title: The Passion of the Christ
decision: PUBLISH: Greydanus's analysis and Ebert's review document a film built around the unity of Calvary and the Mass, with Mary at its centre. The material objection, the 2003 ad hoc scholars' report on the portrayal of Caiaphas, the priests and the crowd, is now stated with the subtitle change, and the Roman Catechism's teaching on who bears the guilt of the Passion is given. The recommendation is for the 2004 theatrical cut (adults only); the 2005 Recut is noted.
summary: Mel Gibson's Passion, spoken in reconstructed Aramaic and Latin, follows Christ's last twelve hours with relentless physical realism and cuts from Calvary back to the Last Supper.
synopsis: At night in Gethsemane, Jesus (Jim Caviezel) prays while a pale, androgynous Satan tempts him. The Temple guard arrests him and beats him on the way to the high priest. Before Caiaphas and the Sanhedrin he is condemned for blasphemy, then handed to Pilate. Pilate sends him to Herod, offers the crowd Barabbas, and orders a scourging in the hope that it will be enough. It is long and savage. Jesus carries the cross to Golgotha, helped by Simon of Cyrene, as Mary (Maia Morgenstern), John and Mary Magdalene follow. Flashbacks to the Sermon on the Mount, the woman taken in adultery and the Last Supper break up the march. Judas, harried by children who turn into demons, hangs himself. After the crucifixion an earthquake shakes the Temple, and a brief final shot shows the Resurrection.
inclusion: The editing carries the argument. As Christ is nailed and the cross raised, the film cuts back to the Last Supper, so the bread and cup are shown as the same offering as Calvary. Steven Greydanus ties this to the Catholic teaching that the Mass and the Cross are one sacrifice. Mary is the other centre. Morgenstern plays her with almost no dialogue, and her run to her fallen Son, intercut with a memory of catching him as a child, is the film's most affecting scene. Caleb Deschanel's dark, candle-lit photography and the dead languages strip away Hollywood-biblical diction. Roger Ebert, who admired it, still called it the most violent film he had ever seen. The violence serves the film's purpose and also limits it. It can numb as easily as it moves, and the Resurrection is a few seconds long.
themes: The Eucharistic frame presents the Mass as a sharing in Calvary. Mary is shown as co-sufferer, and the two Marys wiping up the blood of the scourging with linen is a devotion to the Precious Blood. Satan moves through the crowds and at one point carries a deformed infant, a parody of Madonna and Child that Greydanus links to Genesis 3:15. The film's dramatic weight falls heavily on Caiaphas and the Temple crowd, and the Church's teaching on who bears the guilt (see the theological notes) corrects that.
history: The Gospels tell of the arrest in Gethsemane, the hearing before the high priest, Pilate's sentence, the scourging and the crucifixion briefly and with restraint. Caiaphas held office at the pleasure of the Roman prefect, and only Pilate could order a crucifixion. Crucifixion was a Roman punishment for slaves and rebels, and the Romans scourged those condemned to it. The Gospels differ on points of detail but agree that Jesus died on a Friday on the eve of the Passover Sabbath, that Pilate gave the sentence, and that the body was buried that day.
liberties: Much extra-biblical material comes from Anne Catherine Emmerich's Dolorous Passion: Jesus thrown in chains from a bridge, Pilate's wife bringing linens to Mary, Satan's presence throughout, and the demonic children who drive Judas to despair. Mary Magdalene is identified with the woman taken in adultery. Pilate is more troubled and sympathetic than Philo and Josephus describe him. The Romans speak Latin, where Greek is more likely. Caiaphas's 'His blood be on us and on our children' (Matthew 27:25) is still spoken, but it was left unsubtitled before release.
advisories:
Extremely graphic violence for long stretches: the beating, scourging, carrying of the cross and nailing are shown in detail with heavy bloodshed.

Demonic imagery; a crow pecks out a crucified thief's eye; Judas hangs himself.

The Recut (2005) is shorter but still very violent.

The portrayal of Caiaphas, the priests and the crowd has been criticised as reviving the charge that the Jews as a people killed Christ.

suitability.note: Extended, very bloody scenes of beating, scourging and crucifixion, demonic imagery and a suicide. The original cut was rated 18 in the UK. It is not for children, and many adults find it overwhelming.

doctrine: The Church teaches that Christ's death is a true sacrifice for sin. The Council of Trent (1562) taught that the Mass is the same sacrifice as Calvary, offered in an unbloody manner. The film's flashbacks from the Last Supper to the Cross draw that link. The Roman Catechism (1566) says that the guilt of Christ's death lies on all sinners, and that Christians, who sin knowing him, share it more than the Jews or the Romans. It warns against laying the blame on any one people. The scourging, crowning with thorns and carrying of the cross are the subject of the Sorrowful Mysteries of the Rosary and the Stations of the Cross. Gibson also relies on private visions, notably those of Anne Catherine Emmerich. These are pious writings and not part of the deposit of faith.
production: Mel Gibson financed the film himself through Icon Productions, for about $30 million. The dialogue is in reconstructed Aramaic, Hebrew and Latin, with subtitles. It was shot mostly in Italy, at Cinecittà in Rome and in Matera and the ghost town of Craco. In 2003 a joint committee of the US bishops' conference and the Anti-Defamation League reviewed an early script and warned of its potential for antisemitism. Newmarket Films released it in the US on 25 February 2004, and it earned over $620 million worldwide. A report that John Paul II said 'It is as it was' was denied by Archbishop Dziwisz, who said the Pope told no one his opinion of the film. A shorter Recut opened on 11 March 2005 with about five minutes of the most explicit violence removed.

title: The Song of Bernadette
decision: PUBLISH: AFI's production history, Steven Greydanus and John Clark document a reverent treatment of the Lourdes apparitions and of Bernadette's suffering at Nevers. The Werfel inventions (the Antoine romance, Peyramale at the deathbed, the villainous Dutour, Sister Vauzous's backstory) are now listed and do not change the religious meaning.
summary: Henry King's Oscar-winning Lourdes epic, with Jennifer Jones as a slow, guileless Bernadette, is long and studio-bound but takes her hidden suffering as seriously as the visions.
synopsis: Lourdes, 1858. Bernadette Soubirous, the sickly eldest child of a ruined miller living in a disused jail, sees a lady in white in the grotto of Massabielle. She keeps returning as she was asked; crowds follow, and a spring rises where she digs. The imperial prosecutor Vital Dutour and the police commissioner try to stop the visits and have her declared insane. Dean Peyramale is suspicious until the Lady gives her name, 'I am the Immaculate Conception'. The diocese opens an inquiry and cures are reported. To shield her from the curious, Bernadette enters the Sisters of Charity at Nevers. There her old schoolteacher, now novice mistress Sister Marie Thérèse Vauzous, resents the favour shown to a dull peasant girl. A painful disease of the bone in her leg is kept hidden until it is far advanced, and she dies young.
inclusion: Jennifer Jones won the Academy Award for a performance built on stillness. Her Bernadette is not clever and is not trying to persuade anyone. Arthur Miller's black-and-white photography and Alfred Newman's score also won Oscars, and Gladys Cooper is formidable as Vauzous. Steven Greydanus notes that the third act turns from marvels to the meaning of suffering, and that is the film's best stretch. At about two and a half hours it is slow, Lourdes is a Fox backlot, and Vincent Price's sneering prosecutor belongs in a melodrama. Franz Werfel, the Jewish novelist behind the source novel, adds romance and villainy the real story does not need. It remains the best-known Lourdes film.
themes: The apparitions are treated as real but tested. Clergy, family and state all doubt Bernadette, and the film lets the doubt land. The Lady's name, 'I am the Immaculate Conception', comes four years after the dogma's definition and is the turning point for Peyramale. Greydanus notes that the film never explains why that phrase convinced him. Penance, prayer for sinners and the spring are presented plainly. In the Nevers section, holiness is ordinary work, humiliation and pain accepted without complaint. Linda Darnell plays the Lady, unbilled and briefly glimpsed, which keeps the image modest.
history: Bernadette Soubirous (1844–1879) reported eighteen apparitions at the grotto of Massabielle between 11 February and 16 July 1858. She entered the Sisters of Charity at Nevers in 1866 and died there of tuberculosis of the bone in 1879. She was beatified in 1925 and canonised by Pius XI on 8 December 1933.
liberties: Antoine Nicolau, a historical acquaintance, is turned into a devoted suitor who vows never to marry; no such romance is documented. Peyramale died in 1877, so he was not at Bernadette's deathbed. Vital Dutour, said to have been a practising Catholic who thought her deluded, is played as an anticlerical villain and given an invented end, dying of throat cancer at the grotto; he is also merged with another of Werfel's officials. There is no evidence that Sister Vauzous taught Bernadette in Lourdes, and her final repentance is invented.
advisories: Some priests and nuns behave harshly or unjustly before relenting.

names: The Song of Bernadette, novel by Franz Werfel (1941)

suitability.note: Illness, a painful bone disease and a deathbed, with no violence. At about two and a half hours it is long and slow for young children, but older children usually follow it well.

doctrine: Pius IX defined the Immaculate Conception on 8 December 1854 in Ineffabilis Deus: Mary was preserved from original sin from the first moment of her conception. The Lady's words to Bernadette, 'I am the Immaculate Conception', came on 25 March 1858. Apparitions are private revelation. The Church does not require belief in them, but a bishop may judge them worthy of belief; the Bishop of Tarbes did so in 1862, and Leo XIII authorised a Mass and Office. Pius X extended the feast of Our Lady of Lourdes to the whole Church in 1907 (11 February).
production: Franz Werfel's novel (1941) was written to keep a vow made while he hid at Lourdes in 1940. Twentieth Century-Fox filmed it with George Seaton's screenplay under Henry King, on a budget of about $1.6 million. The running time is 155 minutes. Igor Stravinsky was approached in February 1943 and began writing music, but no contract was agreed, and Alfred Newman scored it instead. The film ends with Bernadette's death and omits the novel's exhumation and canonisation. It opened on 25 December 1943 and earned an estimated $5 to $7 million. It won four Academy Awards (Jennifer Jones, cinematography, art direction, score) and three Golden Globes. Bosley Crowther of the New York Times called the narrative tedious and repetitious but praised Jones. The Legion of Decency classified it A-I.

title: Bernadette
decision: PUBLISH: LUMIERE and Allociné settle identity (CH/FR/LU co-production, French release 17 February 1988). Steven Greydanus's detailed review documents a restrained, historically careful treatment that never shows the Lady. The conflicting accounts of the French and English versions are recorded. Independent secular criticism is thin; Le Monde's 1988 review is paywalled.
summary: Jean Delannoy's plain, careful account of the Lourdes apparitions never shows the Lady, and relies instead on Sydney Penny's spirited, unsentimental Bernadette.
synopsis: Lourdes, 1858. Fourteen-year-old Bernadette Soubirous, from a family sunk in poverty, goes to gather wood by the grotto of Massabielle and sees a small young lady in white in a niche of the rock. She returns again and again. Neighbours, the police commissioner, the imperial prosecutor and the formidable Dean Peyramale question her. Some want her to recant; others want her shut away. She will not add to or subtract from what she has said, even when officials try to trip her up. The crowds grow, a spring appears, cures are claimed, and the Lady at last names herself the Immaculate Conception. The film ends as the apparitions give way to the question of what to do with a girl whom everyone now wants to see. Her life as a nun is left to the sequel.
inclusion: Delannoy, a veteran of postwar French cinema, makes a sober chronicle. Shooting near Lourdes lends weight that Fox's backlot lacked. The visions are staged with sound and faces and no effects: the noise of the river drops away, a simple Francis Lai theme plays, and we watch Bernadette. Steven Greydanus credits fifteen-year-old Sydney Penny with 'spirit, even tartness'. Her Bernadette answers doctors and clerics with disconcerting directness, which is closer to the documented girl than Jennifer Jones's dreamy saint. The look is televisual, the English dub is awkward, and the film was little seen outside France and the shrine, where it was screened for pilgrims for years.
themes: Bernadette is asked again and again to repeat exactly what she saw and heard, and her refusal to embellish becomes the evidence. The Church appears cautious, and Dean Peyramale wants the Lady's name before he will believe anything. The name, 'I am the Immaculate Conception', comes four years after the dogma was defined, from a girl who did not know the term. The Lady's calls for penance and prayer for sinners are given plainly. Because she is never shown, the viewer's attention stays on the witness, which is an honest way to film a private revelation.
history: Bernadette Soubirous (1844–1879), a poor and sickly girl of Lourdes, reported eighteen apparitions of a 'beautiful lady' at the Massabielle rock between 11 February and 16 July 1858. A spring began to flow at the grotto. Officials, including Commissioner Jacomet and Prosecutor Dutour, questioned her and tried to stop the gatherings, and the clergy were at first doubtful. Her interrogations were recorded, and René Laurentin later published the records.
liberties: Dialogue is reconstructed and the eighteen apparitions are selected and compressed. Greydanus judges it unembellished. Accounts of the English version conflict. The distributor says each language was performed directly, while Greydanus says the English track was redubbed.
advisories: Family viewing; Greydanus reports nothing objectionable.

sources.title: Lourdes
sources.claims: Apparition dates, 1862 episcopal declaration, basilica, feast extended 1907, medical bureau

suitability.note: A poor, sick girl is questioned and bullied by officials, which younger children may find upsetting, but it is a gentle, slow-paced telling suited to a family audience.

doctrine: In 1862 the Bishop of Tarbes declared the faithful 'justified in believing the reality of the apparition'. This approves the apparitions as worthy of belief; it is a judgement about a private revelation, not an article of faith, so no Catholic is bound to accept it. The basilica at the grotto was consecrated, and the statue formally crowned, in 1876. Leo XIII authorised a special office and Mass, and Pius X extended the feast to the whole Church in 1907, to be kept on 11 February. The Bureau des Constatations Médicales at Lourdes records and checks medical certificates for claimed cures, and is open to physicians of any belief.
production: Jean Delannoy shot this film in 1987 in and around Lourdes. The original grotto could not be used, so nearby places resembling the scene at the time were found. Each scene was filmed twice, once in French and once in English, and the American lead Sydney Penny did not speak French. It opened in France on 17 February 1988.

title: The Passion of Bernadette
decision: PUBLISH: Greydanus's review documents an earnest, reverent account of Bernadette's convent years, with a specific medical-image advisory. Year corrected to 1990: AlloCiné gives production year 1990 and French release 9 May 1990; the 1989 date used by Decent Films and MUBI has no release behind it that we could find.
summary: Delannoy's sequel follows Bernadette's thirteen years at Nevers, where obscurity, a suspicious novice mistress and bone tuberculosis replace the drama of Lourdes; quieter and less shapely than the first film.
synopsis: In 1866, eight years after the apparitions, Bernadette (Sydney Penny again) enters the Sisters of Charity at Saint-Gildard in Nevers, hoping to disappear. Her superiors decide that the famous visionary must not be allowed to think herself special. The novice mistress watches for pride. Bernadette is corrected for slipping away to pray at the convent's grotto during recreation. She also learns to work in the infirmary, where she nurses a blind old nun with a festering sore and rounds sharply on a postulant who recoils from it. A wounded soldier is brought in. Visitors still ask to see her; she wants none of it. Her own illness, tuberculosis of the bone, worsens year by year, and the film follows her to her death in 1879 at thirty-five.
inclusion: Few films about saints try to dramatise the long middle of a religious life, with its obedience, routine, bad health and other people. This one does. Penny is again strong. The Catholic News Service reviewer praised her 'down-to-earth sanctity', and Delannoy's period detail is careful. Steven Greydanus, who rates it lower than the first film, is right that it does not really tell a story; it is a sequence of convent episodes. The US release defaults to an English dub, which flattens the performances; the original French with subtitles is the better choice.
themes: The film shows a visionary who has to be ordinary. Obedience to superiors, including unjust ones, is shown as costly but not foolish. Charity to the sick is concrete and unglamorous: she cleans a wound others will not touch. She offers her suffering without explaining it, and the film does not turn illness into a spectacle of holiness. The superiors' suspicion of a famous young nun has some historical basis. The film presents it as a trial without making the community villains.
history: Bernadette Soubirous (1844-1879) saw the Blessed Virgin eighteen times in the grotto of Massabielle at Lourdes between 11 February and 16 July 1858. On 25 March the lady told her, in the local dialect, 'I am the Immaculate Conception', four years after Pius IX defined that doctrine on 8 December 1854. Bishop Laurence of Tarbes approved the apparitions and the cult by a pastoral letter of 18 January 1862. Bernadette entered the Sisters of Charity of Nevers in 1866, at Saint-Gildard, where she took the habit and her vows in 1867, and nursed the sick until her bone tuberculosis made her an invalid herself. She died on 16 April 1879, aged 35. Pius XI beatified her in 1925 and canonised her on 8 December 1933.
liberties: Convent episodes are selected and dialogue invented; the long periods of illness are compressed. Greydanus raises in passing the question of whether Penny's mannerisms suggest a developmental condition. That is the reviewer's speculation, not a documented trait of the saint.
advisories:
A brief, graphic glimpse of an ulcerated female breast during a medical procedure; a bloodied soldier; an ugly bedsore.

Greydanus thinks it suitable for children.

suitability.note: Illness and a long deathbed, plus one graphic medical scene that parents should preview for younger viewers.

doctrine: Bernadette's life shows the Church's teaching on private revelation: apparitions approved by a bishop, as at Lourdes in 1862, may be believed as worthy of pious credence, but no Catholic is bound to believe them. The saint's convent trial, in which she was kept humble and told little of her fame, illustrates the traditional spiritual teaching that humility is the foundation of the interior life. She lived the life of a Sister of Charity under vows, in obedience to superiors, nursing the sick as a work of mercy. Her last years of suffering, accepted as a share in Christ's Passion, were understood by her and her superiors as redemptive suffering. Her body, found intact at exhumations in 1909, 1919 and 1925, lies at Nevers.
production: Rachel Productions of France made this sequel to Delannoy's Bernadette (1988), with Sydney Penny again in the title role, and it covers her convent years. It was filmed in colour and ran 106 minutes. The date is given as 1989 in one reference and 9 May 1990 on a technical sheet. Emmanuelle Riva, known from Hiroshima mon amour, plays the superior Mother Vauzou.

title: The Miracle of Our Lady of Fatima
originalTitle: The Miracle of Our Lady of Fatima
decision: PUBLISH: with a historical caution. AFI's detailed production history and Greydanus's review document both the reverent apparition narrative and the specific inventions: the agnostic peddler Hugo, a Cold War 'socialist People's Republic' in place of Portugal's anticlerical liberal republic, and the detention moved and enlarged. All are now disclosed, and none touches the apparitions themselves. This is consistent with La Señora de Fátima (1951) staying on HOLD: that film is held for lack of any treatment evidence, not for having the same problems.
summary: Warner Bros.' colour Fatima drama is reverent toward the children and the Lady but recasts 1917 Portugal as a Cold War police state and adds a lovable fictional rogue.
synopsis: An opening narration tells of a 'socialist minority' that has seized Portugal and built a police state to crush the Church. In May 1917 Lúcia (Susan Whitney) and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta see a Lady above a holm oak at the Cova da Iria. Lúcia's mother calls her a liar, and the parish priest, Father Ferreira, is sceptical. Only Hugo (Gilbert Roland), an agnostic wandering peddler, humours the children, advising them to keep quiet. The local administrator Arturo closes the church, arrests the priest and finally has the children abducted. They are jailed with criminals and Hugo and threatened, but they refuse to recant. On 13 October an enormous crowd waits in the rain. The sun spins and plunges, the sick are healed, the ground dries, and Hugo believes.
inclusion: A well-made studio picture, shot in WarnerColor with location footage from the 1951 anniversary at Fatima. Max Steiner's score was Oscar-nominated, and the miracle of the sun is staged with ambition. The three children are believable, and the film takes their prayer, fear and stubbornness seriously. It has the weaknesses of 1952 Hollywood. Characters are types, and Steven Greydanus finds Susan Whitney's Lúcia mostly anxious tearfulness. Gilbert Roland's charming rogue takes over too much of the story, and the politics are a Cold War sermon. Greydanus judges it short of The Song of Bernadette, and later called it more embellished than The 13th Day. As an introduction for families it still works, provided the history is corrected.
themes: The Lady's requests (the daily Rosary, prayer and sacrifice for sinners, the promise of a sign) are given clearly, and the children's endurance under threat is the film's moral spine. Hugo's arc turns the miracle into a story of conversion. The Cova da Iria is presented as a place of public prayer that the state cannot suppress. The film's dramatisation of the Lady's words is an interpretation, not a record.
history: Portugal's First Republic, set up in 1910, was liberal and fiercely anticlerical. It separated Church and State in 1911 and harassed clergy, but it was not a socialist people's republic. Lúcia dos Santos and Francisco and Jacinta Marto reported six apparitions from 13 May to 13 October 1917, preceded in 1916 by visits of an angel. In August 1917 the Ourém administrator, Artur de Oliveira Santos, took the children away and held and threatened them for about two days. Tens of thousands witnessed the solar phenomenon on 13 October.
liberties: Hugo da Silva is invented, and Father Ferreira and the administrator are fictionalised. The narration's 'socialist' police state recasts the 1910 republic in Cold War terms; Greydanus calls the villains 'militant Marxists'. The angel apparitions of 1916 are omitted. The children's detention is moved to October and enlarged into a jail term among criminals. The narration gives 15 May for the first apparition (it was Sunday 13 May), and the sun falls once instead of twice.
advisories: Children are abducted, jailed and threatened; there are family quarrels and mockery.

title: Our Lady of Fatima
decision: PUBLISH: a contemporary Spanish review (Alfonso Sánchez, Hoja del Lunes, Madrid, 22 October 1951) and María Aimaretti's scene-level study (Accadere 7, 2024) establish a devout pre-conciliar telling of the apparitions, faithful in substance to Lucía's account (rosary, reparation, the warning about Russia, the miracle of the sun), with disclosed political anachronism (a Marxist villain) and an invented convert. Aimaretti is critical of the film's national-Catholic politics but reports no doctrinal problem. The subject is the apparitions approved in 1930, not Francisco and Jacinta (canonised 2017), so rule 1 does not apply. Editor may prefer GREY 'reservations' for the political transposition.
summary: Rafael Gil's Spanish account of the 1917 Fátima apparitions, told through Lucía's trials at home and at the hands of anticlerical officials, ending with the miracle of the sun.
synopsis: Portugal, 1917: the country is at war and its republican government is hostile to the Church. Near Fátima, Lucía, a devout shepherd girl, and her young cousins Francisco and Jacinta see a Lady above a holm oak who asks them to pray the rosary. Lucía's home is falling apart: her father drinks and sells off land, her brother leaves for the front, and her disbelieving mother has the village women try to make her retract; her father beats her. The district chief Oliveira, an atheist revolutionary, and the lawyer Duarte try to stop the cult. Oliveira holds the children and threatens Lucía with a furnace. On 13 October a vast crowd gathers in the rain, the sun spins, the Lady names herself Our Lady of the Rosary, the sick are healed and Duarte is converted.
inclusion: Vicente Escrivá's Aspa Films, the most consistent of the 1950s Spanish Catholic production companies, made the Spanish Fátima film and released it as the Holy Year closed at Fátima. It was a major success. Aimaretti records 56 weeks in a Madrid cinema, national prizes and papal approval at its Rome premiere, and Alfonso Sánchez in Hoja del Lunes praised its simple, fervent telling. Gil shows the Virgin only in fragments (the hem of a mantle, bare feet, light and a voice), and Michel Kelber's photography sets Lucía's moonlit room against a home full of shadows. Inés Orsini, the Maria Goretti of Heaven Over the Marshes, plays Lucía. The Marxist villain is cardboard, and the politics belong to Franco's Spain more than to 1917 Portugal.
themes: The film gives the Fátima message as Lucía recorded it: the rosary, suffering offered in reparation for sin, the warning that Russia would spread her errors, and conversion as the fruit of a child's obedience. Lucía bears beatings, mockery and threats without complaint, and the healings and the lawyer's conversion are shown as the Virgin's answer. Aimaretti reads the film as a hagiography of a Marian daughter. One study notes that the priests, like the politicians, must be won over through Lucía. The anti-communism is explicit, and the ending joins the fictional pilgrims to documentary footage of the sanctuary's later crowds.
history: Between May and October 1917 Lúcia dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto reported apparitions of the Virgin at the Cova da Iria near Fátima. In August the local administrator, Artur Santos, detained and threatened the children. On 13 October a crowd of tens of thousands reported that, after rain, the sun appeared to spin.
liberties: The administrator who detains the children is turned into Oliveira, a Marxist plotting to impose communism, an anachronism Aimaretti reads as aimed at Spain's Second Republic. The lawyer Duarte and his conversion are invented. The threat against Lucía is staged in a cellar furnace room, and the women's attempt to make her recant is presented as a kind of exorcism. The closing documentary montage of later pilgrimages is the film's own addition.
advisories:
A girl is beaten by her father and threatened with burning by an official; the furnace-room scene is intense.

Family poverty and a drunken father.

doctrine: The Bishop of Leiria, José Alves Correia da Silva, declared the apparitions worthy of belief on 13 October 1930. As a private revelation, Fátima adds nothing to the deposit of faith and binds no one to belief, but the Church permits and encourages the devotion, whose requests are traditional ones. In 1925 at Pontevedra Lúcia reported the conditions of the Five First Saturdays: confession, Communion, five decades of the Rosary and a quarter-hour's meditation, in reparation. Pius XII consecrated the human race to the Immaculate Heart in 1942 and had the Fátima image crowned through his legate on 13 May 1946. The year after this film, in the letter Sacro vergente of 7 July 1952, he consecrated the peoples of Russia to the Immaculate Heart.

The Círculo de Escritores Cinematográficos gave José Nieto a supporting-actor medal. Later Spanish critics have read it chiefly as a document of Francoist anti-communism; it was shown in the San Sebastián Festival's 1996 retrospective of Francoist anti-communist cinema.

title: Apparitions at Fatima
decision: GREY: The French subtitle file confirms Greydanus's account of a faithful drama: the Angel of Peace and the Angel of Portugal, the angel's Communion, the vision of hell, the second secret on Russia and the Immaculate Heart with the Holy Father's consecration of Russia, the Lady naming herself Our Lady of the Rosary, and the miracle of the sun. The coda records the deaths of Francisco and Jacinta and then the Pope blessing the three young actors. The drama is pre-conciliar in substance; the reservation is only the coda, which frames it as a tribute to John Paul II.
summary: Daniel Costelle's sober docudrama of the 1917 Fátima apparitions, shot at the Cova da Iria with a largely amateur cast and dialogue taken from Lúcia's memoirs.
synopsis: In 1917, in the hill country around Fátima, the shepherd children Lúcia dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto report that a Lady from heaven has appeared to them at the Cova da Iria. The film follows the apparitions from May to October in a mixture of drama and documentary, with the dialogue drawn from the memoirs Lúcia later wrote. It gives full weight to the vision of hell that terrifies Jacinta, and to the penances the children take on for sinners: going without water in the summer heat and wearing a rope tied tightly round their waists, which the Lady tells them not to wear at night. The film closes with a postscript of premiere footage in which Pope John Paul II and Sister Lúcia greet the three young actors.
inclusion: Steven Greydanus judges this the most faithful screen account of Fátima, more accurate and spiritually serious than Hollywood's The Miracle of Our Lady of Fatima. In a later piece he calls it the film to beat for fidelity, though not compelling art. The mostly amateur cast is good, and the real locations, the Cova da Iria above all, give it an authenticity no studio could. Greydanus finds the effects modest and the narration and music at times intrusive, and the budget was small. It suits families and anyone who wants the events without dramatic invention. The 13th Day (2009) is the more artful film; this is the more literal one.
themes: The message of 1917 is given straight: prayer, sacrifice for sinners and the reality of hell, which Greydanus notes the film does not soften as the Hollywood version did. The apparitions of the angel in 1916, including his Communion to the children, are included, and the second secret, with its call for the consecration of Russia to the Immaculate Heart, is spoken in full. The children's penances are the heart of their response, with the Lady moderating them. Because the dialogue comes from Lúcia's memoirs, the film presents her testimony as she gave it.
history: Lúcia dos Santos (1907–2005) and her cousins Francisco (1908–1919) and Jacinta Marto (1910–1920) reported six apparitions of Our Lady at the Cova da Iria between May and October 1917, preceded by apparitions of an angel in 1916. Both Marto children died in the influenza epidemic. Lúcia became a religious and wrote her memoirs between 1935 and 1941.
liberties: Greydanus notes no significant inventions; the dialogue is drawn from Lúcia's memoirs. A documentary-style voice-over links the episodes. The apparitions are necessarily a reconstruction, staged with very simple effects.
advisories:
The vision of hell is shown directly and may frighten young children.

The children's self-imposed penances, including going without water and wearing a tight rope.

grey.question: The drama follows Sister Lúcia's memoirs faithfully, from the angel's apparitions in 1916 to Our Lady's in 1917, and includes the vision of hell, the second secret on Russia and the Immaculate Heart, and the miracle of the sun. The reservation concerns its ending. After recording the deaths of Francisco and Jacinta, the film closes on footage of John Paul II blessing the young cast at its premiere, presenting the story as a tribute to the post-conciliar papacy. Viewers can stop before the coda, but it is part of the film as released.

suitability.note: Decent Films finds nothing objectionable and rates it for children and up, though the vision of hell may frighten the youngest and the children's penances are severe.

doctrine: The Church has approved the apparitions as worthy of belief, as the Bishop of Leiria declared in 1930. They remain a private revelation, which Catholics are not bound to accept. The Church teaches the reality of hell as everlasting punishment for unrepented mortal sin (Council of Trent, Session 6; Fourth Lateran Council, 1215), and the Lady's request for prayer for sinners rests on that doctrine. The children's penances, going without water and wearing a rope round the waist, are acts of mortification offered in reparation. The Church admires the intention, but prudence in such penances belongs to those who guide the young. The film also shows the Rosary, which she asked them to say every day.
production: Daniel Costelle, a French documentary maker, directed this television docudrama. It is based mainly on Sister Lúcia's Memoirs, and the dialogue quotes them. The script was by an Italian priest living in France, and an international organisation that had earlier made a film on Lourdes commissioned the work, with the support of the Sanctuary of Fátima. Some scenes were filmed at Fátima. It was shown from May 1991 at the Centro Pastoral Paulo VI, and about 20,000 people had seen it there by February 1992. It was dubbed into several languages. The film ends with footage from the premiere of Pope John Paul II and Sister Lúcia greeting the young actors.

title: The 13th Day
decision: PUBLISH: Greydanus's detailed review documents a reverent, artful film that stays close to Lúcia's memoirs, and lists its liberties. The Fátima sanctuary's 2009 announcement and Companies House confirm the British production company, credits and world premiere. A reader's documented objection about frightening scenes is reflected in the advisory.
summary: Two illustrator brothers made this low-budget, mostly black-and-white Fatima film as Sister Lúcia's memory, with painterly images and a closer fidelity to her memoirs than Hollywood managed.
synopsis: In a convent in Spain, Sister Lúcia, now an adult, writes one of her memoirs, and the film unfolds as her recollection. In 1917 Lúcia, Francisco and Jacinta are shepherd children near Fátima when a Lady appears to them at the Cova da Iria and asks them to return on the thirteenth of each month. They pray the Rosary, make sacrifices, and are shown a vision of hell. Lúcia's family disbelieves her; the town administrator abducts the children and threatens them. Crowds grow despite mockery from the press. On 13 October, in pouring rain, tens of thousands see the sun dance. The film closes back with the aging memory of the nun at her desk.
inclusion: Ian and Dominic Higgins were illustrators before directing, and it shows. Shot cheaply on digital video, the film is mostly black and white with spots of colour, soft-focused and composed like paintings. Steven Greydanus compares its frames to Vermeer and the austerity of Bresson. It moves in vignettes, almost like a silent film with dialogue, which some viewers will find static. The digital effects in the miracle of the sun are more effective than the budget suggests. Greydanus called it the best Fatima film, closer to the historical record than the 1952 Warner film and more artful than the 1992 Portuguese Aparição. The acting is modest and the English dialogue a little stiff.
themes: The content of the 1917 message is front and centre: daily Rosary, penance and sacrifice for sinners, the vision of hell, and the call for the consecration of Russia. The children's willingness to suffer for others is treated as the heart of the story. Lúcia's memory frame reminds the viewer that we know these events through her written testimony. That testimony is a private revelation, and the film's images of the Lady and of hell are an artist's rendering of it.
history: Lúcia dos Santos (1907–2005) and her cousins Francisco (d. 1919) and Jacinta Marto (d. 1920) reported six apparitions from May to October 1917. Lúcia wrote her memoirs between 1935 and 1941 as a Dorothean sister in Spain; she entered the Carmel of Coimbra only in 1948. The film was produced by 13th Day Films Ltd and shot in Portugal and England. It had its world premiere at the Fátima sanctuary on 13 October 2009.
liberties: Greydanus notes that the 1916 angel apparitions are omitted and that the six apparitions are condensed to four on screen. Lúcia's father is drawn differently from the account in Fr. John de Marchi's history. Lúcia is played as reserved, where the historical girl was outgoing.
advisories:
A vision of hell and other fleeting infernal imagery; children are imprisoned and threatened.

Greydanus watched it with his young family without trouble, but a reader reported that his children found it frightening.

title: The Miracle of Marcelino
decision: PUBLISH: Two independent Spanish analyses (Instituto Cervantes; Vida Nueva) describe the treatment of the crucifix scenes and the ending in detail, and the Danish Film Institute and festival record settle identity. The film is a literary fable, not a claimed miracle, and the child's death is clearly advised.
summary: Ladislao Vajda's Spanish classic about a foundling raised by friars who feeds bread and wine to the crucifix in the attic: tender, beautifully lit, and unashamedly a tearjerker.
synopsis: At a village feast, a friar (Fernando Rey) visits a sick girl and tells her family how the feast began. After the war against Napoleon, a few Franciscans rebuild a ruined building as their friary and find a baby abandoned at the door. They fail to find him a family, so twelve friars raise Marcelino among them, each with a nickname and a trade. At five he is mischievous, lonely and longs for the mother he never knew. He is forbidden the attic, goes up anyway, and finds a large crucifix. Thinking the man looks hungry, he steals bread and wine from the kitchen for him. The figure comes down from the cross, eats, and talks with him. Asked what he wants most, Marcelino asks to see his mother. Fray Papilla, spying through the door, sees the miracle.
inclusion: Six-year-old Pablito Calvo gives one of cinema's most natural child performances, and the friars, each a gentle comic type, are warmly drawn. Enrique Guerner's lighting makes the attic scenes glow. The Cervantes essay notes that Christ is shown almost only through his hands, and that the miracle is signalled by changes of light. That discretion keeps the film on the right side of kitsch. It was a huge international success, and it is also deliberately heartbreaking. The critic José Luis Guarner called it 'un cuento para niños que parece un cilicio' (a children's tale that feels like a hair shirt). The English dub on some US discs is poor; choose the Spanish track.
themes: The crucifix in the attic becomes a living person to a lonely child, and his instinct is charity, because the hungry should be fed. Bread and wine carried to Christ recall the Eucharist without staging a Mass, and the title, 'Marcelino, bread and wine', makes the link explicit. Christ answers the boy's longing with heaven. He takes Marcelino to his mother, and the boy dies in his sleep. The friars' household shows religious life as a family. Fray Papilla's witness turns the story into the origin of a local devotion.
history: The story is a fable, not a recorded miracle. Its plot is often traced to a medieval legend of a child who feeds Christ on the cross, which the book and the film modernised. It is set in a Spanish friary after the war against Napoleon (1808-14). Stories of crucifixes that speak are old in Franciscan tradition (in 1205-06 the crucifix in the ruined chapel of San Damiano is said to have told St Francis to repair the Lord's house). Spain's friaries were suppressed in the 1830s, a few years after the time the story depicts.
liberties: It is fiction based on a literary fable. Vida Nueva notes that the film heightens the light-and-dark contrasts of the death scene well beyond the book. Later remakes, Luigi Comencini's Marcellino (1991) and a Mexican Marcelino pan y vino (2010), as well as an animated series (2000), are different works.
advisories:
The death of a small child (shown as falling asleep in Christ's arms), and his longing for his dead mother.

No violence or sexual content.

names: Marcelino, pan y vino, novel by José María Sánchez-Silva (1953)

suitability.note: Children usually love the friars, but the ending is sad enough that younger ones may want a parent beside them.

doctrine: The film rests on the Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist, defined by the Council of Trent (Session XIII, 1551): under the appearances of bread and wine, Christ is truly, really and substantially present. Marcelino's gift of bread and wine to the crucifix is a child's offering and not a sacrament, and the film is not a claim about the Mass. Two other points follow. The Church teaches that baptised infants who die before the use of reason go straight to heaven, which is the consolation of the last scene. And it teaches that children should be admitted to Communion as soon as they have the use of reason, about seven years old, as Pius X decreed in Quam singulari (8 August 1910). The Franciscans' care of a foundling is the corporal work of mercy to the orphan.
production: José María Sánchez-Silva's story was filmed by the Hungarian-born Ladislao Vajda, who had settled in Spain, as a Spanish-Italian production. Key scenes were shot at La Alberca in Salamanca and in the chapel of the Cristo del Caloco at El Espinar, though the crucifix in the film was a sculpture by Antonio Simont, now at Don Benito. It opened in Spain on 24 February 1955, in Italy on 8 September 1955 and in the United States on 22 October 1956, distributed there by United Motion Pictures Organization. At Cannes in 1955 the film took the OCIC special mention and Pablito Calvo a special mention; it won the Silver Bear at Berlin. The Legion of Decency classed it A-I.

title: Mary of Nazareth
decision: PUBLISH: The subtitle files for both parts provide the careful check the earlier question asked for. The Annunciation, Visitation and Magnificat follow Luke; Joseph accepts the angel's word; no brothers or sisters of Jesus appear; Mary asks to suffer in her Son's place, renews her consent at the Cross, and the risen Christ appears to her. An early line that no descendant of Eve escapes the dogs that smell sin reads as an oblique allusion to her Immaculate Conception. Modern touches are slight: Mary doubts at Cana and admits breaking the rule that a woman should not interrupt. There is no Assumption. The published reviews are all from present-day Catholic outlets, so the editor may prefer GREY/unverified.
summary: Lux Vide's life of the Virgin Mary from her girlhood in the Temple to Easter morning, carried by Alissa Jung's grave performance.
synopsis: Joachim and Anna give their young daughter Mary to be raised at the Temple. Her childhood friend Mary of Magdala drifts instead into the court of Herod Antipas and Herodias. Betrothed to the carpenter Joseph, Mary receives the angel's message, visits Elizabeth and returns pregnant to a village that scorns her; Joseph, after a dream, takes her as his wife and accepts that their marriage will be unlike others. The Nativity, the Presentation and the flight into Egypt follow. Years later Joseph dies, Jesus begins to preach, and Magdalene, rescued from stoning, becomes His follower. Mary follows her Son to Calvary, and on the third day the risen Christ appears to Magdalene and then to His mother.
inclusion: Most screen lives of Christ treat Mary as a face in the crowd. This one puts her at the centre, and Alissa Jung, a German actress, makes her firm and believable as a young woman whose 'yes' costs her something. Luca Marinelli's Joseph is the supporting performance every reviewer praises. Campiotti grounds the Gospel in daily work, with Mary salting bread as Jesus speaks of the salt of the earth. It is conventional television filmmaking, and David Ives finds it only a little better than most TV fare, while DeCine21 faults the poor ageing of the cast and a melodramatic Herodias. In the shortened version, as Cooney and Ford both note, the cuts leave the two Marys' friendship confusing.
themes: The film presents Mary as the obedient handmaid whose fiat is the hinge of the story. The Annunciation, the Visitation and the Magnificat follow Luke closely, Simeon's prophecy of the sword is given weight, and at the Cross Mary renews her consent and asks to suffer in her Son's place. Her virginal conception is plain, Joseph accepts a virginal marriage after the angel's message, and no brothers or sisters of Jesus appear. An early line about dogs that smell sin in every descendant of Eve, which Ives disliked, works as an oblique hint of her Immaculate Conception. Christ's divinity, Passion and Resurrection are affirmed. Mary's doubt at Cana is a small modern touch.
history: The Gospels say little of Mary's life outside the infancy narratives and the Passion. The film draws on the tradition of her presentation in the Temple and of Joachim and Anna, found in the Protoevangelium of James.
liberties: Mary and Mary Magdalene are made childhood friends, and Magdalene is given a past at Herod's court and identified with the woman saved from stoning and the woman who anointed Jesus' feet, a Western tradition the film follows freely. Herodias is drawn from medieval legend as something of a sorceress. Mary's wedding, Joseph's brother Eleazar, Joseph's death while Jesus is away, and episodes from Jesus' childhood are invented. The 153-minute version drops an early meeting between the two Marys.
advisories:
The massacre of the innocents is violent, and the scourging and crucifixion are shown with some graphic detail, though far less than in The Passion of the Christ.

An attempted stoning.

Magdalene falls into prostitution at Herod's court; implied, not shown explicitly.

An English song over the end credits jars.

title: The Passion of Joan of Arc
decision: PUBLISH: Greydanus's detailed review, Criterion's edition notes and the film's well-documented history establish Dreyer's use of the trial record, the sacramental climax (confession and Communion before the burning) and the unhistorical riot. The judges' cruelty is presented as that of particular men, while Joan seeks Christ through the Church's sacraments.
summary: Dreyer compresses Joan's months of trial into one day of faces in close-up, and Renée Falconetti gives what may be the greatest performance in silent film.
synopsis: Rouen, 1431. Joan (Renée Falconetti), nineteen and in chains, is led before a tribunal of churchmen and university doctors, with English soldiers at the door. They question her about her voices, her male dress and her mission, and try to trap her: will she say the Our Father? Is she in a state of grace? A forged letter from the king is used to deceive her, and she is shown the instruments of torture. Exhausted and ill, she is bled. Facing the fire, she signs a recantation and her head is shaved. Then she retracts, saying she betrayed God to save her life. A sympathetic young priest hears her confession and gives her Communion. She is burned in the market square, and the watching crowd rises against the soldiers and is beaten back.
inclusion: Dreyer built the film almost entirely from close-ups of unpowdered faces against bare white walls. There are hardly any establishing shots, so the viewer is trapped in the interrogation with Joan. Falconetti, a stage actress who never made another major film, plays Joan as frightened, peasant-plain and immovable, and her face is the film. The dialogue intertitles are drawn from the trial record, compressed so that months feel like one day. Steven Greydanus finds some religious films more theologically profound and some of the trial dialogue confusing, but few films convey so physically what it costs to stay faithful. Watch the Gaumont restoration; Richard Einhorn's oratorio Voices of Light is the most admired accompaniment.
themes: Joan's anguish turns on the sacraments. Her judges withhold confession and Communion to break her, and the climax is not the burning but her reception of the Eucharist from a compassionate priest. Greydanus notes that her refusal to say the Our Father, which the judges treated as a test for possession, was historically a request to say it in confession. Dreyer links her mocking by soldiers to the mocking of Christ. The judges are clerics acting for English political interests, and the film shows them as men abusing an office, not as the voice of the Church.
history: Joan of Arc was captured at Compiègne in 1430, sold to the English, and tried for heresy at Rouen under Bishop Pierre Cauchon from January to May 1431. She was burned on 30 May 1431. Dreyer drew on Pierre Champion's 1921 edition of the trial records.
liberties: Many sessions spread over months are compressed into what feels like a single day. The closing riot in the square is Dreyer's invention, inspired by Eisenstein's Battleship Potemkin. Characters among the judges are composites.
advisories:
Burning at the stake shown graphically; the instruments of torture; medicinal bloodletting; the crowd is clubbed by soldiers.

Sustained distress with little gore. Greydanus thinks older children can watch it.

sources.title: Joan of Arc
sources.claims: Voices of Michael, Margaret and Catherine; trial from 21 February 1431; relapse for male dress; confession and Communion before execution on 30 May 1431; beatified by Pius X (decree 1909); canonised by Benedict XV (1920)

names: The trial record of Joan of Arc (1431), in Pierre Champion's edition (1921)

suitability.note: A silent film of constant interrogation, slow and intense. Patient older children can follow it, but younger ones will tire.

doctrine: Joan said her voices were St Michael, St Catherine and St Margaret. The Church did not ask her to prove this. Her trial was a heresy trial, and the verdict turned on whether she would submit her visions to the Church Militant. In 1456 the sentence was annulled after a retrial. Pius X declared her Blessed in 1909 and Benedict XV canonised her on 16 May 1920. The film's climax rests on the Church's rule that a penitent in danger of death is not to be refused absolution and Viaticum; Trent (Session XIII) teaches that the faithful must receive the Eucharist as the food of the soul, and the viaticum prepares the dying for the journey. By tradition she made her confession and received Communion before the pyre on 30 May 1431. Her feast is 30 May.
production: The poet Joseph Delteil, Dreyer's co-writer, had his 1925 book on Joan bought for the production and credited as a source, but Dreyer worked from the trial record. The huge octagonal concrete set, a replica of Rouen castle, cost much of the seven-million-franc budget. It opened in Copenhagen on 21 April 1928 and in Paris on 25 October 1928. The Archbishop of Paris and the censors required cuts, and a fire at UFA in Berlin on 6 December 1928 destroyed the original negative. Dreyer's original cut was found in a hospital near Oslo in 1981. It was banned in Britain for its portrayal of the English soldiers. It was a financial failure. In 1995 the Vatican included it in its list of important films, under religion.

title: Joan of Arc
alternateTitles: The Life of Joan of Arc
decision: PUBLISH (restored 145-minute version): the AFI Catalog's cutting-continuity synopsis and history, Felicia Feaster's TCM production essay and the Fordham Medieval Hollywood entry establish a pious, canonisation-framed portrait: voices of Sts Michael, Catherine and Margaret, confession for the army, a politically driven trial under Cauchon. The trial's hostility matches the Catholic Encyclopedia's account and the Church's own annulment; the film's political compressions are disclosed.
summary: Ingrid Bergman plays Joan in Victor Fleming's lavish Technicolor biography, from Domrémy to the stake, with the trial at Rouen as its strongest stretch.
synopsis: A peasant girl in Lorraine hears the voices of saints telling her to save France. She persuades the governor at Vaucouleurs to send her to the Dauphin at Chinon, convinces the weak and evasive Charles, and is given command at Orleans. She makes the soldiers confess, stop swearing and send away camp followers, then leads them to victory and sees Charles crowned at Reims. When the court makes peace with Burgundy she is pushed aside, her voices fall silent, and she is captured at Compiègne. Sold to the English, she is tried for heresy at Rouen by Bishop Cauchon. Worn down, she signs an abjuration, recants it when she understands she has been tricked, and is burned in the market square.
inclusion: The big Hollywood version has Technicolor, armour made with help from the Metropolitan Museum's armourer, thousands of extras, and Oscars for Winton Hoch's colour photography and Barbara Karinska's costumes. Bergman had played Joan on Broadway and wanted the part for years; her performance is earnest and physical, and José Ferrer, in his first film, makes a memorably slippery Dauphin. The first half is stiff pageantry, a long run of processions and speeches; critics from Bosley Crowther onward found it short on spiritual fire. The trial is better. Joan argues with her judges, insists she is a prisoner of the English and not of the Church, and breaks and recovers. The film never doubts her mission.
themes: Joan's voices are presented as messages from St Michael, St Catherine and St Margaret, not as a psychological symptom. Her campaign is framed as a religious reform as much as a military one: she sends the soldiers to confession and calls them God's army. The trial is a corrupt proceeding run by a partisan bishop for English masters, which is how the Catholic Encyclopedia describes it, and the film shows a sympathetic priest at her side to the end. It does not suggest the Church's faith was on trial; the prologue showing her canonisation makes the point that the Church reversed the verdict.
history: Joan was captured at Compiègne in May 1430 by Burgundian forces and sold to the English. Pierre Cauchon, Bishop of Beauvais and a Burgundian partisan, conducted the trial at Rouen. She abjured at Saint-Ouen, resumed male dress, was declared relapsed and burned on 30 May 1431. A papally appointed court annulled the sentence in 1456.
liberties: Charles VII is made into a villain who effectively sells Joan out for Burgundian money; historically his counsellors arranged a truce and then made no effort to ransom her. The capture is simplified. The Inquisitor of Rouen's arc, from lone defender to accuser, is dramatised. Joan's appeal to the Pope, central to the trial, does not appear in published synopses of the film. The 1950 general-release cut also rearranged scenes and added narration.
advisories:
Medieval battle scenes with arrows, falls and burning; Joan is wounded by an arrow.

The burning at the stake is shown, though without graphic detail.

References to camp followers, and an English captain calls Joan a strumpet.

Choose the restored 145-minute version; the 100-minute cut is confusing.

doctrine: Joan's heavenly counsel is a matter of private revelation, and the Church does not oblige belief in it. The second trial of 1455–56, ordered by Callixtus III, annulled the sentence of 1431 as procured by fraud and malice. Pius X beatified her in 1909 and Benedict XV canonised her on 16 May 1920. Her feast is 30 May. The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that her condemnation was the work of a partisan bishop and an English-controlled court, and adds that she appealed to the Pope, which the judges refused to forward. Her insistence that she would submit to the Church Militant, meaning the Pope and the whole body of the Church, but not to Cauchon's court as the judge of her voices, is the heart of the trial.
production: Maxwell Anderson's Broadway play Joan of Lorraine (1946), in which Bergman won a Tony, led to the film. Sierra Pictures made it for RKO, with Victor Fleming (his last film; he died in 1949) directing. Principal photography ran from 16 September to 18 December 1947 at Hal Roach Studios, with nine days of reshoots, on a budget of $4.6 million. It premiered in New York on 11 November 1948 in a 145-minute roadshow version. For general release in September 1950 about 45 minutes were cut; the full version was restored in 1998. It won Oscars for colour cinematography and colour costume design, and Bergman and Ferrer were nominated. Critics praised the spectacle and Bergman; some found Joan thinly drawn. RKO lost about $2.5 million.

title: The Trial of Joan of Arc
decision: PUBLISH: DVDClassik's analysis and Florence Delay's account establish a film built from the condemnation trial record, with rehabilitation testimony for the final hours. The critical dissent (Time Out's 'voyeurism' reading) is recorded. It won the OCIC prize at Cannes. Its severe material is advised.
summary: Bresson's sixty-five-minute Joan uses only the words of the trial record, delivered flatly by non-actors, and becomes a film of doors, chains, glances and a calm, unbreakable voice.
synopsis: Joan's mother asks for her daughter's rehabilitation, and then the film goes back to Rouen in 1431. Joan (Florence Delay, then a student) is already a prisoner in the castle. The interrogations follow one after another: her voices, her male clothing, her submission to the Church. Between them she is chained in her cell, spied on through a hole in the wall by English soldiers and churchmen, examined to establish her virginity, and threatened. She abjures under the threat of fire, resumes her men's clothes after an attempted assault in her cell, and is condemned as a relapsed heretic. She walks quickly, barefoot, to the stake. The film ends on the empty post and the chain.
inclusion: Bresson rejected Dreyer's expressive acting and made the opposite version, brief, cold and exact. Every word comes from the documents, spoken without emphasis, and the drama lies in what the camera chooses to watch, which is hands, feet, doors opening and closing. DVDClassik singles out the single backward tracking shot as Joan hurries to the stake, as if toward the sky. Delay, twenty and untrained, is remarkable for her stillness. The film won the Special Jury Prize and the OCIC (Catholic film office) prize at Cannes in 1962. Time Out called it Bresson's essay in 'sado-masochistic voyeurism', and many viewers find it too austere to feel. Its brevity and fidelity make it the best companion to Dreyer.
themes: Joan submits to God first and to the Church militant as far as she can without denying her voices. Her abjuration and relapse are not hidden, and her return to fidelity is the turning point. Bresson presents grace as working through constraint, not feeling. The ecclesiastical judges act in concert with English interests, and the film's restraint lets the injustice speak without caricature.
history: Joan was tried at Rouen from January to May 1431 by a court under Bishop Pierre Cauchon and burned on 30 May 1431. The verdict was annulled in 1456 after a retrial in which witnesses described her last days, and which found it tainted by deceit and procedural errors.
liberties: Hearings spread over months are reduced to a handful of exchanges. The scenes of her last hours, including the assault that led her to resume male dress, come from later rehabilitation testimony rather than the condemnation record. Bresson's selection of what to keep is itself an interpretation.
advisories:
Older teens and adults: imprisonment in chains, coercive interrogation, an implied attempted rape, a virginity examination observed by men, and execution by burning (shown with restraint).

UK rating 12.

suitability.note: Brief at 65 minutes but very austere, so teenagers will manage it better than children.

doctrine: The key moment is Joan's reply that she would submit to the Church Militant but not to judges who disowned her voices. The Church distinguishes the Church as a whole, headed by the Pope, from a local court acting for political ends. Joan appealed to the Pope, and the Rouen court disregarded the appeal. Pius X beatified her in 1909 and Benedict XV canonised her on 16 May 1920. Her feast is 30 May. By tradition she received Communion before the stake.
production: Bresson wrote the script from the surviving trial and retrial transcripts and used non-professional actors, a method he had followed since 1945. He shot the film in the summer of 1961 at the Meudon observatory near Paris. Florence Delay is credited as Florence Carrez. The film runs 65 minutes and is in French. It was in competition at Cannes on 18 May 1962. It was shown at the first New York Film Festival in 1963 and had a limited New York release in 1965. It was poorly received at first and long seen as a minor work, but Godard put it first on his 1963 ten-best list, and later reviews were more positive.

title: The Flowers of St. Francis
decision: PUBLISH: Peter Brunette's Criterion essay, Greydanus's review and Chris Shields's Screen Slate piece independently document a film drawn from the Fioretti and the Life of Brother Juniper, centred on poverty, obedience and joy, and played by real friars. Recommended in the original Italian cut; the 1952 US version cut episodes and added a prologue.
summary: Rossellini and Fellini turn the Little Flowers into nine comic, tender episodes of the first friars, played by Franciscan friars: the most joyful film about religious life ever made.
synopsis: In the rain, Francis and his brothers come back to the Portiuncula after visiting the Pope, and find their hut taken over by a peasant and his donkey. They build a new home. Brother Juniper gives away his habit to a beggar and comes back naked. To make soup for a sick brother, he cuts the foot off a living pig, to its owner's fury. Clare visits and the brothers prepare a humble meal. Francis meets and embraces a leper at night. Juniper, sent out to preach, wanders into the camp of the tyrant Nicolaio, is beaten and nearly hanged, and his meekness disarms the warlord. Francis and Brother Leo learn what perfect joy is by being turned away in the snow. At the end, Francis has the brothers spin round until they fall, and each sets off to preach in the direction he faces.
inclusion: It is Rossellini's lightest film, made between Stromboli and Europe '51, and one of his best. He cast friars from the Franciscan house at Nocera Inferiore: Brother Nazario Gerardi plays Francis and Brother Severino Pisacane plays Juniper. Their unaffected faces carry more conviction than actors could. Aldo Fabrizi, the only star, plays Nicolaio as a buffoon trapped in absurd armour, and Brunette reads that scene as the clash between the noisy world and the friars' simplicity. Steven Greydanus notes that Francis is the straight man and the brothers are the holy fools. The episodes do not add up to a plot, and the comedy is slapstick at times.
themes: Poverty here is freedom: the friars possess nothing and are happy. Obedience is literal. Francis commands under holy obedience, and the final spinning game turns obedience into a children's game that sends them out to preach. Charity reaches the leper, the beggar and the tyrant. Juniper's foolishness, as with the pig, shows that zeal without prudence wounds others, and Francis corrects him. Clare's visit gives a glimpse of the Poor Clares' share in the same life. Prayer is constant and unforced. The film makes no claim to biography, and it stays faithful to how the Franciscan tradition remembered its beginning.
history: Francis (c. 1181–1226), son of a cloth merchant of Assisi, gave up his inheritance in 1206 and gathered companions around the chapel of the Portiuncula. The Fioretti ('Little Flowers') were compiled in the later fourteenth century from the Latin Actus beati Francisci, long after his death, and the Life of Brother Juniper gathers legends of one of his early companions. They are edifying stories, not documentary history.
liberties: It is selective and legendary by design: there is no conversion, stigmata or death of Francis. The American release of 1952 cut episodes, including the leper scene, removed the chapter titles and added a prologue of paintings and frescoes. Criterion's restoration is the Italian version, with the prologue as an extra.
advisories: Juniper is beaten and threatened with hanging in the tyrant's camp; a pig's foot is cut off (offscreen) and its owner is enraged; Juniper returns naked after giving away his habit (not shown explicitly).

doctrine: The film shows evangelical poverty as Francis lived it: the Rule that Innocent III approved orally in 1209 and Honorius III confirmed in 1223 binds the friars to hold nothing of their own. The episode of 'perfect joy' (Fioretti, chapter 8) teaches that joy lies in patient suffering of insults for Christ, not in miracles or learning. Francis received the stigmata in 1224 and died on 3 October 1226; Gregory IX canonised him in 1228. Clare founded the Poor Clares under his direction.
production: The film draws on the Fioretti and the Life of Brother Juniper. Fellini co-wrote it with Rossellini but was not present for the shooting. It premiered at the Venice Film Festival in 1950 to a packed and applauding house, though critics were mostly poor. It reached America in 1952 with the chapter markers removed. In 1995 the Vatican included it in its list of 45 important films.

title: Francis of Assisi
decision: PUBLISH: the AFI Catalog establishes the production (Fox/Perseus, shot at Assisi and Rome with Franciscan and Benedictine cooperation) and a full plot; independent contemporary reviews (New York Times, Variety, Harrison's Reports, LA Times, Washington Post, Monthly Film Bulletin, quoted via Wikipedia) and a later British review agree that it is reverent and static, with nothing doctrinally objectionable reported. The invented Paolo plot is disclosed. No Legion of Decency rating located; OSV's A-I is cited only as a fact. Primary 1961 review texts were not opened.
summary: Michael Curtiz's reverent, static CinemaScope life of St Francis, from rich man's son to stigmatic, with Bradford Dillman as Francis and Dolores Hart as Clare.
synopsis: Francis Bernardone, the pleasure-loving son of an Assisi cloth merchant, rides out with his friend Paolo, an impoverished nobleman, to fight for the Pope. In battle he hears a voice telling him to go home; he obeys and is jailed as a coward. Freed, he is told to rebuild a ruined church, gives up his inheritance, gathers followers, and Innocent III approves his order. Clare, his childhood friend, whom Paolo loves, is moved by his preaching and becomes a nun; the embittered Paolo joins the Crusade. Francis goes to the Holy Land, offers to walk through fire before the Sultan, and is appalled by the Crusaders' plundering. Back in Italy he finds friars abandoning poverty, withdraws, loses his sight, receives the stigmata and dies, visited by a repentant Paolo.
inclusion: It is the only Hollywood studio life of St Francis, shot at Assisi and in Rome with the cooperation of the Franciscans and the Benedictines of Assisi, and it covers more of his life than most Francis films: conversion, the rule, Clare, the Sultan, the troubles of the order and the stigmata. Contemporary critics found it respectful and inert. A. H. Weiler in the New York Times compared it to tapestries hanging limp on castle walls, and Harrison's Reports judged it too talky. Bradford Dillman, usually cast as a villain, plays Francis straight. It is more pageant than drama and suits the whole family.
themes: The film takes Francis's spirituality chiefly as poverty and obedience. He hears a voice and obeys, strips himself of his inheritance, rebuilds a church with his own hands, submits his rule to the Pope and fights to keep his friars poor. The Church is shown approving him through Innocent III and Cardinal Hugolino, and the stigmata are presented as a miracle. Prayer and the sacraments are less prominent than renunciation, and one British reviewer complained that the spiritual is smothered by the religiose. The invented rivalry with Paolo supplies most of the conflict.
history: Francis was born at Assisi in 1181 or 1182, son of the cloth merchant Pietro Bernardone. Around 1205 he set out for Apulia to join Walter of Brienne's campaign but turned back at Spoleto after a dream. He renounced his inheritance before the bishop, restored San Damiano, and won Innocent III's verbal approval for his rule. Clare joined him in Lent 1212. In 1219 he went to Damietta and was received by the Sultan. He received the stigmata on La Verna in September 1224 and died on 3 October 1226.
liberties: Paolo, Francis's friend and Clare's suitor, has no counterpart in the early lives of Francis and carries much of the plot, including a pardon he grants Francis at Clare's request. Francis's aborted military venture becomes a papal campaign for Sicily; in fact he set out for Apulia. Clare is given the surname Scefi. Francis's offer to walk through fire before the Sultan is staged as a set-piece. The troubles of the order are compressed into a single crisis.
advisories:
Battle scenes and sword fights; nothing graphic.

Blindness, the stigmata and a deathbed.

names: The Joyful Beggar, novel by Louis de Wohl (1958)

suitability.note: Suitable for all ages. The main obstacle for children is the slow pace and long speeches.

doctrine: Innocent III gave verbal approval to Francis's first rule; the definitive Rule was confirmed by Honorius III in the bull Solet annuere of 29 November 1223, and binds the friars to observe the Gospel in obedience, without property and in chastity. Clare's order followed the same poverty under its own rule. Francis was ordained deacon but, out of humility, never sought the priesthood. The Church keeps a commemoration of the Stigmata on 17 September, close to the feast of the Exaltation of the Cross, when he received them. He was canonised on 16 July 1228 by Gregory IX, who as Cardinal Hugolino had been protector of the order, the role Cecil Kellaway plays. His feast is 4 October.
production: Twentieth Century-Fox made the film, with Michael Curtiz directing. Filming began in Italy on 28 October 1960 and took about five months, in Assisi, elsewhere in Umbria and in Rome; the papal apartment at the Basilica of San Francesco stood in for the Lateran. Reshoots followed at the Fox lot in Los Angeles in March 1961. Mario Nascimbene's score was reported as the first film soundtrack to use Gregorian chant. It premiered in San Francisco on 12 July 1961 and in Assisi on 4 October 1961. Reviews were cool. The New York Times called it serene and static, and Variety missed any sustained dramatic friction and complained of ponderous verbosity. It earned about $920,000 in North American rentals, and Skouras blamed weak support from the Church as well as the reviews. Dolores Hart, who played Clare, entered the Benedictine Abbey of Regina Laudis in 1963.

title: Monsieur Vincent
decision: PUBLISH: Greydanus's review and Steve Vineberg's essay independently document an unsentimental portrait of priestly charity, with specific episodes (the plague village, the Ladies and Daughters of Charity, the foundlings) and a brief war-time assault image advised. AlloCiné settles identity.
summary: Pierre Fresnay's austere Vincent de Paul turns the organisation of charity into high drama in Maurice Cloche's understated, Oscar-honoured 1947 biography.
synopsis: Vincent, a young priest who has been comfortable as chaplain to a great family, takes the poor parish of Châtillon-les-Dombes. Plague has struck it, and the villagers stone him from their windows. He shames a lord who has barred his doors, finds an orphaned girl beside her dead mother, and persuades an overburdened neighbour to take her in. His first confraternity of charity grows from this. In Paris he enlists aristocratic Ladies of Charity, who soon send their maids instead of coming themselves. With Louise de Marillac he forms the Daughters of Charity from country girls. He serves as chaplain to the galley convicts, argues with Richelieu, and struggles over abandoned infants whom even the sisters at first refuse to touch. War ravages the provinces. Old and nearly blind, he charges a young sister with the hardest lesson of service to the poor.
inclusion: Fresnay's Vincent is no plaster saint. He is dry, ironic, sometimes harsh, and always working. Jean Anouilh's dialogue has an edge, and Claude Renoir's black-and-white images are sober and handsome. Steven Greydanus calls it a towering achievement. He praises its refusal to romanticise the poor or excuse the rich, and its sense of Vincent as an organiser who turned almsgiving into institutions. Steve Vineberg singles out the foundling sequence. The film is episodic, and some threads, the galleys and the foundlings, are left hanging; Greydanus calls it a fragment of a larger story.
themes: Charity here is a duty laid on the Christian, and it is uncomfortable. The poor are often ungrateful, dirty and rude, and Vincent insists they are owed help anyway. The rich are criticised not for having money but for wanting the satisfaction of giving without the labour. Vincent's priesthood is the source of his work: he prays, preaches and hears confessions, and the film never presents him as a social reformer who happens to wear a cassock. The Daughters of Charity appear as a new form of consecrated life lived in the streets. The final lesson, that the poor must be served humbly enough to forgive us our bread, is the film's moral centre.
history: Vincent de Paul (1581–1660) was parish priest at Châtillon-les-Dombes in 1617, where he founded the first Confraternity of Charity. He was royal chaplain of the galleys and organised care for foundlings and relief for war-ravaged Lorraine.
liberties: The film omits Vincent's early life, including the disputed story of his capture by pirates. It compresses forty years into a series of episodes and leaves several outcomes unclear. One German plot summary says he takes a galley convict's place at the oar, a hagiographic legend historians reject.
advisories:
Brief violence (stoning); a fleeting war montage with a glimpse of rape, nothing explicit.

Plague, death, misery and abandoned babies.

doctrine: Vincent's work is the corporal works of mercy as the Church has always taught them: feeding the hungry, tending the sick, ransoming captives and burying the dead. Christ says that what is done to the least of his brethren is done to him (Matthew 25:40). Vincent also served the Council of Trent's reform of the clergy: his Congregation of the Mission (founded 1625) gave missions to country people and trained priests, and the Council's decree on seminaries (Session 23, 1563) was in the same spirit. He founded the Daughters of Charity in 1633 with Louise de Marillac as women who lived in the world, not in an enclosure. He was canonised by Clement XII in 1737, and Leo XIII named him patron of all charitable societies in 1885. His traditional feast is 19 July.
production: Maurice Cloche directed. Pierre Fresnay's performance won him the Volpi Cup for best actor at Venice in 1947. The film was released in France on 5 November 1947 and won the Grand Prix du Cinéma Français. It is a black-and-white picture of 114 minutes. In the United States it received an honorary Academy Award (in 1949) as the best foreign-language film released there in 1948, and it was nominated for the BAFTA for Best Film. Sight and Sound called Fresnay's performance 'one of the most perfect pieces of work' seen for many years. In 1995 the Vatican included it in its list of great films.
