title: The Reluctant Saint
decision: PUBLISH: The AFI Catalog gives a detailed plot and production record, TCM's article documents the US–Italian co-production and its reception, and Greydanus's review recommends it for families. It is gentle, accurate in spirit, and has no content concerns beyond a brief exorcism scene.
summary: Maximilian Schell plays Joseph of Cupertino, the slow-witted friar who flew, in Edward Dmytryk's gentle, funny and affecting Italian-shot comedy.
synopsis: In seventeenth-century Apulia, Giuseppe Desa is a clumsy, dim young man whom nobody in his village wants. His mother Francesca, tired of him, gets her brother to have the Franciscan friary take him. Giuseppe is put to work in the stables, where he is happy with the animals and humble before everyone. The kindly bishop sees something in him and lets him try for ordination, and against all expectation he passes the examination when he is asked the one text he knows. Father Raspi (Ricardo Montalban), a strict and learned friar, distrusts him and suspects the devil when strange things start to happen, even attempting an exorcism. Then Giuseppe, praying before a statue of the Madonna, rises into the air, and the whole friary has to reckon with a holiness it did not see coming.
inclusion: A modest film that knows it. Schell, fresh from his Oscar for Judgment at Nuremberg, plays Joseph without condescension: slow, sweet and stubborn. He later counted it among his best performances. Montalban's Raspi is a good foil, a clever man humbled by a simple one. Shot in Rome and Lazio with Nino Rota's score, it looks and sounds Italian. Steven Greydanus calls it fine family viewing and admires the way the film holds back the miracles for over an hour, so that we know Joseph as a person before we see him fly. The comedy is broad and the special effects are dated, and it failed at the box office; Dmytryk called it his biggest flop.
themes: Humility is the subject, and God is shown choosing the weak to confound the strong. Joseph is not clever, and the friars, especially Raspi, assume that holiness must look like learning. His obedience is total: he does whatever task he is given. Raspi's suspicion of the devil reflects the Church's caution about extraordinary phenomena, and the film treats it fairly before showing the truth. Joseph's love of animals and his joy in prayer echo St. Francis. The ordination scene, where he passes by being asked the one thing he knows, is told as Providence. The levitations are a fruit of his love for Our Lady, not a show.
history: Giuseppe Desa (1603–1663) was born at Cupertino in Apulia, was accepted by the Conventual Franciscans after several rejections, and was ordained in 1628. His ecstasies and levitations, witnessed by many, led the Inquisition to examine him and move him from friary to friary; he died at Osimo.
liberties: The film compresses his life to the years up to his first levitations and omits the Inquisition's investigations and his later confinement. Father Raspi is largely an invented composite. The exam story is told as a single scene. The plot puts much of the early action at the friary at Grottella, where the historical Joseph lived.
advisories:
Brief exorcism scene, played seriously but not frightening.

Mild comic slapstick; no violence or sexual content.

Suitable for all ages.

doctrine: Joseph of Cupertino was refused by the Capuchins as well as the Conventual Franciscans and was admitted to the clerical state in 1625. He was kept from public ministry. The Church teaches that such phenomena are gratuitous graces and are not themselves the measure of holiness, which is charity and humility, as Benedict XIV argued in his treatise on beatification. Priests are bound to test claims of the extraordinary, as Father Raspi does. Benedict XIV beatified him in 1753 and Clement XIII canonised him in 1767. His feast is 18 September. He is the patron of students facing examinations.
production: Edward Dmytryk directed this American-Italian comedy-drama. It is in English and runs 105 minutes. A TV Guide review praised the light tone but found the direction lifeless.

title: Heaven over the Marshes
decision: PUBLISH: Identity is established by the Museo Nazionale del Cinema and contemporary Italian criticism, and the treatment by the Centro Cattolico Cinematografico synopsis, Aristarco (1949) and Morandini. The record gives no running time, so the unresolved 111 v. 98 minute discrepancy between festival records and the 2010 Fox DVD does not affect anything published; it is noted for viewers.
summary: Augusto Genina's neorealist-style life of Maria Goretti, filmed in the Pontine marshes with peasant non-actors: the story of a twelve-year-old who resisted, died and forgave.
synopsis: Luigi Goretti, a farm labourer, brings his wife and six children to the malarial marshes near Nettuno, where the landowners lodge them in a farmhouse with the Serenellis, a father and son who resent them. Luigi works tirelessly, but malaria kills him, and the fatherless family is left at the Serenellis' mercy. The drunken old man pursues the widow, who rebuffs him. His son Alessandro becomes obsessed with Maria, the eldest daughter and still almost a child. He tries small gifts, then force; she escapes him, and he threatens her. On a July afternoon, with everyone in the fields, he drags her into the house and, enraged by her refusal, stabs her again and again. Taken to hospital, she suffers for a day, holds firm in her faith, and forgives her murderer before she dies.
inclusion: Genina shot on location in the marshes with non-professional actors, and Ines Orsini, a peasant girl, plays Maria with plain conviction. G. R. Aldo's photography of the flat, fevered landscape won admiration. A 1955 survey of Italian cinema found it lacking in religious depth but called it sincerely affecting and a faithful chronicle of events. Guido Aristarco, writing in Cinema in December 1949, faulted its pictorial calligraphy and sentimental touches with the children, yet judged it the best film Genina had made in Italy. Morandini called it neorealism in a Catholic key.
themes: Maria's purity is presented as a choice of the will, not innocence alone: she knows what Alessandro wants and refuses it, even at the cost of her life. Her forgiveness of her murderer on her deathbed is the film's spiritual climax and the heart of her holiness. The poverty of the family, the fever of the marsh and the absence of the father show the conditions in which sin grows, without excusing it. The title sets heaven against the stagnant swamp. The film ends with Maria's death and leaves the fruit of her forgiveness to the viewer's knowledge.
history: Maria Goretti was stabbed on 5 July 1902 at Le Ferriere di Conca, in the Pontine marshes, by Alessandro Serenelli, and died the next day at Nettuno after forgiving him. Serenelli later repented in prison and was reconciled with her mother.
liberties: Genina compressed and shaped events, and his screenplay was more explicit in its symbolism than the finished film, according to the Torino retrospective essay. Its ending omits Alessandro's later conversion. Andreotti recalled that Pius XII, at a screening, was troubled by one scene that showed more of the girl than he thought fitting.

doctrine: Pius XII beatified Maria Goretti on 27 April 1947 and canonised her on 24 June 1950. The crowd was too large for St Peter's, so the rite was held in the square, with her mother and four of her surviving children present. Her feast is 6 July, and her body rests in the Passionist church of Our Lady of Graces at Nettuno. She is honoured as a martyr in defence of chastity: St Thomas teaches that any virtuous deed referred to God can be a cause of martyrdom, as with St John the Baptist, who died for rebuking adultery (Summa II-II, q. 124, a. 5). Her refusal ('it is a sin') rests on the old teaching, set out by St Augustine in The City of God (I, 16-18), that purity is a virtue of the will: violence suffered without consent is no sin in the victim, while consent is sin even where nothing is done.
production: It was shot in the summer of 1949, with interiors at Cinecittà and exteriors around Nettuno, and Genina cast local peasants beside a few professionals. At the 10th Venice Film Festival in 1949 it won the prizes for best Italian film and best director and the award of the Catholic film office (OCIC). It opened in Italy on 24 November 1949, seven months before the canonisation. Genina won the Nastro d'Argento for direction in 1950. Catholic critics held it up as an alternative to secular neorealism; others found it decorous but on the surface. In 2008 it was named among the 100 Italian films to be saved.

title: Thérèse: The Story of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux
originalTitle: Thérèse: The Story of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux
decision: PUBLISH as a modest family film, with its weaknesses stated: the Austin Chronicle review confirms credits, PG rating and 2004 release; Greydanus's review (Decent Films/National Catholic Register) documents a reverent, faithful outline of Story of a Soul with an engaging lead, while noting thin treatment of the Little Way. Secular reviews (Austin Chronicle, Film Threat) and the Catholic News Service reviewer's 'hagiographic tableaus' confirm the craft is weak. No doctrinal or reverence concerns are recorded by any source.
summary: A sincere, low-budget American biopic of the Little Flower, reverent and family-safe, that walks through Story of a Soul without quite catching its depth.
synopsis: Thérèse Martin grows up the youngest of five sisters in a pious, loving household in Alençon and Lisieux. Her mother dies when she is four, and she becomes her father Louis's 'little queen'. One by one her sisters enter the Carmel, and Thérèse, still a girl, resolves to follow. Refused because of her age, she appeals to the bishop and then, on pilgrimage to Rome, to Pope Leo XIII himself. Admitted at fifteen, she learns to serve awkward, elderly sisters with patience and to make small sacrifices out of love. Her father declines into illness. Thérèse falls ill with tuberculosis and dies in the infirmary at twenty-four.
inclusion: Watch it with children, but do not expect craft. It was made on a small budget, and it shows. The staging is stiff, much of the supporting cast is weak, and the script explains what it should dramatise. What it has is sincerity and an attractive lead. Lindsay Younce plays Thérèse as a normal, likeable young woman, and Steven Greydanus finds her deathbed scenes affecting. Defilippis himself is good as Louis Martin. Passages from Thérèse's own writing are read in voiceover, which is the best thing about it.
themes: The film follows the main events of Story of a Soul: the devout family, the call to Carmel, the appeal to Leo XIII, the patient charity of convent life and the trial of illness. Prayer, the sacraments and religious life are shown with uncomplicated reverence. Greydanus and Marjorie Baumgarten both note that the film gives little sense of the 'little way' of spiritual childhood that made Thérèse a Doctor of the Church, and her dark night of faith is reduced to a voiceover line.
history: Thérèse Martin (1873–1897) entered the Lisieux Carmel at fifteen and died of tuberculosis in 1897. Her autobiography, Story of a Soul, spread her Little Way worldwide.
liberties: The film omits Thérèse's scrupulosity and emotional struggles, the troubles of her sister Léonie, her work with the novices and much of her spiritual trial at the end. The Martin family is presented as almost flawless. Greydanus notes at least one small factual slip in the Christmas conversion scene.
advisories:
The death of a parent and a brief frightening image.

Thérèse's final illness and death are shown plainly.

The film shows the Carmelite life: strict enclosure, the divine office, perpetual abstinence and the Rule of St Albert as reformed by St Teresa of Avila. Her Little Way is confidence in God and the offering of small acts out of love, which the Church teaches is a path to holiness open to all, since every state of life is called to perfection. Pius XI beatified her on 29 April 1923, canonised her on 17 May 1925 and named her, with Francis Xavier, patron of the missions in 1927. Her feast was 3 October.

title: Fray Escoba
decision: PUBLISH: José María Aresté's DeCine21 critique describes specific episodes (the food basket, clashes with the porter, the farewell to his mother) that place Martín's charity and humility at the centre; the ICAA record confirms identity, a Dominican religious adviser and an all-ages video rating. The film's whimsy and anecdotal structure are noted as weaknesses, not doctrinal problems.
summary: A modest Spanish biopic of Martín de Porres, the mixed-race Dominican lay brother of Lima whose broom became the emblem of his holiness.
synopsis: Martín, son of a Spanish nobleman and a freed Black woman, grows up in Lima between his father's world and his mother's poverty. He gives up the advantages his father could offer and asks to serve the Dominicans. Set to sweeping and menial work, he earns the nickname "Fray Escoba" (Brother Broom). Episodes follow his care for the sick and the poor, his friction with the convent porter, Padre Barragán, and a growing reputation for wonders he does not seek: in one scene a basket keeps yielding food for the hungry. The film closes its family story with Martín's emotional parting from his mother.
inclusion: Ramón Torrado made a plain, warm film for a broad audience, and its best quality is that it keeps Martín at floor level. Holiness here is measured by the broom, the infirmary and the begging round. René Muñoz gives Martín a gentle, unpushy presence, and the Círculo de Escritores Cinematográficos gave him a special prize for it in 1961. José María Aresté calls the farewell with his mother the film's strongest moment. It has the faults of Spanish devotional cinema of the period: episodic construction, some sentimental comedy and miracle scenes staged with a fairy-tale touch that Aresté compares to Mary Poppins.
themes: The film's Catholic subject is humility made concrete. Martín chooses the lowest work in a religious house and treats it as service to Christ in the poor and the sick. Miracles are present, but they grow out of works of mercy such as feeding the hungry. Martín's patience with a sharp-tongued superior shows obedience as a daily discipline, not a pious attitude. A Dominican priest, Fr. Antonio Sánchez, served as religious adviser on the production.
history: Martín de Porres (1579–1639) was born in Lima to the Spaniard Juan de Porres and Ana Velázquez, a freed woman of African descent. Barred by colonial rules from entering as a full religious at first, he joined the Dominican convent of the Holy Rosary as a donado (lay helper) and later professed as a lay brother. He was known for nursing the sick, caring for the poor and animals, and for reported miracles.
liberties: The screenplay by Jaime G. Herranz is credited as "inspired by" the life of the then Blessed Martín, and it arranges traditional anecdotes into a loose sequence. Conversations, the porter's characterisation and the staging of individual miracles are dramatic inventions.
advisories:
Rated suitable for all audiences on its Spanish video releases (1988 and 2008).

Illness, poverty and an emotional parting between mother and son.

doctrine: Martín de Porres lived the Dominican life as a lay brother, which the Church honours as a true state of perfection through the vows of poverty, chastity and obedience. His care of the sick and the poor is the corporal works of mercy. The Church teaches that all men are equal before God and redeemed by Christ: Paul III's bull Sublimis Deus (1537) declared the Indians of the New World to be rational men who could not lawfully be enslaved, and the principle governs the case of a mulatto boy who was kept from full profession. Martín was beatified by Gregory XVI in 1837 and canonised by John XXIII on 6 May 1962, before the Council opened in October of that year. He died on 3 November 1639.
production: Ramón Torrado directed this Spanish black-and-white film for Copercines in 1961. The film runs about 101 minutes. It was a success on release, and the Círculo de Escritores Cinematográficos gave García-Herranz its medal for best screenplay. It appeared a year before Martín's canonisation, which made it timely.

title: Un mulato llamado Martín
alternateTitles: La vida de San Martín de Porres
decision: GREY: Identity, credits and the main episodes are established (Sentido Fílmico, Spanish Wikipedia, a Lima devotional blog), but no critic has assessed how the film treats the saint, and its synopses frame his life as a 'fight against slavery' in a 1970s Peruvian production made under the Velasco-era film law. That framing is unexamined. Martín was canonised in 1962, so the post-1965 rule does not apply. Settled by a review or recorded viewing that addresses the miracles, the convent life and the slavery theme. Year: the SIC and INAH listings give 1974 (probably production); IMDb and Sentido Fílmico give the Lima premiere, 25 September 1975.

grey.question: Tito Davison directed this Mexican-Peruvian film, with René Muñoz as Martín, and it opened in Lima in 1975. No independent review exists, so nobody has said how it treats the saint. Its published synopses present his life as a struggle against slavery and against the barriers between slaves, priests and nobles, and it was made under Peru's state film law of the early 1970s. Whether that is the charity of the traditional lives or a social reading of the saint cannot yet be said.

summary: Tito Davison's Mexican–Peruvian life of St Martin de Porres, with René Muñoz returning to the role he first played in Fray Escoba.
synopsis: Martín is the illegitimate son of a Spanish nobleman, Don Juan de Porres, and a woman of African descent. The film follows him from a devout childhood in colonial Lima to the Dominican convent of Santo Domingo, where his birth allows him only the place of a donado, a lay helper, and he takes the lowest work. Episodes described in published accounts include a trader at the port of Callao trying to sell him as a slave until a friar intervenes; his care for Balu, an enslaved man who has turned to violence and later gains his freedom; a temptation by the devil on the convent stairs; and his gift of his father's shirt to Tupac, an Indigenous man whose son is sick. Fray Barragán, the porter, is his companion and a comic foil.
inclusion: Few films about the Lima saint were made in Peru itself, and this one was shot partly in the convent of Santo Domingo, where Martín lived and died, with a largely Peruvian supporting cast drawn from television. René Muñoz, the Cuban actor who first played Martín in the Spanish Fray Escoba (1961), took the part again here and in Mexican television serials. A Lima devotional writer says this film gives more room to Martín's works of mercy than the earlier Spanish one, which he calls sugary. It is of most interest to viewers who know Fray Escoba and want a Latin American treatment of the same saint.
themes: Martín's holiness is shown through humility and charity: a donado who sweeps, serves and gives away what he has. The convent of Santo Domingo frames his religious life, and his temptation by the devil, a traditional element of his legend, is staged on its stairs. The film's synopses also present his life as a struggle against slavery and against the barriers between slaves, priests and nobility.
history: Martín de Porres (1579–1639) was born in Lima, the son of a Spanish nobleman, Juan de Porres, and Ana Velázquez, a freed woman of African descent. He entered the Dominican convent of the Holy Rosary (Santo Domingo) as a lay helper, later professed as a lay brother, and became known for his care of the sick and poor, his penances and reported miracles.
liberties: The devotional account notes that not every episode in the film is historically proven. The enslaved man Balu and the Indigenous father Tupac are not figures of the standard biographies, and the attempted sale of Martín at Callao is not part of the usual record. The friendship with Fray Barragán is played partly for comedy.
advisories:
A violent enslaved character; an attempt to sell the young Martín as a slave.

A scene of diabolical temptation.

Nothing sexual is reported.

summary: Luis César Amadori's Spanish biopic, with Mel Ferrer as the Reims canon who gave up rank and fortune to found the Brothers of the Christian Schools.
synopsis: Set in the France of Louis XIV, the film follows Jean-Baptiste de La Salle, a canon from a well-off family, as he turns to the education of poor children. Catalogue summaries and the Lasallian Brothers' own notice describe its arc: his first involvement with schools, the founding of the Brothers of the Christian Schools, and the hardship and obstacles he meets in trying to offer free schooling to all children. Mel Ferrer plays La Salle, with Fernando Rey, Mabel Karr, Manuel Alexandre and Antonio Ferrandis among the Spanish cast.
inclusion: La Salle is one of the great figures of Catholic education, yet he has rarely been filmed, and this is the only feature about him. Spain put serious resources into it, with Amadori, a veteran of Argentine cinema then working in Spain, directing Mel Ferrer and a strong supporting cast. Paco Casado, reviewing it for Cine y Max, calls Amadori's direction diligent, the colour photography acceptable, Gregorio García Segura's score good and Ferrer well suited to the part. He blames a weak script and a polished, Hollywood-style surface that leaves the saint himself thinly drawn. DeCine21 rates it 5/10. It reached the United States in 1976 as Who Are My Own and returned on DVD in 2010.
themes: The film's subject is the founding of a teaching institute: La Salle's renunciation of comfort and status, and his dedication of his life to free Christian schooling for poor children. DeCine21 presents him as a holy man whose service of others follows Christian teaching.
history: Jean-Baptiste de La Salle (1651–1719), a priest and canon of Reims, founded the Brothers of the Christian Schools in the early 1680s. He pioneered free elementary schools, teaching in French rather than Latin, and the training of teachers. He faced lawsuits from the guilds of schoolmasters.
advisories:
No violence or sexual content is recorded; DeCine21 lists it as suitable for young people.

doctrine: La Salle's Brothers of the Christian Schools are lay religious: he refused to let them become priests, so that they would stay teachers. The aim of the schools was to teach poor boys the catechism and the faith along with reading and writing, in line with the Council of Trent's order that children be taught Christian doctrine (the Roman Catechism, 1566). The Institute was bound by simple vows, and its Rule gained papal approval from Benedict XIII in 1725, after his death in 1719. La Salle gave away his canonry and inheritance, an act of evangelical poverty. He was canonised by Leo XIII on 24 May 1900, and Pius XII proclaimed him heavenly patron of all teachers of youth in 1950.
production: Luis César Amadori directed this Spanish historical drama, released in 1964 as El señor de La Salle and running 138 minutes.

title: Don Bosco
decision: GREY: identity is secure (ACMI, Box Office Mojo, Wikipedia credits) and one independent, scene-level review exists (Avellina Balestri, Catholic Insight, 2016), which is enthusiastic. Not PUBLISH because that is a single modern review that does not address liberties, the film was co-produced by Elle Di Ci (the Salesian publisher's film arm, an interested party), it adds an invented brothel subplot, and its weighting of Bosco's conflict with Archbishop Gastaldi is unexamined. Settles with a second independent review (e.g. the 1988 Italian press: Repubblica, Segnalazioni cinematografiche) or a documented viewing.

grey.question: Only one independent review exists: Avellina Balestri's in Catholic Insight, which finds the film devout and balanced. That is thin for a film co-produced by the Salesians' own publishing house, which adds an invented subplot about a girl and a brothel. Nobody has examined how it presents Bosco's quarrel with Archbishop Gastaldi, his dreams or the Lina story against the historical record.

summary: Leandro Castellani's centenary-year biopic, co-produced by the Salesians' publishing house, with Ben Gazzara as the Turin priest who battles poverty, the state and his archbishop for his boys.
synopsis: In nineteenth-century Turin Don Giovanni Bosco, guided by a dream he has had since boyhood, gathers poor and abandoned boys into his oratory. Officials complain that he is harbouring misfits. During political unrest he is offered money to stop, and there are attempts on his life, among them poisoned wine; a large grey dog that he believes heaven sent turns away an assassin. A subplot follows Lina, a girl whose mother wants her to work in a brothel beside the oratory, and Giuseppe, one of Bosco's boys, who takes her side and is later arrested for robbery. A hostile bishop suspends Bosco's faculty to hear confessions. He goes to Rome, wins the support of Pius IX and founds the Salesians. The film ends with his last days.
inclusion: Ben Gazzara's Bosco is the film's main asset. Avellina Balestri, reviewing it for the Canadian magazine Catholic Insight, calls it his finest performance and praises its mixture of earthy realism and mysticism. She finds the production uneven, thinks Patsy Kensit miscast as Lina, and is irked by the English dubbing of some Italian actors. Unusually for a saint's film, it puts on screen the opposition Bosco met from his own archbishop as well as from the state.
themes: The Catholic content is Bosco's pastoral method and his supernatural life: the oratory as a place of work, prayer and play for boys nobody else wanted; his dreams, treated as true guidance, including visions of the Christ Child and Our Lady that he recounts before the Pope; and the grey dog that protects him. Balestri finds it balanced, showing good and bad churchmen without attacking the Church.
history: John Bosco was born near Castelnuovo in Piedmont in 1815. As a young priest in Turin he began his oratory for poor boys; by 1868 the Salesian Society he founded had fifty priests and teachers. He met complaints from the authorities and even an attempt to have him confined in an asylum. He died in Turin on 31 January 1888.
liberties: Lina, her mother and the brothel, and Giuseppe's romance and arrest, form a subplot that appears to be invented.
advisories:
A subplot involves a brothel and a mother pressing her daughter to work there; sources do not describe explicit content.

Assassination attempts, a poisoning and an arrest.

doctrine: Bosco's method was the preventive system, which the Catholic Encyclopedia describes as gaining love before inspiring fear, with teachers as father, adviser and friend, and the foundation of frequent Confession, frequent Communion and daily Mass. His oratory began on 8 December 1841, the feast of the Immaculate Conception defined by Pius IX in 1854. The church he built at Valdocco was consecrated on 9 June 1868 under the patronage of Our Lady, Help of Christians. The Salesian Society was approved by Pius IX provisionally in 1869 and finally in 1874. The film's dreams are Bosco's own; the Church does not require belief in private visions, and the grey dog Grigio is a popular tradition. Bosco was canonised by Pius XI on Easter Sunday 1934; his feast is 31 January.
production: Leandro Castellani directed this centenary-year film, marking 100 years since Bosco's death in 1888. It was made by Elle Di Ci and Tiber Cinematografica. Ben Gazzara, an American, played Bosco in an English-language version, and some Italian actors are dubbed; the running time is 108 minutes. Columbia Tri-Star distributed it in Italy, where it was released on 30 September 1988. Balestri gave it five stars.

title: Ignatius of Loyola
decision: PUBLISH: Ignatius was canonised in 1622, so rule (a) does not apply. Independent reviews (Oggs Cruz in Rappler; Rome Jorge and Rea Gierran in adobo Magazine) establish a straightforward conversion narrative that sets out the saint's virtues without reinterpreting him, and Brad Miner's detailed review (The Catholic Thing, used for content) confirms the penances, temptations and Inquisition trial are treated reverently. The producer, Jesuit Communications, is an interested party and is disclosed; no source reports post-conciliar framing in the film itself.
summary: Paolo Dy's Filipino-made, Spanish-cast biography follows Iñigo de Loyola from his wound at Pamplona through the cave at Manresa to his trial before the Inquisition.
synopsis: In 1521 Iñigo López de Loyola, a Basque nobleman, defends Pamplona against the French and has his leg shattered. It is set, broken again and reset, and he is left with a limp. Convalescing, he reads a life of Christ and lives of the saints and resolves to change his life. Taken to a brothel by his brother and cousin, he refuses the prostitute Ana and talks with her about Christ instead. He gives up his sword, nurses the sick in a hospital and withdraws to a cave, where he fasts, scourges himself and is tempted by a devil who wears his own face. From this struggle come the notes that become the Spiritual Exercises. When he begins to preach and gather followers without a degree or holy orders, he is brought before an inquisitor, examined and vindicated. The film ends before the founding of the Society of Jesus.
inclusion: It is the first English-language feature about Ignatius, made with unusual ambition for a low-budget Filipino production. Andreas Muñoz, a Spanish stage actor, carries it; Rina Jimenez-David in the Inquirer praised the intensity of his performance, and Miner thought it the best Catholic film he had seen in years. Oggs Cruz in Rappler was cooler. The battles borrow from The Lord of the Rings, the Spanish-accented English grates, and the story lacks a central conflict and circles a point made early. Cruz still found it affecting in its quieter scenes, especially Iñigo's conversation with the prostitute. The adobo reviewers fault thin sound and visible CGI. It is earnest and suits viewers who want a plain account of a conversion.
themes: The conversion story is told in traditional terms. Iñigo's change begins with reading the life of Christ and the saints, passes through renunciation, works of mercy and harsh penance, and is tested by a devil who tempts him with his former self. The penances are shown frankly; the adobo reviewers note that sceptics may read them as madness, while Miner reads them, as the film intends, as the road to sanity and holiness. The Spiritual Exercises appear as the fruit of that struggle. The Inquisition scenes make churchmen the antagonists, but Ignatius submits to examination and is cleared, which is close to what happened. Cruz observes that it seeks only to set out the saint's virtues. Although Jesuit Communications produced it, the reviews report no modern reframing of Ignatius or his mission.
history: Iñigo López de Loyola (1491–1556) was wounded by a cannonball at the siege of Pamplona on 20 May 1521. Recovering at Loyola, he read lives of Christ and the saints. In 1522 he left his sword at Our Lady's altar at Montserrat and spent months in penance at Manresa, where the Spiritual Exercises took shape. Preaching without theological training led to imprisonment and examination at Alcalá and Salamanca. He studied in Paris.
liberties: The inquisitor is named Frías, apparently after Alonso de Salazar Frías, who was born after Ignatius died; Miner notes the anachronism. The separate inquiries at Alcalá and Salamanca are compressed into one trial, and the threat of burning is spoken of but not shown. The brothel scene and the devil in Iñigo's likeness are dramatic inventions. The film stops before Paris and the founding of the Society.
advisories:
Battle violence and a painful leg-setting.

Self-flagellation and severe penances, the main reason for its PG-13 rating according to Miner.

A brothel scene with a prostitute; nothing sexual is shown.

Scenes of diabolical temptation.

doctrine: Ignatius (born 1491, died in Rome 31 July 1556) wrote the Spiritual Exercises, a guided program of meditations that received papal approval in 1548. In 1534 at Montmartre he and his first companions took vows. Paul III approved the Society of Jesus by the bull Regimini militantis Ecclesiae in 1540, and Ignatius was elected first general in 1541. Paul V beatified him in 1609 and Gregory XV canonised him in 1622.
production: Made by Jesuit Communications, the media arm of the Jesuits in the Philippines, as the directorial debut of Paolo Dy. Shooting took about twenty days in Navarra and the Basque Country, on a budget of ₱50 million; the battle scene was the hardest to film and stuntmen came from the Canary Islands. It was screened at the Vatican Film Library on 14 June 2016, the first Philippine film shown in Vatican City, opened in the Philippines on 27 July and in select US cinemas on 26 August 2016.

title: Molokai: The Story of Father Damien
originalTitle: Molokai: The Story of Father Damien
decision: REJECT: Scope (editorial ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's subject is recognised as saint or blessed only through a canonisation or beatification made after the Second Vatican Council (Damien of Molokai, beatified 1995, canonised 2009).
summary: David Wenham plays the Belgian priest who went to the Hawaiian leper settlement of Kalawao in 1873, stayed sixteen years, caught the disease and died there.
synopsis: In 1873 Father Damien, a young Belgian priest of the Sacred Hearts Fathers, volunteers to go to Molokai, where the Hawaiian kingdom exiles people with leprosy. He finds a lawless, filthy settlement where the sick are left to die. He dresses sores, builds houses, digs graves, says Mass and badgers the Board of Health and his own superiors in Honolulu for money, medicine, nuns and a confessor. Officials find him tactless; a cynical Anglican patient enjoys resisting his offer of the sacraments; a shrewd rancher becomes an ally. Years later he learns he has leprosy himself, and he keeps working while new helpers, among them Mother Marianne Cope, arrive to carry on.
inclusion: Cox, a Melbourne director known for small, personal films, plays the material straight and lets the place do the work: the cliffs, the sea, the faces of the sick. Wenham is the reason to watch. His Damien is stubborn, irritable, funny and plainly holy, a man whose charity is practical and whose priesthood is not decoration: he wants souls as well as bandages. David Stratton found the leper scenes and Wenham's performance the heart of a flawed film, and Time Out called it engrossing and often moving. The supporting cast is starry but uneven, the structure episodic, and the music sometimes pushes too hard.
themes: Damien's charity is inseparable from his priesthood. He celebrates Mass, hears confessions, baptises and tries, openly, to bring the dying into the Church. The film shows him, unable to land a confessor, shouting his sins in French to a priest on a ship offshore. His struggles with obedience are treated honestly: he is often in conflict with his superiors, but the film also shows good bishops and sympathetic clergy. He faces sexual temptation and resists it. Greydanus doubts two brief moments, a line about Hawaii's 'old gods' and a wedding Damien performs that would have been invalid.
history: Joseph de Veuster (1840–1889) took the name Damien in the Congregation of the Sacred Hearts and went to Molokai at Easter 1873. Superiors found his zeal indiscreet and his bishop called him tempestuous. Leprosy was confirmed in 1885 and he died on 15 April 1889. Robert Louis Stevenson defended him against a Protestant minister's slanders. He was beatified in 1995 and canonised in 2009.
liberties: Based on Hilde Eynikel's biography, the film compresses sixteen years into episodes and invents or composites some patients and officials. Greydanus could find nothing in the biographies to support the 'old gods' remark or the wedding scene. The producers' 1999 Belgian release was disowned by Cox; the version he later restored runs about two hours.
advisories:
Disfigurement from leprosy, death and burial are shown frequently.

A brief, shadowy massacre; minor profanity; a restrained scene of resisted sexual temptation and a reference to impure thoughts.

Rated PG. Better for teenagers and adults than young children.

title: Claret
decision: GREY: Identity, credits and outline are established (Cine con Ñ interview, DeCine21, Crux), and Claret was beatified in 1934 and canonised in 1950, so rule (a) does not apply. Every substantive review found comes from a Catholic outlet (DeCine21, El Debate, Filasiete, Cinemanet, Catholic Review) and the Claretians co-produced the film, so there is no independent assessment of its treatment; the makers' human-dignity framing of the Cuban years is unexamined. Year: 2020 is the production year given by DeCine21; first release was 24 September 2021 in Spain. Settled by a secular review or a check of the dialogue.

grey.question: No independent review exists of how Pablo Moreno's 2021 Spanish film treats Claret. The reviews so far all come from Catholic outlets, and his own congregation, the Claretians, co-produced it. Its publicity stresses his defence of enslaved people in Cuba and calls him a man for our time, so it is not yet clear that his preaching and priestly work stay at the centre.

summary: Pablo Moreno's low-budget Spanish biography of St Anthony Mary Claret, framed by the writer Azorín's 1930s inquiry into the slanders that pursued the archbishop.
synopsis: In the 1930s the writer Azorín, who had once repeated the hostile legend about Archbishop Claret, discovers that the sources behind it were falsified and sets out to establish the truth, consulting Pío Baroja along the way. His inquiry frames the story of Claret's life. The son of a Catalan textile family, Claret chooses the priesthood, becomes a missionary preacher and founds a congregation. Sent to Cuba as Archbishop of Santiago, he defends enslaved people, makes powerful enemies and survives attempts on his life. Recalled to Madrid as confessor to Queen Isabel II, he is drawn into palace intrigue and the quarrels of the Carlist era while longing to return to the missions; a papal representative tells him to stay. The two timelines run in parallel, and Azorín's own exile is set beside Claret's.
inclusion: Claret is one of the most important Spanish saints of the nineteenth century, and this is the first feature film about him. Moreno's framing device is its best idea: the inquiry of Azorín, an anticlerical writer who came to defend the archbishop, gives the story an argument about how reputations are made and unmade. José María Aresté of DeCine21 found the device effective and praised Antonio Reyes as a Claret both spiritual and approachable, while noting a stock voice-over and abrupt jumps. John Mulderig of the Catholic Review found it informative but stiff, with awkward dialogue made worse by the English dub, and praised its portrait of Claret's opposition to slavery. Alba Recondo's Isabel II has been singled out by Spanish reviewers. The budget is visibly small. It is most useful for viewers who know little of Claret and want the outline of his life.
themes: The film presents Claret's holiness as uncompromising zeal. He preaches, founds a congregation, governs his diocese and refuses to soften the demands of the faith, and this earns him enemies. His defence of the enslaved in Cuba is prominent; the director describes him treating slaves and the queen with the same human dignity. Azorín and Pío Baroja, neither of them practising Catholics, are shown treating his memory with intellectual honesty. His years as royal confessor are shown as a trial of obedience: he wants to go back to the missions and is told to stay.
history: Antonio María Claret (1807–1870), born at Sallent near Barcelona, the son of a small woollen manufacturer, worked as a weaver before entering the seminary at Vic. Ordained in 1835, he became a popular missionary preacher. As Archbishop of Santiago de Cuba from 1851 he survived attempts on his life (at least fifteen are recorded); at Holguín an assassin cut his face open. From 1857 he was confessor to Isabel II. He attended the Vatican Council in 1869 and died at Fontfroide in 1870.
liberties: The 1930s frame rests on an actual episode, Azorín's public change of mind about Claret, but its staging, including the conversations with Baroja and the parallel with Azorín's own exile, is the film's construction.
advisories:
Brief violence with slight gore: an assassination attempt and the aftermath of a lynching and a battle.

Adultery and illegitimacy are part of the court intrigue; a couple of mild oaths.

doctrine: Claret was beatified in 1934 and canonised by Pius XII in 1950. He founded the Missionary Sons of the Immaculate Heart of Mary in 1849, which is why the Claretians take that title. In Cuba he restored clerical discipline, reorganised the seminary and, the Catholic Encyclopedia says, validated over nine thousand marriages in two years, which is a pastoral matter of the sacrament of matrimony. He founded schools and a hospital. As royal confessor from 1857 he held a post that carried considerable political risk, and after the 1868 revolution the pope sent him back to Madrid with faculties to absolve the queen of censures she had incurred. Investigation of his cause began in 1887, and Leo XIII declared him Venerable in 1899.
production: Claret (released in Latin America as Esclavos y reyes, and in the United States as Slaves and Kings) is by Pablo Moreno of Contracorriente Producciones. It is co-produced with Three Columns Entertainment and the Claretians. It was meant to appear in 2020, the 150th anniversary of Claret's death, but COVID-19 delayed it to a Spanish release on 24 September 2021. It runs about two hours. Fathom Events screened it in US cinemas, in English on 22 August 2022 and in Spanish on 23 August.

title: A Man for All Seasons
decision: PUBLISH: The 'autonomous conscience' objection (Duffy; echoed by Weigel) is aimed chiefly at Bolt's preface and at the historical More's omitted record, while the film itself has More defend papal primacy at his trial, refuse a heretic son-in-law and die 'God's first' (Wilson, Weigel, plot record). The omission of More's actions against heretics is disclosed as a historical liberty rather than treated as a doctrinal defect.
summary: Zinnemann's film of Robert Bolt's play follows Thomas More from royal favour to the scaffold as he refuses to accept Henry VIII as head of the Church.
synopsis: Sir Thomas More, a lawyer and devout family man, is admired across England when Henry VIII wants his marriage to Catherine of Aragon annulled. Cardinal Wolsey asks for More's help; More will not give it. After Wolsey's fall More becomes Lord Chancellor, then resigns when the clergy submit to the King. He keeps silent on the marriage and the new oath, trusting that the law protects a man who says nothing. Thomas Cromwell works patiently to break that silence. More is imprisoned in the Tower, separated from his wife Alice and daughter Meg, and finally convicted on the perjured evidence of Richard Rich, a young man he once refused to promote. Only after the verdict does he say plainly what he believes.
inclusion: The film is made almost entirely of conversations, and it grips. Bolt's dialogue is sharp and often funny, and Paul Scofield plays More as a man of wit and warmth who would much rather live than die. The supporting cast is excellent: Orson Welles as a bloated, worldly Wolsey, Leo McKern as Cromwell, Robert Shaw as a boisterous and dangerous Henry, Wendy Hiller as Alice, John Hurt as the weak, ambitious Rich. Ted Moore's photography and Georges Delerue's score keep it handsome without fuss. The Catholic case is clear. More's quarrel is not over a divorce as such but over whether a king can make himself head of the Church. The film lets his conviction emerge slowly, under pressure, through legal caution, family love and finally open witness.
themes: The film turns on papal primacy and the indissolubility of marriage. More refuses to take an oath that would deny the Pope's authority, and at his trial he argues that no temporal ruler may claim the government of the Church, citing Christ's commission to St Peter. He forbids his daughter to marry Will Roper while Roper holds Lutheran views, and his last words are that he dies the King's good servant, but God's first. Critics such as Eamon Duffy argue that Bolt made More a modern hero of personal integrity; Bolt's own preface encourages that reading. Joe Wilson and George Weigel reply that on screen More rarely talks about conscience at all and grounds himself in God. The more convincing reading is theirs, though the film does stress keeping one's 'self'.
history: More resigned as Lord Chancellor in 1532, refused the oath attached to the Act of Succession in 1534, and was tried for treason on 1 July 1535. Accounts of the trial record that, at its close, he declared the Act on which he was indicted contrary to the laws of God and his holy Church. He was beheaded on Tower Hill on 6 July 1535.
liberties: The film leaves out More's writings against Protestants and his part, as Chancellor, in prosecuting heretics; the biographer Richard Marius thought this produced a More who would barely be recognised in his own time. Rich's long acquaintance with More is expanded for dramatic shape. Several private conversations, including those with Norfolk and Cromwell, are invented, though the main events follow the record.
advisories:
More is beheaded at the end; the blow is not lingered on.

No sexual content or strong language.

sources.title: Blessed Thomas More
sources.claims: Act of Succession oath, supremacy statutes, resignation 1532, trial 1 July 1535, beheading 6 July 1535, beatification 1886

names: A Man for All Seasons, play by Robert Bolt (1960)

suitability.note: The film is made of long dialogue scenes about oaths and law, which suit teenagers better than young children.

doctrine: More died for the primacy of the Roman Pontiff. The Act of Succession (1534) required an oath that rejected the Pope's authority, and the Act of Supremacy named Henry Supreme Head of the Church in England. The Church holds that Christ gave Peter the keys (Matthew 16:18-19), and the Vatican Council defined the Pope's universal jurisdiction in 1870. More's refusal is therefore obedience to a divine law above the King's. It is not the modern claim that each man's private conscience is final. He was beatified by Leo XIII in 1886 and canonised, with John Fisher, by Pius XI on 19 May 1935. His silence rests on the legal maxim that silence gives consent, and he did not risk perjury or a lie to save himself.
production: Robert Bolt wrote the play in 1960 and the film keeps its form. Fred Zinnemann insisted on Paul Scofield, who had played More in London and on Broadway, even though the producers doubted his box-office value. The actors took salary cuts to keep the budget under $2 million. John Hurt had his first major film role as Rich. The picture was released by Columbia in 1966 and earned about $28.4 million. It won six Academy Awards, among them Best Picture, Director, Actor, Adapted Screenplay, Colour Cinematography and Colour Costume Design, and also the BAFTA for Best Film.

title: Becket
decision: PUBLISH (teens and up): AFI Catalog identity and synopsis; Greydanus's Decent Films review (+3) judges it reverent, with sincere faith and carefully staged liturgy. The serious historical liberties, above all the invented libertine past and mistress, which the Catholic Encyclopedia flatly contradicts, and the unfair portrait of Alexander III, are stated plainly; they shape the drama but do not turn the martyrdom against the faith.
summary: Richard Burton's Becket and Peter O'Toole's Henry II, drinking companions turned archbishop and king, in a lavish film of Anouilh's play about friendship broken by the honour of God.
synopsis: Henry II spends his days hunting and carousing with his clever friend Thomas Becket and makes him Chancellor, where Becket bleeds the Church for the Crown. When Henry demands Becket's mistress for himself, Becket gives her up and she kills herself. On the death of the Archbishop of Canterbury, Henry forces Becket into the see, expecting a compliant ally. Becket warns him he cannot serve both God and the king, resigns the chancellorship and defends the Church's rights. Henry turns on him with false charges; Becket flees to France and the Pope. A last meeting on horseback produces a hollow peace. Becket returns to Canterbury, Henry cries out to be rid of him, and four barons kill him at the altar.
inclusion: The two performances carry it. O'Toole's Henry is needy, funny, petulant and frightening, and Burton plays Becket with a cool reserve that slowly becomes something like holiness. Steven Greydanus calls the film a reverent masterpiece, though less incisive than A Man for All Seasons, and finds Burton harder to warm to than Scofield's More, which is fair. Geoffrey Unsworth's colour photography and the huge Canterbury set are handsome, and the ceremonies, the consecration, an excommunication, the chant, are staged with care. It is long and theatrical, and Anouilh's dialogue is more epigrammatic than devout. Still, the moment when Becket, having found a cause worthy of his honour, chooses God over his friend is stirring.
themes: The question is the freedom of the Church from the Crown. Once consecrated, Becket gives his goods to the poor, takes up prayer and penance, and refuses to let the king control ecclesiastical courts or appointments. Greydanus judges that he loves God, though Anouilh frames his conversion as the discovery of an honour worth serving, the honour of God. Liturgy and the sacramental office of a bishop are treated with dignity. The papacy fares worse: Alexander III and his court are shown as calculating politicians, which Greydanus thinks unfair. The ending, Henry submitting to a flogging by monks and proclaiming Becket a saint, honours the martyr.
history: Thomas Becket was born in London of Norman parents, served Henry II as Chancellor, and was consecrated Archbishop of Canterbury in 1162. He resisted the Constitutions of Clarendon, spent six years in exile, returned in 1170 and was killed in his cathedral by four knights on 29 December. Henry did public penance at his tomb in 1174.
liberties: Anouilh made Becket a Saxon to set him against the Norman king; he was Norman. The film gives him a mistress and a life of drinking and womanising with Henry; the Catholic Encyclopedia records that no word was ever said against his purity. Gwendolen is invented. The Pope is made a cynic. Gilbert Foliot's role is simplified, and Becket's exile is compressed.
advisories:
Implied sexual immorality and womanising in the early scenes; Henry takes Becket's mistress, who then kills herself.

The murder in the cathedral is violent but brief. Some coarse language and demeaning treatment of women.

Greydanus rates it for teens and up.

doctrine: Becket defended the liberty of the Church against Henry II's Constitutions of Clarendon (1164), above all the claim to try clergy in royal courts. The Church holds that clerics are tried by their own courts (the privilege of the forum). Becket's motto in the play is 'the honour of God'. He was killed at the altar steps on 29 December 1170 and was canonised by Alexander III on 21 February 1173; the pilgrimage to Canterbury lasted until Henry VIII destroyed the shrine in 1538. The historical Becket was only a deacon until ordained priest on the eve of his consecration.
production: Paramount made the film from Anouilh's 1959 play, with Peter Glenville directing. It was shot at Shepperton Studios and on location at Alnwick and Bamburgh castles in Northumberland. The budget was about $3 million. It opened as a roadshow on 11 March 1964 and ran 148 minutes. It took about $9.2 million in the box office and won the Oscar for Best Adapted Screenplay among twelve nominations, including Best Picture, Burton and O'Toole. It won Golden Globes for Best Drama and for O'Toole. A restored print was shown again in 2007.

title: The Carmelites
decision: PUBLISH: Identity confirmed by AlloCiné and the Gaumont catalogue; James Travers's detailed review and the Aleteia appreciation establish a faithful adaptation of Bernanos centred on fear, grace and martyrdom, and the film won the OCIC Grand Prix hors-festival in 1960. The fictional Blanche and the dramatised convent are disclosed; Time Out's dissent concerns style, not doctrine.
summary: A Dominican priest and Bresson's former cameraman film Bernanos's play about the Carmelites of Compiègne and a frightened novice who finds her courage at the scaffold.
synopsis: In 1789 two young women enter the Carmel of Compiègne. Sister Constance is cheerful and ready for the life; Blanche de la Force is crippled by fear of death and doubts her vocation. The dying prioress asks that Blanche be watched over. As the Revolution turns against religious houses, the community shelters Blanche's brother, attends a clandestine Mass said by a hunted priest, and is ordered to disperse. The sisters keep their common life in secret, are arrested and condemned. Blanche has already fled. On the day of the execution she watches her sisters climb to the guillotine, and joins them.
inclusion: Most of Bernanos's dialogue survives, and it is the reason to see the film: hard, plain exchanges about fear, pride and what it costs to give one's life. The cast is remarkable for a religious picture of its day. Jeanne Moreau plays Mother Marie de l'Incarnation, the nun most eager for martyrdom; Madeleine Renaud is the old prioress; Alida Valli the new one; Pascale Audret is Blanche. The style is more conventional and more lavish than Bresson's, and Time Out found it static and pallid. James Travers thought the opposite, judging that it does justice to the play and that the final scaffold sequence is overwhelming. The strength is the subject, a community of contemplatives who choose to die together and refuse to abandon their vows.
themes: Blanche does not overcome her terror by willpower; the story suggests she is carried by the prayer and sacrifice of others, and Bernanos's line that fear is a fantasy of the devil sums up its view. Religious vows, the cloister, the Mass and the Divine Office are treated as realities worth dying for, not as picturesque background. The revolutionary officials are shown as persecutors of the Church, but the film's interest is less in politics than in the different temperaments of the nuns: Constance's simplicity, Marie's zeal, the prioresses' humility. Bernanos was a Catholic novelist and Bruckberger a Dominican, and the treatment of martyrdom is orthodox.
history: Sixteen Discalced Carmelites of Compiègne were guillotined in Paris on 17 July 1794 after offering their lives for peace and for the Church in France. They sang the Salve Regina and the Veni Creator on the way to the scaffold.
liberties: Blanche de la Force is fictional, invented by Gertrud von Le Fort for her 1931 novella and kept by Bernanos. Conversations inside the convent, Blanche's family and her flight are imagined. Jean-Louis Barrault has an odd cameo as a mime. The martyrs' actual vow and community life are compressed into a few scenes.
advisories:
The final sequence shows the nuns going one by one to the guillotine; it is grim rather than graphic.

Revolutionary menace and the execution sequence may disturb younger viewers. No sexual content is reported.

doctrine: The prioress of the Martyrs of Compiègne, Mother Teresa of St Augustine (Madeleine Lidoine), had proposed at Easter 1792 that the community offer itself as a sacrifice for France and for the French Church. Pius X beatified them on 27 May 1906, the first martyrs of the Revolution recognised by the Holy See. Blanche de la Force is not one of the sixteen.
production: In 1947 Raymond-Léopold Bruckberger, a Dominican, and the director Philippe Agostini were preparing a film from Gertrud von Le Fort's novella and asked Georges Bernanos to write the dialogue. The film was not made then. Bernanos died in 1948 and his text was first staged in Zurich in 1951; it was later the basis of Poulenc's opera. Bruckberger and Agostini finally made the film in 1960, in black and white, for Champs-Élysées Productions, with Italian participation from Titanus, and Lux as French distributor. It was released in France on 10 June 1960 and runs about 113 minutes. It won the OCIC Grand Prix hors-festival in 1960. Critics were divided: Films de France thought it faithful and the last scene affecting.

title: Vaincre ou mourir
decision: GREY: Independent treatment exists, so the film is not 'unverified'. Press critics (Le Monde, Télérama, L'Obs, François Huzar) judge the craft poor; historians (Jean-Clément Martin, Paul Chopelin and François Huzar, Guillaume Lancereau) find few factual errors but a narrow, partisan frame. The subtitle file shows more religious substance than the historians allowed: refractory priests hunted and Mass said in hiding, a sworn priest rejected, Sacred Heart badges, the rising fought for God and king and for souls, a treaty valued for freedom of Catholic worship, a Latin Mass, and absolution before the execution. The chaplain refuses Charette's reprisals as a priest. The word genocide is not used in the opening interviews. The reservation is the partisan historical frame.

grey.question: The Puy du Fou made the film, and its opening interviews include Reynald Secher, whose description of the 1794 repression as genocide is widely disputed, though the word is not used in the film. Historians found few factual errors but a narrow and partisan frame: the Republic's massacres are shown and the Vendéen killings at Machecoul are not. The religious side is sound and more present than critics allowed, with Mass in hiding, a chaplain who refuses reprisals and absolution before death. Viewers sympathetic to the Vendéens should weigh that one-sidedness.

summary: The Puy du Fou's first feature tells the Vendée war through Charette, the reluctant former naval officer who led the rising and was shot at Nantes in 1796.
synopsis: In 1793 François-Athanase Charette de La Contrie, a former naval officer living quietly at Fonteclose, is pressed by angry peasants to lead their rising against the Republic. He proves a skilful and charismatic guerrilla leader, fighting with an army of peasants, women and young men, among them the fighter Céleste Bulkeley and his companion Hervouët de La Robrie, with the abbé Remaud at his side. Victories give way to losses and to the reprisals of the Republic's infernal columns. In 1795 he makes peace at La Jaunaye, but the peace breaks down. Betrayed and hunted, he is captured by General Travot and shot at Nantes in March 1796, after receiving absolution. Short interviews with historians open the film, and Charette's voice-over carries it.
inclusion: It is the only recent French feature on the Vendée war, a subject French cinema has largely avoided. Hugo Becker's Charette is the performance reviewers single out. Most notices are poor: Le Monde called it a historical dud, Télérama said it was bad enough to put off royalists, L'Obs found it inert and preachy, and François Huzar, judging it purely as cinema, found the dialogue false, the voice-over constant and the battles illegible. DeCine21 is kinder, praising the costumes and photography and noting the small budget. Jean-Clément Martin found its women fighters, émigré links and infernal columns broadly credible while faulting the narrow focus on Charette. It is a sincere but clumsy attempt at a neglected chapter of Catholic France.
themes: The Vendéens fight for God and the king, and the film shows the reasons. Refractory priests are hunted and Mass is said in hiding, a sworn priest is rejected, the rebels wear the Sacred Heart, and the 1795 treaty is valued for restoring freedom of Catholic worship. A Latin Mass is celebrated in the field, and Charette receives absolution before he is shot; Aleteia's critic reads the execution as a deliberate echo of Calvary. The abbé Remaud refuses, as a priest, Charette's call for reprisals in kind. Paul Chopelin and François Huzar still find the religious crisis thinly explained. The film does not make Charette a saint; he says he is no saint but will not go to hell.
history: In March 1793 the Convention's levy of 300,000 men set the west of France ablaze, and the peasants of the Vendée, who had resented the Civil Constitution of the Clergy (1790) and the persecution of their priests, took up arms. François-Athanase de Charette de La Contrie (1763-1796), a former naval officer, became a leader of the rising and fought the Republican columns in the marshes of Poitou. He agreed the peace of La Jaunaye in February 1795 with the Republic, though the peace broke down. He was captured by General Travot in March 1796 and shot at Nantes on 29 March. The Republic's 'infernal columns' of 1794 devastated the region. Historians still dispute the death toll and the use of the word 'genocide'.
liberties: Jean-Clément Martin points to one clear error: the film shows Charette signing the 1795 peace of La Jaunaye, which, he says, only the Republican side signed. He adds that the Republicans were more numerous and better armed than the film suggests, and Vendéen society more varied and organised. The massacre of Republicans at Machecoul in March 1793 is left out, and rival leaders such as Stofflet are pushed aside by the focus on Charette.
advisories:
Battle scenes, executions, and reprisals against civilians by Republican troops.

Charette is shot by a firing squad.

suitability.note: It was rated for all audiences in French cinemas, but French television advised against it for children under 10.

doctrine: The Vendéens fought for their priests and their altars, and the Church had already condemned the Civil Constitution, which put the clergy under the State, as schismatic and heretical in its principles (Pius VI, Quod aliquantum and Charitas, 1791). The film's last scene, in which Charette receives absolution before the firing squad, shows the Church's teaching that a man in danger of death should receive the sacrament of Penance, and that a priest may absolve anyone in extremis. Whether the Vendée war was a just war is a separate question: the Church teaches that insurrection against an unjust authority is lawful only when tyranny is manifest, prolonged and without remedy, and that the means must be just, so the reprisals on both sides are not excused by the cause.
production: Paul Mignot and Vincent Mottez directed it for Puy du Fou Films and StudioCanal. It was announced in March 2022 as the Puy du Fou park's first feature film, with a budget below €5 million, of which the Pays de la Loire region gave €200,000, and filming began that month in and around the park. The historian Jean-Clément Martin was consulted during development but later asked for his involvement to be withdrawn. It ran 100 minutes, had previews on 8 December 2022 and opened in France on 25 January 2023, drawing about 287,600 admissions. The press was mostly negative, though the traditionalist Catholic monthly La Nef praised it. Two La France insoumise deputies attacked it as anti-republican.

title: The War of the Vendée
decision: GREY: identity, outline, cast and the director's own account of his liberties are documented by several sources, so it is not HOLD; but no independent critic has assessed its history. The only full review by an outsider, Joseph Pearce's (2013), is appreciative, sets historical accuracy aside and has an indirect tie to the DVD's distributor (Ignatius Press). Settles with an independent review, or a scene log checked against academic histories of 1793-94 (Huchet 1988; Jean-Clément Martin), covering Robespierre, the devil figure, Fr Bernier and the morality of the rising.

grey.question: No independent review exists of how this film handles its history. What has been written comes from the director, from Catholic outlets that promoted it and from family-viewing guides. Joseph Pearce's appreciative essay concedes that it gives up historical nuance and shows Robespierre as demonically possessed. Morlino drew mainly on Reynald Secher's disputed genocide thesis and combined people and events, so it still needs checking against academic histories of 1793–94.

summary: Jim Morlino's low-budget drama of the 1793 Catholic rising in western France, played entirely by a cast of some 250 children and teenagers.
synopsis: In 1793 the Revolutionary government has outlawed priests who refuse the constitutional oath and orders a mass levy of conscripts. In a village of the Vendée, peasants and local nobles decide to take up arms for their priests and their king. The film follows the villagers and their families through secret meetings, a Latin Mass celebrated before battle, early victories, losses and reprisals. A boy, Remy, is turned away from the men's council and longs to fight; the village women push the hesitant men to act. In Paris, Robespierre appears as the sinister face of the Revolution. A priest, Fr Bernier, ministers to the rising, and the devil appears as a hooded figure. Every role, the adults included, is played by young performers, more than 250 of them.
inclusion: It is one of very few English-language films about the Vendée, and it keeps the religious cause of the rising at the centre: the persecution of priests who refused the oath, and Mass said in Latin before battle. Morlino made it through his Navis Pictures as a children's cinema project, with a cast all under 21 and a tiny budget. Fr John Zuhlsdorf, writing from a DVD supplied for review, found the acting uneven but praised Kevin Kaska's score. Joseph Pearce, an editor for Ignatius Press, which distributes the DVD, expected a bad film and was charmed, while admitting that it trades historical nuance for plain good against plain evil. Catholic festivals gave it prizes for young audiences. It is made for families and older children.
themes: The film's Catholic content is the defence of the sacraments and of faithful priests. The rising is presented as a response to the persecution of clergy who refused the oath to the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, and the Mass before battle is its central religious image. The devil appears as a hooded figure, and Pearce reads Robespierre as shown possessed.
history: The Vendée rising began in March 1793, when conscription for the levy of 300,000 men set off armed revolt across parts of Maine-et-Loire, Vendée, Deux-Sèvres and Loire-Inférieure. Françoise Huchet's study traces its first days in Maine-et-Loire between 2 and 22 March 1793. Hostility to the Civil Constitution of the Clergy and the persecution of priests who refused the oath were central grievances. The Catholic and Royal Army won early victories before defeat at Cholet and Savenay in late 1793, followed by severe Republican repression in 1794. Historians still argue over death tolls and over Secher's description of the repression as genocide.
liberties: Morlino says he combined characters and events and put historical figures together in one village "for convenience", though several never met. He also says he left out many atrocities because the film was made for young people. His main research source was Reynald Secher's A French Genocide, whose central term he acknowledges is hotly contested by historians. Pearce notes that the film removes the nuance that historical accuracy demands.
advisories:
Battle scenes with swords, muskets and cannon; parent reviews report no blood.

Persecution of priests, deaths and bereavement.

doctrine: The Civil Constitution of the Clergy, passed on 12 July 1790, made bishops and parish priests elected state officials. From 27 November 1790 every priest had to swear to it; seven of 135 bishops did. Pius VI condemned it in Charitas (13 April 1791). He declared the elections of the new constitutional bishops null, suspended the clergy who had sworn unless they retracted within forty days, and told the faithful to shun the intruded pastors and hold to their lawful ones. That explains why Vendéan peasants walked to hidden Masses said by priests who had refused the oath. On armed resistance, St Thomas teaches that a government directed to the ruler's private good rather than the common good is tyrannical, and that overthrowing it is not sedition, unless the disorder causes the people greater harm than the tyranny (Summa II-II, q. 42, a. 2, ad 3).
production: Jim Morlino, a Connecticut actor turned film-maker, made The War of the Vendée as the second film of his company Navis Pictures, after St. Bernadette of Lourdes (2009). He wanted an action story for boys that showed courage and sacrifice; a friend pointed him to the Vendée. He drew on Reynald Secher's A French Genocide, Michael Davies's For Altar and Throne, Warren Carroll's The Guillotine and the Cross, Simon Schama's Citizens and William Bush's To Quell the Terror. The young cast were all unpaid amateurs. Morlino did the writing, lighting, shooting, editing and producing himself, and put out-of-pocket costs at about $30,000. The one large expense was Kevin Kaska's score, recorded by an orchestra of about 80 at Warner Bros. The DVD came out on 24 February 2012, the 219th anniversary of the 1793 levy decree, and was entered in the Mirabile Dictu festival that summer.

title: A Forbidden God
decision: REJECT: Scope (editorial ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's subject is recognised as saint or blessed only through a canonisation or beatification made after the Second Vatican Council (the Claretian martyrs of Barbastro, beatified 1992).
summary: A sincere, cheaply made account of the 51 Claretian seminarians, brothers and priests held and shot at Barbastro in August 1936, notable for its stress on forgiveness.
synopsis: In July 1936, after the military rising, a revolutionary committee takes control of Barbastro in Aragon. The Claretian community is arrested. The superiors are separated and shot first; the young students and brothers are crowded into the assembly hall of the Piarist school. A local CNT leader, Eugenio Sopena, tries at first to protect them, but the arrival of harder men from Barcelona sweeps him aside. The prisoners are pressed to renounce their vocation, mocked and tempted, including by a young militiawoman, Trini, who is drawn to the student Esteban Casadevall. They smuggle the consecrated Host into their breakfast bread, write farewell notes, and go to their deaths in groups in August 1936. Two Argentine students are released.
inclusion: Pablo Moreno, working from Ciudad Rodrigo with a small company and a young cast, took the more difficult route: a martyrdom film about the victims' faith rather than their killers' cruelty. Jerónimo José Martín (Aceprensa) calls it "more religious than denunciatory". Esther Rodríguez (Contraste) credits it with conveying the faith that let the men accept death while forgiving, and with giving human dimensions to characters on both sides. There are real weaknesses. Several performances are amateurish, sound and lighting are poor, some exteriors are obviously faked, and the 39 students blur into a single group. Beatriz Martínez (SensaCine) found it slow, naive and full of stock villains. For viewers interested in the Spanish martyrs, its sincerity and historical grounding outweigh its limits.
themes: The Eucharist is the film's spiritual centre. The prisoners receive Communion secretly for as long as they can, and one priest slips up to the chapel to rescue the consecrated Hosts. The second strand is fidelity to religious vows under pressure, including sexual temptation; the young Claretian courted by a militiawoman answers that he is "married to God". The third is forgiveness. The farewell notes the men left, preserved by the order, forgive their executioners and offer their deaths for the Church and the Congregation. The film shows the anticlerical view of the Church as an ally of the rich without endorsing it, and it does not make the militiamen uniformly monstrous.
history: In July 1936 the Claretian community at Barbastro numbered nine priests, 39 students and 12 lay brothers. A revolutionary committee of anarchists and communists held them from 20 July. Over August 1936, 51 were shot, the superiors first. The two Argentine students who were freed carried testimony and keepsakes to Rome. The same repression killed the Bishop of Barbastro, Florentino Asensio, and the Romani layman Ceferino Giménez Malla ("El Pelé"). John Paul II beatified the 51 Claretians in 1992 and Asensio and Giménez Malla in 1997.
liberties: Moreno says about 90 percent of the screenplay rests on the martyrs' writings and contemporary testimony. Trini's infatuation with Casadevall and Sopena's attempt to protect the prisoners are documented episodes, according to La Vanguardia. Dialogue, the treatment of the student group as a near-collective character and the compression of events across several weeks are dramatic choices. Some comic moments, such as seminarians drilled with wooden rifles, are invented.
advisories:
Imprisonment, humiliation, beatings, torture and mass executions by firing squad.

Sexual temptation of the prisoners, including a militiawoman's advances to a seminarian (rejected).

Best for teenagers and adults.

It shows one local episode of anticlerical violence, not the whole Civil War.

title: For Greater Glory
originalTitle: For Greater Glory: The True Story of Cristiada
decision: REJECT: Scope (editorial ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's subject is recognised as saint or blessed only through a canonisation or beatification made after the Second Vatican Council (José Sánchez del Río, beatified 2005, canonised 2016).
summary: A big, earnest English-language epic of Mexico's Cristero War, built around an unbelieving general and a boy martyr, stronger on conviction than on history or subtlety.
synopsis: In 1926 President Calles enforces the anticlerical articles of the Mexican constitution: foreign priests are expelled, churches closed and public worship suspended. Peaceful protest fails and armed rebels rise under the cry 'Viva Cristo Rey'. The National League for the Defence of Religious Liberty hires Enrique Gorostieta, a retired general and sceptic, to turn the scattered bands into an army. Among them are the rancher Victoriano 'El Catorce' Ramírez and Fr José Reyes Vega, a priest who carries a rifle. A boy, José Sánchez del Río, sees the old priest who taught him shot by federal troops and joins the rebels. Women smuggle ammunition. As Gorostieta's campaign succeeds, the American ambassador Dwight Morrow brokers a settlement between the government and the Church, and José is captured.
inclusion: This is the only large-scale film about the Cristiada in English, and its Catholic stakes are explicit: Mass said in secret, priests killed at the altar, a boy who will not say 'Death to Christ the King'. The martyrdom of José Sánchez del Río, now a canonised saint, is the emotional centre, and it is staged with obvious debts to the Passion. Andy Garcia gives Gorostieta's slow movement towards faith a dry, watchful dignity, and Bruce Greenwood is sharp as Morrow. Location shooting and James Horner's score give it scale. The weaknesses are typical of the faith-based epic: heavy exposition, insistent music, flat villains, too many characters introduced and dropped. Steven Greydanus rates it a flawed but worthwhile film.
themes: The film's subject is religious persecution and martyrdom, and it handles both with conviction: the Mass, the priesthood and the Kingship of Christ are what the Cristeros fight for. It argues that the faithful may defend their liberty by force once peaceful means fail, which is broadly the reasoning Pius XI set out in Firmissimam constantiam (1937): lawful, proportionate means, never an end in themselves. Pius XI also said armed defence is no part of the clergy's task, and the film admires Fr Vega's fighting without much question. The 1929 settlement between the bishops and the government, brokered with Rome's involvement, is presented as a bitter compromise that left the rebels exposed.
history: Calles's enforcement of the 1917 constitution provoked the Cristero rising of 1926–29. Jean Meyer, the war's principal historian, interviewed hundreds of veterans for La Cristiada. Fr José Reyes Vega led the attack on the Guadalajara train near La Barca in April 1927 and, having lost a brother in the fight, set it on fire; Meyer counts 52 soldiers and about 30 civilians dead. José Sánchez del Río was killed in 1928 and canonised in 2016.
liberties: Fr Vega is turned into a pious warrior who burns the train in a moment of confusion and spends the rest of the film seeking forgiveness; the historical Vega had a much worse reputation and burned the train in anger. Gorostieta's arc from unbelief to faith is disputed: Greydanus calls the real man an anticlerical Freemason, while Herodote reports letters to his wife, known to Meyer, showing a convinced Catholic. Anacleto González Flores is reduced to a cameo. Several relationships between characters are invented.
advisories:
Rated R for war violence and executions. Priests are shot and hanged, a boy is hanged, civilians are killed in a church, and José is tortured, including having the soles of his feet cut, before being killed. Screams are heard from a burning train.

Desecration of churches and sacred objects.

Little bad language and no sexual content beyond a married couple in bed. Older teenagers and adults.

A priest takes part in combat and the film largely admires him for it; the Church did not.
