title: The Scarlet and the Black
decision: PUBLISH: Television Academy records confirm the 1983 CBS film; Greydanus's Decent Films review gives a scene-aware positive assessment (priestly charity, accurate closing coda) and flags the invented Pius XII Concordat scene; CNA/Catholic World Report confirms the history of O'Flaherty's escape line and Kappler's 1959 baptism. Dramatic liberties are ordinary for the genre and do not distort the religious meaning.
summary: Gregory Peck plays Mgr Hugh O'Flaherty, the Irish Vatican priest who hid thousands of escaped prisoners and Jews under the nose of the SS in occupied Rome.
synopsis: Rome, 1943. German troops occupy the city, and SS chief Herbert Kappler paints a white line across the edge of St Peter's Square: if Monsignor O'Flaherty steps over it, he will be shot. O'Flaherty, an Irish official of the Holy Office, has already started hiding escaped Allied prisoners and Jews in flats, convents and monasteries, with help from priests, diplomats and Roman families. He slips past the line in disguises, outwits raids and survives an attempt on his life inside the Vatican. As the Allies approach, Kappler, fearing for his own family, asks his enemy for help. A closing coda follows the two men after the war.
inclusion: This is a well-made, old-fashioned television thriller with a priest as its hero, and it never lets you forget he is a priest. Peck plays O'Flaherty as blunt, funny and fearless, a man who boxes and plays golf but treats every life he hides as a charge from God. Christopher Plummer's Kappler is cold and intelligent, and their duel gives the film its spine. The best scenes turn on mercy: O'Flaherty's choice when Kappler pleads for his wife and children, and the true postscript about what the priest did for Kappler in prison. Steven D. Greydanus calls it riveting and edifying. Rome locations and an Ennio Morricone score help, though the pacing sags in the middle.
themes: The film's Catholic heart is the priest's refusal to divide people into those who deserve help and those who do not. O'Flaherty hides Jews, Communists and Allied soldiers alike, and finally extends the same charity to the man who tried to have him killed. The Vatican appears as a place of moral tension: O'Flaherty's superiors worry that his work threatens the Holy See's neutrality, and John Gielgud's Pius XII is sympathetic. Greydanus notes one scene in which the Pope has second thoughts about the Concordat with Germany.
history: Hugh O'Flaherty was born at Kiskeam, County Cork, on 28 February 1898 and ordained in Rome on 20 December 1925. He served in the Vatican diplomatic service in Egypt, Haiti, Santo Domingo and Czechoslovakia and was made a monsignor in 1934. During the German occupation of Rome, from September 1943 to June 1944, he ran what became known as the Rome Escape Line, sheltering escaped Allied prisoners, Jews and others. Estimates of those saved run to about 6,500. Herbert Kappler, head of the SS in Rome, was sentenced to life imprisonment in 1948. O'Flaherty visited him every month and baptised him in 1959. After the war Pius XII made O'Flaherty a domestic prelate and notary of the Holy Office, and he received the CBE and the American Medal of Freedom. He died at Cahersiveen, County Kerry, on 30 October 1963.
liberties: The film compresses events into a cat-and-mouse plot. The SS general Max Helm is a fictionalised stand-in for Karl Wolff, who was still alive, and Hirsch stands for Erich Priebke. The scene of Pius XII doubting the Concordat is invented. Kappler's appeal to O'Flaherty over his family is dramatised for the climax.
advisories:
Wartime violence, including executions, a raid and the murder of a priest; no graphic gore by modern standards.

No sexual content of note.

The Vatican scenes are dramatised and should not be taken as a record of Pius XII's words.

doctrine: O'Flaherty's work is a list of the corporal works of mercy as St Thomas gives them: to feed the hungry, clothe the naked, harbour the harbourless and ransom the captive (Summa II-II, q. 32, a. 2). His treatment of Kappler follows St Thomas's teaching on enemies. Charity must not shut an enemy out of the love owed to all men, and we must be ready to help an enemy in urgent need; going further and overcoming evil with good belongs to the perfection of charity (q. 25, aa. 8-9). The Vatican's caution in the film has a basis in the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929, in which the Holy See pledged itself to perpetual neutrality in international disputes, so a priest using Vatican property for the Allies put it at risk.
production: The film was adapted from J. P. Gallagher's 1967 book The Scarlet Pimpernel of the Vatican and shot in Rome and the Vatican. It won the Emmy for sound mixing and was nominated for editing and title design.

title: The Assisi Underground
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a bishop, a Franciscan priest and enclosed nuns are the rescuers) and securely identified (Box Office Mojo, Wikipedia, Winnert). The reservation is historical and can be stated: the film follows Ramati's book, built on Niccacci's recollections, which Don Aldo Brunacci, the actual organiser, called a novel, and which Michele Sarfatti shows to contain inventions such as Bartali's courier runs. Not PUBLISH because no substantive independent review addresses its treatment of the faith and it is unchecked whether the film carries the anti-Pius XII charge of the book's British title. It would move to PUBLISH if the dialogue shows no such charge, since this record discloses the history.

grey.question: The Assisi Underground honours a real rescue, but tells it through Alexander Ramati's book, built on Padre Rufino Niccacci's own recollections. Don Aldo Brunacci, who actually ran the network for the bishop, called that book a novel and said many details were invented or distorted, including Niccacci's arrest and the cyclist Gino Bartali's courier runs, for which historians have found no documents. Ramati's British edition was titled While the Pope Kept Silent, and the film's treatment of Pius XII is unclear. It dramatises the Church's rescue work and is not a record of it.

summary: Alexander Ramati's Cannon-produced drama of the Franciscan Padre Rufino Niccacci and the Assisi clergy who hid Jews from the Germans in 1943–44.
synopsis: In 1943, after the Germans occupy northern Italy, the Bishop of Assisi, Giuseppe Placido Nicolini, charges the Franciscan Padre Rufino Niccacci with saving Jewish refugees. Rufino hides them in the town's monasteries and convents, one of them under the formidable Mother Giuseppina, dresses some as friars and nuns and teaches them enough Latin prayers to pass. False identity papers are printed in the town, and the cyclist Gino Bartali is among the characters. Rufino guides refugees towards the Allied lines, makes promises to compromised fascists and befriends the German commandant, Colonel Müller, a medical officer who supplies medicines to the town. The SS grow suspicious, arrest Rufino and put him before a firing squad, and Müller uses his influence to save him. Closing titles describe what became of the real people.
inclusion: The rescue was real. Yad Vashem has honoured Niccacci, Don Aldo Brunacci and others among the Assisi clergy and townspeople, and about three hundred Jews survived the occupation there. The film puts the Church's work at the centre, with a bishop, a friar and enclosed nuns risking their lives for strangers. Giuseppe Rotunno's photography of Assisi is a point in its favour, as are James Mason in his last screen role as the bishop, and Irene Papas and Maximilian Schell. Derek Winnert calls it well-meaning but ineptly told and Ben Cross uninspiring, and the theatrical version, cut from a television version of about three hours, shows its seams. It is of interest as a popular film about Catholic rescuers, provided the history is kept apart from Ramati's version of it.
themes: The clergy act on their bishop's orders, so the rescue is shown as the work of the Church, and its subject is charity. Enclosure is opened and habits are lent to save lives, and the Jewish refugees are sheltered without pressure to convert; historically the Assisi nuns even prepared the meal that ended Yom Kippur in 1943. Rufino is a clever, sometimes devious priest who lies to the occupiers and bargains with fascists, and the film treats this as justified by necessity. The good German colonel is a believing Catholic. How the film treats Pius XII is unclear. Accounts of the rescue say the bishop acted on the Pope's wishes.
history: After the German occupation of northern and central Italy in September 1943, Assisi became a refuge for Jews. Bishop Giuseppe Placido Nicolini, with the Franciscan Fr Rufino Niccacci and the priest Aldo Brunacci, sheltered several hundred Jewish refugees in convents and monasteries, and local printers made false papers. Niccacci was named one of the Righteous Among the Nations in April 1974. The cyclist Gino Bartali carried documents for the wider Florence-Assisi network, as Yad Vashem recognised in 2013. Alexander Ramati's 1978 book, on which the film rests, gives an account of the rescue that historians have not accepted in every detail.
liberties: Brunacci, who ran the operation, called Ramati's book nothing but a novel and said many details were invented or distorted. The film makes Niccacci the organiser; Brunacci says it was he, not Niccacci, who was arrested in May 1944. Gino Bartali's role as a courier, taken from the book, has no documentary support, according to the historian Michele Sarfatti. The plan that protected Assisi as a hospital town also happened differently.
advisories:
Wartime menace, arrests, a threatened execution and some violence.

No sexual content reported.

Suitable for older children and adults; slow in places.

Its history follows a contested account that exaggerates Niccacci's role.

title: The Ninth Day
decision: PUBLISH: the Film Fund Luxembourg catalogue confirms identity; Greydanus's detailed review and Thomas Wolter's essay in forum (Luxembourg, 2004) establish both the film's moral seriousness and exactly what is invented. The interrogation is openly a dramatisation of nine days Bernard's diary barely describes. The Pius XII material is a character's doubt answered by his bishop's account of reprisals, not the film's verdict; its one chronological slip (the Dutch reprisals of summer 1942) is noted. A Luxembourg critic's complaint that the film is pro-Church propaganda is recorded.
summary: A starved priest is let out of Dachau for nine days and given a choice by a Gestapo officer: win over his bishop for the Reich, or go back to the camp.
synopsis: Dachau, early 1942. Abbé Henri Kremer, a Luxembourg priest, survives in the priests' block amid hunger, beatings and executions. Suddenly he is released and sent home, apparently for his mother's funeral. In Luxembourg he must report each day to Untersturmführer Gebhardt, a young Gestapo officer who once studied for the priesthood. Gebhardt wants Kremer to persuade the Bishop of Luxembourg, who has shut himself away in protest, to accept the occupation; then a signed declaration will do. If Kremer refuses or runs, the priests in Dachau will pay. Over nine days the two men argue about faith, obedience and the Church's silence while Kremer's family urges him to save himself.
inclusion: Schlöndorff turns a small episode into a tight moral drama in which the arguments carry weight. Ulrich Matthes, gaunt and hollow-eyed, plays Kremer as a man with no heroism left, only conscience. August Diehl's Gebhardt is clever, polite and a theologian of sorts, which makes him more dangerous than a thug. The Dachau scenes are brief and restrained. Steven D. Greydanus gives it his top grade, noting that it shows several kinds of resistance and their costs without offering a simple defence or accusation. It is short and austere.
themes: Kremer's choice is the classic one between apostasy dressed as prudence and fidelity that may cost his life. Gebhardt does not ask him to deny Christ, only to compromise a little for the good of others, and the film is sharp on how temptation works that way. The priests in Dachau pray, say Mass in secret and share bread; some of them are shown collaborating or bitter. The Church's public silence is debated openly. Kremer says he never doubts the Church but sometimes doubts the Holy Father, and his bishop answers that protests have brought reprisals on the very people they were meant to help.
history: Jean Bernard (1907–1994), a Luxembourg priest, was arrested in 1941 and sent to Dachau, where he was among the many priests held in the clergy block. In February 1942 he was released for nine days, apparently to win over Luxembourg's clergy, refused, and returned. He was freed in August 1942, later edited the Luxemburger Wort and led the international Catholic film office (OCIC). His memoir is Pfarrerblock 25487.
liberties: The hero is renamed Kremer. Bernard's diary says almost nothing about the nine days, so the daily interrogations and Gebhardt are invented; Thomas Wolter notes none of the conversations happened as staged. A detail from Primo Levi's memoirs is borrowed. The bishop's reference to reprisals after the Dutch bishops' protest is anachronistic: that protest and the arrests that followed, including Edith Stein's, came in July and August 1942, after the story's February setting.
advisories:
Concentration-camp brutality: beatings, starvation and deaths, shown briefly and without lingering.

Some crude language. No sexual content.

The film raises the question of Pius XII's public silence through its characters, but it is a drama and offers no historical verdict.

title: A Hidden Life
decision: REJECT: Scope (editorial ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's subject is recognised as saint or blessed only through a canonisation or beatification made after the Second Vatican Council (Franz Jägerstätter, beatified 2007).
summary: Malick's long, lyrical film about Franz Jägerstätter, the Austrian farmer who refused to swear loyalty to Hitler and was executed in 1943, and the wife who stood by him.
synopsis: In the mountain village of St Radegund, Franz and Fani Jägerstätter farm, raise three small daughters and go to Mass. After the Anschluss Franz becomes the only man in the village to vote against it, and when he is called up he cannot bring himself to swear the oath to Hitler. Neighbours turn on the family. The parish priest and then the Bishop of Linz urge him to think of his wife and children. Franz reports for duty, refuses the oath and is imprisoned, first in Linz and then in Berlin. Lawyers and officers offer him easy ways out. Fani keeps the farm going alone while letters pass between them. He is tried and condemned.
inclusion: This is Malick's most direct film about faith, and the one where his methods most suit the subject. Long passages of farm work, mountains and weather build a world worth losing. August Diehl's Franz says little; Valerie Pachner's Fani is the film's emotional anchor, and Combs singles out Bruno Ganz, in his last role, as a judge crushed by his inability to save him. Voiceover drawn from the couple's letters carries much of the meaning. At nearly three hours it demands patience, and CNS warns that much of it is domestic routine. For viewers who give it the time, the last hour is overwhelming.
themes: Franz's refusal is grounded in his Catholic faith: he will not swear an oath to a regime he believes evil, whatever it costs. The film shows Mass, prayer and the sacristy as parts of ordinary village life, and its opening scene of a church painter who admits he paints a comfortable Christ sets out its subject: the difference between admiring Christ and following him. CNS's John Mulderig calls the treatment of the parish priest and bishop ambivalent at best; they counsel prudence and family duty. Pappas reads Fani's endurance as a hidden, Marian counterpart to Franz's martyrdom.
history: Franz Jägerstätter (1907–1943), a farmer and sacristan in St Radegund, refused military service in March 1943 on religious grounds. He had sought the counsel of Bishop Joseph Calasanz Fliesser of Linz, who by his own account explained a citizen's duties towards those in authority 'in vain'; Franz came out saying the clergy did not dare speak. He was condemned for undermining military morale and guillotined at Brandenburg on 9 August 1943. He was beatified in Linz on 26 October 2007. Franziska died in 2013, aged 100.
liberties: Dialogue is largely invented around the letters, and the clergy's scenes compress several conversations. The village's hostility is heightened. Combs notes that the film never lets Franz articulate his position as a formal conscientious objection, which leaves his reasoning more mysterious than his writings are.
advisories:
Prison beatings and humiliation, and the threat and fact of execution, handled without gore.

The family is shunned and harassed by neighbours.

Rated PG-13; CNS A-II (adults and adolescents). Running time 174 minutes.

Priests and a bishop are shown urging compromise; the portrayal reflects the historical record but is not flattering.

title: Triumph of the Heart
decision: REJECT: Scope (editorial ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's subject is recognised as saint or blessed only through a canonisation or beatification made after the Second Vatican Council (Maximilian Kolbe, beatified 1971, canonised 1982).
summary: A harrowing chamber drama set almost entirely in the Auschwitz starvation bunker, where Maximilian Kolbe leads nine condemned men in prayer during their last days.
synopsis: After a prisoner escapes from Auschwitz in 1941, the SS deputy commandant Karl Fritzsch picks ten men from the block to starve to death. When one of them cries out for his wife and children, the Franciscan priest Maximilian Kolbe steps forward and asks to take his place. The rest of the film unfolds in the underground cell. The men bring fear, rage, guilt and old injuries with them. Kolbe hears their confessions, leads them in prayer and song, and holds the group together as hunger, thirst and hallucinations take hold. After two weeks only Kolbe and three others are alive, and the guards kill them by lethal injection.
inclusion: Writer-director Anthony D'Ambrosio confines a famous act of self-sacrifice to one dark room, and the confinement works. The story becomes less about the heroic gesture than about what a priest does with the days that follow. Marcin Kwaśny, a Polish actor performing in English, plays Kolbe as steady rather than saintly in a stained-glass way. OSV News's Joseph McAleer and the National Catholic Register's Joseph Pronechen both praise the script and the central performance; Pronechen notes how flashbacks and visions open up the men's inner lives. The film is hard to watch. McAleer rates it for adults only, and the starvation scenes, hallucinations and abuse by guards make that limit essential.
themes: The film is explicitly sacramental. Kolbe hears the condemned men's confessions and makes them a brotherhood of prayer. He asks Our Lady for the words he needs. The men sing a lullaby based on the Salve Regina, which enrages the guards and heartens prisoners who hear it. When despair sets in, Kolbe points to Christ's own cry of abandonment on the cross and urges the men to die with their eyes on God. The film reads his substitution through John 15:13, "greater love hath no man". It does not soften the cost: the men's anger at God is given real voice before it is answered.
history: Maximilian Kolbe (1894–1941), a Polish Conventual Franciscan, founded the Militia of the Immaculata and the friary-publishing centre at Niepokalanów. Arrested in February 1941, he became prisoner 16670 at Auschwitz. In late July 1941, after an escape, ten men were condemned to the starvation bunker. Kolbe volunteered in place of Franciszek Gajowniczek, a sergeant with a wife and sons. Gajowniczek survived the war and died in 1995. Kolbe, still alive after two weeks, was killed by injection of carbolic acid on 14 August 1941. He was beatified in 1971 and canonised as a martyr by John Paul II in 1982.
liberties: Nothing is known of what was said in the bunker beyond survivors' reports that prayers and hymns were heard from the cell. The other prisoners' identities, backstories, quarrels and conversations are invented or composite. The Salve Regina lullaby, the visions and the dialogue are dramatic constructions.

title: Rome, Open City
decision: REJECT: Editor ruling (2026-10-11). The film's centre is the Resistance, not the faith, and it presents a priest's common cause with Communist partisans as exemplary, against Pius XI's Divini Redemptoris (1937). It is not Catholic-centred and its outlook on that point is contrary to pre-conciliar teaching.
summary: Rossellini's raw, half-documentary account of occupied Rome in 1944, in which a parish priest and a Communist resistance leader are hunted by the Gestapo and die together.
synopsis: Rome, winter 1944, under German occupation. Giorgio Manfredi, a Communist leader of the resistance, escapes a Gestapo raid and seeks shelter with Francesco, a fellow resister, whose fiancée Pina is a widow expecting his child. The local parish priest, Don Pietro, carries money and messages to the partisans outside the city and is to marry Pina and Francesco. In a German round-up of their tenement Francesco is arrested, and Pina is shot dead running after the truck. Francesco escapes, and he and Manfredi hide with Manfredi's girlfriend Marina, who depends on drugs supplied by Ingrid, a Gestapo agent. Marina betrays them. Manfredi and Don Pietro are taken to Gestapo headquarters, where Major Bergmann has Manfredi tortured to death while trying to break the priest. Neither talks. Don Pietro is shot by firing squad the next morning.
inclusion: Shot within months of the liberation, on the streets and with scavenged film stock, it made Rossellini and Anna Magnani international names and won the top prize at Cannes in 1946. Its rough, newsreel look is mixed with old-fashioned melodrama, as Alex Barrett notes for the BFI, and the mixture is what gives it force. Pina's death in the street is one of the great shocks of the decade. Aldo Fabrizi's Don Pietro starts as a comic figure, refereeing a boys' football match, and grows into a man who dies with complete resolve. Steven Greydanus grades it A+. The German villains are stereotypes, some scenes are contrived, and the politics are of its moment. It is a primary document of how Rome remembered the occupation, and of a priest's courage in it.
themes: Don Pietro is a recognisable parish priest: he uses his cassock to move after curfew, claims to be going to anoint a dying man to get past German soldiers, and holds firm under interrogation. Barrett notes how heavily the script draws on Catholic symbolism, and Greydanus points to Manfredi's body posed like the crucified Christ. The problem is the frame. The film celebrates a united front of Catholics and Communists, and when Bergmann calls Manfredi an atheist and an enemy, the priest answers that whoever fights for justice and liberty walks in the ways of the Lord. Pius XI had forbidden Catholics to collaborate with Communism in any undertaking, and in 1949 the Holy Office excommunicated Catholics who supported it. The film never raises that question.
history: The story was first planned as a documentary about Don Giuseppe Morosini, a Roman priest executed by the Germans in April 1944 for helping the resistance. Sergio Amidei, Federico Fellini and Alberto Consiglio worked on the script with Rossellini. It opened in Italy on 27 September 1945 and in New York, as Open City, on 25 February 1946, in a cut version.
liberties: Don Pietro is a composite fiction; Morosini was not executed alongside a Communist leader, and the film's events are dramatised rather than reconstructed. The German officers are drawn as decadent stereotypes.
advisories:
Torture: a prisoner is tortured to death largely off screen, and his beaten body is shown.

A pregnant woman is shot dead in the street; a priest is executed by firing squad.

Drug dependency: a Gestapo agent keeps a young woman supplied with drugs; the agent's interest in her is implied to be sexual.

A couple expecting a child before marriage; a nightclub milieu.

For older teenagers and adults.

The Legion of Decency classified the film as objectionable (B or C; sources differ).

title: Network of Freedom
decision: GREY: Identity and content are established (SensaCine, eCartelera, ACI Prensa interview, Almudi). Hélène Studler is not beatified, so rule (a) does not apply. grey.question: Pablo Moreno's 2017 Spanish feature tells the story of Sister Hélène Studler, the Daughter of Charity whose network in occupied Metz smuggled some two thousand prisoners to safety. It was commissioned by the Vincentian Family, and the director says they wanted a figure close to people of today, not a saint's life. A secular review praises Assumpta Serna but says little about how religious life is shown, and no independent review judges it. A fuller review, or a check of the dialogue, showing that her vocation and prayer stay at the centre would settle it.

summary: Assumpta Serna plays Sister Hélène Studler, a Daughter of Charity in occupied Metz whose escape network smuggled some two thousand prisoners of war to safety.
synopsis: Metz, 1940. Sister Hélène Studler, a Daughter of Charity who cares for orphans and the destitute at a city hospice, sees Lorraine annexed and a camp for French prisoners of war built near the city. Under Red Cross protection she and her sisters, with volunteers from the town, bring the prisoners food and water. Relief turns into rescue. The sisters begin smuggling men out of the camp and across the new frontier into unoccupied France, and a clandestine network, linked to the Resistance, grows around them. The work puts her community and her helpers in danger. Among those the network helps, in the film as in history, are the future president François Mitterrand and General Henri Giraud. St Louise de Marillac, co-foundress of her congregation, appears as a figure in the story.
inclusion: Hélène Studler's story is little known outside Lorraine, and no French film has told it. Moreno made this one on a budget of roughly half a million euros, commissioned by the Vincentian Family for the 400th anniversary of its charism, with Burgos standing in for Lorraine and Spanish actors playing French and Germans. Miguel Ángel Pizarro of eCartelera, a secular critic, called Assumpta Serna's performance one of her strongest in years and said she carries the film over its weak early production design, which he compared unfavourably with Spanish television drama. He read the faith as the heroine's inner strength and saw no propaganda. The press average on SensaCine is low.
themes: Sister Hélène acts as a Daughter of Charity, and the film roots her rescue work in the Vincentian tradition of serving the poor. Catholic accounts describe her as sustained by prayer, and St Louise de Marillac appears. The director calls his approach Christian humanism and says the Vincentians wanted a figure close to people of today, not a saint's biography; the anniversary campaign the film served took the text 'I was a stranger and you welcomed me'. Pizarro reads the faith as her inner strength. It is unclear how much the film shows of her religious life, prayer, community and obedience, as against the humanitarian adventure.
history: Marie Joséphine Studler (1891–1944), born at Amiens to an Alsatian family, joined the Daughters of Charity in 1912 and worked at the Saint-Nicolas hospice in Metz from 1918. From 1940 to early 1942 she ran an escape network for prisoners of war, draft evaders and Allied airmen, credited with helping over 2,000 people. She was arrested in 1941 and released for ill health. Her network helped Mitterrand escape in December 1941, and from Lyon she found the guide for Giraud's escape in 1942. She died of cancer at Clermont-Ferrand on 3 December 1944.

Wartime setting with arrests, danger and some violence.

No sexual content reported.

title: Quo Vadis
decision: PUBLISH: Re-checked against the AFI Catalog's full synopsis. The joint suicide is real but belongs to the pagan Petronius and his slave Eunice, while the Christians die by martyrdom and Nero's own suicide is shown as cowardice; the coercive start of the romance is Nero's act, which Lygia escapes and refuses until Vinicius turns towards Christ. Neither is endorsed by the film. Liz Gloyn and the Dickinson College essay give substantive treatment. Both elements are flagged in advisories.
summary: MGM's Technicolor epic of Nero's Rome sets a Roman commander's pursuit of a Christian girl against the Great Fire, the first persecution and the deaths of St Peter and St Paul.
synopsis: In AD 64 the commander Marcus Vinicius returns to Rome and falls for Lygia, a Christian hostage raised by a retired general. When she rebuffs him, his uncle Petronius gets Nero to hand her to Marcus as a gift; her giant servant Ursus rescues her. Marcus tracks her to a secret gathering where St Peter tells of his time with Christ. Lygia will not marry him at the price of her faith. Nero burns Rome to inspire a poem and, to save himself, blames the Christians. On the Appian Way Peter meets his Lord and turns back to Rome. Christians are thrown to the lions, Peter is crucified, Petronius takes his own life, and Lygia is tied in the arena before a bull, with Ursus her only defender.
inclusion: It started the 1950s epic cycle, and it has the virtues and faults of the type. The sets, crowds and Robert Surtees's colour photography are lavish; the burning of Rome is spectacular. Peter Ustinov's Nero, vain, petulant and murderous, steals the picture, and Leo Genn's ironic Petronius runs him close. Robert Taylor and Deborah Kerr are stiff, and the romance is the weakest part. The classicist Liz Gloyn found that modern viewers are surprised by how central the Church is. Peter and Paul appear in person, the catacomb liturgy and Peter's preaching are given time, and the martyrs go to the lions singing. The Christian community is idealised but attractive.
themes: Peter recounts the miraculous catch and the Resurrection, the 'Domine, quo vadis?' legend sends him back to Rome to die, and he is crucified. Paul preaches that Christ conquers by love. Lygia prays for Marcus's conversion and refuses to buy his love with her faith; Peter marries them in prison. Against this the film sets Roman decadence and Nero's claim to divinity. Petronius dies as a cultivated pagan, set against the Christians who 'know how to die'.
history: Rome burned in July 64, and Nero blamed the Christians, whom Tacitus records were killed in his gardens. Early tradition, reported by Origen through Eusebius, says Peter was crucified head downward at his own wish; the date of his death is uncertain within 64 to 68. The Quo vadis encounter on the Appian Way is a legend from the apocryphal Acts of Peter (c. AD 180), not a scriptural event. Petronius's forced suicide is recorded by Tacitus.
liberties: Lygia, Vinicius and Ursus are fictional, from Henryk Sienkiewicz's 1896 novel. The joint suicide with a slave is borrowed from Seneca and Paulina, who survived. There is no evidence that Poppaea proposed blaming the Christians. Nero's death and Galba's arrival are compressed into the aftermath of the persecution. The flowering staff is a pious legend.
advisories:
A long scene shows Petronius and his slave Eunice opening their veins and dying at table; it is calm and bloodless but sympathetic to them.

Christians are killed by lions and burned at the stake, mostly offscreen; Nero strangles Poppaea and is helped to stab himself; sword fights and a man's neck broken.

Nero orders Lygia given to Marcus as a slave at the start; scantily dressed dancers and Roman revels.

Younger children may find the arena scenes frightening.

doctrine: The Church teaches that the Apostle Peter was the first bishop of Rome and the head of the Apostles, a primacy later defined at the First Vatican Council (1870). The Church counts martyrdom, death for the faith, as the baptism of blood. Lygia's refusal to marry a pagan has a basis in the 1917 Code (canon 1070), under which difference in religion between a baptised and an unbaptised person was a diriment impediment to marriage that only dispensation could remove.
production: MGM's first attempt in 1949, with Gregory Peck and Elizabeth Taylor, was postponed; Mervyn LeRoy took over the next year with Robert Taylor and Deborah Kerr. Shooting began on 22 May 1950 at Cinecittà, Rome, and the film cost about $7 million, then the most expensive ever made. Peter Ustinov's Nero and Leo Genn's Petronius were nominated for Oscars, with six other nominations, and none won. MGM released it on 2 November 1951 at 171 minutes. It earned about $21 million and was the highest-grossing film of 1951. The National Legion of Decency classified it A-I.

title: Fabiola
decision: GREY: The reservation is documented by contemporary pre-conciliar Catholic evidence: Paola Palma's archival study (Schermi, 2017) shows the Centro Cattolico Cinematografico classified the Italian release 'adulti con riserva', and Vittorino Veronese of Catholic Action found it 'molto discutibile' for its thesis and sensual material. The English subtitle file shows what that thesis is: not indifferentism, since the Christians say Rome must become Christian and the martyrs confess Christ, but non-violence and human brotherhood. The film is dedicated to the victims of all violence, its Christians speak of a world without masters or slaves, and Rhual's refusal to kill rests on the claim that a Christian never kills. No baptism occurs. Not REJECT; the rating and the sensual material keep it GREY.

grey.question: Fabiola was sold as a Catholic epic, but the Italian Catholic film office of its day classified it 'adults with reservations', and Catholic Action's Vittorino Veronese found its thesis questionable and its sensual scenes gratuitous. Its Christians preach non-violence and human brotherhood, yet they confess Christ plainly. The question is whether that witness outweighs a gladiator romance, the sensual scenes and the loose use of Wiseman's novel.

summary: Blasetti's huge postwar epic, very loosely from Cardinal Wiseman's novel, turns the Church of the catacombs into a gladiator romance and murder plot that ends in the arena.
synopsis: In Rome around 312, Fabiola, a senator's daughter, falls for Rhual, a Gaulish gladiator who is secretly an agent of Constantine. Her father, Senator Fabius, who favours tolerance and the freeing of slaves, is murdered, and the Christians are blamed and put on trial. Rhual is condemned with them to the arena. Fabiola at first suspects him, then takes her stand with the Christians in the arena. Rhual refuses to kill his opponents and the other gladiators follow him. Constantine's army reaches Rome, the city rises, and the film ends under the Christian standards of the new emperor.
inclusion: Fabiola opened the postwar wave of religious epics, as the Treccani film encyclopedia notes. It was the biggest Italian spectacle since the war, with Michèle Morgan, Henri Vidal and Michel Simon and enormous sets. French critics in 1949, as Paola Palma's archival study shows, admired Blasetti's handling of crowds while finding the film too long. Time Out's reviewer finds it dull until the violent climax in the arena; Manny Farber, seeing the shortened American version, called it a chaos of disconnected sequences. Its interest now is largely historical, as an ambitious Catholic spectacle made by a company widely taken for a Vatican enterprise, though the Catholic film bodies of the time publicly disowned its Catholic credentials.
themes: Wiseman's 1854 novel is a Catholic apologetic for the Church of the catacombs, ending in Fabiola's baptism. The film keeps the persecution, the arena and names such as Sebastiano, Cecilia and Sira, but builds its story on a gladiator, a murder mystery and a love affair. A French critic in 1949 complained that Fabiola reaches Christianity by way of profane passion. The dialogue shows what he meant. The film is dedicated to the victims of all violence, and its Christians preach brotherhood, a world without masters or slaves and an absolute refusal to kill, which goes beyond the Church's teaching on just defence. The faith is not diluted, though. The martyrs confess Christ, and Fabiola declares herself a Christian in the arena.
history: The novel and the film are set in Rome at the start of the last great persecution. In 302 Diocletian and his Caesar Galerius agreed at Nicomedia to suppress Christianity. The first edict of February 303 ordered churches destroyed and Scriptures burned, and stripped Christians of rank of their status. Further edicts imprisoned the clergy, then compelled them to sacrifice under torture, and finally extended the order to the laity. Diocletian abdicated on 1 May 305, and the persecution went on in the East under his successors until the toleration granted in 311 and the Edict of Milan of 313. Fabiola herself is Wiseman's invention.
liberties: Rhual, the gladiator-agent of Constantine, the murder of Fabiola's father and the love story are invented. The novel's martyrdoms of Agnes, Pancratius and Tarcisius do not appear among the characters. The film sets its action around 312, on the eve of Constantine's victory, and ends with Constantine's army entering Rome; Wiseman places most of the story in the Diocletian persecution. The baptism of Fabiola and her household that the novel narrates does not occur in the dialogue.
advisories:
Prolonged kisses and love scenes, a banquet dance and semi-nude courtesans; a 1949 Catholic critic asked for this material to be cut.

Arena martyrdoms and mass violence at the climax.

Versions vary widely, from the Italian release of about 164 minutes to an American dubbed cut of about 97, and the French release differed again. Check which version a copy is.

names: Fabiola, or the Church of the Catacombs, novel by Cardinal Nicholas Wiseman (1854)

suitability.note: The full version suits adults and older teenagers. The shorter dubbed versions cut much of the sensual material but keep the martyrdoms.

doctrine: Wiseman wrote the novel as the first of a series of tales on periods of Church history, and it shows the early Church's practice, including the catechumenate, baptism of adults after instruction, burial of the martyrs in the catacombs and veneration of their tombs. Several of its figures are real martyrs. St Sebastian was buried on the Via Appia, as the Depositio martyrum of 354 records, and his feast is 20 January; the Catholic Encyclopedia judges the later Acts of his martyrdom unhistorical. St Cecilia's feast is 22 November, and the date of her martyrdom is uncertain. The Church teaches that martyrdom, the free acceptance of death for the faith, justifies even the unbaptised as baptism of blood.
production: Salvo D'Angelo's Universalia Film made Fabiola with French stars and money through Franco-London Films. At least ten writers worked on a long and troubled script, eight of them credited. It was shot almost entirely at Cinecittà, with the arena combat and martyrdoms filmed in the Arena di Verona. It opened in Italy on 3 March 1949, distributed by Warner Bros., and was the highest-grossing Italian film of the 1948–49 season. The Centro Cattolico Cinematografico classified it 'adults with reservations', and the Dominican Félix Morlion's praise in the OCIC review was later corrected to accept that rating. Critics faulted its history and some bold scenes. Shortened dubbed versions reached Britain, as The Fighting Gladiator, and the United States in 1951. A restoration was shown in Rome in 2001.

title: Diary of a Country Priest
alternateTitles: Le Journal d'un curé de campagne
decision: PUBLISH: Steven Greydanus's detailed review and the critical tradition around the film establish a portrait of priestly perseverance and grace in apparent failure, drawn faithfully from Bernanos. Adult material (an affair, a threatened suicide) is part of the moral drama and is disclosed.
summary: Bresson's spare adaptation of Bernanos follows a sickly young curé whose parish rejects him, and finds holiness in apparent failure.
synopsis: A young priest arrives in Ambricourt, a village in northern France. He is poor, ill, inexperienced and awkward, and his parishioners respond with indifference or mockery. He records everything in a diary. The older curé of Torcy gives him blunt advice about running a parish. At the château, the count is having an affair with the governess, and the count's daughter Chantal hates them both and threatens to kill herself. The priest confronts the countess, who has been bitter towards God since the death of her son. In a long exchange she yields and makes her peace, and she dies that night. Gossip about the encounter turns the village further against him. Diagnosed with stomach cancer, he travels to Lille and dies in the lodgings of a former seminary friend who has left the priesthood.
inclusion: It is one of the essential films about the priesthood. Bresson strips away everything decorative, leaving Claude Laydu's still face, the diary voice-over and Léonce-Henri Burel's grey images of the Artois countryside. What remains is a man trying to do his duty with almost no visible success. The scene with the countess is the dramatic peak; Steven D. Greydanus compares it to the great dialogues in The Brothers Karamazov. André Bazin's 1951 essay, which called the film a masterpiece, helped make it a landmark of modern cinema. The pace is slow and the tone severe, and some viewers find it opaque.
themes: The film shows the priesthood stripped of consolation. The curé suffers spiritual dryness, physical weakness and the contempt of his flock. He feels unable even to pray, yet keeps saying Mass, visiting and hearing confessions. Greydanus notes how he accepts failure, dryness and persecution and turns them into a kind of victory. The countess scene shows the cure of souls in action: he refuses to accept her despair and leads her to surrender her grief to God. The end gives Bernanos's last words to the priest: "All is grace."
liberties: Bresson follows the novel closely but cuts heavily, especially the long reflective passages and several conversations with the curé of Torcy. He invents almost nothing; his changes are mainly omissions and a sharper focus on the priest's isolation.
advisories:
An adulterous affair, which is only implied.

A girl threatens suicide; a death; terminal illness.

suitability.note: Nothing is shown directly, but the film is long, silent in manner and austere, and suits older teenagers and adults better than children.

doctrine: The priest's last words, 'All is grace', are those of St Thérèse of Lisieux in her last conversations; Bernanos borrowed them knowingly. The countess scene turns on despair, which the theologians count among the sins against the Holy Ghost because it refuses God's mercy, and on resignation to His will as its remedy. The curé's own state is the dryness the spiritual writers describe, after St John of the Cross, as a purifying night in which the soul feels abandoned while it is being drawn closer. His priesthood does not depend on his feelings. The Council of Trent (Session XXIII) teaches that ordination imprints an indelible character, and Trent (Session VII) that the sacraments act by the rite performed, not by the minister's holiness. Final perseverance, which he receives without a priest at hand, is a special gift of God (Trent, Session VI, canon 22).
production: Georges Bernanos published the novel in 1936, and it won the Grand Prix du roman of the Académie française. Jean Aurenche and Pierre Bost wrote an earlier adaptation that Bernanos rejected. Bresson wrote his own screenplay after Bernanos died in 1948. He cast mostly non-professionals, whom he called 'models', with Claude Laydu, in his first film, as the curé, and had them repeat takes until their movements became automatic. It was his first use of a voice-over drawn from a diary. The film was shot in northern France. Released on 7 February 1951, it was a financial success in France. At Venice it won the prize for photography, the International Award and the OCIC Catholic award, and it also took the Prix Louis-Delluc. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II on its American release. Tarkovsky called it his favourite film, and it is regularly named in Sight and Sound polls.

title: I Confess
decision: PUBLISH: America's Catholic Movie Club essay, TCM and the AFI Catalog establish the seal of confession as the film's governing moral fact; the priest keeps it at the risk of his life. Mature material (murder, blackmail, a past romance) is disclosed.
summary: Hitchcock's most Catholic film: a Quebec priest hears a murderer's confession and then, bound by the seal, cannot clear himself when suspicion falls on him.
synopsis: In Quebec City, Otto Keller, a German refugee who works at the parish, confesses to Father Michael Logan that he has killed a lawyer named Villette during a robbery, wearing a cassock as a disguise. Witnesses saw a priest leaving the house. Inspector Larrue learns that Villette had been blackmailing Ruth Grandfort, a married woman who had loved Logan before his ordination, and Logan becomes the chief suspect. He will not say what he knows. Keller, increasingly afraid, plants evidence against him. Logan is tried, acquitted for want of proof and jeered by a hostile crowd outside the courthouse, before the truth comes out in a confrontation at the Château Frontenac.
inclusion: Hitchcock, raised a Catholic and taught by Jesuits, built a thriller around a rule most of his audience did not understand, and the film's power comes from treating that rule as absolute. Montgomery Clift plays Logan almost entirely through silence and posture. Robert Burks's location photography makes Quebec's steep streets and churches part of the drama. Hitchcock himself thought the film heavy-handed and humourless, and the Ruth flashbacks are stiff. Few Hollywood films show a priest paying so high a price for keeping the seal.
themes: The seal of confession is the hinge of the plot. Logan may not reveal what Keller told him, even to save himself from the gallows, and he never considers doing so. Hitchcock blamed the film's weak box office on audiences who did not grasp why a priest would stay silent. John Dougherty, writing in America, calls it a uniquely Catholic moral conundrum. The film also sets the penitent's duty against the priest's. Keller confesses but does not make amends, and his fear drives him to frame the man bound to protect his secret.
liberties: This is fiction. The investigation and trial are simplified for suspense, and the play's darker ending and its illegitimate child were removed.
advisories:
A murder, blackmail and a police shooting.

Flashbacks to the priest's pre-ordination romance with a woman who had married another man; restrained.

suitability.note: Nothing is graphic, but the plot turns on adult guilt and suspicion and will mean little to younger children. It suits teenagers and adults.

doctrine: The seal of confession binds the priest absolutely. The Fourth Lateran Council (1215, canon 21) ordered that the priest must not betray the sinner 'by word or sign or by any manner whatever', on pain of deposition and perpetual penance in a monastery. The canon makes no exception. The 1917 Code (canon 889) restates that the seal is inviolable, and that the confessor must not betray the sinner in the slightest, by word, sign or any other way, for any reason. Logan's silence before the police and the court is therefore obedience to the law of the sacrament.
production: Paul Anthelme's play Nos deux consciences was published in 1902. His nephew inherited the rights in 1947 and sold them to the writer and agent Louis Verneuil, who passed them to Hitchcock. In 1951 Hitchcock developed it alongside another property, The Bramble Bush, and chose it. Jack Warner rejected the original ending, in which the priest is hanged before his innocence is proved, and the pre-ordination child, for fear of offending Catholics. Anne Baxter replaced the Swedish actress Anita Björk. The film was shot from 21 August to 22 October 1952, almost entirely on location in Quebec City, including the Château Frontenac, the Lévis ferry and the church of Saint-Zéphirin-de-Stadacona, with Father Paul LaCouline as technical adviser. Montgomery Clift spent a week at a Quebec monastery to prepare. It premiered in Quebec City on 12 February 1953. Contemporary reviews found it slow. America's Catholic Movie Club has since treated it as Catholic noir.

title: Angels of Sin
decision: PUBLISH: Doug Cummings's detailed essay and the BFI record establish a drama of zeal, pride, humility and repentance inside a Dominican congregation that receives women from prison; the ending joins the religious and the legal acceptance of guilt. Murder and emotional cruelty are disclosed.
summary: Bresson's first feature: a novice in a convent for former prisoners sets out to save a hardened young woman, and has to be saved from her own pride first.
synopsis: Anne-Marie, a well-off young woman with a fervent vocation, enters the Dominican Sisters of Bethany, a congregation that welcomes women released from prison. Accompanying the sisters to collect a released inmate, she fixes on another prisoner, Thérèse, who insists she was framed by her former lover. On release, Thérèse shoots him, then takes refuge in the convent as a novice. Anne-Marie's possessive zeal to convert her irritates the community and leads to her own humiliation and expulsion. She keeps vigil by the grave of the congregation's founder and falls gravely ill. Readmitted and dying, she is nursed by Thérèse, who is finally moved by her. As Anne-Marie dies, the police arrive, and Thérèse holds out her wrists.
inclusion: Made under the Occupation by a director just back from a German prison camp, it is a notable debut. The style is not yet the bare Bresson of later films, with professional actresses, a score and Jean Giraudoux's polished dialogue, but the concentration is already there in the white habits, the closed spaces and the faces of Renée Faure and Jany Holt. Doug Cummings shows how carefully the film weighs Anne-Marie's humility against her pride, and the convent's rivalries against its charity. The community is petty at times and the heroine is often wrong, and that honesty makes the final act of grace convincing.
themes: The film follows the purification of zeal. Anne-Marie wants to save a soul, but her charity becomes possessive and proud, and the community's discipline, including penance and obedience, exposes this. Her suffering and death become the means of Thérèse's conversion. The film insists that repentance includes accepting earthly justice, and Thérèse's surrender to the police completes her change of heart. The religious community is shown with its faults, but its vocation and rule are taken seriously.
history: The Dominican Sisters of Bethany (the Congregation of Bethany) were founded in 1866 by the Dominican Jean-Joseph Lataste, O.P., who had preached in women's prisons and wanted a community in which former prisoners and women without a criminal past lived as equals.
liberties: Anne-Marie, Thérèse and the crime are fictional, though the congregation is real. The film condenses its life into a few dramatic months, sharpens its internal rivalries, and gives Giraudoux's literary dialogue to its sisters.
advisories:
A deliberate killing (shown in preparation, act brief).

Humiliation, emotional cruelty, illness and death.

suitability.note: There is no sex or gore, but the story is austere, adult in its psychology and in French; it suits mature teenagers and adults and will mean little to younger children.

doctrine: The Sisters of Bethany live under the Dominican rule with choir, silence and penance. The film's drama depends on the traditional teaching that zeal for souls must be founded on humility. Her vigil at the founder's grave and her death are offered as expiation for another. That one soul may offer sufferings for another rests on the communion of saints and on the teaching that works of satisfaction have their value only in union with Christ (Council of Trent, Session XIV, chapters 8 and 9). Thérèse's surrender to the police reflects the teaching that repentance does not cancel the temporal punishment due to a crime.
production: The Dominican priest Raymond-Léopold Bruckberger proposed a film about the Sisters of Bethany and worked on the script with Bresson and Jean Giraudoux. Bresson, then known only as a stills photographer and an assistant, made his first feature during the German occupation of France. Working titles included Bethany and The Exchange, the latter Bresson's preferred title. Giraudoux's name stood above Bresson's on the posters. It was released in France on 23 June 1943 and runs about 80 minutes. It is usually seen as his most conventional film, though critics find in it the ellipses, close-ups of hands and prison setting of his later work.

title: I Was a Parish Priest
decision: PUBLISH: the Italian Catholic Cinematografo record gives a full narrative and a 1955 Segnalazioni cinematografiche notice; together they establish a priest who sides with exploited miners and is then sent back to them by his bishop. The 2019 diocesan capsule is retained only for production context; its synopsis echoes the DVD blurb and is not independent criticism.
summary: Rafael Gil's prize-winning drama of a young priest who takes the miners' side in a bitter strike and pays for it with his superiors and his own body.
synopsis: In 1930, Father Andrés Mendoza, just out of the seminary, is sent to Aldemoz, a poor mining village full of resentment. The mine owner, Don César, tries to win him over, while the miners, led by the embittered Martín, distrust him. When a worker is unjustly dismissed, the men strike and occupy the mine. Andrés tries to mediate, fails, and then openly backs the strikers. Don César has to give way but complains to the bishop. Later, the owner's son and Martín's small daughter wander into an abandoned, unstable gallery and have to be rescued. Then a cave-in traps several men, among them Martín, Don César and the priest, until their comrades dig them out. Martín will not reconcile with Don César even underground, but does so at his injured daughter's bedside. The bishop summons Andrés and lets him return to his miners.
inclusion: It is one of the more interesting Spanish religious films of the 1950s because it takes sides. Rafael Gil and the writers Vicente Escrivá and Ramón D. Faraldo give the young priest a fight, on the side of the workers, against the man who owns the mine. Claude Laydu, two years after Diary of a Country Priest, plays another young curé, dubbed into Spanish. Francisco Rabal won best-actor prizes as Martín. The 1955 Italian Catholic notice found the opening slow and somewhat naive but called the mine sequence intense and convincing and praised the photography.
themes: The film puts the Church's social teaching into the mouth of a parish priest. Andrés defends a just wage and fair treatment, which he sees as part of caring for souls, and he refuses to be the owner's chaplain. His siding with the strike costs him the trust of his superiors, and the decisive reconciliation comes through suffering and charity in the mine. The bishop's decision to send him back places the priest with his poor parishioners, under obedience. The approach follows Rerum novarum and Quadragesimo anno and has nothing revolutionary in it.
history: The film was declared "of national interest" by the Franco regime's film authorities, which brought official support. The Colegio de Médicos reportedly objected to its portrayal of a doctor and sought to have it banned.
liberties: Aldemoz and its strike are fictional. The film should not be taken as a portrait of Spanish labour relations in 1930. The concentration of rescue and reconciliation into a few days is dramatic shorthand.
advisories:
Mining accidents, trapped men and children in danger; a child is injured.

Class hostility and threats.

Best for older children with an adult, teenagers and adults.

sources.title: Rerum novarum
sources.claims: Just wage and the victim of force in necessity (nn. 43-45); workers' associations a natural right (nn. 49-58); duties of employers and workers (n. 20)

sources.title: Quadragesimo anno
sources.claims: Family wage and the three considerations (nn. 71-74); condemnation of class struggle (n. 112); Catholic workers' associations (nn. 31-36)

suitability.note: The strike, the class hatred and the long scenes of argument suit teenagers better than small children.

doctrine: Leo XIII's Rerum novarum (15 May 1891) taught that a wage must be enough to support a thrifty worker, that necessity does not make a harsh bargain just, and that workers have a natural right to form associations; it urges Christian workers to form their own where others are hostile. Pius XI's Quadragesimo anno (15 May 1931) added that a just wage must keep the worker and his family, and also weighs the state of the business and the common good. Both condemn class hatred and treat the Church as the reconciler of employer and worker, which is the part Andrés plays at the bedside.
production: Aspa Producciones made the film, with CIFESA as distributor. It is set in the early 1930s, shot in black and white, and runs 96 minutes. It was released in Spain on 30 September 1953. It won the Golden Shell at the first San Sebastián festival in 1953 and the Bronze Lion at Venice, and Rabal won a Fotogramas de Plata for his part.

title: Balarrasa
decision: PUBLISH: Independent treatment is now substantial: DeCine21's review, Rubén Higueras Flores's close textual analysis (ZER, 2017), Matt Losada's article (Romance Notes, 2011) and Fernán Gómez's own recollection (via Joan Ripollès, Centro Virtual Cervantes). Higueras finds undercurrents linking religion with coercion and renunciation, but concludes they do not overturn the plain reading: a sinner's conversion, a priestly vocation and the restoration of a family to the faith. That reading is sound, and the adult material serves it. Year 1951 (Cannes competition 1951; scholars date the production 1950).
summary: Nieves Conde's postwar melodrama about a reckless Legion officer whose comrade dies in his place, and who becomes a priest and sets out to save his own family.
synopsis: A Spanish missionary is lost in an Alaskan blizzard, and as he faces death he remembers his life. During the Civil War, Lieutenant Javier Mendoza, known as Balarrasa, is a hard-drinking Legion officer. He gambles away his guard duty to a comrade, Joaquín, who is shot on the watch that should have been Javier's. Shaken, he leaves the army for the seminary in Salamanca. Back home as a seminarian, he finds his family in moral ruin: his widowed father gambles, his brother Fernando trades in black-market currency, his sister Lina is the mistress of the crook their father owes money to, and his youngest sister Mayte drifts between suitors. Javier sets about putting them right. Lina dies in a car crash while fleeing with her lover, and the shock brings the family back to the faith. Javier is ordained and leaves for the missions.
inclusion: Balarrasa was one of the most successful Spanish religious films of its time, and it made Fernando Fernán Gómez a leading man. Vicente Escrivá's script is a moral fable, but Nieves Conde gives it a hard edge. The family scenes have the shadows and night-time look of film noir, and the picture of a prosperous postwar family rotting from within anticipates his social drama Surcos. DeCine21 praises the realism, the humour that leavens the drama and Fernán Gómez's performance, and notes that priests advised the production. Fernán Gómez himself later found the family's sins mild stand-ins for the real problems of the time.
themes: It is a vocation story built on guilt and reparation. Javier reads his comrade's death as a debt, and gives the life left to him to God. The film shows seminary study, Latin and Thomist philosophy, ordination with the kissing of the new priest's hands, and the missions. At home his work is the cure of souls, through grace at table, a Gospel warning about empty hands and steady pressure on each sinner. Lina's death, with her empty hands raised and Javier, not yet a priest, unable to absolve her, is a stark lesson about dying unprepared. Higueras Flores argues that the film ties religion to renunciation and coercion, but he concludes that this does not overturn its plain religious meaning.
history: Balarrasa is fiction. Its writer, Vicente Escrivá, co-founded the production company Aspa Films with the director Rafael Gil in 1950 and became a leading maker of Catholic films in 1950s Spain. The story of a Legion officer who exchanges his uniform for a cassock reflects the early Franco years, when the regime increasingly presented itself through the Church, moving away from the army; Matt Losada and Higueras Flores both read the film in that light.
advisories:
A soldier is shot dead; a fatal car crash; a young woman's deathbed.

An officers' drinking party in a brothel (not explicit); an illicit affair, gambling and black-market dealing.

Javier urges a shy suitor to punch a rival, a scene played for comedy.

DeCine21 recommends it for adults; Spanish television rates it for all audiences.

sources.publisher: Matt Losada, Romance Notes 51/2 (2011), pp. 257–265 (Project MUSE)

suitability.note: Nothing is shown, but the film is in Spanish with subtitles and quite talky, so it suits teenagers better than young children.

doctrine: The story turns on a vocation that follows a bad conscience. The Council of Trent taught that a priest is called by God and tested in a seminary (Session 23, chapter 18, which founded the diocesan seminaries), and the film's Salamanca seminary reflects this. Javier's guilt over a comrade's death and his return to the Faith show the sacrament of Penance: contrition, confession and satisfaction. His family's rescue by a death, and the shock that follows, recall that grace can work through suffering, though the Church does not teach that a particular misfortune is sent as a punishment for a particular sin. Pius XI's Rerum Ecclesiae (28 February 1926) urged the whole Church to support foreign missions.
production: It was shot in Madrid (Centro, Retiro, Salamanca and Ciudad Lineal districts) and in Salamanca province. It was chosen for the Cannes competition in 1951. At the Círculo de Escritores Cinematográficos medals for 1951, Nieves Conde won Best Director and Fernán Gómez Best Actor.

title: The Fugitive
decision: PUBLISH: AFI and TCM establish the film and its changes to Greene; Greydanus (A-, +3) and the 1948 Venice International Award (reported as the first OCIC prize) support a reverent treatment of a hunted priest who baptises, seeks to say Mass and dies rather than apostatise. The reservation about the altered protagonist dissolves: the changes remove the novel's sacrilegious and sexual sins rather than add doctrinal error, at the cost of Greene's complexity. Legion of Decency A-I for the re-edited release (first classed A-II).
summary: John Ford's stark, stylised version of Greene's The Power and the Glory: Henry Fonda's hunted priest, the last in a state where religion is outlawed, walks back towards martyrdom.
synopsis: In an unnamed Latin American state the government has outlawed religion and hunts its priests. One nameless priest remains. He returns to his abandoned village church, where María Dolores, an unmarried mother whose child was fathered by the police lieutenant, finds him, and he baptises the village children in secret. The lieutenant takes hostages to force him into the open. The priest flees towards the port, shadowed by an informer and crossing paths with an American wanted for murder. Unable to say Mass without wine, he is arrested, unrecognised, with a bottle of brandy. Safe over the border, he goes back when a beggar brings a note, supposedly from the dying American, asking for confession. Captured, he refuses to renounce his faith and is shot. At the end another priest comes to the church to pray with the faithful.
inclusion: It is the most openly religious film John Ford made, and Steven D. Greydanus notes that Ford himself thought it his best. Gabriel Figueroa's black-and-white photography is its great strength. Henry Fonda plays the priest as a frightened man whose courage comes late. Greydanus grades it A- and says that, though it softens Greene, it still packs spiritual punch; the debate between priest and lieutenant remains a high point. Dennis Schwartz found it turgid and its religious symbols simplistic, and Bret Wood suggests the images distract from the priest's plight.
themes: The priest baptises children who have had no priest for years. The plot turns on the Mass: without altar wine he cannot celebrate, and his search for it leads to his arrest. An informer betrays him, and he goes back across the border because a dying man may need a priest. Offered his life for apostasy, he refuses. His flaw in the film is pride in his office and fear. That makes him more conventionally edifying, and Greydanus calls the result a softened, conventionalised Greene, while Schwartz thinks it loses the novel's moral urgency. The closing image of another priest arriving to pray shows that the Church outlasts its persecutors.
history: Mexico's 1917 constitution restricted the Church, and in 1926 President Calles enforced it. The bishops suspended public worship at the end of July 1926, foreign priests were expelled, and several states limited the number of priests to a handful or none. In Tabasco, under Governor Tomás Garrido Canabal, churches were closed and priests driven out or forced to marry. The Cristero rising (1926–29) ended in a settlement, but persecution flared again in the 1930s. Graham Greene travelled in Mexico in 1938, when churches in several states were still closed and priests were in hiding, and drew on that for his novel.
liberties: Greene's 'whisky priest' is an alcoholic who has fathered a child with María; the film makes the lieutenant the father and gives the priest only pride and fear. Greene's lieutenant is an idealist who wants to help the poor; Ford's is a harder tyrant. The setting is an unnamed state, and a spoken prologue presents the story as true.
advisories:
Hostages are taken and threatened; a gunfight in a cornfield; the priest is executed (not shown graphically).

An unmarried mother and the officer who fathered her child; she dances in a cantina to distract the police.

Drinking and a jail sequence.

Steady tension and menace; best for teenagers and adults.

names: The Power and the Glory, novel by Graham Greene (1940)

suitability.note: The menace is steady but nothing is graphic, which suits older children.

doctrine: Two points of sacramental law drive the plot. The Mass requires wine of the grape, and the 1917 Code (canon 815) and the long tradition behind it make true wine necessary matter, so brandy will not serve and the priest must hunt for it. A priest's duty to the dying is also grave: where a soul may be lost without absolution, the pastor is bound to go even at risk to his life, which is why the priest crosses back over the border. Pius XI protested against the Mexican persecution in Iniquis afflictisque (18 November 1926), listing the limits placed on the number of priests, the expulsion of foreign clergy and the closing of seminaries and convents, and returned to it in Acerba animi (1932) and Firmissimam constantiam (1937). Baptism of children, shown in the village, is necessary for salvation (Trent, Session VII).
production: Ford and Merian C. Cooper made it as the first of three Argosy Pictures films for RKO, which shared costs and profits while Argosy kept creative control. Dudley Nichols wrote the screenplay, but Ford departed from much of it on location. The film was shot in Taxco, Cholula and Cuernavaca and at Churubusco Studios in Mexico City, with a crew that was Mexican apart from two assistant directors and an editor. Emilio Fernández, the associate producer, brought in Dolores del Río, Pedro Armendáriz and the cameraman Gabriel Figueroa. It cost about $1.5 million, opened on 3 November 1947 and lost money. At Venice in 1948 it shared the International Award and won the OCIC (Catholic film office) prize. Ford defended it; Bret Wood has called it perhaps his last great 'art film'. The Legion of Decency classified it A-I.

title: Léon Morin, Priest
decision: REJECT: The subtitle file shows a heterodox thesis carried by the film's moral centre and never corrected. Explaining that there is no salvation outside the Church, Morin tells Barny she is not damned even if she goes on living as an atheist, and makes the Church an invisible Church of all humanity of goodwill, the reading Pius XII rejected in Mystici Corporis and Humani generis. In the closing conversation he asks why God should not work miracles for heretics, says God is Catholic only in our temporal language, and that the contradictions between the churches are mostly in our minds. Elsewhere he says the bourgeois distorted religion. With the sustained erotic focus already documented, this meets the rule against a heterodox thesis. Editor to confirm.
summary: Melville's Occupation drama of a Communist widow and a young priest whose arguments bring her back to a faith he recasts as an invisible Church of goodwill.
synopsis: A small Alpine town under the Occupation. Barny (Emmanuelle Riva), a widow whose Jewish husband has been killed, is a Communist and a lapsed Catholic bringing up her daughter alone and correcting work for a correspondence school. To mock the Church she goes to confession and baits the young priest, Léon Morin (Jean-Paul Belmondo), with the old line that religion is the opium of the people. He answers her, and she keeps coming back. Over months of private conversations she returns to the faith. Her feelings for him turn romantic, and other women of the town are drawn to him too; none succeeds in seducing him. When the Germans leave, the school returns to Paris and Morin is transferred to another parish. On his last night he sees her once more, tells her they will meet in another life, and she leaves in tears.
inclusion: Jean-Pierre Melville works here in a chamber register: most of the film is two people talking in small rooms, and it holds because the arguments are real. Belmondo plays a quick, blunt priest who questions authority and is not afraid of gossip; Dennis Schwartz found his case for God forceful and intelligent. Riva is the real centre, and even Eye for Film, otherwise cool on the film, praises her nuanced performance. Sean Axmaker in Video Librarian called it a solid chamber drama, respectful of the Church, with a priest who is chaste and devoted; the hosts of the Catholic film podcast Criteria call it one of the best priest films ever made and read it as a study in pastoral prudence. Not every critic agrees: Eye for Film found the theological exchanges grating and the story close to soap opera. It is talky and deliberately low-key. The difficulty is that the faith he argues for is not quite the Church's.
themes: The core is a conversion worked out through argument, and the argument is the problem. Morin answers Barny's Marxist jibes, but his answers reshape the faith: he tells her that no salvation outside the Church means an invisible Church of all people of goodwill, that she is not damned even if she remains an atheist, and at the end that God is Catholic only in human language and that contradictions between the churches are mostly in our minds. Nobody in the film corrects him. Barny's desire for Morin also grows with her faith, and though he keeps his vows and sends her away, he lets the private meetings run on for months.
history: Béatrix Beck's novel Léon Morin, prêtre won the Prix Goncourt in 1952 and was published in English as The Passionate Heart. Melville cut a first assembly of about three hours down to the 117-minute release; a longer director's cut of about 128 minutes was restored in 2019. The film drew 1.7 million admissions in France.
advisories:
Sustained romantic and sexual tension between a widow and a priest; no sex scene. The heroine is also shown as attracted to a female colleague.

Occupation setting, with the deportation of Jews in the background; reviews do not report graphic violence.

Adult in theme and slow in pace; for older teenagers and adults.

The priest teaches that an atheist need not be damned and that the Church is the invisible community of goodwill, and the film presents him as its moral centre. The heroine's conversion is entangled with her desire for him.

title: Going My Way
decision: PUBLISH: The AFI Catalog gives a full synopsis and production record; John Clark (NCRegister), Anthony Esolen and Joe Wilson give detailed Catholic readings of its portrait of parish priesthood. The Criteria critique and David E. White's scholarly chapter (the film nearly omits the supernatural and sacramental) are real limits and are stated in the record, but they describe an emphasis, not a teaching that contradicts the faith.
summary: Bing Crosby's easygoing young curate takes over a debt-ridden New York parish from its stubborn old pastor, played by Barry Fitzgerald.
synopsis: St Dominic's, a poor New York parish, is about to lose its church to the mortgage holder. The bishop sends Father Chuck O'Malley, a former songwriter who wears a sweatshirt and plays golf, ostensibly as curate to the elderly Father Fitzgibbon, in fact to take charge without humiliating him. O'Malley turns a gang of street boys into a choir, helps a runaway girl, marries her to the landlord's son, and sells a song to pay the debt. Fitzgibbon learns the truth and runs away into the rain, then comes round. When the church burns, the parish starts again, and O'Malley moves on to the next troubled parish.
inclusion: McCarey made a comedy about two priests, and it is funny. Barry Fitzgerald's Fitzgibbon, crotchety, vain and devoted, and finally touching, is one of the great character performances of the period, and his scenes with Crosby have an easy rhythm that holds the film together. Crosby underplays O'Malley's tact, taking over without ever saying so. The film is long and loosely plotted, the opera interlude with Risë Stevens stops it dead, and the delinquents reform suspiciously fast. But its picture of a parish as a place where a priest knows the landlady, the policeman and the boys stealing turkeys has warmth and observation. The final scene, with Fitzgibbon's mother, is famous.
themes: The film presents the parish priest as a father to his people, with patience for an older priest, care for the poor and the young, and a refusal to humiliate anyone. Esolen calls its governing virtue tact, a form of charity. John Clark draws out its respect for ordinary priestly service and a line affirming the indissolubility of a valid marriage. What it hardly shows is the supernatural centre of the priesthood. The scholar David E. White notes that it leaves out nearly all supernatural, sacramental and theological reference, and Thomas Mirus and James Majewski argue that O'Malley is admired for singing and charm, not for anything spiritual. That criticism is fair.
liberties: Fiction; no historical persons. The parish is idealised and the plot runs on coincidence and a hit song.
advisories:
No violence beyond a church fire. A runaway girl lives in an apartment paid for by a young man before they marry; nothing is shown.

Suitable for all ages.

suitability.note: There is no coarse language. It runs over two hours and is gentle and episodic, so younger children may drift; the boys' choir and Fitzgerald's comedy keep many of them with it.

doctrine: The film shows the pastor's office as the Council of Trent described it: to know his flock, preach, teach children and relieve the poor (Session 24 and Session 5, decrees on reform). Pius XI's encyclical Ad Catholici Sacerdotii (1935) states the weightier doctrine the film leaves aside: the priest is another Christ, ordained to offer the Mass and forgive sins, and is bound to holiness of life. The O'Malley-Fitzgibbon dialogue on a marriage that lasts "till death" reflects Christ's teaching (Matthew 19:6), which Pius XI restated in Casti Connubii (1930): a valid, consummated Christian marriage cannot be dissolved by any human power. A priest's easy sociability is no fault, but the 1917 Code (canon 124 ff.) expects clerics to live in a manner befitting their state.
production: Leo McCarey, who had a Catholic upbringing, made the film for Paramount. Interiors were made at Paramount; St Monica's Church in Santa Monica stood in for St Dominic's, and the Robert Mitchell Boychoir sang. Risë Stevens was then at the Metropolitan Opera. The film opened in New York on 3 May 1944 and was the highest-grossing film of 1944. It won seven Academy Awards, including Best Picture, Director, Actor (Crosby) and Supporting Actor (Fitzgerald), and Fitzgerald was nominated for the same role as lead and supporting actor. Crosby and McCarey later presented a print to Pope Pius XII at the Vatican. Crosby played O'Malley again in The Bells of St Mary's (1945).
