doctrine: Father Paul's position is the Church's own: the Council of Trent (Session XXV, 1563) ordered that no new miracle be acknowledged until the bishop has examined and approved it, and that superstition be removed from devotion to the saints and their images. A priest therefore has no right to proclaim a miracle, and the film's ending sits uneasily with that rule. Truthfulness is no small matter in Catholic moral teaching, though a pastor may choose what to preach. The St Michael devotion is traditional: he is named in the Mass at the Confiteor and, from 1886 by order of Leo XIII, in the prayer said after low Mass. Olga's film role, Joan of Arc, was canonised in 1920.
production: Exteriors were shot in Glen Lyon, Pennsylvania, the mining town behind Coaltown. The film ran 120 minutes. Critics were hostile: Time said 'St. Michael ought to sue' and James Agee declared himself founder of a 'Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to God'. It lost about $640,000 and was repossessed by Bank of America. The Legion of Decency classified it A-I.

title: The Keys of the Kingdom
decision: GREY: The subtitle file confirms the Legion's likely targets and adds one more. As a student Chisholm asks whether God sets value on creed, an accident of birth, and his rector says that He does. In China Chisholm says heathen priests are often good and noble men, tells the mandarin that the Methodist newcomers serve the same true God, and says no one is a Christian who is not tolerant. At Willie's death he prays the De profundis, tells him his salvation is his own doing and is thanked for not bullying him into heaven. Nothing denies the Church's claim outright, so it stays a weighable reservation rather than REJECT, but the drift towards indifferentism is now documented in the dialogue.
summary: Gregory Peck plays a Scottish priest whose fifty years, most of them as a missionary in China, are read from his diary in Fox's handsome adaptation of Cronin's bestseller.
synopsis: In 1938 a monsignor arrives at a Scottish parish to retire its elderly priest, Francis Chisholm, whose unorthodox preaching has drawn complaints, and reads his journal overnight. Francis's parents died after an anti-Catholic mob attacked his father; the girl he loved bore a child out of wedlock and died; at seminary he was rebuked for questioning what he was taught. Sent to China, he finds his mission church destroyed by flood, turns away converts who come only for rice, cures a mandarin's son but refuses the father's offer to convert out of gratitude, and rebuilds with the land the mandarin gives. An aristocratic nun, Mother Maria Veronica, despises him until his humility wins her over. Civil war reaches the mission, and his unbelieving friend Dr Willie Tulloch is killed. Methodist missionaries arrive and are welcomed. Chisholm goes home, and the monsignor lets him stay.
inclusion: Peck carries the film across half a century of one man's life, and Bosley Crowther praised his force. The film drew four Oscar nominations, among them Peck's first, for best actor, Arthur C. Miller's black-and-white photography and the art direction of its Chinese village. The portrait of a poor, stubborn missionary who will not buy converts with rice or favours is attractive, and Steven D. Greydanus calls the film an edifying celebration of Christian virtue in an imperfect hero. It is also long and vague in its piety. James Agee came to find its sincerity and ethics bland, Crowther thought it a surface shadow of Cronin's novel, and the Church that sent Chisholm barely appears.
themes: The film admires Chisholm's charity, humility and refusal to coerce belief. The Church itself is thin: he is never shown saying Mass or administering a sacrament, and the nearest is a joke about confession. Cronin's novel was openly sceptical of the Church's unique claim, and the film tones this down without removing it. As a student Chisholm asks whether God sets an exclusive value on creed, an accident of birth. In China he speaks well of heathen priests, tells the mandarin that the Methodist newcomers serve the same true God, and says no one is a Christian who is not tolerant. At Willie's deathbed he prays the De profundis but does not press him to believe, and Willie thanks him for it. Taken together, these lean towards the indifferentism Pius XI condemned in Mortalium animos.
history: Francis Chisholm is fictional. A. J. Cronin (1896-1981) was the son of a Catholic father and a Presbyterian mother and was schooled at St Aloysius' College, Glasgow, before becoming a doctor. He lost his faith as a medical student and later came back to belief in a Creator. The Keys of the Kingdom (1941) is his most openly religious novel.
liberties: Fiction, from Cronin's novel. grey.question: The Legion of Decency passed this film for all audiences but flagged statements by the priest open to a meaning not in accordance with Catholic doctrine. Among them are Chisholm's asking as a student whether God values creed, which he calls an accident of birth, and his telling a mandarin that Methodist missionaries serve the same true God. He also lets his unbelieving friend die unpersuaded and is thanked for it. Nothing denies the Church outright, but the drift is towards indifferentism.

suitability.note: At about 137 minutes it is long and slow for younger children, and several of the priest's remarks about other religions need an adult to explain what the Church actually teaches.

doctrine: The film's key lines touch the dogma that there is no salvation outside the Church. Pius IX restated it in Quanto conficiamur moerore (10 August 1863): it is well known Catholic teaching that no one can be saved outside the Catholic Church. In the same letter he allowed that those in invincible ignorance of the true religion who keep the natural law are not punished for that ignorance. That is the narrow ground on which Chisholm's charity towards Willie can be read in a Catholic sense; it does not make creed indifferent. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) defines indifferentism as the denial of a duty to worship God by the one true religion, and calls the view that all religions are equally good a form of it. Refusing 'rice Christians' is sound: the Church has always required that an adult come to baptism freely and with faith, not for material gain.
production: David O. Selznick bought the screen rights to Cronin's novel, planning to produce it for United Artists; when Selznick International closed in 1943, Twentieth Century-Fox acquired them. Nunnally Johnson wrote the first script, and Joseph L. Mankiewicz, who became producer, substantially rewrote it. Alfred Hitchcock was interested in directing but made Lifeboat instead. Gregory Peck, then relatively unknown, took the lead. The film premiered on 15 December 1944, runs 136 minutes and cost about $3 million. Reviews were mixed. The Legion of Decency classified it A-I.

title: God Needs Men
decision: GREY: The English subtitle file, a rough translation, sharpens the reservation. Thomas pronounces absolution over a woman who believes she is dying and gives the full formula to Joseph as he dies after hanging himself. With hosts he has baked, and prompted by an islander, he recites the Mass as far as the words of consecration; only the gendarmes' arrival stops him, after which he says he will not say Mass. The curé tells him he does not know what sacrilege is and later calls the islanders pagans and savages. The ending is the burial at sea, not a return to Mass. REJECT is arguable, since the film presents simulated sacraments with sympathy; kept at GREY for the editor because Thomas knows he is not a priest, submits, and the film never claims his acts are valid.
summary: On a priestless Breton island, a fisherman-sacristan is pushed by his parish into the priest's role, and the film watches him go too far.
synopsis: Île de Sein, off Brittany, in the mid-19th century. The islanders fish and loot wrecks, and their discouraged rector leaves. They will not do without the sacraments, so they turn to the sacristan, Thomas Gourvennec (Pierre Fresnay), a fisherman who can barely write. He agrees to lead prayers and preach on Sundays, insisting that he is not a priest. The pressure grows. He pronounces absolution over a woman who thinks she is dying, hears the confession of the young Joseph Le Berre (Daniel Gélin), who admits to a crime, and, with hosts he has baked, recites the Mass as far as the consecration. Gendarmes arrive escorting a priest from the mainland. Joseph hangs himself, and Thomas absolves him as he dies. The islanders defy the curé over the burial, and Thomas leads them out to give the body to the sea.
inclusion: Few films ask so bluntly what a priest is for, and what happens to people who lose one. Jean Aurenche and Pierre Bost adapted Henri Queffélec's novel, and Delannoy stages it with care. Robert Lefebvre's photography gives strong high-angle views of the island and of Thomas hemmed in by his parishioners, and the choral music is used heavily. Fresnay dominates as a decent, unlettered man frightened by what is being asked of him. The International Catholic Film Office (OCIC) gave it its prize at Venice in 1950, and the Canadian Catholic film review Séquences called it frankly religious. It also has faults. Séquences found the acting theatrical, Fresnay's gestures included, and the island's poverty too polished and picturesque; Fr Beirnaert of the Jesuit review Études, quoted there, missed the novel's sea and wind.
themes: The islanders' faith is crude but sincere: they want sacraments, not ideas, and they fear damnation. Thomas knows he is not a priest and says so, yet he pronounces absolution twice and recites the Mass as far as the consecration. The film treats him with sympathy. The curé who comes with gendarmes is cold and authoritarian; he tells Thomas he does not know what sacrilege is and later calls the islanders pagans and savages. Séquences noted that the film sets a 'democratic' lay leader against an odious cleric, which is why Protestants and anticlericals liked it. Against that, Thomas refuses to say Mass and accepts that a parish must obey its priest, and the story rests on the need for an ordained priest.
history: Queffélec based his novel, Un recteur de l'île de Sein, loosely on events on Sein in 1641. When two Jesuit missionaries landed, they found that a fisherman, François Le Su, had acted as catechist and preacher since the rector's death. They sent him to study on the mainland; he was ordained and returned as the island's priest.
liberties: The film moves the story from the 17th century to the mid-19th century and drops the ending of both the history and the novel, in which the sacristan becomes a priest. It enlarges the two confession scenes and creates an open conflict between Thomas and an authoritarian curé, which is not in the novel. Bretons objected that the real Church had welcomed the fisherman instead of opposing him.
advisories:
A suicide, and the crime confessed by Joseph, are central to the plot.

The islanders loot shipwrecks; there are scenes of anger and confrontation with gendarmes.

No sexual content of note. Suitable for older children with an adult; the story's questions are for adults.

A layman pronounces absolution and recites the Mass over hosts as far as the consecration, and the film is more sympathetic to him than to the lawful priest.

names: Un recteur de l'Île de Sein, novel by Henri Queffélec (1944)

suitability.note: Nothing is graphic, but the film asks adult questions and needs explanation.

doctrine: Only a priest can validly absolve and consecrate. Trent teaches that the priest alone has the power to forgive sins in the sacrament of penance (Session XIV, chapter 6 and canon 9) and that the power to consecrate belongs to those ordained (Session XXIII). A layman who pronounces the words of absolution or of consecration confers and effects nothing. In danger of death, the Church allows anyone to baptise, but not to absolve. A suicide who dies impenitent was refused ecclesiastical burial under the 1917 Code (canon 1240); this is the point on which Thomas and the curé clash. The rule is a discipline and does not judge the soul. The Church allows that God may be merciful to one who repents at the last. The film's Thomas is unsure of his powers and stops short of the consecration.
production: Jean Delannoy's film was produced by Paul Graetz's Transcontinental Films. Location work began on the Île de Sein, but the islanders' distrust of the unit led the crew to shoot the exteriors at Plouguerneau and to build a model of the village at Pantin, outside Paris, with interiors at the Billancourt studios. It was released on 4 October 1950 and runs 100 minutes. The French delegation first withdrew it from the 1950 Venice Festival for fear of offending the Church, then accepted it for screening because of its popularity, including among Catholics. It won a special prize at Berlin in 1951.

title: The Unfrocked One
decision: GREY: The film's thesis is plainly orthodox: holy orders leave an indelible mark, so the apostate's mock consecration is valid and therefore sacrilegious, the young priest consumes the wine to stop its profanation, and the ending gives the dying priest's absolution and the apostate's contrition. The sacrilege is shown as horror, not approved, so REJECT does not apply. It is grey because a valid-in-the-fiction consecration is staged in a cabaret for shock, and because no contemporary Catholic review (Centrale Catholique cote, Radio-Cinéma, La Croix) has been found; present treatment evidence is a ciné-club note, a traditionalist recommendation, a hostile blog and viewer reviews. Finding the 1954 Centrale Catholique cote would settle it.
summary: Pierre Fresnay plays an apostate priest who mocks the Church, and Pierre Trabaud the young convert who becomes a priest to win him back, in Joannon's blunt, provocative drama.
synopsis: In a German officers' camp in 1945, Maurice Morand reveals that he is a priest when he gives the last rites to the dying chaplain. Morand has left the Church and despises it, but the young Gérard Lacassagne is moved and decides to become a priest himself, against his family and his fiancée. After the war Morand, back at the Sorbonne, publishes an attack on religion, while Gérard, in the seminary, keeps trying to bring him back. In a cabaret Morand mockingly says the words of consecration over white wine; since he is still a priest, Gérard takes it for the Blood of Christ and drinks it rather than leave it to be profaned. After his ordination Gérard visits Morand once more. They quarrel and Morand strikes him, reopening an old wound. Dying, Gérard absolves him, and Morand is left in tears and prayer.
inclusion: Fresnay, who had played St Vincent de Paul in Monsieur Vincent and a lay 'rector' in Dieu a besoin des hommes, gives the film its force. Even the hostile blogger Narkissos admires his conviction, though some viewers find him overemphatic. The opening, with a sick chaplain collapsing at Mass and Morand forced to reveal himself, is the passage even detractors praise. The ciné-club de Montereau calls the film incisive and violent, the dialogue often brilliant, and praises Trabaud and Nicole Stéphane. It is a thesis film in the old French Catholic manner, built on the sacramental character of the priesthood, and it argues its case with melodrama. Its detractors find the later scenes close to grand guignol, and Narkissos, comparing it with Bresson and Melville, dismisses it. A traditionalist reviewer, by contrast, praises its classical theology and calls the craft exceptional.
themes: Everything rests on the doctrine that ordination imprints an indelible character. Morand is still a priest, so his cabaret consecration is real and his blasphemy a sacrilege. Gérard treats the wine as the Blood of Christ and consumes it to stop its profanation. The film also shows the last rites and the slow growth of a vocation against family opposition, and the ending turns on absolution given by a dying priest to the man who has killed him. Its detractors' complaint, that it relies on shock where Bresson worked by restraint, has force.
advisories:
A sacrilege against the Eucharist is shown on screen: an apostate priest mockingly consecrates wine in a cabaret, and a seminarian drinks it to prevent its profanation.

A newly ordained priest is fatally struck by the man he is trying to save; a death in a wartime prison camp.

Adult themes of apostasy and self-hatred. Older teenagers and adults.

grey.question: The film's theology is traditional. An ordained man stays a priest, so Morand's mock consecration in the cabaret is real and sacrilegious, and the young priest drinks the wine to save it from profanation. The sacrilege is shown as horror, and the ending turns on absolution and contrition. What is in doubt is taste and reverence. Does staging a valid consecration for shock, with the drunkenness and vomiting viewers describe, serve the argument or cheapen the Sacrament?

sources.title: Holy Orders
sources.claims: Indelible character of Orders; validity independent of minister's holiness

suitability.note: Besides the sacrilege there is a drinking scene and suicidal despair. The ideas are heavy and the staging melodramatic; older teenagers who know what the Mass is can handle it, younger children cannot.

doctrine: Holy Orders imprints an indelible character. The Council of Trent (session 23, canon 4, 1563) anathematised anyone who denies that the sacrament of Order imprints a character or that a man once a priest can become a layman again. A priest who has apostatised therefore keeps the power to consecrate, and if he says the words with the intention of doing what the Church does, the consecration is valid, though the act is a grave sacrilege. Trent also teaches that the validity of a sacrament does not depend on the minister's state of grace. In danger of death any priest, even one suspended or excommunicated, absolves validly (Trent, session 14, chapter 7), which explains why the film's absolutions hold. The film's assumption that a mock consecration in jest would still be valid is disputed by theologians: validity needs the intention to do what the Church does.
production: Made for Gaumont and the Société Française de Cinématographie from Joannon's own idea, with no source novel. It was shot in late 1953 at La Celle-Saint-Cloud and Joinville and released in France on 26 February 1954. It runs 107 minutes and won the Bronze Bear at the 4th Berlin International Film Festival.

title: The Secret Conclave
originalTitle: Gli uomini non guardano il cielo
alternateTitles: Men Do Not Look at Heaven
decision: PUBLISH: The National Legion of Decency classified The Secret Conclave A-I (1952–53 season), a contemporary Catholic judgment, and Variety's review (Hift, May 1953) gives an independent, substantive assessment: a moving lead performance and a fine conclave sequence in a cheaply made, static film. The Exhibitor's 1953 review and the Diocese of Treviso production history establish the content. Pius X was beatified in 1951 and canonised in 1954, so rule (a) does not apply. Invented elements (the final Mass, a fictional countess) are disclosed.
summary: Umberto Scarpelli's biography of St Pius X frames the Pope's last weeks in 1914, as war approaches, around flashbacks to his country priesthood, Venice and the 1903 conclave.
synopsis: Summer 1914. The Archduke has been murdered, and Pius X, old and ill, does what he can to stop the coming war. When the Austrian ambassador asks him to bless his country's troops, he refuses to bless a war. His nephew, a young priest, comes to Rome to help him, and in a night of prayer the Pope's life is recalled in flashback: a poor boyhood, a scholarship to the seminary, years as a country priest caring for the poor and for families struck by cholera, charitable work as bishop of Mantua and patriarch of Venice. The 1903 conclave is staged at length: Austria's veto against Cardinal Rampolla, rejected by the cardinals, and the ballots that elect Cardinal Sarto against his own pleas. The film ends with the Pope going to say Mass for the last time, offering his life with the sacrifice of the altar.
inclusion: It is the only feature film about Pius X, made within months of his beatification by a Venetian company with a historian and a priest as advisers. Its strength is Henri Vidon, a Vatican Radio employee cast for his likeness to Sarto. Variety's reviewer in 1953 called his performance affecting and thoroughly expert, and praised the conclave in the Sistine Chapel, staged with a documentary sobriety. The same review found the script static, the treatment sometimes amateurish, the photography and editing weak and the English dubbing spotty. The acting, largely by stage actors, is slow and the style old-fashioned for 1952. It suits viewers who want the history of a modern saint told plainly.
themes: Pius X is shown as a priest who never stopped being a parish priest. Sarto's motto frames the story, and his nephew lists the work of the pontificate: the fight against Modernism, the reform of sacred music, the clergy and canon law, the abolition of the veto, and the admission of children to Holy Communion. The conclave shows the Church refusing a secular power's interference. The Pope's counsel to the countess, to bear her cross and stay in her marriage, is traditional spiritual direction. The ending presents the Mass as sacrifice, and the Pope's death as an offering for peace.
history: Giuseppe Sarto (1835–1914), born at Riese near Treviso, was a curate and parish priest in the Veneto, then bishop of Mantua (1884) and patriarch of Venice (1893). He was elected Pope on 4 August 1903 after Austria-Hungary's veto against Cardinal Rampolla was announced in the conclave. He died on 20 August 1914, weeks into the war. Pius XII beatified him in 1951 and canonised him on 29 May 1954.
liberties: Pius X died in bed, not at Mass; the closing Mass is a dramatic compression. The scene with the Austrian ambassador dramatises a story told after his death that historians treat with caution. The countess played by Isa Miranda is a composite, and the nephew's night of remembrance is the film's framing device.
advisories:
Deaths from cholera; the Pope's illness and death.

Talk of the coming war; a woman betrayed by her husband.

Slow and old-fashioned; the English-dubbed version is uneven.

Suitable for all ages.

doctrine: Pius X took as his motto 'to restore all things in Christ'. In 1903 he confirmed in the Motu proprio Tra le sollecitudini the use of Gregorian chant. He condemned Modernism in the decree Lamentabili (3 July 1907) and the encyclical Pascendi (8 September 1907). By the decree Sacra Tridentina (20 December 1905) he urged frequent, even daily, Communion, and by Quam singulari (8 August 1910) he lowered the age of first Communion to the age of discretion, about seven. The conclave sequence concerns the 'veto' of Austria, which Pius X abolished in 1904 under penalty of excommunication for any cardinal who conveyed such a veto. His counsel to the countess matches the indissolubility of marriage as the Church has always taught it.
production: Cinelia Film of Venice made it in 1951–52, before the canonisation, with the Diocese of Treviso supplying historical advice, and released the film in Italy in the second half of 1952. It ran about 94 minutes in black and white, as Gli uomini non guardano il cielo, and in English as The Secret Conclave. The National Legion of Decency rated it A-I. Prints are scarce: the Cineteca Nazionale and the Vatican Film Library hold copies.

title: Jesus of Nazareth
decision: REJECT: Editor ruling (2026-10-11). Zeffirelli shaped the film by Nostra Aetate, and that conciliar reading is built into the drama: the invented scribe Zerah engineers the arrest and Judas becomes a well-meaning dupe, shifting the Gospel account of responsibility. This is the post-conciliar outlook applied to the Gospel itself, not a reservation a viewer can set aside.
summary: Zeffirelli's six-hour Gospel life, from the Annunciation to the empty tomb, with Robert Powell's grave Christ and an invented scribe who engineers the arrest.
synopsis: In occupied Judea, Mary is betrothed to Joseph and receives the angel's message. The Nativity, the Magi, Herod's massacre and the Holy Family's return to Nazareth take up much of the first part. John the Baptist preaches at the Jordan and Jesus begins His ministry, calling Peter and Matthew, healing the sick, raising Jairus's daughter and Lazarus, and teaching in parables and the Sermon on the Mount. Zerah, a scribe of the Sanhedrin, watches the new rabbi with growing alarm and draws Judas into a plan to bring Jesus before the council. After the Last Supper Jesus is arrested in Gethsemane, tried before Caiaphas and Pilate, scourged and crucified. The tomb is found empty, and the risen Christ appears to His disciples.
inclusion: This is still the screen life of Christ most people picture. Powell plays Him grave and hieratic, with a fixed, piercing gaze; Steven Greydanus finds the Shakespearean diction stiff, but the performance has outlasted its rivals. The first ninety minutes are the strongest. Greydanus calls them the best screen telling of the Christmas story to date, and he ranks the Annunciation, built almost entirely on Olivia Hussey's reactions to an unseen presence, among the best ever filmed. Zeffirelli gives the miracles naturalistic touches, such as a paralysed man's limbs slowly unlocking. Rod Steiger's troubled Pilate and Peter Ustinov's witty, frightened Herod are memorable. The film is also slow to start, uneven in the middle, and its post-Resurrection ending is hasty and muted. Only the complete version, about six hours, is worth seeking; the 270-minute abridgement cuts too much.
themes: Christ is presented as the Son of God who works real miracles, forgives sins, dies and rises. The Last Supper is reverently staged, Mary is shown with tenderness and restraint, and the Passion is grave rather than sensational. The reservations concern who is responsible for the Cross. Zeffirelli cited Nostra Aetate, the Council's 1965 declaration on non-Christian religions, as a guiding influence, and the film moves the plot against Jesus onto Zerah, an invented scribe, while rewriting Judas. The Gospels show a thief who sells his Master (John 12:6; Matthew 26:15). Ian McShane's Judas is a well-meaning zealot who wants Jesus to prove Himself before the council, and the silver is an afterthought. Greydanus calls this the film's most troubling departure from the Gospel story.
history: Lew Grade's ITC and the Italian broadcaster RAI produced the film after, by Grade's account, Paul VI suggested a life of Jesus. Anthony Burgess, Suso Cecchi d'Amico and Zeffirelli wrote it, consulting experts of several religions, and it was shot in Morocco and Tunisia over 186 days. RAI broadcast it in five weekly episodes from 27 March 1977; ITV and NBC showed it in two parts on Palm Sunday and Easter Sunday, 3 and 10 April 1977. Paul VI praised it publicly.
liberties: Zerah is invented and drives the plot against Jesus; Judas's motive is rewritten so that greed largely disappears. The Magi's visit to Herod, the Temptation in the desert, Jesus weeping at Lazarus's tomb and Simon of Cyrene are omitted. Mary Magdalene is played as a repentant prostitute, following the traditional Western identification. Peter is called Simon Peter from the start. The post-Resurrection appearances are brief and hurried.
advisories:
The scourging and crucifixion are shown with some blood but without the extended brutality of later Passion films.

The Massacre of the Innocents and an exorcism may frighten young children.

Brief, discreet sexual reference in the Magdalene scenes.

Suitable for most ages with parents present for the Passion. Watch the complete version, about six and a quarter hours depending on the release; the 2000 Carlton 270-minute abridgement and the shorter cinema cut lose much of the film. It is usually watched in two or four sittings.

Judas is portrayed contrary to the Gospel account of his motive, and an invented scribe carries most of the plot against Jesus.

title: Teresa de Jesús
decision: PUBLISH: Gil de Muro's Carmelite survey, Alonso Franch's production study and the decine21 review give accessible, specific evidence of fidelity to Teresa's life and writings and of how the series stages prayer, the Inquisition and opposition to the reform; RTVE and the Universidad de Navarra fix identity. RTVE's 'modernity' framing and the medical aside in Alonso Franch are disclosed; neither is shown to be the series' own account of Teresa's mysticism.
summary: Josefina Molina's eight-hour TVE series, carried by Concha Velasco, follows Teresa of Ávila from the Encarnación to her death through illness, prayer, reform and opposition.
synopsis: The series picks Teresa up at twenty-three, a nun in the large, sociable Carmelite convent of the Encarnación in Ávila. Years of sickness and half-hearted prayer give way to a deeper conversion. Against the hostility of the town council and of many in her own order she founds San José, a small, poor, enclosed house, and then takes to the roads to found more. Her autobiography attracts the attention of the Inquisition; the friars opposed to the reform imprison John of the Cross. Each episode takes its title from one of her books. The eighth, 'Hija de la Iglesia', covers her last hours and her death as, in her own words, a daughter of the Church.
inclusion: It is the most ambitious attempt Spanish film or television has made at Teresa. Carmen Martín Gaite wrote the dialogue, the Teresian scholar Víctor García de la Concha advised on the scripts, and the Encarnación was rebuilt in the studio down to the colour of the habits and the refectory bowls. It was shot on 35mm, like a cinema feature. Concha Velasco spent days studying Discalced Carmelite life before filming; her Teresa is shrewd, funny, stubborn and often ill, and both the Carmelite writer Eduardo Gil de Muro and decine21 call it the performance of her career. At that length the series has time for what most saints' films skip, from convent politics, money and letters to long dry stretches of prayer and the slow cost of a vocation.
themes: Mental prayer is the centre. Teresa struggles to pray, has visions and raptures, and builds a reform so that nuns can pray in poverty and enclosure. Molina, an agnostic, set out to show a woman still walking towards holiness, and the ecstasies are played physically; Velasco arches and cries out. Alonso Franch writes that Molina filmed them without violating their mystery, and the series does not offer a medical explanation. RTVE's catalogue blurb sells Teresa as a pioneer of 'liberation of the spirit' and European modernity, a framing the series' own ending, on her dying profession of loyalty to the Church, does not bear out. Alonso Franch's article also repeats a modern claim that she was neurotic and epileptic, an aside of his that the drama does not share.
history: Teresa de Cepeda y Ahumada (1515–1582) entered the Encarnación in 1535 and founded San José in 1562, the first of her reformed Carmels. The Inquisition held her autobiography for years but never condemned it. She was canonised in 1622 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1970. The series was filmed in 1983 and premiered in Ávila.
liberties: Dialogue is newly written to sound natural, not quoted from her books, and events years apart are brought together in single scenes. The physical staging of rapture and levitation is an interpretation. Eight hours still leave out a good deal of her life, and Gil de Muro records that the Teresian scholar Tomás Álvarez had reservations he does not spell out. Shorter versions exist: a 222-minute film and a four-episode cut.
advisories:
Prolonged illness, convulsive ecstatic states, a death-bed scene and the imprisonment of John of the Cross.

Slow and dialogue-heavy over about eight hours; best for teenagers and adults.

Spanish with subtitles. The Ignatius Press DVD carries the full series.

doctrine: The Catholic Encyclopedia dates her profession to 1536, the year after she entered in November. San José was founded on 24 August. She was beatified in 1614 and canonised by Gregory XV. Her teaching is that mental prayer, the conversation of the soul with God, is open to all who persevere, and that visions and locutions are to be tested by learned confessors, as she did with Dominicans and Jesuits. The reform, begun with St John of the Cross among the friars in 1568, met opposition before the discalced province was set up on 22 June 1580 with the support of Philip II. She died at Alba de Tormes on 4 October 1582, a day reckoned as 15 October because of the calendar reform, and her feast is 15 October.

title: Clare and Francis
decision: PUBLISH: Greydanus's review and the reported reaction of the Assisi friars document a reverent, Church-loyal portrait with no invented romance; the producer's catalogue confirms Clare's vows are shown. Invented-material threshold applied to the Lux Vide/Rai saint dramas: invented scenes, composite characters, compressed chronology and renamed antagonists are acceptable when they dramatise the documented character and vocation; a record goes to HOLD when an invention changes the saint's own choices about vocation, chastity or obedience in a way the historical record contradicts (e.g. a romance for the saint, an unauthorised absence from the convent). Here the inventions are dramatic connective tissue, and the friars' objections concern depth and craftsmanship, not distortion of either vocation.
summary: A two-part Rai drama that tells the conversions of Francis and Clare side by side; its Clare is convincing, its young Francis less so.
synopsis: Assisi, 1198: the merchant families storm the towers of the nobility. Francesco, the cloth merchant Bernardone's son, is throwing stones; Chiara, a girl of the noble Offreduccio household, is trapped inside her besieged home. Years later the two meet again across a family table. Francesco renounces his father's wealth, rebuilds a ruined chapel with his own hands and attracts companions to a life of poverty. Chiara watches, and on the night of Palm Sunday she slips out of her house. In the little church Francesco has restored she lays aside her shoes and fine clothes, he cuts her hair, and she vows poverty, chastity and obedience. The rest of the drama follows the two communities, and the two friends, as they grow.
inclusion: Most films about Francis treat Clare as a footnote; this one gives her equal weight, and Mary Petruolo plays her as calm and self-possessed from the start. Steven D. Greydanus judged it a 'pick' and found the converted Francis 'joyful in humility' and devoted to the Church, though he thought the drama much less successful with Francis's worldly youth. It is a conventional Lux Vide production of the kind Rai made often in the 2000s, and some Assisi friars complained about its sets and images. Father Vincenzo Coli of the Sacro Convento praised it for avoiding the cliché of the 'two little sweethearts', a romance for which there is no historical evidence.
themes: The vows are shown explicitly and treated as the climax: Clare's flight, tonsure and profession are staged as a consecration, not an elopement. Poverty is a choice for Christ and not a social programme, and Francis's submission to the Church is part of his character. The friendship between the two saints is presented as love of each other in Christ. The drama is stronger on gesture than on prayer.
history: Clare (1194–1253) left her family on Palm Sunday night 1212 and was received by Francis at the Porziuncola. She led the Poor Ladies at San Damiano for over forty years and outlived Francis by twenty-seven. Her rule was the first written by a woman to receive papal approval.
liberties: The early meetings between the two, their families' dinner and much of the dialogue are invented. The siege that opens the film draws on Assisi's civil conflict of 1198–1200 but is shaped for drama. The film calls the church of Clare's profession simply one Francis restored; tradition places it at the Porziuncola.
advisories:
Mild violence in the street fighting that opens the film.

A few unpleasant images of leprosy.

Two long episodes (about 200 minutes); younger viewers may need it in parts. The US DVD offers Italian or an English dub.

doctrine: At the Porziuncola, the Catholic Encyclopedia records, Francis cut Clare's hair and clothed her in a rough tunic and veil. Gregory IX granted the Poor Ladies the Privilege of Poverty in 1228, securing their right to own nothing. Innocent IV confirmed Clare's own rule, keeping absolute poverty, on 9 August 1253, two days before her death. Alexander IV canonised her in 1255; her feast is 12 August. Gregory IX canonised Francis on 16 July 1228; his feast is 4 October, and the Impression of his Stigmata is kept on 17 September. Innocent III gave verbal approval to Francis's first rule; Honorius III approved the final rule in 1223. Pius XII named Clare patroness of television in 1958.
production: Lux Vide made the two-part drama with Rai Fiction and Rai Trade. Rai 1 broadcast it on 7 and 8 October 2007, around the feast of St Francis, to 6.7 and 7.8 million viewers. summary: Lux Vide's two-part Italian television life of Rita of Cascia: unwilling bride, peacemaking wife and widow, and finally Augustinian nun, amid the blood feuds of fourteenth-century Umbria.
synopsis: Rita Lotti, the only child of elderly parents in the hills above Cascia, wants to become a nun, but her parents arrange her marriage to Paolo Mancini, a hot-tempered young man from a family caught up in local feuds. Through patience and prayer she draws him away from violence, and they raise two sons. The feud does not end with his change of heart. After she loses her husband and her sons, Rita seeks admission to the Augustinian convent in Cascia, where she must first make peace between the families before she can begin her life as a religious.
inclusion: It is the fullest screen life of Rita of Cascia, one of the most popular saints of Italian devotion. Vittoria Belvedere plays Rita from girlhood to old age, and Mgr Marco Frisina, the Roman priest-composer, wrote the score. Steven D. Greydanus gave the Ignatius Press DVD a short 'Pick' in the National Catholic Register, calling it engaging and edifying, with a crisp screenplay, solid performances and good production values, and comparing its feud plot to The Godfather. He recommended the Italian soundtrack with subtitles over the English dub.
themes: The film concerns forgiveness in a culture of vendetta: a wife who draws her husband away from violence, a mother who wants her sons to forgive their father's killers, and a widow who enters religious life only after reconciling the feuding families. Marriage, motherhood and the convent appear as stages of one vocation, which is the traditional shape of Rita's life. Greydanus raises no doctrinal objection.
history: Rita (c. 1381–1457; the 1912 Catholic Encyclopedia gives 1386–1456) was married at twelve, saw her husband murdered and prayed that her sons would not avenge him. Refused at first by the Augustinians of Cascia, she was admitted after persistent pleading.
liberties: Greydanus says the film takes licence with the few known facts and singles out the arranged marriage against her wish for the convent, though that marriage is the traditional account given by the Catholic Encyclopedia.

Restrained menace and violence, including killings in a feud and a possible threat of rape.

Suitable for older children and up with parents; not rated.

doctrine: The Catholic Encyclopedia (1912) gives the traditional account that the film dramatises. Rita was born at Rocca Porena and died at the Augustinian convent of Cascia. title: Padre Pio: Miracle Man
decision: REJECT: Scope (editorial ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's subject is recognised as saint or blessed only through a canonisation or beatification made after the Second Vatican Council (Padre Pio, canonised 2002).
summary: Sergio Castellitto plays Padre Pio as gruff, funny and suffering in Carlei's Mediaset biopic, framed by an invented night-long interrogation by a sceptical envoy from Rome.
synopsis: Shortly after midnight on 22 September 1968 a prelate from Rome arrives at San Giovanni Rotondo, where crowds already wait for the morning Mass. Sent to expose the old friar's stigmata and miracles as a fraud, he questions the dying Padre Pio, and Pio answers by telling his life. We see Francesco Forgione as a peasant boy in Pietrelcina, tormented by the devil and drawn to God; his entry into the Capuchins; his illnesses; the stigmata; the crowds; and the long investigations by Church authorities, who for years restrict him to saying Mass in private. In the end the hostile cross-examination turns into the visitor's own confession, and Pio dies the next night.
inclusion: Castellitto is the reason to watch. He ages Pio from thirty to eighty and catches the dialect, the temper and the dry humour as well as the piety, and decine21 counts it among his best work. Steven Greydanus thought it the most consistently edifying of the Italian saints' miniseries he reviewed: vivid, unsentimental about the saint's irascibility, and serious about the priesthood. It is a hagiography in television form: the flashbacks march through the life in order, and Italian viewers' complaints were that it is a pious biography rather than a probing one. But the drama keeps the confessional and the Mass at the centre of Pio's life, and it is honest that a saint can be hard to like and still be obeying God.
themes: Pio's priesthood is shown through what he spent his life doing: saying Mass and hearing confessions, often sternly. Diabolical attacks are treated as real, as Pio himself described them. The Church's scrutiny of him, from the Holy Office's verdict that his phenomena were not proven supernatural to the restrictions on his ministry, is part of the story, and Pio submits to it; one scene even has him rounding on a local mayor who attacked the bishop. The frame turns on confession: the man sent to judge him ends on his knees. Mediaset's publicity, which spoke of a friar who rejected authority, does not describe the film or the man.
history: Pio (1887–1968) received the stigmata in 1918. The Holy Office sent Mgr Raffaele Rossi to investigate in 1921, declared in 1923 that the supernatural character of the phenomena was not established, and in 1931 confined him to private Mass; Pius XI lifted the ban in 1933. In 1960 John XXIII approved an apostolic visitation by Mgr Carlo Maccari, after which Pio's Masses and concelebration were limited; Paul VI removed those limits. He was canonised in 2002.
liberties: No Roman visitor interrogated Pio on the night before his death. The frame is a composite of real investigators such as Rossi (1921) and Maccari (1960), compressed into one fictional prelate. Dialogue and many incidents are invented or arranged for effect. Phillip Campbell notes that the film shows Pio slapping the mayor of San Giovanni Rotondo, where sources record him grabbing the man by the collar. The film is based on Renzo Allegri's popular biography rather than on the archival scholarship.
advisories:
Frightening scenes of diabolical attack, including the devil as a black dog, and some disturbing images of suffering.

References to misconduct by priests and one brief apparent instance (Greydanus).

Pio's temper includes physical blows. Teenagers and adults; not for young children.

Runtimes vary: about 206 minutes on Italian television, with shorter DVD cuts. The Ignatius DVD offers Italian, Spanish or an English dub.

title: Saint Philip Neri: I Prefer Heaven
decision: PUBLISH: Edoardo Aldo Cerrato of the Oratorian Confederation's procura, the best-qualified critic available, judges the portrait of Philip's priesthood, confession and obedience 'sostanzialmente positiva' while listing the historical errors, which are disclosed here. Invented-material threshold applied to the Lux Vide/Rai saint dramas: invented scenes, composite characters, compressed chronology and renamed antagonists are acceptable when they dramatise the documented character and vocation; a record goes to HOLD when an invention changes the saint's own choices about vocation, chastity or obedience in a way the historical record contradicts (e.g. a romance for the saint, an unauthorised absence from the convent). Unlike Bakhita and Moscati, the inventions here alter chronology and the Oratory's social make-up, not Philip's own vocational choices or his obedience.
summary: Gigi Proietti makes a warm, mischievous Philip Neri in Campiotti's two-part Rai drama, which is generous with invention but true to the saint's spirit.
synopsis: Filippo, already a priest, arrives in sixteenth-century Rome meaning to join Ignatius of Loyola's missionaries bound for the Indies. Instead he finds his mission in the streets around him: gangs of half-starved boys, families in debt, young men drifting. He gathers the boys, feeds them, teaches them to pray and plays with them, and his house becomes the Oratory. Opposition comes from the powerful and from Church authority, which at one point suspects him, and he bears it without breaking with the Church. In the second part the Oratory opens to adults, and young men formed there, among them a fictionalised Cesare Baronio, become priests of a new congregation.
inclusion: Gigi Proietti, a great Roman comic actor, was a natural Philip: shrewd, playful, quick to deflate pride, and plainly a man of prayer. Cerrato praised both him and the sets, and the drama mixes comedy with child poverty and illness. Its spiritual instincts are good. Cerrato, who saw it before broadcast at the producer's invitation, singled out a priest who goes to confession as well as hears it, who stays humbly faithful to the Church under trial, and who joins work and contemplation without setting them against each other. Several of the saint's own short prayers are woven into the dialogue. It is unreliable history but a convincing picture of a joyful priest.
themes: Confession is central. Philip hears the confessions of the boys and of Rome, and the film also shows him going to confession himself. Obedience under pressure is the other thread: when Church authority doubts him, he submits. His humour serves holiness, and the recurring line 'State buoni, se potete' ('Be good, if you can') is invented, as Cerrato notes, but it fits the saint's gentle realism. The Oratory's prayer, music and charity are shown as means of bringing young people to the sacraments, not as social work alone.
history: Philip Neri (1515–1595) came to Rome as a young layman and lived there for years as a lay catechist and hermit in the city. The Oratory grew from informal gatherings for prayer and spiritual conversation open to men of every class.
liberties: The liberties are large. Philip arrives as a middle-aged priest when he was in fact a young layman; his meeting with Persiano Rosa is rearranged; the Oratory becomes chiefly a refuge for street boys, where it was a gathering of young men and adults of all classes; Baronio is heavily fictionalised; and many episodes are invented outright. Cerrato lists these 'incongruenze storiche' while defending the film's spirit.
advisories:
Child poverty, hunger, illness and death, including the deaths of children.

Some menace from street gangs and from powerful enemies; no graphic violence is described.

Suitable for families with older children; the history needs correcting with a biography.

doctrine: Philip Neri, born at Florence on 22 July 1515, lived in Rome as a layman for years and was ordained priest in 1551 at his confessor's bidding. He spent long hours in the confessional and urged frequent confession and Communion. He kept up monthly exposition of the Blessed Sacrament and the Forty Hours' Devotion, and took groups on the visit to the Seven Churches of Rome. His Oratory drew people of every rank to prayer, sermons and sacred music. Gregory XIII recognised the Congregation in 1575 and gave it Santa Maria in Vallicella. He refused the cardinalate, died at Rome in May 1595, was beatified by Paul V in 1615 and canonised by Gregory XV in 1622. Reported gifts include the 1544 'heart miracle' and the reading of consciences.

title: Saint Anthony: The Miracle Worker of Padua
decision: GREY: Identity and broad content are established (Italian and English Wikipedia, AlloCiné, the Città Nuova preview, the Messenger of Saint Anthony), but every account of the film's treatment comes from interested Catholic sources, and the March 2002 La Repubblica and Corriere della Sera notices cited for its historical failings could not be read. Not HOLD, because the film is clearly identified. An independent review or a transcript checking the invented early life, Teresa's role and the 'human rights' framing would move it to PUBLISH or to reservations.
summary: A Lux Vide television life of the Portuguese Franciscan, told in flashback by the sick friar, with Daniele Liotti as Anthony and an invented companion friar.
synopsis: In 1221 a ship bringing two friars back from Africa is wrecked off Sicily. Antonio is gravely ill; his companion, Giulietto, is a cheerful, simple brother. Sheltered by a community of friars, Antonio tells them his life. Born into the Portuguese nobility, he turns down the knighthood and the war his father intends for him and enters religion instead. He joins the Franciscans, goes as a missionary to Morocco and is driven back by illness. In Italy he meets Francis of Assisi and is sent out to preach and teach. His sermons attack pride and usury, he takes the side of the poor, and the healings attributed to him make him famous. He insists that God, not he, works the miracles.
inclusion: This was the first substantial screen life of Anthony since Pietro Francisci's little-known film of 1949, and Italian television treated it as an event. Daniele Liotti plays Anthony as a learned, ascetic preacher, set against Enrico Brignano's Giulietto, an invented friar who stands for Franciscan simplicity. The friars' own Messenger praised the casting and the staging of the miracles. It is widely available with English subtitles on DVD and Catholic streaming services.
themes: The film's Catholic content includes a vocation chosen against a father's ambitions, the Franciscan ideal of poverty, preaching against sin and usury, and miracles worked through prayer. The Messenger of Saint Anthony points to Anthony's line that he does not work miracles, God does, which ties the wonders to grace. The publicity leans towards a modern reading. The Città Nuova preview calls Anthony a forerunner of human-rights defenders, and the stress on his campaign for the poor may tilt the story towards social reform.
history: Fernando de Bulhões was born at Lisbon about 1195 and joined the Canons Regular of St Augustine. In 1220 the bodies of five Franciscans killed in Morocco were brought to Coimbra, and he left to join the Friars Minor, taking the name Anthony. He sailed for Morocco but fell ill, and the ship was driven to Sicily in 1221. He attended the Franciscan chapter at Assisi that year, was sent to a hermitage, and his gift for preaching was discovered by chance at an ordination. St Francis made him the order's first lector in theology. He preached in northern Italy and southern France against heresy, usury and injustice, and settled at Padua, where he died on 13 June 1231 at Arcella, aged about thirty-six. Gregory IX canonised him at Spoleto on 30 May 1232, within a year, and Pius XII declared him a Doctor of the Church on 16 January 1946.
liberties: The makers acknowledge that little is documented of Anthony's early years, so they are largely invented, including the clash with his father over knighthood and war; historians and the Basilica's friars were consulted. Giulietto is an invented character. Teresa, played by Vittoria Puccini, is not a known historical figure. La Repubblica and Corriere della Sera reportedly faulted the film's historical fidelity at its premiere.
advisories:
A shipwreck, serious illness and scenes of miraculous healing.

No sexual content or strong language is reported; the role of a young woman in Anthony's early life is unverified.

Suitable for families; distributed unrated.

The early life is largely invented and is not a reliable guide to the saint's biography.

grey.question: This Lux Vide television film is a devout life of St Anthony, made with the cooperation of the friars of Padua. No independent review of it exists; the detailed accounts come from the friars' own Messenger and from the producers. The makers admit the early life is largely invented, Italian critics reportedly faulted its history, and its publicity presents Anthony as a forerunner of human rights. A review by an independent critic, or a transcript showing how it handles his preaching, miracles and invented characters, would settle it.

doctrine: Anthony is the Doctor Evangelicus, so named for his sermons on Scripture. Canonisation is the Church's infallible declaration that a servant of God is in heaven. The Church teaches that miracles are works of God and that a saint intercedes (Council of Trent, Session 25, on the invocation of saints), as Anthony insists in the film. The devotion to St Anthony as the finder of lost things, and the 'Anthony's bread' for the poor, grew from the later Middle Ages; the Church allows but does not require them. His feast is 13 June.
production: An Italian television film for Canale 5, made by Lux Vide with the cooperation of the friars of the Basilica in Padua and shot in Spain in five weeks. It runs 102 minutes and was first broadcast on 1 April 2002, to more than seven million viewers.

title: Saint John Bosco: Mission to Love
decision: PUBLISH: A detailed Salesian review (interested but specific and critical) documents catechesis, Dominic Savio, Bosco's own words on holiness and his obedience to the Pope in the conflict with his archbishop, and lists the compressions and renamed characters disclosed here. Rai Teche and RaiPlay fix identity. Invented-material threshold applied to the Lux Vide/Rai saint dramas: invented scenes, composite characters, compressed chronology and renamed antagonists are acceptable when they dramatise the documented character and vocation; a record goes to HOLD when an invention changes the saint's own choices about vocation, chastity or obedience in a way the historical record contradicts (e.g. a romance for the saint, an unauthorised absence from the convent). Here inventions are composites and telescoping that do not alter Bosco's vocation or obedience.
summary: Flavio Insinna plays Don Bosco in a brisk, compressed Rai/Lux Vide life of the Turin priest who built schools and a religious family for abandoned boys.
synopsis: A Piedmontese farm boy who lost his father young, Giovanni Bosco follows his mentor into the seminary and arrives in Turin as a young priest. The city is full of hungry, exploited and violent boys, some in prison. He gathers them on Sundays, feeds them, teaches them catechism and a trade, and is chased from site to site by suspicious neighbours, officials and clergy. A wealthy noblewoman, the Marchesa Barolo, helps and then drops him. His mother Margherita comes to cook for the boys. Dominic Savio arrives. A liberal official, played by Charles Dance, schemes against him, and his friendship with the archbishop turns to conflict, which Bosco ends by submitting at the Pope's request. The Salesian congregation is founded to carry the work on.
inclusion: Flavio Insinna, later a popular television host, plays Bosco. Like the best Bosco lives, the film shows a priest whose kindness to delinquent boys always aims at their souls. It quotes Bosco's own sayings on holiness and gives time to the catechism lessons, and it introduces Dominic Savio, the pupil he raised to sanctity. The Salesian reviewer FrMike judges that it presents Don Bosco's mission and personality well, while poking at details such as the repeated 'Father Bosco' of the dub. He also found the Italian-origin lines well dubbed into English for the US DVD.
themes: The Preventive System is shown as religion, reason and kindness, with the sacraments and catechism at its heart. Bosco's priesthood is active and pastoral, and his holiness is ordinary hard work and trust in Providence. By the Salesian reviewer's account the best scene is his conflict with the archbishop. The film shows an early friendship, the archbishop's zeal for training priests, his view of Bosco as proud, and Bosco's eventual humbling of himself in obedience to the Pope to end the dispute. Anticlerical politics of the Risorgimento form the background.
history: John Bosco (1815–1888) opened his Oratory at Valdocco in 1846, founded the Salesians in 1859 and the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians in 1872. His long dispute with Archbishop Lorenzo Gastaldi of Turin in the 1870s–80s was settled under Leo XIII. Dominic Savio died in 1857 aged fourteen.
liberties: Events from 1844 to 1882 are telescoped, so Mamma Margherita (d. 1856) and Joseph Cafasso (d. 1860) are present at a finale set decades after their deaths. Opponents are renamed: the Salesian reviewer notes that the vicar Cavour becomes the 'Prefect Clementi', who later absorbs Urbano Rattazzi, and that in the version he saw Archbishop Gastaldi becomes 'Cardinal Fassati'. The Oratory is placed in open country, and in fact it stood on Turin's edge.
advisories:
Neglected and abused children, prison scenes, illness and death.

Scuffles and street violence of a mild, television kind.

Good for families with children over ten, with an adult on hand to correct the compressed history.

Italian and English tracks exist, and the English-subtitled Italian version condenses the dialogue.

title: Maria Goretti
decision: GREY: The English subtitles settle what the earlier record left open. Maria refuses Alessandro by naming the sin and warning him of hell, the assault is brief and not lingered on, and on her deathbed she forgives him and asks to have him with her in heaven; his repentance follows. On the saint the film is sound. The reservation (editor ruling, 2026-10-11) is liturgical: Mass and Communion in 1902 are given in post-conciliar vernacular form ("The Body of Christ. Amen"; "Go, the Mass is over"), which places the reformed rite in a pre-conciliar saint's life as if it were the Church's worship of her day.
summary: Giulio Base's Rai film of the Goretti story, told in flashback from a hospital bed, with Martina Pinto as the devout farm girl killed in 1902.
synopsis: July 1902, the Pontine Marshes. Maria Goretti, not yet twelve, is rushed to hospital with stab wounds while carabinieri protect twenty-year-old Alessandro Serenelli from a lynch mob. As her mother Assunta waits and the Passionist Padre Basilio prays at her bedside, the film goes back. The Gorettis and the Serenellis share a farmhouse as illiterate labourers on a landowner's estate, in a district ravaged by malaria. Maria is cheerful, generous and preparing for her First Communion. Alessandro, raised by a drunken, irreligious father who resents Luigi Goretti's help, clings to his friendship with the girl. Illness and death strike the Goretti family, poverty deepens, and Alessandro's attention turns to menace. When Maria resists his assault, he stabs her. Dying, she forgives him.
inclusion: Steven D. Greydanus, in the National Catholic Register, judged it dramatically effective, devout and responsible with the historical facts. Other notices are cooler: the most-read FilmTV.it review calls it conventional television drama, slow, didactic and peopled with one-dimensional characters, though it credits Martina Pinto and Fabrizio Bucci, and ranks it below Genina's 1949 Heaven over the Marshes. It is the more literal of the two films, framed through the memories of a Passionist priest, and keeps close to the familiar account of the martyrdom and the forgiveness.
themes: Purity and forgiveness run through it. Maria's piety is shown through prayer and her preparation for First Communion, which she receives; her father calls hatred a disease whose only cure is Jesus. When Alessandro attacks her she refuses by naming the sin and warning him of hell, and dying she forgives him and asks to have him with her in heaven, the traditional reading of her death. Alessandro is given a background of neglect and an irreligious, drinking father, which explains him without excusing him; his repentance is shown at her bedside and in a closing title. Padre Basilio, who cites Rerum novarum against the landowners, recovers from a crisis over his vocation through her example.
history: Maria Goretti was born at Corinaldo in 1890. Her family, ruined by poverty, settled in 1899 at Le Ferriere near Nettuno, sharing a house with the Serenellis; her father died of malaria soon after. On 5 July 1902 Alessandro Serenelli tried to rape her and, when she refused, stabbed her fourteen times. She forgave him and died the next day. He repented in prison, was released after twenty-seven years, asked her mother's pardon and became a Capuchin lay brother.
liberties: The framing through Padre Basilio's memories is a dramatic device, and his crisis over leaving the priesthood and the Countess Mazzoleni (Claudia Koll) appear to be inventions. Alessandro's plea for forgiveness at Maria's hospital bedside is invented; historically his repentance came in prison years later. The Communion and dismissal formulas, as subtitled, are those of the modern rite, an anachronism for 1902.
advisories:
Restrained but frank sexual menace and an attempted rape; a fatal stabbing (Greydanus). The dialogue of the assault is brief.

Death of a parent from illness; poverty and a drunken, abusive father.

Teens and up.

sources.claims: Art. 5: faith is not the only cause of martyrdom; all virtuous deeds referred to God are professions of faith

grey.question: On St Maria Goretti herself the film is sound. She refuses Alessandro by calling the act a sin, the assault is handled briefly, and she dies forgiving him and wanting him with her in heaven. The reservation concerns the liturgy. Mass and Communion in 1902 are shown with the vernacular formulas of the post-conciliar rite, an anachronism that presents the reformed Mass as the worship of her time. Viewers who accept that liberty will find a faithful account otherwise.

suitability.note: The assault is brief and not shown in detail, but the menace is plain and her death in hospital is hard to watch. Older children who know the story will find a clear example of purity and forgiveness; a parent should watch with them.

doctrine: Pius XII beatified Maria Goretti on 27 April 1947, with her mother present, and canonised her on 24 June 1950 in St Peter's Square before a crowd of about half a million. She is venerated as a martyr. St Thomas Aquinas teaches that faith is not the only cause of martyrdom: any virtuous act referred to God is a profession of faith, so a death suffered in defence of chastity can be martyrdom (Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 124, a. 5). The Passionists guided her spiritual formation and promoted her cause, and her remains rest in their basilica at Nettuno. Her feast is 6 July, the day she died. Her deathbed forgiveness of Alessandro follows Our Lord's prayer for His executioners (Luke 23:34).
production: Lux Vide and Rai Fiction made the film in 2002 for the centenary of Maria's death, with the patronage of the Passionist Congregation. Giulio Base, who directed, also plays the hospital doctor. Rai 1 broadcast it on 23 February 2003 to about 9.9 million viewers, a 35 per cent share, and TV2000 and Rai Premium have repeated it.

title: Joseph of Nazareth
alternateTitles: Gli amici di Gesù – Giuseppe di Nazareth
Joseph of Nazareth: The Man Closest to Christ
decision: GREY: The subtitle file corrects the record and sharpens the question. Joseph is not a widower: his betrothed was killed at Bethlehem years before and he has never married, and the brethren are his nephews Joses, Simon and Judas, so Mary's perpetual virginity is kept on St Jerome's reading. The virginal conception is plain, and at his death Joseph addresses Jesus as Lord and God. The weak point is the annunciation to Joseph: he asks whether Mary was forced, suspects a village youth and says he trusts his eyes, and a rabbi advises marrying her and repudiating her quietly. That suspicion, allowed by some Fathers but rejected by Jerome and St Thomas, is for the reader to weigh. Not REJECT; not PUBLISH while the only assessment is one present-day Catholic critic.
summary: Lux Vide's television life of St Joseph, with Tobias Moretti as a carpenter who works on Herod's Temple, accepts Mary's child, and raises Jesus in Nazareth.
synopsis: Joseph, a carpenter of David's line who has mourned for ten years a betrothed killed in Bethlehem, works on Herod's rebuilding of the Temple, where the king learns his name and praises his skill. He lives with his nephews Joses, Simon and Judas; Judas dies after a clash with Roman soldiers. Joseph is betrothed to the young Mary. When he learns she is pregnant he asks whether she was forced or unfaithful and will not believe her, and a rabbi advises him to marry her and put her away quietly. An angel in a dream tells him the child is conceived by the Holy Spirit. After the birth in Bethlehem, Herod identifies the child through the craftsman he knows, and the family flees into Egypt. Back in Nazareth, Simon joins the Zealots and kills Joses as a traitor. Joseph dies with Jesus beside him, and Simon repents.
inclusion: Joseph seldom gets a film of his own, and this one, the first of Lux Vide's Friends of Jesus films and first shown on Canale 5 in January 2000, takes him seriously as a man with a trade, a family and a conscience. Tobias Moretti plays him as a vigorous craftsman, not an old man, and Steven D. Greydanus found the result an attractive picture of Joseph as head of the Holy Family. There are good ideas: Joseph's distaste for the state of Herod's Temple foreshadows Christ's cleansing of it, and his resistance to early zealots anticipates Christ's refusal of armed means. It is weaker where it invents. Greydanus finds Herod's acquaintance with Joseph unconvincing and the plotting round Mary's silence frustrating. Marco Frisina wrote the score. It suits families who know the Gospel accounts well enough to tell the inventions from the text.
themes: At the centre is Joseph's obedience: he is a just man who accepts the angel's word and the care of the incarnate Son. The film keeps the virginal conception and Mary's perpetual virginity. Mary offers to accept punishment and calls him a just man. At his death Joseph addresses Jesus as the Lord's anointed, his Lord and his God.
history: The Gospels say little of Joseph: a just man of David's line, a craftsman of Nazareth, betrothed to Mary, who took her as his wife after an angel's message, went to Bethlehem, fled into Egypt and returned to Nazareth. He last appears when Jesus is twelve. That he was an older widower with children from an earlier marriage comes from the second-century Protoevangelium of James; St Jerome held instead that he was a virgin and that the brethren were cousins. The film follows Jerome.
liberties: Joseph's earlier betrothed, Herod's acquaintance with him through the Temple works, and the king's identification of the child through him are invented. The plan to marry Mary and repudiate her quietly is a speculative reading of Matthew. The Lord's brethren become Joseph's nephews Joses, Simon and Judas; James is left out, Judas dies young, and Joses is killed by his brother Simon, a Zealot, who repents at Joseph's deathbed. This sits awkwardly with the tradition linking Simon and Jude to the apostles of those names.
advisories:
Herod's threat to the child and the flight into Egypt; a clash with Roman soldiers; one nephew is killed by his brother.

Joseph suspects Mary of infidelity and confronts her angrily.

Suitable for older children and families.

Several episodes in the Holy Family's life are invented, and Joseph's suspicion of Mary goes beyond the reading of St Jerome and St Thomas.

grey.question: This Lux Vide film keeps the doctrine intact. The virginal conception is plain, Joseph has never married, and the Lord's brethren are his nephews, as St Jerome held. The doubt concerns Joseph's first reaction. Before the angel speaks he asks whether Mary was forced, suspects a village youth and says he trusts his eyes over her word, and a rabbi advises him to marry her and repudiate her quietly. Some Fathers allowed such a suspicion, but Jerome and St Thomas held that Joseph never doubted her. The film also invents Herod's acquaintance with Joseph and has one nephew killed by his brother.

doctrine: On Joseph the Gospels say little, and the Catholic Encyclopedia (1912) calls the first chapters of Matthew and Luke practically the only reliable sources. It says he was a craftsman, a tekton, and that the marriage to Mary was intended to be a virgin marriage, citing Augustine and Aquinas. The apocryphal tales of an older widower with children are unreliable; Jerome called them 'dreams'. In its article on the Brethren of the Lord the Encyclopedia says most Latin Fathers held the brethren to be the Lord's cousins, while most Greek Fathers made them sons of Joseph by an earlier marriage, and it notes the great antiquity of belief in Mary's perpetual virginity. Sixtus IV (1471-84) saw Joseph's feast of 19 March included in the Roman Calendar, and Pius IX declared him patron of the Catholic Church in December 1870.

title: Saint Peter
decision: PUBLISH: The English subtitle file supplies the transcript the earlier question asked for. Peter's primacy is explicit: Christ's promise at Caesarea Philippi, on this rock I will build my church, is given in full; Peter is called first among the apostles; and at the Council of Jerusalem he closes the debate on his own authority and rules that Gentiles are to be baptised and saved by the grace of the Lord. The Last Supper presents Christ's body given in sacrifice and the new and eternal covenant. Quo Vadis and the inverted crucifixion follow tradition. Talk of embracing everyone refers to the Gentiles' admission, not to modern dialogue. Identity: Italian Wikipedia; content: Dove, CatholicMom and the dialogue check.
summary: Omar Sharif plays Peter from the days after the Crucifixion to his own death in Nero's Rome, in Lux Vide's two-part drama drawn from Acts and tradition.
synopsis: After the Crucifixion Peter is crushed by his denial and doubts he can lead the apostles. The risen Christ appears and forgives him, and at Pentecost the apostles receive the Holy Spirit and preach openly. Stephen is stoned, Saul persecutes the Church and is converted on the road to Damascus, Peter baptises the centurion Cornelius, and the apostles meet in Jerusalem to settle the admission of Gentiles before dispersing. In the second part an aged Peter reaches Rome in 64, on the day Paul is arrested. He works among the poor while invented subplots follow a gladiator and his family and a pair of young lovers. After the great fire Nero blames the Christians. Peter leaves the city, meets Christ on the road, turns back, gives himself up so that others may go free, and is crucified upside down at his own request.
inclusion: Omar Sharif's Peter is the reason to watch. Reviewers of different stripes single him out. The Dove Foundation's Edwin Carpenter calls the performance compassionate and strong, and Stuart Dunn at CatholicMom finds Sharif the highlight. The first part follows the Acts of the Apostles closely, and Dunn notes how much of the dialogue comes straight from Scripture. The second is looser, padding the Roman years with invented melodrama about a gladiator and two young lovers. It keeps the Church at the centre, with Peter a weak man made strong and the first community growing under persecution.
themes: The drama turns on Peter's repentance, as the forgiven denier becomes the rock who leads the others. His primacy is explicit. Christ's promise at Caesarea Philippi is given in full, Peter is called the first of the apostles, and at the Council of Jerusalem he ends the debate on his own authority and rules that the Gentiles are to be baptised and saved by grace. Pentecost, the conversion of Saul and the baptism of Cornelius are decisive steps in the mission. At the Last Supper the Eucharist is Christ's body given in sacrifice and the new and eternal covenant. The Quo Vadis episode and the inverted crucifixion follow the ancient tradition of Peter's martyrdom in Rome.
history: Simon Peter, a fisherman of Bethsaida and Capernaum, was called by Christ and named Cephas, the Rock (John 1:42; Matthew 16:18). He denied his Master three times and was restored after the Resurrection (John 21). After Pentecost he led the Church in Jerusalem, baptised the centurion Cornelius, the first Gentile convert (Acts 10), and spoke the decisive word at the Council of Jerusalem about AD 49-50 (Acts 15). Tradition places him at Rome, where, as the Catholic Encyclopedia holds, he died in the persecution of Nero, probably between 64 and 67, crucified head downwards, as Origen reports. He was buried on the Vatican hill, where Constantine built the basilica over his tomb. Paul was beheaded at Rome in the same persecution.
liberties: The gladiator Davide, his wife Anna, and the young lovers Claudio and Silvia are invented. Dunn calls a market scene in which Jesus appears to Peter fictitious and unnecessary, and the subplot about Cornelius's family padding. Chronology is compressed: Peter reaches Rome on the day of Paul's arrest, and Paul is executed before the fire, although tradition places his death after it.
advisories:
Frequent violence: the stoning of Stephen, gladiator fights, an off-screen throat-cutting, a man set on fire, and Peter's crucifixion with brief blood (Dove).

Prostitutes approach Peter; brief romantic embraces; some cleavage.

Ages 12 and up.

Invented subplots fill much of the Roman half.
