doctrine: Peter holds the primacy among the Apostles. The Church reads Matthew 16:18-19 and John 21:15-17 as Christ's grant to Peter of the keys and the care of the whole flock, and the First Vatican Council defined in 1870 (Pastor aeternus) that the Roman Pontiff succeeds him in this primacy and teaches infallibly ex cathedra on faith and morals. The film's meeting with Christ on the Appian Way, 'Quo vadis?', comes from the apocryphal Acts of Peter (late second century) and not from Scripture. The film's Council of Jerusalem presents the Church's teaching that the Gentiles are not bound by the Mosaic law.
production: A long, earnest television miniseries made for Rai by Lux Vide with San Paolo Film. It was released in 2005 as San Pietro and is known in English as Imperium: Saint Peter. About eight million Italians watched each night in October 2005.

title: Pius XII: Under the Roman Sky
decision: GREY: Independent coverage (Angela Cinicolo's Movieplayer.it review, Il Post's report, Donatella Di Cesare's essay in the Rome Jewish community's Moked dossier, Corrado Augias via Wikipedia) establishes the content and documented historical distortions, and Lux Vide itself conceded inaccuracies. The English subtitle file adds detail: the Pope orders enclosed convents opened and offers gold towards the ransom; a priest's appeal to General Stahel is shown halting the arrests; and the Pope explains his public silence by the Dutch bishops' protest, citing an unsupported figure of forty thousand deported. There is no doctrinal problem, and Pius XII is only Venerable, so rule (a) does not apply. The reservation is historical.
summary: James Cromwell plays Pius XII in Lux Vide's two-part drama of the German occupation of Rome, a sympathetic account of papal caution that Rome's Jewish community attacked as apologetic.
synopsis: September 1943: after the armistice, German troops occupy Rome, and Pius XII stays in the city. The Germans extort fifty kilograms of gold from the Jewish community under threat of deporting two hundred people. The Pope deals with the German commander, General Stahel, has Jews sheltered in convents and seminaries, and weighs whether to protest publicly, while Berlin considers abducting him. On 16 October about a thousand Jews are rounded up, among them the father of Miriam, a young Jewish woman. She escapes and is hidden in a convent with help from Davide, a black-market charmer who loves her, and Marco, a student who has joined the partisans. Stahel is replaced by the SS general Karl Wolff. Marco dies after the Via Rasella attack. Rome is liberated in June 1944, and Miriam finds her brother and marries Davide.
inclusion: It is the most substantial screen defence of Pius XII's conduct in occupied Rome, and part of its interest is the argument it provoked. Duguay stages the occupation well. Movieplayer.it's Angela Cinicolo praised the depiction of the German encirclement and the mounting fear in the ghetto, while finding the papal scenes almost didactic and the young people's romance sentimental. Cromwell plays Pius as reserved, prudent and troubled, a man who opens convents and churches but will not denounce the deportations publicly. The makers drew on testimony gathered for his beatification cause, and the distributor says so. Its critics, from Rome's chief rabbi Riccardo Di Segni to the philosopher Donatella Di Cesare, called it apologetic.
themes: The Catholic subject is the Pope as shepherd under occupation, with prayer before the crucifix, the duty to protect his flock, and charity to the Jews through religious houses. The film presents his public silence as prudence. Pacelli says he cannot take one people's side against another, and fears that open protest would cost more lives. A German general keeps a rosary in his desk, and the ending points towards reconciliation. Di Cesare objected that the film casts Pius as carrying the cross, and that scenes of hidden Jews dressed as priests and nuns hint at conversion. Nothing here departs from Catholic teaching.
history: German troops occupied Rome on 10 September 1943. On 26 September the SS demanded fifty kilograms of gold from the Jewish community in exchange for the Jews not being deported, and the gold was collected, with the Vatican reportedly offering to lend part of it. On 16 October the Germans arrested over a thousand Jews in the old ghetto and deported them to Auschwitz; only a handful returned. Many others were hidden in convents, monasteries and Vatican properties. On 23 March 1944 partisans attacked a German column in the Via Rasella, and on 24 March the Germans shot 335 men at the Ardeatine Caves. Rome was liberated on 4 June 1944. Pius XII (Eugenio Pacelli, pope 1939-1958) made no explicit public protest naming the Jews; historians still dispute whether more could have been done. The Vatican opened its archives for his pontificate in March 2020.
liberties: Miriam, Davide and Marco are invented. Critics identified concrete distortions: the film shows a priest's appeal to General Stahel cutting short the ghetto round-up, which Di Segni and many historians deny; the Italian Fascists all but vanish; Via Rasella and the Fosse Ardeatine get only passing notice; and, according to Corrado Augias, it credits Vatican pressure with a peaceful German withdrawal and omits the La Storta massacre. The Pope justifies his silence by the Dutch bishops' protest, with an unsupported figure of forty thousand deported. The kidnap plot rests on disputed sources.
advisories:
Round-ups, deportations and shootings; the Via Rasella attack and its aftermath.

A wartime romance between young adults; no explicit sexual content is reported.

Teens and up.

A one-sided treatment of a disputed history, with documented distortions.

grey.question: The film defends Pius XII's wartime conduct. He opens enclosed convents to Jews, offers gold for the ransom, and explains his public silence by the deportations that followed the Dutch bishops' protest. That is a legitimate view, but the film reaches it partly by altering the record. It shows a priest's appeal to the German commander cutting short the October 1943 round-up, nearly erases the Italian Fascists, and passes quickly over the Fosse Ardeatine. Rome's chief rabbi called it propaganda, and its producer admitted inaccuracies. Treat it as advocacy drama and read a serious history alongside it.

doctrine: In Mystici Corporis (1943) Pius XII taught that the Church is the Mystical Body of Christ and that Christ's charity extends to every person, and in Summi Pontificatus (1939) he affirmed the unity of the human race. The film leans on the Church's teaching on works of mercy: shelter for the hunted and fugitive. It also touches the difficult prudential question the Pope faced, whether public condemnation of a persecutor would save those in danger or provoke greater reprisals. The Church teaches that a pope's governance and prudential judgments are not infallible; infallibility is limited to definitions of faith and morals ex cathedra (Vatican I, 1870), so the debate about his silence is a question of historical judgment, not doctrine.
production: An Italian-German television film, shown on Rai 1 in 2010. Di Segni called it propaganda and apologetics full of errors. Corrado Augias criticised it as a work meant to shape Pius XII's image for sainthood and listed historical falsehoods, among them the claim that the Pope personally stopped the raid on the Roman ghetto. The producer Bernabei admitted some inaccuracies but said it was not a documentary, and the writers said they aimed at storytelling, not historical judgment.

title: God's Mighty Servant
alternateTitles: God's Mighty Servant: Sister Pascalina Lehnert
God's Mighty Servant: Sister Pascalina Lehnert, Secretary of Pius XII
decision: GREY: Dating settled: Ziegler Film gives production year 2009; first broadcast on Das Erste on 22 and 23 April 2011 (Good Friday and Holy Saturday, per the Abendzeitung review of 20 April 2011); repeated 13 June 2012. Two independent reviews (Abendzeitung, evangelisch.de) establish the content and its historical liberties. The reservations are historical and concern the picture of convent life; neither hard rule applies (Pius XII is Venerable only; Pascalina has no cause). A editorial ruling that the convent portrayal is fair would move it to PUBLISH.
summary: A two-part German drama of Sister Pascalina Lehnert, the Bavarian nun who ran Eugenio Pacelli's household for forty years, with Christine Neubauer and Remo Girone as Pius XII.
synopsis: Josefine Lehnert, a Bavarian farmer's daughter whose father opposes her schooling, enters a convent as Sister Pascalina. She is sent to keep house for the papal nuncio in Munich, Eugenio Pacelli, and becomes his secretary. After her father dies unreconciled, her superiors and fellow sisters turn against her; she is accused of an improper relationship with Pacelli, confined, and sent away to recover from asthma. She returns to him when he becomes Cardinal Secretary of State and slips into the Vatican. In the second part she helps with the Reich Concordat and the encyclical Mit brennender Sorge, sees Pacelli elected Pius XII, and runs his war relief. The Pope weighs whether to protest the persecution of the Jews, opens church buildings to refugees and is warned of a plan to abduct him. He dies in 1958, still doubting his choices.
inclusion: It gives an unusual view of the Vatican from inside the papal household, and of a woman who held influence there without any office. The evangelisch.de reviewer found it gripping and free of religious kitsch, and thought Neubauer, a much-mocked star, right for the stubborn, practical nun. Robert Braunmüller in the Abendzeitung was scathing. He found it dull, repetitive, sentimental at the end, and a whitewash of Pius XII. The Lexikon des internationalen Films called it sprawling. Its value is the household view of a pontificate, and the history should be checked against better sources.
themes: The religious substance is Pascalina's vocation, with obedience to superiors who mistreat her, fidelity to the priest she serves, and practical charity in the papal relief work. The convent scenes are unflattering. The evangelisch.de reviewer found the order's ways medieval and unworldly, and the drama of jealous sisters and a false charge of impropriety turns religious life into an obstacle course. Pius XII is devout, anxious and burdened by his silence, which Braunmüller reads as Catholic apologetics. The film does not mock the faith, but it treats Church institutions mainly as power and politics, with the heroine's common sense as the corrective.
history: Josefine Lehnert (1894–1983) joined the Holy Cross Sisters of Menzingen and from 1917 kept house for Pacelli as nuncio in Munich, and from 1925 in Berlin. She followed him to Rome, stayed throughout his pontificate and directed his private charity office from 1944 to 1958. Her memoir, written in 1959, was not allowed to appear until 1982. John XXIII gave her the Pro Ecclesia et Pontifice medal. She died in Vienna.
liberties: Braunmüller notes that the film brings Pascalina into Pacelli's household earlier than in fact, likens the Allied bombing of Rome to the deportation of its Jews, idealises King Ludwig III, and gives the Pope a line about his silence that predates knowledge of the Holocaust. The evangelisch.de reviewer adds that the second part makes Pascalina rescue Rome's Jews almost single-handedly. The house arrest and the accusations against her are dramatised from Schad's account.
advisories:
Wartime violence: revolutionary fighting in Munich, the 1923 putsch, the bombing of Rome and the deportations.

An accusation of an improper relationship between a nun and a prelate; no sexual content is reported.

Teens and up.

Historical compressions, and a heroine whose role is enlarged.

grey.question: This German two-parter is sympathetic to Sister Pascalina and to Pius XII, but its history is loose. Critics note that it enlarges her role until she seems to rescue Rome's Jews almost alone, shifts dates, and handles the Holocaust question sentimentally. Its picture of convent life is harsh, with jealous sisters, a false charge of impropriety and superiors who block her at every turn. Viewers should weigh whether that picture of religious life is fair, and treat the wartime episodes as drama and not as history.

doctrine: The film touches the papacy under Pius XI and Pius XII. The Church holds that the Roman Pontiff has full and supreme power over the whole Church (Vatican Council, 1870). Pius XI's encyclical Mit brennender Sorge (14 March 1937) condemned Nazi doctrine on race and the state, after repeated violations of the Reich Concordat of 20 July 1933. Pius XII defined the dogma of the Assumption in Munificentissimus Deus on 1 November 1950 and wrote on the Church as the Mystical Body in Mystici Corporis (1943). Pascalina's life is that of a Sister of the Holy Cross of Menzingen, bound by vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, serving a Cardinal Secretary of State and a Pope. Whether he should have protested publicly against the persecution of the Jews is still disputed by historians.
production: Ziegler Film made this two-part German television film of about 180 minutes for ARD (Das Erste), which showed it in 2011. The crew moved fourteen times and shot in Germany and Italy. The Munich putsch of Hitler was staged on the Odeonsplatz with about 350 extras, and since filming in the Vatican was not possible a balcony was built for the papal coronation scene. About 4,000 costume pieces were made. Remo Girone was nominated at the Monte-Carlo Television Festival, and the film for best film at the Mirabile Dictu Catholic film festival.

title: Blessed Duns Scotus: Defender of the Immaculate Conception
decision: REJECT: Scope (editorial ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's subject is recognised as saint or blessed only through a canonisation or beatification made after the Second Vatican Council (John Duns Scotus, cult confirmed 1993).
summary: A low-budget Italian drama in which the Franciscan theologian Duns Scotus teaches, prays and argues for Mary's Immaculate Conception: earnest, talky and unusually serious about ideas.
synopsis: In Paris in 1303 the friar John Duns Scotus refuses to sign King Philip IV's appeal against Pope Boniface VIII and is expelled from the university. The film moves between his teaching, his memories of a Scottish boyhood spent wanting to join the Franciscans, and the formation of three novices, one of whom falls for a pious orphan girl and must decide whether he has a vocation. Scotus tells a brilliant student that he studies too much and prays too little, and grounds his own theology in adoration before the Eucharist. The climax is an open-air disputation with Dominican masters over whether Mary was conceived without original sin.
inclusion: Films about theologians are rare because argument is hard to film; this one makes a real attempt. Adriano Braidotti plays Scotus with quiet conviction and makes dry scholastic reasoning sound like something worth living by. The film's point is that thinking about God is a form of prayer and needs prayer: study grows from contemplation of the Eucharist, and the doctrine defended is understood as an act of love for Our Lady. The blog critic Mercuriade called it a successful experiment that avoids the syrup of most saints' films. Its faults are plain. The budget is small, the debates rely on exposition, the novices' subplot is formulaic, and the devotional tableaux are sugary.
themes: The Immaculate Conception is presented as Scotus argued it: Christ, the perfect Redeemer, preserved his Mother from original sin by a more perfect redemption, in view of his merits. That is substantially what Pius IX defined in Ineffabilis Deus in 1854. Before then the question was open. St Bernard opposed the feast, and St Thomas Aquinas and St Bonaventure did not accept the doctrine in the form Scotus later defended, and in 1483 Sixtus IV forbade either side to call the other heretical. The film is a Franciscan partisan of a side that the Church later vindicated; viewers should not take its Dominicans as villains. Loyalty to the Pope and devotion to the Eucharist frame the argument.
history: John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a Scottish Franciscan, taught at Oxford, Paris and Cologne. Contemporary sources on his life are thin. He was among the friars expelled from Paris in 1303 for siding with Boniface VIII against Philip IV, and his Sentences commentary laid out the argument from preservative redemption. His cult was confirmed, amounting to beatification, by John Paul II in 1993.
liberties: The novices, their romance and much of the dialogue are invented. The climactic public disputation with the Dominicans comes from later Franciscan tradition about a Paris debate and is not documented in contemporary sources; the arguments are Scotus's, the event is staged. Scenes of his boyhood vocation are imaginative.
advisories:
A brief, sudden image of Christ's scourging (about 16 minutes in).

A chaste romantic subplot about discernment.

Dense philosophical dialogue; best for older teenagers and adults.

Available in English as Blessed Duns Scotus: Defender of the Immaculate Conception (Ignatius Press DVD, Italian or English audio).

title: Into Great Silence
decision: REJECT: Scope (editorial ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's Catholic content is the post-conciliar Church, presented as normal or exemplary: the Grande Chartreuse as it lives today, after the Carthusians' post-conciliar liturgical revision.
summary: Philip Gröning's near-wordless documentary about the Carthusian monks of the Grande Chartreuse: almost three hours of prayer, work and seasons, with no narration at all.
synopsis: Gröning asked the Carthusians for permission to film in 1984; they answered sixteen years later. He then lived at the Grande Chartreuse, the order's mother house in the French Alps, for about six months, shooting alone with available light. The film follows the cycle of the year and of the day: night Office in the dark church, solitary meals passed through hatches, wood-chopping, tailoring, a barber's chair, snow. Two postulants are received as novices and tonsured. On the weekly walk the monks talk and laugh. Late in the film an old, blind monk speaks about death, God's Providence and the loss of faith in the world outside.
inclusion: This is cinema used for something it rarely attempts: making time felt. There is no commentary, no interview to explain things, and no music except the monks' chant. Scripture verses return as intertitles, and the repetitions build up the rhythm of a life given entirely to prayer. Gröning's images, many of them grainy from the low light, have a painterly patience, and the film rewards a viewer who stops waiting for events. The monks' weekly walk, full of talk and laughter, comes as a welcome surprise. At 164 minutes it is long and some find it stupefying; it is best watched in one sitting in a dark room, or not at all.
themes: The content is unmistakably Catholic. The monks chant a patristic text on the Holy Spirit that is, as Greydanus puts it, a small catechesis in Trinitarian doctrine. The intertitles quote the Gospels and the prophets on giving up everything to follow Christ. The reception of novices and the blind monk's reflections show vocation as an answer to God, not a lifestyle. The Carthusians kept their own ancient rite, and much of what is seen and heard, from Latin chant to the night Office, would be recognisable to monks of earlier centuries, but this is a community filmed in the early 2000s, not a reconstruction of older practice.
history: St Bruno founded the Carthusians in 1084 in the Chartreuse massif. The Grande Chartreuse is the order's mother house and admits no visitors; the monks live as hermits in community, meeting for the Office, Sunday meal and a weekly walk.
liberties: A documentary still shapes what it shows. Gröning shot more than 120 hours and arranges his material by season rather than strict chronology. Nothing is explained, so the Carthusian rule, the order's history and the meaning of particular customs stay off screen.
advisories:
Nothing problematic in content, according to Greydanus.

Very slow, almost silent and 164 minutes long; most children will not sit through it.

The little speech there is is French, with Latin chant; subtitled.

title: No Greater Love
decision: REJECT: Scope (editorial ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's Catholic content is the post-conciliar Church, presented as normal or exemplary: a present-day Carmel filmed in 2009.
summary: Michael Whyte spent a year filming the enclosed Carmelite nuns of Notting Hill; the result is quieter than Into Great Silence and more personal, because the sisters talk.
synopsis: Behind a wall in St Charles Square, Notting Hill, a community of Discalced Carmelite nuns lives an enclosed life of prayer and work. Whyte, who lived across the square for years without knowing it was still occupied, took about ten years to gain permission and then filmed alone over a year. The film runs two lines side by side, a single day and a whole year, centred on Holy Week. A nun rattles a clapper down a dark corridor to wake her sisters; they sing the Office, garden, and bake altar breads by the million for the churches of Westminster. A young sister makes her profession. An old sister dies and is buried. Between these events the nuns talk about their vocations, about prayer, and about long years when God seemed absent.
inclusion: The interviews make the film. The sisters are clever, funny and candid, quote Gerard Manley Hopkins and St John of the Cross, and talk about the habit and gardening as easily as about the dark night of the soul. Whyte's camera has a Vermeer-like feel for light at a window, and the editing sets the old nun's death against the community's Easter in a way that gives the whole film its shape. Greydanus called that juxtaposition its most inspired stroke. It is less austere and less ambitious than Gröning's Carthusian film, and more accessible: a good introduction to what contemplative life is for.
themes: The Resurrection is the film's spine: Holy Week, including the Mandatum in which the prioress washes her sisters' feet, leads to Easter, and a sister's death is placed inside that faith. The nuns pray for people who do not pray for themselves. Their accounts of spiritual darkness are the heart of the interviews: one went two years without any sense of God's presence, the elderly prioress around eighteen. Laughing, the prioress admits she sometimes thinks the atheists could be right, and adds that if she is wrong nobody will be there to tell her, and if she is right someone will meet her. It is the dark night described by John of the Cross, recounted by someone still living through it, not a profession of doubt.

liberties: A year of footage is cut into a day-and-year structure, and the interviews are personal testimony chosen by the director. Liturgical music and practice are those of an English community in the 2000s.

title: Two Crowns
decision: REJECT: Scope (editorial ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's subject is recognised as saint or blessed only through a canonisation or beatification made after the Second Vatican Council (Maximilian Kolbe, beatified 1971, canonised 1982).
summary: A Polish docudrama on Maximilian Kolbe that mixes interviews, archive material and staged scenes with Adam Woronowicz; devout and informative, but stiff as cinema.
synopsis: The title comes from Kolbe's childhood vision, in which Our Lady offered him two crowns, one white for purity and one red for martyrdom, and he chose both. Michał Kondrat follows him from his boyhood in Zduńska Wola through the Franciscans, the founding of the Militia of the Immaculata, the vast friary-publishing house of Niepokalanów, and the mission to Japan, to Auschwitz, where in 1941 he offered to take the place of a condemned prisoner. Franciscans and historians speak to camera, and Kondrat addresses the viewer himself. Staged scenes with Adam Woronowicz as Kolbe and Cezary Pazura as Brother Zeno fill in episodes, and the Auschwitz survivor Kazimierz Piechowski, who knew Kolbe, gives testimony.
inclusion: The value here is information and witness, not drama. The film gathers material that is hard to find elsewhere in one place, especially on the Japanese mission and Niepokalanów, and Piechowski's testimony is moving. Woronowicz's Kolbe is, in Przewodnik Katolicki's words, full of patience and peace. As cinema it is weak: Filmweb's Jakub Popielecki gave it two stars out of ten and called it a hagiographic primer, and even the friendly Przewodnik Katolicki review found it lacking in dynamism and too reluctant to show human weakness. Best used as a well-researched introduction for parishes and schools.
themes: Marian consecration runs through every chapter: Kolbe's movement, his presses and his missions are all offered to the Immaculata. The film presents his zeal for the Pope and the Church, his patience and generosity at Auschwitz, and his teaching that holiness means submitting one's will to God's. A healing with Lourdes water is presented as a miracle. His death is shown as the end of a lifetime's consistent self-offering rather than a single heroic gesture.
history: Maximilian Kolbe (1894–1941), a Conventual Franciscan, founded the Militia of the Immaculata in 1917 and Niepokalanów in 1927, and worked in Nagasaki from 1930 to 1936. Arrested in 1941 and sent to Auschwitz, he volunteered to die in place of Franciszek Gajowniczek and was killed by lethal injection in the starvation bunker on 14 August 1941. John Paul II canonised him as a martyr in 1982.
liberties: Dialogue and gestures in the staged scenes are invented. Reviewers note the interview-and-reconstruction pattern becomes repetitive and the portrait is idealised. The film's world premiere was an event screening alongside the 2017 Cannes festival, not a festival selection.
advisories:
Concentration-camp imprisonment and Kolbe's death; the sources do not describe how graphically the bunker is shown.

No other content of concern is reported.

Suitable for older children and up; slow and explanatory.

title: Faith of Our Fathers: In Search of the English Martyrs
originalTitle: Faith of our Fathers: In Search of the English Martyrs
decision: REJECT: Rule (b), editor ruling (2026-10-11). The recusant history it tells is sound and well located, but serving post-conciliar bishops speak as the authorities throughout and the film celebrates the 1970 canonisations as the culmination of the martyrs' story. Rule (a) does not apply: the martyrs it centres on were beatified in 1886 and 1929.
summary: Two London priests visit the places of England's Reformation martyrs, from Tyburn to Stonor's priest holes, in a sincere, low-key guide to the martyrs and the families who hid them.
synopsis: Fr Marcus Holden of Southwark and Fr Nicholas Schofield, archivist of the Archdiocese of Westminster, set out from the Westminster diocesan archives on a pilgrimage through the places of the English martyrs. At Allen Hall, on the site of Thomas More's Chelsea house, More's stand is recalled. At Stonor Park, Lord Camoys shows the hiding place of Edmund Campion's secret press and describes the exclusion of Catholics from public life. They visit the priest holes at West Grinstead, the skull of Ambrose Barlow at Wardley Hall, Arrowsmith House, the shrine at Ladyewell, Rievaulx and Ampleforth, Margaret Clitherow's shrine at York and the Tyburn convent. Along the way Westminster Cathedral's master of music discusses Byrd's Masses, once sung in secret, and Archbishop Vincent Nichols and Bishop Terence Brain reflect on the martyrs.
inclusion: The film's value is in the places. Few documentaries show so many of the sites of recusant England: the chapel at Stonor, where Mass has been said since the thirteenth century, the priest holes at West Grinstead built by Nicholas Owen, relics kept by families and shrines that sheltered priests. The presenters know the history, Schofield being a church historian, and they let lesser-known martyrs such as Robert Wrenno, whose first hanging failed when the rope broke, stand beside More, Campion and Clitherow. It is a modest production, presenter-led and partly improvised, and the original two-part version runs nearly two hours; Ignatius Press issued a 95-minute cut in North America. Charles Cole called it beautiful and fascinating. It suits parishes and schools wanting a guided tour of recusant history.
themes: The martyrs are presented as dying for the Mass, the priesthood and the Pope's supremacy, and the recusant families as keeping the faith through fines, exclusion and hidden altars. In interviews about the film Holden draws a providential lesson, that persecution strengthened the Church, and stresses that the martyrs prayed for England and forgave their persecutors. The frame is present-day. Archbishop Nichols and Bishop Brain speak as authorities, and Brain recalls the campaign for the 1970 canonisation of the Forty Martyrs. Most of the martyrs shown, including Campion and Clitherow, were beatified long before 1965 and are properly Blessed; Francis Bell, whose hidden altar appears, was beatified only in 1987.
history: Between 1535 and 1679 several hundred Catholics were put to death in England and Wales for the faith, beginning with the Carthusian priors and Thomas More under Henry VIII and continuing through the Elizabethan and Stuart mission priests and those who sheltered them. Leo XIII beatified the first group, including More, Fisher and the London Carthusians, in 1886, and further groups followed in 1895 and 1929.
advisories:
The martyrs' imprisonment, torture and executions are described; relics include a martyr's skull.

No sexual content or bad language. Suitable for older children and adults.

Present-day bishops speak as authorities, and the 1970 canonisations are recalled with approval.

title: Finding Fátima
decision: REJECT: Rule (b), editor ruling (2026-10-11). The 1917 material is sound, but the documentary's climax and interpretive voice are the post-conciliar Church: it presents John Paul II's survival in 1981 and the Vatican's 2000 reading of the third secret as the fulfilment of Fátima, with present-day clergy and shrine officials as its authorities. A coda would be a reservation; here the post-conciliar reading is the film's conclusion.
summary: The makers of The 13th Day mix interviews, archive footage and reused dramatic scenes to retell the Fátima apparitions and trace their meaning through the twentieth century.
synopsis: The film opens at Hiroshima in August 1945, with the story of a small community of German priests whose survival near the blast was later linked to the Fátima message. It then goes back to 1916 and 1917: the Angel's visits to Lúcia, Francisco and Jacinta, the apparitions of Our Lady at the Cova da Iria, the vision of hell, the hostility of the anticlerical Republic, and the Miracle of the Sun on 13 October 1917. Reconstructions taken from The 13th Day alternate with archive footage and interviews with commentators, shrine figures and descendants of witnesses. The last part follows the message forward: the Second World War, the spread of the devotion, John Paul II's survival of the assassination attempt of 13 May 1981, the publication of the third part of the secret in 2000, and Sister Lúcia's death in 2005.
inclusion: Finding Fátima is a companion to The 13th Day, and its most striking images are borrowed from it: the sepia-tinted reconstructions, with their stark rendering of the Lady and of hell. Around them Ian and Dominic Higgins build a brisk 90-minute documentary. Catholic reviewers praised its pace and its short interview clips; Sr Helena Burns suggested it could be called "Fatima Then and Now". The interviews add what the drama cannot: recollections handed down in the witnesses' families, and the memories of Fr Luciano Guerra, rector of the shrine from 1973 to 2000. For viewers who know the story only in outline, it sets out the 1917 events in order and makes the content of the message (prayer, penance, the Rosary, reparation) unmistakable. Its account of what happened afterwards is more debatable.
themes: The message comes through plainly: the Angel's prayers of adoration and reparation, the daily Rosary, sacrifice for sinners, devotion to the Immaculate Heart, and the vision of hell, which the commentator Timothy Tindall-Robertson presents as showing that damnation is a real possibility. That is sound and traditional in substance. The difficulty is the frame. The film links the third secret's images to Hiroshima and to the 1981 attack on John Paul II, which the Pope believed it foretold, and treats the Vatican's publication of 2000 as the close of the story, with present-day clergy and shrine officials as its interpreters. Traditional Catholic writers dispute that reading, and the film does not say so.
advisories:
A dramatised vision of hell, images of war and of the atomic bombing of Hiroshima. The distributor suggests age 12 and up; one reviewer warned that these scenes may disturb children under eight.

No sexual content or bad language reported.

The film presents John Paul II's reading of the third secret and the Vatican's interpretation of 2000 as the culmination of Fátima.

title: The Miracle of Father Kapaun
decision: GREY: Identity: a Wichita Eagle documentary by Travis Heying made with Roy Wenzl's December 2009 series (Newman University notice, 17 December 2009), distributed by Ignatius Press from 1 August 2010 (45 minutes). The subject's history is verified by the US Army's Medal of Honor page. Kapaun is Venerable (2025), so rule (a) does not apply. No independent assessment of the film's treatment, and the healings in its title are unapproved claims: unverified.
summary: Wichita Eagle journalists tell the story of Fr Emil Kapaun, the Kansas army chaplain who served fellow prisoners in a Korean War camp until his death in 1951.
synopsis: Emil Kapaun, the son of Czech immigrant farmers in Kansas, becomes a priest of the Diocese of Wichita and an army chaplain. In Korea in November 1950, at Unsan, he crosses open ground under fire to reach the wounded, refuses chances to escape, and is captured when he stays behind with injured men. In the camps at Sambukol and Pyoktong he forages for food, nurses the sick and leads prayers and services in defiance of the guards. He dies at Pyoktong in May 1951, aged 35. Men who were imprisoned with him, military historians and church officials tell the story. The last part follows his cause for canonisation and a Kansas family who believe his intercession saved their son's life, among recoveries that were then under Church investigation.
inclusion: The film began as journalism. Travis Heying, a Wichita Eagle videographer, made it alongside Roy Wenzl's eight-part series for the paper in December 2009; the Diocese of Wichita then screened it and Ignatius Press took it on. Its strength is testimony from men who were in the camps with Kapaun, filmed while some were still alive to speak. It is a short portrait, not a full biography, and Heying and Wenzl later returned to the subject. It is a good introduction to a pre-conciliar priest whose service was practical, physical and sacramental.
themes: Kapaun is presented above all as a priest. He leads prayers and services in the camp at the risk of punishment, cares for the sick and keeps faith among starving men under captors hostile to religion. That is a strong picture of the priesthood as sacrifice. The title is the difficulty, because the miracle refers to recoveries that families attribute to his intercession, which the Church has not approved. Rome declared him Venerable in 2025 under the "offering of life" category introduced in 2017, not on the strength of a miracle.
history: Emil Kapaun was captured at Unsan on 2 November 1950 after volunteering to stay with the wounded, and was held at Sambukol and Pyoktong, where he died on 23 May 1951. He received the Distinguished Service Cross from the Army in August 1951, while still listed as missing, and the Medal of Honor, presented by President Obama, on 11 April 2013. He was declared a Servant of God in 1993 and Venerable in February 2025.
advisories:
Accounts of combat, starvation and death in a prison camp.

No sexual content. Suitable for older children and adults.

The title's miracle refers to claimed healings the Church has not approved; Kapaun is Venerable, not Blessed or Saint.

grey.question: The Miracle of Father Kapaun is a short documentary made by Wichita Eagle journalists, built on interviews with men who survived the camp with him. The record of his heroism is solid. The film's treatment of the healings in its title, which the Church has not approved, is unassessed, because no independent review of the film exists. Kapaun was declared Venerable in 2025, not on the basis of a miracle. A review or a transcript of its closing section would settle how it presents those claims.

suitability.note: It is a documentary, so no violence is dramatised and nothing sexual appears. Older children can watch it with a parent.

doctrine: A priest's first duty is the care of souls, and the film's account of Kapaun saying prayers and giving the sacraments to starving prisoners shows that duty at its limit. A priest may absolve a man in danger of death, and in grave necessity the sacraments are given as circumstances allow. The film's title refers to healings that families attribute to his intercession. Under the traditional procedure (Urban VIII, Benedict XIV), the Church examines a cause for proof of heroic virtue and then for miracles after death; a reported cure is not a miracle until the Church has examined and approved it. The claims of healing in the film are therefore those of the families and the film-makers, not of the Church. The Medal of Honor is a military decoration, not a judgment on his sanctity.
production: The Miracle of Father Kapaun is a 45-minute documentary from 2009 with interviews of former prisoners who were in the camp with him, church officials, military historians and the Kansas family who credit his intercession for their son's recovery. title: The Blood & the Rose
decision: GREY: Identity is established (Renegade Productions press releases of 2011 and 2012; benefit premiere at the Warner Theatre, Washington, 24 January 2013, reported by the Catholic Review). Content is documented by Alberto González's detailed review for Aleteia and by CNA's interview with the director, both present-day Catholic outlets, so there is no independent assessment. Reservations: disputed claims about the tilma presented as findings, historical errors in the Spanish survey, and New Evangelization framing. Would move only with an independent review.
summary: Tim Watkins's documentary sets Our Lady of Guadalupe against Aztec sacrifice and the Marian history of Spain, then examines the tilma with claims that outrun the evidence.
synopsis: Narrated by Eduardo Verástegui and shot in Spain and Mexico over four years, the film is built in three parts. The first is history: Constantine, the Marian shrines and victories of Christian Spain from Covadonga to the Guadalupe of Extremadura, and the Aztec cult of human sacrifice as Bernal Díaz described it. The second tells the apparitions of December 1531 on Tepeyac: Juan Diego's errands to Bishop Zumárraga, the request for a church, the roses and the image found on his cloak. The third turns to the tilma itself, presenting claims about figures reflected in the Virgin's eyes and stars on her mantle said to match the sky of 1531. It ends by linking Guadalupe to the Marian apparitions of the twentieth century and by calling Catholics to follow Juan Diego as messengers of the faith today.
inclusion: The film's strength is its first half. Watkins starts in Spain and argues that the Guadalupe story only makes sense against two backgrounds: a Spanish Catholicism shaped by centuries of war under Marian patronage, and an Aztec religion that fed its gods with human hearts. That contrast, which Alberto González's review for Aleteia follows closely, makes the scale of the conversions after 1531 intelligible. The apparition narrative is told straightforwardly and keeps the details of the traditional account. Watkins, a Baltimore businessman and documentary maker, made it as a catechetical film and toured it through parishes with study materials, so it is pitched at Catholics who know the image but not the history behind it.
themes: The film reads Guadalupe as a chapter in the enmity between the woman and the serpent of Genesis 3:15 and Revelation 12, and as the means by which Mary brought a people to her Son. That reading is traditional, and the image is treated as a sign pointing to Christ: Watkins stresses the bowed head and folded hands. The scientific section presents disputed claims about the eyes and the stars as findings. The closing section frames the story in John Paul II's language of the New Evangelization, with Juan Diego, beatified in 1990 and canonised in 2002, held up as the model evangelist.
history: The 1910 Catholic Encyclopedia gives the traditional account. On 9 December 1531 the Virgin appeared to Juan Diego, a recent convert, on Tepeyac and asked for a church. Bishop Zumárraga asked for a sign. On 12 December she cured Juan's dying uncle and sent Juan with roses in his cloak, which, opened before the bishop, bore the image.
liberties: The historical survey is triumphal and sometimes wrong. As González summarises it, Alfonso XI's victory at the Río Salado is said to have ended the Moorish presence in Europe, though Granada did not fall until 1492; Covadonga is told as a Marian victory without qualification. The claims about the tilma are presented as settled discoveries, though they are contested interpretations.
advisories:
Descriptions and reconstructions of Aztec human sacrifice.

No sexual content reported. Suitable for older children with an adult.

The scientific claims about the image are presented as findings; they are disputed and have no Church endorsement.

grey.question: The Blood & the Rose tells the Guadalupe story in its traditional form and sets it against Aztec sacrifice and the Marian history of Spain. Its weaker parts are presented with the same confidence. They include claims that figures appear in the Virgin's eyes and that the stars on her mantle map the sky of December 1531, and a survey of Spanish history with plain errors. It also closes in the post-conciliar language of the New Evangelization. No independent review of the film exists; one would show how much weight the scientific section can bear.

doctrine: Apparitions are private revelation: the Church does not oblige belief in them, but approves devotion where she finds nothing contrary to faith. Benedict XIV declared Our Lady of Guadalupe patroness of New Spain in 1754 and approved a proper Mass and Office for 12 December. Leo XIII had the image crowned in 1895. The film reads the story through Genesis 3:15 and Apocalypse 12, passages the Church has long applied to Our Lady; Pius IX appeals to Genesis 3:15 in Ineffabilis Deus (1854). The claims that figures can be seen reflected in the Virgin's eyes and that her mantle maps the sky of 1531 have never been endorsed by Church authority and cannot be treated as proof.
production: Tim Watkins, who runs Renegade Productions and co-directed In the Face of Evil on Reagan, made the documentary with Leo McWatkins Films. Eduardo Verástegui, who narrates, is the actor from Bella. A benefit premiere for Catholic Charities of Washington was held at the Warner Theatre in Washington, D.C., on 24 January 2013.

title: Guadalupe: Mother of Humanity
decision: REJECT: Rule (b), editor ruling (2026-10-11). Half the film is present-day testimony, with Archbishop José Gómez and other post-conciliar clergy as its authorities, and it makes claims about the tilma (including "music" in its proportions) that the Church has never endorsed. The 1531 account is not the film's centre.
summary: A Spanish docudrama that pairs reconstructions of the 1531 apparitions with present-day testimonies of conversion and healing, and with contested claims about hidden details in the tilma.
synopsis: The actress Karyme Lozano guides the viewer between three settings: New Spain in 1531, present-day Los Angeles and Barcelona. Reconstructions directed by Pablo Moreno show pre-Hispanic Mexico, the arrival of the Spaniards and the turn from human sacrifice, then follow Juan Diego (Mario Alberto Hernández), a recent convert, through the apparitions on Tepeyac, his visits to the bishop and the sign of the roses and the image, with Angélica Chong as the Virgin. Between them come testimonies: a Hollywood producer who credits Our Lady with saving his life, an actress, two men who left crime and drug trafficking, and a former abortionist. Archbishop José Gómez of Los Angeles speaks of miracles attributed to Guadalupe there, and a final section examines the tilma, presenting claims about figures in the Virgin's eyes, the meaning of the stars on her mantle and music derived from the image's proportions.
inclusion: This is the most elaborate recent film on Guadalupe. It was shot in Mexico, the United States, Spain and Germany and released in early 2024 across the Americas and in Spain. The reconstructions give the 1531 story a full dramatic treatment with Mexican actors, and the colonial background is part of the story rather than a footnote: John Mulderig's review notes that the apparitions came when many of the conquered Indians were disoriented and despairing. The testimonies are the film's other half and, for its makers, its main point: they present the devotion as alive, especially in the defence of the unborn, of whom Our Lady of Guadalupe is patroness. Andrés Garrigó's Goya Producciones specialises in this mixture of drama and testimony, and viewers who know its other films will know what to expect.
themes: The apparition narrative carries the traditional content: Mary as Mother who asks for a church, the conversion of a people, the image as a sign given to the bishop. The present-day half is more uneven. Its testimonies of healing and conversion are personal, not judged miracles, and the film leans on modern authorities, chiefly Archbishop Gómez, rather than on the Church's historic acts concerning the shrine. Its claims about the tilma, including music drawn from its proportions, go well beyond anything the Church has affirmed. Juan Diego was beatified in 1990 and canonised in 2002, so his cult as a saint rests wholly on post-conciliar acts.
history: According to the 1910 Catholic Encyclopedia, the Virgin appeared to Juan Diego on Tepeyac on 9 December 1531, and on 12 December the image was found on his cloak as he opened it before Bishop Zumárraga. Pilgrimage to the shrine has been almost continuous since 1531 and 1532. Benedict XIV made Our Lady of Guadalupe national patron, with a proper Mass and Office, and Leo XIII had the image crowned in his name.
advisories:
References to abortion, serious illness and accidents in the testimonies; OSV News judged it too intense for small children.

No sexual content or bad language reported. Spanish, released in the United States with English subtitles.

The scientific claims about the image are presented as discoveries; they are contested and have no Church endorsement.

decision: GREY: Identity is established by TheTVDB (CCC of America's Saints and Heroes series; 30 minutes; United States), retailer and Formed listings, and the Dove Foundation's series review (based on a text by Fr Robert J. Fox). Content is known only in outline from these interested or series-level sources, and no independent assessment of its treatment exists. The year is disputed (1988 TheTVDB, 1989 fan wiki, ©1991 VHS in WorldCat per earlier research, 2005 DVD in TMDB); 1988 used provisionally. Would move with a transcript or a review.
summary: An animated retelling of the Fátima apparitions for young children, made by CCC of America and based on a text by Fr Robert J. Fox.
synopsis: In Portugal in 1916, during the First World War, an angel appears to three shepherd children, Lúcia, aged ten, and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta, aged nine and seven. He teaches them a prayer of adoration and tells them that the Hearts of Jesus and Mary are listening. In 1917 the Lady appears to them while they are minding their sheep near Fátima, again and again, asks them to pray the Rosary, since she can end the war, and entrusts them with secrets meant for the whole world. Few believe them, and they suffer for their testimony. Finally, before a great crowd in the rain, the sun appears to dance in the sky, and the children are accepted as the messengers of Our Lady of Fátima.
inclusion: It is one of the few versions of Fátima made for young children, and it has stayed in circulation for over three decades. It runs under half an hour, which suits a classroom, and Seton's catalogue places it at third grade.
themes: The film keeps the core of the message for a young audience, to judge by its catalogue descriptions: the Angel's prayer of adoration, the Hearts of Jesus and Mary, the Rosary, prayer for peace and for sinners, and the Lady's secrets, with the Miracle of the Sun as their vindication. The Dove Foundation's notes for the series mention the Virgin described as sinless and people kneeling before her image. One unverified viewer complaint says the Russia request is left out; if so, the story is simplified, not falsified.
advisories:
No violence, sexual content or bad language reported for this episode; made for young children.

The Dove Foundation's content notes and its 12+ seal cover the whole Saints and Heroes series, not this episode alone.

Whether the vision of hell and the request for the consecration of Russia are included has not been verified.

grey.question: The Day the Sun Danced is a short animated version of the Fátima story for young children, from CCC of America and based on a text by Fr Robert J. Fox. Catalogue descriptions and the Dove Foundation's notes show the Angel, the Rosary, the secrets and the Miracle of the Sun. No independent review of the film exists, so nothing checks how closely it follows Lúcia's memoirs, or whether it includes the vision of hell and the request for the consecration of Russia. sources.title: Our Lady of Fátima
sources.claims: Angel 1916; apparitions 13 May-13 October 1917; custody 13 August and Valinhos 19 August; crowd estimate; deaths of Francisco 1919 and Jacinta 1920; Lúcia memoirs 1935-41; Bishop of Leiria approval 13 October 1930; Pius XII consecrations 1942 and 1952; coronation 1946; basilica 1954

names: An original text by Fr Robert J. Fox

suitability.note: Nothing frightening is reported. The children's persecution by unbelieving adults and the secrets may need a word of explanation for the youngest.

doctrine: The Bishop of Leiria, José Alves Correia da Silva, declared the apparitions worthy of belief on 13 October 1930 and authorised the cult of Our Lady of Fátima. Pius XII consecrated the human race to the Immaculate Heart of Mary on 31 October 1942, naming the peoples of Russia, and consecrated Russia itself in the apostolic letter Sacro vergente anno of 7 July 1952. He had the Fátima statue crowned by a papal legate on 13 May 1946 and raised the sanctuary to a basilica in 1954. The Lady's requests, daily Rosary, reparation and prayer for sinners, rest on long-standing devotion; the Angel's prayer is one of adoration of the Holy Trinity. Private revelations, however approved, are not part of the deposit of faith.
history: In 1916 Lúcia dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto, shepherd children of Aljustrel near Fátima, reported three visits from an angel. From 13 May to 13 October 1917 they reported monthly apparitions of the Virgin at the Cova da Iria. On 13 August the district administrator, Artur Santos, took them into custody, and the August apparition came on the 19th at Valinhos. On 13 October a crowd estimated at 30,000 to 100,000 saw the Miracle of the Sun. Francisco died in the influenza pandemic on 4 April 1919 and Jacinta in Lisbon on 20 February 1920. Lúcia became a religious and wrote down the secrets in her memoirs of 1935 to 1941.
production: CCC of America, which produced animated lives of saints for the home market in the late 1980s, made the film as part of its Saints and Heroes series for home and school. The series also covers Bernadette and Juan Diego, and this film is sold in a Marian set. The story follows an original text by Fr Robert J. Fox, a priest known for his books on Fátima. Dates are uncertain: TheTVDB gives 1988, other listings 1989, a VHS copyright is dated 1991, and a DVD followed in 2005. It first circulated on video and runs about thirty minutes. It is still sold on DVD by Catholic school suppliers and streamed on Formed.

title: Silence
decision: REJECT: Too grave to leave to the reader (editorial standard, 2026-10-11), not a scope ruling. At the climax a voice from the fumie, presented as Christ's, tells the priest to trample His image, and the film's added final image (his wife placing a hidden crucifix in his hands at his Buddhist cremation) presents his public apostasy as compatible with a fidelity kept in secret. Catholic critics who admire the film (Greydanus, Mirus, Fr Martin) and those who condemn it (Miller) agree on these facts; they disagree only about the voice's source, which Scorsese leaves open. A film whose climax puts permission for apostasy in Christ's mouth and whose ending honours a hidden faith contradicts the duty to confess the faith under persecution (Mt 10:33; Summa II-II q.3 a.2). That is the question the brief asked to be judged, and the answer is yes.

title: Conclave
decision: REJECT: a fictional papal-election thriller whose resolution argues for change in Catholic teaching, as secular and Catholic critics agree. Stephanie Zacharek (TIME) reads its point as that the Church 'must change' its views on women and LGBTQ people; Kayleigh Hearn (Looper) calls it a film about tradition versus progress in which 'progress prevails'; Nina Starner (SlashFilm) reads the ending as challenging the Church's patriarchy, quoting the director that it is 'not a takedown of the church' but that 'not everyone needs to agree with the movie'. Brad Miner (The Catholic Thing) objects that the plot ends with the cardinals knowingly electing a pope who, by the film's own account, is a woman. A drama built to advocate positions contrary to the Church's teaching on holy orders falls outside a Catholic-centred recommendation list. Its craft is a separate question.

title: Brother Sun, Sister Moon
decision: REJECT: Editor ruling (2026-10-11). The film recasts St Francis as a 1970s counter-cultural figure, makes the bishop and papal court the antagonists, and stages vernacular worship with the priest facing the people at San Damiano as the purified Church: the post-conciliar reform presented as the ideal (hard rule 2 in substance).
summary: Zeffirelli's lyrical, flower-power life of the young Francis of Assisi, from his return from war to his audience with Innocent III, with songs by Donovan.
synopsis: Francesco Bernardone, the spoiled son of a rich Assisi cloth merchant, comes home sick from the war with Perugia. During a long fever he turns from his old life to the fields, birds and flowers. In his father's dye-works he sees the workers' misery, frees them and throws his father's cloth to the poor. Pietro drags him before the bishop, where Francesco strips off his clothes, renounces his inheritance and leaves the town. At the ruined chapel of San Damiano a voice tells him to rebuild the church, and he begs for stones. Friends join him, among them Bernardo, back from the Crusade, and Clare, who nurses lepers. Their chapel is burned and one brother dies. Francesco walks to Rome, abandons the speech prepared for him and rebukes the papal court with the Sermon on the Mount. Innocent III calls him back, kisses his feet and approves the brotherhood.
inclusion: The film's strongest case is visual. Ennio Guarnieri's photography of Umbrian poppy fields and the grey rubble of San Damiano won the Nastro d'Argento, the art direction was nominated for an Oscar, and the closing audience, shot among the gold mosaics of Monreale standing in for Rome, is real spectacle. Alec Guinness gives Innocent III weight in a few minutes. The film also takes Francis's poverty seriously: Ron Reed in Christianity Today points out that the words viewers find naive are mostly Christ's own. The weaknesses are as well known. Graham Faulkner is wide-eyed and fey, Donovan's songs date it badly, and Roger Ebert and Vincent Canby found it sugary and simple-minded. It stops in 1210, so there are no stigmata, no sickness and no Rule.
themes: Francis's conversion comes through nature, the crucifix and the Gospel: he quotes Christ on God and money, rebuilds San Damiano and embraces poverty, chastity and obedience. Clare's vocation is treated delicately. But the film frames all this in the terms of 1972. ACEC Toscana's critic contrasts a cathedral Mass, where the rich stand frozen while the bishop celebrates with his back to them, with San Damiano, where the poor sing in the vernacular and the priest faces them across the altar, and reads it as a probable allusion to the Council's liturgical reform. The papal court is a gilded trap. The Pope's best-known line, as Reed quotes it, is 'In our obsession with original sin we too often forget original innocence', which sits badly with Trent's decree on original sin.
history: Francis Bernardone (c.1181–1226) was held prisoner for a year after a skirmish with Perugia, renounced his inheritance before the bishop of Assisi, and rebuilt San Damiano after hearing a voice there. Bishop Guido commended him in Rome, where Innocent III gave verbal approval to his way of life and permission to preach. Clare joined him in Lent 1212. Honorius III approved the Rule in 1223; Francis received the stigmata in 1224, died in 1226 and was canonised by Gregory IX in 1228.
liberties: Bishop Guido, who supported Francis, is made an opponent. The father's dye-works, the freeing of the workers, the burning of San Damiano and a brother's death are invented or reworked. Paolo, the worldly friend, is a composite. The Pope's public foot-kissing and his confession of the Church's wealth are invented. The film ends in 1210, omitting the Rule, the stigmata and Francis's death. The Italian and international cuts differ in order, dialogue and songs.
advisories:
Francis strips off his clothes in front of the bishop and walks out of the town naked: brief, non-sexual nudity. Rated PG in the United States.

Fevered flashbacks of war; a chapel is burned and one of the brothers dies.

Suitable for older children and up.

Two versions exist: the international English-language cut (about 121–122 minutes, songs by Donovan) and a longer Italian cut (about 135 minutes) with a different order of scenes and songs by Claudio Baglioni. The English-language reviews cited here are of the international version.

The film's picture of the Church is shaped by the late 1960s: the hierarchy appears mainly as wealth and power, and one line sets 'original innocence' against original sin.

title: Fátima
decision: REJECT: Content, editor ruling (2026-10-11). The transcript shows Our Lady's words reworked ("praying for me", "do not hurt yourselves with ropes") and the request concerning Russia and the consecration left out, so the film misrepresents the message it claims to tell. Its invented 1989 frame adds a sceptical present-day interviewer. Wikipedia reports that the end credits use footage of the 2017 canonisation Mass, which would also bring it under rule (b); the ruling does not depend on that.
summary: Marco Pontecorvo's handsome, earnest dramatisation of the 1917 apparitions, framed by an invented 1989 interview between the elderly Sister Lúcia and a sceptical professor.
synopsis: In 1917, with Portuguese soldiers dying in the First World War, ten-year-old Lúcia dos Santos (Stephanie Gil) and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta say that a Lady has appeared to them at the Cova da Iria. Lúcia's mother, Maria Rosa, thinks her daughter is lying and suffers the village's scorn with her; the parish priest is cautious; the anticlerical mayor, Artur Santos, closes the church and detains the children to make them recant. Each month the crowds grow, and the children are shown a vision of hell and of a worse war to come. On 13 October the Lady names herself the Lady of the Rosary and the sun seems to fall towards the crowd. In 1989 the elderly Sister Lúcia (Sônia Braga) recounts all this in her Carmel at Coimbra to Professor Nichols (Harvey Keitel), who doubts every word.
inclusion: This is the best-made of the recent Fátima films. Pontecorvo, a former cinematographer, shot it entirely in Portugal, and Brad Miner and Steven Greydanus both single out the look of Aljustrel and the 1917 sequences. The children are well cast, and Lúcia Moniz gives Lúcia's mother more depth than any earlier film: devout, loving and convinced her daughter has gone too far. The Lady's appearances are filmed impressionistically rather than with glowing effects. The weak part is the frame. Keitel and Braga are good company, but Greydanus finds the professor's questions sophomoric and Miner calls the exchanges static and didactic. Secular critics were cooler: Film Threat found it sincere but tedious, and Dennis Schwartz thought it would change no one's mind.
themes: The film takes the supernatural at face value and gives the children's penances and the vision of hell their place. But the Lady's words are reworked. The dialogue never mentions Russia, its consecration or the Communion of reparation; the Angel's prayer is cut down; Our Lady thanks the children for praying "for me"; and in July she tells them not to hurt themselves with ropes, which reverses what Lúcia records of September, when they were told to wear the cord by day only. The 1989 frame is invented, and the professor's argument that visions merely mirror local iconography is answered only with Lúcia's testimony.
history: Lúcia dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto reported apparitions at the Cova da Iria each month from May to October 1917 (August's took place on the 19th, at Valinhos, after the children's detention). The solar phenomenon of 13 October was witnessed by a large crowd. The bishop of Leiria approved the apparitions in 1930. Lúcia became a Carmelite at Coimbra and died there in 2005, aged 97.
liberties: Professor Nichols is fictional, and the Fatima Center notes that Lúcia received few visitors in her later years. Greydanus notes that the soldier on the casualty list, Lúcia's brother Manuel here, was in fact a cousin. The mayor's Catholic wife is an addition. The Angel's appearances are moved and multiplied, the August and September apparitions are dropped, and the Lady's words are paraphrased throughout, with the Russia request omitted.
advisories:
Visionary images of battlefield violence and a brief vision of hell; rated PG-13 in the United States.

No sexual content.

Our Lady's words are paraphrased and partly altered, and the request for the consecration of Russia is left out. The end credits reportedly include footage of Pope Francis's 2017 Mass at Fátima.

title: Thérèse
decision: GREY: The subtitle file settles part of what Greydanus described. The dream of a man dragging someone into the woods is told in a letter from Thérèse's sister Céline, not dreamt by Thérèse. Lucie's fixation is spoken plainly; Thérèse rebuffs her, the two are kept apart and Lucie later leaves the order. An old nun asks Thérèse for a kiss. Thérèse's trial of faith in her last illness is given in words close to her own writings. The host scene has no dialogue, so the subtitles cannot settle it. Nothing in the dialogue sexualises her love of Christ, so not REJECT; the surrounding material keeps it GREY.
summary: Cavalier's austere portrait of Thérèse Martin, from her girlhood longing for Carmel to her death at twenty-four, told in spare vignettes against a bare backdrop.
synopsis: Thérèse Martin, the youngest daughter of a devout Normandy family, wants to follow two of her sisters into the Carmel at Lisieux, though she is only fifteen. She presses her case as far as Pope Leo XIII. Admitted, she lives the enclosed life of work, silence and prayer among sisters who are sometimes petty, sometimes eccentric, and one of whom, Lucie, becomes fixated on her. Thérèse speaks of her vocation as a love affair with Jesus and prays for sinners, among them the condemned murderer Pranzini. At Christmas the nuns celebrate the birthday of the Child they call their husband. After her father's death, the hardships of the convent wear her down; she suffers physically, is shaken by doubt, and dies of tuberculosis.
inclusion: On artistic grounds it is among the most honoured saint films. Catherine Mouchet plays Thérèse as a determined teenager whose love for Christ is concrete and urgent, and the scholar Mary Bryant called the film the most effective and challenging screen version of her story in its decade. Cavalier strips everything away, paring sets and props to a minimum against a neutral backdrop. Vincent Canby noted that there are no heavenly choirs and no visions bathed in light, and that the beauty of the images is not ornament. Steven D. Greydanus compares the restraint to Bresson, as Marina Warner did. The film follows Thérèse's own conviction that love, not suffering for its own sake, is the point of sacrifice. Its weakness is that it observes her without explaining her. Greydanus calls it a reverie and not a meditation, leaving her a riddle.
themes: The film draws on Story of a Soul for Thérèse's vocation, her small sacrifices, her prayer for Pranzini, the daily life of the Carmel and her last illness. Her love for Jesus is the centre of her life and is spoken in the romantic language she herself used. The film passes no judgment on her, and some critics have read it through Freud; Greydanus answers that psychoanalysis cannot account for her selflessness. The trouble lies around her, not in her. Her trial of faith at the end is taken from her own writings.
history: Thérèse Martin (1873–1897) entered the Lisieux Carmel at fifteen, after asking Leo XIII in person for permission, and died of tuberculosis at twenty-four. Her spiritual memoir, Story of a Soul, made her and her 'little way' known worldwide after her death.
liberties: Sister Lucie is a fictional character, and the film has her leave the order. The film works in elliptical vignettes and omits large parts of the life, including much of the family background. The dream imagery, given to a letter from Céline, is Cavalier's invention.
advisories:
Several sexual allusions; a dream, recounted in a letter from her sister, that mixes martyrdom with sexual violence imagery; a nun's declared attachment to Thérèse, which she rebuffs.

An accidental desecration of a consecrated host.

Illness and death from tuberculosis. Adults and older teenagers.

French with subtitles.

grey.question: Cavalier's Thérèse is restrained and largely reverent, and her own love of Christ is not sexualised. The difficulty is the material around her. An invented nun, Lucie, declares her love for Thérèse, is rebuffed and later leaves the convent; an old nun asks her for a kiss; a letter from her sister Céline recounts a dream of being dragged into the woods that blends martyrdom with sexual violence; and a host is accidentally desecrated. The film passes no judgment, and some critics read it through Freud. Viewers should judge whether this is honest observation of a convent or a slight on the saint.

names: Histoire d'une âme (Story of a Soul), autobiography of Thérèse of Lisieux (1898)

suitability.note: The material is adult, and the film is slow and in French with subtitles; it is best for adults and older teenagers.

doctrine: Thérèse entered the Carmel at Lisieux on 9 April 1888. The Carmelite life is enclosed prayer and penance offered for sinners and for priests, as she offered hers for the murderer Pranzini, executed in 1887. Her 'little way' of spiritual childhood is trust, humility and love in small duties. In her day the sisters received Holy Communion only a few times a week. Pius X's decree Sacra Tridentina (1905) encouraged frequent and daily Communion, and his decree Quam singulari (1910) lowered the age of First Communion to the age of reason. The Church teaches the Real Presence in the Eucharist (Council of Trent, Session 13, 1551), which is why the dropped host in the film matters. She was beatified in 1923 and canonised by Pius XI on 17 May 1925, and he declared her patroness of the missions in 1927.
production: Cavalier visited the Lisieux Carmel and spoke with its sisters but did not film there. It was shown at Cannes in 1986, where it won the Jury Prize. At the 1987 César Awards it won five: best film, screenplay, cinematography and editing, and most promising actress for Mouchet. Pauline Kael wrote that the viewer was 'trapped inside his glass bubble'.

title: The Mission
decision: GREY: The subtitle file confirms the reservation and corrects one point. Altamirano threatens the priests with excommunication if they stay; Mendoza renounces his vow of obedience to fight; Gabriel refuses him a blessing, telling him that dying with blood on his hands betrays everything and that if might is right love has no place. The film does state its verdict, through Altamirano, whose closing reflections say that he and men like him made the world as it is and that he is the one who is dead while the slain live. Its sympathy for disobedience is therefore explicit, but Gabriel's refusal is non-violent and the Catholic substance is strong (Greydanus, A−): a weighable reservation, not REJECT.
summary: Bolt and Joffé's epic of the Jesuit missions of Paraguay, destroyed after a 1750 treaty, with Jeremy Irons as a peaceful priest and Robert De Niro as a penitent slaver.
synopsis: In the 1750s Father Gabriel climbs the cliffs beside the Iguazú Falls, above which the Guaraní have sent a missionary to his death, and wins their trust by playing the oboe. Rodrigo Mendoza, a mercenary who captures Guaraní for slavers, kills his brother in a fit of anger. Gabriel sets him a penance: to haul his armour up the falls. He reaches the Guaraní he once hunted, is received among them and becomes a Jesuit. Then the Treaty of Madrid hands the territory to Portugal. A papal envoy, Cardinal Altamirano, tours the missions and must decide their fate, knowing that defending them could bring the Society of Jesus down in Europe; he orders them abandoned. Gabriel and Mendoza refuse to leave. Mendoza breaks his vows and trains the Guaraní to fight; Gabriel leads a procession with the Blessed Sacrament. Colonial troops destroy the mission and both priests are killed.
inclusion: Chris Menges's photography of the falls and the forest and Ennio Morricone's score are widely praised. Its finest passages are thoroughly Catholic. Mendoza dragging his armour up the cliff as penance is a strong image of contrition, and the closing procession of the Blessed Sacrament through gunfire, the monstrance taken up by a Guaraní when Gabriel falls, is the film's best scene. The drama is weaker than the images. Steven D. Greydanus finds the structure diffuse and Altamirano, the narrator, underwritten, and the film never quite settles whose story it is. Roger Ebert was harsher. Every moment is watchable, he wrote, but the moments never add up to a story, and the final battle dissolves into chaos.
themes: Penance and forgiveness drive the first half, and the missions are shown as an attempt at a Christian society in which the Guaraní can live in peace. The second half turns on obedience. Gabriel defies his superiors but refuses violence and dies carrying the monstrance, while Mendoza takes up the sword. The film prefers Gabriel, but it treats both men's disobedience as nobler than the Church's compliance. Greydanus argues that grave danger to souls could justify Gabriel's refusal and that a priest may not take up arms; the film does not weigh obedience itself.
history: The 1750 Treaty of Madrid transferred seven Jesuit missions east of the Uruguay River from Spain to Portugal. The Jesuits petitioned the king against it, but their General, Ignazio Visconti, ordered compliance and sent Fr Lope Luis Altamirano to enforce it. The Guaraní refused to move against the orders of both governor and missionaries, and fought under their own leaders, Sepé Tiaraju and Nicolás Ñeenguirú. They were crushed at Caaybaté in 1756. Madrid and Lisbon blamed Jesuit intrigue. The treaty was annulled in 1761.
liberties: The real Altamirano was a Jesuit sent by his own General, not a cardinal sent by the Pope. Some individual Jesuits were accused of helping the rebels, but the Guaraní fought under their own leaders, whom the film leaves out, and historians now credit them with organising their own resistance. Gabriel and Mendoza are invented.
advisories:
Bloody battle violence and killings, including the shooting of priests and villagers in a procession.

Non-sexual ethnographic nudity among the Guaraní.

A man kills his brother in a fit of anger. Rated PG in the United States but better for teenagers and adults.

The film presents disobedience to religious superiors, and a Jesuit's armed resistance, as admirable, and it inverts the Society's official obedience.

grey.question: The Mission ends by honouring two Jesuits who disobey an order to abandon their missions despite a threat of excommunication. Mendoza renounces his vow of obedience and leads an armed defence; Gabriel refuses him a blessing, rejects violence and dies carrying the Blessed Sacrament. The film's verdict is spoken by the envoy himself, who concludes that he and men like him made the world as it is, and that he is dead while the slain live. It also turns history round: the real Altamirano was a Jesuit sent by his own General, and the Society ordered the missions surrendered. Viewers must weigh the film's view of obedience.

doctrine: The film sets Mendoza's penance, in which he drags his armour up the falls and is absolved, beside the Church's teaching on sacramental confession: sorrow, confession, absolution and satisfaction (Council of Trent, session XIV, 1551). Mendoza's slaying of his brother in a duel is mortal sin. Father Gabriel refuses to bless the sword; yet Catholic teaching allows a just war and the defence of the innocent (St Thomas, Summa II-II, q. 40), and the film leaves the question open. The Jesuit vow of obedience, which makes the superior's command as that of Christ, is central to the Society (Ignatius's Constitutions), and Father Fielding's armed resistance goes against it. Clement XIV suppressed the Society in 1773; Pius VII restored it in 1814.
production: David Puttnam championed the project, recommended Roland Joffé as director and joined as co-producer; Goldcrest came in and Warner Bros. supplied $5 million. Filming began in April 1985, chiefly in Colombia, with Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay also named. Robert De Niro had bodyguards after the cartel led by Pablo Escobar threatened Americans in Colombia. The Jesuit C. J. McNaspy, whose book The Lost Cities of Paraguay lies behind the story, consulted. It premiered in competition at Cannes on 16 May 1986 and won the Palme d'Or. It won the Academy Award for cinematography and BAFTAs for Ray McAnally, editing and score. At $17.2 million against a budget of £16.5 million it was a commercial disappointment, and Goldcrest's losses contributed to that company's end.

title: The Exorcist
decision: REJECT for scope as a recommendation, in every edition: the film's force depends on extended obscene and sacrilegious material — a child possessed by a demon masturbating with a crucifix, the desecration of a church, and sustained sexual obscenity and blasphemy — which its own Jesuit adviser Fr John Nicola protested and the U.S. Catholic Conference's film office publicly judged unsuitable for a wide audience (A-IV, adults with reservations). Chambers (History of the Human Sciences, 2021) and America's 1974 symposium document a divided Catholic reception, including private readings of the film as favourable to faith. That defence is real, but no edition can be recommended without a substantial reservation on reverence and moral content. This is not a claim that the film is condemned or that its picture of priesthood and the rite is false.
summary: Friedkin's horror film about two Jesuits who attempt to exorcise a possessed twelve-year-old girl in Georgetown.
synopsis: Regan MacNeil, the daughter of an actress filming in Washington, begins to behave violently and obscenely. Doctors find nothing. Fr Damien Karras, a Jesuit psychiatrist losing his faith after his mother's death, is asked to help, and the Church sends the elderly Fr Lankester Merrin to perform the rite. Merrin dies during the exorcism, and Karras, taking the demon into himself, throws himself from the window.
