title: Au revoir les enfants
decision: REJECT on scope only, and narrowly. The film is excellent and its priest is a genuine hero, but its subject is a boy's friendship with a hidden Jewish classmate, his unwitting betrayal and his loss of innocence; Catholic life is the setting, not the subject. Catholic critics who admire it (Mary Joseph in The Catholic Weekly; Criteria at CatholicCulture.org) describe Mass, prayer, a confession and a sermon as texture around a coming-of-age and Holocaust story, with the headmaster's sacrifice as its climax. Under the editor's Catholic-centred bar, which excludes On the Waterfront despite its central priest, consistency requires exclusion. This is not a judgment against the film; if the editor treats the priest's witness as central, it can move straight to PUBLISH on the existing evidence.
summary: Louis Malle's memory of the winter of 1944 at a Carmelite boarding school, where a rich boy befriends a new pupil who turns out to be a Jew hidden by the headmaster.
synopsis: Julien Quentin, eleven, returns after Christmas to a Carmelite school near Fontainebleau. The headmaster, Père Jean, brings in three new boys, among them Jean Bonnet, clever and aloof. Julien resents him, then discovers that his real name is Kippelstein and that the monks are hiding him. They become friends over books and the piano. A kitchen hand is sacked for black-market dealing. In January 1944 the Gestapo arrive, tipped off by him. Julien's glance gives Bonnet away, and the boys watch the priest led off with the three Jewish pupils.
inclusion: This is Malle's finest film: restrained, precisely observed, and devastating in its last minutes. The school's routines, cold dormitories, Mass and the Our Father said for a classmate are rendered without sentiment or satire. Père Jean, based on the Carmelite Père Jacques de Jésus, is a portrait of quiet priestly courage. The film won the Golden Lion at Venice and the César for best film. Its centre, though, is the friendship of two boys and the guilt of the survivor.
themes: The Catholic material is real and respectful: the boys pray, serve Mass, confess; Père Jean preaches to wealthy parents about the poor of a starving country and hides Jewish children at the cost of his life. Mary Joseph notes the film's feel for the sacramental life. The faith is the atmosphere of the school rather than the question the film asks.
history: Malle attended the Petit Collège d'Avon, run by Discalced Carmelites. On 15 January 1944 the Gestapo arrested its headmaster, Père Jacques de Jésus (Lucien Bunel), and three Jewish pupils. The boys died at Auschwitz; Père Jacques died in June 1945 shortly after the liberation of Mauthausen. Yad Vashem recognised him as Righteous Among the Nations; his cause for beatification opened in 1990.
liberties: Names are changed, and the friendship and its details are Malle's reconstruction of a childhood memory.
advisories:

title: The Innocents
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a Benedictine community, its vows and its Office) and well documented: Danish Film Institute and Wikipedia for identity, Kevin Jagernauth (The Playlist) and A. G. Harmon (Image) as independent treatments, Brad Miner (The Catholic Thing) for content. The Portuguese subtitle file confirms the reservation without turning it into a thesis. The abbess says she entrusted the baby to God and calls it Providence, then admits she damned herself to save the community and is called a murderer. One sister keeps her son and means to live her vocation differently; another gives up her child. The novice mistress defends faith through long doubt, and the closing letter credits God with sending the doctor. Not REJECT; not PUBLISH while the affair, an attempted assault and the departures need stating.

grey.question: The Innocents treats the nuns' faith and vows seriously and gives their prayer weight. The reservation lies in where it places blame and how it ends. The abbess, fearing scandal, abandons a newborn and calls it Providence, later admitting she damned herself to save the community; a young nun kills herself; the way out is found by an unbelieving doctor, and some sisters leave religious life with the film's sympathy. The doctor's affair is shown without comment. Much of this is invented around a true episode. Viewers able to weigh a religious superior as the main wrongdoer will find a serious, restrained film.

summary: Anne Fontaine's restrained drama of a French Red Cross doctor who secretly delivers the babies of Benedictine nuns raped by Soviet soldiers in Poland in 1945.
synopsis: Poland, December 1945. Mathilde Beaulieu, a young French Red Cross doctor caring for French soldiers before their repatriation, is begged by a nun to come to her convent. She finds that soldiers have raped the Benedictine sisters and that several are pregnant. The abbess, afraid that scandal will destroy the community, insists on secrecy, and some sisters resist examination, fearing it breaks their vows. Mathilde returns in secret, helped by Samuel, a Jewish doctor in her unit with whom she has an affair, and wins the trust of Sister Maria, the novice mistress. As the births come, the abbess says she is placing the babies with families; in fact she leaves one at a wayside cross, and its mother, Sister Zofia, kills herself. Maria confronts the abbess. Mathilde proposes that the sisters take in the town's orphans, and the convent becomes an orphanage; some nuns leave with their children.
inclusion: Fontaine handles a grim subject with restraint. Caroline Champetier's wintry photography, the sung Office and the faces of the sisters do much of the work, and Agata Buzek and Agata Kulesza give strong performances; Brad Miner of The Catholic Thing called Buzek the film's soul. It takes seriously what most films about nuns do not: what vows, enclosure and prayer mean to women who have suffered this. Critics praised it widely. Dissent centres on the ending. Kevin Jagernauth in The Playlist thought the first two-thirds a nuanced study of devotion meeting a modern outlook, but found the rosy finale dishonest and one character clumsily pushed into a villain's role. A. G. Harmon, writing in Image, admired its account of faith enduring in a ruined place.
themes: The film asks how faith survives violation. Without a priest the community has no Mass and lives by the Office alone. The sisters fear damnation for a chastity they did not choose to lose, and Maria defines faith as twenty-four hours of doubt and one minute of hope. Some lose their faith, some leave, some endure. Miner reads the film as about hope, its answers given in action. The gravest wrong is the abbess's. Her fear for the convent leads her to abandon a newborn and to call it Providence, and the film places the moral failure in her rigid authority. The resolution, an orphanage run by the sisters, depends on Mathilde, a non-believer, showing them their duty, and those who leave religious life are treated with sympathy.
history: Madeleine Pauliac (1912-1946) was a French doctor who headed the French Red Cross mission in Warsaw after the war and treated French soldiers awaiting repatriation. Her diary, kept by her nephew Philippe Maynial, records that Soviet soldiers had raped nuns in a convent near Warsaw, and that she delivered babies there in secret. She died in a car accident in 1946, aged 33. The numbers of nuns attacked in Poland in 1945 are not firmly established.
liberties: Mathilde is a junior doctor, whereas Pauliac headed the Warsaw hospital, and Samuel and the affair are not in the published accounts of Pauliac. Her notes say that pregnant nuns raised the question of abortion with her in veiled terms, which the film leaves out. The abbess's abandonment of a baby, Zofia's suicide and the orphanage ending are not attested and appear to be invention.
advisories:
The rapes take place before the story and are not shown, but they are described. Soviet soldiers at a checkpoint come close to assaulting the heroine.

A brief non-marital bedroom scene between Mathilde and a colleague.

Childbirth scenes, including a Caesarean section; venereal disease; a nun's suicide; an abbess abandons a newborn.

For adults.

A religious superior is the film's chief wrongdoer, and leaving religious life is shown sympathetically.

title: A Birth
decision: PUBLISH: Tentative. The English subtitle file, a poor machine translation, answers the question the record left open. The faith is at the centre: baptisms, including a fellow prisoner's before his death; Kim's ordination as the first Korean priest; an Easter Mass whose consecration is heard in Latin in the traditional form; and a martyrdom presented as a confession of love made without fear, with last words that he gains eternal life by dying for the Catholic faith, followed by his farewell letter. summary: Park Heung-sik's lavish Korean biography of Andrew Kim Taegon, the first Korean priest, from his seminary years in Macau to his beheading in 1846.
synopsis: The film opens in 1836 with the French missionary Pierre Maubant crossing secretly into Korea, where Catholicism is outlawed. Kim Taegon, a teenager from a Catholic family, is sent with Choe Yang-eop and Choe Bang-je to study for the priesthood in Macau, where he learns Latin, French and Chinese as well as theology. War in China blocks the way home, and he spends time in the Philippines and China before making perilous journeys across frozen country and open sea to open a route for missionaries into Korea, helped by Yu Jin-gil, the Church's interpreter in its dealings with China. In 1845 he is ordained priest in Shanghai, the first Korean to be so, and returns to Joseon in a small wooden boat. Arrested in a new persecution, he is beheaded at Saenamteo in 1846, aged twenty-five.
inclusion: It is the first feature film about Korea's first priest, made for the bicentenary of his birth, and it is the only screen treatment of the Korean martyrs on this scale. Its money is on the screen in snowfields, storms at sea and the streets of Macau. Yoon Si-yoon plays Kim and speaks four languages; the reviews single him out, and Ahn Sung-ki adds weight as the interpreter Yu Jin-gil. Park Ji-yoon of The Fact found it crammed, packing ten years of events into a breathless sequence and assuming knowledge many viewers lack. Kim Jung-ki in Maeil Shinmun calls it sincere and praises the lead. Its dialogue keeps the sacraments and the martyrdom at the centre.
themes: Kim's priesthood and martyrdom frame the film, and the faith is at its centre. Converts are baptised, one of them a fellow prisoner shortly before his death; Kim is ordained in Shanghai; and at Easter he celebrates Mass, with the consecration heard in Latin in the traditional form. The pioneer material, his maps, the sea route and the Opium War, serves the aim of opening a way for missionaries. He is shown with fears and doubts as well as conviction, and his last words are that he gains eternal life by dying for the Catholic faith, which presents his martyrdom as a confession of love made without fear.
history: Andrew Kim Taegon (1821–1846), from a Catholic family that had already given martyrs, was sent to Macau in 1836 to train for the priesthood. He was ordained in Shanghai in 1845, the first Korean priest, and returned to bring missionaries into the country. Arrested in 1846, he was beheaded at Saenamteo by the Han River in September 1846. With 78 other martyrs of the 1839 and 1846 persecutions, among them Augustine Yu Jin-gil and Pierre Maubant, he was beatified by Pius XI in 1925; the group was canonised in 1984.

Persecution, imprisonment and a beheading.

title: Fátima, Terra de Fé!
decision: GREY: Identity, outline and production context are established by the Cinemateca Portuguesa and Público's Cinecartaz. The Cinemateca's programme note and the Diário de Notícias comment on its craft and its place in the Estado Novo's official cinema, but no source assesses how it treats the apparitions or the faith. Settle with a 1943 Portuguese Catholic review (e.g. Novidades, Voz da Fátima) or a recorded viewing of the Cinemateca print, checking especially the staged apparition episode and the fictional cure.

grey.question: The film is well identified as Jorge Brum do Canto's 1943 feature, preserved and screened by the Cinemateca Portuguesa. No independent review of how it treats Fátima exists. Its story of a sceptical doctor converted by his son's cure is fiction, set beside a staged account of the 1917 apparitions, and the only critical comments, from the Cinemateca and the Portuguese press, concern its craft and its official character under the Salazar regime. A contemporary Catholic review or a recorded viewing would settle it.

summary: Jorge Brum do Canto's wartime Portuguese drama of a sceptical doctor converted by his son's cure, set beside a staged account of the Fátima apparitions.
synopsis: A doctor without faith has become estranged from his family over religion and devotes himself to his patients. When his son is badly injured in an accident, his medicine proves insufficient, and the boy's recovery, attributed to the intervention of Our Lady of Fátima, brings the father to belief. The film sets this invented story against the shrine and includes an episode that reconstructs the 1917 apparitions to the shepherd children. The father's struggle between science and faith is the dramatic spine.
inclusion: The Cinemateca Portuguesa calls it the classic Portuguese sound film on Fátima. It was an ambitious studio picture, and Brum do Canto was one of the leading directors of the period. He himself dismissed it as commissioned work with little of himself in it, except the apparition episode and the doctor's religious dilemma, and the Diário de Notícias presents the film as an example of the Estado Novo's official production. The Cinemateca nonetheless singles out passages of documentary interest and some well-directed sequences. It is a document of how Portugal presented Fátima to itself in wartime, a quarter-century after the apparitions.
themes: The film turns on a healing and the conversion it brings, with a man of science confronted by a cure his medicine could not achieve. That pattern reflects Fátima's place as a shrine of pilgrimage and prayer for the sick, and the film adds a staged account of the apparitions themselves.
history: Three shepherd children, Lúcia dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto, reported six apparitions of Our Lady at the Cova da Iria, near Fátima, between May and October 1917, ending with the solar phenomenon seen by a large crowd on 13 October. By 1942 Fátima was a national shrine.
liberties: The doctor, his family and the cure are invented for the film. The 1917 apparitions appear as a reconstructed episode within the fiction.

suitability.note: The film is slow and talky by modern standards, and nothing violent or frightening is recorded. Children who know the Fátima story may follow the apparition episode.

doctrine: The apparitions at the Cova da Iria were reported between 13 May and 13 October 1917. On 13 October 1930 Bishop José Alves Correia da Silva of Leiria declared them 'worthy of belief', which allowed public devotion; this is a judgment that belief is permitted, not a doctrine that Catholics must accept. The Lady's reported message asked for the daily Rosary for peace, prayer and sacrifice for sinners, devotion to the Immaculate Heart and the consecration of Russia. On 31 October 1942 Pius XII consecrated the human race to the Immaculate Heart of Mary in a radio message to Portugal, naming the peoples of Russia, and repeated the act at St Peter's on 8 December 1942. Healings attributed to Our Lady are for the bishop to examine.
production: Jorge Brum do Canto's fourth feature was the first production of Filmes Portugueses, a company set up by the cinematographer José César de Sá, who also directed production. It was shot at Tóbis Portuguesa in Lisbon and released in 1943 at 102 minutes.

title: Coroação de Nossa Senhora de Fátima
originalTitle: Coroação de Nossa Senhora de Fátima
decision: HOLD: The film exists (Cinemateca Portuguesa, 1946, 19 minutes, Eduardo García Maroto) but nothing beyond the Cinemateca's two-sentence programme note describes it. A further search of the Cinemateca's digitisation catalogue (no entry), RTP Arquivos, the Santuário de Fátima site, the 2017 press coverage (DN, Time Out) and Spanish sources on García Maroto found no fuller description, no online copy and no 1946 notice. It needs the Cinemateca's catalogue record or a viewing there, or a 1946 notice (Voz da Fátima, Novidades, Diário de Notícias) via the Biblioteca Nacional Digital.
summary: A 19-minute Portuguese record of the coronation of the Fátima statue by Pius XII's legate in May 1946, made by the Spanish director Eduardo García Maroto.
synopsis: The film records the ceremonies of 13 May 1946, when Cardinal Benedetto Aloisi Masella, sent by Pius XII as papal legate, crowned the statue of Our Lady of Fátima at the Cova da Iria. According to the Cinemateca Portuguesa, it also shows the pilgrimage and the route and region around the shrine. The crown, made in Lisbon, was the gift of Portuguese women in thanksgiving that the country had been kept out of the Second World War. The archive's note does not describe the film's narration, music or structure, and no other account of its contents has been found.
inclusion: Its value is as a record. The 1946 coronation was a papal act that gave a shrine not yet thirty years old Rome's public recognition. García Maroto, a Spanish director who made the Luso-Spanish co-production A Mantilha de Beatriz the same year, filmed it. The Cinemateca Portuguesa preserved it and screened it in 2017, before Brum do Canto's Fátima, Terra de Fé!, in a season of seven films about Fátima, and the Diário de Notícias presented the pair as a contrast between the regime's official fiction and the record of the event. Nothing is known about its quality as filmmaking. It is chiefly for viewers interested in the history of the shrine.
themes: The film's Catholic content is a liturgical and devotional event: the solemn crowning of an image of Our Lady by a papal legate, an honour granted by the Pope to images with a long and fervent cult. The coronation followed Pius XII's 1942 consecration of the world to the Immaculate Heart of Mary and showed Fátima as a shrine with Rome's explicit approval. How the film frames the event, whether chiefly as devotion, as national celebration, or both, is not described in any source.
history: Pius XII authorised the canonical coronation of the Fátima statue, carved by José Ferreira Thedim and enthroned in the Chapel of the Apparitions in 1920. His legate, Cardinal Benedetto Aloisi Masella, crowned it on 13 May 1946 before a large crowd of pilgrims. The crown, of gold set with pearls and precious stones and made without charge by Lisbon craftsmen, had been offered by the women of Portugal in 1942 in thanksgiving for the country's neutrality in the war.
advisories:
A short documentary with no known violence or sexual content.

The Cinemateca screened it, with Fátima, Terra de Fé!, under an M/12 classification.

No commercial edition is known; access is through the Cinemateca Portuguesa.

title: Faustina
decision: REJECT: Scope (editorial ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's subject is recognised as saint or blessed only through a canonisation or beatification made after the Second Vatican Council (Faustina Kowalska, beatified 1993, canonised 2000; her Divine Mercy writings were also placed under restriction by the Holy Office in 1959).
summary: A spare Polish television-produced portrait of Sister Faustina Kowalska, the peasant nun whose visions of Christ became the Divine Mercy devotion, told by an elderly sister looking back.
synopsis: An old nun, Sister Feliksa, remembers the young Faustina, a barely educated peasant girl who joined the Congregation of Our Lady of Mercy and worked in its kitchens and gardens. Faustina reports that Christ appears to her and asks for an image of His mercy to be painted. Her superiors and sisters doubt her; some mock her. Her confessor, Fr Michał Sopoćko, takes her seriously and has the picture made. Sick with tuberculosis, she keeps a diary of her visions. Feliksa's memories are coloured by regret for how the community treated her.
inclusion: Dorota Segda's performance as a sickly but joyful mystic is the film's strength. Wojciech Kilar wrote the score. The film's interest lies in its picture of an ordinary convent, its kitchens, rivalries and suspicion of a sister claiming visions. Frank Swietek found it reverent but too fragmentary and elliptical, with an unnecessarily intricate flashback structure.
themes: The film concerns religious life, obedience under suspicion, and the claim of private revelation. It treats Faustina's visions of Christ sympathetically. The devotion she promoted was placed under a Holy Office prohibition in 1959, and the film's handling of that history has not been documented.
history: Helena Kowalska (1905–1938) entered the Congregation of the Sisters of Our Lady of Mercy in 1925 as Sister Maria Faustina. Her confessor in Vilnius, Fr Michał Sopoćko, had the Divine Mercy image painted in 1934. She died of tuberculosis in Kraków in 1938. On 6 March 1959 the Holy Office prohibited the spread of images and writings promoting the devotion in the forms she proposed; the prohibition was rescinded in 1978. She was canonised in 2000.
liberties: Sister Feliksa's narration is a framing device; how far the film dramatises or composites the convent's treatment of Faustina has not been established.
advisories:
Illness and death from tuberculosis; scenes of a sister being mocked by her community.

No known violence or sexual content, but no source confirms this in detail.

The film presents private revelations that the Holy Office restricted in 1959.

title: The Bells of Nagasaki
decision: GREY: identity is secure (Shochiku, NFAJ: 94 min, 22–23 September 1950, script by Shindō, Mitsuhata and Hashida from Nagai's books) and the outline and censorship history are documented (Seid/PFA, Shibata). Treatment of the faith is described only in a paragraph each by Shibata and Seid, who disagree on whether the conversion is shown; Nipponica judges it a good Ofuna-style work but says nothing of faith. Not HOLD because identity and content are established. Settles with a scene-level account (viewing or the 1950 Kinema Junpō review; Tadao Satō) of the conversion, Midori's faith and death, the treatment of the bomb as providence, and the ending.

grey.question: The film's identity is secure, but no independent review describes in any detail how it presents Takashi Nagai's Catholic faith. The two scholarly accounts give a paragraph each and disagree on whether his conversion happens on screen. Nagai's own reading of the bomb as a burnt offering to God is disputed, and it is not known whether the film adopts it. A scene-level account of the conversion, his wife Midori's faith and death, and the ending, from a viewing or from the 1950 Japanese reviews, would settle it.

summary: Shochiku's occupation-era melodrama of Takashi Nagai, the Catholic radiologist of Nagasaki, and the first Japanese feature to approach the atomic bombing, made under heavy American censorship.
synopsis: Takashi Nagai, a medical student in Nagasaki, turns to radiology at a time when older doctors scorn the field. He is supported by his wife Midori. His early X-ray work exposes him to radiation, and he learns that he is dying before the war ends. Through the years of war he balances his research against duty to his wife and children, and he is drawn towards the Catholic faith of the city's Urakami Christians. In the last third of the film the atomic bomb falls on Nagasaki; the explosion is seen only as a cloud over the mountains. Afterwards the dying Nagai and the survivors set about rebuilding the city, and the bell of the ruined cathedral rings again.
inclusion: It is the first Japanese feature to approach the atomic bombing, made under Occupation censorship. The Nipponica encyclopedia counts it among the good films that showed the best side of Hideo Ōba's Ofuna studio style; Steve Seid of the Pacific Film Archive calls it a somewhat sentimental melodrama. For a Catholic viewer the interest is that a major Japanese studio built a 1950 film round a convert's faith and death.
themes: The archive notes and Yuko Shibata's study describe Nagai as drawn to the Catholic faith of his wife Midori and of the Urakami Christians, and accepting his own death from radiation with resignation; Shibata says he treats the bombing as a test given by God. The closing bell is the Angelus bell of Urakami Cathedral. Nagai himself taught that the bomb was a burnt offering accepted by God, a reading later criticised by some survivors.
history: Takashi Nagai was a radiologist at Nagasaki Medical College who was baptised a Catholic at 26, influenced by his wife Midori's faith. His X-ray work had already given him a fatal dose of radiation when the bomb of 9 August 1945 devastated Urakami, the Catholic district, and killed Midori. His book The Bells of Nagasaki was cleared by the Occupation censors only on condition that it appeared with an account of Japanese atrocities in Manila; it was published in 1949, and the film followed the next year.
liberties: Shibata calls the film a "somehow fictionalized" version of Nagai's story. The bombing is shown only as a distant cloud over the mountains.
advisories:
Terminal illness from radiation, and a wife's death in the bombing; the explosion itself is seen only at a distance.

Wartime hardship.

No English-subtitled home-video edition is known; the Pacific Film Archive holds a restricted subtitled print.

sources.title: Angelus
sources.claims: Angelus said morning, noon and evening at the bell; indulgences of John XXII (1318, 1327) and Benedict XIII (14 September 1724)

names: Nagasaki no kane (The Bells of Nagasaki, 1949), Kono ko o nokoshite and Rosario no kusari, books by Takashi Nagai

suitability.note: The dying man and his wife's death are the hard parts, and the film is slow and sentimental, so it suits older children watching with a parent.

doctrine: Urakami was the home of Japan's hidden Christians. On 17 March 1865 a group of them made themselves known to Père Petitjean at the new church in Nagasaki; persecution resumed in 1867, the Urakami faithful were sent into exile, and many died before the survivors came home in 1873. Nagai entered that community by baptism in June 1934, taking the name Paul. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1907) records the Angelus said morning, noon and evening at the bell, indulgenced by John XXII in 1318 and by Benedict XIII in 1724. Nagai's teaching that the dead of Urakami were a burnt offering accepted by God is his own reading, not a doctrine of the Church. It rests on the traditional teaching that suffering joined to Christ's Passion can be offered in reparation, but the Church has never declared any particular calamity to be such an offering.
production: Shochiku's Ōfuna studio made the film the year after Nagai's book appeared, with the support of Nagasaki City and Prefecture, the Society of St Paul and Toshiba. The Occupation authorities rejected the first two outlines, many scenes were cut from Shindō's script, and the censors required a finale of survivors rebuilding the city; the bombing was a forbidden subject, so the studio cast the story as melodrama. Hideo Ōba directed. Liturgical music was sung by the St Gregory Choir. Yūji Koseki's theme song, with words by Hachirō Satō and sung by Mariko Ike, became very popular. The film opened on 23 September 1950, while Nagai was still alive; he died on 1 May 1951.

title: Nazarín
decision: REJECT: Not a problem a reader can weigh but the film's thesis. Buñuel, an atheist, uses Galdós's Christ-like priest to argue that literal Christian charity is futile and that the Church disowns it. The film invents scenes the novel lacks for that purpose: a dying woman rejects the priest and heaven for her lover, and in prison a thief tells him that his good life is worth no more than the thief's bad one, with no answer given. Ambiguity that almost won it an OCIC prize in 1959 does not change the argument; the director rejected the religious reading.

title: All That Remains
decision: PUBLISH: Respinti's review and the distributor and festival records document a Catholic conversion and family story, the bombing of Nagasaki, Nagai's illness and writing, and an imagined closing reunion; Higgins's account of five years' work and survivor interviews supports the seriousness of the research. Nagai is a Servant of God, not a canonised saint.
summary: A British low-budget hybrid of drama, CGI and archive footage about Takashi Nagai, the Nagasaki radiologist and convert who lost his wife to the atomic bomb.
synopsis: Takashi Nagai is a brilliant, sceptical young doctor in Nagasaki who lodges with a family of Catholics descended from Japan's hidden Christians. Their faith and their daughter Midori draw him, slowly, into the Church, and they marry. He throws himself into pioneering radiology, neglecting his family and his health, and is diagnosed with leukaemia. On 9 August 1945 the atomic bomb falls on Urakami, the Catholic heart of the city. Midori is killed. Nagai, injured and dying, works among the survivors, cares for his two children and, increasingly bedridden, writes the books that made him famous. The film ends with an imagined reunion with Midori at the cathedral, as on their wedding day.
inclusion: Nagai's story is important and little known outside Japan, and the Higgins brothers treat it with care. Dominic Higgins spent about five years on the project and interviewed survivors. The mix of live action, CGI and archive footage is a resourceful answer to a small budget. Marco Respinti found the archive images of the bombing chilling and called it a film about the saint who beat the bomb. Faith carries the story. Conversion, Christian marriage and a doctor's charity are its subject, and the film shows Nagai reading the catastrophe in the light of Providence and the Cross, as he did in his writings.
themes: The film is a conversion story first: an atheist scientist is drawn to Christ through the witness of a Catholic family and community with centuries of hidden fidelity behind them. Marriage is shown as a vocation, and its loss as a grief. Nagai's response to the bomb, serving the wounded, raising his children and praying, is presented as Christian hope. The closing reunion is a poetic image of hope in the resurrection, not a claimed vision.
history: Takashi Nagai (1908–1951) was baptised in 1934 and married Midori Moriyama, whose family had kept the faith in secret through the persecutions. Already diagnosed with radiation-induced leukaemia, he survived the bombing of 9 August 1945, which killed Midori. He spent his last years in a tiny hut, writing; his books include The Bells of Nagasaki. His cause for beatification was opened in 2021.
liberties: Dialogue is invented and the narrative selects heavily from Nagai's life. The final reunion is imagined. CGI reconstructions stand in for prewar and bombed Nagasaki. The film is a family story and does not attempt a full account of the war or of the decision to use the bomb.
advisories:
Archive images of the atomic bombing and its victims, described by one reviewer as chilling; mass death and severe injury.

Bereavement, terminal illness and children who have lost their mother.

Best for teenagers and adults.

doctrine: Nagai came to the Church as an adult convert. The Church teaches that Baptism is necessary for salvation and that adults must be instructed and freely seek it (Council of Trent, Session 6; Roman Catechism). His wife's family belonged to the hidden Christians of Urakami. Their ancestors kept the faith after the persecutions of the Tokugawa period without priests, and in 1865 the Christians of Nagasaki made themselves known to Fr Petitjean at Oura. The Church teaches that suffering borne in union with Christ can be offered for the sanctification of the soul. Nagai's own reading of the bomb as a providential sacrifice for peace was his own view and is not Church teaching. He died on 1 May 1951. He is not a canonised saint.
production: Pixel Revolution Films, the makers of the Fátima film The 13th Day, made it. To save money the Higgins brothers did the visual effects themselves, and production took almost four years. The film was crowdfunded in its early stages. Members of the local Japanese community appeared as extras. Ignatius Press lists the DVD, with a documentary on Nagai told by Fr Paul Glynn, SM, under a publication date of 6 May 2016. The running time is given as 114 to 120 minutes. It was shown at the Uranium Film Festival in Berlin in 2017.

title: Don Bosco
decision: GREY: identity and production history are secure (ANICA visa, Torino Film Festival restoration, Enciclopedia del Cinema in Piemonte). The only independent critical text read is Cinema Illustrazione (1935), which judges craft, not faith. Pre-conciliar Catholic approval (Segnalazioni cinematografiche; L'Osservatore Romano and Rivista del Cinematografo) is known only at second hand, via Salesian ANS and an unpublished essay quoted by Prono. Salesians wrote the treatment, negotiated the script and later owned the negative. Settles with the 1935 Segnalazioni/Rivista del Cinematografo texts or a documented viewing of the 2021 restoration (dreams, Generala episode, Church–State material).

grey.question: The film's identity and production history are well documented, but no independent review describes how it treats the faith. Approval from the Catholic film press of 1935 survives only at second hand, in Salesian accounts and an unpublished essay. The Salesians supplied the story, negotiated the script and later owned the film. A reading of the 1935 Catholic reviews, or a documented viewing of the restored version that covers Bosco's dreams, the reshot Generala episode and the Church–State material, would settle it.

summary: Lux's first production, made the year after John Bosco's canonisation: a Turin-shot life of the saint with one professional actor, Gian Paolo Rosmino, and real Salesians around him.
synopsis: A Monferrato farm boy who has lost his father clashes with his older half-brother Antonio and finds a mentor in the old priest Don Calosso, who teaches him Latin. After Calosso's death Giovanni leaves home to study at Chieri, where the death of his friend Luigi Comollo marks him. Ordained, he goes to Turin, where townspeople distrust his rowdy Sunday gatherings of poor boys. Help comes, surprisingly, from anticlerical authorities, who suggest a society whose members keep their civil rights. The Oratory becomes schools and workshops, the Salesians and the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians follow, and missionaries leave for Patagonia. The film ends with his death in 1888 and a coda of his canonisation in St Peter's.
inclusion: It is the first sound feature about Don Bosco and the first production of Lux, later one of the major Italian studios. It was shot in a snowbound Turin, at Chieri and in the Monferrato, with non-professionals around Gian Paolo Rosmino, real Salesians among them. The director Goffredo Alessandrini, by his own account not a practising Catholic, said he kept to Bosco's memoirs and the historians and invented only linking scenes. Contemporary opinion was mixed. Cinema Illustrazione's critic praised Rosmino and the death scene but found the film disjointed, often superficial and close to an informational documentary. It failed in first-run cinemas and found its audience in parish halls.
themes: Salesian accounts and archive synopses agree on its shape. A vocation grows into institutions, from a priest's Sunday gatherings of poor boys to schools, workshops, two religious congregations and missions in Patagonia. The Salesian historian Fr Rufillo Uguccioni wrote the first treatment, and the order's delegate negotiated the script throughout.
history: John Bosco was born on 16 August 1815 at Becchi near Castelnuovo, Piedmont, and lost his father when he was two. He was ordained in Turin on 5 June 1841. In the 1840s he gathered poor and abandoned boys in the Oratory, which settled at Valdocco in 1846, and added workshops and schools. He founded the Salesians in 1859 and, with Maria Mazzarello, the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians in 1872. His missionaries reached Patagonia in 1875. He died in Turin on 31 January 1888.
liberties: The first version, released in April 1935, included an episode at the Generala reformatory that the Salesians considered invented. After their protests the scene was reshot, with a caption stressing Bosco's role, and a second version reached cinemas in September 1935. A third version became the standard print. The 2021 restoration reconstructs the second version. Bosco's real outing with Generala inmates in 1855 suggests the scene dramatised an actual episode, but this is unresolved.
advisories:
Poverty, the death of a friend and a deathbed scene.

An early sound film with period acting and recording; patience required.

No age classification found.

doctrine: Bosco's work was a work of Christian education: to keep poor boys from sin and bring them to the sacraments of penance and Holy Communion. His method, which he called the preventive system, rests on reason, religion and loving-kindness. The Salesian Society, which he founded under the patronage of St Francis de Sales, received final approval from Pius IX in 1874. He had a strong devotion to Our Lady Help of Christians, a title whose feast, on 24 May, Pius VII established after his return to Rome. Pius XI, who had known Bosco, beatified him in 1929 and canonised him on Easter Sunday, 1 April 1934. His feast is 31 January.
production: Goffredo Alessandrini directed the film for Lux Film, then run by the industrialist Riccardo Gualino, who had been sent into internal exile on Lipari by the Fascist regime. It was made a year after the canonisation, in the climate that followed the Lateran Pacts of 1929. The film runs about 90 minutes in black and white. Gualino later ceded the negative to the Salesians, who held it in their archive. A restored version made from that negative, deposited at Ivrea in 2016, was shown at the Torino Film Festival in 2021.

title: La mies es mucha
decision: PUBLISH: Ernesto Fayé's detailed 1949 review in Cristiandad, read in full, documents a restrained, humorous and devout missionary drama with named religious advisers and judges the one doubtful Christmas Mass gag innocent; RTVE fixes the plot and audience guidance. The director's role as the Franco regime's official filmmaker and the film's place in national-Catholic cinema are disclosed; neither source shows the film carrying political propaganda.
summary: Sáenz de Heredia's missionary drama sends a young Spanish priest to a plague-stricken Indian village, and balances sacrifice with gentle comedy.
synopsis: Father Santiago, a young Spanish missionary, arrives at Kattinga in India to replace the ailing Father Daniel, who dies soon after. He finds the villagers in the grip of Sandem, a trader and moneylender whose loans end in forced labour in a mine. To free them, Santiago signs for the debts of the whole village. When the note falls due, Sandem demands payment. At the same moment people sick with plague begin arriving, and Santiago gives himself to their care. The comedy of a newcomer learning the mission's ways, including a Midnight Mass where the wrong gramophone record plays, gives way to the cost of staying with his flock.
inclusion: Unlike much Spanish religious cinema of the 1940s, it keeps to the facts and spares the rhetoric. The 1949 Cristiandad critic praised its 'gran contención', with no showy technique, no melodramatic tricks and humour that makes it a pleasure, not a seminary lecture. A Vincentian missionary who had served at Cuttack advised on the village, and the Augustinian Félix García advised on religious matters. The story of a priest who pledges himself for his people's debts and then serves them through an epidemic is a clean, strong one. The Indian characters are seen through a 1940s Spanish lens, with all its limits.
themes: The film's Catholic case is missionary charity in its literal form. The priest takes on his people's debt, then gives his life in the plague. The Midnight Mass gag, in which an unexpected record replaces the carols, worried some contemporaries. Cristiandad's critic, who was alert to irreverence elsewhere, judged it innocent and typically Spanish, with no offence to the Mass itself. Evangelisation is presented as service to the poor against exploitation, not conquest.
liberties: An original story, not a biography. The Indian setting is reconstructed with Spanish locations and actors in some roles, and the picture of Indian society is simplified. Recorded runtimes vary widely between versions.
advisories:
Plague, illness and the death of priests and villagers.

Forced labour and debt bondage.

RTVE rated its broadcast not recommended for under-12s.

A comic mix-up during Midnight Mass may bother some viewers; contemporary Catholic critics judged it harmless.

suitability.note: The comic first half is easy going, but the plague and the deaths make it a film for older children, who will find something to think about in the priest's self-giving.

doctrine: The title is Matthew 9:37: 'The harvest indeed is great, but the labourers are few.' The years before the film saw the popes press hard for missions: Benedict XV's Maximum illud (1919) and Pius XI's Rerum Ecclesiae (1926) urged the training of native clergy and the support of missionaries, and in 1927 Pius XI named St Francis Xavier, apostle of India, and St Thérèse of Lisieux patrons of the missions. Father Santiago's signing for his people's debts is a corporal work of mercy, the ransoming of captives, and his staying with the plague-stricken follows the traditional teaching that a pastor must give the sacraments to the dying even at risk to his own life. Midnight Mass belongs to the old Christmas privilege by which every priest may say three Masses on the feast.
production: The film was made under the patronage of Bishop Ángel Herrera Oria of Málaga. José Luis Sáenz de Heredia, a first cousin of José Antonio Primo de Rivera and the regime's leading director, made it in 1948. India was recreated in Málaga, in the tropical gardens of La Concepción. It was a large box-office success. The Círculo de Escritores Cinematográficos gave it its medals for best film and best director, and for supporting performances by Rafael Romero Marchent and Julia Caba Alba. It belongs to the national-Catholic cinema of the 1940s, and Catholic critics such as Cristiandad's praised it partly as a credit to Spanish missions.

title: Le Sorcier du ciel
decision: GREY: identity is secure (CNC visa 8067, Unifrance, Cinematografo). A brief pre-conciliar Catholic critical judgment now exists: Séquences no. 16 (January 1959) cites the film as an example of the artifice Pius XII warned against, the director having gone astray by chasing the sensational side of the saint, notably the devil. Kind 'reservations' rather than 'unverified' because the concern is now stated by an independent source. Not REJECT: Vianney was canonised in 1925. Settles with the Centrale Catholique cote, a 1949 Radio-Cinéma or La Croix review, or a documented viewing of the devil scenes.

grey.question: Le Sorcier du ciel gives the Devil a speaking part and stages the Curé d'Ars's night-time struggles with him as set-pieces. The question is one of emphasis. Writing in 1959, the Quebec film review Séquences cited it as an example of the artifice Pius XII warned against: the director went astray chasing the sensational side of the saint's life, and spiritual combat sits badly in a presbytery bedroom. A contemporary French Catholic review or rating, or a documented viewing, would show whether the saint or the spectacle dominates.

summary: A French life of the Curé d'Ars, with Georges Rollin as Vianney facing a hostile village and a Devil who argues with him at night.
synopsis: In 1818 the young priest Jean-Marie Vianney is sent to Ars, a village of unbelievers and anticlericals, and is met with jeers from the blacksmith Sanson and the innkeeper Mairey, whose wedding is being celebrated. Poor and worn by work and fasting, he preaches boldly, while the Devil works against him and the two of them argue at night. Falsely accused of plotting against the government, he is about to be arrested when he cures Mairey's crippled son, and the father returns to the faith. His fame grows, and he confesses day and night and reads souls. He tries to flee the celebrity but is brought back. At the end only Sanson resists, until the old curé's death.
inclusion: The subject is the patron of parish priests, and the film builds its story round what made him famous: preaching, penance, the long hours in the confessional and a village won back to the faith. It was selected for Venice in 1949. It is one of the few films to take the saint's reported struggles with the devil literally and put them on screen, which is what its critics questioned. Bresson's Diary of a Country Priest followed two years later, a useful comparison for how French cinema of the period filmed the priesthood.
themes: The film presents the conversion of a parish through a priest's suffering and prayer. It shows him preaching against the tavern and the dance, the confessional as the place where souls are won, and the devil's attacks as a sign that the work is succeeding. The cure of the innkeeper's son and the last holdout's conversion at Vianney's death make grace visible. In 1959 Séquences judged that Blistène had gone astray in pursuing the surprising side of the saint's life, and that spiritual combat is poorly contained in the closed, material space of a presbytery room.
history: Jean-Baptiste-Marie Vianney became parish priest of Ars in 1818, when his bishop warned him there was little love of God in the parish. He made the church his home and disciplined himself with vigils and fasts. In his last years he spent sixteen to eighteen hours a day in the confessional and was credited with reading souls and healing the sick, especially children. He longed to flee into solitude but never abandoned his post. He died at Ars on 4 August 1859.
liberties: Unifrance's synopsis says the film presents his life "en forme un peu romancée", and it gives him invented adversaries in the village. The departure and return compress his recorded longing to leave Ars into a single episode. The Devil appears as a speaking character, a dramatic device Séquences considered misjudged.
advisories:
Night scenes in which the Devil harasses and argues with the priest; these may frighten children.

Village hostility and mockery of a priest; a crippled child; a deathbed.

General-audience classification in France (CNC).

doctrine: The sacrament of penance is central. The Council of Trent (Session 14, 1551) taught that priests have the power to forgive sins, and that sacramental confession of all mortal sins is necessary to salvation. The Church also holds that devils are fallen angels who were created good (Fourth Lateran Council, 1215) and who tempt men but cannot compel them. Accounts of Vianney's harassment by the devil are traditional, but the film dramatises them freely. Vianney was beatified in 1905 and canonised by Pius XI on 31 May 1925. Pius XI named him patron of parish priests in 1929. His feast is 4 August.
production: Made for Ydex Films in black and white. Raymond Loyer was Satan as a voice or shadow. The film was released in France on 14 October 1949 and runs about 100 minutes. It was shown in Italy as Il paese senza Dio.

title: Caterina da Siena
decision: PUBLISH: The contemporary judgment of the Centro Cattolico Cinematografico (preserved in the Italian bishops' film-commission archive) approves the film for all audiences as made with elevated intentions, finds Catherine's mysticism well conveyed and asks parish halls to cut one bedroom scene; ANICA and Film Atlas establish identity and the 1947 censorship certificate. Intermezzo's hostile review and Gianluca della Maggiore's account cover craft and reception. The weak craft and the parish-hall cut are disclosed; neither is a doctrinal problem. Distinct from Palella's later Io, Caterina (1956).
summary: Oreste Palella's modest postwar life of St Catherine of Siena, from her childhood vision to her death in Rome, approved by Italy's Catholic film office.
synopsis: In Siena, the young Caterina Benincasa has a vision of Christ and gives herself to prayer and penance. Her forceful mother, Lapa, wants her married; Caterina answers that she is already the bride of Jesus, and her father and her confessor take her side. She joins the Mantellate, the Dominican women of penance, while still living at home, and the order approves her teaching. After a stay in Florence she returns to nurse the victims of plague in Siena. In 1376 she persuades Pope Gregory XI to bring the papacy back from Avignon to Rome, and miracles are attributed to her. She dies in Rome on 29 April 1380, her last words recorded as 'Blood, blood, blood.'
inclusion: It is an early screen life of Catherine of Siena, made in the poverty of postwar Italy by Oreste Palella, a minor director who returned to the saint in Io, Caterina (1956). The script draws on Catherine's life and letters. The contemporary verdicts are mixed. Italy's Catholic Film Centre found passages of good workmanship and judged Catherine's mysticism well conveyed, but thought the whole rather fragmentary and her political work poorly drawn; it praised the score. The magazine Intermezzo was harsher, saying such a subject needed more preparation and less limited means. The historian Gianluca della Maggiore records that it won over neither critics nor audiences. It is a period piece, not a lost classic.
themes: Catherine's mystical life is the centre of the film: the childhood vision, her refusal of marriage because she is already given to Christ, penance, and her life as a Dominican tertiary living in the world. Her nursing of the plague-stricken shows prayer turning into charity. Her mission to Gregory XI presents loyalty to the Pope as part of the same holiness. The Catholic Film Centre's moral verdict was that the film had been conceived and made with elevated intentions.
history: Caterina Benincasa (1347–1380), the daughter of a Sienese dyer, joined the Dominican Mantellate as a laywoman and became known for her prayer, her penances, her care for the sick and her letters to popes and princes. She urged Gregory XI to return the papacy from Avignon to Rome. Her Dialogue and nearly four hundred letters survive.
advisories:
Plague scenes and a deathbed.

The Catholic Film Centre asked parish halls to cut a first-half sequence showing the character Monna Gioiosa in her bedroom or dressing room.

Cheaply made and, by contemporary accounts, fragmentary; copies are scarce.

title: John of the Cross
decision: GREY: Identity settled: 1997, Saint Luke Productions, directed by K. C. Lynch (Spirituality & Practice and Katoflix; the IMDb credit to Leonardo Defilippis likely reflects his role as producer-performer), with Leonardo and Patti Defilippis in the main roles; 56–60 minutes by edition. Content is clear from the producer's description and a brief Spirituality & Practice notice, but no independent review assesses its treatment, and how it frames the Calced–Discalced conflict is unchecked. A transcript or independent review would move it to PUBLISH or to reservations.
summary: Saint Luke Productions' hour-long drama of John of the Cross, from a poor childhood to the prison cell where he wrote his poems, played by a husband-and-wife company.
synopsis: John grows up in poverty and is drawn early to contemplative prayer. As a young Carmelite friar and priest he finds his order lax, and his austerity offends many of his brethren, including his superiors. In 1567 he meets Teresa of Ávila, who is seeking a partner for her reform; she makes him prior of the first house of Discalced friars, and he later serves as confessor at her convent. Friars opposed to the reform seize him and shut him in a cell for nine months. There he composes much of his poetry and reaches the mystical union he has longed for, before an escape the producers call miraculous. The story is told through the eyes of one of his patrons, and passages from the Spiritual Canticle run through it.
inclusion: Made as a modest video drama by a small American Catholic theatre company, it is one of very few English-language films about John of the Cross, and it puts his poetry at the centre, not treating him as a footnote to Teresa. Frederic and Mary Ann Brussat of Spirituality & Practice, a multifaith review site, describe a drama of the saint's longing for union with God, built round his meeting with Teresa and his imprisonment. Mother Angelica of EWTN endorsed it, according to the producer. At under an hour it is necessarily a sketch, and the tiny cast limits its scale; it is pitched at parish and classroom use.
themes: The film treats John's life as a path to union with God through suffering: the Carmelite rule taken seriously, Teresa's reform, and the dark cell where he writes. Its religious content is traditional: the contemplative vocation, obedience and the cross. The framing invites caution, since the producer's copy says his brethren imprisoned him out of resentment at his holiness, and the Brussats speak of an order that found his devotion excessive and of corruption in it. The actual conflict was a jurisdictional dispute between Calced and Discalced Carmelites under the Church's law, and a holy-reformer-against-the-institution reading would distort it.
history: Juan de Yepes (1542–1591) entered the Carmelites at Medina del Campo in 1563 and was ordained in 1567, the year he met Teresa of Ávila. In 1568 he helped found the first Discalced friary at Duruelo. In December 1577 friars of the Observance seized him at Ávila and held him in their Toledo priory, where he composed much of the Spiritual Canticle; he escaped in August 1578. He was beatified by Clement X in 1675, canonised by Benedict XIII in 1726 and declared a Doctor of the Church by Pius XI in 1926.
advisories:
Imprisonment and harsh treatment of a friar by his brethren.

No sexual content or strong language is reported.

The producer suggests ages 8 and up.

title: The Dark Night
alternateTitles: The Dark Night of the Soul
decision: REJECT: problem too grave. Saura described his subject as John's inner process and a 'secular mysticism' rather than religion. Mariona Visa Barbosa's scene-by-scene study (2009) records that the film has St John of the Cross tell his jailer that he sinned when he met a nun, Ana de Jesús, at a convent; shows that nun succumbing to lust and possessed; casts the same actress as the Virgin Mary; and stages the soul's union with the Bridegroom as John and the Virgin kissing on the mouth and embracing. The Cinémathèque française confirms Julie Delpy plays both the Virgin and a temptress. An invented sin tied to a lustful nun for a canonised Doctor of the Church, and an erotic treatment of Our Lady, presented approvingly as mystical union, cannot be listed even with reservations. The hard rule on post-1965 canonisations does not apply (John was canonised in 1726).

title: Saint John Houghton
decision: GREY: Identity and content are established only by the producer: the Mary's Dowry product page (archived 2021) and production blog (filming July 2015, editing November 2015, DVD release announced 26 March 2016). Houghton was beatified by Leo XIII in 1886, so rule (a) does not apply; he is styled Bl. No independent treatment exists, so unverified rather than PUBLISH.
summary: A half-hour devotional film from Mary's Dowry Productions on Bl. John Houghton, the Carthusian prior who was the first martyr of Henry VIII's royal supremacy.
synopsis: Mary's Dowry films tell a saint's life through silent reconstructed scenes, a devotional narration and original contemplative music, and this one follows that pattern. Houghton flees a marriage his parents have arranged, studies for the priesthood and later enters the London Charterhouse, where he is elected prior. When Henry VIII demands the oath acknowledging his supremacy over the Church in England, Houghton refuses. He and his companions are imprisoned in the Tower, pressed by Thomas Cromwell, tried at Westminster and condemned for high treason. On 4 May 1535 they are dragged on hurdles to Tyburn, and Thomas More watches them go from his cell. Houghton urges his brethren to confession, goes first to the gallows in his habit and forgives his executioner. The reconstructions show him teaching novices, at prayer, in prison and at Tyburn.
inclusion: Houghton is the protomartyr of the English Reformation, yet he has almost no presence on film, and this short is the only dedicated treatment. Mary's Dowry Productions, a small family company in West Sussex, has been making low-budget lives of the English martyrs for parishes and schools since 2007, and describes its approach as prayer as much as information, with silent tableaux, narration and contemplative music in place of drama. That makes it suitable for a classroom or an evening at home, and unsuitable for anyone expecting a dramatised biography. The scenes were filmed over a day in July 2015 in a barn beside a parish church in Goring, which gives a fair idea of the scale.
themes: The Catholic content is unambiguous: the Pope's primacy against the royal supremacy, the Carthusian life of prayer and silence, and a martyrdom met with confession, forgiveness and joy. The producers' text includes More's remark that the monks went to death like bridegrooms to their marriage. As described, it has none of the post-conciliar framing common in recent productions. The producers' own account is plain hagiography, with a terrified jury and a horrified crowd, and it leaves out complications such as Houghton's qualified acceptance of the oath of succession in 1534.
history: Houghton, born in Essex about 1487, entered the London Charterhouse in 1516 and was elected prior in 1531. In 1534 he was imprisoned for refusing the oath of succession, then took it with the qualification "as far as the law of Christ allows". In 1535 he and the priors of Beauvale and Axholme refused the oath of supremacy, and on 4 May they were hanged, drawn and quartered at Tyburn with Richard Reynolds of Syon. Leo XIII beatified him in 1886.
advisories:
The execution at Tyburn is shown in reconstruction; the producers present the film as devotional, not graphic.

Suitable for older children and adults.

The producers call him Saint; he is only beatified, and is styled Bl. John Houghton here.

title: Golgotha
decision: PUBLISH: Identity from Unifrance and AlloCiné; substantive treatment from James Travers's detailed review and K. V. Turley's National Catholic Register essay, which together establish Scripture-based dialogue for Christ, a reverent Passion and a depicted Resurrection. The portrayal of the Temple authorities is disputed in secondary comment and is flagged rather than treated as resolved by silence.
summary: The first sound film of the Passion: Duvivier's dark, crowded Holy Week, with Jean Gabin's Pilate and Harry Baur's Herod, and a crucifixion staged as a cosmic storm.
synopsis: Christ enters Jerusalem to the crowd's acclaim. The high priests, fearing his popularity, plot with Judas and press the Roman authorities. At the Last Supper Christ foretells his betrayal. He is arrested, taken before Caiaphas, Herod and Pilate, mocked and scourged. Pilate, warned by his wife Claudia, tries to release him, but the crowd chooses Barabbas. Christ carries the cross to Golgotha and is crucified as a storm breaks over the city. The film continues past his death and burial to the Risen Christ.
inclusion: Duvivier keeps Christ at a distance for the first half, seen from behind or across a crowd, and lets us read him through the people around him: Our Lady, Peter, Judas, Caiaphas, Herod, Pilate. K. V. Turley, writing for the National Catholic Register, finds the method illuminating and the film well judged at about ninety minutes. Robert Le Vigan speaks only words from the Gospels and plays the part with restraint. The supporting cast is the strength: Harry Baur's massive Herod, Gabin's tired, almost decent Pilate, Edwige Feuillère as his wife. Jules Kruger's photography and Ferdinand Earle's Jerusalem give it scale for a French production, and James Travers singles out the crucifixion sequence. The script is thin and the characters stay at arm's length; some viewers will find it stiff.
themes: The Passion is played straight from the Gospels, without invented speeches for Christ. Travers stresses the film's emphasis on Christ's humanity and suffering. That is a matter of emphasis, not denial, since the film shows the Risen Christ with the wounds of the nails, and Turley calls it a cinematic icon for praying through Holy Week. Our Lady's presence is reverent. The Last Supper is staged after Leonardo. The film locates guilt in a small group of conspirators and in Pilate's weakness.
liberties: Pilate is made more sympathetic than the Gospels require, and Claudia Procula's role is enlarged. Herod's scene is built up for Harry Baur.
advisories:
Scourging, mockery and crucifixion, shown without modern graphic detail but with force.

Some viewers consider the costuming and casting of the Jewish authorities stereotyped in the manner of 1930s European films.

Suitable for older children and up; the crucifixion storm is frightening.

suitability.note: It is a French black-and-white film of about 95 minutes, best for older children who already know the Gospel story.

doctrine: The film's reverent Last Supper and its Resurrection follow the Creed: Christ 'suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried', and rose again. On the question the film is sometimes asked about, who killed Christ, the Roman Catechism of the Council of Trent is plain. Under the Fourth Article it teaches that our sins consigned Christ to the cross, that sinners were the 'authors and ministers' of his Passion, and that 'this guilt seems more enormous in us than in the Jews', since they would not have crucified the Lord had they known him, while Christians who know him deny him by their deeds. Claudia Procula, Pilate's wife, is named in tradition, and the Greek Church keeps her feast on 27 October.
history: Pontius Pilate governed Judaea for Rome from about AD 26 to 36, an unusually long term, and was recalled after complaints from the Samaritans. The Gospels name Caiaphas as high priest and Annas as his father-in-law, and St Luke alone records that Pilate sent Christ to Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee. St Matthew alone records the message from Pilate's wife about her dream. Golgotha, the place of the skull, lay outside the walls of Jerusalem.
production: The project began with Canon Joseph Reymond. Duvivier took it on after Maria Chapdelaine, and the film was shot in 1934 for the company Ichthys Film, with exteriors at Fort-de-l'Eau near Algiers and interiors at Boulogne. Jean Perrier built solid sets. It was a costly production by French standards. Jacques Ibert's score makes extensive use of the ondes Martenot, an electronic instrument then still a novelty, and Ibert later drew a concert suite from it. Golgotha opened in France in April 1935, played across Europe, and reached the United States in 1937 as Behold the Man, when the National Board of Review named it the sixth best foreign film of the year. The British censors refused it.

title: Miracle of Saint Thérèse
decision: PUBLISH: Unifrance confirms identity (FAF / Films Fernand Rivers, released 29 August 1952); Steven Greydanus's Decent Films review (A+, +4, nothing objectionable) gives detailed evidence of a reverent biography that presents the Little Way, Carmelite life and her death faithfully. Main checks against Thérèse's own Story of a Soul show no material distortion; minor chronological points are noted.
summary: A plain, reverent French biography of St Thérèse of Lisieux, from her childhood at Les Buissonnets to her death in Carmel, framed by her cause for canonisation.
synopsis: Framed by documentary-style scenes of her canonisation cause, the film tells Thérèse Martin's life. A pious child in a devout family, she hears her father read about Joan of Arc and wants to be a saint. Gravely ill as a girl, she is cured when a statue of Our Lady seems to smile at her. She follows two sisters into the Carmel of Lisieux, overcoming the objections of the convent's ecclesiastical superior. Inside, a prioress rebukes her ambition to be a saint as presumptuous; she answers with Christ's call to be perfect. As novice mistress she teaches her 'little way' of spiritual childhood. She dies young of tuberculosis after a painful illness.
inclusion: Greydanus gives it his highest grade and calls it an excellent, reverent biopic. By his account it takes Thérèse's spirituality seriously instead of turning her into a sugary icon. Her 'little way' is shown in friction with the more severe piety around her, and the film is willing to show a young nun correcting her elders. France Descaut is a sincere Thérèse, Jean Debucourt plays her father, Suzanne Flon is among the nuns, and the black-and-white photography and convent sets are convincing. The canonisation-process frame is stiff, and the titles in both languages promise something it is not. The only English home release is dubbed.
themes: Sanctity in small things is the film's concern. Thérèse wants to be a saint, is told that this is presumption, and replies that Christ commanded it. Her 'little way' is love expressed in ordinary duties and acceptance of suffering; as novice mistress she spares a novice a harsh penance that harms body and work. Greydanus draws out her childhood devotion to Joan of Arc and her love for the missions. The Marian cure and a snowfall are shown as signs of grace without exaggeration, and her death of tuberculosis is treated as a consuming of love.
history: Thérèse Martin was born at Alençon in 1873. In May 1883, aged ten, she was cured of a grave illness when the statue of Our Lady seemed to smile at her. On 20 November 1887 she asked Leo XIII to let her enter Carmel at fifteen; he replied that she would if it was God's will. She entered on 9 April 1888 and died in 1897.
liberties: Greydanus's account places her cure at about eight; she was ten. The film's snowfall at her entry to Carmel may shift a later event. Convent dialogue is invented. Some English-language summaries wrongly say her father opposed her vocation; in the film, as in history, the opposition came from the convent's superior.
advisories:
A long final illness and death from tuberculosis.

Greydanus rates it for children and up.

doctrine: Benedict XV declared Thérèse's virtues heroic on 14 August 1921 and presented her way of spiritual childhood, reliance on God and surrender to His guidance, as a way for all the faithful. Pius XI beatified her on 29 April 1923 and canonised her on 17 May 1925. On 14 December 1927 he named her principal patroness of the missions, equal with St Francis Xavier, although she never left her cloister, in recognition that prayer and sacrifice in an enclosed convent serve the apostolate. Pius XII named her secondary patroness of France, with St Joan of Arc, on 3 May 1944. Her feast is 3 October. The film includes the murderer Henri Pranzini, for whose conversion she prayed in 1887; reports that he kissed the crucifix before his execution illustrate the Church's teaching on prayer for sinners.
production: Procès au Vatican was made by Les Films Fernand Rivers with Les Films Artistiques Français. The film runs 115 minutes and opened in France on 29 August 1952; it was also known as La Vie de Sainte Thérèse de Lisieux. In America Ellis Films released it as Miracle of St. Therese (formerly Trial at the Vatican), and the National Legion of Decency classified it A-I.

title: Teresa de Jesús
decision: PUBLISH (judgment call): Fernando Sanz Ferreruela's archival study (Artigrama, 2023) establishes identity (Agrupa Films; shot September to December 1961; Madrid premiere 14 May 1962; Interés Nacional, 8 June 1962) and shows that the Carmelite objections often attached to this title were made against an earlier, banned script; the filmed script was passed by a Carmelite adviser appointed by the Order and by the Bishop of Madrid in July 1961. Tracie Amend's scene-by-scene study guide supplies substantive treatment. The invented courtship and forced entry are a real distortion and are disclosed.
summary: Aurora Bautista plays St Teresa of Ávila from courted girl to dying foundress in Juan de Orduña's long-delayed, Carmelite-approved Spanish biography.
synopsis: In Ávila the young Teresa is courted by her cousin Pedro and by Álvaro. When the two men duel in the garden, her father sends her to the convent of the Encarnación the next morning. Years later, as a nun, she fasts and scourges herself until she collapses, and her prioress calls it pride. Learned men fear her prayer is the devil's work and her confessor burns her books, until St Francis Borgia tells her to obey God and found a reformed house. With Doña Guiomar's help she opens a poor convent despite a hostile town. She travels Castile founding more houses, drives the Princess of Eboli out of Pastrana and answers the Inquisition in Seville. She dies asking her daughters' pardon.
inclusion: Aurora Bautista carries the film, and the verdicts on her divide: Fernando Méndez-Leite counted it among her best performances, while Eduardo Gil de Muro thought casting her a mistake. Sanz Ferreruela, who reconstructed the production from the censorship file, calls the finished script a hagiography full of commonplaces and regrets the bolder script the censors banned. The conventional choices are mostly sound ones. The film follows Teresa's own account of her long trial by suspicious confessors, Borgia's discernment, the poverty of St Joseph's, the road with her coachman, Pastrana and Seville. Its picture of a mystic tested by the Church is the right one.
themes: Teresa's early penances are sincere but excessive. The prioress who calls them pride is not a villain, and Teresa confesses pride more than once. Her prayer is treated as genuine, yet the learned men's fear that it may be diabolical is given full weight, and she herself panics that the devil has taken Christ's form. The reform concerns poverty and enclosure, set against an Encarnación whose parlour has become a salon for well-dressed visitors. At the trial she answers that she was led by God and denies calling herself a saint. Her death is penitent.
history: Teresa de Ahumada (1515–1582) was sent by her father to the Augustinian nuns of Ávila to be educated. In November 1535 she entered the Carmelite Incarnation, leaving home without his consent; he then yielded. After years of illness, St Francis Borgia and St Peter of Alcántara guided her through her mystical experiences. She founded St Joseph's at Ávila on 24 August 1562, and later houses included Pastrana and Seville. Jerónimo Gracián's appointment as apostolic visitor was followed by four years of persecution of the reform. She died at Alba de Tormes on 4 October 1582.
liberties: The opening is invented, and it reverses the history. There were no rival suitors and no duel, and her father did not order her into the convent the next morning: he sent her to the Augustinians for schooling, and she entered Carmel against his wishes. Álvaro's later visits and roses are also fiction. The Encarnación's laxity is sharpened for drama; a Carmelite historian asked in 1957 that the script not show the Order as persecuting innocence. One detailed summary has her travelling to Ávila to die, but she died at Alba de Tormes.
advisories:
Self-flagellation and fasting to the point of collapse, shown as excess and rebuked.

An opening arrest of a fraudulent stigmatic, with a bloody knife; a sword duel; a torch-bearing mob; Inquisition interrogations; a deathbed scene.

Suitable for teens and older.

doctrine: Teresa was beatified by Paul V in 1614 and canonised by Gregory XV on 12 March 1622 with Ignatius Loyola, Francis Xavier, Philip Neri and Isidore the Farmer. Her feast is 15 October, because the Gregorian reform of 1582 skipped the days after the night of her death. Her reform of Carmel returned the order to the primitive rule, with strict enclosure, poverty and silence, in the spirit of Trent's decrees on religious life (Session XXV). The film shows her obedience to confessors and the testing of her visions. The Church's teaching is that private revelations are not part of the deposit of faith, are to be tried by learned directors, and may be believed only with human faith. The Transverberation, the piercing of her heart by an angel's flaming dart, was given its own feast in the Carmelite calendar.
production: This Spanish religious drama was filmed in 1961 by Estela Films and Agrupa Films Cooperativa Cinematográfica and released in 1962. Bautista had starred in Orduña's Locura de amor (1948). The film runs 131 minutes and was distributed by CEA. In 1962 it won the special prize of the Sindicato Nacional del Espectáculo. In 1984 Spanish television made a series, Teresa de Jesús, starring Concha Velasco, and a film cut of it, which Spanish Wikipedia describes as based on Orduña's film.

title: The Gospel According to St. Matthew
decision: PUBLISH: Identity and awards confirmed by the Italian Cultural Institute (Venice Special Jury Prize; OCIC prize); Greydanus's detailed Decent Films review (A+, +4) shows near-verbatim fidelity to Matthew, matter-of-fact miracles and a contemplative rather than political Christ. Pasolini's Marxism and unbelief are a documented context, but the critical evidence shows the text of the Gospel is not reinterpreted; the film shows the Resurrection.
summary: An atheist Marxist poet filmed St Matthew's Gospel almost word for word, with peasants for actors and southern Italy for Palestine, and made the most austere of Jesus films.
synopsis: The film follows Matthew's Gospel in order. Joseph learns that Mary is with child and is reassured by an angel; Christ is born, the Magi come, the Holy Family flees and Herod kills the infants. John baptises in the Jordan. Jesus, young and severe, calls fishermen, preaches, heals, walks on water, and confronts the scribes and Pharisees. The Sermon on the Mount comes as a barrage of close-ups. He enters Jerusalem, drives the traders from the Temple, eats the Passover with the Twelve, is betrayed, denied by Peter, tried and crucified, watched by his aged mother. On the third day the tomb is empty and he sends his disciples to all nations.
inclusion: Pasolini took no liberties with the words: the dialogue is Matthew's, cut and sometimes reordered, but not rewritten. He cast non-professionals, including a Spanish student as Christ, and shot in central and southern Italy. The result looks like no other Bible film: weathered faces, bare landscapes, abrupt cuts, and long stretches where the images carry the narrative that Matthew's own voice would supply. Greydanus gives it his highest artistic grade and calls it one of the most contemplative Jesus films made. It is demanding, since the long silent passages assume you know the text and the Passion is restrained, but few films let the Gospel speak so directly.
themes: Miracles happen without fuss: an angel simply stands there, Christ walks on the water, the loaves multiply. Enrique Irazoqui's Christ is urgent, stern and fully human. Pasolini called himself an unbeliever with a nostalgia for belief, and critics have long read the film as a Marxist allegory of the poor; Greydanus answers that the text is not bent to politics. Our Lady is played in youth by a silent teenager and at the Cross by Pasolini's own mother.
history: Pasolini had been convicted in 1963 of insulting the state religion for his short film La ricotta. The Gospel premiered at Venice on 4 September 1964 and won the Special Jury Prize and the prize of the Office Catholique International du Cinéma. Pasolini dedicated it to the memory of John XXIII, who had died the year before.
liberties: Matthew's genealogy and the Transfiguration are omitted; some episodes are reordered or compressed. The Pharisees' tall hats are borrowed from Renaissance painting. Settings are southern Italian, not Palestinian, and the music is anachronistic by design.
advisories:
Massacre of the Innocents and the Crucifixion are shown, but with little blood.

No sexual content. Greydanus rates it suitable for children and up.

doctrine: The Pontifical Biblical Commission, in answers reproduced in the 1911 Catholic Encyclopedia, held that the Apostle Matthew wrote the first Gospel, first in the language of the Palestinian Jews, that the Greek Gospel is identical in substance with it, that it was not written after the destruction of Jerusalem, and that doubts about its first two chapters and about the passages on Peter's primacy are unfounded. Those passages matter in the film, which includes the charge to Peter. The First Vatican Council (Pastor Aeternus, 18 July 1870, chapter 1) defined that Christ gave Peter a primacy of jurisdiction over the whole Church.
production: He scouted the Holy Land and rejected it as too modern, and shot instead in southern Italy, at Barile, Matera and Massafra, using the Sassi of Matera for the family home. Much of the dialogue was dubbed. The film was made by Arco Film and Lux Compagnie Cinématographique, and after Venice it was released in Italy in October 1964, in France in March 1965 and in the United States in 1966. It earned three Oscar nominations. Left-wing critics were less impressed.
