title: The King of Kings
decision: PUBLISH: AFI Catalog identity; Steven Greydanus's detailed Decent Films review, Charles Musser's Criterion essay and K. V. Turley's National Catholic Register piece establish a reverent Gospel film with a Eucharistic Last Supper, a reverent Our Lady and a careful handling of guilt for the Crucifixion. The invented Magdalene prologue, Protestant-default intertitles and one unscriptural intertitle are disclosed rather than disqualifying.
summary: DeMille's silent life of Christ opens as a lurid Hollywood spectacle, then settles into a surprisingly reverent Gospel film, with H. B. Warner's gentle Christ and a Resurrection in colour.
synopsis: Mary Magdalene, a rich courtesan, is told that her lover Judas has gone off after a carpenter from Nazareth. She drives out in a chariot drawn by zebras to win him back, meets Jesus, and is freed of seven devils. The film then follows Christ through healings, the call of the disciples, conflict with the Temple authorities and the Roman occupiers, and into Holy Week: the Last Supper, Gethsemane, Judas's betrayal, the trial before Pilate, the way of the cross and the Crucifixion, cut against Judas's suicide, with an earthquake that splits the Temple. The Resurrection follows, in colour.
inclusion: Greydanus calls it flawed but powerful, and the description holds. The first reel is pure DeMille: a half-dressed Magdalene, an orgy, zebras. Then the tone changes. H. B. Warner, past fifty and rather old for the part, gives Christ dignity and gentleness; his scenes with children, including one where he mends a child's doll, are the warmest in the film. DeMille's craft is formidable: the crowds, the lighting, the cutting between the Crucifixion and Judas's death, the storm that follows. Musser, in his Criterion essay, finds Warner's divinity rendered by lighting more than by acting and some of the halo effects kitsch, and he has a point. For a silent epic it holds attention, and its seriousness about the Passion is unmistakable.
themes: The Last Supper is handled with reverence: Peter holds the chalice to his heart, while Judas crumbles the host and lets it fall, a clear sign that the film treats the Eucharist as sacred. Our Lady appears with dignity throughout. The intertitles are mostly from the King James Bible and the sensibility, as Greydanus says, is Protestant by default, but nothing in it attacks Catholic belief. Turley objects to one intertitle in which Mary urges her Son to go back to Nazareth, which is unscriptural. On the Crucifixion, the film places guilt on Caiaphas as a Roman appointee and has him plead that he alone is guilty, a deliberate attempt to avoid blaming the Jewish people.
liberties: The opening, with Mary Magdalene as a courtesan and Judas's lover, is invented. Events are rearranged thematically: episodes about taxes are merged and crowd scenes moved. Caiaphas's final prayer is DeMille's invention. The 1927 roadshow version (about 155 minutes) and the 1928 general release (about 112) differ; the longer cut adds an exorcism and other material but also puts the opening in colour, which weakens the colour Resurrection.
advisories:
The opening shows a decadent party and a scantily dressed Magdalene; it is brief.

The scourging and Crucifixion are restrained by modern standards; Judas's suicide is cut against the Crucifixion; earthquake and storm.

Greydanus rates it suitable for children and up, with these caveats.

suitability.note: The brief opening party and the Passion scenes are mild by modern standards. It is silent with intertitles, so younger children may need the cards read to them; the Last Supper and the colour Resurrection reward the effort.

doctrine: The Last Supper scene rests on the Church's teaching on the Real Presence: the Council of Trent (Session XIII, 1551) defined that after the consecration Christ is truly, really and substantially present under the appearances of bread and wine, which is why Judas's dropping of the host reads as sacrilege. The film follows the old Latin tradition, accepted by St Gregory the Great and set out in the Catholic Encyclopedia, that Mary Magdalene is the sinful woman of Luke 7 and the sister of Lazarus; her feast was kept on 22 July. Her deliverance from seven devils is from Luke 8:2. On guilt for the Crucifixion, the Roman Catechism (Part I, article 4) teaches that sinners of every age are its cause.
history: Jesus of Nazareth taught and worked in Galilee and Judaea under the emperor Tiberius. Pontius Pilate governed Judaea as procurator from AD 26 to 36, a term that covers the whole of Christ's public ministry, and Caiaphas was high priest in Jerusalem at the time of the Passion. The Gospels record that Christ was betrayed by Judas, condemned by the Sanhedrin, handed over to Pilate, crucified outside the city at Passover, and rose on the third day.
production: After The Volga Boatman (1926) DeMille dropped a planned film about the Flood when he learned Warner Bros. was making Noah's Ark; Denison Clift suggested the life of Christ instead, and Jeremiah Milbank put up the money. H. B. Warner was cast as Christ in June 1926. It was shot in 1926 on Santa Catalina Island and at the DeMille Studios in Culver City, with the opening and Resurrection in two-colour Technicolor. It premiered in New York on 19 April 1927 and opened Grauman's Chinese Theatre on 18 May. It cost about $1.27 million and earned about $2.64 million. The Memphis censors ordered 900 feet cut, mainly the scourging and crucifixion, and the London County Council banned it. The Legion of Decency classified it A-I.

title: The Nun's Story
decision: PUBLISH (adults and older teens): The AFI Catalog and Greydanus's Decent Films review show a serious, largely respectful account of pre-conciliar religious formation whose heroine leaves by lawful dispensation after judging herself unable to keep obedience, not a film that attacks the vows. Zinnemann deliberately withholds a verdict on her departure (AFI: no end-title music for that reason); Greydanus calls it neither anti-religious nor anti-Catholic. The film's ambiguity about whether the Rule or the nun is at fault is recorded plainly in the text and advisories.
summary: Audrey Hepburn plays a Belgian surgeon's daughter who becomes a nursing sister, serves in the Congo, and after years of struggle with obedience asks to be released from her vows.
synopsis: In the 1920s Gabrielle Van der Mal enters a nursing order in Bruges, hoping to serve in the Congo. As Sister Luke she learns the Rule: silence, custody of the eyes, obedience to the bell. Her superiors test her pride; one even urges her to fail an exam as an act of humility. She is sent to an asylum, then at last to the Congo, where she works beside a brilliant, irreligious surgeon and falls ill with tuberculosis. Recalled to Belgium, she faces the German occupation. Ordered to show charity to the enemy, she secretly helps the Resistance, and when her father is killed she finds herself full of hatred. Concluding that she can no longer be a true nun, she asks for release, signs the papers, changes into a dress and walks out of the convent.
inclusion: No Hollywood film before or since has shown the formation of a religious so carefully. The first hour, which the New York Times likened to a documentary, explains the vows through the words of superiors, and the rituals of the novitiate are filmed with patience. Hepburn is superb, entirely inward; Edith Evans is formidable as a superior, and Peter Finch plays the atheist surgeon who tells her she is a 'worldly nun' and that her real illness is the struggle to conform. Franz Planer's photography of Bruges and the Congo is beautiful. The film is long, its second half loses some of the first half's concentration, and it is not a happy story. It does treat the religious life as a serious calling, and its sisters include warm and holy women as well as harsh ones.
themes: Obedience is the subject. Sister Luke's struggle is not with faith in God but with the surrender of her will: leaving a dying patient at the sound of the bell, accepting humiliation, forgiving the men who killed her father. The Rule is presented in its own terms, and the superiors explain why the sacrifice of liberty matters. Greydanus notes that the bad advice to fail an exam is later corrected by another superior. The Congo scenes include a priest serving lepers in penance for his sins, and a sister murdered by a man in thrall to a witch doctor, whose fellow nuns' forgiveness draws villagers to the Christmas Eve service. The film is open to question in refusing to judge the outcome. It never settles whether the fault lies with the Rule, the community or Sister Luke herself, and some viewers will read her departure as liberation. Read faithfully, it is the story of a vocation honestly found wanting, and not of a vocation exposed as false.
history: Kathryn Hulme's 1956 novel was based on Marie-Louise Habets, a Belgian nursing sister of the Sisters of Charity of Jesus and Mary, who left religious life during the Second World War. Hulme met her among refugees in 1945. The novel changes names and events.

suitability.note: The main difficulty is the ending, and a parent should be ready to discuss vows. The violence in the asylum and the Congo, the leprosy wards and the wartime death are lesser concerns.

doctrine: Religious profession binds by the three vows of poverty, chastity and obedience. A vow, once made to God, obliges in conscience until the Holy See or the competent authority dispenses it. The religious state is, in the traditional teaching, the way of the evangelical counsels, and the vow of obedience is the surrender of one's own will to a lawful superior, as the film shows. Obedience does not require sin. Under the 1917 Code the Holy See grants dispensations or secularisation to religious of simple vows, which is why Sister Luke has to wait for her release. The Church holds that a woman may leave her Institute only by lawful permission.
production: Warner Bros. consulted the Production Code Office in March 1956. The Catholic Church in Belgium disliked the novel and at first refused to cooperate. The Sisters of Charity of Jesus and Mary at Ghent then submitted their own version of the script, many of whose suggestions were used, and allowed observation and guidance but refused to appear on camera. Filming was in the Belgian Congo, near Stanleyville, with Belgian interiors made in Rome (Cinecittà) and exteriors in Bruges. Hepburn prepared by meeting Kathryn Hulme and Marie Louise Habets. The final scene has no music. It premiered at Radio City Music Hall on 18 June 1959, cost $3.5 million and took $12.8 million in the US. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II, 'morally unobjectionable for adults and adolescents'. It earned eight Oscar nominations but won none.

title: Barabbas
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (Christ, St Peter, the Roman martyrs), Legion of Decency A-II (Motion Picture Exhibitor Legion tables, 1962), independent reviews (Hannan, Cinefile). Reservation: the hero's faith stays ambiguous to the end, and his doubt of the Resurrection and his part in the burning of Rome are the core of the story; Peter's rebuke and the martyrs' witness keep it from contradicting doctrine. Would move to PUBLISH if the editor accepts an ambiguous convert as protagonist. The English subtitle file confirms the rebuke (the fire is Nero's, not God's, 02:11:56–02:12:40) and Peter's consolation that Christ has never left Barabbas's side (02:13:44–02:13:59); the last words are addressed into the dark without naming God (02:16:23–02:16:35).
summary: Anthony Quinn's Barabbas, freed in Christ's place, spends twenty years haunted by the man who died for him, in Richard Fleischer's grim and intelligent epic.
synopsis: Pilate offers the crowd Jesus or Barabbas, and they choose Barabbas. Freed, he finds that his lover Rachel has become a follower of the condemned man. He watches the Crucifixion under a darkened sky, finds the tomb empty and refuses to believe; Rachel preaches and is stoned. Back at his old trade, he is caught and sent for life to the sulphur mines of Sicily, chained to Sahak, a Christian. An earthquake frees them, and they are taken to Rome to be trained as gladiators. Sahak is executed for his faith; Barabbas wins his freedom in the arena. When Rome burns he thinks the end of the world has come, sets fires himself and declares himself a Christian. In prison St Peter tells him Christians do not do such things. He is crucified with the Christians.
inclusion: Barabbas is the most searching of the epics of its era, made in Italy by Dino De Laurentiis with serious ambition. Anthony Quinn plays a slow, bewildered man who keeps failing the people around him, and Brian Hannan rightly calls the performance excellent and the film overlooked. Fleischer keeps piety at arm's length; the mine, the arena and the burning of Rome are brutal and convincing. The dialogue can be stiff, and David Clare at Cinefile finds it a Christian-era Spartacus without that film's vision.
themes: Barabbas lives because Christ died, and he cannot escape that fact. Rachel, Sahak and Peter are clear witnesses; Barabbas is not. He doubts the Resurrection, mistakes the fire of Rome for the end of the world, and joins in the arson for which the Christians are blamed. Peter tells him plainly that the fire is Nero's work and not God's. In prison Peter tells him that Christ died for him because he was farthest away, and has never left his side. Barabbas dies on a cross among the martyrs, giving himself up 'into your keeping' in the dark, without saying to whom. Catholic Culture's Criteria podcast calls him an archetype of human resistance to grace.
history: The Gospels say only that Barabbas was released at the Passover instead of Jesus. His later life is unrecorded. The Great Fire of Rome broke out in July AD 64; Nero blamed the Christians, and the persecution that followed is described by Tacitus.
liberties: Barabbas's later life is wholly invented. Against the novel, the film sends him to Sicilian sulphur mines rather than copper mines in Cyprus, frees him by an earthquake rather than a sympathetic overseer, and adds the gladiatorial scenes.
advisories:
Brutal violence: a stoning, a mine disaster, gladiatorial combat, the burning of Rome and mass crucifixions.

Barabbas's relationship with Rachel is implied.

For teenagers and adults.

The hero's faith is left ambiguous.

grey.question: Barabbas follows a man who cannot believe. He doubts the Resurrection, helps set fire to Rome in the belief that he is serving the Christians, and dies on a cross with words that may be faith or only surrender. The martyrs around him, Rachel, Sahak and St Peter, are drawn with conviction, and Peter corrects his error plainly. Viewers who want a clear conversion story will not find one; those willing to watch a portrait of resistance to grace will.

sources.claims: Pilate's offer of Barabbas in the Gospel accounts

suitability.note: The violence is brutal throughout, and the film is long.

doctrine: The exchange of Jesus for Barabbas, a prisoner held for insurrection and murder, is recorded at Matthew 27, Mark 15, Luke 23 and John 18. Christian writers have long seen in it a picture of the Atonement: the guilty man goes free because the Innocent One dies. Trent teaches that Christ merited justification for us by His Passion, and that men can resist grace. Peter, the first Pope, was crucified in Rome under Nero according to ancient tradition. The Church holds that no good end justifies a wicked act, and Barabbas's part in the burning of Rome is such an act, done in the belief that he served the Christians.
production: Pär Lagerkvist, a Swedish Nobel laureate, published his novel in 1950. Christopher Fry was the main writer of the film, helped uncredited by Nigel Balchin, Diego Fabbri, Ivo Perilli and Salvatore Quasimodo. It was shot in Verona and Rome. The darkness at the Crucifixion was filmed during the total solar eclipse of 15 February 1961. Yul Brynner was considered for the title role. Mario Nascimbene's score has a theme based on the Kyrie of Mass XI. It opened in Italy on 23 December 1961 and in the US on 10 October 1962, running 137 minutes, and took $2.9 million in the US and Canada. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.

title: Ben-Hur: A Tale of the Christ
originalTitle: Ben-Hur: A Tale of the Christ
decision: GREY: Identity is secure (AFI Catalog, BFI) and the treatment is established by Greydanus (moral/spiritual +3, Kids & Up*), who calls it arguably the best version of the story. Christ is shown reverently, never with his face, in Technicolor sequences framing the drama: the Nativity, the cup of water, the raising of a child, the healing of the lepers on the way of the cross, the Crucifixion. Two reservations stop it at PUBLISH: Christ is the background to a revenge melodrama from a Protestant novelist rather than its centre, and the restored version contains brief nudity (bare-breasted women in a procession, a nude galley slave) that censors cut in 1931.
summary: MGM's silent Ben-Hur sets Lew Wallace's revenge tale inside the life of Christ, from a Technicolor Nativity to the Crucifixion, with a still-astonishing sea battle and chariot race.
synopsis: The film opens in Bethlehem with Joseph and Mary, the birth in the cave, the shepherds and the Magi. Years later in Jerusalem, Judah Ben-Hur, a Jewish prince, is betrayed by his Roman boyhood friend Messala; Judah is sent to the galleys and his mother and sister are imprisoned. On the road a young carpenter of Nazareth gives him water. Judah survives a sea battle, wins his freedom and returns to defeat Messala in the chariot race. He gathers men to fight for the foretold king, but the Nazarene, carrying his cross, heals Judah's mother and sister of leprosy, and before the Crucifixion Judah lays down his sword when Christ speaks of a kingdom not of this world.
inclusion: This was the most expensive silent film ever made, and it still looks it. Greydanus judges the sea battle the best of any version and the chariot race at least equal to the 1959 remake; Kevin Brownlow compared the race to the Odessa Steps in Potemkin. Ramon Novarro plays Judah, and at around two and a half hours it is an hour shorter than Wyler's version and better paced; Greydanus notes that it delays the rescue of Judah's mother and sister, which helps the drama. The Christ scenes were shot in two-strip Technicolor, considered lost until the 1980s and restored in 1987, so the Gospel episodes glow against the tinted story. Photoplay singled out Betty Bronson's Madonna.
themes: Christ is never seen full-face; he is a hand, a figure, a presence, and the title cards quote the Gospels. That restraint is the film's best religious decision. The Nativity is staged with Mary and Joseph at the centre and treated with reverence. Judah's journey moves from vengeance towards Christ: he plans an army for a political Messiah and learns at the foot of the cross that the kingdom is not of this world. Greydanus approves of keeping the Gospel in the background, but notes that Hollywood's melodramatic spectacle sits uneasily with sacred subjects. The novel's author, Lew Wallace, was a Protestant, and the faith in the film is a broad, undogmatic Christianity.

grey.question: Christ appears in Ben-Hur with reverence, in the Nativity, the healing of the lepers and the Crucifixion, but the film belongs to Judah's revenge and the chariot race, and its faith is the general Christianity of Lew Wallace's novel and not anything specifically Catholic. The full restoration also includes brief nudity cut by censors in 1931. Viewers will want to decide whether a spectacle in which Christ is the frame, and not the subject, belongs alongside films about Him.

history: The film's frame is the Gospel history: the birth of Christ at Bethlehem under Herod, the ministry in Judaea under Roman rule, and the Crucifixion at Jerusalem under Pontius Pilate, prefect from AD 26 to 36. Judah Ben-Hur, Messala and the Ben-Hur family are inventions of the novelist Lew Wallace, a Union general who published the book in 1880. The Roman galleys and chariot racing are period colour, not recorded events.
liberties: Judah, Messala and the Ben-Hur family are Wallace's inventions. The film follows the novel's main line but ends at the Crucifixion, whereas the novel continues into the reign of Nero. Christ's words and the healing of the lepers are placed on the way of the cross for dramatic effect.
advisories:
Battle violence at sea, galley brutality and the chariot race crash.

Brief partial nudity (women in a procession, a galley slave) and a sequence of mild sensuality.

The Crucifixion is shown without graphic detail.

Greydanus rates it Kids & Up with these cautions.

names: Ben-Hur: A Tale of the Christ, novel by Lew Wallace (1880)

suitability.note: Parents may prefer to preview it, since the restored print has brief nudity and the action scenes are violent. The Nativity and Gospel scenes are reverent and suit older children.

doctrine: The film frames Wallace's tale with the Incarnation: the Nativity at Bethlehem, the shepherds and the Magi. Judah's error is the one the Gospels record in the disciples, the hope of a political Messiah. Christ's answer to Pilate, 'My kingdom is not of this world' (John 18:36), is the turning point. Pius XI taught the same truth in Quas Primas (11 December 1925), less than three weeks before the film opened, when he instituted the feast of Christ the King. The film's refusal to show Christ's face accords with the long Christian custom of reverence in depicting Him. The Crucifixion is Gospel history, and the Church holds that Christ died for all men.
production: The 1880 novel was a stage hit for twenty-five years before Goldwyn bought the film rights in 1922. Shooting began in Rome in October 1923 under Charles Brabin; Fred Niblo is the credited director. George Walsh was fired as Ben-Hur and replaced by Ramon Novarro. After two years of trouble the production moved to MGM at Culver City, resuming in spring 1925. Costs reached about $3.9 million. About 200,000 feet of film were shot for the chariot race, cut to 750 feet. William Wyler was an assistant director. It premiered in New York on 30 December 1925 and was reissued in 1931 with a musical score and sound effects added. It took $10.7 million but showed a loss after costs. Reports say about a hundred horses died during the race scenes.

title: Ben-Hur
alternateTitles: Ben-Hur: A Tale of the Christ
decision: PUBLISH: Christ is the hinge of the drama (Crowther, 1959: Judah's emergence from hatred is achieved through the example and teachings of Jesus), so it qualifies under the Bible-epic rule despite its Protestant-authored source; nothing in it contradicts Catholic teaching. Legion of Decency A-I (Motion Picture Exhibitor Legion tables); independent treatment from Crowther (NYT review reprinted in Motion Picture Exhibitor) and Greydanus; identity from AFI.
summary: Wyler's epic of a Jewish prince betrayed by his Roman friend, whose hatred is finally dissolved at the foot of the Cross; the grandest of Hollywood's biblical films.
synopsis: Judea, AD 26. Judah Ben-Hur, a wealthy Jewish prince, welcomes back his boyhood friend Messala, now a Roman tribune. When Judah refuses to inform on his countrymen, Messala seizes on an accident to send him to the galleys and imprison his mother and sister. On the march to the coast a carpenter in Nazareth gives the parched Judah water. Years later Judah saves the life of the Roman commander Arrius in a sea battle, is adopted as his son, and returns to Judea seeking revenge. He beats Messala in the chariot race; the dying Messala tells him that his mother and sister are lepers. Embittered, Judah follows the condemned Jesus to Calvary, recognises the man who gave him water, and tries to give Him water in turn. At the Crucifixion his mother and sister are healed, and Judah's hatred leaves him.
inclusion: It is the summit of the Hollywood biblical epic. The chariot race, with Charlton Heston and Stephen Boyd doing much of their own driving, remains one of the great action sequences. Steven D. Greydanus notes that it does not transcend its genre of spectacle and melodrama, but does those things about as well as they could be done. Bosley Crowther in 1959 thought it the most stirring of all the Bible-fiction pictures and singled out Judah's meetings with Jesus as dignified and true. Its weaknesses are length and stiffness, and Greydanus finds Judah's loss of faith once his fortunes improve hard to follow.
themes: The subtitle is A Tale of the Christ, and Wallace's design holds. Christ appears only at the edges of the story, His face never seen and His voice never heard, yet every turn of Judah's life passes through Him. The water given at Nazareth is returned on the road to Calvary. The healing of the lepers comes with the death on the Cross, and Greydanus points to the image of Christ's blood running into the rain that washes the hillside. Judah's conversion is from vengeance to forgiveness rather than a full confession of faith, so the religious meaning is present but understated. The Nativity, the Sermon on the Mount and the Passion are treated with reverence.
history: The film is set in Judea in the reign of Tiberius. Pontius Pilate governed Judea as prefect from AD 26 to 36. Rome ruled the province through its governors and its garrisons, and the Jews were divided between those who accepted the occupation and those who resisted it. Rome sent condemned men to the galleys and fought pirates in the eastern Mediterranean. Jesus was crucified at Jerusalem under Pilate, at the Passover. The Gospel narrative of his birth, ministry, trial and death underlies the story.
liberties: Judah, Messala, Arrius and their families are fictional, from Wallace's novel. Judah's meetings with Jesus, the water given and returned, and the healing of the lepers at the Crucifixion are invented around the Gospel scenes, in keeping with Wallace's design.
advisories:
Battle and arena violence: the sea battle and the chariot race, with a trampled, mangled charioteer.

The lepers' disfigurement; the scourging and Crucifixion are shown with restraint.

Suitable for older children and up.

names: Ben-Hur: A Tale of the Christ, novel by Lew Wallace (1880)

suitability.note: Nothing is graphic, but the running time of over three and a half hours is the main test for children.

doctrine: The story is framed by the Nativity (the film opens with the Magi) and the Crucifixion, both set down in the Gospels. The Gospel names no number of Magi; the names Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar are tradition, and the film's Balthasar is one of them. The Creed confesses that Christ 'suffered under Pontius Pilate', and the Roman Catechism (Part I, article IV) teaches that He died freely for the redemption of all. Judah's change from hatred to forgiveness at the Cross follows the teaching that Christ's blood was the price of pardon, and that love of enemies is a commandment (Matthew 5:44). Leprosy in the Law (Leviticus 13) is a state of ritual separation, which explains the lepers' exile from the city.
production: MGM remade its own 1925 silent film from Lew Wallace's 1880 novel. The screenplay is credited to Karl Tunberg, with contributions from Maxwell Anderson, S. N. Behrman, Gore Vidal and Christopher Fry. Filming ran from 18 May 1958 to 7 January 1959, mostly at Cinecittà in Rome, in the MGM Camera 65 widescreen process. The chariot race of about nine minutes was directed by Andrew Marton and Yakima Canutt. The budget of about $15.2 million was the largest of any film at the time. The producer Sam Zimbalist died during the shoot. It opened at Loew's State in New York on 18 November 1959, ran 212 minutes, and was the highest-grossing film of 1959. It won eleven Academy Awards, a record then. The Legion of Decency classed it A-I.

title: Black Robe
decision: GREY: Identity and content are well established (Australian Screen curator's notes, Video Librarian, the Lehigh 'Reel American History' scene log, Wikipedia). No Catholic review was found. The reservation is real but can be weighed: an ambivalent, partly sceptical view of the mission from Brian Moore's script, a priest who questions whether an unbaptised friend is lost, and several on-screen sex scenes that pre-conciliar standards would not pass. Not REJECT because the priest's faith and endurance are treated with respect and the film ends in an act of charity and a baptism. The editor may prefer REJECT on the sexual content. The English subtitle file shows that Laforgue does not deny that the unbaptised are lost: he anguishes over it in prayer ('Why is Father Jerome with you in Heaven while Chomina lies forever in utter darkness?', 01:28:30). He baptises a dying child, makes his confession to a fellow priest, refuses to present baptism as a cure, and baptises the Hurons at the end after they ask whether he loves them. That strengthens GREY rather than REJECT.
summary: Bruce Beresford's austere adaptation of Brian Moore's novel follows a young Jesuit through the winter wilderness of New France in 1634, testing his faith against an alien world.
synopsis: In 1634 Samuel de Champlain sends Father Paul Laforgue, a young Jesuit newly arrived in New France, to a distant mission among the Hurons. He travels by canoe with a party of Algonquins led by Chomina, together with Daniel, a young Frenchman who falls in love with Chomina's daughter Annuka. Laforgue, shaken by desire and by the Algonquins' ways, does penance in the forest. A shaman calls him a demon and the party abandons him; Chomina, ashamed, turns back. An Iroquois war party then captures them, kills Chomina's wife and young son and tortures the prisoners until Annuka helps them escape. Chomina dies without accepting baptism. Laforgue reaches the mission alone and finds the Hurons dying of fever. Asked whether he loves them, he says yes, and baptises them.
inclusion: Black Robe is one of the few films to take seventeenth-century missionaries seriously on their own terms. It is often cited for the care of its research into Algonquin and Huron life. Peter James's photography of the wilderness won awards in Canada and Australia, and the film took six Genie awards, including best picture and best direction. Lothaire Bluteau plays Laforgue as an inward, uncertain man; Randy Pitman of Video Librarian found him a bit of a cipher who cries a lot and says little. Roger Ebert, quoted by later writers, praised its realism but was left depressed by the ending. The case for it is that Laforgue is no caricature, since he endures cold, hunger, contempt and torture to reach his mission and the last scene is a baptism. The difficulty is that the film keeps its own view of that mission at a distance.
themes: Laforgue holds to prayer, the sacraments and the conviction that the unbaptised are lost, and the film tests all three. He baptises a dying child, flogs himself after watching Daniel and Annuka together, and confesses to a fellow priest. Chomina refuses baptism because his people will not be in the Christian paradise, and Laforgue later asks God why a dead priest is in heaven while Chomina lies in utter darkness; he grieves at the doctrine without denying it. He will not offer baptism as a cure for fever, but baptises the Hurons when they ask whether he loves them. The Algonquins' dream-world is given as much weight as his faith, and the ending can be read as charity or as defeat.
history: Moore based his 1985 novel on the Jesuit Relations, the annual reports that missionaries in New France sent to their superiors, and the Australian Screen notes add Francis Parkman's history as a source. The closing title is broadly historical: the Huron missions were destroyed by Iroquois attacks at the end of the 1640s, and the surviving Jesuits withdrew to Quebec.
liberties: Laforgue, Daniel, Chomina and Annuka are invented, and the journey is a composite of episodes from the Relations. The film's portrait of Indigenous life is widely praised for its research, but Ward Churchill criticised historical inaccuracies and its portrayal of the Mohawks.
advisories:
Several sex scenes: a couple in a shared lodge, Daniel and Annuka in the woods, and Annuka seducing a guard to free the prisoners.

Graphic torture and killing by an Iroquois war party, including the killing of a child, an arrow through the neck and a severed finger.

A priest flogs himself.

The film's view of the mission is ambivalent, and the priest's anguish over an unbaptised friend is left unresolved.

grey.question: Black Robe takes a Jesuit missionary seriously, gives him the sacraments and ends with a baptism, but it keeps its own judgment of the mission at arm's length. It sets the priest's faith beside the Algonquins' dream-religion as near equals, lets him cry out to God over an unbaptised friend he believes lost, and closes on the destruction of the Christian Hurons. It also contains several sex scenes and graphic torture. Viewers who know the Jesuit Relations and the story of the North American Martyrs can weigh how much of the film's ambivalence is honesty and how much is scepticism.

names: Black Robe, novel by Brian Moore (1985)

suitability.note: The sex scenes and graphic torture put it firmly in adult territory. It is rated R in the United States.

doctrine: The Jesuit missionaries in New France held that baptism is necessary for salvation (Council of Trent, session VII, canon 5; Baltimore Catechism), and so they baptised the dying. Laforgue's anguish over his unbaptised friend meets the Church's teaching on baptism of desire, which the Council of Trent mentions in session VI, chapter 4, and which the Catholic Encyclopedia describes: a perfect act of charity with the will to receive the sacrament can supply it. The Jesuit Relations record martyrdoms, among them the eight North American Martyrs killed by the Iroquois between 1642 and 1649, whom Pius XI canonised in 1930. The film's view of the mission is bleak and ambiguous, so a reader should not take its Native religion scenes as Church teaching.
production: The film was a Canada-Australia co-production by Alliance Communications, Samson Productions and Hoyts, under a treaty that required 30 per cent Australian financing. It was shot mainly in the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean region of Quebec, with a few scenes in Rouen. It was shown at the Toronto festival in 1991, opened in Canada in October 1991 and in Australia in February 1992. It grossed about $8.2 million, the highest of any Canadian film that year. Variety praised it.

title: Brideshead Revisited
decision: GREY: Identity is secure (ACMI; Wikipedia credits and broadcast record) and fidelity is documented (Sturridge's 95 per cent claim; Spectator 2021 retrospective; Seeing Things Secondhand episode review). The Catholic thesis is Waugh's and orthodox: deathbed absolution and the sign of the cross, Julia's renunciation, Charles before the sanctuary lamp. The reservation is moral, not doctrinal: brief nudity and an intimate scene (the 'bottoms' debate recorded by the Spectator), a long adulterous affair and a homoerotic undercurrent. The editor may judge this PUBLISH with advisories, as with Diary of a Country Priest; it is not REJECT, because the story judges the sins it shows.

grey.question: The serial keeps Waugh's Catholic argument whole: a dying man returns to the sacraments, a woman gives up the man she loves rather than live in sin, and an unbeliever ends on his knees. To make that argument it shows the sins at length: an adulterous affair over several episodes, brief nudity and an intimate scene, and a romantic friendship between two young men that some critics at the time thought overplayed. The question is whether what is shown along the way is acceptable for the sake of an ending that judges it.

summary: Granada's eleven-part, near-verbatim adaptation of Waugh's novel, in which an agnostic painter is drawn, through his love for a Catholic family, towards the faith that divides them.
synopsis: In wartime, Captain Charles Ryder's company is billeted at Brideshead, and the house brings back his past. At Oxford in the 1920s he befriends Lord Sebastian Flyte, charming and evasive, and is drawn into the life of his Catholic family: the devout, possessive Lady Marchmain; her estranged husband, living in Venice with his mistress; and their children Bridey, Julia and Cordelia. Sebastian sinks into drink, escapes abroad and ends as a hanger-on at a North African monastery. Years later Charles, now an unhappily married painter, begins an affair with Julia, who is married to the divorced Rex Mottram, and they plan to divorce and marry. Lord Marchmain comes home to die. He sends the priest away, but at the last accepts absolution with the sign of the cross. Julia breaks with Charles. In 1943 Charles prays in the reopened chapel.
inclusion: Granada's serial is often named the finest literary adaptation British television has made; Anthony Burgess called it the best piece of fictional television ever made. Its distinction is fidelity, and Charles Sturridge said 95 per cent of the dialogue is Waugh's. Jeremy Irons's narration carries long stretches of the prose. Laurence Olivier's dying Lord Marchmain is the dramatic peak, and John Gielgud's dry Mr Ryder is a comic treasure. Length is the obvious weakness, with eleven episodes, some of them static, and contemporary critics such as Richard Ingrams found it too long and the score too insistent. Because it keeps nearly all of Waugh, it keeps the novel's Catholic argument intact, including the parts that secular viewers in 1981 found hardest to accept.
themes: The serial keeps the novel's subject, grace working on very different people. Each of the Flytes is caught by the 'twitch upon the thread' in a different way: Sebastian in drunken exile beside a monastery, Lord Marchmain at his deathbed, Julia when she gives up the man she loves rather than set up a rival good to God, and Charles, the sceptical narrator, who ends praying before the relit sanctuary lamp. The faith is shown as costly and inconvenient, and Lady Marchmain's possessive piety does harm. Sin is not softened: adultery, divorce, drunkenness and the romantic friendship of the two young men are shown at length, and judged by the end and not along the way.
history: Evelyn Waugh, a convert since 1930, published the novel in 1945. ITV broadcast the serial from 12 October to 22 December 1981, and PBS from January 1982.
liberties: Very few. Descriptive detail is cut and the narration lifts whole passages of Waugh's prose. The serial makes visible, briefly, things the novel only implies, such as the young men sunbathing naked on the roof.
advisories:
Brief rear male nudity (two young men sunbathing on a roof) and a scene in which Charles touches Julia's breast.

An adulterous affair across several episodes, with the couple living together; divorce.

The Charles and Sebastian friendship has a romantic undercurrent; a scene in a gay nightclub.

Heavy drinking and alcoholism.

For older teenagers and adults.

The religious resolution comes only in the last episodes; viewers who stop midway see the sin without its judgement.

sources.title: Extreme Unction
sources.claims: Remission of sins, unconscious recipients, absolute administration, Trent Session XIV on matter.

names: Brideshead Revisited, novel by Evelyn Waugh (1945)

suitability.note: Eleven episodes of adultery, heavy drinking and romantic friendship, shown at length, make it a series for older teenagers and adults.

doctrine: For Lord Marchmain's deathbed, the Catholic Encyclopedia teaches that extreme unction remits sins, mortal as well as venial, in a person who has attrition, and that a man who has lost consciousness can still receive it if he was sorry earlier and had not withdrawn that sorrow. It is normally given absolutely, not conditionally, so that its effect can revive once the obstacle is removed. Marchmain's sign of the cross, made as the priest anoints him, is the kind of sign a priest looks for. The Council of Trent (Session XIV) taught that the matter of the sacrament is oil blessed by the bishop.
production: Granada began filming in April 1979 as a six-hour serial. A technicians' strike and Jeremy Irons's commitment to The French Lieutenant's Woman interrupted it, and Michael Lindsay-Hogg, who began as director, left for another commitment and was succeeded by Charles Sturridge. The script was expanded, then restructured into eleven episodes (659 minutes) at ITV's request. Principal photography ended in January 1981 after 42 weeks. Castle Howard stood in for Brideshead, Oxford scenes were shot at Hertford, Wadham and Christ Church, and Venice, Malta and Gozo and the liner Queen Elizabeth 2 were also used. John Mortimer's script was set aside and the producer, Derek Granger, built much of the screenplay from Waugh's text, although Mortimer kept the credit. It won the BAFTA for Best Drama Series and the Golden Globe for Best Miniseries or Television Film, Anthony Andrews won the BAFTA and Golden Globe for best actor, and Laurence Olivier won an Emmy for supporting actor. The BFI placed it tenth in its 2000 list of the 100 greatest British television programmes.

title: Christus
decision: GREY: Identity is secure (Silent Era; Wikipedia citing Pucci 2016; cinemaitaliano.info) and the content is a Life of Christ and of Our Lady built from tableaux after Fra Angelico, Leonardo and Michelangelo, with Leda Gys as the Madonna. The Vatican helped send it into Germany in 1917, which shows contemporary Church favour but is not an assessment of its treatment. No independent review describing the film's handling of the Gospel was found. It would move to PUBLISH with a substantive review or scholarly description of the restored print (Cineteca di Bologna 2000), or a contemporary Catholic notice.
summary: Cines' four-year Life of Christ, shot partly in Egypt and Palestine, stages the Gospel as a series of living pictures after Fra Angelico, Leonardo and Michelangelo.
synopsis: Christus tells the life of Christ from the Annunciation, staged after Fra Angelico, through his childhood (Renato Visca plays Jesus at twelve) and public ministry to the Passion. Leda Gys plays the Virgin Mary and Amleto Novelli plays Pontius Pilate; Alberto Pasquali plays Christ and Augusto Mastripietri plays Judas. The Last Supper is staged as a living reproduction of Leonardo's fresco, placed at the centre of the film. Michelangelo's Pietà, Mary holding her dead Son, is among the works of art the film reproduces. The scenario, by Antamoro and Ignazio Lupi, follows a poem by Fausto Salvatori.
inclusion: Christus was the first Italian epic of the life of Christ and an international hit, and Wikipedia quotes Pucci calling it a milestone of Italian religious epic cinema. Its method is pictorial. It brings famous religious paintings to life, which places it in the tradition of the Pathé Passion and of sacred art. Leda Gys, then a leading Italian star, plays the Madonna.
themes: The film's Catholic character lies in its sources. It takes its images from the great Catholic painters of the Annunciation, the Last Supper and the Pietà, and the institution of the Eucharist is given the central tableau. Salvatori's poem frames the Gospel as a sacred narrative rather than a historical reconstruction.

grey.question: Christus is a Life of Christ built from Catholic sacred art, with the Annunciation after Fra Angelico, the Last Supper after Leonardo and a Pietà after Michelangelo, and the Vatican helped distribute it in 1917. No independent review of the restored film exists, so nothing tells us how it handles the Gospel: its intertitles, its miracles, its Resurrection. A review of the 2000 Bologna restoration, or a contemporary Catholic notice, would settle the matter.

history: The film tells the life of Christ as the Gospels record it, from the Annunciation and the childhood at Nazareth through the public ministry to the Passion and death in Jerusalem. Leonardo's Last Supper is in the refectory of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, and Michelangelo's Pietà in St Peter's.
advisories:
Passion scenes are staged in tableau form, with no graphic violence reported.

Silent.

sources.title: The Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist
sources.claims: Trent, Sess. XIII, can. i-ii: Christ truly, really and substantially present; conversion of the whole substance, only the appearances remaining; words of institution are the words of transubstantiation

suitability.note: The Passion is staged as a series of still, painting-like tableaux, so it is gentle for children who know the Gospel. It is about an hour and a half long, which will try the patience of younger viewers.

doctrine: In the Last Supper tableau, the Council of Trent (Session XIII, 1551) defined that Christ is 'truly, really, and substantially' present under the appearances of bread and wine, and that the whole substance of the bread and wine is changed into his Body and Blood, only the appearances remaining. The words of institution, 'This is my body', are at once the words of consecration. The Annunciation after Fra Angelico and the image of Mary holding her dead Son after Michelangelo's Pietà place Our Lady at the beginning of the Incarnation and at the foot of the Passion, the two points at which the Church has always joined her to the work of her Son.
production: Cines, the leading Roman studio, gave Giulio Antamoro four years, 1912 to 1916, for its first Italian epic of the life of Christ. Much was shot in Egypt and Palestine; many scenes were filmed in Italy at Cori, south of Rome. It opened in Italy in November 1916 and in the United States in April 1917; its Paris premiere at the Trocadéro had an orchestra under Victor Charpentier. During the war the Vatican helped bring it into Germany through Switzerland. It stayed popular until sound arrived, after which prints disappeared. Cineteca di Bologna and Titanus, headed by Leda Gys's son Goffredo Lombardo, reconstructed it from fragments in foreign archives, with a new score by Mgr Marco Frisina, and it was shown at the 57th Venice Film Festival in 2000.

title: Conspiracy of Hearts
decision: PUBLISH: Catholic-centred in that a community of nuns and its charity are the subject. Legion of Decency A-I and a detailed contemporary trade review (Motion Picture Exhibitor, 16 March 1960: 'a reverent, potent drama'); identity and production history from Wikipedia and the Exhibitor credits. The English subtitle file shows the one romantic thread is the Italian major's courting of a novice, who rebuffs him; the Mother Superior counsels her soundly about her vocation, and refuses on the ground of the sisters' vows to let him kill to save them. Nothing there unsettles PUBLISH.
summary: Lilli Palmer's prioress and her nuns smuggle Jewish children out of an internment camp beside their Italian convent in 1943, in a well-made British weepie.
synopsis: Northern Italy, 1943. Beside a convent stands a camp where Jewish children are held under Italian guard. Mother Katharine and her nuns smuggle the children out, hide them and pass them on to safety. Major Spoletti, the Italian commander, hates the job and looks the other way. Not every sister agrees: Sister Gerta fears for the community. Then the Germans take over the camp, and Colonel Horsten and his zealous lieutenant Schmidt tighten the watch and investigate the escapes. A rabbi is caught leading a secret Yom Kippur service for the children in the convent cellar and is shot. The Germans raid the convent and condemn Mother Katharine and two sisters to death. The Italian firing squad fires over their heads, the Germans are killed, and the Italian soldiers leave to join the partisans.
inclusion: The film holds up as solid, emotional studio filmmaking. Lilli Palmer is the reason to see it. Motion Picture Exhibitor thought her performance worthy of an Oscar, called the film reverent and heart-rending, and singled out the cellar service as the scene to remember. Sylvia Syms and Yvonne Mitchell give good support as a young sister and a doubting one. David Parkinson of Time Out is less kind, calling it a synthetic weepie, and the plotting is conventional, with stock German villains and a last-minute rescue.
themes: The sisters' charity to the children grows out of their religious life, and the drama turns on what a community is prepared to risk for strangers. Mother Katharine's authority, Sister Gerta's prudence and the younger sisters' courage give a fair picture of obedience under pressure. A subplot has the Italian major court the novice Mitya; she rebuffs him, and the Mother Superior tells her not to force herself into religious life if her heart is elsewhere, sound counsel to a novice. At the climax the Mother forbids him to kill a German to save them, because the sisters live by the law of God they promised to keep.
history: The story is invented, but its setting is real. Fascist Italy interned foreign Jews in camps, Ferramonti di Tarsia in Calabria among the largest. After the armistice of 8 September 1943 German forces occupied northern and central Italy, and the murder of Italy's Jews began. On 16 October 1943 more than a thousand Roman Jews were seized and deported to Auschwitz; all but sixteen were killed. By Martin Gilbert's count, 477 Jews were then sheltered in the Vatican and its properties and 4,238 in Rome's monasteries and convents, and religious houses elsewhere in Italy hid many more. Almost 8,600 Jews from Italy and Italian-held territory were deported to Auschwitz by the end of the war, and all but about a thousand died.
advisories:
Wartime menace: executions are threatened, a rabbi is shot, and several Germans are killed at the end.

Children in danger throughout.

An Italian officer courts a novice, who turns him away; nothing more.

Suitable for older children and up.

suitability.note: There is nothing sexual, but it is a war story with children in danger throughout, so it suits children old enough for one.

doctrine: Sheltering the homeless and visiting prisoners are among the corporal works of mercy, and the sisters practise them under their vows of poverty, chastity and obedience. Their community is one of active Sisters of Charity rather than an enclosed order. The novice Mitya's position is as the Church defines it: the Council of Trent required a full year of novitiate before profession, on pain of nullity, and the novice keeps 'full and entire liberty' to leave (Catholic Encyclopedia), which is why the Mother Superior can tell her to test her heart. The Church had already condemned the racial creed behind the camp: in Mit brennender Sorge (14 March 1937) Pius XI wrote that whoever raises race, people or state to an idolatrous level distorts the order God created. The Mother's refusal to let a man kill for them rests on the fifth commandment as she and her sisters vowed to keep it.
production: The story began as a 1956 Goodyear Playhouse television play, directed by Robert Mulligan and set in 1946, about nuns helping Jewish children reach Palestine. Its true author was the blacklisted Adrian Scott, one of the Hollywood Ten, writing under the name of his friend Dale Pitt. Robert Presnell Jr. wrote the screenplay and moved the story to 1943; he was himself reportedly fronting for Dalton Trumbo. Albert C. Gannaway optioned it in 1958 but could not raise the money. Betty Box took it to a reluctant Rank, which agreed on the strength of her Doctor comedies with Ralph Thomas. It was shot in Italy, partly at the Certosa di Galluzzo near Florence, and at Pinewood. Released in Britain on 19 February 1960, it was the fifth most popular film of the year there. Paramount paid Rank a record sum for American rights; the Legion of Decency rated it A-I, and it was nominated for a Golden Globe.

title: Loyola, the Soldier Saint
decision: PUBLISH: Pablo Úrbez Fernández's scholarly study (Trasvases entre la literatura y el cine 4, 2022), based on the Spanish censorship files, establishes a near-complete and largely faithful life of St Ignatius, from his youth at court to his death in Rome in 1556, drawing on his Autobiography for Pamplona, the Montserrat vigil, the encounter with the Moor, Manresa, the Paris companions and Montmartre. A Jesuit, Fr Carlos María de Heredia, was adviser. The liberties (an invented infanta, an invented antagonist and his mistress, a strong militarist-patriotic colouring) are disclosed. Wikipedia gives identity; no doctrinal problem is reported.
summary: A Spanish biopic of St Ignatius from courtier and soldier to founder of the Jesuits, faithful to his Autobiography but coloured by the military patriotism of 1940s Spain.
synopsis: Íñigo leaves Loyola as a boy for the Castilian court, grows into an idle young gallant who dreams of the Infanta Catalina, and enters the service of the Duke of Nájera. Made captain, he leads the defence of Pamplona against the French in 1521 and is struck down by a cannonball. Convalescing at Loyola, he asks for books and is given lives of St Francis and St Dominic; his brother Martín warns him against vague dreams. He leaves for Montserrat, keeps vigil and lays down his arms before Our Lady, and on the road argues with a Moor who denies Mary's virginity, letting his mule decide whether to pursue him. He lives in prayer at Manresa and Barcelona. In Paris he meets Francis Xavier, is accused of heresy over his Exercises, and founds the Society at Montmartre. In Rome he converts the scoffer Beltrán and dies in 1556.
inclusion: Unlike most saint films of its day, this one covers almost the whole life, and Úrbez shows how closely it follows Ignatius's own Autobiography in the episodes that matter most: the reading at Loyola, the armour laid before the Virgin of Montserrat, the comic and revealing incident of the Moor and the mule, Manresa, the meeting with Xavier. Rafael Durán plays Íñigo. The production was serious, with a Jesuit adviser, a censor's report praising the dialogue and the name of the Catholic poet and monarchist José María Pemán on the script, though Úrbez notes that Pemán supplied only a short outline. It is also a document of its time. Contemporary provincial reports were mixed, criticising the Pamplona scenes and calling the direction inexperienced and the ending forced. The Roman section turns to fiction to illustrate Ignatian spirituality through the conversion of an invented sinner.
themes: The spine of the film is conversion: the gallant who reads the lives of the saints and resolves to outdo them, the knight who keeps vigil before Our Lady and gives up his sword, the penitent of Manresa. A censor summed up its thesis as conquering the passions through the Spiritual Exercises. Our Lady's virginity is defended in the Moor episode, and the founding of the Society is a Mass at Montmartre celebrated by Peter Faber. In Rome Ignatius sends his men out to defend the Church against heresy and carry the Gospel to the Indies. Úrbez notes that the film fuses soldier and saint more than conversion strictly allows, and that its title cards include 'war against the enemies of God'.
history: Íñigo López de Loyola (1491–1556), a Basque nobleman, was wounded at Pamplona in 1521 and converted while convalescing. He kept vigil at Montserrat in March 1522, lived as a penitent at Manresa, where the Spiritual Exercises took shape, studied at Alcalá, Salamanca and Paris, and with six companions took vows at Montmartre in 1534. He died in Rome on 31 July 1556.
liberties: The Infanta Catalina as Íñigo's ideal lady is invented, and the film makes him eight when he leaves home rather than sixteen. It makes him leader of the Pamplona defence. The tavern brawl and the shipwreck he providentially misses in Barcelona are invented. Jerusalem, Alcalá, Salamanca and Venice are skipped. The Roman section is largely fiction, built around Beltrán and his mistress Marcelilla.
advisories:
Battle violence at Pamplona; Íñigo's wound.

An invented sinner keeps a mistress in the Roman section; no explicit content is reported.

The film presents Ignatius in strongly military and Spanish-nationalist terms typical of its period.

doctrine: Ignatius's conversion at Loyola in 1521 came through reading the lives of Christ and the saints while he recovered from his wound at Pamplona. The Spiritual Exercises, composed from his experience at Manresa, are a month-long course of meditation on sin, the life of Christ and the end of man, and they were approved by Paul III in 1548. The Society of Jesus was approved by Paul III in 1540 with a fourth vow of special obedience to the Pope concerning missions. Ignatius was beatified by Paul V in 1609 and canonised by Gregory XV on 12 March 1622 together with Francis Xavier, Teresa of Avila, Philip Neri and Isidore. His feast was 31 July.
production: A Spanish production by Producciones Calderón and Intercontinental Films. It ran about 100 minutes and opened in Spain on 1 April 1949 through CEPISCA. It belongs to the group of lavish historical pictures that the Franco-era industry made in the 1940s. A Spanish academic article on the film (Trasvases) discusses its military and nationalist treatment of the saint.

title: From the Manger to the Cross
originalTitle: From the Manger to the Cross
alternateTitles: From the Manger to the Cross; or, Jesus of Nazareth
decision: GREY: Identity and content are well established (AFI Catalog; Greydanus, moral/spiritual +3, Kids & Up). The reservation is the film's shape: Greydanus describes it as Protestant in sensibility, built on King James title cards, with the Baptism of Christ left out, Mary's part at Cana removed and no Resurrection; it ends at the death of Christ with John 3:16. Nothing is contrary to faith, but the omissions are real and a reader can weigh them. It would move to PUBLISH if the editor judges a Life of Christ ending at Calvary acceptable when the omission is disclosed.
summary: Kalem's Life of Christ, shot in Palestine and Egypt in 1912, has authentic locations and reverent staging, but stops at Calvary without the Resurrection.
synopsis: The angel's message comes to Mary, though the angel himself is never seen. Joseph is shown struck by a light from outside the frame. Christ is born in Bethlehem, the Magi and shepherds come, and the Holy Family flees into Egypt, filmed in front of the real Sphinx and pyramids. Scenes of the boy Jesus in Nazareth follow. John the Baptist points out the Lamb of God, though Christ is only a distant figure. The disciples are called, and the ministry includes the wedding at Cana, healings and the raising of Lazarus. The Passion follows from the Last Supper to the Crucifixion. Most of the title cards are verses from the King James Bible. The film closes with the death of Christ and a final card quoting John 3:16.
inclusion: Shooting on location makes the film unusual. The hills of Galilee and Nazareth are real, and the flight into Egypt passes the Sphinx, an image Greydanus thinks later films should have copied. Costumes follow James Tissot's watercolours of the life of Christ. The Annunciation, with Mary addressed by an angel we never see, is simply and memorably done. The acting is more natural than in earlier Passion films, but the pace is slow, and the reliance on long Bible quotations makes it a reading film as much as a visual one. The National Film Preservation Foundation ranks it as the most important silent film about Christ.
themes: The film treats the Gospel with reverence: Christ is played with restraint and the Passion is not sensationalised. Greydanus, though, calls its approach Protestant, since it lets the scriptural text speak for itself and does not draw on the visual tradition of the Church. The omissions follow from this. Christ's Baptism is never shown. At Cana, Mary does not bring the shortage of wine to her Son, so her intercession, which Catholic tradition draws from that scene, is lost. Above all there is no Resurrection: the story ends with Christ's death and a verse about God's love.

grey.question: This is a reverent and in places beautiful Life of Christ, but it is shaped by a Protestant reading of Scripture. It leaves out Christ's Baptism, cuts Mary's request at Cana, the Gospel basis of her intercession, and ends at Calvary with John 3:16, so the Resurrection never appears. Nothing in it contradicts the faith; the question is whether a Gospel film that stops at the Cross gives a true account of the Gospel. Greydanus pairs it with Pathé's Life and Passion for the Resurrection and Ascension.

history: The film follows the Gospel narrative, taken from Matthew, Luke, Mark and John. It tells of the birth of Jesus at Bethlehem in the reign of Herod the Great, the flight into Egypt, the baptism by John, the wedding at Cana, the raising of Lazarus, the Last Supper, and the trial before Pilate and the Crucifixion at Jerusalem around AD 30. The Gospels give few details of the hidden life at Nazareth, and the film fills it with simple, pious scenes.
advisories:
Mild depiction of the Passion and Crucifixion.

Silent, with many long Bible-verse title cards.

Suitable for children.

doctrine: The film follows the four Gospels in order from the Annunciation to the Crucifixion, and so shows the mysteries of the Rosary's Joyful and Sorrowful decades in sequence. The Church teaches that Christ's Passion is the sacrifice by which he redeemed mankind (Council of Trent, Session 6, 1547), and that the Resurrection is the proof of his divinity and the foundation of the faith (1 Corinthians 15:14). A reader should therefore not take the ending as the end of the story. The Church's Easter liturgy completes it. The flight into Egypt, the raising of Lazarus and the wedding at Cana are all in the Gospels or in Matthew's infancy narrative. The film shows the Holy Family at the Sphinx, which is not a Gospel detail.
production: Kalem sent director Sidney Olcott and his unit to Palestine and Egypt in 1912, and the film was shot on location, including at Jerusalem and before the Sphinx and pyramids. Olcott took many compositions from James Tissot's illustrated Life of Our Saviour Jesus Christ. The film ran about 71 minutes, making it one of the longest of its day. It opened in London in October 1912, at Queen's Hall, where it ran for eight months, and in New York. The clergy were mostly approving, though the Daily Mail asked whether nothing was sacred to filmmakers, which helped bring about the British Board of Film Censors in 1913. Kalem's directors refused Olcott a rise, and he left. Vitagraph reissued it in 1919, after buying Kalem. The Rev. Brian Hession found negatives and re-released it in Britain in 1938 with music and commentary. The Library of Congress added it to the National Film Registry in 1998.

title: Ida
decision: GREY: Identity (Danish Film Institute, Wikipedia) and content (Globe and Mail and Time Out, independent; Catholic Herald, Aleteia and US Catholic, content only) are established. Reservations: a novice sleeps with a man before her vows, the ending leaves her profession open, and the film draws a parallel between a parish priest's certainty and a party official's (US Catholic). Not REJECT because the pre-conciliar convent and the vocation are treated with respect and the film argues no anti-Catholic thesis.
summary: Paweł Pawlikowski's spare black-and-white film about a Polish novice who learns, days before her vows, that she was born Jewish and her family murdered in the war.
synopsis: Poland, 1962. Anna, an orphan raised by nuns, is about to take her vows when her superior sends her to meet her only relative, her aunt Wanda, a hard-drinking judge who was once a Stalinist prosecutor. Wanda tells her she was born Ida Lebenstein, a Jew. The two drive into the countryside to find where her parents are buried. They learn that Feliks Skiba, whose family had sheltered the Lebensteins, killed them, and killed Wanda's small son too. Ida gives up any claim to the farm, and the two rebury the bones in a Jewish cemetery. Back in the city, Wanda jumps from her window. After the funeral Ida tries her aunt's life: she drinks, smokes, dances with the young saxophonist Lis and sleeps with him. He offers marriage and an ordinary life. At dawn she puts her habit back on and walks away.
inclusion: The film's reputation rests on its form: black-and-white images, long, still takes and very little dialogue. It runs eighty minutes and wastes none of them. Agata Kulesza's Wanda, worldly, sardonic and broken, is the performance critics singled out, and Agata Trzebuchowska, a newcomer, is all stillness; Kiva Reardon in the Globe and Mail calls her masterful. Reviewers compared the film to Dreyer and Bresson. For Catholic viewers its interest is that a film of this standing takes a novice's vocation seriously, sets it in a pre-conciliar convent of Latin prayer and silent meals, and does not mock it. Mark Judge at Aleteia called it the kind of film Catholics say is never made any more. It is also bleak, and its ending can be read more than one way.
themes: The convent is shown plainly: the nuns pray in Latin, eat in silence and work, and Anna kneels at a wayside shrine and blesses an infant. Wanda's taunt that Jesus did not hide from the world puts the film's question: is Anna's vocation a flight or a choice? Her night with Lis is the film's answer, of a kind. She tries the world, and in the morning goes back to the habit. Pawlikowski does not show whether she makes her profession. Patrick McCormick in US Catholic notes an unsettling parallel between the certainty of the parish priest and that of the party official. The guilt of Polish villagers in Jewish deaths is at the film's centre.
history: Many Jews in occupied Poland survived by hiding with Polish families, and some were betrayed or killed by those who sheltered them; Poles who helped Jews also risked execution. Ida's story is fictional. The post-war setting is the Stalinist Poland of the early 1960s, where the character of Wanda was inspired by Helena Wolińska-Brus, a Jewish-Polish prosecutor of that period.
advisories:
A novice sleeps with a man before returning to the convent; her aunt's casual affairs are shown.

A suicide.

The exhumation of murdered family members, including a child.

grey.question: Ida is a serious, respectful film about a novice in a pre-conciliar Polish convent, and it does not mock her faith. Yet the decisive episode before her vows is a night in which she drinks, dances and sleeps with a musician, and the film leaves open whether she goes back to make her profession. Some viewers will see a soul choosing God with open eyes; others, an ambiguity the film never resolves. It also draws a parallel between a priest's certainty and a communist official's.

sources.claims: A vow requires full knowledge and liberty; earlier vows cease on solemn profession

suitability.note: The novice's night with a man, the suicide and the exhumation of murdered family members, including a child, make it a film for older teenagers and adults. It is rated PG-13 in the United States.

doctrine: The Church's law on the novitiate is built to test a vocation of this kind. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1912) says the Council of Trent required a full year's novitiate, in which the novice is trained by a novice-master and tests the life, and that during it she is free to leave. Trent set sixteen as the earliest age for the profession that follows. Simple vows taken before solemn profession cease to bind on that profession, and a vow is a promise made to God that presupposes sufficient knowledge and freedom (Encyclopedia, 'Vows'). The film does not name her order or say whether she has taken any vow, so the choice that remains is hers to make.
production: Pawlikowski wrote the first draft in English with Rebecca Lenkiewicz under the working title Sister of Mercy, then translated and adapted it in Polish. The Polish Film Institute gave early funding and the producer Eric Abraham later underwrote the production. He cast Agata Trzebuchowska, a non-actor, after interviewing more than 400 actresses. Filmed in black and white in 4:3, it uses no score but a piece of Bach over the final scene. Łukasz Żal took over from Ryszard Lenczewski when Lenczewski fell ill, and an early snowstorm stopped production for two weeks. It premiered at the Toronto festival in 2013, opened in the United States on 2 May 2014, and won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film, the first Polish film to do so. Polish nationalists objected to its portrayal of Christian-Jewish relations. A petition with more than 40,000 signatures asked for title cards stating that thousands of Poles were executed for helping Jews; Abraham refused.

title: Bernadette of Lourdes
decision: PUBLISH: Catholic-centred life of St Bernadette (canonised 1933). Identity from Unifrance, Cinema Belgica and eofftv; independent treatment from Stuart Galbraith IV (DVD Talk, 2008, via the Wayback Machine); Legion of Decency A-I (Motion Picture Exhibitor Legion tables, 1962). Year 1961: French release 4 February 1961, after Belgian censorship in December 1960 and a Variety review in September 1960.
summary: A modest French life of St Bernadette, scripted by the Catholic novelist Gilbert Cesbron, that keeps the Lady unseen and follows Bernadette from the grotto to the convent at Nevers.
synopsis: Lourdes, 1858. Bernadette Soubirous is the eldest child of a destitute family, asthmatic and slow at her lessons with the sisters, but given to answers of surprising depth. Gathering wood by the river with her sister and a friend, she sees a lady in the grotto of Massabielle. The secret gets out and the town takes sides. The curate believes her; the parish priest, Abbé Peyramale, and the Bishop of Tarbes are slower to be convinced. The imperial police and magistrates question her and forbid her to go to the grotto, and her own family joins them. The apparitions continue: the spring appears, and the Lady names herself the Immaculate Conception. To shield her from the crowds the Church sends her to the sisters at Nevers, where she lives out her life hidden, ill and serving others.
inclusion: It is the sober French counterpart to The Song of Bernadette. Danièle Ajoret looks right as Bernadette. Stuart Galbraith IV, reviewing the American DVD, finds its approach more poetic and less literal than the Hollywood film: the Virgin is neither seen nor heard, only suggested, as in The Miracle of Our Lady of Fatima. He is equally clear about its faults: a tight budget, too many scenes of people talking about events instead of showing them, a restless zoom lens, and a jaunty score that undercuts the drama.
themes: The apparitions are treated as real, and the film follows the Church's own sequence: the parish priest's and the bishop's caution, the test of asking the Lady's name, and the answer, the Immaculate Conception, which Galbraith notes the unschooled girl could hardly have known. The emphasis falls on Bernadette's simplicity and obedience. The title, 'It is enough to love', points to the last part, where her vocation at Nevers is shown as hidden suffering and service rather than glory. Beyond the spring, no miracles are shown, partly for want of money, so the weight falls on her witness.
history: Bernadette Soubirous (1844–79) was the eldest child of a very poor family at Lourdes. Between 11 February and 16 July 1858 she saw eighteen apparitions of a lady at the grotto of Massabielle. A spring appeared on 25 February. On 25 March the lady told her 'I am the Immaculate Conception', four years after Pius IX defined that doctrine (8 December 1854). The parish priest, Abbé Peyramale, demanded proof, and the police commissioner Jacomet and the imperial magistrates tried to stop her. The Bishop of Tarbes, Mgr Laurence, set up an inquiry and declared the apparitions authentic on 18 January 1862. In 1866 Bernadette entered the Sisters of Charity at Nevers, where she died on 16 April 1879. Pius XI beatified her in 1925 and canonised her on 8 December 1933.
advisories:
Illness and poverty are shown plainly.

Suitable for all ages.

doctrine: Bernadette's lady named herself the Immaculate Conception: Mary was preserved from original sin from the first instant of her conception, by a singular grace of God and in view of the merits of Christ (Pius IX, Ineffabilis Deus, 1854). The Church does not oblige Catholics to believe in apparitions. Approval means that the bishop finds nothing contrary to faith or morals and permits the devotion; Bishop Laurence's judgment of 1862 was of this kind. The film's lesson on suffering follows the Church's old teaching on redemptive suffering and reparation: Bernadette's last illness is offered for sinners, for whom the Lady had asked her to pray and do penance.
production: This French-Italian production was filmed in black and white in the Hautes-Pyrénées, at Lourdes and at Nevers. Belgian censors passed it in December 1960. It opened in France on 4 February 1961 under the title Il suffit d'aimer ('Love is enough') and was released in America by Janus Films as Bernadette of Lourdes. The usual English version is dubbed and runs about 94 minutes. The Legion of Decency rated it A-I.

title: Joan the Woman
decision: GREY: Identity and content are established (AFI Catalog; Giornate del Cinema Muto 2019 note by Anne Morey; Movies Silently review). St Joan was canonised in 1920, so no hard rule applies. The reservations are concrete: an invented English lover, Eric Trent, whose betrayal leads to her capture; a First World War frame in which Joan's ghost urges a soldier to a suicide raid to atone for English sins; and a film more interested in Joan as patriot and woman than as saint. Not REJECT because her mission, visions and martyrdom are treated with respect; not PUBLISH because the inventions change the meaning of her story.
summary: DeMille's lavish 1916 epic of Joan of Arc, framed by the First World War trenches, has fine battle scenes and Handschiegl colour, and an invented English lover.
synopsis: In a French trench in 1916 an English officer, Eric Trent, finds an old sword in the earth and dreams of Joan of Arc. In the fifteenth-century story, his ancestor, also called Eric Trent, raids Joan's village of Domrémy, is wounded and is hidden and nursed by Joan, who is fond of him. Her visions then call her to the Dauphin, and she sets him aside. She persuades Charles, leads the French army, raises the siege of Orléans and sees Charles crowned. Trent, now an English commander, captures her at Compiègne and tries to ransom her, but his actions help her enemies. Bishop Cauchon tries her for heresy and she is burned at Rouen. In the trench Joan's spirit appears and tells the officer to expiate English wrongs; he volunteers for a night raid on the German lines and is killed.
inclusion: This was DeMille's first historical epic and one of the most expensive American films of its day. Its strengths are visual: storybook sets and costumes, clearly staged battles at Orléans, and the burning at Rouen tinted in red and yellow by the new Handschiegl process. Anne Morey's note for the 2019 Pordenone restoration describes Joan as a sturdy, honest country girl shown in Christ-like images, crucified in the shadow of the fleur-de-lis, and surrounded by men who are cruel, weak or cowardly. Geraldine Farrar, the opera star, is uneven: Movies Silently finds her strong in quiet and combat scenes but stiff in the visions and the trial, and Leonard Maltin thought her miscast. Raymond Hatton's Charles VII is a standout. It repays viewing for its scale and as a comparison with Dreyer and Gastyne.
themes: Joan's visions send her on her mission and she follows them faithfully; once called, she never looks back at Trent. Her death at the stake is presented as martyrdom, and Morey notes the film's repeated Christ-like imagery around her. But the film's centre of gravity is elsewhere. It treats Joan chiefly as a patriot and a woman, as the title says, and its romance and wartime frame turn her into a sponsor of Anglo-French alliance. The ghost who urges a soldier to die to atone for her death is an invention with no basis in her life or in Catholic teaching on expiation. The trial judges, in white pointed hoods, are villains.

grey.question: DeMille honours Joan's courage and her death, but he reshapes her story. He invents an English lover whose betrayal causes her capture, and he wraps the film in First World War propaganda: Joan's ghost urges a modern soldier to a suicidal raid to atone for her burning. The voices are treated respectfully but briefly; the film's subject is Joan as patriot and woman. Viewers who know the history can enjoy the spectacle; those wanting her sanctity should start with Dreyer.

history: Joan of Arc (c. 1412–1431) raised the siege of Orléans in 1429 and saw Charles VII crowned at Reims. She was captured at Compiègne by Burgundian forces in 1430, sold to the English, tried for heresy at Rouen by a court under Bishop Pierre Cauchon and burned on 30 May 1431. She was rehabilitated in 1456.
liberties: Eric Trent and the romance are invented; Joan was captured by Burgundians, not betrayed by an English lover. The modern frame is wholly fictional. The scenario also drew on Schiller's play rather than the trial records. The film was cut from eleven reels to eight soon after release, and the French version dropped the English frame.
advisories:
Battle violence and the burning of Joan at the stake.

An attempted seduction in Domrémy; no nudity reported.

A soldier is sent on what amounts to a suicide mission at the urging of Joan's ghost.

Older children and up; long (about 140 minutes restored).
