sources.title: Joan of Arc
sources.claims: Her voices; appeal to the Pope; abjuration and relapse; judgement of 29 May 1431; papal annulment; cause introduced 1869; Pius X decree 11 April 1909; canonised 1920 by Benedict XV

suitability.note: The battle scenes and the burning at the stake may upset younger children, and it is a silent film of about two and a half hours, which few children under twelve will sit through.

doctrine: Joan said her voices were those of St Michael, St Catherine of Alexandria and St Margaret of Antioch, whom she claimed to see and touch. At Rouen she appealed to the Pope, and the court went on without reference to him. After her abjuration at Saint-Ouen she resumed male dress, and on 29 May 1431 the judges declared her a relapsed heretic. The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that the retrial, held with the consent of the Holy See, ended with a papal court annulling the sentence. Her cause was introduced in 1869 by Bishop Dupanloup of Orléans. Pius X published the decree of beatification on 11 April 1909, and Benedict XV canonised her in 1920. Her feast is kept on 30 May, the day of her death.
production: Joan the Woman was the first large-scale film about Joan of Arc and the fourth collaboration between Cecil B. DeMille and the opera singer Geraldine Farrar. Jesse Lasky persuaded DeMille in May 1916 to merge two planned Farrar pictures into one epic. Jeanie Macpherson's scenario drew on Mark Twain's Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc (1896). It was shot at the Lasky studios in Hollywood between 19 June and 7 October 1916, with Alvin Wyckoff leading a team of seventeen cameramen. Some scenes, above all the flames at the stake, were coloured by the Handschiegl process, billed as the Wyckoff process. A prologue and epilogue set in the trenches of 1917 tie the story to the Anglo-French alliance. It opened in New York on 25 December 1916 and cost $302,976. It did poorly outside the big cities. The George Eastman Museum print was restored and shown at Le Giornate del Cinema Muto in 2019, running 148 minutes.

title: King of Kings
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred life of Christ. The reservation is documented by contemporary Catholic evidence: the Legion of Decency gave it a Separate Classification (Motion Picture Exhibitor Legion tables, 1962; AFI: 'taking poetic license with the life of Christ'), while the Vatican's Catholic Cinematographic Centre later gave it its highest classification. Invented Zealot subplot, political Judas, reduced role of the Sanhedrin. Not REJECT: no heterodox thesis; not PUBLISH because of the Legion reservation.
summary: Nicholas Ray's life of Christ, with Jeffrey Hunter, sets the Gospel inside a Zealot revolt and makes Judas a disappointed rebel: handsome, reverent and freely rewritten.
synopsis: Narrated by Orson Welles, the film opens with Pompey's capture of Jerusalem in 63 BC and the Roman occupation. Jesus is born in Bethlehem, escapes the massacre of the innocents and grows up in Nazareth. Meanwhile Barabbas and Judas lead Zealot raids against Pilate. Jesus is baptised by John, tempted in the desert, gathers the apostles and preaches the Sermon on the Mount, and Judas leaves Barabbas to follow Him, hoping He will lead the revolt. Herod Antipas has John beheaded. Barabbas launches a Passover rising, and Pilate's legions crush it. Judas, wanting to force Jesus' hand, betrays Him. Pilate condemns Him and releases Barabbas, and Judas hangs himself. After the Crucifixion the risen Christ speaks to the apostles by the sea, His shadow falling in the shape of a cross on the fishing nets.
inclusion: Samuel Bronston's production is handsome: shot in Spain in 70mm, with a Miklós Rózsa score and a long Sermon on the Mount staged as an exchange with the crowd. Ray's widescreen compositions are often arresting. Jeffrey Hunter's Christ is gentle and remote, and Siobhán McKenna's Mary is dignified. The critics divided, and Variety and Harrison's Reports were among those who praised it. DeCine21 finds it respectful and faithful to Scripture in many respects, though drawn as much from Tacitus as from the Gospels; Cinefile, more enthusiastic, calls it the most satisfying film of the Passion of its time but notes its liberties.
themes: The film affirms the Nativity, the miracles, the Passion and the Resurrection, and it treats Christ with reverence. Its trouble is emphasis. Long stretches belong to Barabbas and the Zealots, and Judas betrays Christ to force Him into leading a revolt, a modern theory with no basis in the Gospels. The part of the Jewish authorities in the Passion is reduced and Rome made chiefly responsible; John Farrow left the project rather than make that change. Christ's divinity is stated more than dramatised, and Richard Coe complained that the film made Him uncontroversial. Vatican reviewers rated it highly; the American Legion objected to its poetic licence.
history: Jesus of Nazareth was born in Bethlehem in the reign of Herod the Great and grew up at Nazareth. Judaea had been under Roman power since Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC. John the Baptist baptised in the Jordan and was imprisoned and beheaded by Herod Antipas. Jesus preached in Galilee, chose the Twelve and went up to Jerusalem for the Passover, where Judas Iscariot betrayed Him, the high priests delivered Him to Pontius Pilate, and Pilate had Him crucified. The Gospels say He rose on the third day. Barabbas, released by Pilate at the Passover, is named in all four Gospels as a prisoner; Luke and Mark call him an insurrectionist.
liberties: The Zealot revolt led by Barabbas, Judas's political motive, Christ's visit to John the Baptist in prison and the Roman centurion Lucius, who follows Christ's career, are invented. The Sanhedrin's role is minimised and Pilate's enlarged. The Resurrection is shown only by a shadow and a voice.
advisories:
The massacre of the innocents, the beheading of John and battle scenes; the scourging and Crucifixion are restrained.

Suitable for older children and up.

grey.question: King of Kings is reverent, but it rewrites the Gospel in significant ways. Much of its running time goes to an invented Zealot rising; Judas betrays Christ to provoke a revolt; and the part of the Jewish authorities in the Passion is played down so that Rome bears the guilt. The Legion of Decency, finding that it took poetic licence with the life of Christ, gave it a Separate Classification outside its ordinary ratings. Viewers who know the Gospels well can enjoy its images while setting its inventions aside.

sources.title: Judas Iscariot
sources.claims: Gospel accounts of the motive and the thirty pieces; the theory that he wished to force a revolt rejected as contrary to Scripture and tradition

suitability.note: The violence is restrained. The film is long and slow, and a parent should be ready to correct the Zealot plot, which is not in the Gospels.

doctrine: The Gospels give no single motive for Judas's treachery: Luke and John say Satan entered him, John calls him a thief who kept the purse, and only Matthew names thirty pieces of silver. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) rejects the view that he betrayed Christ to force a revolt as contrary to Scripture and tradition, so the film's central invention is one that the older writers refuted. The Roman Catechism teaches that all sinners were the cause of Christ's Passion, so that guilt cannot be laid on one race or on Rome. Christ's divinity was defined at Nicaea (325) and Chalcedon (451); in the film Rózsa's score and the narration carry the weight. The Legion of Decency gave it a Separate Classification for taking poetic licence with the life of Christ.
production: John Farrow developed the project as Son of Man in the early 1950s and left in 1959 over differences. Nicholas Ray was hired to direct for the producer Samuel Bronston, with a new script by Philip Yordan, and biblical scholars hired to check it against the Gospels. Pope John XXIII reportedly approved the script in March 1960. Filming ran in Spain from April to October 1960, followed by reshoots in late 1960 and London in May 1961. MGM took it over, and Ray Bradbury wrote the narration, spoken by Orson Welles, and a new ending. It opened in New York on 11 October 1961 and ran well over two and a half hours. Time called it 'the corniest, phoniest, ickiest' of recent Bible films; Crowther called it an 'illustrated lecture'. It earned $8 million in North America and $5.4 million abroad.

title: The Saint Who Forged a Country
originalTitle: La virgen que forjó una patria
alternateTitles: The Saint That Forged a Country
decision: GREY: Identity and content are established (Wikipedia citing Rodríguez and BAMPFA; a detailed credits-and-plot page reproducing Jesús Ibarra's commentary; UnoTV). The core is Catholic: the evangelisation of New Spain, a friar's defence of the Indians, and the 1531 apparitions to Juan Diego with the miraculous image presented to Bishop Zumárraga. The reservation is the frame: the story is told by Fr Miguel Hidalgo to justify taking Our Lady of Guadalupe as the banner of armed insurrection, and the film closes on that banner. Hidalgo was excommunicated by his bishop in 1810; the film presents his use of the image approvingly. Juan Diego was beatified only in 1990 and is a character, not the subject (rule (a) does not apply; he must not be called saint or blessed). Not REJECT because the apparitions are central and reverently told.
summary: Julio Bracho's Guadalupe film has Fr Hidalgo, on the eve of revolt in 1810, recount the conversion of Mexico and the apparitions to Juan Diego, played by Ramón Novarro.
synopsis: Querétaro, September 1810: Hidalgo, Allende and the other conspirators plan a rising against Spain and Hidalgo chooses the Virgin of Guadalupe as its banner. When the plot is discovered, Hidalgo tells Allende how the Virgin came to Mexico. In 1528 the Spaniard Pedro de Alonso enslaves and brands Indians, and the Aztec noblewoman Xochiquiahuit, who has taken up with him, is rejected by her father. A friar, Fray Martín, opposes the abuses, baptises the weaver Cuauhtlatoa as Juan Diego and brings Alonso to court; Alonso's own child is born branded, and he blinds himself and dies. Fray Martín wins from Charles V a school for Indians at Tlatelolco and dies on the voyage home. In 1531 the Virgin appears to Juan Diego on Tepeyac, and her image appears on his cloak before Bishop Zumárraga. The film returns to 1810 and the insurgents raise her banner.
inclusion: This is one of the most ambitious religious films of Mexico's golden age, and it gave Ramón Novarro, the silent star of Ben-Hur, a late role as Juan Diego. The commentary reproduced from Jesús Ibarra praises Bracho's direction, the cast, especially Novarro, and Jorge Bustos's editing, which binds the two periods together. A recent programme note calls it an icon of Mexican kitsch, love it or hate it. Its interest lies in the colonial half: the clash between the conquistador and the friar, the founding of the college at Tlatelolco and a careful, reverent staging of the Tepeyac apparitions and the image on the tilma. The 1810 frame is talky and patriotic.
themes: Our Lady of Guadalupe is presented as the Mother who unites Indian and Spaniard in one faith: the apparitions come after the friar's fight against slavery and the first baptisms, and the image on Juan Diego's cloak persuades the bishop. The Church is shown on the side of the Indians against the conquistador, and the miracle is treated as real. The frame is another matter. The film makes the apparition the foundation of Mexican nationhood and ends with a priest raising the image as the standard of a revolt that his bishop condemned. Devotion and insurgent nationalism are run together without comment.

grey.question: The heart of this film is a reverent telling of the Guadalupe apparitions and the conversion of Mexico. But the whole story is framed as Fr Miguel Hidalgo's justification for taking Our Lady's image as the banner of the 1810 insurrection, and the film ends on that banner. Hidalgo was excommunicated by his bishop that year. Viewers should know that the film presents the Virgin of Guadalupe as patroness of a priest-led revolt and treats this as her purpose.

history: Catholic tradition holds that in December 1531 Our Lady appeared four times to the Indian convert Juan Diego on the hill of Tepeyac, and that her image appeared on his tilma before Bishop Juan de Zumárraga. Pius X named her patroness of Latin America in 1910. On 16 September 1810 Fr Miguel Hidalgo began the war of independence at Dolores and took up a Guadalupe banner at Atotonilco.
liberties: Fray Martín, Pedro de Alonso, Xochiquiahuit and their story are invented to dramatise the conquest and evangelisation. The link between the apparitions and the independence movement is the film's thesis, not history; one critic calls the historical frame a pretext for justifying the Guadalupe banner, and commentators note errors in the colonial and 1810 sections.
advisories:
The branding and enslavement of Indians; a man blinds himself.

An unmarried liaison between a Spaniard and an Aztec woman; a child born of it.

The frame presents the 1810 insurrection, led by a priest later excommunicated, as the fulfilment of the apparition.

doctrine: The Church never defined the Guadalupe apparitions as a matter of faith, but the popes honoured them repeatedly. Benedict XIV declared Our Lady of Guadalupe patron of New Spain, made 12 December a holyday with an octave and granted a proper Mass and Office; Leo XIII approved a historical lesson for the Office and had the image crowned in his name (1895). On the frame story the traditional teaching is plain: St Paul's command to be subject to the higher powers (Romans 13), repeated by Leo XIII in Diuturnum (1881), forbids rebellion against lawful authority. Manuel Abad y Queipo, Bishop-elect of Michoacán, excommunicated Hidalgo and his followers in 1810, and other bishops followed him. Hidalgo was degraded from the priesthood before he was shot at Chihuahua on 30 July 1811.
production: Films Mundiales made the film. It was Bracho's third feature and the only Mexican film of Ramón Novarro. Shooting began on 5 October 1942 at the CLASA studios, and the film premiered at the Cine Palacio Chino in Mexico City on 11 December 1942, the eve of the Guadalupe feast. It runs about 110 minutes and reached English-speaking audiences as The Saint Who Forged a Country in 1944. The critic Jesús Ibarra records that it was received less warmly than Bracho's two earlier films, though he praised Villarreal's Hidalgo. A priest, José A. Romero, wrote to Bracho to praise it.

title: Lourdes and Its Miracles
decision: PUBLISH: Catholic-centred documentary on Lourdes. Identity from Unifrance (Fiches du Cinéma synopsis) and French Wikipedia; independent treatment from Jean Collet (Encyclopædia Universalis), who calls it the most honest and moving document on the Lourdes pilgrimages; the National Legion of Decency rated the US release A-I (1958–59).
summary: Georges Rouquier's three-part documentary on Lourdes: cures examined by the Medical Bureau, a pilgrim's day of devotions, and two sick women filmed before and after their cures.
synopsis: The film is built as three linked short documentaries, narrated by Rouquier himself. The first, 'Témoignages', opens on the commercial bustle of the town and then examines three cures recorded by the Bureau des constatations médicales: a nurse from Rennes cured of intestinal tuberculosis, a naval officer from Toulon whose stubborn fistula closed, and a boy, blind and paralysed at three, who recovered sight and movement. The second, 'Pèlerinage', follows a pilgrim's whole day: Mass, prayer at the grotto, the sick immersed in the baths, the rosary, the procession of the Blessed Sacrament and the candlelit night procession. The third, 'Imprévus', stands apart. Rouquier's camera had filmed two sick women hours or days before they were cured, and he shows them again afterwards.
inclusion: Rouquier made his name with Farrebique (1946), a year in the life of a peasant family in the Rouergue, and he brings the same patience to Lourdes. The film was commissioned, and it could easily have been an apologetic tract. Jean Collet, writing on Rouquier for the Encyclopædia Universalis, judges it instead the most honest and affecting record of what happens at Lourdes during the pilgrimages, and perhaps the finest and least known of Rouquier's films. Its strength is its method: it lets the Medical Bureau's files, the pilgrims and the sick speak, and it does not hide the souvenir trade. The young Jacques Demy was Rouquier's assistant. It is rarely shown and hard to find.
themes: The film treats the shrine as a place of prayer and of cures, and takes both seriously. The Medical Bureau's procedure, by which doctors examine a cure before the Church is asked to judge it, is shown in detail. The second part records the devotions that fill a Lourdes day: Mass, the rosary, the baths, the blessing of the sick and the eucharistic procession. Rouquier's narration does not overstate. He presents the cures as facts the doctors could not explain and leaves the viewer to weigh them, which is close to the Church's own caution about Lourdes.
history: Between 11 February and 16 July 1858 Bernadette Soubirous, aged fourteen, reported eighteen apparitions of the Virgin at the grotto of Massabielle; only she saw and heard the Lady. Organised national French pilgrimages began in 1873, and by the end of 1908 more than five thousand pilgrimages, with some 4.9 million pilgrims, had been registered. The Bureau des constatations médicales at the shrine allows doctors of any nationality or belief to examine the certificates of illness and cure, and selects cases that appear both real and medically inexplicable before any bishop is asked to rule on them.
advisories:
Sick and disabled people are shown in their illness; nothing graphic.

Suitable for all ages.

doctrine: The Church judges a reported cure at Lourdes in two stages: physicians first establish that the illness was real and the cure sudden, complete and lasting without medical explanation, and only then does the bishop of the person cured decide whether to declare it miraculous. The criteria go back to Benedict XIV's rules for miracles in causes of canonisation (De servorum Dei beatificatione, 1734–38). The bishop of Tarbes declared in 1862 that the faithful were justified in believing the apparitions. Leo XIII granted a proper Office and Mass of the Apparition, and Pius X extended the feast to the universal Church in 1907, on 11 February. The devotions shown, the blessing of the sick with the Blessed Sacrament and the eucharistic procession, are the shrine's daily practice.
production: Lourdes et ses miracles was made by Les Productions du Parvis. The film runs about ninety minutes. It opened in France on 9 November 1955. In the United States it was distributed by Brandon Films, and the National Legion of Decency classified it A-I.

title: Paul, Apostle of Christ
decision: PUBLISH: Richard Roeper's independent Chicago Sun-Times review (3/4, a 'thoughtful and faithful' telling) and Steven Greydanus's detailed review (B+, used for content only) establish a reverent, Scripture-based account of St Paul's last days and martyrdom that rejects violence against persecutors. The English subtitle file confirms the theology stays scriptural (grace in Pauline words, 2 Timothy read at the end) with no 'faith alone' framing, and that nothing presents the post-conciliar Church. St Peter is named only twice in passing, and no Eucharist or breaking of bread is spoken of; both omissions are disclosed.
summary: Andrew Hyatt's chamber drama of St Paul's last weeks in Nero's Mamertine prison, where St Luke visits him to record his memories while Rome's Christians face persecution.
synopsis: After the fire of Rome, Nero blames the Christians and has them burned as torches and thrown to beasts. Paul, old and worn, waits in the Mamertine prison under sentence of death. Luke slips into the city and gets into the cell, where he persuades Paul to recount his life so that it can be written down. Paul is haunted by the Christians he persecuted as Saul, and remembers his conversion and his baptism at the hands of Ananias. Outside, Priscilla and Aquila shelter the community, whose younger men want to fight back, and a failed rescue lands Luke in prison too. The prefect Mauritius, whose daughter is dying, turns in desperation to Luke, a physician. Luke heals the girl while Christians die in the circus. The community leaves Rome carrying Luke's writings, and Paul is beheaded.
inclusion: This is a small, talky film, not the epic some expected, and it is better for it. James Faulkner gives the strongest performance as a worn, combative Paul, and Richard Roeper singles him out; Jim Caviezel's Luke is steady and restrained. Steven D. Greydanus calls the screenplay intelligent and thoughtful, and finds Paul's remorse over the Christians he persecuted the film's most effective thread. The story turns on a question for a persecuted Church, whether to answer Nero with force. The film says no, and argues the point. Malta's half-burned Rome looks convincing for the budget. Some scenes play like stage dialogue, a few lines sound too modern, and Greydanus finds the timeline of the closing scene confusing.
themes: Paul insists that love, not vengeance, is the answer to Nero, and the young men who want to free him by force are shown to be wrong. His guilt over his years as a persecutor gives the theme of forgiveness weight: his sins, he says, were washed away by God's grace. Luke's healing of the prefect's daughter is presented as a miracle and as charity to an enemy, and Paul's death is martyrdom accepted. The language is Pauline and scriptural, with no 'faith alone' slogan. The Church's structure is missing, with no Eucharist, no clergy and St Peter named only in passing. Greydanus calls the absence of Peter, Linus and Clement an odd missed opportunity.
history: The Second Letter to Timothy, written from Paul's last imprisonment, says that only Luke was with him. Tacitus records that Nero blamed the Christians for the fire of AD 64 and put many to death in cruel spectacles, some burned as torches. Priscilla and Aquila were tentmakers and co-workers of Paul named in Acts and in his letters.
liberties: Scripture places Luke with Paul in his last imprisonment, but the scheme of secretly taking down his memories, the prefect Mauritius and his daughter, and the armed faction among the Christians are invented. St Peter, traditionally martyred in the same persecution, does not appear and is mentioned only twice, as part of Paul's past. Greydanus notes that the story tracing the term 'Roman candle' to burning Christians is a late folk etymology.
advisories:
Bloody images of persecution: Christians burned alive as torches, burned bodies, and martyrs sent to the beasts in the circus.

names: Andrew Hyatt (story by Andrew Hyatt and T.J. Berden)

suitability.note: The film is far less bloody than The Passion of the Christ, but the long dialogue scenes will lose younger children.

doctrine: St Paul's conversion is kept on 25 January; with St Peter he is honoured on 29 June, and his own commemoration falls on 30 June. The Catholic Encyclopedia gives the tradition that he was beheaded at Aquae Salviae (Tre Fontane) on the Ostian Way at the end of Nero's reign, and that he lies at San Paolo fuori le mura. The film's closing reading of 2 Timothy 1:9, saved by God's 'purpose and grace' and not by our works, matches the Council of Trent (Session VI, 1547, ch. 8): nothing that precedes justification, 'whether faith or works', merits the grace itself. Trent also condemned justification 'by faith alone' (canon 9). Tradition names St Luke, Paul's companion of 2 Timothy 4:11, as the author of the third Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles.
production: Andrew Hyatt, a Catholic, developed the story with the producer T.J. Berden. The film was made by Affirm Films (Sony's faith-market label) with ODB Films, Giving Films and Mandalay Pictures, on a budget of about $5 million. Principal photography began in September 2017 in Malta, which stands in for Rome. Sony released it in the United States on 23 March 2018, at 106 minutes; it took about $23 million worldwide. Reviews were mixed: Richard Roeper gave it three stars out of four, while Todd McCarthy in The Hollywood Reporter found it 'missing passion'. Greydanus also gave it three stars out of four.

title: Quo Vadis?
decision: PUBLISH: Maria Wyke's scholarly study documents a faithful set of 'moving illustrations' of Sienkiewicz's Catholic novel: Peter preaching in the catacomb, Christ appearing to Peter on the Via Appia, Paul baptising the repentant Chilo, the martyrs in the arena, and a closing vision of Christ breaking the chains of the faithful. Giovanni Lasi's Cinema Ritrovato note confirms identity, the 2026 restoration and the film's standing. Cines, the producer, was funded by the Vatican's bank; the film's sympathies are plainly with the Church.
summary: Guazzoni's 1913 Cines spectacle of Sienkiewicz's novel, with Peter in the catacombs, the burning of Rome and the arena martyrs, was the first great epic of cinema.
synopsis: In Nero's Rome the patrician officer Vinicius falls for Lygia, a Christian hostage guarded by the giant Ursus. Following her with the informer Chilo, he comes to a night gathering of Christians outside the city, where the apostle Peter preaches to them. His pride gives way as he comes to respect Lygia's faith. Nero burns Rome and blames the Christians, and a persecution follows; the faithful are condemned to the Circus and die among the lions. Lygia is tied to the back of a bull and Ursus saves her by breaking its neck. Peter, leaving the city, meets Christ on the Appian Way and turns back to Rome to die. The penitent Chilo is baptised by Paul. Nero, abandoned, dies, and the film ends with a vision of Christ freeing the faithful from their chains.
inclusion: Quo Vadis? changed what audiences expected from a film. Giovanni Lasi credits Guazzoni, a trained painter, with a new sense of depth and spectacle: crowds arranged in great masses, strong contrasts of light and silhouette, real Roman locations for the Appian Way and the Borghese gardens. Wyke shows how scenes quote Gérôme's paintings of the Christian martyrs. The acting and the tableau construction are of their time, and the French critic René Doumic found the whole thing stupefying. Its importance in film history is beyond dispute.
themes: Sienkiewicz wrote a Catholic novel, ending at Peter's basilica on the Vatican hill, and Wyke reads the film as an Italian Catholic allegory: the persecuted early Christians stand for Catholics under a hostile secular state. Peter is shown preaching in the catacomb, his presence in Rome given the weight of archaeology, and the Quo vadis, Domine? meeting on the Appian Way, where Christ turns Peter back towards martyrdom, is filmed on the real road. Conversion runs through the story: Vinicius is won by Lygia's purity, and Chilo the betrayer is forgiven and baptised by Paul. The film adds a final vision of Christ breaking the chains of kneeling believers.
history: Lygia, Vinicius, Ursus and Chilo are Sienkiewicz's inventions. His novel appeared in 1896 and won him wide fame before his Nobel Prize in 1905.
liberties: The film follows the novel's main line but compresses it into a sequence of illustrated episodes linked by long titles. Its last shot, Christ breaking the chains of the faithful, has no source in the novel. Lasi's note dates it 1912/13; it premiered in Berlin in March 1913.
advisories:
Arena violence: Christians thrown to lions, a gladiator fight, a woman bound to a bull.

The burning of Rome and scenes of Nero's court and banquets.

Silent, with long explanatory titles; older children and up.

names: Quo Vadis, novel by Henryk Sienkiewicz (1896)

suitability.note: It is all in silent-film style, without gore. The long title cards and two-hour length are hard going for young children.

doctrine: The film rests on the Church's tradition of the Roman persecution under Nero. Tacitus (Annals XV) records the punishment of the Christians after the fire of AD 64. Tradition, witnessed by Eusebius, holds that Peter and Paul both died at Rome under Nero, Peter crucified and Paul beheaded. Their joint feast is 29 June. The 'Quo vadis, Domine?' meeting comes from the apocryphal Acts of Peter and is a pious tradition, not a defined fact. The film also shows the early Church's teaching that the martyr's blood is the seed of the Church (Tertullian) and that baptism and the Faith bring a pagan convert to renounce the sins of the old life.
production: Cines of Rome made the film. It ran about two hours, very long for 1913, and used some 5,000 extras and large built sets. It premiered in Berlin on 19 March 1913, at the opening of the Ufa-Pavillon, and was shown to King George V at the Royal Albert Hall. In the United States it was the first film shown at the Astor Theatre on Broadway, where it ran for nine months from April 1913.

title: Quo Vadis
decision: GREY: Identity and fidelity are established (Wikipedia, Kino Muranów, Ewa Skwara in Classica, Marek Zieleniewski in Wprost, Jonathan Rosenbaum). The English subtitle file narrows the coda question: the last dialogue is the Quo vadis scene, Peter turning back to Rome (02:10:18–02:10:52), and nothing is spoken between it and the end titles (02:11:06). The present-day coda is therefore wordless and brief, a passing modern image rather than the film's interpretive voice, so rule (b) does not apply. It stays GREY for the nudity at Nero's feasts and because what the closing images show of modern Rome is still undescribed.
summary: Jerzy Kawalerowicz's lavish, faithful Polish adaptation of Sienkiewicz's novel of Nero's persecution, with Franciszek Pieczka as St Peter and an added ending in modern Rome.
synopsis: In Nero's Rome the young patrician Marcus Vinicius falls for Lygia, a Christian hostage of barbarian birth raised in the house of Aulus Plautius and Pomponia Graecina. His uncle Petronius, Nero's arbiter of taste, contrives to have her handed over to Vinicius, but she escapes with her giant protector Ursus and hides among the Christians. Vinicius tracks her down with the wrestler Croton; Ursus kills Croton and Vinicius is wounded. Nursed by the Christians he came to rob, he is converted and baptised. When Rome burns, Nero blames the Christians and sends them to die in the arena. Lygia is bound to the back of a bull, and Ursus wrestles it down; Nero spares them. Peter, urged to flee, meets Christ on the Appian Way and turns back to Rome. A brief wordless coda shows him in the Rome of today.
inclusion: This is the most faithful screen version of Sienkiewicz's novel, made by one of Poland's most respected directors as his last film. Kawalerowicz said repeatedly that he wanted to follow the book and its moral message; Ewa Skwara's study finds that the result looks like the nineteenth century's idea of Rome, closer to Alma-Tadema's paintings than to modern scholarship, and that Polish audiences loved it. Critics were cooler. Marek Zieleniewski in Wprost praised Jerzy Trela's Chilon, Michał Bajor's Nero and Bogusław Linda's restrained Petronius, but found the film static and stagey and the romance rushed. Jonathan Rosenbaum thought it stacks up well against the 1951 MGM version, though he preferred Ustinov's Nero.
themes: The novel's Christian substance is the conversion of a pagan through charity and the witness of the martyrs, and the film keeps it. Vinicius is won less by argument than by the Christians who nurse the man who came to seize Lygia, and he is baptised in the name of the Trinity; so, at the last, is the informer Chilon. The persecution after the fire is presented as martyrdom. St Peter is the apostle of the Roman Christians, as in the book. The last spoken scene is the legend that gives the story its title: Peter meets Christ on the road, asks where He is going, and turns back to Rome.
history: Sienkiewicz published Quo Vadis in 1895–96 after close study of Tacitus and other Roman writers; its title comes from the legend of Peter meeting Christ on the Appian Way as he fled Rome.
liberties: Kawalerowicz follows the novel closely, compressing its many strands. His main addition is a brief, wordless closing image that brings St Peter into present-day Rome. Zieleniewski found the arena deaths, in the version he saw, oddly bloodless.
advisories:
Bare-breasted dancers at Nero's feasts; Rosenbaum calls the film far racier than the 1951 version.

Christians killed by lions in the arena, with severed limbs shown in at least one cut; the burning of Rome; a man killed in a wrestling fight.

grey.question: Quo Vadis (2001) follows Sienkiewicz faithfully and ends, as the title promises, with Peter meeting Christ on the Appian Way and turning back to Rome to die. Nero's feasts include bare-breasted dancers, and the arena scenes show some gore, so this is not the family film the 1951 version was. Kawalerowicz also added a brief closing image of Peter in the Rome of 2001. It is wordless and says nothing about the present-day Church; a description of what it shows would settle whether it is more than a visual flourish.

names: Quo Vadis, novel by Henryk Sienkiewicz (1896)

suitability.note: It is a long film, in Polish with subtitles, and best for older teenagers and adults.

doctrine: Tacitus records that Nero blamed the Christians for the fire of AD 64 and killed many in cruel spectacles; tradition puts the martyrdom of Peter in the same persecution. The film's conversions are by baptism in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, the form the Church has always required; the informer Chilon is baptised before his death, which fits the Church's teaching that a sincere desire for baptism, or martyrdom, can save. The 'Domine, quo vadis?' scene is not in the Gospels but in the apocryphal Acts of Peter (c. AD 180), and the Church treats it as pious legend. The Roman see is Peter's: the Church holds that the bishop of Rome succeeds him in the primacy, as the First Vatican Council defined in 1870.
production: Jerzy Kawalerowicz's film was the most expensive Polish production to date, at about $18 million. It was released on 14 September 2001 and was seen by 4.2 million in Poland, the most popular Polish film of the year. It was Poland's entry for the 74th Academy Awards Best Foreign Language Film but was not nominated.

title: Saint Joan
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (St Joan of Arc) but built on Shaw's thesis that Joan was a Protestant and a nationalist before her time (Shaw's Preface and Scene IV, per Gale's Drama for Students). Legion of Decency A-II. Not REJECT because the thesis is argued rather than preached, the churchmen are given serious speeches and Greene's adaptation softens Shaw by blaming individual judges; not PUBLISH because the film's framing of Joan's sanctity against Church authority is a real doctrinal question.
summary: Preminger's film of Shaw's play, adapted by Graham Greene, with eighteen-year-old Jean Seberg as Joan: intelligent talk, a miscast lead and Shaw's argument with the Church.
synopsis: In 1456, after Joan's sentence has been annulled, the ageing Charles VII dreams that she visits him, and the story unfolds in flashback. A farm girl who hears the voices of saints persuades a local captain, then the feeble Dauphin, to let her lead the army. She raises the siege of Orléans and sees Charles crowned at Reims. Then the court and the generals tire of her. Captured and sold to the English, she is tried at Rouen by Bishop Cauchon and the Inquisitor, while the Earl of Warwick wants her burned whatever the verdict. Frightened, she signs a recantation; when she learns that she will be imprisoned for life, she tears it up and goes to the stake. The film returns to Charles, waking from his dream.
inclusion: This is the most serious screen version of Shaw's play, with a fine supporting cast: John Gielgud as Warwick, Anton Walbrook as Cauchon, Felix Aylmer as the Inquisitor. Graham Greene cut a play of three and a half hours to under two, and the pressbook claimed nearly all the dialogue was still Shaw's. The trial scenes, where Shaw gives the churchmen real arguments, are the strongest part. Much of the rest was poorly received: critics found Seberg out of her depth, the London Times faulted a scrappy, rearranged first half, and Dennis Schwartz grades it C-minus. Preminger later blamed himself, saying he had treated the play as an intellectual debate about religion instead of a legend.
themes: Shaw admired Joan but built his play on a thesis. His Preface calls her a Protestant martyr and an early apostle of nationalism, as well as a pious Catholic, and in the tent scene Cauchon and Warwick name the threat she poses: private judgment set against the Church. Shaw's churchmen are not villains; Cauchon is sincere and the Inquisitor reasoned. That fairness carries the problem with it, because Joan's sanctity becomes the triumph of the individual conscience over the Church's authority. Greene, a Catholic, shifted the blame from the whole Church to individual judges. Her voices are presented as real to her and left unexplained.
history: Joan of Arc was burned at Rouen in 1431, and Shaw wrote Saint Joan in 1923. Preminger paid Shaw's estate $100,000 for the rights. Shaw had written his own screen version in the 1930s, which Preminger and Greene said they did not know. The film premiered at the Paris Opéra in May 1957.
liberties: The film opens with Shaw's epilogue, played as a dream of Charles VII, and returns to it afterwards. Shaw's anachronisms remain, with talk of Protestantism and nationalism a century before either existed. The film makes no mention of Joan's beatification or canonisation. The trial is heavily compressed.
advisories:
Joan's burning is shown, briefly.

Battle scenes are short and not graphic.

Suitable for teenagers and adults.

Shaw's reading of Joan as a champion of private judgment against the Church runs through the dialogue.

grey.question: Shaw's Joan is a great woman, but his play presents her as a forerunner of Protestantism and nationalism, a private conscience defying the Church, and the film keeps much of that argument. The churchmen are given fair speeches, yet the drama turns Joan's sanctity into a victory of the individual over ecclesiastical authority, which is not why the Church canonised her. Greene's script softens this by blaming individual judges rather than the Church. Viewers who know the history, and the Church's own verdict on Joan in 1456 and 1920, can weigh Shaw's case.

names: Saint Joan, play by George Bernard Shaw (1923)

suitability.note: The dialogue is dense and talky, and the burning and the battle scenes are brief.

doctrine: Shaw makes Joan a Protestant before Luther, answerable to her own voices and not to the Church. The Church teaches the opposite. Private revelation is never of faith and must be tested by the Church. The Church's retrial of 1456 found the Rouen proceedings tainted by deceit and procedural errors and overturned the verdict. Pius X beatified Joan on 18 April 1909 and Benedict XV canonised her on 16 May 1920. The Church's judgment on her visions is therefore a judgment of sanctity, not of rebellion. Her feast is 30 May.
production: United Artists released the British-American film on 8 May 1957; it ran 110 minutes. Preminger tested more than 18,000 girls for the lead and chose the unknown Jean Seberg, who made her film debut. Two reviews in The Times found Greene's condensation made 'some odd omissions, interpolations and additions'. It lost money: the budget was about $1 million and the domestic gross is recorded as only $250,000. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.

title: Saint Joan the Maid
originalTitle: La Merveilleuse Vie de Jeanne d'Arc
alternateTitles: La Merveilleuse Vie de Jeanne d'Arc, fille de Lorraine
The Marvellous Life of Joan of Arc
decision: GREY: Identity is secure (Silent Era; Wikipedia citing Nowell-Smith; Internet Archive copy) and the film's course is known: Joan's life from the first visions at Domrémy in 1428 to her burning at Rouen, made for the fifth centenary of her death after her 1920 canonisation, with Simone Genevois praised for her fervour and purity (BAMPFA 1987 note; Girls with Guns review). No source assesses how it treats her voices, her faith or her judges. Not HOLD, because identity and content are clear. It would move to PUBLISH with a review that addresses the religious content, a 1929 Catholic press notice (La Croix, Centrale Catholique), or a reading of the French intertitles of the Internet Archive copy.
summary: Marco de Gastyne's two-hour French epic of St Joan, shot at Carcassonne, Chinon and Mont-Saint-Michel, with seventeen-year-old Simone Genevois as the Maid.
synopsis: The film follows Joan from 1428, when the shepherd girl first hears her voices at Domrémy, to her death at Rouen in 1431. She goes to the Dauphin Charles (Jean Debucourt) at Chinon, is given command alongside captains such as La Hire and Gilles de Rais, and leads the relief of Orléans, including the assault on the Tourelles. Later she is captured, and at Rouen she is tried by a church court in which the informer Nicolas Loiseleur plays his part. The trial ends in her condemnation. She walks to the stake and is burned, and the film stops abruptly at her death.
inclusion: Gastyne's film was made in 1927–28, in the same years as Dreyer's Passion of Joan of Arc, and was buried by its reputation. The two are opposites: Dreyer confines himself to the trial and the faces; Gastyne gives the whole life, with the castles and towns themselves as settings and thousands of extras for the siege of Orléans, filmed at Carcassonne, and the trial at Mont-Saint-Michel. A 1987 Pacific Film Archive note calls it the more commercial of the two and praises Genevois's youthful fervour, mysterious purity and very human terror. Jim McLennan of Girls with Guns found the trial slow but the battles and the walk to the stake compelling. The Cinémathèque française reconstructed it in the 1980s, and a copy is on the Internet Archive.
themes: The film's frame is Joan's sanctity: it was made for the 500th anniversary of her death, shortly after her canonisation in 1920, and its French title presents her life as marvellous. It begins with her visions and treats her mission as a call from God that she obeys. Reviewers stress her purity and courage rather than any modern psychological reading.

grey.question: This French epic tells the life of St Joan from her first visions to her burning, and reviewers praise Simone Genevois's purity and fervour. No independent review says how it treats the faith itself: how her voices are shown, how the church court and Bishop Cauchon are portrayed, and what is said at the stake. A review addressing these points, a 1929 French Catholic press notice, or a reading of the French intertitles would settle the matter.

history: Joan of Arc (c. 1412–1431) heard her voices at Domrémy, raised the siege of Orléans in 1429 and saw Charles VII crowned at Reims. She was captured in 1430, tried for heresy at Rouen under Bishop Pierre Cauchon and burned on 30 May 1431. She was rehabilitated in 1456.
advisories:
Large-scale battle violence and the siege of Orléans.

Joan's burning at the stake.

title: Under the Sun of Satan
decision: GREY: Identity is secure (Cannes festival record, KVIFF archive, Wikipedia). Independent reviews (Harvard Film Archive, Reeling Reviews, Movies That Make You Think) establish a close adaptation of Bernanos centred on a priest, penance, confession and a personal Devil, and also its open questions: the film leaves the source of Donissan's gifts ambiguous, Mouchette kills herself after his intervention, and the director was an avowed atheist. These are reservations a reader can weigh, not a heterodox thesis. A scene-level French study comparing the dead-child episode with the novel would settle whether Pialat's ambiguity is Bernanos's own (then PUBLISH) or his addition.

grey.question: Pialat follows Bernanos closely: a real, personal Devil, a priest of heroic penance and a battle for a sinner's soul. But the film, made by an avowed atheist, leaves open whether Donissan's power to read souls, and his attempt to raise a dead child, come from God or from Satan's flattery of his pride. A young woman kills herself after he confronts her, and he carries her body into the church. Viewers who know the novel will read it as a Catholic tragedy; others may take it as a study of religious obsession.

summary: Pialat's harsh, Palme d'Or-winning version of Bernanos's first novel: a clumsy, self-scourging country priest meets Satan on a night road and fights for a murderess's soul.
synopsis: Donissan, a young priest of peasant stock, is a poor preacher and an awkward curate under the shrewd, experienced Menou-Segrais, and he punishes himself with a hair shirt and the discipline. Mouchette, a sixteen-year-old in the district, shoots her lover, the Marquis de Cadignan, and his death passes for suicide. Pregnant, she turns to another lover, Dr Gallet, who refuses to help her end the pregnancy. Walking at night to a distant parish, Donissan falls in with a friendly horse-dealer who is Satan; afterwards he finds he can see into souls. He meets Mouchette and urges her to repent. Soon after, she kills herself, and Donissan carries her body into the church, a scandal that gets him sent away. Years later, a priest with a reputation for holiness, he prays over a dead child, whose eyes open. He dies alone in his confessional.
inclusion: Pialat, a professed unbeliever, made one of the most physical films about a priest. Gérard Depardieu's Donissan is a big, clumsy man who scourges himself, walks for miles and cannot preach, and the Harvard Film Archive singles out the vulnerability Depardieu finds in him. Sandrine Bonnaire's Mouchette is fierce and scornful of God. The photography of the Pas-de-Calais is cold and grey, and the supernatural, as the HFA notice puts it, surfaces inside an ordinary realism: the Devil is simply a talkative man on a dark road. The film is also elliptical, hard to follow without the novel, and at times stagey. Pialat said he had, if anything, been too faithful to Bernanos, and the film keeps the novel's core: a war for souls fought by a man who doubts himself.
themes: Bernanos's Catholicism is at its darkest here. Satan is real, personal and patient, and holiness is a combat. Donissan's penances, his gift of reading souls, his long hours in the confessional and his sense of being a mere zero beside other numbers all come from the novel. So does the ambiguity, and that is the difficulty. The film never settles whether his gift comes from God or from the Devil who has marked him, and his prayer over the dead child can be read as spiritual pride. Mouchette's suicide follows his intervention. Some reviewers, quoting Richard Brody, read the whole as a nonbeliever's study of religion's psychological power; the Catholic reading is equally open.
advisories:
A teenage girl's affairs with two older men are discussed frankly, and she seeks an abortion and is refused.

A shooting, a suicide, and the priest carrying the dead body.

Self-flagellation and other bodily penance.

The Devil appears in human form and kisses the priest.

For adults.

The film leaves open whether the priest's gifts come from God or from Satan.

names: Sous le soleil de Satan, novel by Georges Bernanos (1926)

suitability.note: Dark and oppressive, and its meaning depends on an adult grasp of sin and grace.

doctrine: Bernanos writes from the Church's teaching that the devil is a real, personal fallen angel who tempts men, as the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) and the Roman Catechism state. The priest's penances, the hair shirt and the discipline, belong to the Church's tradition of mortification, and his gift of reading hearts (cardiognosis) is a recognised charism of saints such as the Curé d'Ars, on whom Bernanos modelled Donissan. The Church teaches that such gifts and wonders are not proof of holiness, and that a priest must test them against pride. Under the 1917 Code (canon 1240) a person who deliberately killed himself was refused ecclesiastical burial, unless proved insane, which explains the scandal when Donissan carries Mouchette into the church. Despair is a sin against hope, and the confessional is the place of mercy.
production: Georges Bernanos published his first novel in 1926. Filming began on 20 October 1986 at Fressin and Montreuil-sur-Mer in Pas-de-Calais. Pialat himself plays the Canon Menou-Segrais. The film premiered at Cannes on 14 May 1987 and was met with boos and whistles, then won the Palme d'Or unanimously, the first French winner in 21 years. Mitterrand congratulated Pialat. It was nominated for César awards including best film and director, and opened in France on 2 September 1987, drawing 815,748 admissions.

title: The 26 Martyrs of Japan
decision: PUBLISH: Goffredo Fofi's review (Il Sole 24 Ore, 2017, summarised in the Cinema Ritrovato note) is an independent, substantive treatment: he praises the film's skill and its respectful view from inside Japanese culture and its Christian community, and contrasts its decency with later propaganda. The film depicts the 1597 Nagasaki martyrdom faithfully in four chapters ending with the crucifixions. The martyrs were beatified in 1627 and canonised in 1862, so no hard rule applies. Made with Catholic help and co-written by a Jesuit, Fr Hermann Heuvers; Japanese Catholic hierarchy received it well (contemporary Catholic press cited by Wikipedia).
summary: A Nikkatsu silent epic, made by Japanese Catholics in 1931, of the Franciscans, Jesuits and Japanese tertiaries crucified at Nagasaki in 1597.
synopsis: The Spanish Franciscan Pedro Bautista preaches in the Kyoto region, where a Christian community grows among ordinary Japanese, many of them members of the Franciscan Third Order. When a Spanish ship, the San Felipe, is wrecked on the coast, suspicion grows that the missionaries are the vanguard of conquest, and the ruler Toyotomi Hideyoshi orders a persecution. Missionaries and laymen are arrested, among them a child and a converted thief who becomes the first victim. The film, told in four chapters that follow the phases of the mission, ends on a beach at Nagasaki, where the twenty-six are crucified and run through with lances. An epilogue recalls their canonisation at the Vatican in 1862.
inclusion: This is a major Japanese studio film about the Japanese martyrs, made in the last years of silent cinema by people who shared their faith. The Jesuit Hermann Heuvers co-wrote the script. Goffredo Fofi, reviewing the 2017 restoration, praises Ikeda's command of late silent technique, the way the drama and documentary-style passages support each other, and the respect with which it shows Japanese life from inside its Christian community. He faults it for not exploring the political motives behind the persecution. The surviving version, found among Salesian holdings and restored in 4K in Turin, runs about 65 minutes.
themes: The victims include European friars and Jesuits, but most are Japanese lay tertiaries, and a child among them is given particular attention, so the faith appears as fully Japanese. A thief converted by the missionaries is the first to die. The ending reproduces the crucifixion at Nagasaki, deliberately echoing Calvary. Fofi notes the film's decency and restraint. Its makers intended it partly as a defence of Japanese Catholics, honoured by Rome, against suspicion at home.
history: On 5 February 1597, twenty-six Christians were crucified on a hill above Nagasaki on the order of Toyotomi Hideyoshi. They were six Franciscan missionaries, including Peter Baptist, three Japanese Jesuits, among them Paul Miki, and seventeen Japanese laymen, most of them members of the Franciscan Third Order. The youngest, Louis Ibaraki, was a boy of about twelve. Hideyoshi had issued an edict against the missionaries in 1587 and was provoked afresh by the wreck of the Spanish ship San Felipe off Shikoku in October 1596, when the pilot was reported to have spoken of conquest following the missionaries. The prisoners were marched in winter from Kyoto to Nagasaki, with part of an ear cut from each. Pius IX canonised them on 8 June 1862. Their feast is 6 February.
liberties: Only about 65 minutes survive of a film originally around 150 minutes long, so the restored version compresses the story. The film's account of the San Felipe affair and Hideyoshi's motives is simplified, as Fofi notes. The converted thief's role reflects the film's dramatisation rather than any established detail of the martyrs' lives.
advisories:
The crucifixion of the martyrs, with lances; the death of a child.

Scenes of arrest and persecution.

Silent, with Japanese intertitles (the restoration is subtitled).

suitability.note: The crucifixions are handled in a restrained silent style, but the film is slow, so it suits older children who can read subtitles and want the story.

doctrine: The Church counts as martyrs those killed out of hatred for the Faith, and the 1597 victims were canonised by Pius IX, with the usual process of beatification first (Urban VIII had beatified them in 1627). A martyr dies for the Faith and forgives his killers; the Roman Catechism, treating the Creed's article on the communion of saints, teaches that the saints in heaven may be invoked, for they pray for us. Tertullian's saying that the blood of martyrs is the seed of Christians was borne out: the Japanese Christians went underground and kept the Faith for over two centuries without priests, until they were found at Nagasaki in 1865. Third Order membership, shown in the film, is the lay association of Franciscan tertiaries, approved by the Holy See.
production: Nikkatsu made the film in 1931 for Seiju Hirayama, a Catholic landowner who invested a large part of his own fortune in it. The budget was reported at 300,000 yen. Tomiyasu Ikeda directed, after a book by Aimé Villion. The original ran about 152 minutes. It was generally well received by film critics and the Japanese Catholic hierarchy. Hirayama toured the United States with it despite racist opposition, and it was also shown in Europe.

title: The Cardinal
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a priest's vocation; Church teaching on mixed marriage and on the unborn child). Legion of Decency A-III (Motion Picture Exhibitor Legion tables, 1963–64); contemporary reviews (Exhibitor; James Daane in Christianity Today; Crowther and Crist via TCM and Varden). The English subtitle file shows the closing speech is anti-totalitarian Americanism ('That is America's creed. That is the Gospel of the Church') ending in a prayer 'for the liberty and exaltation of our church', not a case for conciliar religious liberty; the Vienna section defends the Church's rights over family and schools against the Nazis; the Georgia section is about a segregated Catholic school and a church burned by the Klan, with no interracial marriage. The one line to state is the hero's unqualified answer to a parish class that anyone following conscience can reach heaven. Not REJECT: the film's thesis is not the post-conciliar programme. Joseph Ratzinger's role as Vatican liaison is a fact only.
summary: Preminger's three-hour saga of an Irish-American priest's rise from Boston curate to cardinal, through family tragedy, the Klan and the Anschluss: sincere, handsome and uneven.
synopsis: In 1939 Stephen Fermoyle is created a cardinal in Rome, and his life returns in flashback. Newly ordained in 1917, he comes home to Boston, where his sister Mona wants to marry a Jewish man who will not promise to raise their children Catholic. Stephen advises her to give him up, and she leaves home and goes astray. Sent to a poor country parish under the dying Father Halley, he learns humility. When Mona, pregnant out of wedlock, is in a fatal labour, the doctor says only killing the child can save her; Stephen refuses, and she dies. Shaken, he takes leave in Vienna, where a young woman, Annemarie, falls in love with him; he keeps his vows. Back in service, he confronts the Klan in Georgia, becomes a bishop and confronts Cardinal Innitzer over the Nazis.
inclusion: It is one of the few big Hollywood films to take a priest's whole career seriously, and it was shot on location, including Santa Maria sopra Minerva in Rome and St Stephen's Cathedral in Vienna. John Huston as the shrewd Cardinal Glennon and Burgess Meredith as the dying country priest are excellent. Tom Tryon is the weak point. Bosley Crowther called his priest a callow cliché, and Judith Crist found the whole a mélange of melodrama and mouthed pieties, while Motion Picture Exhibitor called it provocative and dignified. Bishop Erik Varden, watching it sixty years later, is struck that a mainstream film could show the Church as a source of moral authority.
themes: The film takes Catholic teaching seriously enough to dramatise its cost. Stephen tells his sister plainly what a mixed marriage requires and that a civil wedding would be no marriage, and in the childbirth scene he refuses to let her child be killed to save her. He takes leave from the priesthood but keeps his vows. Two passages trouble. He tells a parish class that anyone who does God's will according to conscience can reach heaven, and a boy's 'Then what's the use of being Catholic?' goes unanswered. The closing speech calls 'life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness' both America's creed and the Gospel of the Church, the confusion Leo XIII warned against in 1899, though it ends with a prayer for the liberty and exaltation of the Church.
history: The film's Archbishop of Vienna, Cardinal Theodor Innitzer (1875-1955), was real. He became a cardinal in 1933. After the German annexation of Austria in March 1938 he and the Austrian bishops signed a declaration on 18 March welcoming the change, with his own hand adding 'Heil Hitler'. Rome rebuked him, and Pius XI summoned him to the Vatican in April 1938. After he preached on the Rosary at the Cathedral of St Stephen, the Hitler Youth attacked the archbishop's palace on 8 October 1938. Pius XI had condemned National Socialism's racial doctrines in Mit brennender Sorge (1937). Stephen Fermoyle is fictional; the novel is thought to have drawn on Cardinal Spellman.
liberties: Fermoyle is fictional. The Vienna episode built around Innitzer and the Nazis was Preminger's most significant addition to the novel. The Georgia episode with the Klan and a Black priest is freely dramatised.
advisories:
A woman's death in childbirth after a refusal to kill the child; the dilemma is explicit.

A young woman's promiscuity and an out-of-wedlock pregnancy, implied rather than shown.

A priest is beaten by the Klan; a suicide; Nazi violence.

For adults and older teenagers.

A loose statement on the salvation of non-Catholics goes unqualified, and the closing speech equates American liberty with the Gospel.

grey.question: The Cardinal upholds Catholic teaching at its hardest points: its hero refuses to let his sister's unborn child be killed, and keeps his vows when a woman falls in love with him. But it presents those rules as costly and doubtful and the Church as rigid. The hero tells children that anyone who follows his conscience can be saved, without the qualifications the Church attached, and the film ends on a speech calling the American creed the Gospel of the Church. Viewers can admire its seriousness while asking whose side it is really on.

names: The Cardinal, novel by Henry Morton Robinson (1950)

suitability.note: The Legion of Decency rated it A-III, and the film runs nearly three hours.

doctrine: Several questions are decided by the pre-conciliar Church. Mixed marriage: the 1917 Code (canon 1060) forbade a Catholic to marry a non-Catholic without dispensation, and canon 1061 required guarantees that all the children be baptised and raised Catholic; Mona's fiance refuses these. The Fermoyle birth scene follows the teaching of the Holy Office and Pius XI's Casti Connubii (1930): the direct killing of the unborn child to save the mother, including craniotomy, is never lawful; the Holy Office condemned it in 1884 and 1889. The film's remark that non-Catholics can be saved is incomplete: the Church teaches that outside her there is no salvation (Unam Sanctam, 1302; Florence, 1442), with the qualification that those in invincible ignorance may be saved by the grace of God (Pius IX, 1863). A priest's celibacy is a discipline of the Latin Church; Stephen's keeping his vows in Vienna is simply fidelity.
production: Preminger made it for Columbia through Gamma Productions, from Henry Morton Robinson's 1950 novel, with uncredited screenplay work by Ring Lardner Jr. It was shot in Rome, Vienna, Boston and Stamford, Connecticut. Saul Bass designed the titles and poster. It premiered in Boston on 12 December 1963, opened in the United States on 23 December, and ran 175 minutes. It was among the first films shown in 70 mm via blow-up from 35 mm. Its US rentals were about $5.5 million. It had six Academy Award nominations and won none, though it won two Golden Globes (Best Drama and John Huston as Best Supporting Actor).

title: The Greatest Story Ever Told
decision: GREY: AFI (identity, production) and Steven Greydanus (B+, +3, a substantive review) establish a reverent, Christ-centred film released in February 1965, before the Council closed; its non-denominational production does not put it out of scope because Christ, the Eucharist and the Resurrection are central and nothing contradicts Catholic teaching outright. The reservation is the Gospel revisionism Greydanus flags: Judas half-excused and given an invented death, Lazarus merged with the rich young man. This is a milder form of the Judas problem in Jesus of Nazareth, without that film's Nostra Aetate framing. The Legion of Decency classed it A-I (Motion Picture Exhibitor, 1965); it stays GREY because the reservation concerns the Gospel changes, which that rating does not address.

grey.question: Stevens's film is reverent, and it plainly presents Christ as the divine Word who works miracles, institutes the Eucharist, dies, rises and ascends. It departs from the Gospels in ways that matter. Judas becomes a half-sympathetic figure and dies by walking into a Temple fire rather than by hanging; Lazarus is merged with the rich young man; Satan appears as an invented hermit. Greydanus counts the Judas change the most damaging. Viewers who know the Gospel text will notice and can correct these changes; younger viewers should be told.

summary: George Stevens's slow, reverent, star-crowded Life of Christ, from the Nativity to the Ascension, with Max von Sydow as a grave and sovereign Jesus.
synopsis: The Magi follow the star to Bethlehem; Herod the Great orders the massacre of the infants, and the Holy Family flees to Egypt. Years later John the Baptist preaches at the Jordan and baptises Jesus, who goes into the wilderness and is tempted by a sinister hermit. Jesus calls the Twelve, teaches, heals and raises Lazarus, which alarms Caiaphas and Herod Antipas. He enters Jerusalem and eats the Last Supper with His disciples, instituting the Eucharist and foretelling Judas's betrayal and Peter's denials. Judas hands Him over in Gethsemane for thirty pieces of silver. He is tried before the Sanhedrin, Pilate and Herod, scourged and crucified, with Simon of Cyrene carrying His cross. Judas throws himself into a Temple fire. Jesus rises, appears to Mary Magdalene and the disciples, convinces Thomas, and sends them out to all nations.
inclusion: Stevens spent years on the film, and it shows both ways. The images are its strength: shot in the American Southwest, the canyons stand in for an empty, monumental Holy Land, and many compositions look like devotional paintings. Alfred Newman's score is lush, and the raising of Lazarus, cut to Handel's Hallelujah Chorus, is the sequence Greydanus rates highest. Max von Sydow plays Christ as the sovereign Lord of St John's Gospel; Greydanus finds him persuasively authoritative, if not warm. The faults are well known. The pace is stately to the point of torpor, the star cameos distract, and Charlton Heston's Baptist is overblown. Time called it impeccable boredom; Greydanus still ranks it above most Hollywood Bible epics for its prayerful spirit. Watch a long version: the 1967 general release lost more than an hour.
themes: Christ's divinity is never in doubt. The film opens on the prologue of St John and presents Him as the eternal Word, who forgives sins, works miracles, institutes the Eucharist at the Last Supper, dies, rises and gives the Great Commission. Dorothy McGuire's Mary is reverent. Judas is made an almost sympathetic figure, and Greydanus calls his death in the Temple fire the departure that hurts most. Beyond what the Gospels give, there is nothing distinctly Catholic, and nothing anti-Catholic either.
history: Twentieth Century-Fox bought Fulton Oursler's 1949 bestseller in 1954; Stevens took the project to United Artists, consulted dozens of Bible translations and sought the advice of Pope John XXIII. John E. Fitzgerald of Our Sunday Visitor advised on the script.
liberties: Judas dies by throwing himself into the Temple's sacrificial fire, not by hanging (Matthew 27:5). Lazarus is merged with the rich young man. Satan is an invented 'Dark Hermit'. The four Gospels are blended freely, the Holy Land is the American Southwest, and dialogue sometimes slips into flat modern idiom.
advisories:
The scourging and crucifixion are restrained, as Greydanus says.

No sexual content or bad language.

Suitable for all ages, though the length (about 3 hours 20 minutes in the usual restored version) and pace will tax children.

Judas's motive and death are changed from the Gospel account.

suitability.note: The main difficulty is length, about three hours twenty in the usual restored version, and the slow pace will tax children.

doctrine: The Last Supper is the centre of the film's doctrine. The Council of Trent (Session 13) defined that at the words of consecration Christ is truly, really and substantially present, and that He instituted the priesthood at the same Supper (Session 22, can. 2). The film shows Peter's denials and Christ's words to him; the Church reads Matthew 16:18-19 and John 21:15-17 as the grant of primacy to Peter, which the Vatican Council defined in 1870. Judas's death is told differently in the Gospels: Matthew 27:5 says he hanged himself and Acts 1:18 that he fell and burst open. Mary's perpetual virginity and the Immaculate Conception, defined in 1854, are not shown.
production: George Stevens shot in the American Southwest, at Utah sites including Lake Powell, Canyonlands, Dead Horse Point and Lake Moab. Principal photography ran from 29 October 1962 to 1 August 1963. The cinematographer William C. Mellor died during the shoot and Loyal Griggs replaced him; David Lean directed second-unit scenes with Claude Rains as Herod, and Jean Negulesco filmed the Jerusalem street and Nativity sequences. The budget was about $20 million, the most expensive film shot in the United States to that time. The original cut ran about 260 minutes. The New York premiere at the Warner Cinerama Theatre on 15 February 1965 ran 221 to 225 minutes, and the general release 137 to 141. It earned about $15.5 million and lost money. Bosley Crowther called it the 'world's most conglomerate Biblical picture'. It had five Oscar nominations and no wins. Stevens replaced Alfred Newman's choral finales with Handel's Hallelujah Chorus, which critics ridiculed.

title: The Hoodlum Priest
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a Jesuit's apostolate to ex-convicts; the good-thief theme). Strong pre-1965 Catholic recognition: the International Catholic Office for the Cinema award at Cannes 1961 (AFI); Cardinal Ritter attended the premiere (TCM). Reservations: the film argues against capital punishment, and the real Fr Clark repudiated it (TCM; Motion Picture Exhibitor reports the Globe-Democrat controversy). Legion rating not found (OCR gap). Would be PUBLISH if the editor treats the anti-death-penalty thrust as a tolerable prudential view.
summary: Don Murray plays the real Jesuit Fr Charles Dismas Clark, who works with ex-convicts in St Louis and walks a young killer to the gas chamber.
synopsis: St Louis, around 1960. Fr Charles Clark, a Jesuit known on the streets as the Hoodlum Priest, works with delinquents and men out of prison, speaking their language and finding them work. He takes on Billy Lee Jackson, a young thief just released from the state penitentiary, clears him of a false charge and gets him a job at a produce market, where Billy falls for a girl from a wealthy family. With the help of a criminal lawyer, Louis Rosen, Clark raises money to open a halfway house for ex-convicts. Then Billy is fired for a theft he did not commit, and in a botched robbery he kills a man. Clark persuades him to surrender. Billy is sentenced to death, and before the gas chamber Clark tells him about Dismas, the good thief promised Paradise.
inclusion: It is a sober, unsentimental film about a working priest, made cheaply on location, including Dismas House and the Missouri State Penitentiary, and shot in hard black and white by Haskell Wexler. Don Murray plays Clark as tough and quick rather than saintly, and Keir Dullea, in his first film, is affecting as Billy. A. H. Weiler in the New York Times praised its authentic look and pace. It competed at Cannes in 1961, where it received the award of the International Catholic Office for the Cinema, and the National Board of Review named it one of the year's ten best. The second half becomes an argument against the death penalty, and the execution is long and harrowing.
themes: The film shows a priest's apostolate among the lost, and its Catholic substance is concrete: a Jesuit meeting criminals on their own ground, finding them work and a roof, and staying with them when they fail. The centre is the last night of Billy's life. Clark cannot save his life, so he works to save his soul, and the spiritual climax is the story of Dismas, the thief who repented on the cross and was promised Paradise. That is sound. The film's other aim, to show the gas chamber as an atrocity, sits uneasily with the Church's traditional teaching.
history: Charles Dismas Clark, a Jesuit of the Missouri province, worked in St Louis with convicts and ex-convicts from the 1940s. He took his second name from Dismas, the Good Thief of Luke 23:39-43. He opened Dismas House, a halfway house for men released from prison, in St Louis in 1959, and died in 1963.
liberties: Billy Lee Jackson and his story are fiction built around Clark's work. The St Louis Globe-Democrat disputed the film's truthfulness at its premiere, and Clark himself later repudiated it for reasons he did not make public.
advisories:
A killing in a robbery and a long, distressing execution in the gas chamber.

A criminal milieu, drinking and rough language for its period.

The film argues against the death penalty.

grey.question: The Hoodlum Priest is sound on what matters most: a Jesuit's care for criminals, and his effort to bring a condemned man to repentance through the example of the good thief. But it is also a case against capital punishment, built on a sympathetic young offender and a drawn-out gas-chamber scene, whereas the Church's traditional teaching upheld the State's right to execute murderers. Fr Clark himself repudiated the film after its premiere. Viewers can take its portrait of a priest while weighing its thesis.

doctrine: Dismas, promised Paradise on the cross (Luke 23:43), is the traditional patron of the condemned, and the visit to prisoners is a corporal work of mercy (Matthew 25:36). The film's argument against the death penalty is not the Church's teaching. The Roman Catechism, in its commentary on the Fifth Commandment, says the lawful use of capital punishment by the civil power is not forbidden but is an act of obedience to that Commandment. What the Church does ask is that a condemned man be given the sacraments and a chance to repent, which is what Clark offers Billy. The Jesuit's tactics, such as speaking the criminals' language, stand in a tradition of missionary adaptation, but the film puts the priest's social work ahead of his sacramental role.
production: Don Murray, who played Clark, co-wrote the script under the name Don Deer and co-produced through Murray-Wood Productions with Walter Wood. Irvin Kershner directed, and the film was shot largely on location in St Louis. United Artists released it on 26 March 1961 at about 101 minutes. It grossed about $1.3 million. Weiler of the New York Times also called it an unrelievedly grim, serious case against harsh attitudes to ex-convicts and capital punishment.

title: The Life and Passion of Jesus Christ
originalTitle: La Vie et la passion de Jésus-Christ
decision: PUBLISH: Steven Greydanus's detailed review (A+, moral/spiritual +4, Kids & Up) establishes a reverent tableau Life of Christ from the Annunciation to the Ascension, drawing on Catholic tradition (Veronica's veil, St Michael in the flight to Egypt) with no doctrinal objection. Silent Era's independent DVD review confirms the surviving 44-minute Pathécolor print. Its place on the 1995 Vatican list is recorded as a fact only.
summary: Pathé's hand-coloured tableau Gospel, staged after Doré, runs from the Annunciation to the Ascension in short scenes that work like a moving set of holy pictures.
synopsis: The film is a chain of short scenes, each announced by a title card naming the event, as in a book of devotional pictures. It opens with the Annunciation and the Nativity, where shepherds and Magi gather at the manger, then follows the flight into Egypt, in which St Michael hides the Holy Family from Herod's soldiers. Episodes from the public life follow, among them a miraculous catch of fish combined with Christ walking on the water. The Passion follows, staged in the same pageant manner, including the way of the cross, where Veronica wipes Christ's face and finds his image on the cloth, and the Crucifixion. The film closes with the Resurrection and an Ascension in which Christ is seated at the Father's right hand, with the Holy Spirit, among saints and angels.
inclusion: One of the first long films ever made, it was built and rebuilt by Pathé between 1902 and 1905 until it ran about three-quarters of an hour, at a time when most films lasted a few minutes. The staging is frankly theatrical, with painted backdrops, a static camera and broad gestures. Steven D. Greydanus argues that this stiffness works like the stylisation of an icon, and the Pathécolor stencil tinting, applied by hand to single objects in each frame, still gives some tableaux the look of coloured prints. There are no dialogue titles, so it assumes the viewer knows the Gospel; Greydanus found it among the most accessible Jesus films for small children. The surviving print, preserved by Haghefilm and Lobster Films, is clean and complete enough to be watched as a whole.
themes: The film follows the shape of Catholic devotion more than any single Gospel. It harmonises the evangelists and adds traditional material: Veronica's veil, the archangel guarding the Holy Family, and a Nativity in which Christ appears in the manger, an image Greydanus links to the patristic figure of light passing through glass. Mary is present throughout, from the Annunciation to Calvary. The ending goes on to the Resurrection and Ascension instead of stopping at the tomb. Greydanus contrasts it with the more literal From the Manger to the Cross and prefers this pageant.
history: Pathé first released a Passion film in 1902 under Ferdinand Zecca and kept revising it. Greydanus dates the completed form to 1905, after Lucien Nonguet added the final scenes. Pathé made an entirely new version in 1907.
advisories:
Mild, stylised depiction of the scourging and Crucifixion.

Silent, with title cards that name each scene but carry no dialogue; viewers need to know the Gospel story.

Suitable for children.

suitability.note: Children who know the Gospel will follow it, and at 44 minutes it is short enough to hold them.

doctrine: Several things in the film come from Catholic tradition and are not in the Gospel text. Veronica wiping Christ's face on the way of the cross is the sixth Station, a pious tradition outside Scripture. The closing Ascension, with Christ seated at the right hand of the Father, follows the Creed ('he ascended into heaven, and sitteth at the right hand of God'). The Council of Trent (Session 25) taught that images of Christ and the saints may be kept and honoured, because the honour passes to the person shown.
production: Pathé Frères made the film in Paris. Many scenes copy Gustave Doré's Bible illustrations. Pathé revised the film several times, which is why dates and running times differ between sources. Wikipedia gives a May 1903 French release for the expanded version; it opened in the United States in June. A 1932 US reissue was printed on red-tinted stock with a new score by James C. Bradford. Historians often call it the first feature-length narrative film, though others dispute this because it was issued in separate parts. The Vatican's 1995 list of important films included it, as the oldest title under 'Religion'.
