title: The Miracle of Father Malachia
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a monk's answered prayer and the world's response). Independent treatment from the Harvard Film Archive and the Zeughauskino programme (Ralf Schenk); Silver Bear for direction, Berlin 1961. Reservation: the satire extends to the hierarchy and to a religious order, and no pre-1965 Catholic rating (Film-Dienst, Legion) was found to judge its fairness. The Film-Dienst 1961 review or subtitles of the clergy scenes would settle it.
summary: Bernhard Wicki's satire from Bruce Marshall's novel: a simple monk's prayer removes a nightclub from beside his church, and the boom-town world turns the miracle into business.
synopsis: In a prosperous industrial town in the Ruhr, the Eden Bar, a dance club with a bad name, stands opposite a church. Father Malachias, a simple and unworldly monk, prays that it be taken away, and overnight the building and everyone in it vanish and reappear on a rocky island in the North Sea. Journalists, politicians and scientists look for explanations, and the Church is slow to call it a miracle. The empty plot becomes a fairground where traders sell holy water and souvenir models of the bar; a girl who was inside becomes a celebrity; investors build a casino on the island, which turns into a club for the rich. Dismayed by what his miracle has caused, Malachias prays again, and the Eden Bar returns to its old place.
inclusion: Wicki, fresh from The Bridge, made this as a broad satire of West Germany's economic miracle, plainly influenced by La Dolce Vita. Introducing it at the Zeughauskino in 2012, Ralf Schenk described it as a dance round the golden calf in which nearly everyone takes part, from waitress to tycoon, and called it still relevant. The Harvard Film Archive notes how unusual it is among West German films in daring to show God acting. Horst Bollmann's Malachias is the one calm figure in a crowded, episodic and often frantic film, which ends in a long party sequence.
themes: The film takes its miracle seriously. Malachias's prayer is answered, and the satire is aimed at the world's response to the sign. Its Catholic heart is the monk's simple faith, which the film never mocks. How it treats the Church itself is the question. The hierarchy is slow to recognise the miracle for fear of losing control or being embarrassed, and the satire is said to reach the upper levels of a religious order. That could be fair comment on worldly churchmen or a jibe at the Church's proper caution about miracles, and the film does not settle which.
history: Bruce Marshall (1899–1987) was born in Edinburgh and received into the Catholic Church in 1917. Father Malachy's Miracle, his comic novel of a monk whose prayer moves a dance hall, appeared in 1931. Brian Doherty adapted it for the stage in the late 1930s, and American television presented it in 1950. Wicki and Heinz Pauck moved the story to West Germany during the economic boom of the 1950s, the 'miracle on the Rhine'.
advisories:
A nightclub and striptease milieu; sensuality is implied rather than explicit.

For older teenagers and adults.

Versions of 88, 122 and 126 minutes are recorded.

grey.question: The Miracle of Father Malachia believes in its miracle and loves its monk; its scorn is for a materialist society that can only sell what God has done. The satire also reaches the Church. The hierarchy is shown as reluctant to admit the miracle for fear of losing face, and commentators speak of corruption reaching the upper levels of a religious order. Viewers must decide whether the portrait of churchmen is fair satire or mockery.

names: Father Malachy's Miracle, novel by Bruce Marshall (1931)

suitability.note: The German film service Filmdienst and the German censors both recommend it from 16. The party and the satire of sex, money and churchmen are aimed at adults, though nothing is explicit.

doctrine: The film's premise is orthodox. The Vatican Council (Dei Filius, 24 April 1870) anathematised anyone who says miracles are impossible or can never be known with certainty, and taught that miracles are 'the most certain signs of revelation'. The Catholic Encyclopedia gives their primary ends as the glory of God and the good of men; the secondary ends include attesting the holiness of God's servants. It also notes that the faithful are not obliged to accept every alleged miracle and that testimony must be carefully examined, so a bishop's caution is in itself proper. The trade in 'miracle water' and souvenirs touches simony: the Catholic Encyclopedia defines it as buying or selling for a temporal price things spiritual or annexed to them, counts sacramentals among spiritual things, and notes that Church law forbade the sale of blessed rosaries and crucifixes.
production: Shooting ran from 10 October 1960 to the end of January 1961 at the Berlin-Tempelhof and Göttingen studios, with outdoor shoots in northern and western German cities and on Sylt; many central scenes were shot in Gelsenkirchen, where local residents appeared as extras. Horst Bollmann was a stage actor; Loriot has a small role. It premiered in Berlin on 3 July 1961, where Wicki won the Silver Bear for direction. It also won a Bambi, German film awards (gold for Richard Münch and for production design, silver for best film) and a prize at Valladolid in 1963. The Filmdienst review finds the satire of only limited success, overloaded with ideas and gags.

title: The Nativity Story
decision: GREY: Identity (Danish Film Institute, Wikipedia) and content (Greydanus B+, used for content only; Jeffrey Overstreet in Christianity Today, independent of Catholic outlets) are established. The reservation is doctrinal: Mary is shown in labour pain (Fr John Zuhlsdorf; Br André Marie), contrary to the Roman Catechism's teaching that she gave birth without pain, and the specifically Marian texts are trimmed. Not REJECT because the film affirms the virginal conception and does not argue error as a thesis; the editor may judge the birth scene grave enough to REJECT. The English subtitle file confirms the pain in dialogue: Joseph begs for shelter because 'my wife, she's in pain' (01:17:08), Mary calls out for him (01:17:27), and a cry is heard in the stable (01:19:37). It also shows that Mary does answer the angel 'Let it be done to me, according to your word' (00:21:43), so the earlier note that her answer is dropped is corrected.
summary: Catherine Hardwicke's sober, earthy telling of the Annunciation, Joseph's trial and the birth at Bethlehem, carried by Oscar Isaac's Joseph and marred by a labouring Mary.
synopsis: In Nazareth the teenage Mary is betrothed by her parents, Joachim and Anna, to the carpenter Joseph, a match she accepts without enthusiasm. The angel Gabriel tells her she will bear the Son of God, and she goes to her kinswoman Elizabeth, who is expecting John. Mary returns pregnant to a village that suspects the worst, and Joseph is in anguish until a dream tells him to take her as his wife. A census sends them on a hard journey to Bethlehem, while three Magi follow a star from the East and Herod grows uneasy. There is no room in Bethlehem, and Mary gives birth in a stable, where shepherds and the Magi come to worship. Warned in a dream, Joseph takes the family to Egypt before Herod's soldiers reach the town.
inclusion: Most screen Nativities are pageants. Hardwicke shot this one as rural life in first-century Palestine, with mud-brick villages, hard labour, Roman soldiers and Middle-Eastern accents; Steven D. Greydanus notes it may have the least Caucasian cast in the history of Hollywood Bible films. Its best asset is Oscar Isaac's Joseph, whom Jeffrey Overstreet in Christianity Today calls a detailed portrait of a virtuous man accepting enormous responsibility. Mychael Danna's score draws on 'O Come, O Come, Emmanuel'. Overstreet finds Keisha Castle-Hughes's Mary flat. The comic Magi jar, and the birth itself passes quickly in a stable that looks like a greeting card. A. O. Scott in the New York Times found an interesting film buried in the pageantry, while most critics were unimpressed.
themes: The film follows the Gospel infancy narratives closely, and Greydanus finds its faults mostly of omission. Gabriel greets Mary as 'favoured one' instead of 'full of grace'; she answers 'Let it be done to me according to your word', though not as the Lord's handmaid; the Magnificat is a short voice-over at the end. The virginal conception is plain: Mary has been with no man, and Joseph, having resolved not to accuse her, learns in a dream that the child is of the Holy Spirit. Her perpetual virginity is neither affirmed nor denied. The serious problem is the birth. Joseph begs for shelter because she is in pain, and she cries out in the stable.
liberties: Mary is drawn as an ordinary, at first reluctant teenager, a characterisation meant to make her accessible to young viewers. Joseph is young. Elizabeth's labour and John's birth are shown. The Magi are played partly for comedy, and Herod's consultation with the scribes over Micah's prophecy is omitted.
advisories:
Two brief childbirth scenes, not graphic but intense: Elizabeth's and Mary's.

The massacre of the innocents is mostly implied; a Jewish girl is taken from her parents by Roman soldiers.

Rated PG in the United States; suitable for families.

grey.question: The Nativity Story is reverent and close to the Gospels, but it shows Our Lady in labour pain at Bethlehem. Joseph begs for shelter because she is in pain, and she cries out in the stable. The Roman Catechism teaches that she gave birth without pain, a virgin in giving birth as before and after, and traditional Catholic critics objected when the film opened. The script also thins out what is specifically Marian, with no 'full of grace', no 'handmaid of the Lord' and a shortened Magnificat. Viewers can weigh whether these are tolerable simplifications or a Protestant reading of Mary.

history: The Gospels of Matthew and Luke give the accounts of the birth of Christ. Herod the Great ruled Judaea as Rome's client king until his death in 4 BC, so Christ was born before that date. Luke ties the journey to Bethlehem to a census under Augustus. Matthew records the visit of the Magi, Herod's order to kill the infants of Bethlehem and the flight into Egypt. The Gospels do not state the number or names of the Magi, nor Mary's age, nor the names of her parents. The names Joachim and Anna come from the apocryphal Protoevangelium of James, which the Church has never put on a level with Scripture.

suitability.note: Families can watch it, with one caution: the birth of Christ is shown with pain, against traditional teaching.

doctrine: The Council of Ephesus (431) defined Mary as Theotokos, Mother of God. The Church holds that she conceived by the Holy Ghost without a human father, as St Luke (1:26-38) and St Matthew (1:18-25) say, and that she remained a virgin before, in and after the birth. The Lateran Council of 649 taught her perpetual virginity. The Roman Catechism (1566) teaches that Christ was born without injury to her virginity and without pain to her, which the film's labour contradicts. Pius IX defined her Immaculate Conception in 1854 (Ineffabilis Deus). Joseph was her true husband, though not Christ's father, and in Jewish law betrothal was already a marriage bond. The Magi are honoured at Epiphany (6 January) and the Holy Innocents on 28 December.
production: New Line Cinema made the film on a reported budget of $35 million. It was shot in Matera and Craco in southern Italy, at Cinecittà in Rome, and in Ouarzazate in Morocco. It was the first film to have a world premiere in Vatican City, on 26 November 2006. It opened in the US on 1 December 2006. Critics were divided, with Rotten Tomatoes listing 37 per cent approval. It earned about $46 million worldwide, which was a disappointment.

title: The Prisoner
decision: PUBLISH: Catholic-centred (a cardinal's faith under communist interrogation). Pre-1965 Catholic judgments are favourable: Grand Prize of the International Catholic Office for the Cinema 1956 (AFI, citing the NYT of 12 July 1956), commendation by Cardinal Griffin (Wikipedia), Legion of Decency A-II. Independent treatment from the Monthly Film Bulletin and NYT (via Wikipedia) and Roger Moore (2023). The open question about the cardinal's motives is disclosed.
summary: Alec Guinness plays a cardinal in a communist state whose interrogator breaks him without torture, by turning his own humility against him.
synopsis: In an unnamed country of eastern Europe after the war, the government arrests its popular cardinal for treason. He resisted the Nazis and survived their torture, so his interrogator, a former comrade from the Resistance now loyal to the party, avoids physical violence. Forged evidence fails, and the interrogator turns to sleeplessness, solitary confinement and the disruption of every routine, searching the cardinal's past for a weakness. He finds it in his poor childhood, and in his fear that he became a priest out of vanity and a wish to escape it. Broken, the cardinal confesses at a show trial to everything he is charged with. His sentence is commuted so that he cannot become a martyr, and he walks out into a silent crowd. A subplot follows a young guard and a married woman.
inclusion: Guinness and Jack Hawkins have the film almost to themselves, and their duel is the reason to see it. The Monthly Film Bulletin praised Peter Glenville's first film and Guinness's soberly convincing cardinal, while finding the manner sometimes portentous; the New York Times called it grim and gripping. Its origin as a stage play shows. Roger Moore, reviewing it in 2023, found it stagebound and the guard's romance corny. In 1955 it was attacked from both sides. The International Catholic Office for the Cinema gave it its Grand Prize for 1956, and Cardinal Griffin of Westminster commended it.
themes: It turns on a priest's interior life under assault. The cardinal's strength is his faith, and the interrogator wins only by persuading him that his vocation was mixed with pride. The confession that follows is false, but it is also an act of self-abasement, and in the dock he seeks forgiveness from God, not from the court. He then accepts his survival, discredited, as a penance. The film leaves open how far his self-accusation is true; it never doubts the faith itself, and it is the interrogator who is left unsettled. Glenville insisted the film was not a tract for either side but the encounter of a man of God and a man of the State.
history: József Mindszenty, Archbishop of Esztergom and Primate of Hungary, was arrested on 26 December 1948 and in February 1949 sentenced to life imprisonment after a show trial in which he confessed to treason and currency offences. He had said beforehand that any confession of his would be the product of duress. The Hungarian rising freed him in October 1956 and he took refuge in the American legation in Budapest, where he stayed until 1971. In Yugoslavia, Alojzije Stepinac, Archbishop of Zagreb, was sentenced in October 1946 to sixteen years in prison and later confined to his village; Pius XII made him a cardinal in 1953.
liberties: The cardinal and his country are fictional, a composite of the Mindszenty and Stepinac cases. The psychological method of the interrogation is the play's invention, not a reconstruction of either trial.
advisories:
Psychological cruelty: sleep deprivation, solitary confinement and humiliation; no torture is shown.

A subplot about a guard's love for a married woman; nothing explicit.

For teenagers and adults. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.

The cardinal's false confession, and his doubts about his own motives, are central and partly left open.

doctrine: The Church teaches that a confession or act extorted by fear is not freely made. The film's cardinal is broken by pressure on the mind, and the interrogator exploits his fear that he entered the priesthood from pride. Trent taught that the efficacy of the Church's ministry does not depend on the priest's worthiness (Session 7, can. 12). The Holy Office decree of 1 July 1949 excommunicated Catholics who knowingly profess and spread communist doctrine. The Church honours those who endure imprisonment for the Faith as confessors, a title below that of martyr.
production: Bridget Boland's play opened in London in 1954, and Peter Glenville, who had directed it on stage, adapted it for the screen. It was shot in England and in Ostend and Bruges. It was controversial: Ireland banned it as pro-Communist, it was dropped from Cannes and refused at Venice as anti-Communist, and some Italian critics called it anti-Catholic. Because of the resemblance to Stepinac it was not shown in Yugoslavia until after communist rule ended. It received five BAFTA nominations, including Best Film and Best British Actor for both Guinness and Hawkins.

title: The Robe
decision: PUBLISH: The National Legion of Decency classified the finished film A-I (morally unobjectionable for general patronage) and it received a Christopher Award, both pre-conciliar Catholic judgments recorded in the AFI Catalog; the Legion had warned against Lloyd C. Douglas's novel in 1948 (B), so the A-I marks a deliberate judgment on the film itself. Greydanus (B-, moral/spiritual +2, Kids & Up) establishes reverent content with Christ seen only from outside and St Peter as leader of the community, and is candid about its dramatic weakness. Christ, the Passion, Peter and martyrdom are central; nothing contrary to Catholic teaching is reported. Protestant authorship is disclosed.
summary: The first CinemaScope film follows the Roman tribune who crucified Christ and won His robe, through guilt and conversion under St Peter, to martyrdom under Caligula.
synopsis: Marcellus Gallio, a dissolute Roman tribune, is posted to Jerusalem after offending Caligula, taking with him the Greek slave Demetrius. He commands the detail that crucifies Jesus and wins the robe in a dice game at the foot of the cross. Demetrius, who has seen Christ on Palm Sunday, follows Him. Marcellus is tormented by guilt and fits of madness. The Emperor Tiberius sends him back to Palestine to find and destroy the robe and to spy on the Christians. In Cana he meets the followers of Jesus, among them Peter, comes to faith and joins them. Back in Rome he helps rescue Demetrius, who has been tortured, and Peter's prayer restores him. Caligula, now emperor, tries Marcellus for treason. He confesses Christ and walks to his death with Diana, who chooses to die with him.
inclusion: The Robe is best known as the film that launched CinemaScope, and it won Oscars for its sets and costumes. It was shot in Technicolor and nominated for Best Picture. As drama it is uneven. Steven D. Greydanus singles out the Roman prologue and Demetrius's frantic search through Jerusalem on Holy Thursday night, and Peter's account of his denial and forgiveness, but finds Richard Burton stiff, the action scenes weak beside Ben-Hur, and the conversion more a matter of special effects than of a changed life. Bosley Crowther and Richard L. Coe were also unimpressed at the time. Its virtues are reverence and clarity, and Greydanus rates it suitable for children.
themes: Christ is never shown full-face. Demetrius is overwhelmed by a glance on Palm Sunday, and Calvary is seen through the soldiers who carry out the sentence. The robe is treated almost as a relic, an idea Greydanus finds intriguingly sacramental, though the film does not develop it. Peter recounts his triple denial and Christ's forgiveness, and leads the community that receives Marcellus. The ending is a confession of faith before the emperor and a martyrdom accepted freely. The film's Christianity is broad, from a Lutheran-trained novelist, but its subjects, the Passion, repentance and martyrdom, are wholly within Catholic tradition.
history: Pontius Pilate was prefect of Judaea from about AD 26 to 36 and ordered the crucifixion of Jesus under Tiberius. St John records that the soldiers divided Christ's garments and cast lots for the seamless tunic. Caligula became emperor in AD 37 and was murdered in AD 41. The Gallio family name comes from the proconsul of Achaia before whom St Paul appeared at Corinth (Acts 18:12), but the tribune is not a historical figure. The accounts of Roman persecution of the first Christians belong to a later period than the film places them.
liberties: Marcellus, Diana, Demetrius and their story are fictional. Greydanus notes the film exaggerates the prominence of the early Church in Rome and invents a direct clash with Caligula, for which there is no historical basis. Peter is gentler than the Peter of the Gospels and Acts.
advisories:
Stylised action violence, a sword duel and the torture of a prisoner.

The Crucifixion is seen at a distance; mild Passion imagery.

Some veiled innuendo at Caligula's court.

Legion of Decency A-I; suitable for children.

suitability.note: None of it is graphic. Older children can follow it, though the story is long and talky.

doctrine: The seamless tunic for which the soldiers cast lots is in St John's Gospel (19:23-24). The Fathers read it as a sign of the unity of the Church. Tradition names the centurion who confessed Christ at the cross as Longinus, whom the Roman Martyrology keeps as a saint. The film's Peter is the leader of the disciples. The Church holds that Christ made Peter the rock on which the Church is built (Matthew 16:18), a primacy that the Vatican Council defined in 1870. Marcellus is converted by grace and by the witness of the faithful, and he ends in martyrdom, which the Church honours as the highest proof of faith. Two relics claim to be the seamless robe (Trier and Argenteuil). The Church has never defined that either is authentic.
production: Frank Ross bought the film rights to Lloyd C. Douglas's novel in 1942, before the book was finished, for $100,000. A first attempt at RKO stalled and the property passed to Twentieth Century-Fox. Jean Peters was first cast as Diana, but became pregnant and was replaced by Jean Simmons. Victor Mature signed as Demetrius in December 1952. Each scene was shot in both wide and standard versions. Filming ended on 30 April 1953, two weeks early. It opened at the Roxy, New York, on 16 September 1953 and was the top US film for nine weeks. It also won the Golden Globe for best drama. The Legion of Decency classified it A-I.

title: The Shoes of the Fisherman
decision: REJECT: Rule (b) (editorial ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's exemplary pope is a figure of the conciliar aggiornamento: he befriends and defends a Teilhard-like theologian whose heterodoxy the film treats as a tragedy rather than an error (Greydanus: 'Teilhard de Chardin by way of Hans Küng'), prays a Jewish prayer at a deathbed as a model of dialogue, and at his coronation takes off the tiara and pledges the Church's wealth, to applause, as the climax. These gestures, modelled on the 1960s Church, are presented as the ideal of the papacy. Greydanus also flags 'muddled or misguided religious themes'. The conclave and coronation pageantry are pre-conciliar in form, which is why the case is close.

title: The Sign of the Cross
decision: REJECT: content, problem too grave. DeMille's Neronian martyr drama was itself one of the films that provoked the Catholic campaign which produced the Legion of Decency: a bishop cited it among Hollywood's 'vile and nauseating' films (OUP blog, Romanowski). The version now in circulation, restored to 125 minutes (UCLA; Universal 1993; Kino Lorber Blu-ray 2020), reinstates the erotic 'Dance of the Naked Moon' performed to seduce the Christian heroine, Poppaea's milk bath with partial nudity, and arena sequences of naked women set upon by beasts, the material cut for the 1938 reissue under the Code. Impurity staged as spectacle around the martyrs is not something a reader can weigh with a warning. A cut reissue (1938, or the 1944 version with a war prologue) could be reconsidered only if a copy is identifiable and the Legion's classification of it is found.

title: The Trouble with Angels
decision: PUBLISH: The AFI Catalog settles identity and source. Independent secular criticism (Films and Filming, quoted by TCM; Christian Sauvé) and Simcha Fisher's Catholic review (used for content) agree that the film treats the sisters and Mary's vocation with sympathy, with religious life in its pre-conciliar form shown as normal. No doctrinal problem is reported; the only advisory is a few leering gags. A 1966 Catholic film-office classification was not found and would strengthen the record.
summary: Ida Lupino's convent-school comedy follows Hayley Mills as a prank-playing pupil whose long war with Rosalind Russell's Mother Superior ends in a vocation.
synopsis: Mary Clancy arrives at St Francis Academy, a girls' school run by nuns, and at once teams up with Rachel Devery. Over three years the pair stage a string of pranks that test the patience of the Mother Superior, who comes close to sending Mary away; Mary's uncle, her guardian, lets her stay on. When Mother Superior learns what lies behind Mary's behaviour, she shows mercy and sees promise in her. Left at school over Christmas, Mary watches the sisters at Midnight Mass from the wings of the chapel. When old Sister Liguori dies in her sleep, Mary slips into the chapel and sees Mother Superior's private grief. At graduation Mary announces that she will stay and enter the order. Rachel feels betrayed, but comes to accept her friend's choice.
inclusion: A mild studio comedy, but an unusually honest one about a vocation. It comes from Jane Trahey's memoir of a Catholic girls' school in the 1930s, and the sisters are individuals rather than saints or tyrants: Simcha Fisher notes that several carry painful pasts and share friendships. Rosalind Russell, a devout Catholic, gives Mother Superior dry wit and authority, and her grief at a sister's death is the best scene in the film. Hayley Mills is better than her material. Variety found the plotting repetitive, most contemporary critics thought it formulaic, the slapstick has dated, and Fisher would cut twenty minutes. The turn from farce to vocation is abrupt; Christian Sauvé finds the late revelation forced. It was Lupino's last feature, and it remains a good family film that treats the convent as a way of life.
themes: Religious life is shown in full habits, community prayer, Midnight Mass and obedience to a superior. The film takes the vocation seriously without preaching. Mary is not converted by argument. She is drawn by seeing the sisters at prayer at Christmas and by the way the community meets a death, and her choice is a free answer to a call. Mother Superior disciplines, then forgives, and her authority rests on charity. There are no doctrinal statements to weigh. The Catholic content is the witness of a community living its rule, seen through the eyes of a girl who begins by mocking it.
history: Jane Trahey published Life with Mother Superior in 1962, drawing on her own schooldays at a Catholic girls' school near Chicago in the 1930s; she was a day pupil, while the book's school is a boarding school.

title: Vision
originalTitle: Vision – Aus dem Leben der Hildegard von Bingen
alternateTitles: Vision: From the Life of Hildegard von Bingen
decision: GREY: Rule (a) does not apply. Hildegard was never formally canonised in the Middle Ages, but she was venerated as a saint and her name stands in the Roman Martyrology, as the Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) records; Benedict XVI's 2012 extension of her cult adds nothing needed here. Identity (filmportal.de) and content (Christianity Today, Time Out, One Guy's Opinion, Wikipedia) are established. Reservations: von Trotta's feminist framing, ambiguity over whether Hildegard feigns illness, little sense of the mystical, and an intense, possessive attachment to Richardis.
summary: Margarethe von Trotta's handsome, measured life of St Hildegard of Bingen, with Barbara Sukowa as the visionary abbess who founds her own convent against male resistance.
synopsis: Hildegard is given as a child to the Benedictine house at Disibodenberg, where she grows up among the nuns enclosed beside the monks' abbey. As a nun she has visions, which she keeps hidden until the monk Volmar encourages her to write them down. Elected to lead the sisters, she clashes with Abbot Kuno over penitential severity, the study of medicine and the sisters' welfare, and her visions are examined and in the end accepted by Church authority. Closely attached to the young nun Richardis, she resolves to found her own convent at Rupertsberg near Bingen, against the monks' opposition. A nun's pregnancy and suicide shake the community. When Richardis's family secures her an abbacy elsewhere, Hildegard fights bitterly to keep her and is devastated by her departure. At the end Hildegard announces that she will go out and preach.
inclusion: Hildegard was a composer, a writer on medicine and nature, a correspondent of popes and emperors and a reformer of her own community, and von Trotta's film gives a solid outline of that life. Kenneth Morefield in Christianity Today credits it with careful research and much detail of convent life. Barbara Sukowa's Hildegard is formidable, even haughty, and her chant runs through the film. It is slow and severe, and a reviewer at One Guy's Opinion warns that the pacing is very deliberate. Joshua Rothkopf in Time Out finds the performance over-restrained and the abbess's famous independence in short supply. It is most alive in the Richardis story, which von Trotta called its emotional climax.
themes: The visions are treated as real events, and they are tested and approved by the Church, but Morefield, citing the medievalist Elizabeth Rambo, finds little sense of the transcendent; the Hildegard on screen can look more like a shrewd politician than a mystic. Von Trotta frames the story around a woman resisting male superiors, and the film leaves open whether some of Hildegard's illnesses are feigned to get her way. The Benedictine life itself, with its Office, enclosure and obedience, is shown with respect, and questions of penance and learning are raised, though not resolved. Hildegard's possessive love for Richardis is presented as an intense friendship; Rothkopf hints at an unspoken subtext, while One Guy's Opinion finds nothing improper.
history: Hildegard (1098–1179) entered religious life as a child at Disibodenberg and in about 1147–48 settled with eighteen sisters at Rupertsberg near Bingen under the Benedictine Rule, and she died there. The Catholic Encyclopedia records that no formal canonisation ever took place, though Gregory IX and Innocent IV ordered inquiries; she was venerated as a saint, her name is in the Roman Martyrology and her feast is 17 September. Benedict XVI extended her cult to the whole Church in 2012.
liberties: The film compresses decades into a few conflicts, concentrated on Abbot Kuno and on Richardis. Morefield notes that it raises disputes over penance and secular learning and then drops them. The nun's pregnancy and suicide and Hildegard's possible feigned illness are dramatic conjecture, not documented fact.
advisories:
Two scenes of self-flagellation, and nuns removing a belt of thorns from a dead sister's scarred body.

A nun becomes pregnant and later takes her own life; no sexual activity is shown.

Rated 12 in Germany; suitable for teenagers and adults.

The film reads Hildegard partly through a modern feminist lens.

grey.question: Vision gives a careful, well-researched outline of St Hildegard's life and treats Benedictine life with respect. Its angle is open to question. Von Trotta frames the abbess as a proto-feminist resisting male superiors, lets the film wonder whether some of her illnesses were feigned to get her way, and conveys little of the mystical depth of her visions. Her attachment to Richardis is shown as intense and possessive, and some critics read more into it. Viewers can judge whether this is a fair portrait or a modern projection.

suitability.note: Slow and talky, so younger children will be bored, and there is at least one curse.

doctrine: From 1141 Hildegard wrote down her visions at the command, she said, of a voice from heaven; her major work, Scivias, was begun then. Bishop Henry of Mainz and his clergy judged the writings divinely inspired, and Pope Eugene III, informed while at Trier in 1147, had Albero of Verdun examine them; his report was favourable. This is the Church's normal way with private revelation: examination by bishops and the Holy See before anything is accepted. Near her death the Mainz chapter laid an interdict on her convent because she would not remove from its cemetery the body of a young man she said had been reconciled and had received the last sacraments. She eventually had the interdict lifted.
production: Vision (Aus dem Leben der Hildegard von Bingen) was written and directed by Margarethe von Trotta. She first thought of Hildegard while working on Rosa Luxemburg (1983), but could not find a producer and set the idea aside. It reunited her with Barbara Sukowa, who has described the finished film as more like Gregorian chant than a Beethoven symphony. It was shot in original medieval cloisters, chiefly the Cistercian abbey of Maulbronn and also Eberbach, and uses candle and torch lighting. Hildegard's own music joins the score. It premiered at Telluride on 4 September 2009, played at Toronto, and opened in Germany on 24 September 2009 (111 minutes). Zeitgeist Films released it in the United States from 13 October 2010. Morefield also found it loosely structured.

title: A Man for All Seasons
alternateTitles: Robert Bolt's A Man for All Seasons
decision: PUBLISH: The TNT film follows Bolt's play more literally than the 1966 film (Wikipedia, Cinema e Medioevo), and the play text (1960 edition, archive.org) was checked: More calls the divorce a matter for the Holy See, refuses a heretic son-in-law, and argues at his trial that Parliament cannot confer a spiritual supremacy. A contemporary Catholic review of the play (Theophilus Lewis, America, 1961) is the independent judgment. The Bolt 'self' caveat is the same as in the 1966 record. No independent review of the 1988 production itself could be opened (TCM and KQEK pages failed); if the editor wants one, GREY/unverified is the fallback.
summary: Charlton Heston directs himself as Thomas More in a close, stagy version of Bolt's play that keeps the Common Man the 1966 film dropped.
synopsis: Henry VIII wants his marriage to Catherine of Aragon annulled and needs his Lord Chancellor, Sir Thomas More, to approve. More will not. He resigns the chancellorship and keeps silent, trusting the law to protect a man who says nothing. Thomas Cromwell sets out to break him, with the help of the ambitious Richard Rich. More refuses to let his daughter Margaret marry William Roper while Roper holds heretical views, and he will not take the oath required by the new Act. Imprisoned in the Tower, he resists the pleas of his wife Alice and his friend the Duke of Norfolk. Rich's perjury convicts him, and only then does More speak his mind on the Act before going to the block. The Common Man steps in and out of the action as chorus and plays several small parts.
inclusion: Heston had played More on stage and adapted his own production for TNT, the network's first made-for-television film. He told critics that Paul Scofield's screen performance was definitive and that he was not trying to copy it. The production is plainly theatrical, runs about half an hour longer than Zinnemann's film and follows Bolt's text more literally. The cast is strong, with John Gielgud as Wolsey, Vanessa Redgrave as Alice, Richard Johnson as Norfolk and Roy Kinnear as the Common Man. Redgrave's casting earned a Golden Globe nomination. Beside the 1966 film, its interest is the text: this is Bolt's play much as he wrote it, with the Common Man's ironic commentary restored and More's argument for the Church given in full. Anyone who knows the Zinnemann film will find it stagier and less polished.
themes: More dies for the papacy and for the indissolubility of marriage. In Bolt's text he calls the King's case a matter for the Holy See, refuses Roper while Roper is a heretic, and at his trial argues that Parliament cannot give the King the Supremacy of the Church because it is a spiritual supremacy, adding that the Church's immunity is promised in Magna Carta and the coronation oath. Bolt's preface describes More as a man who would not retreat from the place where he located his self, and that modern language of selfhood colours the play. On stage, though, his reasons are God and the Church. Theophilus Lewis, reviewing the Broadway production for America in 1961, called it magnificent and read More as a man of conscience rather than a seeker after martyrdom.
liberties: Bolt compresses More's last years and leaves out his record as Lord Chancellor against heretics. The Common Man is Bolt's invention, a chorus figure who comments on the action and plays servants, officials and the executioner's kind. Rich's perjury follows the traditional accounts of the trial.
advisories:
More's execution ends the film; there is no sexual content or strong language.

The play omits More's part in the prosecution of heretics, so it is not a complete biography.

sources.title: Pastor Aeternus

names: A Man for All Seasons, play by Robert Bolt (1960)

suitability.note: The only violence is More's execution at the end, and there is no sexual content or strong language. The long legal dialogue and political argument suit teenagers and adults better than young children.

doctrine: More refuses the oath because it repudiates papal authority. The Council of the Vatican (1870) later defined that Christ gave Peter a true primacy of jurisdiction over the whole Church (chapter 1) and that the Roman Pontiff has full, supreme, ordinary and immediate power over it (chapter 3). The Act of Succession of 1534 required an oath accepting the heirs of Henry and Anne Boleyn and contained a clause rejecting any foreign authority, prince or potentate. When Cromwell pressed More in 1535 on the new statutes naming Henry Supreme Head of the Church, he would say only that he was a faithful subject of the king. Beatified by Leo XIII on 29 December 1886, More was canonised by Pius XI in 1935.
history: Thomas More succeeded Wolsey as Lord Chancellor in October 1529, the first layman to hold the office. He resigned in May 1532, after the clergy were required to acknowledge Henry as Supreme Head of the Church. On 14 April 1534 he refused the oath demanded by the Act of Succession and was moved to the Tower four days later. He was attainted of misprision of treason in November 1534. On 1 July 1535 he was tried for high treason at Westminster Hall, where he denounced the solicitor-general Richard Rich as a perjurer. He was beheaded on Tower Hill on 6 July 1535.
production: It was made through Agamemnon Films and British Lion Films, with Peter Snell as executive producer. It premiered on TNT on 21 December 1988 and runs about 150 minutes.

title: Acts of the Apostles
decision: GREY: Identity (MUBI; Brunette) and content established by independent scholarship (Peter Brunette, UC Press 1996; Tag Gallagher, Senses of Cinema 2004; Adriano Aprà via Bible Films Blog). Not PUBLISH because the adaptation removes the Ascension and almost all the miracles and frames the faith in humanist terms; not REJECT because Luke's text and the apostles' preaching are largely kept and no explicit heterodox thesis is voiced in the film. The editor may prefer REJECT; a subtitle check of Pentecost and Peter's sermons would decide.
summary: Rossellini's five-part RAI series stages the Acts of the Apostles in Tunisian locations, from the first community in Jerusalem to Paul in Rome, with the miracles almost all removed.
synopsis: The series begins in Jerusalem after Christ has gone, with the apostles gathered and waiting. It follows the first conversions and baptisms, the life of the community and its sharing of goods, disputes over the meaning of Christ's words and over the Law, the stoning of Stephen and the persecution led by Saul, Philip's baptism of the Ethiopian eunuch, and Saul's conversion. The later episodes follow Paul on his journeys, preaching to Jews, Greeks and Romans, through riots, arrests and trials, to his arrival in Rome. The great events are given no more weight than the business of daily life.
inclusion: Tag Gallagher calls it perhaps the aesthetic culmination of Rossellini's late historical work, and Adriano Aprà ranks it the warmest of his television films. Shot in south-east Tunisia, with the mosque of Kairouan standing in for the Temple, it looks like no other Bible film: long takes, slow zooms, white light, largely non-professional actors, and constant attention to how people ate, worked, kept accounts and prayed. Jacques Siclier in Le Monde called it anti-dramatic, the objective description of a phenomenon. It is also long, talky and deliberately flat, and its padded costumes and painted backdrops have been mocked. It drew an average of 8.6 million homes per episode on RAI. For patient viewers it is the most serious attempt on film to show the Church of the Acts as a community living in the real world.
themes: Much of Luke's text is there: the community of goods, baptism, Stephen's martyrdom, Paul's conversion and his argument that salvation comes through faith in Christ, not the letter of the Law. What Rossellini leaves out is the difficulty. He omits the Ascension and nearly all the miracles and, as Peter Brunette notes, refuses any outside confirmation that the apostles are guided from heaven. Rossellini said he made the series because Christianity changed man's relation to nature and so made Western civilisation, and Brunette concludes that it shows Christianity as a carrier of Hebrew ideas rather than as the true religion. The Church's beginnings are respected as history; its supernatural foundation is muted.
history: The Acts of the Apostles is the second part of St Luke's work, continuing his Gospel. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1907) ascribes it to Luke, the companion of Paul, on the evidence of the 'we' passages, and dates its completion to about 64, since it ends after Paul's two years in Rome, which it places at about 62. It opens with the promise of the Holy Ghost and the Ascension, then tells of Pentecost, Peter's preaching and the first baptisms at Jerusalem. The deacon Stephen is stoned after a false accusation, and the persecution that follows is led by Saul, who is converted and becomes Paul. The book follows the faith from Jerusalem to Rome and from the Jews to the Gentiles.
liberties: Rossellini invents speeches for Saul before and after his conversion and adds detailed scenes of daily life; Aprà notes that he synthesises, expands, cuts and invents freely within Luke. The Ascension and most of the apostles' miracles are left out.
advisories:
The stoning of Stephen, riots and a food riot, staged without gore.

Very long: about 340 minutes in five episodes; a shorter theatrical version exists.

Suitable for older children and adults with patience.

The supernatural is largely removed; viewers should know Luke's account.

grey.question: Rossellini's series keeps much of the text of Acts and treats the first Christians with respect, but it removes the Ascension and almost all the miracles by which Peter and Paul show their authority, and it declines to show the apostles' inspiration as more than their own conviction. By Rossellini's own statements and Peter Brunette's reading, it presents Christianity as a turning point in civilisation rather than as revealed truth. Viewers who know Luke's account can weigh what is missing.

names: The Acts of the Apostles, attributed to St Luke
Orizzonte 2000 for RAI and ORTF (production companies)

suitability.note: Nothing sexual appears. The difficulty is a slow documentary style that suits older children and adults with patience.

doctrine: Acts presents the Holy Ghost, sent at Pentecost, as the guide of the Church's first preaching. The baptisms of the first converts illustrate the teaching that baptism is necessary for salvation, which the Council of Trent defined (Sess. VII, can. v on baptism). Stephen is the first martyr. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1907) reads the book as showing the promises of Christ fulfilled, with the Holy Spirit guiding the work.
production: Rossellini made the series for Italian television (RAI, with the French ORTF) through his company Orizzonte 2000. It was broadcast in five episodes from 5 April to 4 May 1969, running about 340 minutes, and a shortened version of about 280 minutes also exists.

title: A.D.
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred in its apostolic core, which follows Acts and Eusebius (McNulty; Unger in the Christian Science Monitor, 1985). But a large share of the running time goes to invented romance and Roman court drama, with some sexual content (McNulty rates sex and nudity 3/10). That is a reservation a reader can weigh. A detailed episode guide or a subtitle check of the Roman episodes would settle how much sexual material there is.
summary: A six-part account of the Apostles from Pentecost to Nero's persecution, half the Acts of the Apostles and half Roman court drama and invented romance.
synopsis: After the Crucifixion, the Apostles in Jerusalem receive the Spirit at Pentecost and begin to preach. Peter and John stand before the Sanhedrin, Stephen is stoned, Philip baptises the Ethiopian, and Saul the persecutor is converted. After his vision, Peter visits a Roman officer. Alongside the Church's story runs the history of the Caesars, from Tiberius through Caligula and Claudius to Nero, and two invented love stories between Jews and Romans: the Zealot Caleb becomes a gladiator in Rome while searching for his sister Sarah, who is enslaved and then marries the soldier Valerius. After the fire of Rome, Nero blames the Christians. Peter is crucified head downwards and Paul is beheaded. At the end Linus, Peter's successor, entrusts an orphaned boy to Caleb and Corinna.
inclusion: This was the last of Vincenzo Labella's biblical productions with Anthony Burgess, after Moses the Lawgiver and Jesus of Nazareth, and it has the same kind of large international cast. Denis Quilley's Peter and Philip Sayer's Paul are its core, and Ed McNulty singles them out. Arthur Unger, in the Christian Science Monitor, found it a serious, perhaps too serious, attempt to recreate the years after the Crucifixion rather than camp spectacle, and praised James Mason's Tiberius and Anthony Andrews's Nero. He also found the Jerusalem episodes slow and the Roman ones livelier. The Acts material is good, but it has to be extracted from a great deal of imperial intrigue and fiction. The DVD runs about six hours, cut from a broadcast that took nine with commercials.
themes: The apostolic material is substantial. Pentecost, the Apostles before the Sanhedrin, Stephen's martyrdom, Philip and the Ethiopian, Peter's vision and visit to the Roman officer, Saul's conversion, and the house church of Aquila and Priscilla in Rome are all dramatised, drawing on Acts and on Eusebius. Peter is crucified head down, and the closing scene with Linus shows the succession continuing in Rome. McNulty notes, as a quibble, that baptisms are by pouring. Much of the running time goes to the Caesars and to invented romance, which at times pushes the Apostles to the margins.
history: Acts records Pentecost, Stephen's death, Philip and the Ethiopian, Peter and Cornelius, Paul's conversion and his journeys, and ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome. Peter's crucifixion and Paul's beheading under Nero come from early tradition recorded by Eusebius. Tacitus records that Nero blamed the Christians for the fire of 64. Linus is listed as Peter's first successor as bishop of Rome.
liberties: Caleb, Sarah, Valerius and Corinna are invented, and their stories, including Corinna's turn as a gladiator and two love affairs between Jews and Romans, take up much of the series. The imperial scenes draw on Suetonius rather than Acts. The final scene with Linus is invented.
advisories:
Persecution and martyrdom: stoning, crucifixion, beheading and arena violence. McNulty rates the violence 5 out of 10.

Some sexual content and nudity; McNulty rates it 3 out of 10.

Invented romances run through the series alongside the apostolic story.

For older teenagers and adults.

sources.title: St. Peter
sources.claims: Peter crucified at Rome, head downward (Origen); date; Vatican tomb; primacy; 29 June feast; Pentecost.

grey.question: The apostolic story is told seriously and with care, from Pentecost and Stephen to Paul's conversion, the house church in Rome and the martyrdoms of Peter and Paul. A large share of the series, though, goes to the vices of the Caesars and to two invented romances between Jews and Romans, with some sexual content and arena violence. Viewers who want the Acts of the Apostles will find it here, but they will have to sit through, or skip, a good deal of Burgess's own invention.

names: The Kingdom of the Wicked, novel by Anthony Burgess (1985)

suitability.note: The other difficulty is length, with the apostolic scenes spread thin.

doctrine: The Church's tradition is that Peter was crucified at Rome under Nero. Origen, quoted in the Catholic Encyclopedia, says he was crucified head downwards at his own wish. The year is not settled: Eusebius and Jerome give 67 or 68, and the Encyclopedia places it between July 64 and 68. His tomb lay in the Vatican area, where Constantine later built a basilica. The Church has always rested the primacy of the Roman see on Christ's charge to Peter in Matthew 16 and on the fact that Peter died at Rome. The Roman feast of Saints Peter and Paul is 29 June, observed since the third or fourth century, though the date of the deaths is not known. Pentecost, shown in the first episode, is the descent of the Holy Ghost on the Apostles, after which Peter preached the first public sermon.
production: A.D. was an American-Italian co-production in six parts, about 600 minutes, shown from 31 March to 5 April 1985. Anthony Burgess adapted his own novel The Kingdom of the Wicked (1985).

title: Agnes of God
decision: REJECT: Content (editorial ruling, 2026-10-11). The film sets faith against psychiatry in a modern convent: a novice's claim of a virgin conception after her newborn is found dead is treated as a case for hypnosis, and the investigation points to a human explanation while leaving a parody of the Incarnation open as a possibility. Religious life is framed as repression and pathology. The question is not one a reader can weigh as a reservation.

title: Anthony of Padua
decision: PUBLISH: The Legion of Decency classed the American release A-I (1951-52), the pre-conciliar Catholic judgment, and The Exhibitor's 1952 review gives an independent account: made with care and sincerity, with Aldo Fabrizi's Ezzelino sequence the best thing in it. The content (vocation, preaching, bilocation, raising a dead man to clear his father, confronting Ezzelino) follows the traditional legends. Anthony was canonised in 1232.
summary: Pietro Francisci's modest biography of St Anthony, framed by a modern mother's prayer, moves from Lisbon to the Franciscans and ends with the saint facing down the tyrant Ezzelino.
synopsis: After the First World War a young mother refuses to believe her husband has been killed. She almost agrees to marry a rich suitor, but her prayers to St Anthony are answered and her husband comes home. Her small son becomes fascinated by the saint's story, which the film then tells. Fernando, son of a noble family in Lisbon, enters the Augustinian canons and later becomes a Franciscan, taking the name Antonio. He preaches in Africa, France and Italy. Preaching in Paris, he learns that his father is on trial in Lisbon for murder; by bilocation he appears in the court and raises the dead man, who names his real killer. Settled in the Veneto, he confronts the tyrant Ezzelino da Romano, whose massacres have become unbearable, and persuades him to open his prisons. He dies near Padua.
inclusion: This was the first sound feature on St Anthony, made by Pietro Francisci a few years before his Hercules films, with Mario Bava, later known for horror films, as cinematographer and Silvana Pampanini, soon a star, as the mother in the frame story. It is a small film. The Exhibitor found it made with care and sincerity but limited in appeal, and singled out the one sequence with Aldo Fabrizi as Ezzelino as easily the best in it. What it offers is the popular St Anthony: the preacher, the wonder-worker of the bilocation and the Lisbon trial, the patron who answers prayers, and the friar who stands up to a tyrant. The modern frame shows why he was the most invoked saint in Italian homes. It suits families who want a plain, devout saint's life rather than a work of art.
themes: The frame story turns on intercession: a widow's prayers to St Anthony are answered, and her son's devotion leads into the saint's life. That life is told through his vocation, first as an Augustinian canon and then as a Franciscan, his preaching against heresy and sin, and his miracles, which the film presents as real: bilocation and the raising of a murdered man to save an innocent. The confrontation with Ezzelino shows the saint's preaching as a public force, persuading a tyrant to release prisoners. It is devotional in the traditional sense, close to the Fioretti-style legends rather than to critical biography.
history: Fernando Martins de Bulhões was born in Lisbon about 1195, joined the Augustinian canons and in 1220 became a Franciscan after seeing the relics of the friars martyred in Morocco. Shipwrecked in Sicily on the way back from Africa, he became a celebrated preacher in Italy and France.
liberties: The bilocation to Lisbon and the raising of the murdered man are traditional legends, presented as fact. His preaching in Africa is a stretch: he went to Morocco to seek martyrdom but fell ill and never preached there. The modern frame story is invented. The meeting with Ezzelino follows a later legend.
advisories:
Violence: a murder trial, massacres ordered by a tyrant.

A widow nearly remarries while her husband is missing in war.

Suitable for older children and up.

sources.publisher: National Legion of Decency, via Internet Archive
sources.claims: Anthony of Padua (Italian) (Trans-Global Pictures): Legion of Decency A-I, 1951-52

suitability.note: The violence is handled without gore, and the story is simple and devotional. Young children may find the pace slow, but older children will follow it easily.

doctrine: Anthony died near Padua on 13 June 1231 and was canonised by Gregory IX on 30 May 1232, less than a year later, at Spoleto. His feast is 13 June. Pius XII declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1946 with the title Doctor Evangelicus, honouring his sermons, which were built on Scripture and aimed at heresy and at the sins of usury and tyranny. The Council of Trent (Session 25, 1563) taught that the saints reign with Christ, offer their prayers to God for men, and that it is good and useful to invoke them. The film's frame, a mother asking the saint's help for a missing husband, rests on that teaching. Anthony's tongue was found incorrupt when his relics were moved in 1263, in the presence of St Bonaventure. The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that the story of Ezzelino's humbling is legend, though Anthony's plea for prisoners at Verona is documented.
production: Oro Film made the picture; its director, Pietro Francisci, went on to make the 1950s Hercules films. The cast was led by the unknown Aldo Fiorelli as Anthony, with the comic star Aldo Fabrizi in a serious part as the tyrant Ezzelino da Romano and Silvana Pampanini as the saint's mother. The film runs 81 minutes and was released in Italy in June 1949. It was later shown in the United States in the Trans-Global dubbed version, reviewed in the trade press as an Italian-made picture.

title: Augustine of Hippo
decision: PUBLISH: Identity from the Pacific Film Archive catalogue record (Italy 1972, made for Italian television, 120 min, screenplay Rossellini, Mariani, Scaffa) and the Gulbenkian programme. Peter Brunette's chapter (UC Press, 1996) is an independent, scene-aware treatment showing a film centred on the bishop's defence of Catholic unity against the Donatists, with Augustine given the answer to the pagans' objections. No hard rule applies; the 1972 date is noted and no post-conciliar framing is reported. The absence of Pelagius and the didactic flatness are stated.
summary: Rossellini's spare RAI film follows St Augustine as Bishop of Hippo, defending the unity of the Church against the Donatists while the Western Empire falls apart.
synopsis: The film skips the Confessions and begins with the bishop. Valerius, the aged Bishop of Hippo, chooses the reluctant Augustine (Dary Berkani) as his successor, and Augustine leaves his home for his new diocese. After the sack of Rome, Romans blame the Christians, and Augustine argues that the empire fell through its own corruption and that hope lies with the Church. Much of the film follows his long struggle with the Donatists, who reject Catholic unity and attack other Christians, and his eventual recourse to Roman law against them. He sits as judge in a civil case and insists that justice matters more than legality; he persuades a Christian magistrate that public duty and the law of charity cannot be separated; he answers pagans who accuse the Christians of hating beauty and pleasure. The Vandal advance on Roman Africa darkens his last years.
inclusion: Rossellini wanted to film a turning point in civilisation, and he chose what Peter Brunette calls the life of a small-town bishop over the convert of the Confessions. That choice is the film's strength. Shot among the ruins of Pompeii, Paestum and Herculaneum and composed like a late Roman mosaic, it shows how a fifth-century bishop preached, judged disputes and held his flock together while the world he knew collapsed. Brunette reports that the Catholic critic Trasatti thought its religious inspiration the highest in Rossellini's work. It is austere and talky, the acting is deliberately flat, and anyone hoping for Augustine the theologian of grace will find little of him.
themes: Augustine fights the Donatists for the unity of the Church because, in a line Brunette quotes, they want to destroy the unity of the Church of Christ, and the film shares his view that truth and unity go together. Original sin is stated through a pagan who mocks the Christians for calling human nature wounded, and Augustine answers the pagans that Christians do not reject art or history but see through them the Word made flesh. The scenes with the magistrate teach that morality is one, in public office as in private life. Brunette notes the irony that Augustine finally calls on Roman law to suppress the schismatics; the film does not condemn him for it.
history: Augustine (354–430) was ordained priest at Hippo in 391 and, from about 396, was coadjutor and then successor to the aged Bishop Valerius, holding the see for thirty-four years. The Donatist schism dominated his early episcopate; at the Conference of Carthage in 411 the Catholic case prevailed and imperial authority enforced it. He also wrote against the Pelagians. He died on 28 August 430 while the Vandals besieged Hippo.
liberties: The film omits Augustine's youth, his conversion and his mother, St Monica, and gives almost no room to his writings or to the Pelagian controversy. Its debates with pagans, magistrates and litigants compress arguments into short set-piece scenes.
advisories:
Donatist mobs attack other Christians; little else in the way of violence.

No sexual content; Augustine's early life is left out.

Slow and dialogue-heavy; best for adults and older students.

sources.title: Donatists
sources.claims: Donatist schism, Arles 314, Conference of Carthage 411, validity of sacraments independent of minister.

suitability.note: It is a slow, talky two-hour film about church unity and grace. Older children who like history may follow it; younger ones will be lost.

doctrine: The Donatists held that sacraments given by sinful ministers, or by 'traditors' who had surrendered the Scriptures in the persecution of 303-305, were invalid. The Catholic answer, developed by Optatus and Augustine, is that Christ is the true minister, so the minister's holiness does not decide the validity of a sacrament. The Council of Arles (314) condemned the Donatists and forbade rebaptism. Augustine's second great struggle was with the Pelagians, who denied original sin. A council at Carthage condemned them in 412, Pope Innocent I confirmed this in 417 and Pope Zosimus condemned them in 418. Against the Semipelagians Augustine argued that grace governs predestination.
production: Rossellini made Agostino d'Ippona for Italian television in 1972. It is a 120-minute colour film in Italian. The Pacific Film Archive's print has faded to red.

title: Barabbas
decision: GREY: Same story and grounds as barabbas-1961 (GREY): Christ's Passion, St Peter and the Roman martyrs surround a protagonist who never clearly believes. This version is closer to the source, since Lagerkvist co-wrote it, and the novel ends with Barabbas surrendering his soul to the darkness. Identity from the Cannes festival record and Wikipedia; content from the novel and a Church of Sweden screening note. No review of the film's own treatment was found. A review, or the film's final dialogue, would settle whether the ending is despair or a hidden act of faith.
summary: Alf Sjöberg's austere Swedish film of Pär Lagerkvist's novel about the robber freed in Christ's place, who spends his life unable either to believe or to forget.
synopsis: The film follows Lagerkvist's novel. Barabbas, a brigand condemned to death, is released by Pilate at the Passover in place of Jesus, and watches the crucifixion from the crowd. The event takes hold of him. He seeks out the followers of the crucified man and questions them, but what they say does not match what he has seen, and he cannot share their faith. Years later he is a slave in the mines, chained to a Christian, Sahak, who believes and who dies for it. Taken to Rome, Barabbas still tries to understand. When fire breaks out in the city he joins in, thinking he is serving the Christians, and is imprisoned with them. St Peter is among the prisoners. Barabbas is crucified with them, and dies alone.
inclusion: This is the first film of Lagerkvist's novel, which helped win its author the Nobel Prize in 1951, and Lagerkvist shares the screenplay credit. Sjöberg was Sweden's leading stage and film director before Bergman. The film is much harder to see, and much less spectacular, than the 1961 Hollywood version with Anthony Quinn, and it is likely to be closer to the book's bleak, questioning spirit. That is both its interest and its difficulty. It suits viewers who know the novel and want its most faithful screen form.
themes: The story is told from outside faith. Barabbas wants to believe but must first understand, and never does. Around him are believers who understand less and believe more: Sahak, the martyrs in Rome and Peter. The novel's great antithesis is that Christ dies among friends and speaking to God, Barabbas alone and speaking to the darkness. Read as a Catholic, it is a portrait of a soul resisting grace and of what faith asks: trust before understanding. The danger is that the film, like its author, may leave the darkness the last word.
liberties: Barabbas's life after his release is wholly invented by Lagerkvist; the Gospels say nothing of it. The novel's account of the Christians setting fire to Rome reflects Nero's accusation, not their guilt, and Barabbas's part in it is his own mistake.
advisories:
The Crucifixion and later crucifixions; harsh slavery in the mines; a martyr's death.

No sexual content of note is reported.

A bleak story of unbelief; for adults and older teenagers.

sources.title: Douay-Rheims Bible, Matthew 27
sources.claims: Gospel account of Barabbas (Matthew 27:15-26)

grey.question: Barabbas cannot believe. He is freed in Christ's place and haunted by the crucifixion, surrounded by believers who die for their faith, St Peter among them, yet never reaches faith himself. In Lagerkvist's novel, which he co-adapted, Barabbas dies on a cross speaking to the darkness. The film is a study of unbelief that respects the believers but may give doubt the last word, and whether its ending leaves any opening to grace is open.

suitability.note: A slow, bleak Swedish drama about unbelief. Not suited to children; mature teenagers and adults may follow it.

doctrine: Barabbas appears in all four Gospels. In the Douay-Rheims text of Matthew 27:15-26 the governor was accustomed on the solemn day to release to the people one prisoner, whom they would. Barabbas is called a notorious prisoner (v. 16). Pilate offers the crowd a choice between Barabbas and Jesus, the chief priests and elders persuade the multitude to ask for Barabbas (v. 20), and Pilate releases him (v. 26). The Church teaches that Christ died for all men, and that faith is a gift of grace which man may refuse. The film's Barabbas is a figure of one for whom the Passion was endured and who cannot yet accept it.
production: The film is a Swedish adaptation of Pär Lagerkvist's 1950 novel Barabbas. Filming began in spring 1952 in Israel and Rome and moved to Sweden for interiors in the summer, continuing into December 1952. Göran Strindberg fell ill early on, and Sven Nykvist, then an up-and-coming cinematographer, shot the exteriors. Sandrews distributed it, and it was one of the largest Swedish productions of its time. It opened in Sweden on 5 May 1953 and was entered at the 1953 Cannes Film Festival. It runs 119 minutes and is in Swedish.

title: Cardinal Messias
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred and morally clean - the Legion of Decency classed the US release A-I (1951-52), and Italian reviews of 1939 and The Exhibitor (1952) agree on a dignified missionary drama. The reservation is political and historical: made in Italian East Africa three years after the conquest of Ethiopia, funded partly by a religious order, awarded the Coppa Mussolini, and described by the Museo Nazionale del Cinema as a manifesto of italianità and of the regime. Massaia is a Servant of God (declared Venerable only in 2016); rule (a) does not apply and he is not given a title.
summary: A Fascist-era epic of the Capuchin bishop Guglielmo Massaia's mission in Ethiopia, his friendship with Menelik and his expulsion, shot on location and awarded the Coppa Mussolini.
synopsis: Massaia, a Capuchin bishop who has spent years in Ethiopia, travels on foot with his companion Fr Leone, caring for the poor and freeing a slave. Menelik, King of Shewa, receives him warmly and lets him found a mission; the two become friends. Massaia fights an epidemic with a rough smallpox vaccine and settles his mission among the people he has nursed. His success provokes the Coptic Abuna Atanasio, who excommunicates anyone who deals with him and persuades the Emperor Yohannes to demand his expulsion. Menelik refuses and war follows; a princess slighted by Menelik joins his enemies. Massaia, knowing he is the pretext, offers to give himself up. Yohannes wins with the help of the Galla, spares Menelik but orders Massaia out to satisfy the Copts. Fr Leone dies on the journey, and crowds escort the bishop to the border.
inclusion: Camillo Pilotto's Massaia was widely praised. Mario Gromo in La Stampa called the film a major achievement and admired Pilotto and Enrico Glori's ambiguous Menelik, and Umberto Barbaro found it dignified and serious though spectacular and crudely edited. The battle and crowd scenes, shot in Eritrea with thousands of extras, were what impressed contemporary audiences. The Exhibitor, reviewing the American release in 1952, admired the authentic background but felt the film never got below the surface of its political and religious struggle. The Museo del Cinema's programme note, presenting a restored copy in 2009, judged that Massaia himself is spared the propaganda rhetoric given to other characters.
themes: Massaia is presented as an apostle in the full sense: he preaches, baptises, heals and frees slaves, and he is ready to give himself up to prevent bloodshed. The Coptic hierarchy, in the person of Abuna Atanasio, is shown as envious and political, using excommunication to drive out the Catholic mission. The Church's work is given a clear supernatural purpose, the salvation of souls and works of mercy, but the film also makes the missionary a forerunner of Italian influence in Ethiopia and celebrates Italy as a civilising power.
history: Guglielmo Massaia (1809-1889), a Piedmontese Capuchin, worked in Ethiopia for some thirty-five years, much of it in Shewa under Menelik, whose favour he won partly through medicine, including vaccination against smallpox. He was forced out of Ethiopia under the Emperor Yohannes IV in 1879-80, returned to Italy and wrote his memoirs. His cause for beatification is open.
liberties: The plot compresses decades of missionary work into a single conflict, and the princess and some episodes are dramatised. The film presents Italian interest in Ethiopia through a friendly Menelik, passing over the later war of 1896 and the invasion of 1935-36, which the film was made to justify.
advisories:
Battle scenes with many deaths; an epidemic.

Slavery, including a slave being freed.

Suitable for older children and up.

The film was made as colonial propaganda and presents Fascist Italy's claims in Ethiopia favourably.

grey.question: The missionary portrait is sound, and the Legion of Decency passed the film for all audiences. Its purpose is another matter. It was shot in occupied Ethiopia in 1939 and is described by the Museo Nazionale del Cinema as a manifesto of Italian identity and of the regime: Massaia's mission is presented as the forerunner of Italy's civilising role in Africa. Viewers should weigh how far the film enlists a missionary bishop for the Fascist colonial cause.

doctrine: Massaia was a Capuchin who received the habit on 25 September 1825, was consecrated at Rome on 24 May 1846 as first vicar apostolic of the Gallas in Abyssinia, and was made a cardinal by Leo XIII on 10 November 1884. The Catholic Encyclopedia records that he was exiled seven times in thirty-five years but kept returning, and that he freed Galla boys from slavery and started a school for them at Marseilles. He ordained native priests for the Coptic Rite and consecrated Giustino de Jacobis as vicar apostolic for the Copts, which brought opposition from the Coptic Patriarch of Egypt. Massaia was banished and fled under an assumed name. In 1880 he resigned his mission because of ill health.
production: Cardinal Messias (Il cardinale Messias or Abuna Messias) was made by Romana Editrice Film and released on 31 August 1939 at about 96 minutes. It won the Mussolini Cup at the 1939 Venice festival. Because it was made under the Fascist regime, after Italy's conquest of Ethiopia, it should be read as colonial propaganda around a historical missionary.

title: Near the City
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a young priest's first parish and his catechism of the children). Identity and outline are established (Spanish Wikipedia), and decine21 gives a short descriptive note. No independent or contemporary Catholic assessment of how the film treats the priest and the faith was found. A Spanish Catholic rating (the 1950s Oficina Nacional Permanente de Vigilancia de Espectáculos or Ecclesia listings) or a 1952 review would settle it.
summary: Luis Lucia's modest Spanish social drama of a newly ordained priest who takes charge of a destitute parish on the edge of Madrid and wins it over through its children.
synopsis: Padre José, newly ordained and the son of a variety ventriloquist, is sent as curate to a poor parish on the outskirts of Madrid. He arrives to find that the parish priest has died, and he must run the church himself until the bishop decides what to do. The district is poor in every sense: bad housing, poor health and moral neglect. Ramón, the old sacristan, explains its troubles to him. Doña Casilda, owner of the best house in the neighbourhood, practises her religion in her own fashion. With the help of the sacristan, a doctor who gives his services, and Pepito, his father's ventriloquist's dummy, the young priest begins to draw the neighbourhood's children to catechism, the first step in reclaiming a parish that has drifted from the Church.
inclusion: It belongs to a strand of early-1950s Spanish films that put a priest among the urban poor. Adolfo Marsillach, later a leading theatre director, plays the young curate, with the great character actor Pepe Isbert as the sacristan. Decine21 calls it an interesting example of the social cinema of the period, though it rates it only 4 out of 10. The ventriloquist's dummy as an instrument of catechesis is an engaging, unusual idea.
themes: The subject is the pastoral care of a dechristianised suburb. The young priest's tools are humble: catechism for the children, the help of a sacristan and a charitable doctor, and a dummy that makes the children laugh. The film appears to set the priest's patient work against both material poverty and a self-satisfied piety, in Doña Casilda, who keeps religion on her own terms.
advisories:
Poverty and illness in a shanty district.

Nothing objectionable is reported.

Suitable for families.

doctrine: The film's centre is a young priest teaching catechism to neglected children. Pius X's Acerbo Nimis (15 April 1905) made this the first duty of a parish priest. Every Sunday and holy day, 'with no exception', pastors were to give boys and girls an hour of catechism (paragraph 19). They were to prepare children for Penance and Confirmation (paragraph 20) and, especially in Lent, for a holy first Communion (paragraph 21). Every parish was to have a Confraternity of Christian Doctrine, whose lay members help the priest where priests are few (paragraph 22).
production: This is a 90-minute black-and-white Spanish film directed by Luis Lucia. It received a cash prize of 300,000 pesetas from the awards of the Sindicato Nacional del Espectáculo. Spanish Wikipedia says Jaime García-Herranz co-wrote the script with Lucia, while Decine21 names José Luis Colina.

title: An Ardent Heart
decision: REJECT (rule a): the devotion is presented through Bernardo de Hoyos (beatified 2010) and the Divine Mercy shrine at Łagiewniki (St Faustina, canonised 2000), alongside present-day testimonies. Prior assessment: Identity from the Comunidad de Madrid film catalogue and Kino Kraków; content only from the producer and Catholic press (ACI Prensa, interested). The pre-conciliar devotion is central, but post-1965 figures and shrines are included and the treatment is unverified. Could become REJECT under rule (b) if present-day clergy or the Divine Mercy shrine frame its climax; subtitles or a detailed review would settle it.
summary: Goya Producciones' docudrama on devotion to the Sacred Heart, from St. Margaret Mary's revelations at Paray-le-Monial to the consecration of nations, framed by a novelist's search for a story.
synopsis: Lupe Valdés, a best-selling novelist carrying old wounds, looks for the subject of her next book and settles on the apparitions of the Sacred Heart. María, an expert in mysteries played by the Spanish writer María Vallejo-Nágera, becomes her guide. Their search begins in France, where Christ showed his Heart to St. Margaret Mary Alacoque and made promises to those who honour it, and where her body lies. It continues through the Spanish Jesuit Bernardo de Hoyos, the Vatican, the shrine at Łagiewniki in Kraków and sites of Eucharistic miracles. On the way they meet, in drama or documentary, saints, exorcists, popes, presidents and conspirators. Interviews are woven through the fiction, and Lupe's inquiry becomes a personal reconciliation.
inclusion: The film was conceived for the centenary of Alfonso XIII's consecration of Spain to the Sacred Heart in 1919, and its subject is one of the great devotions of the pre-conciliar Church: the revelations at Paray-le-Monial, the promises and the consecration of families and nations. Andrés Garrigó directed the documentary parts and Antonio Cuadri the fiction; it was partly crowdfunded and released by Goya Producciones, the Catholic company behind Fátima, el último misterio. Karyme Lozano leads the dramatised frame. It reached cinemas in Spain, Poland and Latin America in 2020 and the United States in 2022. No independent critic is known to have reviewed it in detail.
themes: The core is solidly traditional: the Sacred Heart as the sign of Christ's love and of reparation, St. Margaret Mary's revelations, the promises, and the consecration of nations that Leo XIII extended to the whole human race in 1899. The difficulties lie in the company it keeps. Bernardo de Hoyos was beatified only in 2010, and the film's route also takes in Łagiewniki, shrine of a devotion recognised after the Council, and modern Eucharistic miracles. The producers' material mentions popes and exorcists without naming them, so how far present-day churchmen act as the film's authorities is not known.
history: Margaret Mary Alacoque (1647–1690) entered the Visitation convent at Paray-le-Monial in 1671 and there received the revelations by which Christ asked for devotion to his Sacred Heart, a Holy Hour and a feast on the Friday after the octave of Corpus Christi. Leo XII declared her Venerable in 1824, Pius IX beatified her in 1864 and Benedict XV canonised her in 1920.
advisories:
No reported sexual content or bad language. The synopsis mentions murders, crimes and exorcists, so some scenes may frighten young children.

The film draws in post-conciliar devotions and figures, including the Łagiewniki shrine and Bernardo de Hoyos, beatified in 2010.

title: Joan of Arc
decision: REJECT: content and scope (editorial ruling standard, 2026-10-11). UFA's state-rated film ('staatspolitisch und künstlerisch besonders wertvoll') recasts St Joan inside a National Socialist leadership myth. Its hero, as Graham Greene and Klaudia Knabel argue (via Koletzki, Skript 2020), is Charles VII, who calls Joan 'my tool, never anything but a tool' and decides 'she must burn' because a dead martyr is more useful; Joan accepts death 'so that my fatherland may be free'. The people turn on her as a heretic when plague follows the coronation. Her mission and sanctity are subordinated to political expediency: not Catholic-centred and too grave to weigh.
