title: Demetrius and the Gladiators
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred enough under the Bible-epic rule (a Christian's fall and repentance, St Peter as shepherd, the relic of Christ's robe), and the Legion of Decency rated it A-II. The English dialogue (read 2026-10-12) confirms the shape and sharpens the reservation: the apostasy is explicit (he swears there is no king but Caesar and sacrifices to Isis), the return is private prayer without any sacramental reconciliation, and the middle third relishes the arena killings, an attempted gang rape and the affair with Messalina. The robe is handled correctly as a memorial, not a charm. AFI, Bryant Frazer and Wikipedia remain the critical sources.
summary: Fox's sequel to The Robe sends the Christian freedman Demetrius into the arena, out of his faith and into Messalina's arms, before St Peter brings him back.
synopsis: After Marcellus and Diana are martyred, Peter leaves Christ's robe in the keeping of Demetrius, the Greek freedman who knew Christ. Caligula, who believes the robe can make him immortal, has it hunted; Demetrius strikes a soldier and is sentenced to the gladiator school owned by Claudius. In the arena he refuses to kill. Messalina, Claudius's wife, takes an interest in him. When gladiators assault Lucia, the Christian girl who loves him, and she seems to die, Demetrius cries out against God, kills his opponents, declares before Caligula that there is no king but Caesar, sacrifices to Isis and becomes Messalina's lover. Peter visits and is mocked. Sent to seize the robe, Demetrius finds Lucia alive but sunk in a stupor; he prays for forgiveness and she wakes. Caligula's test of the robe fails, the Praetorians kill him, and Claudius promises loyal Christians safety.
inclusion: It was a bigger hit than many better films, and contemporary critics liked it more than The Robe. Bosley Crowther enjoyed its mix of spectacle, action, sex and reverence, and Richard L. Coe found it less stuffy. Delmer Daves directs with energy and makes good use of CinemaScope, Susan Hayward is a vivid Messalina, and Jay Robinson's Caligula is grand camp. Victor Mature is wooden. Bryant Frazer gives the modern view: a Bible picture that condemns its hero's killing and adultery while letting the audience enjoy both, then turns preachy. Its religious core, a believer's fall and return through prayer and the patience of Peter, is stronger than its reputation as a gladiator movie suggests. Michael Rennie's Peter, who answers mockery with pity, is the best thing in it.
themes: Demetrius loses his faith when God seems to let Lucia die, and the denial is explicit: he swears there is no king but Caesar and offers sacrifice to Isis. Peter does not argue him back. He comes to the villa, is mocked, and answers with pity; later he tells Demetrius that if he wants the robe he must pray for it, as he once knew how. The return is a prayer to the Father for forgiveness, set against Christ's words from the cross, and Lucia's waking answers it. The robe is treated as a relic and memorial: Demetrius says its only spell is memory, and when Caligula fails to raise a murdered man with it, he is told no one ever claimed it had powers. The repentance stays private; nothing sacramental is shown.
history: Caligula reigned from 37 to 41 and was murdered by officers of the Praetorian Guard led by Cassius Chaerea, who appears in the film. Claudius succeeded him; Messalina was his wife. There is no evidence that Claudius protected Christians, and he expelled Jews from Rome in about 49, an episode that may have involved early Christians.
liberties: Demetrius, Lucia and the robe's history are fiction from Lloyd C. Douglas's characters. The film makes Messalina a predator at Caligula's court who publicly renounces her adultery at the end, and has Claudius promise the Christians they have nothing to fear while they stay loyal, which is invention. Peter's presence in Rome under Caligula is unhistorical.
advisories:
Arena combat, with killings; tigers; an attempted gang rape of a young woman.

An adulterous affair with Messalina, implied rather than shown.

The hero denies Christ and sacrifices to Isis before his repentance.

grey.question: Demetrius is a story of apostasy and return. A Christian curses God, swears there is no king but Caesar, sacrifices to Isis and becomes Messalina's lover, then repents in prayer after St Peter answers him with pity. The faith wins and Christ's robe is treated soberly as a relic, not a charm. But the film spends its middle third enjoying the sin it condemns, with arena killings, an attempted gang rape and the affair at court.

names: Characters created by Lloyd C. Douglas in The Robe

suitability.note: It is not a film for younger children.

doctrine: Demetrius lapses in the manner of the third-century lapsi. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1912) describes them as Christians who denied the faith under persecution, the sacrificati who offered sacrifice and the thurificati who burned incense before idols; Demetrius's sacrifice to Isis puts him in the first class. Many fell from fear, not conviction. After the Decian persecution (250-251), synods at Carthage and Rome agreed with Cyprian that the lapsed should be encouraged to repent and admitted to public penance, though the Encyclopedia records that the sacrificati and thurificati were readmitted only at the point of death. Novatian refused all readmission and went into schism. Demetrius's private prayer, 'Father, forgive me', is far from that discipline.
production: The sequel to The Robe (1953) was first titled The Story of Demetrius, and Victor Mature repeated his role. 20th Century Fox made it, and filming was finished by September 1953, at a budget of about $1.99 million. It opened in Los Angeles on 16 June 1954 at 101 minutes. Variety called it 'a worthy successor' to The Robe, and it grossed about $26 million in North America.

title: The Galilean
decision: PUBLISH: Identity from filmdienst.de (45 min, tinted, restored 1996 by the Bundesarchiv-Filmarchiv) and the 4enoch catalogue. Grzegorz Nadgrodkiewicz's scholarly article (Kwartalnik Filmowy 87–88, 2014), an independent source drawing on Reinhold Zwick's study, establishes a Gospel Passion adapted from the Fassnacht family's Freiburg play, itself based on the Oberammergau text, with the Christ–Judas conflict at its centre. Reservation stated in advisories: the Sanhedrin priests are drawn with anti-Jewish stereotyping.
summary: Dimitri Buchowetzki's film of the Fassnacht family's Freiburg Passion play, a self-styled Oberammergau, with Adolf Fassnacht as Christ and his brother Georg as Judas.
synopsis: The film follows the last days of Christ as the Passion plays did. Christ enters Jerusalem on foot at the head of a great crowd and heals a blind man, while Judas watches from the edge, apart and hostile. Other teachings and miracles are reported by the characters in the titles rather than shown. Parallel scenes show the Last Supper, staged after Leonardo, and Judas before the Sanhedrin taking the thirty pieces of silver; he returns to the upper room and faces Christ in silence. The arrest, the trial and the way of the cross follow, ending with the Crucifixion. Throughout, the drama turns on Christ and his betrayer rather than on Pilate or the crowd.
inclusion: The Galilean is the founding film of German religious cinema and a record of a popular Passion play that has otherwise vanished. The Fassnacht family had toured Germany with a Passion 'after Oberammergau' before settling in Freiburg in 1921, where they built a huge open-air stage. Buchowetzki, fresh from his hit Danton, filmed it that September with more than 3,000 extras. Nadgrodkiewicz shows that he did more than record the play: the entry into Jerusalem is cut quickly from several angles, and the Last Supper is intercut with Judas's bargain and closes on alternating close-ups of Christ and Judas. Other passages remain static and stagey. Reviews in 1921 were mixed but praised the crowd scenes.
themes: The film is a straightforward Gospel Passion drawn from a Catholic popular tradition: the Fassnachts' text was an adaptation of the Oberammergau play as revised by its parish priest, Joseph Alois Daisenberger. Christ is shown praying before the miracle at the gate, instituting the Eucharist at the Last Supper and going to his death. Judas is the dramatic counterweight, a brooding loner bought with silver, not a political rebel. The Sanhedrin is another matter: Nadgrodkiewicz notes that the priests are drawn as stereotypes, with sneers and horned caps, a feature for which the Fassnachts' stage play drew protests in America.
history: The Passion play is a medieval form. Easter plays grew out of the liturgy in the tenth century, and Passion plays proper flourished from about 1400 to 1515. The Oberammergau play dates from a vow made in 1633 during the plague. Imitators followed. The Fassnacht family of Freiburg claimed a Passion tradition going back to 1264, a claim one Polish scholar (Nadgrodkiewicz) treats as publicity.
advisories:
The scourging and Crucifixion, in the restrained manner of a stage Passion.

The Jewish priests of the Sanhedrin are drawn as hostile caricatures.

Silent, in a tinted restoration.

Suitable for older children and up.

sources.title: Passion Plays
sources.claims: Origins of Passion plays, Church restrictions, Oberammergau first mentioned 1633 and the vow to stage it every ten years.

names: The Freiburg Passion play of the Fassnacht family, derived from the Oberammergau text

suitability.note: The film is silent and slow, and a parent should be ready to explain the caricatured priests. The German film database allows it from twelve.

doctrine: The Gospel Passion is the whole subject. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1911) traces the history of church drama to a tenth-century Easter trope, through the thirteenth-century Benedictbeurn play, to the height of the Passion play between 1400 and 1515. It records that in 1471 the Bishop of Havelberg ordered his clergy to suppress Passion plays because crude farces had been added, and that the Parliament of Paris banned the Mysteries of the Passion in 1548 and the Synod of Strasbourg opposed religious plays in 1549.
production: Express-Film made the film in Germany in 1921, with Dimitri Buchowetzki directing. Both leads came from the family's Freiburg company. In 1921 the Oberammergau players sued over the use of their name, and the film was released as Der Galiläer, a mystery in five acts. The German premiere was put off until 1923. In the United States it appeared in the mid-1920s as The Passion Play and helped launch the Fassnachts' 1929 tour; the company performed the play at the New York Hippodrome that year. The film survives as a tinted print of about 45 minutes, restored in 1996 by the Bundesarchiv-Filmarchiv.

title: Don Camillo and the Youth of Today
originalTitle: Don Camillo e i giovani d'oggi
decision: GREY: Identity from ComingSoon and Avvenire (Fulvio Fulvi, 2025); content from ComingSoon's plot and Gordiano Lupi's review (Futuro Europa, 2015). The film satirises post-conciliar novelties from the side of tradition (so not rule b), but it is set inside the reformed Church, and how it shows the new liturgy and Don Camillo's relation to his bishop is unverified; it is also weak by all accounts.
summary: The last Don Camillo film, with Gastone Moschin and Lionel Stander, sets the old rivals against 1968's youth and a young curate determined to reform everything, liturgy included.
synopsis: Peppone (Lionel Stander) has a rebellious son, Michele, whose long-haired gang splits his party, and a Maoist cell gives him further trouble. Don Camillo (Gastone Moschin) is saddled with his niece Caterina, a young protester, and with a curate, don Francesco, who wants to reform everything, the liturgy included. Caterina wins a contest at the Communist Festa dell'Unità and causes a scandal, and the bishop, who also wants to take away the old wooden crucifix Don Camillo talks to, transfers him to a small mountain parish. To repair matters Caterina pretends to have fallen in love with don Francesco, who falls into a spiritual crisis and asks to go to the mountain parish himself. Don Camillo quietly helps Peppone win re-election, and Michele and Caterina, now in love, are married in church with the traditional rite.
inclusion: Guareschi's last, unfinished book, Don Camillo e don Chichì, turned his parish priest against a new adversary: not Communism but the fashions that followed 1968 and the Council. The film keeps Guareschi's central idea: the old priest, the crucifix that answers him, and the folly of a reforming curate and a bishop who would clear it all away. The execution is weak. Gordiano Lupi finds Moschin and especially Stander shouting where Fernandel and Cervi were restrained, and the humour mild and rose-tinted. It is of interest to admirers of the series and of Guareschi's resistance to the post-conciliar changes.
themes: The faith here is under pressure from within. Don Camillo's crucifix, the voice of Christ throughout the series, is threatened by a bishop who wants it removed, and his parish by a curate who would remake the liturgy; the film takes Don Camillo's side, and it ends with a church wedding in the traditional rite. Guareschi's point, kept here, is that the novelties of 1968, in Church and party alike, are fashions that pass, while the old priest's plain faith and charity remain.
history: Guareschi died in 1968 without finishing Don Camillo e don Chichì, the last part of his Mondo piccolo, and his children prepared the text for publication. Christian-Jaque began filming it with Fernandel and Cervi at Brescello in July 1970; Fernandel collapsed on set on 31 July and died in February 1971. Camerini's film, with Moschin and Stander, used a revised script approved by Guareschi's children and had little success.
advisories:
Fights between rival youth gangs.

Caterina feigns a romance with the curate as a trick, and some accounts say a pregnancy; nothing is shown.

Miniskirts and mild sensuality around Carole André's character.

Suitable for teenagers and adults.

sources.claims: Paras 58, 60, 68, 109: liturgy regulated by the Holy See; Latin; the Mass a true sacrifice; no experiments

grey.question: The film satirises the post-conciliar Church from the side of tradition: a bishop who wants to remove Don Camillo's crucifix, a curate who would reform the liturgy, and a closing wedding in the traditional rite. It is set inside the reformed Church, though, and it is not clear how far Don Camillo resists his bishop or how the new liturgy is shown. By most accounts it is also a weak film.

names: Don Camillo e i giovani d'oggi, a free adaptation of the novel by Giovanni Guareschi (Rizzoli)

suitability.note: Nothing is shown, but the themes suit teenagers and adults more than small children.

doctrine: The film sets a priest who holds to the old ways against a curate who would change the liturgy. Pius XII's Mediator Dei (20 November 1947) is the standard here. Only the Sovereign Pontiff may establish worship practices, introduce new rites or alter existing ones, and private persons, even clerics, may not decide these matters for themselves (paragraph 58). Latin is a sign of unity and a safeguard of doctrinal truth, and any use of the mother tongue needs the Holy See's permission (paragraph 60). No priest may use the sacred edifices 'according to his whim to try out experiments' (paragraph 109). The Mass is a true sacrifice, in which Christ offers himself through an unbloody immolation (paragraph 68). By that standard a priest has no authority to remake the liturgy on his own.
production: Rizzoli Film of Rome and Francoriz Production of Paris made the film and released it in 1972, running 111 minutes in Eastmancolor.

title: Judas' Kiss
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred Gospel drama of the betrayal, told from Judas's side, with Christ's face kept off screen. Identity is secure (Wikipedia; Venice 1954 competition list). Content comes from decine21 (present-day, content only), Entreletras and viewers' reviews; none examines the film's account of Judas's motive and end, and an OCIC mention at Venice claimed by decine21 could not be confirmed (the 1954 OCIC prize went to On the Waterfront). A contemporary review or Catholic rating would settle it.
summary: Rafael Gil's large-scale Spanish Passion drama tells the story of the betrayal through Judas Iscariot, played by Rafael Rivelles, with Christ seen only from behind or in part.
synopsis: The film follows the public life and Passion of Jesus as Judas Iscariot lives it. Judas joins the disciples driven by ambition, and over time his ambition and greed harden into betrayal. He sells Jesus to the priests for thirty pieces of silver and identifies Him with a kiss. A young Roman soldier, Quinto Licinio, comes to plead for clemency for the man he recognises as the Son of God, and Pilate, under pressure, gives Jesus up to be crucified. Judas lives on to see the suffering he has caused.
inclusion: This was the most ambitious production of the religious cycle Rafael Gil made with Vicente Escrivá for their company Aspa: 82 sets by Enrique Alarcón, Holy Land exteriors and dramatic black-and-white photography by Alfredo Fraile, which viewers still single out. The press of the day was dazzled by its scale. It was shown in competition at Venice in 1954 and declared of National Interest. Rafael Rivelles gives Judas an intense, brooding presence, and Francisco Rabal, as the Roman soldier, tends to overact. Viewers note that the film is at its best when it stays close to Judas in a dark, almost noir mood, and weaker when it retells the Gospel at a distance. Entreletras calls it monumental and dogmatic, and finds it has aged into a curiosity.
themes: The Passion is seen from the traitor's side. Judas betrays out of ambition and greed, as the Gospels suggest, and the film shows him watching the consequences of what he has done. Christ is never shown full-face: His figure is seen from behind or in part, a reverent convention of the period. Licinio's plea for 'the Son of God' affirms Christ's divinity within the drama. Entreletras reports that the film presents the betrayal as a step in the work of Redemption.
advisories:
The scourging and Crucifixion; Judas's end may be shown.

Nothing sexual of note is reported.

Suitable for older children and adults.

sources.title: Judas Iscariot
sources.claims: Gospel facts on Judas's motive, kiss, silver and death; fall as a warning

grey.question: Judas' Kiss is a reverent Spanish Passion film that keeps Christ's face off screen and tells the betrayal through Judas. No independent review of it exists, so it is not known whether the film shows his betrayal as a free act of greed and ambition, as tradition holds, or as a predestined role, or how it presents his despair and death.

suitability.note: Nothing sexual appears. Decine21 classes it for young people.

doctrine: The betrayal is told in all three synoptic Gospels with a kiss as the sign; St Matthew alone records the thirty pieces of silver and says Judas repented, returned the money and hanged himself. St Luke and St John attribute the act to Satan, while Matthew and Mark have Judas go to the chief priests on his own initiative. According to the Catholic Encyclopedia, John calls him a thief who kept the common purse. The same article holds that his fall shows that being chosen by Christ does not save a man who proves unfaithful, and that betrayal can grow out of small failings in lesser matters. It rejects the Cainite idea of Judas as an enlightened man, and the view that he was never a true disciple. Entreletras says the film's Judas is an instrument of a necessary betrayal and ends in suicide.
production: Rafael Gil made the film for Aspa Producciones Cinematográficas with the writer Vicente Escrivá, retelling the story of Jesus from Judas's point of view. Escrivá pitched the idea in 1952 and United Artists received it enthusiastically, which helped secure distribution in several American countries. Gil took a crew to the Holy Land in summer 1953 for exteriors. Arturo Fernández is said to have dubbed Christ's voice without credit. CIFESA released it on 28 February 1954. It is black and white and runs about 90 minutes. The magazine Primer Plano, according to an essay on Entreletras, treated it as a national monument and a lesson in visual theology.

title: The Cock Crow
decision: PUBLISH: The film's dialogue (Spanish auto-captions, read in machine translation, 2026-10-12) settles what was unverified. The priest's denial, his refusal of confession to a dying man and his betrayal of a fellow priest are named as grave sins; the enforced cohabitation is explicitly chaste; the climax is sacramental confession to a bishop, with absolution and a penance, followed by restitution to the dead man's companion and the commissar's reconciliation before death. Identity from Wikipedia (Bentley) and the SSIFF 1996 record; craft from Decine21. No contemporary Catholic rating found; the captions are imperfect, so wording is approximate but the substance is unambiguous.
summary: Rafael Gil's Cold War parable on Peter's denial: a priest under a Communist regime disowns his priesthood to save his life, sinks further, then confesses, does penance and returns.
synopsis: Communist troops raid a church refuge in Hungary and beat Father Gruber to death. Father Muller (Francisco Rabal) flees, is arrested and denies he is a priest; in the cells he refuses to hear a dying prisoner's confession. The commissar Gans (Gérard Tichy), his old schoolfellow, spares him once he signs a statement that he has deceived the people, and lodges him with Elsa, a hard-drinking woman separated from her husband. Neighbours discover him; he is made to marry a young couple, and to save himself he points out a fellow priest, then tries in vain to retract. Drunk, he proclaims his priesthood. After the war he confesses to his bishop, who absolves him and sends him back to his old parish as penance, and he tells the dead prisoner's companion what he did. When Gans, now hunted, returns, Muller offers him God's forgiveness, and the commissar dies reconciled.
inclusion: Rafael Gil and the writer-producer Vicente Escrivá made a run of Catholic films in 1950s Spain, and this is one of their Cold War pair with Rabal, after Murió hace quince años. Its idea is a good one, Peter's denial at cockcrow transposed to a priest in a Communist state, so that the drama is weakness and return instead of heroic resistance. Rabal, a few years before Buñuel's Nazarín, plays the fallen priest without vanity, and Tichy's commissar, a man whose hatred of God is grief, won a Círculo de Escritores Cinematográficos medal. The Spanish site Decine21 finds it well made and tense despite its political message, with a memorable chase through the sewers and touches of film noir. The confession scene with the bishop is the heart of it. The regime declared it of national interest. It is hard to see outside Spain.
themes: The film follows Peter's denial closely and treats the priest's fall with Catholic precision. Muller's sins are named in his own confession: refusing a dying man the sacrament, denying his priesthood in writing, betraying a brother priest and living under one roof with a woman, an arrangement the film makes clear stays chaste. The bishop answers with Peter, the power to bind and loose, and the joy over one sinner who repents; he calls Muller's despair and his wish for martyrdom forms of pride, absolves him and imposes a penance. The priesthood is indelible: even drunk and apostate, Muller insists his hands can still absolve and consecrate. The ending carries the same logic to his persecutor. A passing scene has a mother rebuked for calling a cure miraculous before the Church has judged.
advisories:
The killing of a priest in a raid (heard, not shown); a shoot-out and a pursuit through the sewers; nothing graphic.

The priest is made to live in the same room as a hard-drinking woman, and soldiers make drunken advances to her.

For teenagers and adults.

A priest's apostasy and betrayals are central before his confession and penance.

sources.title: Apostasy, Catholic Encyclopedia
sources.claims: Definition of apostasy; lapsi after the Decian persecution; Carthage 251

suitability.note: Nothing is graphic, but the subject of apostasy, drink and persecution is for teenagers and adults.

doctrine: The priest's fall is apostasy in act if not in will. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1913) defines apostasy from the faith as the complete and voluntary abandonment of the Christian religion, and notes the early Church's severe penance for those who denied the Lord. After the Decian persecution (249-250) many lapsi sought readmission. St Cyprian and the Council of Carthage (251) affirmed the Church's authority to forgive apostasy even before death, and Pope Cornelius and a Roman council confirmed it. That is the pattern of the film: a bishop absolves the repentant priest and imposes a penance, and the priest in turn offers a persecutor God's forgiveness. The priest's denial echoes St Peter's, which the title recalls (the cock crow, Matthew 26:74-75).
production: El canto del gallo is a Spanish drama of 1955 made for Aspa Producciones Cinematográficas, the company of Vicente Escrivá. It runs 95 minutes and was released in Spain on 26 September 1955.

title: The Judas
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a village Passion play as the means of a sinner's conversion; a monk of Montserrat as counsellor). Identity and outline are established by independent Spanish reviews (Alberto Mateos at Camino de Emaús; DQVlapeli; Entreletras). None describes the ending in detail, and no contemporary Catholic assessment was found; Entreletras reports that Catholic critics of the time argued over it. The ending and the period Catholic verdict would settle it.
summary: Ignacio Iquino's drama, shot at the Esparreguera Passion play with its villagers, about a grasping man who schemes his way into the role of Christ and is changed by it.
synopsis: In Esparreguera, a Catalan town famous for its Holy Week Passion play, Mariano Torné is cast as Judas, and in life he resembles him: proud, envious, a usurer who has ruined neighbours and cheated his own brother Fermín of his inheritance. He wants the part of Christ for his vanity, not from any belief. He frames Jaime Soler, the man cast as Jesus, for thefts at the textile mill where Jaime works, and takes over the role. Rehearsing the Passion begins to work on him. A conversation with a monk of Montserrat shakes him, and the people he has wronged, the children he drove off, a shopkeeper he meant to evict, relatives he cheated, return to confront him. The performance of the Way of the Cross becomes his own Calvary.
inclusion: Iquino, a prolific Barcelona genre director, made this in 1952, the year of the International Eucharistic Congress in Barcelona, and filmed it in Esparreguera with the town's own Passion company as cast and extras; only Antonio Vilar and Manuel Gas were professionals. Reviewers single out Vilar's embittered Mariano and Iquino's skill in weaving rehearsals into the story without trying to stage the whole Passion. Alberto Mateos compares the use of non-actors to Italian neorealism. Entreletras finds it the more lasting of the two Spanish Judas films of the period, against Rafael Gil's monumental Judas' Kiss, and notes the expressionist chiaroscuro of Pablo Ripoll's photography.
themes: The film rests on an old Catholic idea, that representing the Passion can convert the one who represents it. Mariano begins as a Judas in fact, playing Christ out of vanity, and the role, the monk's counsel and the reappearance of those he has injured press him toward repentance. Entreletras describes salvation in the film as an uncertain, interior process, and reports that Catholic critics at the time argued whether a man who played Judas could aspire to holiness.
advisories:
The Passion is re-enacted, with the Way of the Cross.

Fraud, usury and family betrayal; threats of revenge.

Nothing sexual of note is reported.

Suitable for older children and adults.

grey.question: El Judas is built on a Catholic idea: a man who plays Christ in his village's Passion is brought by the role, a monk's counsel and the faces of those he has wronged toward repentance. How the story ends is unknown, and no independent review exists to say; the period's Catholic critics reportedly disagreed about it.

suitability.note: Camino de Emaús recommends it from 13.

doctrine: The film leans on the Gospel figure of Judas, whom the Catholic Encyclopedia describes as the keeper of the common purse, a thief according to St John, who sold Christ for thirty pieces of silver (recorded only by St Matthew) and betrayed him with a kiss. Matthew says he repented, returned the silver and hanged himself. The Encyclopedia argues that his fall shows that friendship with Christ and privileged grace do not save a man who is unfaithful, and that betrayal may grow out of small failings that were never corrected. It does not say Scripture rules out true repentance, and it rejects the Cainite claim that Judas was enlightened. Mariano's story runs the other way: the part he coveted out of vanity leads him to restitution to those he wronged. The Entreletras essay reports that the more conservative Catholic critics distrusted the film's humanising of the traitor.
production: The film was shot on natural locations in Esparreguera. Rafael J. Salvia received the Cinematographic Writers' Circle medal for best original screenplay in 1952. Iquino originally filmed in Catalan; censorship banned that version and the film was dubbed into Castilian. The magazine Imágenes praised its raw realism and Vilar's human Judas, while some Catholic critics accused it of ugliness. Spanish Wikipedia gives 102 minutes and Camino de Emaús 93.

title: The Martyr of Calvary
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred life of Christ from the call of the Apostles to the Resurrection, with Our Lady present. Identity from Wikipedia (citing the Cannes festival record); content from Infobae (2021, secular press) and blog and user reviews that call it faithful to the Gospels. No substantive independent critique or contemporary Catholic rating was found (it is not in the US Legion list). A 1952 Mexican review or a Legión Mexicana de la Decencia rating would settle it.
summary: Mexico's best-loved Holy Week film: a studio-bound, theatrical life of Christ with Enrique Rambal, still shown on Mexican television every Lent.
synopsis: The film follows Jesus from the gathering of His first disciples to His Resurrection on the third day. It takes in the Sermon on the Mount, the multiplication of the loaves and fishes, the healing of a blind child and of a paralytic, His disputes with the scribes and Pharisees, the repentance of Mary Magdalene and the raising of Lazarus. Peter, Andrew and the other Apostles follow Him, and His Mother is present through the story. Judas, played by Manolo Fábregas, betrays Him to the priests. He is condemned, handed over by Pilate, scourged and crucified on Calvary. The film closes with the Resurrection.
inclusion: For Mexican Catholics this is the Passion film, broadcast every Lent and still a fixture of Holy Week. Its reputation rests on Enrique Rambal, a Valencian actor of 28, whose voice and bearing became the model for later portrayals of Christ in Mexico, including the great Passion of Iztapalapa. Miguel Morayta, a Spanish Republican exile, shot it entirely on interior sets at the Tepeyac studios on a small budget, and it looks like a stage play. Admirers find that its plainness gives it force, and Fábregas's Judas was hated by audiences of the day. Viewers used to later, grander Gospel films will find it stiff; those who value an unembellished telling may respond to its simplicity.
themes: The film keeps close to the Gospel narrative, according to its admirers, and presents the miracles and the Resurrection without softening them. Christ is shown as a Man who teaches, heals and suffers, and the Passion is the climax. Our Lady, played by Consuelo Frank, has a place throughout. The film was made as Holy Week devotion for a Catholic audience and has served that purpose for seventy years.
advisories:
The scourging and Crucifixion are shown with some force.

Nothing sexual of note; Magdalene's past is treated discreetly.

Suitable for older children and families in Holy Week.

title: Entertaining Angels: The Dorothy Day Story
originalTitle: Entertaining Angels: The Dorothy Day Story
decision: REJECT (rule b): a 1996 Paulist production whose interpretive frame is post-conciliar “social justice” Catholicism, opening and closing on the elderly Day in jail; it also shows her pre-conversion abortion. Prior grey assessment: Catholic-centred and pre-conciliar in period (Day's conversion in 1927 and the founding of the Catholic Worker in 1933), and Day is only a Servant of God, so rule (a) does not apply. The reservations are moral and of framing: the film spends much of its length on her pre-conversion affairs and abortion, it is the work of a post-conciliar Paulist producer whose audience was the peace-and-justice wing (Pax Christi), and it stages her clash with a bishop over the paper's name. Subtitles would settle how that clash and the Church are framed.
summary: Paulist Pictures' biography of Dorothy Day, from bohemian journalist with an abortion behind her to convert and co-founder, with Peter Maurin, of the Catholic Worker.
synopsis: The film opens with an elderly Dorothy Day in a jail cell, comforting an addicted cellmate, and then goes back to her youth. In New York around the Great War, Day (Moira Kelly) is a socialist journalist and suffragette among the radicals of Greenwich Village. An affair ends in an abortion that she comes to regret. She later lives with the anarchist Forster Batterham and has a daughter, Tamar. Visiting a Catholic church, she befriends a nun, Sister Aloysius, and her spiritual hunger grows until she chooses baptism over the union. In the Depression she meets the French itinerant Peter Maurin (Martin Sheen), and together they start the Catholic Worker newspaper and houses of hospitality. A bishop's demand that she drop 'Catholic' from the paper's name tests her loyalty.
inclusion: Dorothy Day's conversion is one of the great American Catholic stories, and this is the only feature film about her. Its best material is the cost of conversion: the film shows that entering the Church meant losing the man she loved, because she would not go on living with him unmarried. Moira Kelly's Day has real moments, and the houses of hospitality are filmed with some sense of the squalor Day chose. The film was produced by the Paulist priest Ellwood Kieser, who knew Day. Critics were lukewarm. Marjorie Baumgarten (Austin Chronicle) found it a basic introduction with a confusing timeline, sterile sets and a comic French accent for Sheen's Maurin. Stephen Holden (New York Times) thought it reduced her life to rigged confrontations, and Day's former colleague Jim Forest called it disappointing.
themes: The centre is conversion and its price. Day's turn to the Church comes through gratitude for her daughter's birth, prayer and the patient instruction of a nun, and she chooses baptism over her common-law union. The abortion is shown as part of the life she left, and the film presents it as a wound. The Catholic Worker is shown as works of mercy, feeding and housing the poor, rather than as politics, though its utopian strain is present through Maurin. The film is a product of the post-conciliar American Church's 'peace and justice' circles, and its emphasis falls more on social witness than on sacraments.
history: Dorothy Day (1897–1980) had an abortion in 1919 and lived in a common-law union with Forster Batterham, by whom she had a daughter, Tamar, in 1926. She had Tamar baptised and was received into the Church in December 1927. With Peter Maurin she launched The Catholic Worker on 1 May 1933. Her cause for canonisation was opened in 2000; she is a Servant of God.
liberties: Reviewers note that the timeline is compressed and confusing, and that the screenplay reduces long processes to set-piece confrontations. The framing scene of the elderly Day in jail draws on her later arrests, the last in 1973 at a farmworkers' protest. The film otherwise stops well before her later pacifism and decades of public controversy.
advisories:
Rated PG-13. Day's pre-conversion affair and abortion are depicted, with bed scenes and innuendo but no explicit sex; a common-law union and an out-of-wedlock birth.

A woman is found dead with cut wrists; a tenement fire kills children; street assaults; frequent profanity and racial slurs; heavy drinking.

Suitable for older teenagers and adults.

A post-conciliar production with a 'social justice' emphasis, framed by Day's late activism; the bishop scene presents tension between Day and Church authority.

title: Fabiola
alternateTitles: Fabiola ou a igreja das catacumbas
decision: GREY: Identity is established (Silent Era's Progressive Silent Film List and home-video page; Wikipedia citing Sorlin). The cast list (St Sebastian, St Agnes, St Cecilia, Fulvius, Eurotas, Quadratus, Afra, Lucina) shows it follows Cardinal Wiseman's novel of the Diocletian persecution, but no source describes the film's own treatment or its ending. The 1949 remake is GREY for a different reason (CCC reservation). An independent description of the surviving print would settle it.
summary: Guazzoni's silent Fabiola brings Cardinal Wiseman's novel of the Diocletian persecution to the screen, with St Sebastian and St Agnes among the martyrs.
synopsis: This summary follows the cast list and the novel it adapts. In Rome under Diocletian, Fabiola is a rich and proud pagan woman. Around her are the hidden Christians of the city: the soldier Sebastian, the young Agnes and Cecilia, and Fabiola's own slave Afra among her household. The informer Fulvius and his servant Eurotas hunt the Christians for profit, and the persecution claims Agnes and Sebastian among others. In Wiseman's novel, the witness of the martyrs and of those close to her leads Fabiola to the faith and to baptism.
inclusion: Enrico Guazzoni had made the Quo Vadis of 1913 that defined the Italian Roman epic, and Fabiola, produced by Palatino Film in 1918, belongs to the same tradition of crowds, arenas and catacombs. Its source is one of the most widely read Catholic novels of the nineteenth century, written by Cardinal Wiseman to show the life of the early Church. The cast includes Elena Sangro, later a star of the 1924 Quo Vadis, and Amleto Novelli as Fulvius. A print survives; an 87-minute version with English intertitles is available on disc, probably from a 16mm reduction print.
themes: The source gives the film its Catholic shape: martyrdom as witness, the hidden life of the Roman Church in the catacombs and the conversion of a proud pagan through the example of the Christians around her. The saints in the cast, Sebastian, Agnes and Cecilia, are among the best-known martyrs of the Roman calendar.
history: Nicholas Wiseman, first Archbishop of Westminster and a cardinal, published Fabiola, or the Church of the Catacombs in 1854. It is set in Rome around 302–305, during the persecution under Diocletian, and weaves the martyrdoms of St Sebastian, St Agnes and others into the fictional story of Fabiola's conversion.
advisories:
Persecution and martyrdom, including arena scenes typical of the genre.

Silent; the surviving copy has English intertitles.

Age guidance is provisional.

grey.question: Fabiola adapts Cardinal Wiseman's novel of the Roman persecution, and its cast list names St Sebastian, St Agnes and St Cecilia. No independent review exists of what the film itself shows: how it treats the martyrs, whether Fabiola's conversion and baptism are kept, and how much is romance and spectacle.

sources.title: Agnes of Rome
sources.claims: Martyrdom 21 January 304, feast, lambs and pallia

names: Fabiola, or The Church of the Catacombs, novel by Nicholas Wiseman (1854)

suitability.note: Older children who know the saints may follow it; younger ones will find the silent pace slow.

doctrine: The novel is built round the martyrs of the early persecutions. St Agnes died young, about twelve or thirteen (Ambrose says twelve, Augustine thirteen). The Catholic Encyclopedia says the year of her death is not known with certainty, once placed in Diocletian's persecution about 304 and now argued by some to fall in a third-century persecution. Her feast is kept on 21 January, and on that day two lambs are blessed and their wool is used for the palliums the Pope sends to archbishops. The Church honours the martyrs as witnesses who chose death rather than deny the faith. In Wiseman's story the slave Syra and the martyrs bring the proud pagan Fabiola to the faith by their example. Fabiola herself is fictional; Agnes and Sebastian are historical martyrs.
production: The screenplay is by Fausto Salvatori. Fabiola was released in Italy on 25 March 1918 and runs about 85 minutes. A sound film of the same novel followed in 1949. The Legion of Decency rating A-II in its later lists belongs to the 1949 English version.

title: Father Brown, Detective
decision: PUBLISH: Identity and full synopsis from the AFI Catalog (PCA no. 374; passed by the National Board of Review). Independent reviews (Home Theater Forum, 2025; Editor Eric's Chesterton essay) establish a priest whose aim is the thief's soul: he lures Flambeau, lets him go without the diamonds, prays for him, and Flambeau gives himself up. Softer and more romantic than Chesterton, as the reviewers note, but no doctrinal problem. Pre-Legion list; no rating found.
summary: The first Father Brown film: Walter Connolly's priest guards a diamond cross from Paul Lukas's Flambeau, less to catch the thief than to save him.
synopsis: The jewel thief Flambeau falls for Evelyn Fischer and announces that he will steal the ten diamonds of the 'Flying Stars': six belong to her uncle, Sir Leopold, and four are set in a gold cross that Father Brown keeps for his church. Father Brown wants to reform Flambeau before the police catch him. When Flambeau turns up at the presbytery posing as a stranded motorist, the priest recognises him and hides the stones in a glass of milk. Flambeau steals the Fischer diamonds, but Evelyn rejects him because of what he is. At a Eucharistic Congress in London, Flambeau, disguised as a priest, tries for the cross again; Father Brown leads him on a trail of odd incidents that brings the police, then lets him escape without the jewels. Father Brown prays for him, and Flambeau gives himself up.
inclusion: This is a modest Paramount programme picture of 68 minutes and the screen's first Father Brown. Walter Connolly's priest is warm and avuncular, a long way from Chesterton's sharp little paradox-monger, and Editor Eric's essay regrets the loss of the books' cleverness and the romance that does much of the converting. Paul Lukas has a rogue's charm, though one reviewer notes that his accent gives away every disguise. Home Theater Forum's 2025 review calls it a quick B-picture that punches above its weight and one of the underrated Father Brown adaptations. The chase across London, taken from 'The Blue Cross', is the highlight. Kino Lorber issued it on Blu-ray in 2025 with a commentary by Jason A. Ney.
themes: The film keeps Chesterton's central idea that the priest's business is the criminal's soul, not his punishment. Father Brown sets the cross where Flambeau can reach it, beats him at his own game and then lets him go free, trusting grace to finish the work. The climax is Father Brown's prayer, after which Flambeau surrenders of his own will. The setting of the Eucharistic Congress places the Church in public view. The weakness, as reviewers note, is that Evelyn's love does as much as the priest to reform the thief.
history: G. K. Chesterton, who became a Catholic in 1922, published the first Father Brown story, 'The Blue Cross', in 1910, and the collection The Innocence of Father Brown in 1911. In the stories Flambeau, the great French thief, is gradually converted by the priest and becomes a private detective and his friend.
liberties: The film combines 'The Blue Cross' and 'The Flying Stars', invents the romance with Evelyn Fischer as a motive for Flambeau's reform, and compresses his conversion, which in the stories takes several adventures, into one.
advisories:
No violence beyond a car accident and a chase.

Flambeau enters Evelyn's bedroom after the theft; nothing improper occurs.

Suitable for all ages.

doctrine: The film rests on a point of Catholic teaching: conversion begins with God, not with the sinner's own cleverness. The Council of Trent teaches that the beginning of justification comes from prevenient grace through Jesus Christ, and that man cannot by his own free will move himself to justice without it (Session 6, chapter 5). Chapter 6 describes the path of an adult sinner: he sees himself as a sinner, passes from fear of divine justice to hope in mercy, begins to love God and turns against sin with hatred and detestation. Father Brown's treatment of Flambeau follows this order. He does not arrest him but leaves him free to choose, and he prays for him.

title: Miraculous Fátima
decision: GREY: Identity is established by the contemporary trade advertisement and news item in Cine – Revista Mensal (October 1928) and the Cinemateca Portuguesa's 2017 Fátima cycle as reported by Diário de Notícias. Content is known only in outline (Time Out Lisboa): an impoverished noblewoman serving incognito in Lisbon goes on pilgrimage to Fátima to obtain the cure of a paralysed girl, with footage of the 1927 pilgrimage. Time Out calls it melodrama, devotion and propaganda. No independent assessment of its treatment; survival in full not confirmed.
summary: The first fiction feature about Fátima: Rino Lupo's melodrama of a ruined noblewoman's pilgrimage for a paralysed girl's cure, built round footage of the 1927 pilgrimage.
synopsis: Maria Helena, a noblewoman from an impoverished provincial family, takes work as a servant in the house of a Lisbon aristocrat without revealing who she is. The butler's young daughter is paralysed. Maria Helena first asks Our Lady of Lourdes for help, but the girl does not recover. She then goes on pilgrimage to Fátima, joining the crowds that travel to the Cova da Iria, and the girl is cured.
inclusion: Fátima Milagrosa is the oldest fiction feature about Fátima, made only eleven years after the apparitions and two years before the bishop of Leiria declared them worthy of belief. Rino Lupo, an Italian who had founded an acting school in Porto, brought the realist method of his Mulheres da Beira and Os Lobos to a popular melodrama, and he worked in footage of the 1927 pilgrimage, the oldest known film of the subject. Manoel de Oliveira made his screen debut in a small part. It was a provincial hit: in October 1928 the magazine Cine reported bookings across the country until the end of the year. Time Out Lisboa sums it up as melodrama, devotion and propaganda.
themes: The film's religious content is the devotion of pilgrimage and the hope of a cure through Our Lady's intercession, shown through a woman who gives up her rank to serve. One element needs care. According to Time Out, the story makes Fátima succeed where a prayer to Our Lady of Lourdes has failed, which sets one Marian shrine above another and is a promotional idea more than a theological one.
history: Three shepherd children reported apparitions of Our Lady at the Cova da Iria, near Fátima, between May and October 1917, ending with the 'miracle of the sun' on 13 October. Pilgrimages grew through the 1920s. The bishop of Leiria declared the apparitions worthy of belief in October 1930.

title: Philip of Jesus
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred: a life of St Philip of Jesus, the Mexican Franciscan crucified at Nagasaki in 1597 and canonised in 1862, ending with his martyrdom and the legendary flowering of the dead fig tree. Identity and plot are established by the English encyclopaedia entry and a reproduction of Jesús Ibarra's account. The reservation is the invented love story that fills most of the film: the novice leaves his convent for a married woman, takes the blame for her stabbing her husband, and meets her double, a leprous prostitute, in Manila. A Mexican critic later noted its sensuality and ironic commentary. No contemporary Catholic rating was found.
summary: Julio Bracho's life of the Mexican martyr of Nagasaki, which surrounds his conversion and crucifixion with an invented double romance.
synopsis: In sixteenth-century Mexico City, the young Felipe de las Casas, a novice, falls in love with Rosalía, who is engaged to another man, and leaves the friary. When she stabs her husband Cristóbal in her bedroom, Felipe takes the blame, and he escapes punishment by enlisting and sailing for the Philippines. In Manila he meets María, a prostitute who is Rosalía's double and has leprosy. He returns to religious life as a Franciscan, and when he sets sail for home María stows away on his ship, where the crew nearly burn her as a witch. Storms drive the ship to Japan. There Felipe joins the friars preaching the faith, until the authorities arrest the missionaries and their converts; they are crucified, and Felipe is pierced with lances. In Mexico City, a dead fig tree bursts into bloom.
inclusion: Felipe de Jesús is the first canonised saint born in Mexico, and his crucifixion at Nagasaki in 1597 is the high point of this film; the miracle of the fig tree, a beloved piece of Mexico City legend, closes it. Julio Bracho, one of the leading directors of the Mexican golden age, made it for Clasa Films Mundiales with Ernesto Alonso as Felipe, Rita Macedo in the double role of Rosalía and María, and Julio Villarreal as Fray Pedro Bautista, the leader of the martyrs. Jesús Ibarra describes a film that was controversial in its day but has come to be valued as a work of art. Its value is in the closing martyrdom; the hour of invented melodrama before it is another matter.
themes: A worldly young man who abandons his vocation for a woman is led back, through sin, guilt and the sight of misery in Manila, to the Franciscan habit and finally to a martyr's death. The double role of Rosalía and María makes the point that the woman he once desired becomes the sick and outcast soul he must serve. The Japanese episode presents the martyrs as missionaries dying for preaching Christ, and the flowering fig tree as Heaven's answer. The romance, the bedroom killing and the prostitute plot, however, take up much of the film.
history: Felipe de las Casas was born in Mexico City around 1572, entered the Franciscans, left, travelled to Manila, and there returned to the order. He is the patron saint of Mexico City.
liberties: Rosalía, the stabbing of Cristóbal, Felipe's taking of the blame and his enlistment, and María the leprous prostitute who stows away on his ship are all invented. Felipe's actual youthful waywardness is known only in outline from the hagiographical tradition. The fig tree is a popular legend, not part of the canonisation record.
advisories:
A love affair with an engaged and then married woman; a stabbing in a bedroom; a prostitute and a near-burning as a witch.

The crucifixion and lancing of the martyrs.

For adults and older teenagers.

grey.question: The film ends well, with St Philip's martyrdom at Nagasaki and the miracle of the fig tree. Yet it fills his life with an invented double romance: a married lover who stabs her husband, a prostitute double, and a sensual treatment that a later Mexican critic remarked on. The saint's actual waywardness was nothing like this. Viewers should weigh whether the invented sins illuminate his conversion or simply exploit it.

doctrine: Philip of Jesus joined the Discalced Franciscans of the Province of St Didacus, and left them in 1589 to take up trade. He was readmitted at Manila in 1590. In 1596 a storm drove his vessel onto the coast of Japan, and he died at Nagasaki in early February 1597, bound to a cross and pierced with spears. The Catholic Encyclopedia counts twenty-six Christians crucified at Nagasaki on 5 February 1597, six of them Franciscan missionaries. Urban VIII beatified him in 1627 and Pius IX canonised him on 8 June 1862. The Church honours such a death as martyrdom, the shedding of blood for the faith, which the Catholic Encyclopedia counts as a baptism of blood.
production: Felipe de Jesús (Philip of Jesus) was made in 1949 by Clasa Films Mundiales and released in Mexico on 5 August 1949, at about 106 minutes. Wikipedia records no awards for it.

title: St. Francis
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred and sincere by the account of the one independent critic found (James Steffen, TCM), with Pope Innocent III's approval of the Rule and the Canticle of the Creatures at its close. The reservations: a large amount of invented material, including a childhood friendship between Francis and Clare from the opening scenes, and a framing that, in Steffen's words, sets Francis's spirituality of nature and the poor against faith coerced through fear, which risks the familiar opposition of the free saint and the institutional Church. Contemporary Italian praise (l'Unità) reads it in modern terms of fraternity, peace and simplicity. Subtitles would settle how Clare's vocation, the Pope and the Church are framed against the clare-and-francis threshold.
summary: Michele Soavi's two-part Canale 5 life of St Francis, with Raoul Bova, from a childhood alongside Clare to the Canticle of the Creatures.
synopsis: The film opens in Francis's childhood in Assisi, where the boy plays with the young Clare, who is already carrying bread to lepers and the poor. Grown up, Francesco (Raoul Bova), son of the cloth merchant Pietro di Bernardone (Mariano Rigillo), carouses with friends, rides to war and comes back a prisoner. Shaken, he gives away his goods, breaks with his father before the bishop, dresses in rags and nurses lepers. Companions join him: Bernardo (Gianmarco Tognazzi), Pietro, Silvestro and others, and Clare (Amélie Daure) follows him into poverty. Francis goes to Rome and wins Innocent III's (Toni Bertorelli) blessing for his brotherhood. As the brotherhood grows, Francis, worn out, dies singing the Canticle of the Creatures.
inclusion: Soavi, known for horror films such as The Church and Cemetery Man, made a serious and ambitious life of Francis, with a strong sense of medieval texture and faces. James Steffen (TCM) found Raoul Bova lively and charismatic and his portrait credible, and preferred the film to Zeffirelli's Brother Sun, Sister Moon. He also found the style overwrought, with too much slow motion and a clichéd score, and called it no masterpiece but worth a look. It was a ratings success on Canale 5, and l'Unità praised lines such as Francis's answer that the Gospel speaks a language he understands. Rossellini's Flowers of St Francis and Curtiz's Francis of Assisi remain the better films.
themes: The film covers Francis's conversion, his embrace of poverty and the lepers, the Gospel as rule of life and the approval of his order by Innocent III. Clare is present throughout, from an invented childhood to her own consecration. Its weaker side is the framing. Steffen describes a contrast between Francis's reverence for nature and the poor and a faith imposed by fear, and Italian praise in 2002 read it as a message of fraternity, peace and simplicity. How far it presents Francis against the Church of his time, rather than within it, is the open question.
history: Francis of Assisi (c. 1181–1226), son of a cloth merchant, was a prisoner of war after the battle of Collestrada, renounced his inheritance before the Bishop of Assisi, and in 1209 or 1210 received oral approval of his rule from Innocent III.
liberties: Reviewers note much speculative material: the first hour, before Francis's break with his father, is largely invented, and Francis and Clare are shown as childhood companions, which the sources do not support.
advisories:
Battle violence and the suffering of lepers; Francis's illness and death.

No sexual content reported.

Suitable for older children and up.

Much invented material, including an early bond between Francis and Clare; the film's picture of the Church of his time should be weighed.

doctrine: Formal papal approval of the Second Rule came from Honorius III on 29 November 1223, in the bull Solet annuere. On or about 14 September 1224, the feast of the Exaltation of the Cross, praying on Mount La Verna, Francis is said to have received the stigmata. He composed the Canticle of the Sun at San Damiano in September 1225, in his last illness, and died at the Porziuncola on 3 October 1226. Gregory IX canonised him at Assisi on 16 July 1228, and his feast is kept on 4 October. Clare joined him in 1212 and was settled at San Damiano, the first house of the Second Order, now the Poor Clares. The Porziuncola, a small chapel of St Mary of the Angels, became the order's first convent.

title: The Passion of St. Francis
alternateTitles: A Vida Humilde de S. Francisco de Assis
decision: GREY: Identity is established (Silent Era's Progressive Silent Film List: I.C.S.A., 3,700 m, April 1927, from a story by Johannes Jørgensen; US release 1932 as The Passion of St. Francis). Content is known from Christensen's and Van Yperen's scholarship as summarised in the Anglican Third Order survey: a complete life from youth to death at the Portiuncula, with the Sultan and the stigmata, plus an invented melodramatic subplot with a villain, Clare's uncle Monaldo. No independent assessment of its treatment, and its survival is uncertain (Silent Era: unknown; TSSF: lost, with fragments online). Settled by locating a print and a description of it.
summary: Giulio Antamoro's big-budget life of St Francis for the saint's seventh centenary, from a story by the Danish Catholic writer Johannes Jørgensen, with Alberto Pasquali as Francis.
synopsis: Francis, son of a cloth merchant, works in his father's business, fights in the war with Perugia, is wounded and sets out as a knight for Apulia, then turns away from war. Before the crucifix of San Damiano he hears the command to rebuild the church, and he strips himself before the bishop of Assisi to renounce his inheritance. He receives Clare when she runs away to a life of poverty, and goes to Rome with his first followers to seek Innocent III's approval. A melodramatic subplot gives the story a villain in Clare's uncle Monaldo. Later Francis goes before the Sultan and receives the stigmata. Sick and failing, he returns to Assisi on a donkey, hailed by the crowd, and dies at the Portiuncula.
inclusion: Frate Francesco was the third Italian film about the saint and much the most ambitious, made by the director of the 1916 Christus for the 700th anniversary of Francis's death. The story came from Johannes Jørgensen, whose 1907 biography of Francis was widely read. The Sole 24 Ore describes it as a blockbuster with wide international distribution, reaching Portugal and Spain. Scholars note how it stages Francis as a second Christ: wounded at Perugia, he is held like the dead Christ in a Pietà; he stands before the San Damiano crucifix with arms outstretched; and he returns to die riding a donkey, as on Palm Sunday.
themes: On the scholarly accounts, the film keeps the traditional life complete: conversion, renunciation, Clare's vocation, papal approval, the Sultan, the stigmata and a holy death. Its distinctive idea is the conformity of Francis to Christ, carried through the staging from the Pietà image to the entry into Assisi. Jørgensen was a Catholic convert and his life of Francis is devout. No critic's account suggests the Church is shown as an opponent.
history: Francis Bernardone (c. 1181–1226) fought for Assisi against Perugia and was imprisoned, renounced his inheritance before the bishop, restored San Damiano and won verbal approval of his rule from Innocent III. He went before the Sultan in Egypt in 1219, received the stigmata in September 1224 and died at the Portiuncula on 3 October 1226.
liberties: The villain Monaldo, Clare's uncle, and his subplot are invented melodrama. The repeated staging of Francis as a figure of Christ is the film's own emphasis rather than the early biographers'. The American release of 1932 cut the film heavily.

title: Brother Sun
decision: GREY: Identity is established (Wikipedia, citing the Cineteca Milano listing; IIC Beirut; the TSSF survey). Content is described by the IIC Beirut screening note and by two Third Order (Anglican Franciscan) viewers quoted in the TSSF survey, who note an invented strand in which Clare guides Francis and sees his stigmata in a vision. No independent critical assessment of the religious treatment exists. A detailed review of the restored print would settle it.
summary: Mario Corsi's four-part 'Franciscan recreation' follows St Francis and St Clare from the kiss of the leper to the stigmata, restored by the Cineteca Italiana in 1998.
synopsis: The film is in four episodes. In the first, Francis, the pleasure-loving son of a merchant, is drawn to God through the prayers and example of Clare, who has turned down rich suitors to give herself to God; she shames him into kindness to a beggar, and he overcomes his disgust to embrace a leper. In the second, he gives to the poor and hears a voice telling him to rebuild the church, and followers gather round him. The third episode, called Time in some sources and The Temple in others, follows the growth of the brotherhood and Clare's religious life. In the last, Francis receives the stigmata on La Verna, and Clare, in her distant cell, sees it in a vision.
inclusion: Mario Corsi, a writer and critic from Pistoia, made Frate Sole soon after coming back wounded from the front, with the playwright Ugo Falena. He billed it as a 'Franciscan recreation in four cantos', with a sacred poem for orchestra and chorus by Luigi Mancinelli, and the episodic structure anticipates Rossellini's Flowers of St Francis. The Sole 24 Ore calls it one of the historical masterpieces of early Italian cinema, though only in passing. The 70-minute restoration by the Fondazione Cineteca Italiana has been shown with live music in Foligno, Assisi, Manila and Beirut. Viewers who have written about it find the vignettes somewhat disjointed. Its unusual feature is the weight it gives to Clare.
themes: The film's Franciscan content is traditional: conversion through the leper, poverty, the call to rebuild the church, the brotherhood and the stigmata. What is unusual is Clare's role. One Third Order viewer noticed that she takes the moral lead: she prays for Francis's conversion, rebukes him over a beggar and explains to him what his embrace of the leper meant. The vision in which she sees his stigmata from afar is in the spirit of the legends.
history: Francis's embrace of a leper, recorded by his early biographers, marked his conversion. He restored San Damiano after hearing a voice there. Clare, a noblewoman of Assisi, joined him. Francis received the stigmata on La Verna in September 1224 and died in 1226.
liberties: Clare's guiding role in Francis's conversion is invented: in the early sources she joined him years after it. Her vision of the stigmata is also invented. The four-episode form leaves out most of the familiar events, such as the renunciation before the bishop and the papal approval.
advisories:
A leper is shown; no violence or sensual content reported.

Silent, with Italian intertitles.

Suitable for children.

title: Garabandal, Only God Knows
decision: REJECT (content): advocacy for apparitions that the Bishops of Santander held unproven from 1961 and declared in 1967 not to have occurred; the film sets itself against the ordinary’s judgment. Prior assessment: Identity from BBFC and La Capital; content from the producers' statements (via Catholic Stand and La Capital) and one Catholic blog review. The apparitions lack ecclesiastical approval and the film is advocacy for them; no doctrinal error is reported. Reservation rather than REJECT because the events are pre-conciliar and the messages traditional; the editor may judge that promoting an unapproved apparition against the ordinary's judgment warrants REJECT.
summary: An amateur-cast Spanish dramatisation of the disputed apparitions reported by four girls at San Sebastián de Garabandal from 1961, seen through the village priest and a Civil Guard officer.
synopsis: On 18 June 1961 four girls in the Cantabrian mountain village of San Sebastián de Garabandal, Conchita, Mari Loli, Jacinta and Mari Cruz, say that St. Michael the Archangel has appeared to them. On 2 July they report a visit from Our Lady of Mount Carmel. Ecstasies and messages follow over the next years, and crowds of visitors arrive. The parish priest, Don Valentín, is caught between the girls, the villagers and a perplexed hierarchy. Juan Álvarez Seco, the Civil Guard officer sent to keep order, begins as a sceptic and ends persuaded. A brief flashback implies executions by firing squad. The film presents the events as genuine.
inclusion: Mater Spei, a non-profit set up to promote Garabandal, made the film with a cast of unpaid amateurs, some of them from the village, and shot it on location. Its interest is as the only feature film on these much-debated events, which fall in the last years before the Council and carry messages of a traditional kind: penance, visits to the Blessed Sacrament, and a warning that many cardinals, bishops and priests are on the road to perdition. The one Catholic reviewer found, Donald McClarey of The American Catholic, liked its drama and its humour. No independent critic appears to have reviewed it, and the producers say openly that they want the Church to complete its study of the case.
themes: The film treats the visions as real and centres on the priest's and the guard's discernment. That is its difficulty. The bishops of Santander from 1961 to 1970 held that the supernatural character of the events could not be confirmed; in 1967 Bishop Puchol stated that there had been no apparition, and the Holy See supported him. The messages the film dramatises are traditional, and nothing reported in it contradicts Catholic doctrine. But a film that presents an unapproved apparition as fact, made to press for a different verdict, asks viewers to take a side the competent bishop did not.
history: Between June 1961 and 1965 four girls of San Sebastián de Garabandal reported more than two thousand encounters with Our Lady of Mount Carmel, with messages in October 1961 and June 1965. In July 1965 Bishop Eugenio Beitia of Santander found nothing deserving censure in the messages, while holding that their supernatural origin was not established. In 1967 his successor declared that there had been no apparition, and the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith upheld him.
advisories:
One brief flashback implies executions by firing squad; the BBFC notes infrequent mild violence.

Scenes of ecstasy and trance that may unsettle young children.

No sexual content or bad language reported.

The apparitions are not approved: the diocese of Santander has consistently held that their supernatural character is not established.

title: Joan of Arc at the Stake
decision: PUBLISH: A filmed staging of Claudel and Honegger's Catholic oratorio on St Joan of Arc (canonised 1920). Identity from the Cinema e Medioevo filmography and the oratorio's record; independent substantive treatment from Phil Hall (Film Threat, 2005) and Hal Erickson (AllMovie, quoted by Cinema e Medioevo): Joan's unwavering faith, the saints' voices, her ascent to heaven. The satire of her judges as beasts is Claudel's, aimed at a tribunal the Church itself later annulled; it is disclosed.
summary: Rossellini's filmed staging of Claudel and Honegger's oratorio, with Ingrid Bergman as St Joan reliving her life from the stake before her soul rises to heaven.
synopsis: The film opens with a cosmic flourish: statue-like angels descend in a spiral while Joan's soul rises. Joan, at the moment of her death at Rouen, is met by Brother Dominic, who leads her back through her life so that she can understand it. She sees her trial again, in which her judges appear in the masks of beasts, the presiding bishop as a pig, and then, in gentler scenes, her childhood at Domrémy and the voices of St Catherine and St Margaret that called her. Returned to the stake, she breaks her chains and goes to the fire with joy, as the voices of heaven receive her and she ascends among the angels.
inclusion: It is a strange, neglected film by a major director: Rossellini filmed his own stage production of the oratorio, first given at the San Carlo in Naples in December 1953, in Gevacolor and largely on painted sets. Ingrid Bergman, too old for Joan, compensates with conviction; Phil Hall of Film Threat calls her performance extraordinary, and Hal Erickson finds her more impressive than the presentation. Honegger's score, with its choruses and unusual orchestra, carries much of the film. It was a box-office failure, partly because the Bergman–Rossellini scandal was stale news, and the French version was never released. Hall argues it is far better than its reputation, and the opening flight of angels is pure cinema. It is static and theatrical, and suits those who know the music or the play.
themes: Claudel wrote the oratorio as a Catholic meditation on Joan's death, and the film keeps it. Her faith never wavers, Hall notes, and the voices of the saints confirm her place in heaven. The mocking of her judges as animals is Claudel's judgment on the court at Rouen, which condemned her for political ends; it does not mock the Church. The childhood scenes set her holiness in the simple piety of a French village, and the end is the triumph of a martyr, not a victim. The Virgin is among the heavenly voices of the score.
history: Joan of Arc (c.1412–1431) led French forces from 1429, was captured, tried for heresy at Rouen and burnt on 30 May 1431. A papal commission annulled the sentence in 1456.
liberties: The film is an oratorio, not a historical reconstruction. The trial is allegory, with Cauchon as a pig and the assessors as animals, and the events of her life return as memories in no strict order. Brother Dominic is Claudel's invention as her guide.
advisories:
Death by burning, stylised rather than realistic.

The judges are shown as grotesque animals in a satirical trial.

Nothing sexual of note.

title: Guilty of Treason
decision: PUBLISH: The National Legion of Decency classified it A-I (1936–59 list on archive.org), a contemporary Catholic judgment. The AFI Catalog establishes the content: the arrest, interrogation and show trial of Cardinal Mindszenty, with a priest as technical adviser and the Cardinal's public papers as a source. Dennis Schwartz's independent review confirms the treatment while judging it cheap propaganda. Mindszenty is not a canonised saint, so rule (a) does not arise.
summary: A low-budget, urgent dramatisation of the communist persecution and 1949 show trial of Hungary's primate, Cardinal József Mindszenty, with Charles Bickford in the role.
synopsis: At a meeting of the Overseas Press Club, the American correspondent Tom Kelly tells what he saw in Soviet-dominated Hungary in 1948. He meets Stephanie Varna, a music teacher in love with a Russian officer, Colonel Melnikov, and the two visit Cardinal Mindszenty at his mother's farm. The Cardinal expects to be arrested and says so. Stephanie refuses to sign a petition demanding his arrest and is taken by the secret police. The regime spreads lies about the Cardinal, arrests him and interrogates him for more than thirty days; a police doctor recommends a drug to break his will. Stephanie, charged with espionage, refuses to confess and dies under torture. Melnikov, faced with what he has served, is shot by his own side. The Cardinal is tried, convicted of treason and sentenced to life imprisonment.
inclusion: This was Hollywood's rapid response to a trial that shocked the Catholic world in February 1949, made within months of the verdict. Charles Bickford gives the Cardinal a stolid, unshowy dignity, and the film draws on Mindszenty's own public statements. As cinema it is weak. Dennis Schwartz calls it cheaply made and over-moralising, and the framing device of a journalist addressing a press club is stiff. The love story was pushed in the advertising because the anti-communist message did not sell. Its value is as a document of its time, since an American film treated the persecution of a Catholic bishop as front-page news and showed the methods of the show trial plainly.
themes: The Cardinal is shown as a pastor who expects arrest and meets it calmly, with Bickford playing him steady and without heroics. The film's interest is in how a regime destroys a churchman, through slander, a manufactured petition, prolonged interrogation and the use of drugs to obtain a confession. Stephanie's refusal to sign against him is the lay counterpart of his witness, and she dies for it. Religion appears mainly as the conscience the state cannot own.
history: József Mindszenty (1892–1975), Archbishop of Esztergom and Primate of Hungary, was arrested on 26 December 1948 and, after weeks of interrogation, tried in February 1949 and sentenced to life imprisonment. Freed briefly in the 1956 uprising, he took refuge in the United States legation in Budapest for about fifteen years, leaving in 1971, and died in exile in Vienna in 1975.
liberties: Stephanie Varna, Melnikov, Tom Kelly and the commissar Belov are fictional. The trial is compressed. The film's account of drugging reflects contemporary Western reports and is not borne out by the biographies. The final sentence and the dedication follow the real record.
advisories:
Torture is depicted, and a young woman dies under interrogation; a beating; a man is shot.

No sexual content of note.

The political propaganda is heavy.

title: The Messiah
decision: REJECT: The English subtitles (read 2026-10-12) show a systematic reduction of Christ to the perfect man, as Rossellini intended and as its Catholic co-producer, Fr Patrick Peyton, objected. The Gospel words of divinity are kept where they stand (Nathanael's and Peter's confessions in John's form, 'Thou hast said it' before Caiaphas, the words of institution), but every miracle happens off screen, Christ's prophecy of his Passion is cut before 'the third day he shall rise again', the film ends on the cry that the tomb is empty, and two reductive glosses go uncorrected: a disciple explains Christ's divine sonship as all men being children of one Father, and Mary, the film's moral centre, teaches that the Kingdom of Heaven is on this earth and comes when everyone is good. Earlier critics (Brunette, Page, Vera) support the reading.
summary: Rossellini's last film tells the Gospel story in long, quiet takes, with every miracle kept off screen and a strikingly young Mary at its emotional centre.
synopsis: The film opens about 1050 BC, as the tribes of Israel demand a king from Samuel, and traces the people's long hope of a just Messiah through Herod's death. Jesus (Pier Maria Rossi) grows up in Nazareth, where Mary (Mita Ungaro) gives him his prayer shawl and teaches him about the Kingdom. John baptises him and is beheaded for rebuking Herod. Jesus calls the fishermen, preaches the Sermon on the Mount and the parables, and clashes with the Pharisees; the great catch of fish is seen only as the nets are hauled, and the cure of the man born blind and the raising of Lazarus are reported. He washes the disciples' feet and institutes the Eucharist, is arrested, admits before Caiaphas that he is the Christ, and is handed to Pilate. Mary hurries to Golgotha. After the burial, Mary Magdalene finds the tomb empty, and the film ends.
inclusion: Peter Brunette calls it a great if flawed film and Rossellini's most beautifully photographed, shot by Mario Montuori in Tunisia; Noel Vera prefers its restraint to the spectacle of Gibson's Passion and notes that Scorsese borrowed from it. Its strengths are real: Gospel words spoken plainly, the Last Supper with the words of institution, Mary's grief at the Cross, and a sense of Christ's world as a working Jewish society. Its history is curious. Father Patrick Peyton of the Family Rosary Crusade co-financed it, then rejected the finished film for its lack of miracles, and associated distributors kept it out of the Americas for years. Matt Page finds its ending far from solid.
themes: Rossellini, who called himself an atheist, said he saw Christ as the perfect man rather than God, and the dialogue bears this out by omission and gloss. Christ's own claims survive where the Gospel puts them, but no miracle happens on screen, the Passion prophecy stops at his death, and nothing follows the empty tomb. When a Pharisee says Jesus suggests he is the Son of God, a disciple answers with the psalm 'You are gods' and adds that we are all children of one Father. Mary tells the boy Jesus that the Kingdom of Heaven is here on this earth and will come when everyone remembers to be good. The Baptist's last words to Herod are that all men are brothers and equal.
liberties: The film opens in the time of Samuel, gives Mary a scene teaching the child Jesus, gives a disciple an invented gloss on Christ's sonship, cuts the promise of rising on the third day from the Passion prophecy, keeps Mary young throughout, shows no miracle, and ends at the empty tomb without the risen Christ.
advisories:
The scourging and Crucifixion are shown without dwelling on violence; a Jewish animal sacrifice is shown in some detail.

No sexual content.

Slow and deliberate.

Christ's divinity is reduced throughout: no miracle is shown, the Resurrection is not, and the Kingdom is presented as an earthly hope.
