title: The Poor Man of Assisi
decision: GREY: Identity is established (Il Cinema Ritrovato's 2008 programme record of the Cineteca Nazionale print). Content is known in outline from Kevin Harty's plot summary (quoted in the Anglican Third Order's 2025 survey) and the Italian Cultural Institute's screening note. The only critical comments (Elena Mosconi via Il Cinema Ritrovato) concern direction and acting, not the treatment of the saint. Nothing suggests a problem; an independent assessment of the content would settle it.
summary: The first film about St Francis: a 24-minute Cines short, shot in Assisi, with Emilio Ghione as the saint and the main episodes of his life in tableaux.
synopsis: Francis, son of a rich Assisi merchant, has a dream in which poverty appears to him in person. He breaks with his father, Pietro Bernardone, and gives himself to poverty and the service of the poor, and other men join him. Clare becomes his spiritual companion. Francis travels to the East and preaches before the Sultan at Damietta, who treats him with respect but will not be converted. The Pope approves his order, and in one scene Francis dictates the Canticle of the Sun. At the end, dying, he blesses Assisi, surrounded by his friars, Clare and her sisters.
inclusion: Enrico Guazzoni, who two years later made the Quo Vadis that set the pattern for the Italian epic, shot it in Assisi itself for the Turin International Exhibition of 1911. It made Emilio Ghione's name. The Il Cinema Ritrovato notes say his first leading role was his first big success, and quote critics on a performance that held together the worldly young man and the ascetic. Elena Mosconi praised the direction and Ghione's restraint. It is a short film, and judging by its plot it passes through the familiar episodes without dramatising any of them.
themes: The film follows the traditional life of the saint, from the call to poverty to a holy death. The visit to the Sultan is shown as an act of preaching, with the Sultan respectful but unconverted, which matches the early sources. Nothing in the accounts of the film casts the Church as an obstacle, as later Francis films do.
history: Francis Bernardone (c. 1181–1226) renounced his inheritance before the bishop of Assisi and restored the chapel of San Damiano. Clare joined him in Lent 1212. In 1219 he sailed for the East and was taken before the Sultan in Egypt. He received the stigmata at La Verna in September 1224, died at the Portiuncula on the evening of 3 October 1226 and was canonised by Gregory IX at Assisi on 16 July 1228.
advisories:
No violence or sensual content reported.

Silent, with Italian intertitles; short.

grey.question: This 1911 short is the earliest film about St Francis, and its outline is known: the vision of poverty, the break with his father, Clare, the Sultan, papal approval, the Canticle of the Sun and a holy death. Festival notes praise Ghione's performance and Guazzoni's direction. What no independent critic has yet described is how the film handles its religious material scene by scene. A detailed review or archival study of the surviving Cineteca Nazionale print would settle it.

doctrine: His feast is 4 October. At La Verna he received the stigmata, the first recorded case of a stigmatist; Benedict XI later allowed the Friars Minor a feast of the Impression of the Stigmata, and Paul V extended it to the universal Church in 1615. Francis was never a priest. He was ordained deacon and obtained from Innocent III in 1209 verbal approval of his Rule, which Honorius III confirmed in 1223. The Order he founded holds the Church's teaching on poverty as a counsel of perfection, not a duty on all, and Francis insisted on obedience to the Pope and reverence for priests. Clare took the veil from him and founded the Poor Clares.
production: Il poverello di Assisi was made in 1911 by Cines of Rome, the leading Italian studio, which made Guazzoni’s Quo Vadis? in 1913. Emilio Ghione, who played Francis, was later famous as the Parisian-gangster hero of Italian serials. The film is 443 metres long, about 24 minutes, in black and white with Italian intertitles. The surviving print comes from the Cineteca Nazionale in Rome and was shown at the Il Cinema Ritrovato festival in Bologna in 2008. The Third Order of St Francis lists it as the first film about the saint.

title: I.N.R.I.
decision: GREY: Identity and content are established (Wikipedia citing Jung and Schatzberg's Beyond Caligari; Paul van Yperen's notes; the Humanities Institute study guide giving a scene-by-scene account of the Gospel section). The Gospel story is told conventionally, and Christ affirms that he is the Son of God. Reservations: the source is Peter Rosegger's novel, in which a condemned anarchist writes his own Gospel; the frame story (often cut) concerns a political assassin; Judas is reconceived as a disillusioned political revolutionary; and the surviving version ends at the death on the cross, with no Resurrection. Not REJECT because the core Gospel content is orthodox in the account available.
summary: Robert Wiene's star-studded Passion, after Rosegger's novel, sets the Gospel inside the story of a condemned Russian anarchist and makes Judas a disappointed revolutionary.
synopsis: In the full version, a revolutionary in modern Russia assassinates a minister and is sentenced to death. Waiting for execution, he begins to doubt the meaning of what he has done, and the story of Christ unfolds. It runs from the Nativity and the boy Jesus in the Temple through the healings, the blessing of children and Mary Magdalene washing his feet, to the entry into Jerusalem, where the crowd hopes he will break the Roman yoke. He drives out the money-changers. Judas, who wanted a leader of revolt, betrays him for silver. Christ is tried before Annas, where he declares himself the Son of God, and before Pilate, who finds him innocent but releases Barabbas. He is crucified, forgives his executioners and dies; a centurion declares him a righteous man.
inclusion: I.N.R.I. was the biggest film Robert Wiene made after Caligari, with expensive sets, hundreds of extras and a remarkable cast. The staging was praised, but German reviews were mixed and it soon left cinemas. It remains of interest as a document of Weimar cinema at full stretch, and of how European film treated the Gospel in the 1920s.
themes: The Gospel section is conventional and largely scriptural. Christ heals and raises the dead, declares himself the Son of God before the high priest and a king whose kingdom is not of this world before Pilate, institutes the Eucharist and forgives his executioners. The difficulties lie around it. Peter Rosegger's novel was a free retelling of the Gospel by an imprisoned anarchist, and Rosegger reinterpreted many dogmas symbolically. Wiene's Judas betrays Christ out of political disappointment, a reading meant to tie the Gospel to the assassin of the frame.
liberties: Judas's motive is changed from greed to political disillusionment, though he still takes the silver. The frame story of a Russian assassin is added from Rosegger's premise and transplanted to Russia. Mary is given a prophecy that his followers will desert him. The film stops at the Crucifixion.
advisories:
The scourging, mocking and Crucifixion, not graphic by later standards.

An assassination in the frame story (absent from many prints).

Silent; prints vary in length and content.

Suitable for older children and up.

grey.question: I.N.R.I. tells the Passion conventionally, and its Christ declares himself the Son of God. But it comes from Peter Rosegger's novel, a Gospel rewritten by a condemned anarchist, and it frames the story with a modern political assassin. Judas becomes a revolutionary who betrays Christ out of political disappointment, and the surviving version ends at the death on the cross without the Resurrection. Viewers should weigh whether the frame and these choices bend the Gospel towards a merely humanitarian Christ.

sources.title: Pascendi Dominici Gregis
sources.claims: Formulas as symbols (paras 12-13); Christ of history and Christ of faith (paras 30-31)

sources.title: Resurrection of Christ
sources.claims: Resurrection attested in the Gospels and 1 Corinthians 15; fundamental apologetic argument; Christ rose by his own power

names: I.N.R.I.: Frohe Botschaft eines armen Sünders, novel by Peter Rosegger (1905)

suitability.note: The scourging, mocking and Crucifixion are restrained, and the frame story includes an assassination (cut from many prints). Judas is recast as a political revolutionary and the film stops at the death, so a parent will need to supply the Gospel's account.

doctrine: Pius X's Pascendi Dominici Gregis (8 September 1907) condemned the modernist habit of treating doctrinal formulas as changeable 'symbols' (paragraphs 12-13) and of separating the 'Christ of history' from the 'Christ of faith' (paragraphs 30-31). Rosegger's novel belongs to that climate, and Wiene's film makes the same move by turning Judas's betrayal into political disillusion. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1912) treats the Resurrection as the fundamental argument for Christian belief, attested by the Gospels and by St Paul (1 Corinthians 15:3-8) and rising by Christ's own power. A film that ends at the cross omits what the Church holds to be the proof of his divine mission.
production: Wiene's film was made by Neumann-Filmproduktion and shot over 90 days from May to September 1923 at the Staaken studios in Berlin. Its Berlin premiere is given as Christmas Day 1923 in one source and 1925 in another. Censors objected to the modern Russian frame, and the film was often shown without it. It was reissued in the United States in 1933 as Crown of Thorns, with music and narration added. A complete 16mm print turned up in an Italian archive in 1999, and a tinted 35mm print with English titles was shown in Tokyo in 2006.

title: My Name Is Bernadette
decision: GREY: Identity from Offi and French Wikipedia; content from distributor material and one short independent review (Unidivers) that judges craft rather than treatment. The subject is pre-conciliar (apparitions approved 1862). Subtitles or a substantive review of the apparition, Peyramale and Nevers scenes would settle it.
summary: Jean Sagols's modest French retelling of Lourdes, from Bernadette's visions at Massabielle through her trials with clergy and officials to the convent at Nevers.
synopsis: In February 1858 Bernadette Soubirous, the fourteen-year-old daughter of a destitute family in Lourdes, sees a Lady in the grotto of Massabielle. Over eighteen apparitions, ending in July, the crowds grow until a town of four thousand is overrun by pilgrims. The parish priest, Abbé Peyramale, is gruff and suspicious; Commissioner Jacomet questions her, and the imperial prosecutor, Vital Dutour, is charged with restoring order. Her parents, Louise and François, suffer poverty and gossip, and Bernadette is examined by the town doctor. She holds to her account, will not embellish it, and has to fight to be heard by Church and State alike. The film then follows her into religious life at Nevers.
inclusion: This was the first cinema feature for Jean Sagols, a veteran of French television serials, made on modest means. Its strength, by every account, is Katia Miran as Bernadette, a determined, unsentimental girl who will not be talked out of what she saw; she won a best-actress prize at the Mirabile Dictu festival in 2013. The distributor says the script draws on Abbé René Laurentin's documentary volumes on Lourdes. Reviews were lukewarm. David Norgeot of Unidivers found the direction and story thin and preferred Jean Delannoy's two Bernadette films of 1988.
themes: The subject is the apparitions and Bernadette's fidelity to them. She is a poor, unlettered girl who reports what she has seen, asks nothing for herself and submits to questioning by the Church and the State. Unidivers found the spiritual message conveyed with some warmth but felt the film reduced the drama to a contest between those two authorities. French Wikipedia describes a strong-willed Bernadette who suffers for her testimony.
history: Between 11 February and 16 July 1858 Bernadette Soubirous reported eighteen apparitions at the grotto of Massabielle outside Lourdes. In 1862 the bishop of Tarbes declared the faithful justified in believing them. Bernadette later entered the Sisters of Charity of Nevers, where she died in 1879. She was beatified in 1925 and canonised in 1933.
advisories:
No reported sexual content, violence or bad language.

Interrogations, official harshness and scenes of family poverty.

grey.question: My Name Is Bernadette tells a canonised saint's story from the traditional sources, and nothing reported about it raises a doctrinal problem. The only independent review, a short notice in Unidivers, judges its craft and does not assess its handling of the faith, and the distributor's claim that it follows Abbé Laurentin's documentation has not been checked. A detailed review, or the dialogue of the apparition and Nevers scenes, would settle it.

title: Joan of Arc
decision: PUBLISH: Identity and content are well documented (Wikipedia drawing on the Méliès catalogue scholarship; Cinemedioevo's catalogue entry; Antti Alanen's and an archive.org note collected on The Early Silent Era blog). The film presents Joan's voices as real, her condemnation as unjust and closes on her reception in heaven. No doctrinal question. A ten-minute tableau short, so 'Silent feature' is the nearest format.
summary: Méliès's hand-coloured pageant tells St Joan's story in a dozen painted tableaux, from her voices at Domrémy to the stake at Rouen and her welcome in heaven.
synopsis: At Domrémy, Joan is visited by St Michael, St Catherine and St Margaret, and leaves home against her parents' pleas. At Vaucouleurs she wins over the captain, Robert de Baudricourt, who gives her men to lead. Orléans greets her with a long triumphal procession, and Charles VII is crowned in the cathedral at Reims. At Compiègne she is captured during an assault on the castle. In prison she has a second vision. Brought before her judges, she refuses to sign a retraction and is condemned as a heretic. She is burned in the market-place at Rouen. In a final apotheosis she rises into heaven, where God and the saints receive her. The surviving print lacks the opening scene.
inclusion: This was Méliès's second long tableau film after Cinderella, and his most ambitious to that date, running about ten minutes when most films lasted one or two. It was a hit in France and abroad, reaching Montreal and Havana, and Edison sold pirated copies in America. The hand-colouring is the main pleasure, with bright costumes against the painted backdrops and a sudden red at the burning. The staging is frankly theatrical, and the procession at Orléans is padding, the same extras running behind the backdrop to cross the frame again. Antti Alanen places the film at the head of the lavish Joan tradition, the opposite of Dreyer's and Bresson's austerity.
themes: The film takes Joan on her own terms. Her voices are not explained away. The saints appear to her at Domrémy and again in prison, and her mission is from God, fulfilled at the coronation at Reims. Her trial is an injustice, and she is condemned for refusing to deny what she has seen. The closing apotheosis shows her received into heaven by God and the saints, two decades before Rome canonised her in 1920. It is popular French devotion of its day, told as a sequence of holy pictures.
history: Joan was born at Domrémy, probably in 1412. Guided by the voices of St Michael, St Catherine and St Margaret, she persuaded Robert de Baudricourt at Vaucouleurs to send her to the Dauphin, entered besieged Orléans on 30 April 1429 and saw Charles VII crowned at Reims on 17 July. She was captured at Compiègne in May 1430, tried at Rouen by a court under Bishop Pierre Cauchon, and burned as a relapsed heretic on 30 May 1431.
liberties: The film compresses Joan's career into single images. Orléans appears as a victory procession with no siege, Chinon and the recognition of the Dauphin are left out, and the trial is reduced to one interrogation and her refusal to sign.
advisories:
The burning at the stake is shown briefly and in stylised form, with the flames coloured red.

Silent.

suitability.note: A silent ten-minute pageant of painted sets. The burning at the stake is brief and stylised, so it suits children, though a young child will need the story explained.

doctrine: The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) says Joan first heard her voices in the summer of 1425, at about thirteen and a half, and names St Michael, St Margaret and St Catherine. It calls their supernatural character something it would be rash to question. At Rouen a large majority of twenty-two judges declared her visions and voices false and diabolical, and on 29 May 1431 a court of thirty-seven judges unanimously declared her a relapsed heretic. The Church later reversed that verdict, and the rehabilitation trial opened in Paris twenty-four years after her death. Pius X published the decree of beatification on 11 April 1909, and Benedict XV canonised her in 1920.
production: Méliès made the film in spring 1900 for his Star Film Company. It has twelve scenes, one per set, and was his first film of more than 200 metres. Méliès played seven parts himself, among them Robert de Baudricourt and Joan's father. It was thought lost until 1982, when a hand-coloured print was found.

title: Joan the Maid
alternateTitles: Jeanne la Pucelle I: Les Batailles
Jeanne la Pucelle II: Les Prisons
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred, serious and close to the record: Joan names St Michael, St Catherine and St Margaret, is examined and approved at Poitiers, recants her abjuration with 'God sent me', receives Communion before the stake and dies calling on Jesus. The reservation is Rivette's stance. Rosenbaum calls it a 'materialist version' with no miracles, and Dennis Schwartz finds it sceptical of her voices and of the miracles attributed to her; the Church at Rouen is shown as a political instrument. A reader can weigh that; it is reticence, not Besson's psychological debunking.
summary: Jacques Rivette's two-part, five-and-a-half-hour chronicle of St Joan, with Sandrine Bonnaire as a down-to-earth Maid, witnesses speaking to camera and no miracles on screen.
synopsis: In the first part, Les Batailles, Joan (Sandrine Bonnaire), a farm girl from Domrémy who has heard St Michael, St Catherine and St Margaret since she was thirteen, persuades the captain at Vaucouleurs to send her to the Dauphin. At Chinon she convinces Charles (André Marcon); at Poitiers churchmen examine her for weeks and approve her. She relieves Orléans, is wounded, and brings Charles to his crowning at Reims. In the second part, Les Prisons, the court loses interest. She is captured at Compiègne, held by the Burgundians and sold to the English. At Rouen the bishop's court tries her for heresy; she abjures to save her life, is put back in an English prison, resists an attempted rape, and takes back her abjuration. She receives Communion and is burned on 30 May 1431. Participants address the camera throughout.
inclusion: Rivette made the most patient and historically grounded of the Joan films. It is built on long takes, real landscapes and the plain business of medieval war, with horses, mud, waiting and councils. Sandrine Bonnaire's Joan is a believable country girl, devout and stubborn, who giggles, weeps and is frightened. Jonathan Rosenbaum calls it a plausible portrait of the teenage Joan, and Glenn Kenny calls it 'essential cinema', praising its long takes and camera movements. The second part, on her captivity, is the stronger. It lacks the intensity of Dreyer and the spiritual concentration of Bresson, and Dennis Schwartz finds it more pleasing than scintillating.
themes: Joan's faith is shown as simple and sincere, in her saints, her prayers, her loyalty to the anointed king, and her refusal at Rouen to deny that God sent her. She receives Communion before her death and dies calling on Jesus. The film itself keeps its distance. Rivette shows no miracles and keeps the camera outside her visions, so her mission is presented as something she believes and the film does not affirm. The Rouen trial is a political deal between Church and English power, which matches the history of a partisan court but leaves out the Church that later annulled the verdict and canonised her.
history: Joan of Arc (c. 1412–1431) was examined by theologians at Poitiers in 1429 before relieving Orléans. Captured at Compiègne in 1430, she was tried at Rouen under Pierre Cauchon, signed an abjuration in May 1431, resumed male dress days later and was burned as a relapsed heretic on 30 May. A papal retrial annulled the sentence in 1456.
liberties: Few factual inventions are reported. The main choices are omissions and stance. No visions or miracles are shown, and witnesses address the camera as if testifying.
advisories:
Battle scenes, wounding and an attempted rape in prison; the burning at the stake.

Long and slow by design; the full version runs over five and a half hours in two parts.

title: Jeannette: The Childhood of Joan of Arc
decision: GREY: Content from Greydanus (Decent Films, B+, and Arts & Faith), Tushnet (The American Interest), Wikipedia and Eyefilm. The text is Péguy's and its theology is corrected within the film; the deliberately incongruous staging and the unresolved revolt are reservations a reader can weigh, not sacrilege presented approvingly.
summary: Bruno Dumont stages Charles Péguy's verse drama of Joan's childhood vocation as a musical for untrained children, from a cappella song to thrash metal, on the dunes of northern France.
synopsis: Domrémy, 1425, during the Hundred Years' War. Eight-year-old Jeannette minds her sheep, shares her bread with refugee children and cannot accept that God permits the war, the suffering and the damnation of souls; she turns the Our Father into a lament. Her friend Hauviette counsels trust. A Franciscan nun, Madame Gervaise, answers her at length: evil is real and all share in it, but Christ's redemption is present now, and Jeannette's wish to suffer hell in place of the damned is blasphemous. Jeannette is not fully satisfied. She has a vision of three saints, who call her to lead France against the English. Years later she persuades her uncle to help her reach the army, hesitates at the last moment, and finally slips away on the pretext of nursing a relative.
inclusion: Dumont shot on the dunes of the Côte d'Opale, cast local children who sing off-key and dance awkwardly to Philippe Decouflé's choreography, and gave the score to the metal musician Igorrr. Every word is Péguy's, from his 1910 Mystère de la charité de Jeanne d'Arc and his 1897 Jeanne d'Arc. Critics are divided. Variety's Peter Debruge called it a blasphemous assault. Eve Tushnet found it strange and often thrilling, a portrait of how unpredictably God breaks in. Steven D. Greydanus gave it B+ and called the eighteen-minute exchange with Madame Gervaise sublime, if close to ridiculous. Most agree the second half drags. Cahiers du cinéma placed it second in its 2017 list.
themes: The first half is a theological drama about the problem of evil and the damnation of souls, posed by a child and answered by a nun. Gervaise's reply is orthodox. The Redemption is present, suffering can be offered, and no one may wish to take on the pains of hell for others. The film leaves Jeannette restless and unconvinced, which is Péguy's point but also a risk. The vocation scene treats the saints' call as real. The style is deliberately incongruous: nuns pull off their wimples and headbang, and the dances are comic. Greydanus and Tushnet argue it is playful and not mocking; Dumont himself is an unbeliever. The second half, from Péguy's earlier socialist play, is more patriotic than religious.
history: Joan was born at Domrémy, probably in 1412, and first heard the voices of St. Michael, St. Margaret and St. Catherine in the summer of 1425, aged about thirteen. In 1428 and again in 1429 she went to Vaucouleurs, accompanied by a kinsman, to seek Robert de Baudricourt. She was burned at Rouen on 30 May 1431.
liberties: Dumont uses Péguy's words but cuts them heavily and stages them anachronistically, with modern dance, rap and metal. Joan's first call is moved from about thirteen to eight. Madame Gervaise is Péguy's invention, and the long theological debate is his and has no basis in the historical record.
advisories:
No violence beyond talk of war; no sexual content or bad language.

Long sung theological disputation.

Nuns headbang and the dancing is comic; some viewers will find this irreverent.

grey.question: Dumont, an unbeliever, stages Péguy's Catholic verse as a punk and metal musical: children dance, a nun pulls off her wimple and headbangs, and the saints sing. Catholic critics who know the film well, Greydanus and Tushnet, find it playful and orthodox in substance; Variety called it blasphemous. Jeannette's revolt against the damnation of souls is answered but leaves her unconvinced. Viewers must decide whether the style serves the text or cheapens it.

title: Everyman
decision: PUBLISH: Hofmannsthal's text (Projekt Gutenberg) is a Catholic morality: contrition, a monk's cleansing and the sacrament, faith joined to good works, and the Devil answered with Christ's atonement. Paimann's Filmlisten (contemporary Austrian trade review, via de.wikipedia) found the film faithful to the play apart from Salzburg-inspired settings, choreography and costumes, and the film-dienst review (organ of the German Catholic film commission, carried in the Lexikon des internationalen Films) called it a remarkable screen record of the Salzburg staging. Identity: filmdienst.de, Wikipedia.
summary: Gottfried Reinhardt films the Salzburg Festival's Everyman, Hofmannsthal's morality play of a rich man summoned by Death, deserted by friends and money, and saved by Faith and Good Works.
synopsis: God, grieved that men forget him, sends Death to summon Everyman (Walther Reyer), a rich man in his prime. Before Death comes, Everyman turns away a poor neighbour, has a debtor taken off to prison, brushes aside his mother's pleas to think of his soul, and feasts with his mistress (Ellen Schwiers). Death interrupts the banquet. Everyman begs for company on his journey and is refused by his friends, his cousins and his servants; Mammon (Paul Dahlke) mocks him. His Good Works (Sonja Sutter) are too weak to stand. Her sister Faith (Paula Wessely) teaches him the mercy of God and the power of contrition. He goes to be cleansed and returns in a white robe; the Devil (Heinrich Schweiger) comes to claim him and is turned away. Everyman goes into his grave with Good Works beside him.
inclusion: Hofmannsthal's Everyman has opened the Salzburg Festival almost every summer since 1920. This film preserves the 1961 production, with Walther Reyer, the festival's Everyman through the 1960s. Film-dienst called it a remarkable screen record of the Salzburg staging. It is filmed theatre and best taken as such, with rhymed verse, pageantry and a strong ensemble. For anyone who cannot get to Salzburg it is the nearest thing.
themes: The play is a Catholic morality about death and the particular judgement, the uselessness of wealth and friends at the end, and salvation through faith joined to works. Faith hears Everyman recite the articles of the Creed learned in childhood, teaches him Christ's atonement and the transforming power of contrition, and sends him to a monk to be cleansed; he later says he has received the sacrament. Good Works, crippled by his neglect, rise and go with him into the grave, and Faith answers the Devil that Christ has paid the debt. His mother, on her way to early Mass, hears the angels.
history: Hofmannsthal drew on the late-medieval morality plays, the English Everyman, the Dutch Elckerlijc and Hans Sachs's Hekastus among them. Max Reinhardt first staged it in Berlin in December 1911, and in 1920 it opened the first Salzburg Festival in front of the cathedral. Gottfried Reinhardt directed the festival production in 1961 and 1962, and the film was made during the 1961 festival.
advisories:
No violence; Death and the Devil may frighten young children.

A banquet with the rich man's mistress; nothing explicit.

In German; English subtitles may be hard to find.

Film-dienst recommended it from 14.

cast.name: Ewald Balser

names: Jedermann, play by Hugo von Hofmannsthal (1911)

suitability.note: Death and the Devil are played as frightening figures, and as filmed theatre in German verse it will be slow going for younger children.

doctrine: The play rests on the particular judgment. The Catholic Encyclopedia teaches that the eternal destiny of each soul is decided by God immediately after death, a doctrine drawn from the Second Council of Lyons (1274), the Council of Florence (1439) and Benedict XII's Benedictus Deus (1336). Everyman's abandonment by friends and wealth illustrates that nothing but grace and merit goes with the soul. The Council of Trent (Session VI) taught that faith, unless hope and charity are added to it, neither unites a man perfectly with Christ nor makes him a living member of His body (chapter 7), while faith is the beginning, foundation and root of all justification (chapter 8). That is the sense of Faith and Good Works standing together at the end. Trent also taught that grace is lost by mortal sin (chapter 15) and that no one can know with the certainty of faith that he has obtained the grace of God (chapter 9).
production: The running time is 96 minutes. It premiered on 24 November 1961 in Vienna and Salzburg, with a German release on 21 December 1961. Austria submitted it for the 34th Academy Awards, but it was not nominated. German film-service sources gave it an FSK 6 rating. Paimann's Filmlisten found it a faithful adaptation apart from its Salzburg settings, choreography and costumes.

title: Jesus
decision: REJECT (content): Christ is shown unsure of his mission until his mother pushes him, the Baptist asks him to confess his sins, and Satan’s visions of the Crusades frame the Church’s history as his failure; it ends with Christ in modern dress. Prior grey assessment: A Catholic-produced (Lux Vide/Rai) Life of Christ that keeps the Passion and Resurrection and, per the English bishops' film note, presents a Jesus aware of his divinity. The reservations are serious but weighable: a deliberately 'human' Jesus who seems unsure of his mission and is pushed into it by his mother; a Baptist who asks him to confess his sins; Satan's visions of wars fought in Christ's name, Crusades included, offered as an argument against the Cross; Mary Magdalene as a prostitute with brief nudity; and a closing scene of the risen Christ in modern dress. Subtitles would settle the Baptism and Gethsemane dialogue; if Jesus confesses sin, or the visions are endorsed rather than refused, it should be REJECT.
summary: Lux Vide's two-part Life of Christ for Rai and CBS, with Jeremy Sisto as a laughing, dancing Jesus and Satan in a modern suit.
synopsis: In Nazareth, Jesus (Jeremy Sisto), a carpenter troubled by recurring dreams of battles fought in his name, mourns Joseph (Armin Mueller-Stahl). Urged by his mother (Jacqueline Bisset), he goes to John for baptism, is tempted in the desert by a Satan in a modern suit, and gathers Peter and the others by the Sea of Galilee. He dances at Cana, heals, forgives the woman taken in adultery, takes in Mary Magdalene (Debra Messing) and is close to Mary and Martha of Bethany. A Roman courtier, Livio, explains events to Pilate (Gary Oldman), who watches Jesus as a political problem. After the entry into Jerusalem and the Last Supper, Satan returns in Gethsemane to show him the evil that will be done in his name. Jesus is arrested, denied by Peter, condemned and crucified, and rises. The film ends with him walking out among children in the present day.
inclusion: This was the most widely seen of Lux Vide's Bible films, a four-hour Life of Christ shot in Morocco and Malta with an international cast and an Emmy nomination. Its aim is a Jesus people can warm to. Sisto laughs, splashes his friends at a fountain and dances at Cana; the English bishops' film note credits him with breaking the habit of a Jesus who never smiles. The adultery scene and the walking on water are well handled, and Plugged In praises Peter's denial and the political scenes around the trial. Gary Oldman's Pilate gives the Roman side weight. Its weaknesses are a script that softens the Gospel's hard sayings, Satan's modern-dress visions, which date the film, and a television look. It is an example of how the post-conciliar 'human Jesus' approach looks on screen.
themes: The Incarnation is the film's concern, tilted heavily towards the human side; the bishops' note says it assumes Jesus is conscious of his divinity, and he speaks of himself as the way and the resurrection and the life. The Passion is told conventionally and the Resurrection is real. The problems lie in emphasis. Sin is played down, John preaches against injustice more than for repentance, and Jesus seems to need his mother's push to begin. The temptations show Satan arguing that the Cross will be wasted because Christians will kill in his name, a modern indictment of Christendom put in the devil's mouth. Mary Magdalene is a prostitute, a traditional Western identification.
liberties: Livio, the Roman courtier, is invented. Satan appears as a modern businessman and as a woman in red. Visions of medieval and modern wars, a witch-burning and a First World War battlefield are added. Joseph dies on screen and Jesus prays for him to be raised. A near-romantic closeness with Mary of Bethany is implied. The final scene moves the risen Christ into the present day.
advisories:
Crucifixion and scourging shown with moderate violence; battle scenes in the visions.

Mary Magdalene is presented as a prostitute, with brief nudity.

Suitable for teenagers and up; parents may want to watch with younger children.

A humanised Jesus who doubts his mission, a Baptist who asks him to confess sins, and visions blaming Christendom's wars on the Gospel: read the question above first.

title: Jesus of Nazareth
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred by subject: the first Mexican sound film on the life and Passion of Christ, with José Cibrián as Jesus and Aurora Walker as Our Lady. Identity is established by the New York State Motion Picture Division's licence record and a 2024 Mexican press article. But no source I could open describes how the Gospel is treated, which episodes are included or invented, or how Our Lady and the Apostles are presented, and no contemporary Catholic rating was found. Unverified, not PUBLISH, until the content is checked.
summary: José Díaz Morales's life of Christ, the first made in Mexico in the sound era, with José Cibrián as Jesus.
synopsis: The film follows the life of Christ as told in the Gospels, from His public ministry to the Passion and Crucifixion, with Aurora Walker as the Blessed Virgin, Adriana Lamar as Mary Magdalene, José Pidal as Judas and José Baviera as Pontius Pilate. Its characters include John the Baptist, the Samaritan woman at the well, the woman taken in adultery, the rich young man, the supper at Simon the Pharisee's house, Nicodemus, the trials before Annas, Caiaphas, Herod and Pilate, Barabbas, Veronica, and the two thieves crucified with Christ. It is not known whether the film shows the Nativity or the Resurrection, or how far it adds invented incidents.
inclusion: Made by Pereda Films in 1942 and released in the United States through Cinespano in 1943, Jesús de Nazareth was the first Mexican feature on the life of Christ, and it made a star of José Cibrián in the title role. The director, José Díaz Morales, was one of the Spanish exiles newly arrived in the Mexican studios, as were many of his crew. The film belongs to the cycle of Mexican religious pictures of the 1940s that also produced La Virgen Morena and Felipe de Jesús.
themes: As a Passion film, it deals in Christ's teaching and miracles, His rejection by the authorities, the betrayal by Judas, the trial before Pilate and the Crucifixion. The cast list suggests the familiar emphases of the period: the sorrowing Mother, the penitent Magdalene and a Judas given motives of his own.
history: Mexico's film industry boomed during the Second World War, and religious subjects were popular with audiences. Spanish exiles who had fled after the Civil War found work in the Mexican studios.
advisories: The scourging and Crucifixion of Christ.

grey.question: This is a life of Christ from Mexico's golden age, made for Catholic audiences. No independent review of it exists, and nothing describes which Gospel episodes it shows, what it invents, how it presents Our Lady, or whether Christ is shown as the Son of God. It is listed here pending a check of the dialogue script held by the New York State Archives, a contemporary review, or a viewing.

sources.title: Council of Trent, Twenty-second Session
sources.claims: Mass and the sacrifice of the Cross, chapters 1 and 2

suitability.note: The scourging and the Crucifixion are shown, though a 1942 black-and-white production is unlikely to be graphic. Older children familiar with the Gospels should manage it.

doctrine: The Council of Trent teaches that Christ instituted the Mass at the Last Supper to leave the Church a visible sacrifice that represents the bloody sacrifice of the Cross and applies its saving power (Session 22, chapter 1). The victim is one and the same, and only the manner of offering differs: Christ offered Himself once in blood on the Cross, and is offered in an unbloody manner on the altar (chapter 2). The Mass is truly propitiatory, for the living and for the dead not yet fully purified. A Passion film must therefore be judged by whether it shows the Cross as a true sacrifice for sin, and Christ as God and man and not as a martyr to a cause.
production: José Díaz Morales directed this 100-minute black-and-white sound film. A Mexican newspaper account (Crónica) calls Díaz Morales the first director to make the Passion the central subject of a film, and José Cibrián the first Christ on the Mexican screen in 1942. Cibrián, a Spanish actor, had a heavy-lidded expression, caused by ptosis, that suited the role. Díaz Morales helped begin the habit of casting Spanish actors as Jesus in Mexican cinema. It was licensed for exhibition in New York State in 1943 at 8,463 feet.

title: Jesus, Our Lord
decision: GREY: Identity from Wikipedia and Hispanopedia (both thinly referenced; García Riera's Historia documental del cine mexicano is the print source cited for production history). summary: The last of Miguel Zacarías's Mexican Gospel trilogy, with Claudio Brook as Christ, covers the public ministry, Passion and Ascension and was released on Holy Thursday 1971.
synopsis: Drawn from the four Gospels, the film covers Christ's public life (Claudio Brook) from his baptism by John to his death and the Ascension. Its scenes include the baptism, at which the young apostle John is shown seeking the Messiah through the Baptist; the Sermon on the Mount, filmed with Popocatépetl behind the crowd and with the Our Father placed in it; and the entry into Jerusalem, shot in the streets of Guanajuato. Rita Macedo appears as Our Lady. After the Crucifixion the film passes directly to Christ's appearance to the apostles and the Ascension, without showing the burial or the empty tomb.
inclusion: Mexican cinema produced a steady line of Gospel films, and Miguel Zacarías, a veteran of the industry, closed his trilogy, after Jesús, el niño Dios and Jesús, María y José, with this account of the ministry and Passion. It is a popular colour production made for Holy Week and shot on Mexican locations, with the volcano and colonial streets standing in for Galilee and Jerusalem, and Claudio Brook cast as Christ on his return to Mexico from Europe.
themes: The film is based on the four Gospels and keeps the familiar shape of a Life of Christ, with Our Lady present.
liberties: The apostle John appears at the Baptist's preaching seeking the Messiah, the Our Father is placed within the Sermon on the Mount, and the burial and Resurrection are skipped between the Crucifixion and the appearance to the apostles before the Ascension.
advisories:
The Passion and Crucifixion are shown; their intensity is not documented.

No other content concerns are reported.

title: Joan of Arc
alternateTitles: Joan of Arc: The Virgin Warrior
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred and broadly sympathetic, and St Joan was canonised in 1920. Not PUBLISH because the independent reviewer (Jim McLennan) notes the film declines to say whether her voices came from God, and the history is bent in ways that change the meaning of her trial: Cauchon is made Charles VII's own spiritual adviser and Charles is made more responsible for her death than the evidence allows, with hints of a romance with Jean de Metz. The only Catholic endorsement is from its present-day distributor, Ignatius Press. Subtitles of the voices and trial scenes would settle whether the treatment of her mission is sceptical or simply reticent.
summary: Christian Duguay's lavish two-part CBS/CBC Joan of Arc, carried by Leelee Sobieski's steady Joan and Peter O'Toole's Emmy-winning Cauchon, with large liberties in the politics.
synopsis: The film opens with Joan's burning and then returns to Domrémy, where a girl her parents (Powers Boothe and Jacqueline Bisset) had not wanted begins at eleven to hear voices. When soldiers burn the village and kill her blind friend, the voices tell her to put the Dauphin on the throne. At Vaucouleurs she wins an escort; at Chinon she sees through a courtier posing as Charles (Neil Patrick Harris) and convinces him. She raises the siege of Orléans and sees Charles crowned at Reims, but the court tires of her. Captured at Compiègne, she is sold to the English and tried at Rouen by Bishop Cauchon (Peter O'Toole), a churchman the film has placed at Charles's side. Abandoned by the king she crowned, she is condemned and burned.
inclusion: It is the most widely seen Joan of the television era, with thirteen Emmy nominations, an award for O'Toole as supporting actor, and a cast that includes Shirley MacLaine, Maximilian Schell, Olympia Dukakis and Robert Loggia. Leelee Sobieski, herself a teenager, plays Joan with a calm, unforced certainty that reviewers single out; Jim McLennan finds it the thing that holds the film together. The early scenes, with Joan feeding the poor and putting heart into her village, give her charity as well as courage. The middle is slow, the battles nearly bloodless, the Middle Ages are filmed in Czech snow, and the script reshapes the politics freely.
themes: Joan's voices, her loyalty to the anointed king and her trial before churchmen are all central. The film shows her praying, receiving guidance and holding to it under interrogation. Reviewers note that it does not commit itself on whether the voices were from God, and its star said publicly she was undecided. The trial is presented as a political manipulation, which matches the history.
history: Joan of Arc (c. 1412–1431) left Domrémy in 1429, relieved Orléans and saw Charles VII crowned at Reims. Captured at Compiègne in 1430, she was sold to the English and tried for heresy at Rouen by a court under Pierre Cauchon, Bishop of Beauvais, a partisan of the Anglo-Burgundian side. She was condemned as a relapsed heretic and burned on 30 May 1431. A papal retrial annulled the verdict in 1456.
liberties: Cauchon is made Charles VII's spiritual adviser, though he was always of the English and Burgundian party. Charles is shown as more responsible for her death than the evidence supports. Joan is an unwanted daughter whose blind friend is killed; her brother dies in battle, though in fact he lived to see her rehabilitated; a romance with Jean de Metz is hinted at. Several supporting characters are composites.
advisories:
Battle scenes, mostly bloodless; a village burned and a child killed; Joan's burning at the stake, shown at the start and end.

No sexual content beyond hinted romantic feeling.

grey.question: Sobieski's Joan prays, obeys her voices and holds firm at her trial, and the film is broadly sympathetic. But it does not commit itself on whether her voices came from God, and it reshapes the history in ways that alter the meaning of her death: Bishop Cauchon, who was always of the English party, is made Charles VII's own spiritual adviser, so the blame falls on the king and his churchmen. doctrine: Joan said her voices began in the summer of 1425, when she was about thirteen and a half, and named them as St Michael, St Margaret and St Catherine. The Catholic Encyclopedia notes she told her judges she saw them with her own eyes. The Church does not oblige belief in private revelations; approval says only that nothing in them is contrary to faith or morals, and the assent owed is human, not divine, faith (Benedict XIV). Her cause was introduced in 1869 by Mgr Dupanloup, Bishop of Orleans. Pius X published the decree of beatification on 11 April 1909 and Benedict XV canonised her in 1920.
production: This was a two-part miniseries produced by CBC and Alliance Atlantis, directed by Christian Duguay. It ran 140 minutes (180 uncut) and aired on CBS from 16 to 18 May 1999. title: The Annunciation of Marie
decision: PUBLISH: A faithful adaptation of Claudel's play, Catholic-centred throughout. Séquences (1992) gives a substantive independent account of its treatment: Violaine's threefold sacrifice, the communion of saints and the Christmas-night miracle. 24 Images (1992) dissents on style only. The 1992 Berlin ecumenical jury prize is a post-conciliar body and is cited for fact only.
summary: Alain Cuny's only film as director is a severe, stylised staging of Claudel's medieval mystery: a girl kisses a leper, loses everything, and revives her sister's dead child.
synopsis: On the farm of Combernon in medieval Champagne, Violaine Vercors is betrothed to Jacques Hury. Pierre de Craon, a master builder working on a church at Reims, has leprosy, and Violaine gives him a kiss of pity in farewell. Her sister Mara, who wants Jacques for herself, sees it and uses it against her. Violaine catches the disease and is cast out to live apart as a leper, and Jacques marries Mara. Years later, on Christmas night, Mara brings her dead baby to Violaine and demands that she give the child back to her alive. The child lives, and opens eyes the colour of Violaine's. At the end Violaine is brought home to die at the great farm table, as her father, Anne Vercors, returns.
inclusion: Cuny acted in Claudel's plays for decades, and before the poet died in 1955 he asked Cuny to film this one. Cuny made it in his eighties. The result is formal to the point of rigidity, with tight framing, slow, measured movement and verse spoken with deliberate solemnity. Opinion split along that line. Séquences, in 1992, called it a work of sublime elevation that asks the viewer to leave everyday concerns behind. 24 Images found Cuny's emphatic acting and over-worked photography at odds with the Bressonian austerity he was reaching for, while granting it some moments of grace. A 4K restoration was released in French cinemas in 2022.
themes: Claudel's subject is sacrifice and the communion of saints. As Séquences notes, following Claudel, Violaine gives herself three times, in pity for the leper, in love for the sister who takes her betrothed, and in faith, when she obtains the child's life. The child's new eyes, the sign of the miracle, bind the two sisters together. Suffering is shown as something that can be offered for others, a fully traditional idea. Cuny keeps the religious world of the play in view: a crucifix on the farmhouse wall, and the dalmatic lent by the nuns of Monsanvierge that Violaine wears at her betrothal.
liberties: The film follows Claudel's text and keeps its verse, so the changes are only in the staging. Exteriors were shot partly in Quebec, standing in for medieval Champagne, and the cast is largely non-professional.
advisories:
Leprosy is shown, and a dead infant is central to the climax.

No sexual content or strong language; a kiss of pity sets the plot in motion.

sources.claims: Roman Catechism principle; merits and satisfactions exchanged; Aquinas.

names: L'Annonce faite à Marie, play by Paul Claudel

suitability.note: Nothing graphic, but a leper, a dead infant and a miracle drive the story, and it is spoken in formal verse at a slow pace. Teenagers used to stage plays may follow it; younger children will not.

doctrine: The play rests on the communion of saints. The Catholic Encyclopedia states, from the Roman Catechism, that every pious and holy action done by one belongs and is profitable to all. Merits and satisfactions can be offered for others, which is the sense of Violaine's sacrifice for her sister and the child. Aquinas teaches that the measure is the degree of charity. Violaine's kiss to the leper is an act of mercy, and her miracle comes on Christmas night, the feast of the Incarnation. Claudel (1868-1955) wrote as a convert and set the play in the Middle Ages.
production: The film was shot in Montreal and at Civry-la-Forêt in France. It opened in France on 18 December 1991 and played at the Berlin festival in February 1992. It won the Prix Georges Sadoul in 1991. It was never released widely abroad.

title: The Apparition
decision: REJECT (editorial ruling, 2026-10-12): the catalogue does not include films about modern alleged apparitions; this one concerns a present-day apparition and its investigation by the post-conciliar Church. Prior assessment: Content from Greydanus (NCRegister), Brad Miner (The Catholic Thing), Aleteia, Johnny Alucard and CNC; identity from CNC and Wikipedia. Respectful and orthodox where it touches doctrine, but agnostic, set in the present-day Church, with a twist not yet verified. Subtitles are needed to state the ending exactly; if it mocks the faith rather than exposing a deception the Church was right to doubt, REJECT.
summary: Xavier Giannoli's long, serious mystery puts an agnostic war reporter on a Vatican commission examining a young novice's claim that the Virgin Mary appeared to her in south-eastern France.
synopsis: Jacques Mayano, a veteran reporter for Ouest-France, is back from the Middle East, where his photographer friend was killed. An official of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith asks him to join a canonical inquiry. In a small town in south-eastern France, Anna, an eighteen-year-old novice raised in foster homes, says she has seen the Virgin; thousands of pilgrims are coming. Her mentor, Father Borrodine, defies his bishop on her behalf, and a German Catholic promoter, Anton Meyer, is marketing her. The commission includes a sceptical theologian and a psychiatrist who wants to believe. Anna guards a bloodstained cloth she says Mary gave her. Jacques's search into her past leads to a missing friend, Meriem, and finally to the Middle East, where the truth about the apparition comes out.
inclusion: This is one of the few recent European films to take Catholic piety and Church procedure seriously. Giannoli built it from an article on canonical inquiries, and the detail of the process, the archive work, interviews and medical examinations, and the commerce round a new shrine, is unusually exact. Vincent Lindon is excellent as the grieving investigator, and Galatéa Bellugi keeps Anna opaque. Greydanus calls it an earnest, curious exploration of doubt and faith; Brad Miner calls it a very Catholic film; Aleteia's critic found it honest and respectful of the Church's judgment. Its faults are length (144 minutes), sprawling subplots and a resolution that Greydanus finds clever but thinly worked out.
themes: The film treats the Church's caution as a virtue: the commission exists to separate fact from fraud, and Jacques's honesty is put at its service. Anna's message, to help the poor and build a house of prayer, is simple and orthodox, and her prayer is shown as sincere. Greydanus corrects the film's sceptical theologian, who argues that Mary cannot be linked with violence, by pointing to the Sorrowful Mother. The relic is the weak point, since apparitions do not traditionally leave objects behind. The ending is agnostic about the supernatural; its interest is in the cost of truth. The setting is the present-day Church, presented without irony.
advisories:
Brief medical nudity: a woman's breasts are exposed during defibrillation.

Several obscenities.

Disturbing images and themes, including war trauma and a death; better for older teenagers and adults.

sources.title: Revelations, Private
sources.claims: Meaning of Church approval; Benedict XIV on human faith; criteria of discernment.

suitability.note: Brief medical nudity, some obscenities, war trauma and a death. It is a long, quiet investigation that younger viewers will find slow and teenagers will need some background to follow.

doctrine: The film's central point is the Church's traditional caution toward private revelation. The Catholic Encyclopedia says that when the Church approves such a revelation it declares only that there is nothing in it contrary to faith or morals and that it may be read with profit; belief is not required, and the assent owed is human, not Catholic, faith (Benedict XIV). Divine origin is best shown by miracles or exactly fulfilled prophecy; otherwise judgement rests on the visionary's character, the agreement of the message with Church teaching, and its fruits. Visionaries can be wrong about details. The message the film gives Anna, to care for the poor and build a house of prayer for Christ, is orthodox.
production: Xavier Giannoli co-wrote the script with Jacques Fieschi and Marcia Romano, and Olivier Delbosc produced. Filming took place in Gap in the Hautes-Alpes, in Rome, at the Zaatari refugee camp in Jordan and in the Île-de-France. Éric Gautier shot it. It opened in France on 14 February 2018, and Music Box Films released it in the United States on 7 September 2018. It runs 144 minutes. Critics were generally positive (73 per cent on Rotten Tomatoes). The reviewer for the National Catholic Register praised its focus on the Church's investigative process but found the ending unsatisfying and disputed the theologian's objection to the bloodstained shroud.

title: Faith
decision: REJECT (content): forbidden at release by Cardinal Segura of Seville under pain of mortal sin and condemned by the Bishop of Barcelona. Under the pre-conciliar standard the ordinaries’ prohibition outweighs Ecclesia’s adults-only rating. Prior grey assessment: Content is established in detail by Fernando Sanz Ferreruela's 2018 study: a young priest's doubts, raised by an unbeliever's books, are resolved; the unbeliever converts and dies reconciled; a devout young woman who falls in love with the priest falsely accuses him, and repents and confesses on her deathbed. The film was declared of National Interest, and the scholar reads it as an exaltation of the priesthood. But the contemporary Church judgment was sharply divided: Bishop Modrego of Barcelona warned his faithful not to see or promote it, and Cardinal Segura forbade it in Seville under pain of mortal sin, while Ecclesia rated it 3 (adults only, of formed judgment). A pre-conciliar episcopal condemnation is more than a Legion B, so this is a serious reservation; the editor may judge it REJECT.
summary: Rafael Gil's adaptation of Palacio Valdés: a young Asturian curate's faith is shaken by an atheist's books and a penitent's infatuation, and restored by a false accusation and prison.
synopsis: Newly ordained, Fr Luis Lastra is sent as curate to Peñascosa, in Asturias, and lodges with the gruff old parish priest, Don Miguel. He takes on the spiritual direction of Marta Osuna, a rich young woman given to fasts and mortifications, and sets out to win back Don Álvaro Montesinos, a cultivated man who lost his faith when his wife left him. To answer Montesinos he reads his rationalist books, with permission, and begins to doubt; he burns them. When Montesinos lies dying, Luis can barely pray, but the atheist, moved by the priest's goodness, asks for him, believes and confesses. Marta asks Luis to escort her to a convent; on the way she declares her love, her father overtakes them, and she accuses Luis of seducing her. He is tried, convicted and accepts prison. A train crash leaves Marta dying; she confesses the truth and Luis absolves her.
inclusion: The novel's reputation in Catholic Spain was poor, and that is the background to the film's story. Rafael Gil, who made Reina santa the same year, and the producer Cesáreo González reworked Armando Palacio Valdés's 1892 novel under close censorship, and the result won Gil a special prize from the Círculo de Escritores Cinematográficos and medals for Amparo Rivelles and Camino Garrigó. Sanz Ferreruela points to an effective scene in which the voices of the rationalist book and the Gospel alternate in the priest's head over images of the crucifix. The two plots are cut together like instalments, and the ending, with a train crash conveniently delivering a deathbed confession, is pure melodrama. Its interest is as the first Spanish film of the period to put a priest's doubts and good name at the centre, and as a case study of how the Church of its day judged such a film.
themes: The film is about faith tested and confirmed. Fr Luis's doubts come from reading forbidden rationalist books, and he answers them by returning to the Gospels; the atheist's deathbed conversion, prompted by the priest's goodness, restores the priest's own faith. The second test is calumny, which he bears as Christ bore it, accepting prison with 'Thy will be done'. Both stories end in confession and absolution. The film keeps the priest chaste and orthodox throughout, but it does show a priest whose prayers falter at a deathbed, and a penitent's infatuation with her confessor; that is what the bishops objected to as an affront to the dignity of the clergy.
history: Armando Palacio Valdés published La fe in 1892; parts of Spanish Catholic opinion called it impious and anticlerical, and he later added a preface defending himself. Rafael Gil submitted his outline to the censors in 1945; the religious member of the board judged the difficulties almost insuperable. The film opened in October 1947, was declared of National Interest, and was then condemned by the Bishop of Barcelona, Gregorio Modrego, whose warning was taken up by the Archbishop of Zaragoza, and forbidden in Seville by Cardinal Pedro Segura on 1 December 1947.
liberties: The film softens the novel throughout: it removes much of the debate between faith and science, keeps the priest's conduct beyond reproach, and adds the deathbed conversions and confessions that close both plots. Peñascosa stands for Luanco in Asturias.

A young woman's infatuation with her confessor and a false accusation of seduction; nothing improper occurs.

Contemporary Catholic judgment: condemned by the Bishop of Barcelona and forbidden by Cardinal Segura in Seville; rated adults only by Ecclesia.

title: The Birth, the Life and the Death of Christ
decision: PUBLISH: Identity from Silent Era's Progressive Silent Film List and Wikipedia (citing Abel, McMahan, Hebron and Foster); Dennis Schwartz's independent review and the scholarship summarised by Wikipedia establish a traditional 25-tableau Gospel life from Bethlehem to the Resurrection, modelled on Tissot's Bible, with Jesuit consultants per Guy's memoirs (via McMahan). The NCRegister piece is present-day Catholic and used for content only. No doctrinal objection.
summary: Alice Guy's Gaumont Life of Christ stages the Gospel in 25 tableaux modelled on Tissot's paintings, from the arrival at Bethlehem to the Resurrection.
synopsis: Mary and Joseph arrive in Bethlehem, Christ is born and the Magi come to the manger. Short scenes of the public life follow: the Samaritan woman, the raising of Jairus's daughter and the woman who washes Christ's feet. After the entry into Jerusalem on Palm Sunday and the Last Supper, the film follows the Passion closely: the agony in the garden, the night watch, Judas's betrayal, Christ before Caiaphas, Peter's denial, the trial before Pilate, the scourging and the Ecce Homo. On the way of the cross Christ falls, Veronica wipes his face and the procession climbs to Golgotha. After the Crucifixion, the agony and the descent from the cross, Christ is laid in the tomb. The last tableau is the Resurrection.
inclusion: Gaumont's answer to Pathé's Passion was the most ambitious film Alice Guy made in France, with some 300 extras and sets by Henri Menessier. Guy based the sets and costumes on James Tissot's watercolours of the life of Christ, and the compositions often look like them. The exteriors give the film more air than its rivals. Historians single out a cut-in to a medium shot as Veronica holds out the veil, and a pan following the climb to Golgotha, both unusual in 1906. Richard Abel notes the attention given to the women around Christ. The acting is broad and the camera mostly static.
themes: This is a traditional Gospel harmony in Catholic dress. Most of the running time goes to the Passion, which follows the order of the Gospels and adds the third-century tradition of Veronica's veil, a scene of the Stations of the Cross. Christ's miracles and his forgiveness of the penitent woman are shown plainly. Guy recalled in her memoirs that she hired two Jesuits who had recently been in the Holy Land as advisers. Gwendolyn Audrey Foster criticises its casting of Black figures, apart from one of the Magi, in hostile roles.
advisories:
Stylised scourging and Crucifixion.

Silent, with title cards naming each scene.

Suitable for children.

sources.claims: Name from vera icon; legends vary; pious traditions cannot be documented

sources.title: Way of the Cross
sources.claims: Veronica as sixth station; fourteen fixed by Clement XII in 1731; general erection from late seventeenth century

names: The illustrated Bible of James Tissot (French edition, 1896), used as documentation for sets and costumes

suitability.note: The scourging and Crucifixion are stylised and bloodless. The main hurdle for young children is reading the titles and knowing the Gospel story.

doctrine: Most of the film follows the Gospels. The exception is Veronica wiping Christ's face on the way to Calvary. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1912) says the name comes from vera icon, 'true image', the title of the oldest Roman image of the Holy Face, which popular belief turned into a woman's name; it adds that the pious traditions about her 'cannot be documented', and the Gospels do not name her. It is a devotion, not a doctrine. She is the sixth of the fourteen Stations of the Cross. The Encyclopedia notes that many earlier accounts omit her, that the Stations were not widely erected until about the end of the seventeenth century, and that Clement XII fixed the number at fourteen in 1731.
production: Alice Guy (1873-1968), head of production at Gaumont, made the film in 1905-06, with Victorin Jasset handling exteriors and extras; for decades it was credited to Jasset alone. It was shot at the Buttes-Chaumont studios and in the forest of Fontainebleau, in 25 tableaux, and runs about 33 minutes. Gaumont sold it as single scenes or as a whole. It came out in January 1906 in France and the United States. The American release by the Mutoscope and Bioscope Company followed on 5 January 1907, and the surviving print is of that version.

title: The Virgin of Guadalupe
decision: PUBLISH: The Legion of Decency classed it A-I as The Virgin of Guadalupe (La Virgen Morena), the pre-conciliar Catholic judgment. Independent contemporary reviews in Motion Picture Herald (John Stuart Jr.), The Exhibitor and Variety (May-June 1943) describe a reverent, well-made telling of the Tepeyac apparitions within a story of the Church defending the Indians against Spanish soldiers. The scenario was by the Jesuit Carlos M. de Heredia and carried the Archbishop of Mexico's endorsement. Juan Diego (beatified 1990) is a character, not the subject; rule (a) does not apply, and he is not given a title.
summary: Gabriel Soria's account of the 1531 apparitions at Tepeyac, written by a Jesuit historian of the shrine, sets Juan Diego's vision against the last struggle between Spaniards and Aztecs.
synopsis: December 1531. Spanish soldiers under a ruthless captain burn and pillage villages of Indians who have become Christians. The Bishop of Mexico begs the Viceroy to stop the cruelty, which is turning the Indians against the faith and keeping the Aztec prince Temoc from agreeing a truce. In reprisal Temoc seizes the Viceroy's daughter, Doña Blanca, as a hostage; the captain recovers her and nearly wipes out the prince's people. Temoc, who has fallen in love with her, brings her back himself and surrenders. Meanwhile the Virgin appears to a poor Indian, Juan Diego, on the hill of Tepeyac and asks for a church there. The bishop's household demands a sign. She sends him to gather roses, and when he opens his cloak before the bishop and the people, her image is on it. Temoc kneels, and the Viceroy has the captain arrested.
inclusion: This is the more straightforward of the two Guadalupe films Mexico made in 1942. Its story came from Fr Carlos M. de Heredia, SJ, a historian of the shrine, and the film opened with the endorsement of the Archbishop of Mexico. The trade press in New York liked it. Motion Picture Herald called the screenplay well contrived and the production values excellent, The Exhibitor found it attention-holding and authentic, and Variety said it was done in excellent taste. José Luis Jiménez, as Juan Diego, was named Mexico's outstanding screen discovery of 1942.
themes: The apparition is presented as a miracle and as the turning point in the conversion of Mexico. The film sets the bishop and the friars against the soldiers. The Church defends the converted Indians against Spanish cruelty, which threatens their faith. Our Lady appears to the poorest of them, the bishop asks for a sign, and the image on the cloak convinces both the Spanish and the Aztec prince, who kneels in submission to the faith. Motion Picture Herald summed up its theme as the simple, sincere faith that is credited with evoking miracles.
history: According to the tradition recorded in the Nican Mopohua, Our Lady appeared four times in December 1531 to Juan Diego, a baptised Indian, on the hill of Tepeyac north of Mexico City, asked that a church be built there, and left her image on his tilma as a sign for Bishop Juan de Zumárraga. The image is venerated in the basilica at Tepeyac.
liberties: Temoc, Doña Blanca, the captain and the hostage story are inventions to dramatise the conquest. The reviews describe the bishop's household doubting Juan Diego and the image appearing before a large gathering; tradition has the tilma opened before the bishop in his house. The 'last battle between Spaniards and Aztecs' in 1531 is a dramatic licence, since Tenochtitlan fell in 1521.
advisories:
Burning of villages, battle scenes and killings.

An abduction; a chaste romance between the prince and the hostage.

Suitable for older children and up.

doctrine: The Church has not defined the apparitions as an article of faith. Pious belief in them rests on tradition and on the cultus the popes have approved. Benedict XIV declared Our Lady of Guadalupe patroness of New Spain in 1754, and Leo XIII authorised her canonical coronation in 1887, carried out in 1895. The bishop's demand for a sign is the Church's ordinary prudence in testing alleged apparitions.
production: The film was made in Mexico for Maya Films and shot in 1942; it opened on 15 May 1943 and runs about 98 minutes. Julián Carrillo composed the music for the apparition scene in his microtonal 'Sonido 13' system, which a Spanish-language source calls the first experimental non-tonal score in Mexican film. In the United States it was released as The Virgin of Guadalupe, and the Legion of Decency listed it in class A-I.

title: The Miracle Roses
decision: GREY: Identity (Wikipedia citing García Riera, Historia documental del cine mexicano) and outline (ADN40, Posta) are established: a conquest-era drama ending in the 1531 Guadalupe apparitions and the miracle of the roses. No review or Catholic rating found. Juan Diego (beatified 1990) is a character, not the subject; rule (a) does not apply, following la-virgen-que-forjo-una-patria-1942. Unverified.
summary: Julián Soler's historical drama of the conquest of Mexico and the 1531 apparitions of Our Lady of Guadalupe to Juan Diego, ending with the roses and the image.
synopsis: The film is set in the years of the Spanish conquest. Its characters include Moctezuma (Crox Alvarado), an Aztec high priest (Andrés Soler) and invented Aztec figures, among them Tlaltecalzin (Armando Silvestre), Nanoaltzin (Jaime Fernández) and Citlali (Magda Urvizu), with Hernán Cortés (Manuel Calvo) and Bishop Juan de Zumárraga (Francisco Jambrina) for the Spaniards. The story leads to 1531, when the Virgin (Lilia del Carmen Camacho) appears to the Indian Juan Diego (Jorge Martínez de Hoyos) at Tepeyac and asks for a church to be built there. The title refers to the sign she gives: Castilian roses gathered out of season, and her image on Juan Diego's cloak before the bishop.
inclusion: Mexican cinema returned several times to Guadalupe. This 1960 version, written by Alfonso Patiño Gómez and directed by the experienced Julián Soler, sets the apparitions against the conquest itself. Jorge Martínez de Hoyos, a respected character actor, plays Juan Diego. Present-day Mexican press pieces call it a forgotten landmark and describe a mix of historical drama and spirituality in which the Virgin's image is offered as a sign of hope for the Indian people. Emilio García Riera covers it in his documentary history of Mexican cinema.
themes: The film dramatises the apparition of Our Lady of Guadalupe in 1531, long venerated and approved by the Church, and the foundation of Mexican Catholic devotion. By the press accounts, it presents the Virgin's image as a sign of hope for the Indians and shows the meeting of Aztec religion and the Catholic faith.
advisories:
Conquest-era conflict and Aztec religion are part of the story; how violence or sacrifice is shown is not documented.

Juan Diego was beatified only in 1990; he is a character here, not the subject, and is given no title.

grey.question: This pre-conciliar Mexican film tells the Guadalupe apparitions against the Spanish conquest, with Moctezuma, Cortés and Bishop Zumárraga among its characters and the miracle of the roses as its climax. No independent review or contemporary Catholic rating of it exists, so how it handles the conquest, Aztec religion or the apparitions themselves is unknown. A Mexican Catholic rating, García Riera's entry or the film itself would settle it.

suitability.note: Nothing about it suggests a problem for families, though how violence or sacrifice is shown is not documented.

doctrine: The cult is old and has been honoured by several popes. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1912) records that Bishop Montúfar opened a canonical inquiry in 1556, that Benedict XIV named Our Lady of Guadalupe national patron and made 12 December a holy day of obligation with an octave, that Leo XIII ordered the picture crowned in his name, and that Pius X allowed the Mass of Our Lady of Guadalupe on the twelfth of each month and granted indulgences. The Encyclopedia also states what approval of a private revelation means: the Church declares only that there is nothing in it contrary to faith or morals; no one is obliged to believe it. The feast is 12 December.
history: According to the account in the Catholic Encyclopedia, on Saturday 9 December 1531 a neophyte, fifty-five years old, named Juan Diego was going down Tepeyac hill to hear Mass in Mexico City when the Virgin appeared and sent him to Bishop Juan de Zumárraga to ask for a temple on the spot. The bishop had not immediately believed him and had him watched, then asked for a sign. On 12 December, when Juan Diego unfolded his cloak before the bishop, roses fell out and the image of the Virgin was on the cloak.

title: The Satin Slipper
decision: PUBLISH: A Catholic-centred adaptation of Claudel's play. Gonçalves (Études littéraires) establishes that it keeps the essentials of Claudel's text, and two independent critics, R. Emmet Sweeney and Joe Bendel, document the religious frame: the Jesuit's prayer for his brother, the slipper left with the Virgin, the Guardian Angel and the lovers' renunciation. The adulterous love is renounced, not approved, and that is stated in the advisories. No contemporary Catholic rating was found.
summary: Manoel de Oliveira films most of Claudel's vast Catholic drama as open theatre: a married woman and a conquistador love each other, renounce each other, and are parted for decades.
synopsis: Spain's Golden Age, with the whole world for a stage. A Jesuit lashed to the mast of a sinking ship prays for his younger brother, Rodrigue, that he may come to God even by way of his passions. Doña Prouhèze, married to an older nobleman, loves Rodrigue and is loved in return. Before going to meet him she leaves her satin slipper with a statue of the Virgin, so that if she runs towards evil it will be with a limping foot. Her Guardian Angel keeps watch over her. The King sends Rodrigue to govern in the Americas and Prouhèze to hold the African fortress of Mogador. Her letter reaches him ten years late. When he finally comes to Mogador they are kept apart, and she dies in the fortress. Years later the maimed and disgraced Rodrigue meets her daughter, Sept-Épées.
inclusion: Claudel's play runs about eleven hours uncut and is rarely staged. Oliveira's version keeps the essentials of the text, as Luís Carlos Pimenta Gonçalves notes, and refuses to make it realistic. It opens on an audience filing into a theatre; the camera is mostly static, the takes are long, the sea is painted papier-mâché and the whales are cardboard. Joe Bendel argues that this stylisation lets the angel scenes work where 1980s effects would have failed, and he singles out Patricia Barzyk's Prouhèze as a great tragic heroine. R. Emmet Sweeney credits the film with making the religious fire of Claudel's world recognisable again. It is talky, heavy with exposition, and some of the comic interludes drag. It is the only complete screen version of the play.
themes: The play is about desire offered up and not indulged. Prouhèze's gesture with the slipper is its emblem, since she does not trust herself and binds herself through Our Lady. The Jesuit's prayer in the opening scene and the Guardian Angel who argues with her make it plain that the lovers' separation is the work of grace. The question the play asks is how God can use even a forbidden love, and its answer is renunciation. The setting is the Spanish Catholic empire at full stretch, and Rodrigue's worldly ambitions are judged as well as admired.
history: Paul Claudel (1868–1955) published Le Soulier de satin in 1929. It was first staged in 1943 in an abridged version prepared by Claudel and Jean-Louis Barrault; complete stagings came only later, notably at the Avignon Festival in 1987.
liberties: Oliveira keeps the play's structure and most of its text, so the changes are only in form. He frames the action as a performance, opens on an audience entering a theatre, and keeps painted backdrops and visible stage artifice throughout. Some secondary material is shortened.
advisories:
No sexual scenes. The love is spoken of and the lovers never consummate it.

Very long (about seven hours, with an intermission) and wordy.

The central love is adulterous in desire, and the play judges it.

suitability.note: It runs about seven hours and is dense, wordy French verse theatre, which only patient adults and older teenagers will sit through.

doctrine: The play touches two points of doctrine. The first is the Guardian Angel, who argues with Prouhèze. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) says the doctrine that every soul has a guardian angel has never been defined and is not an article of faith, but is the mind of the Church; it cites Matthew 18:10 and St Thomas (Summa I, 113, 4), who held that only the lowest order of angels guard men and that they act on our senses and imagination, not directly on our will. The second is marriage. Pius XI's Casti Connubii (31 December 1930) taught that 'what God hath joined together let no man put asunder' (paragraph 32) and that adultery does not loose the bond (paragraph 88, citing Trent). Prouhèze is married.
production: Oliveira's film runs 410 minutes and is in French and Portuguese. It was shown at the Venice Film Festival in 1985, where it won the Sergio Trasatti Award, and was released on 8 January 1986. A drastically shortened version was shown at the New York Film Festival the same year.
