title: Miracles of Thursday
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (apparitions, popular devotion, St Dismas); the Spanish Church's rating was 3R, adults with reservations (La Cabecita), and the censorship history is from es.wikipedia (citing Marcos Molano and Álvarez Sanz, 2019). The English-subtitled version read 2026-10-12 is the pious one: the stranger calls himself a good thief saved by a miracle, cures seem real, the parish priest keeps his distance from the fraud, and the closing reveal identifies Martino as St Dismas. Reservation stands: the 'saint' works through mirrors, staged illnesses and a gold bribe, the mockery of credulous devotion remains, and the plotters' confession is a farce.
summary: Berlanga's satire of a spa town that fakes a saint's apparition to bring back visitors, turned by the censors into a fable in which the real St Dismas intervenes.
synopsis: Fontecilla's spa is dying. Envying Lourdes and Fátima, five notables, the mayor, the doctor, the schoolmaster, a landowner and the spa owner, stage an apparition of St Dismas, the Good Thief, with one of them dressed as the saint. Fireworks fool Mauro, the village simpleton; the next Thursday a devout woman sees it too, and crowds gather. The parish priest, Don Fidel, takes their money for the poor but will not endorse a miracle. On the third Thursday the stunt collapses. A mysterious stranger, Martino (Richard Basehart), then arrives, knows all about the hoax and seems to help it along with tricks of his own, while a lost dog comes home and a sick child recovers. When the plotters try to confess publicly, the crowd will not listen. In his long-empty room they find a picture of the real St Dismas: the stranger himself.
inclusion: Berlanga, the great Spanish satirist of the 1950s, wanted a sharp comedy about the commercial use of religion. A Dominican, Father Garau, was imposed as adviser, and extra scenes were shot by Jorge Grau. The result is two films in one: a funny, well-cast village comedy with José Isbert and Manuel Alexandre, and a pious fable grafted on. It flopped on its Spanish release in 1959 and drew objections from both traditionalists and progressives. Spanish critics now count it among Berlanga's classics, and the Filmoteca Española has restored it from two versions.
themes: Its subject is the abuse of devotion, with notables who manufacture a miracle for money and a gullible faithful. The imposed ending turns this round. The stranger calls himself a thief made good by a miracle, says St Dismas will return with a single word, faith, and is finally revealed as the saint, so grace works through and despite human fraud. But his methods are tricks, staged illnesses and a bribe of gold, which leaves the miraculous ambiguous. The parish priest is the sanest figure. He clears the church of a mob seeking cures.
history: In the 1950s reports of the Virgin appearing to children every Thursday at Cuevas de Vinromà, in Castellón, drew pilgrims. Berlanga visited the site with his family and took the idea for the film from it.
advisories:
No violence or sexual content of note.

Comic mockery of credulous devotion and a staged apparition; the 'saint' uses tricks and a bribe.

For teenagers and adults. The Spanish Catholic rating was 3R (adults, with reservations).

Two versions exist, and the English-subtitled copy has the pious ending.

sources.title: Private Revelations
sources.claims: Meaning of Church approval; Benedict XIV on human faith; signs of genuine revelation; fraud and diabolical deception

grey.question: Berlanga set out to satirise a town that fakes a saint's apparition for profit; the censors, a Dominican adviser and new producers turned the ending into a fable in which the real St Dismas arrives in disguise. In the version with English subtitles the parish priest refuses to endorse the fraud and cures seem real, but the stranger works through tricks and bribes, and the mockery of credulous devotion remains. Whether the satire of popular faith outweighs the pious ending is for the viewer to weigh.

suitability.note: The concern is the comic mockery of a staged apparition and of credulous piety. Teenagers who know what a real approved apparition is will follow the joke.

doctrine: The film plays on the Church's caution about apparitions. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1912) says that when the Church approves a private revelation she declares only that it contains nothing contrary to faith or morals and may be read with profit; no one is bound to believe it, and Benedict XIV described the assent due as human faith resting on prudence, not Catholic faith. Its tests of a genuine revelation include a holy, humble visionary with no self-interest, content that agrees with Church teaching, and fruits of peace. The same source warns that the devil can deceive visionaries and that enthusiasm and frivolous content are suspect. Don Fidel's refusal to call the Thursday events a miracle, and his statement that priests are not miracle workers, are the Church's own prudence.
production: This was Berlanga's fifth feature. Censors rejected the first script in 1956 because it showed a false miracle, which they thought could make people doubt real apparitions. Filming began in June 1956 at the Chamartín studios, mostly at Alhama de Aragón with additional scenes at Bubierca. Midway through production the company was sold to a firm linked to Opus Dei, and further scenes were shot later under government orders. The film premiered in Madrid on 2 February 1959. It won a prize at the Valladolid Catholic film festival in 1958 and the Círculo de Escritores Cinematográficos medal for best original screenplay.

title: Magnificat
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (Holy Week, a pilgrimage to a Marian monastery, the monastic office, a girl's entry into the cloister) and taken seriously by independent critics, who call it Avati's best film and a study of the human need for faith. The reservations are content and stance: graphic executions (a drowning and a drawing and quartering), a young couple subjected to the jus primae noctis, a concubine's desperate efforts to bear a son, and a narrator who stresses the period's superstition; La Stampa's critic asked whether it is a religious work at all. Its Italian age rating is 16+. No CCC/CNVF judgment has been traced.
summary: Pupi Avati's austere Cannes competition film follows pilgrims, an executioner and a girl entering the cloister through one Holy Week in tenth-century Italy.
synopsis: In Holy Week of the year 926, in a small kingdom of the Pentapolis, several journeys converge on the Monastery of the Visitation at Malfole. The executioner Folco, still grieving for his son, takes on a young assistant, Baino, and travels to carry out a drowning and a quartering. The king's concubine Roza, pregnant, goes to the monastery, whose relic of Our Lady's garment is said to protect women in childbirth. Margherita, a fourteen-year-old girl, is brought there by her father to enter the cloister. A monk tours the religious houses recording those who died over the winter. The dying lord of Malfole divides his goods among his bastard sons, and a young peasant couple marry under their lord's right to the wedding night. A narrator comments on the customs and fears of the age.
inclusion: Avati, better known abroad for comedies and gialli, made this as a near-documentary of belief in the early Middle Ages, and Italian critics often name it his best work. It has no single plot. Matt Blake (The Wild Eye) compares it to Pasolini's medieval films with the bawdiness removed and calls it an almost anthropological study of trials, executions, weddings, childbirth and monastic rule; he finds it slow and unstructured but compulsive. Cesare Bastelli's photography of Abruzzese abbeys and churches, Riz Ortolani's spare score and the costumes are its strengths. The Christian Science Monitor's Cannes reviewer called it brilliant and noted how one faith yields both brutal violence and the comfort of the Church's rites.
themes: The film is about faith in a hard world, with Holy Week, pilgrimage, relics, monastic life and death set under the title of Our Lady's canticle. Avati said he went back a thousand years to a time when faith was needed to face God's silence. Margherita's entry into the cloister is its clearest image of consecration. But the film is as interested in superstition and cruelty as in grace. Christian justice is shown through executions, and a lord's claim on a peasant bride stands unchallenged.
advisories:
Graphic executions, a woman drowned and a man drawn and quartered.

A lord exercises the 'right of the first night' over a peasant bride; a concubine's pregnancy; implied sexual content.

sources.title: Magnificat
sources.claims: Luke 1:46-55, use at Vespers in the Roman Breviary, Caesarius of Arles.

grey.question: Magnificat is built around Holy Week, a pilgrimage to a Marian monastery and a girl's entry into the cloister, and critics read it as a film about the need for faith. But it lingers on cruelty. A drowning and a drawing and quartering are shown, a lord claims a peasant bride's wedding night, and a narrator stresses the superstition of the age. One leading Italian critic asked whether it is a religious film at all. It is for adults, and viewers must judge whether it treats medieval faith as true or only as a refuge.

suitability.note: Graphic executions and a lord's claim on a peasant bride, with implied sexual content, make it a film for adults.

doctrine: The title is the canticle of Mary in Luke 1:46-55, which the Catholic Encyclopedia calls the last canticle of the Old Testament and the first of the New. The Roman Breviary assigns it to Vespers every day, and the Rule of Caesarius of Arles (before 502) already gave it to Lauds. At solemn Vespers the celebrant incenses the altar during it. Its place in the Divine Office is why a convent of nuns is the film's goal, since the choir's daily prayer is the work the girl is entering.
production: Part of it was shot in Abruzzo: at the abbey of San Liberatore a Maiella, the church at Bominaco and Santa Maria in Valle Porclaneta at Rosciolo dei Marsi. It was in competition at the 1993 Cannes Festival. Cannes sets the story at the end of the tenth century, and Italian Wikipedia dates it to Holy Week 926. Sissi Parravicini won the 1994 Ciak d'oro for costumes. Cannes lists 100 minutes.

title: Marcellino
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (friary, foundling, crucifix in the attic) with identity established (offi.fr, Movieplayer, Box Office Mojo), and the original author, Sánchez Silva, shares the screenplay credit. No review of how it treats the faith was found. Subtitles of the crucifix scenes and the ending would settle it.
summary: Luigi Comencini's remake of Marcelino, pan y vino: a foundling raised by friars, who longs for his mother and finds a friend in the crucifix in their attic.
synopsis: A baby boy is left at a small, poor friary. The friars cannot trace his parents and raise him themselves. Marcellino grows up happy and mischievous, but he longs for the mother he has never known, whom he imagines as the Virgin Mary. A local count takes him in and has him educated, but the boy runs back to the friars. In the attic he finds a large crucifix, and a friendship begins between the child and the Christ on the cross that changes his life. In the original story the boy brings food to the figure, Christ speaks to him, and the friendship ends with the boy's death as he asks to see his mother. It is unknown how far the remake follows that ending.
inclusion: José María Sánchez Silva's story was filmed by Ladislao Vajda in 1955 as Marcelino, pan y vino, and that version is the classic. Comencini, best known for his films about children, among them Incompreso and the television Pinocchio, remade it near the end of his career.
themes: The original story turns on a child's simple charity towards Christ crucified, answered by Christ himself, and on the boy's longing for his mother, fulfilled in death. Comencini's version keeps the friary, the foundling, the boy's longing for a mother he pictures as Our Lady, and the crucifix in the attic.
liberties: The remake adds a nobleman who takes the boy in and has him educated before he returns to the friars. Listings disagree on the period, with an Italian one placing it in fifteenth-century Italy and a French one in seventeenth-century Tuscany.
advisories:
No violence or sexual content is reported.

Made as a family film.

doctrine: The central scene is a child bringing food to the crucifix. The Council of Trent (session 13, 11 October 1551) taught that Christ, true God and true man, is truly, really and substantially present in the Eucharist under the appearances of bread and wine (chapter 1), that the whole substance of the bread and wine is converted into his body and blood, 'Transubstantiation' (chapter 4), and that the faithful may give the sacrament the worship of latria, due to God alone (chapter 5). title: Margaret of Cortona
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred life of St Margaret of Cortona (canonised 1728); identity and plot are established (Italian and English Wikipedia). The Legion of Decency rated it A-I, but only for prints shown in the continental United States, which implies the Italian original differed. The film recasts her nine years as a nobleman's mistress as a doomed romance with invented villains. No critical review of its treatment was found. A review or a full Italian synopsis would settle it.
summary: Mario Bonnard's Italian life of the thirteenth-century penitent St Margaret of Cortona, from a shepherd girl's love affair with a nobleman to her service of the sick.
synopsis: Margherita, a beautiful shepherd girl of Laviano near Cortona, lives with her father and a young stepmother, Lucia. She falls in love with Arsenio, a young nobleman she meets while minding the sheep. When a rival, Marco, betrays the affair, her father has her sent to a convent, but Arsenio takes her to his house. Marco and Rinaldo degli Uberti murder him, and Francesca, the woman promised to Arsenio, poisons herself. Margherita is despised and persecuted by the villagers and begins to receive visions. When plague strikes the district, she nurses the sick, and she stays at the side of her stepmother, Lucia, until Lucia dies of the disease.
inclusion: St Margaret of Cortona is one of the great penitents of the Franciscan tradition, and this is the only feature film of her life. Bonnard was a veteran of Italian costume pictures. The plot owes as much to melodrama as to the saint's legend, with murderous rivals, a jilted fiancée's poisoning and a vigil at a stepmother's deathbed. It is a curiosity for those devoted to the saint.
themes: The film's arc is conversion, from a girl's sin through the death that ends it, rejection and humiliation, to penance expressed as service of the sick. Margaret's visions after Arsenio's death mark the turn, as they do in her legend. Charity in time of plague, and her care for the stepmother who had never loved her, are the visible signs of her change.
history: Margaret (1247–1297) left her father's house at about seventeen to live with a young nobleman near Montepulciano. She lived with him for nine years and bore a son. After he was murdered, his hound led her to the body. Refused a home by her stepmother, she went to Cortona, became a Franciscan tertiary, lived in severe penance, and founded a hospital for the sick poor.
liberties: The film invents the rival Marco, the murderers, and Arsenio's fiancée and her suicide, and appears to make the affair a brief romance and not nine years' cohabitation. Her son, her years in Cortona under Franciscan direction, and the founding of her hospital do not appear in the synopses. The plague-nursing and reconciliation with the stepmother are dramatised.
advisories:
An unmarried love affair, implied.

A murder and a suicide by poison.

Plague deaths.

doctrine: In Cortona she put herself under the direction of the Franciscan friars. After three years of probation she was admitted to the Third Order of St Francis, lived in strict poverty, begged her bread and nursed the sick poor. She began a congregation of nursing sisters and a confraternity of Our Lady of Mercy. Her director, Fra Giunta Bevegnati, wrote her Legend from her own dictated revelations, so the account of her visions rests on his record. She was honoured as a beata from her death and canonised on 16 May 1728.
production: Scalera Film produced the picture, directed by Mario Bonnard from a story by Guglielmo Zorzi. Maria Frau made her film debut in the title role. Virgilio Marchi, a leading Italian designer, built the sets, and Bonnard's relative Giulio Bonnard wrote the music. It runs about 100 minutes in black and white and opened in Italy on 22 February 1950, the anniversary of the saint's death. It reached Portugal in 1954 and New York in January 1957. The Legion of Decency rated the prints shown in the United States A-I.

title: Mary of Nazareth
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred, from a director whose two Bernadette films are in the same vein, and nothing in the available accounts suggests unsound content: all the infancy episodes, Cana, the Passion with Mary at the Cross, John taking her in, and the Resurrection announced to her by John. But no independent critical assessment has been found, only database entries, audience comments and a 2024 ACI Prensa recommendation, and it was co-produced by the Catholic broadcasting committee C.F.R.T. A contemporary French review (La Croix, Télérama, Le Monde, March 1995) or the subtitles would settle it.
summary: Jean Delannoy's last film, made at 87, tells the Gospel from the Annunciation to the Resurrection through the eyes of Our Lady, played by Myriam Muller.
synopsis: In Nazareth under Herod and Augustus, the young Mary (Myriam Muller) receives the angel's message and is betrothed to Joseph (Francis Lalanne). The film follows all the infancy episodes, from the Visitation and the birth at Bethlehem to the threat from Herod (Marc de Jonge). In the public ministry, the wedding at Cana is the only miracle shown. Mary follows her Son (Didier Bienaimé) to Jerusalem and watches his condemnation by Pilate (Jean-Marc Bory) and his scourging and crucifixion. From the Cross Jesus entrusts her to John. The film does not show the risen Christ appearing to the disciples; John brings Mary the news of the Resurrection. Georges Wilson narrates.
inclusion: Jean Delannoy had made Bernadette (1987) and La Passion de Bernadette (1988) late in a long career, and he called this third religious film his testament. It is one of very few features centred on Our Lady, keeping to the Gospel episodes in which she appears and adding her presence at others. It was shot in Morocco. French audience comments call it stagey and literal but faithful, and praise Muller's simple performance; one English-language comment finds the North African settings handsome but the rest flat, and another notes that much of the film is about Jesus more than Mary. ACI Prensa recommended it in 2024 as an intimate, human portrait.
themes: Mary's divine motherhood is the frame, from the Annunciation and the virgin birth to her watch at the foot of the Cross and her entrustment to St John, the scene tradition reads as her motherhood of the Church. Viewers describe the film as strongly Catholic in tone and close to the Gospels. Its restraint with miracles keeps the focus on Mary's part.
liberties: Mary is placed in scenes where the Gospels do not mention her. Most public-ministry miracles are omitted; Cana is the only one shown. The deposition is not shown, and the Resurrection is only reported, by John.
advisories:
The scourging and crucifixion are shown, with a 'tous publics' French certificate.

No sexual content or strong language reported.

Suitable for families.

grey.question: Delannoy's film keeps closely to the Gospel episodes involving Our Lady, from the Annunciation to the foot of the Cross, and nothing reported about it raises a doctrinal problem. No independent review of how it treats her exists; the available accounts are database entries, audience comments and a recent Catholic news recommendation, and a Catholic broadcasting committee helped produce it. A contemporary French review from 1995, or a check of the dialogue, would settle whether it can be recommended outright.

suitability.note: The pace is slow and stage-like, so younger children may lose interest, but nothing in it is beyond a general audience.

doctrine: Two Marian doctrines bear on the film. The Council of Ephesus met in 431, was the third ecumenical council, and condemned Nestorius, whose teaching on the Godhead of the Word made man was at issue. The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that its fourth session was held in the cathedral of the Theotokos, the Mother of God. On 8 December 1854 Pius IX, in Ineffabilis Deus, defined that Mary was kept free from original sin from the first moment of her conception, in view of the merits of Jesus Christ. The film presents Mary as humble and without sin, which accords with that definition.
production: The film runs about 105 minutes. It was also Marc de Jonge's last film. French Wikipedia notes that many Gospel episodes are left out.

title: Marie's Story
decision: GREY: Identity from NZIFF and Wikipedia; content from independent reviews (Independent Ethos, NZIFF notes) and Catholic sources (The Record; a note by the French bishops' Jeunes & Vocations service, interested). Pre-conciliar religious life shown positively, but no independent source describes how the film handles doctrine or Marie's religious instruction. Subtitles would settle it and could move it to PUBLISH.
summary: Jean-Pierre Améris's restrained true story of a nun at Larnay in the 1890s who teaches a deaf-blind girl to communicate, with Isabelle Carré as the ailing Sister Marguerite.
synopsis: In 1895 a poor artisan brings his daughter Marie, born deaf and blind, to the convent of Larnay near Poitiers, where the Daughters of Wisdom run a school for deaf girls. A doctor has advised an asylum. Marie is wild and violent, and the Mother Superior refuses her, since the sisters have never taught a deaf-blind child. Sister Marguerite, young and already ill, persuades her to relent and takes Marie on. For months she tries to reach her by touch, through tantrums and physical struggles. The breakthrough comes when Marie grasps that a sign made in her hand stands for an object, starting with her treasured knife. Language opens the world to her. Then Marguerite's illness confines her to bed, and she must teach Marie what death means.
inclusion: Améris spent time at Larnay and among deaf-blind people while preparing the film, and he cast Ariana Rivoire, a deaf teenager, as Marie; her physical performance carries the first half. Isabelle Carré, who learned tactile signing for six months, gives Sister Marguerite both delicacy and stubbornness. The camera keeps its distance and the emotion stays low-key; Hans Morgenstern of Independent Ethos praised it for refusing to manipulate, and the NZIFF notes praise the climax. Comparison with The Miracle Worker is unavoidable, and the film holds up. It is also a plain, respectful picture of a teaching congregation before the Council, with sisters in habit, a superior of authority, and a nun who believes it is God's will that she reach this child.
themes: Sister Marguerite sees Marie as a soul imprisoned and believes God wills that she free her; the NZIFF notes describe the story as driven by a divine mission. She presses this against her superior's caution, and the conflict is settled within obedience. The convent is a working community, and its charity is concrete. Death is handled seriously. Marguerite prepares Marie for her own, and the Mother Superior tells the grieving girl that faith does not make loss less painful.
history: Marie Heurtin (1885–1921), born deaf and blind at Vertou, was brought to Notre-Dame de Larnay in March 1895. Sister Sainte-Marguerite of the Daughters of Wisdom taught her tactile signs, the alphabet and Braille, and Marie learned to read, write and knit; she later helped teach her deaf-blind sister Marthe. Louis Arnould made the case famous in Âmes en prison (1910). Sister Marguerite died in 1910 and Marie at Larnay in 1921.
advisories:
Marie's early tantrums and the struggles to restrain and wash her are long and sometimes rough.

A death from illness, and grief.

No sexual content or bad language reported. Suitable for older children and up.

grey.question: Marie's Story shows a pre-conciliar teaching congregation with evident respect, and its Catholic setting is integral to the story. It is not clear how much of the faith itself is on screen, whether Marie is taught about God, prayer and the sacraments, as the real Marie was, or whether religion stays a matter of habit and good works. Independent reviews praise the film but say little on this; its dialogue would settle it.

doctrine: The convent of Notre-Dame de Larnay near Poitiers was run by the Sisters of La Sagesse (the Daughters of Wisdom). It had long specialised in the education of deaf girls, and some of its pupils became sisters. The central claim is the traditional one that every human soul, however shut in by affliction, is made by God and capable of knowing Him, so that teaching a deaf-blind child to communicate is a work of mercy, the instruction of the ignorant.
production: Marie's Story (Marie Heurtin) was produced by Escazal Films, with France 3 Cinéma and Rhône-Alpes Cinéma, and distributed in France by Diaphana. Reviewers note a change from history, since the film shows Marie arriving at 14 while the real Marie was about ten. It premiered at the Locarno festival on 10 August 2014, where it won the Variety Piazza Grande Award, and opened in France on 12 November 2014. It runs about 95 minutes.

title: Mary, Mother of Jesus
decision: REJECT: problem too grave. The producer, Eunice Kennedy Shriver, set out to make a Mary 'more appropriate for our time', and the film rewrites the Gospel to that end: Joseph rejects the pregnant Mary in anger ('You're dead to me'), Mary teaches the boy Jesus his parables, Mary is baptised by John, Jesus tells Peter that women are fit to guide, and James appears as Jesus's 'younger brother', which on its face denies Our Lady's perpetual virginity. Mary, not the Apostles, delivers the Great Commission. If subtitles showed James to be a cousin, the editor could reconsider GREY/reservations, but the feminist recasting of Our Lady and St Joseph remains.

title: Mater Dei
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred life of Our Lady, made by the Society of St Paul from a treatment by its founder, Fr Giacomo Alberione. Content is established by Virgilio Fantuzzi's review of the 2005 restoration in La Civiltà Cattolica (present-day Catholic outlet: content only) and production facts by Fabrizio Natalini's study in Schermi (2017). No independent or pre-1965 assessment of its treatment was found. A Centro Cattolico Cinematografico rating or a 1950–51 review would settle it.
summary: The Pauline Fathers' naive, devotional life of the Virgin Mary, from the Fall to the Assumption, shot in a Roman crypt and billed as Italy's first colour feature.
synopsis: The film opens in Eden after the Fall and then follows Mary's life in a sequence of episodes linked by narration: her childhood, the Annunciation, the Visitation, the Nativity, the visit of the Magi, the flight into Egypt, Christ's public life, Calvary, the Resurrection and the Assumption. The second half moves from the Gospel to the Church. Mary, now in heaven, watches over the faithful, guides and protects them, and receives the devotion of people of every condition, which the film presents as an offering to her.
inclusion: This is an early example of what Virgilio Fantuzzi calls catechetical cinema, made by a religious congregation for its own network of parishes and halls. Fr Giacomo Alberione, founder of the Society of St Paul, wrote the treatment and asked a young Pauline priest, Emilio Cordero, to direct. The whole community took part: the sisters made the costumes, Alberione appears performing a baptism, and the superior of the Daughters of St Paul plays the prophetess Anna. It was shot in Ansco colour in the crypt of the Regina Apostolorum church in Rome, with prints made in New York. Fantuzzi likens its scenes to a gallery of ex-votos, simple and naive. Cordero himself put its faults down to his inexperience.
themes: The structure is Marian doctrine in pictures. The story begins with the Fall, then shows Mary as Mother of God at the Annunciation and the Nativity, the Mother of Sorrows at Calvary, and the Queen assumed into heaven. The film was planned for the definition of the Assumption. Its second half shows her intercession and the devotion of the faithful. Fantuzzi compares the whole to a Biblia pauperum, a picture-book of the faith.
advisories:
The Crucifixion is depicted.

Nothing else of concern is reported.

Simple, slow and amateur in places.

grey.question: Mater Dei is a straightforward devotional life of Our Lady by the Society of St Paul, and everything known of it is orthodox: the Gospel episodes, the Assumption, and Mary's care for the faithful. The only detailed account is a 2005 review in a Jesuit journal, and the production facts come from the Paulines' own history. No independent critic or contemporary Catholic film office has assessed it. A 1950–51 review or a Centro Cattolico Cinematografico rating would settle it.

suitability.note: Nothing in it is a concern beyond the depicted Crucifixion, and its slow, simple manner suits family or parish audiences.

doctrine: Pius XII defined the Assumption, the film's last episode, in the apostolic constitution Munificentissimus Deus, dated 1 November 1950: 'the Immaculate Mother of God, the ever Virgin Mary, having completed the course of her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory'. He declared it a divinely revealed dogma. Before that, the belief was held as pious tradition, and the feast of 15 August was kept as a major feast of Our Lady; the Catholic Encyclopedia (1907) records that Benedict XIV called denial of the belief impious. The film's earlier scenes (Annunciation, Visitation, Nativity, Calvary) follow the Gospels and the mysteries of the Rosary.
production: Mater Dei is an Italian film of 1950 running about 90 minutes, with thirteen listed actors.

title: Ash Wednesday
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a priest serving in hiding under the Calles persecution) but lurid: the premise is a priest's rape of the heroine, much is set in her brothel, and she tries to seduce the hidden priest. Content from the San Sebastián 2019 retrospective record and a fan page reproducing García Riera's documentary history. No Catholic rating found. Editor may prefer REJECT if the priest-rapist premise is judged too grave to weigh.
summary: María Félix plays a brothel-keeper who hates the Church after being raped by a priest, until she falls for a doctor who is secretly a priest during the Cristero persecution.
synopsis: In the 1920s, during the Cristero conflict, young Victoria Rivas falls from a boat on Lake Pátzcuaro and is assaulted by the man who rescues her. At the Ash Wednesday service she recognises him as the priest. Hardened, she leaves the Church, becomes a rich brothel-keeper in Mexico City and informs for the government against the Cristeros. On a train she meets Dr Federico Lamadrid (Arturo de Córdova), who treats the wounded of both sides; later she finds a notebook of his that could ruin him and keeps it rather than betray him. He reveals that he is a priest in hiding and insists on bringing confession to a dying girl in her house. Victoria, in love with him, tries to seduce him and fails. He compares her to Mary Magdalene and leaves her.
inclusion: Gavaldón was one of the great directors of Mexico's golden age, and this was a prestige production with two of the country's biggest stars. Its interest lies in the portrait of the priesthood under the Calles persecution, in a priest who serves in secret as a doctor, tends the wounded of both sides and risks exposure to bring the sacraments to the dying. Arturo de Córdova had played priests before, and Félix's hard, glamorous Victoria is a role built for her. The story, from Luis G. Basurto, is lurid melodrama, and its premise is a priest's crime. The San Sebastián festival revived it in its 2019 Gavaldón retrospective.
themes: Two priests stand at either end of the film. The first commits a grave crime against Victoria and drives her from the faith; the second, Federico, lives his priesthood in hiding, keeps his vows when she tries to seduce him and seeks to bring a dying woman to confession. The film sets the faithful priest against the unworthy one, and shows Victoria's hatred of the Church resting on one man's sin. The Cristero war is background: Victoria informs against the rebels, while Federico treats both sides.
advisories:
The rape of a young woman by a priest is the premise (reported as taking place off screen).

A brothel setting; a woman's attempt to seduce a priest.

Civil-war violence, including a train hold-up and wounded men.

For adults.

grey.question: The heroine's hatred of the Church begins when a priest rapes her, and much of the film takes place in her brothel. Against that crime it sets a priest who serves secretly as a doctor during the Cristero persecution, brings the sacraments to the dying and refuses her when she tries to seduce him, comparing her to Mary Magdalene. The material is grave, and how the film treats it is not known from any review or Catholic rating. A Mexican Catholic rating or García Riera's full entry would show how it is handled.

suitability.note: The sexual assault at the heart of the story, and the brothel setting and attempted seduction that follow, make it a film for adults.

doctrine: The film's unworthy priest raises the question the Council of Trent answered. Session 7, canon 12, condemns the opinion that a minister in mortal sin who observes all the essentials does not confer a sacrament, so the sin of a priest does not void his sacramental acts, though it is a grievous sin against his office. The film's faithful priest acts on Trent's Session 14, chapter 7, under which at the point of death all priests may absolve every penitent from every sin and censure, so Lamadrid's insistence on bringing confession to a dying girl in a brothel is the priest's duty. The setting is the Mexican persecution: Pius XI's Iniquis afflictisque (18 November 1926) described the laws that limited and registered priests, the jailing of some and attacks on others at Mass, and praised the clergy who refused to obey them under the rule that one must obey God rather than men.
production: This Mexican black-and-white drama runs 112 minutes. It premiered in Mexico on 2 October 1958 and was entered in the Berlin International Film Festival.

title: White Mission
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred and established in detail by Diana Arbaiza's 2020 study and the Claretians' own account: a young missionary in Spanish Guinea, his abandoned father turned brutal planter, the father's repentance and death in his son's arms. The reservation is the colonial-nationalist frame. The film opens by praising missionaries for sowing 'religion and the fatherland', presents the natives as childlike, and its key flashback has a missionary cut Our Lady's mantle to make a Spanish flag, then offer the flag back to her. Arbaiza is independent; no contemporary Catholic rating was found.
summary: Juan de Orduña's Spanish missionary melodrama, shot in Guinea: a young priest finds that the brutal planter terrorising the Africans of his mission is his own father.
synopsis: Fr Javier arrives at a Spanish mission in continental Guinea to work under the veteran Fr Urcola, who runs the church and school of a peaceful Christian village. The neighbouring lands belong partly to Brisco, a fugitive Spanish banker who fled the country after a great fraud and now runs a lumber mill with the whip, beating his workers Minoa and Souka. Javier tells him plainly that the Africans hate him because he mistreats them. Brisco is in fact Javier's father, who abandoned him long ago. Brisco burns Urcola's chapel; the old priest rescues a Spanish flag from the fire and explains, in a flashback, how as a young missionary on Annobón he made that flag from altar curtains and the red mantle of the Virgin to turn away a foreign warship. In the end the repentant Brisco dies in his son's arms.
inclusion: Arbaiza argues that its melodrama, with emotional music, close-ups and sentimental acting, makes the missionaries' sacrifice more convincing than the regime's documentaries managed, and that it quietly criticises colonial exploitation by concentrating it in one villain. The father-son story of sin, rejection and deathbed repentance is the film's engine. Its picture of Africans, in broken Spanish and as easily led children, has dated badly.
themes: The missionaries are shown living among the people, teaching, baptising and defending them against exploitation; a priest's line that the mission must sometimes save 'the black souls of white men' sums up its moral. Brisco's story is one of conversion: a fugitive and a cruel master, confronted by the son he abandoned, who repents and dies reconciled. Against this sits the film's equation of the Church's mission with Spain's empire.
history: The Claretian missionaries ran most of the Catholic missions in Spanish Guinea from 1883. The Annobón episode is based on Fr Joaquín Juanola, a Claretian who died in Guinea in 1912; according to the Claretian historian Tomás Luis Pujadas, as cited by Arbaiza, he simply pointed out the Spanish flag already flying to a German commander and did not improvise one under fire.
liberties: Fr Urcola's flag made under fire from a warship dramatises a much smaller incident involving Fr Juanola. Brisco, Javier and the rest are fictional. The film places colonial brutality in the past and in one villain, while forced labour on Guinea's plantations was still common when it was made.
advisories:
Beatings and whipping of African workers; a chapel burned; a deathbed.

Racial caricature typical of its time: African characters speak broken Spanish and are portrayed as childlike.

grey.question: The missionary drama is sound, with priests who serve and defend the Africans and a cruel colonist who repents in his son's arms. But the film fuses the faith with Franco-era imperial nationalism. It opens by praising missionaries for sowing religion and the fatherland together, it portrays Africans as childlike, and its emotional climax has a missionary tear Our Lady's mantle to make a Spanish flag, presented as an act of devotion. Viewers should weigh that use of a sacred object and the patriotic frame.

suitability.note: The African characters are drawn as childlike and speak broken Spanish, so older children will need the colonial context explained.

doctrine: The film joins the mission to Spain's empire, and the Church taught otherwise. Benedict XV's apostolic letter Maximum Illud (30 November 1919) told missionaries to set aside national interests. The missionary is an ambassador of Christ, not of his own country, and one who busied himself with the interests of his earthly homeland instead of his homeland in heaven would 'infect his apostolate like a plague' (paragraph 19). It separated the Church's mission from political alliances and urged the training of local clergy. The film's flag, cut from altar curtains and the Virgin's red mantle and offered to her, turns the Mother of God's mantle into a national banner, the confusion of the two homelands the letter warned against.
production: Colonial AJE, headed by Jesús Rubiera, produced the film with a state credit, and it was classified of National Interest. The Claretian Fr Olangua was religious adviser, and the film opens with a tribute to missionaries sowing 'religion and the fatherland'. It was shot in Spanish Guinea and in a Spanish studio and runs 88 minutes. It was an enormous public success in 1946, and Manuel Luna won the special medal of the Círculo de Escritores Cinematográficos for his Brisco.

title: Monsignor Quixote
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred, with identity established (Wikipedia; BAFTA shortlist) and content established through Greene's novel. But the film's handling of Quixote's doubts, of the satirical bishop and of the delirious Mass with communion given to an unbeliever has not been verified against the film itself. If the dialogue has Quixote voicing heterodoxy that goes uncorrected (for example, rejecting hell), move it to REJECT under the editor precedent. If it is faithful to the novel's sympathetic but ambiguous ending, keep it as reservations.
summary: Alec Guinness plays Graham Greene's unworldly Spanish priest, made a monsignor by chance, on a road trip across post-Franco Spain with the Communist ex-mayor he calls Sancho.
synopsis: Father Quixote, parish priest of El Toboso in La Mancha, believes he is a descendant of Cervantes's knight. After he helps a stranded Italian bishop, Rome makes him a monsignor, to the displeasure of his own bishop, who sends him on holiday. He sets out in his old Seat 600, Rocinante, with the town's Communist former mayor, Sancho (Leo McKern). Their arguments about the Church and Marx bring them closer and unsettle each of them. Recalled and suspended by his bishop, Quixote escapes and takes to the road again. He is hurt trying to rescue a statue of Our Lady from a procession where people pin money to her. Sheltered at a Trappist monastery, he rises in delirium and says Mass in the night with no bread or wine, gives communion to Sancho, and dies in his arms.
inclusion: Guinness and Leo McKern are a well-matched pair, and their scenes together are what viewers remember. Greene's story is a comedy of ideas, with a believer and a Marxist on holiday, each finding the other more human than his creed allows. Its sympathy is with the old priest, who keeps the old Mass and is an embarrassment to his suspicious bishop. That makes it warmer towards the Church than much of Greene, but its Catholicism is the doubting kind, and its ending raises questions.
themes: Quixote's faith is simple and sincere. Greene also gives him doubts, and lets the Communist argue his case, so the faith is tested and not simply affirmed. In the novel the climax is a Mass in the old rite said in delirium, with nothing on the altar, followed by communion given to an unbeliever. The scene raises plain questions. A Mass without matter is no Mass, and communion is not given to a man outside the faith, yet the scene is presented as an act of love. The bishop who suspends Quixote is drawn satirically. The Spain of the film is post-Franco and post-conciliar, but the story's sympathy lies with the priest who keeps the old ways.
advisories:
Long theological arguments between a priest and a Communist, some left unresolved.

Comic episodes touch on sexual subjects.

The ending shows a Mass said in delirium without bread or wine, and communion given to an unbeliever.

Suitable for adults and older teenagers.

grey.question: Greene's story is sympathetic to its old-fashioned priest, but its faith is the doubting kind and its climax is troubling. In the novel, the dying Quixote says the old Latin Mass in delirium with no bread or wine, then gives communion to his Communist friend, a scene offered as an act of love and not judged. names: Monsignor Quixote, novel by Graham Greene (1982)

suitability.note: Long talk about theology and politics between a priest and a Communist, some comic sexual references and a death scene. Nothing is graphic, but it will bore younger viewers and some of the ending needs a parent's explanation.

doctrine: The ending turns on the matter of the Eucharist. The Catholic Encyclopedia gives the valid matter as unadulterated wheat flour, mixed with natural water and baked, and notes that unleavened bread is the uniform practice in the Western Church; the wine must be the naturally fermented juice of the grape. The Council of Trent set out Eucharistic doctrine in Sessions XIII, XXI and XXII, the last on the sacrifice of the Mass. Without the matter there is no consecration, so the priest's good intention does not make the sacrifice.
production: Thames Television made the film for ITV from Greene's 1982 novel, a comic pastiche of Cervantes' Don Quixote. It was shot in Spain about ten years after Franco's death, in locations Greene had written about, including the Valley of the Fallen. It was first shown in Germany on Christmas Eve 1986, and on PBS in the United States in Great Performances on 13 February 1987. It was shortlisted for the 1986 BAFTA for best single television drama, and Alec Guinness received a BAFTA nomination for best actor. Sources variously date the film to 1985 and 1987.

title: Murder in the Cathedral
decision: PUBLISH: Legion of Decency A-I (1936–59 list on archive.org), a contemporary Catholic judgment. Identity from the BFI. Independent substantive treatment from Wheeler Winston Dixon (Senses of Cinema, 2016) and Tom Birchenough (The Arts Desk, 2015): a faithful, austere film of Eliot's play on the martyrdom of St Thomas Becket (canonised 1173). Eliot was an Anglican, but the subject is a Catholic archbishop who dies defending the liberty of the Church, and nothing in the play contradicts Catholic teaching.
summary: George Hoellering's severe, verse-spoken film of T. S. Eliot's play about the last days and martyrdom of St Thomas Becket, with Eliot himself as the unseen fourth tempter.
synopsis: December 1170. Thomas Becket, Archbishop of Canterbury, returns from long exile in France to a cathedral city that fears what his return will bring. A new opening scene, written by Eliot for the film, shows the quarrel with King Henry II that drove him abroad. At Canterbury four tempters come to him in turn: one offers him safety and the pleasures of his youth, one power as the King's chancellor again, one an alliance with the barons against the King. The fourth, the most dangerous, urges him to seek martyrdom for the glory it will bring. Becket refuses them all. On Christmas Day he preaches on the meaning of martyrdom. Four knights arrive from the King and demand that he submit. He will not, and they cut him down in his own cathedral.
inclusion: It is one of the very few serious British films about a saint, and one of the strangest. Hoellering, an Austrian émigré who ran London's Academy Cinema, worked closely with Eliot, who recorded the whole play to guide the actors. Becket is played by Fr John Groser, a London East End clergyman with no acting experience; Tom Birchenough finds his calm dignity remarkable, and Bosley Crowther of the New York Times, who found the verse drama not felicitous for the screen, praised that dignity in 1952. The chorus of Canterbury women, the stark interiors and the bleak exteriors give the film the severity that Dixon compares to Dreyer and Bergman. It is static and wordy, and some will find the verse hard going. The 114-minute cut is the director's preferred version.
themes: The fourth temptation, to die for one's own glory, is the heart of the film. Becket must die for God and the Church, and Dixon reads his death as the King's act and not one Becket contrived. The quarrel is the liberty of the Church against the Crown, and Becket's refusal to yield the rights of his see is presented as fidelity. The Christmas sermon sets his coming death against the feast of Christ's birth and the martyrs who follow it.
history: Thomas Becket (c.1119–1170), Henry II's chancellor, became Archbishop of Canterbury in 1162 and resisted the King's claims over the Church. After six years in exile he returned in December 1170 and was murdered in his cathedral by four knights on 29 December.
liberties: The film adds an opening that dramatises the conflict with Henry, who is seen on screen, unlike in the play. At Hoellering's request Eliot cut most of the knights' direct address to the audience after the murder and replaced it with a shorter speech. A church in St John's Wood stood in for Canterbury.
advisories:
The murder at the altar is brief, with one bloody image (BFI rates it PG).

No sexual content or bad language.

Legion of Decency A-I.

suitability.note: The verse dialogue and slow pace make it best for older teenagers and adults, though the murder at the altar is brief.

doctrine: The quarrel between Becket and Henry II turned, in the Catholic Encyclopedia's account, on whether the royal courts could try clergy accused of crimes. These were the 'criminous clerks', and Henry sought to enforce the custom through the sixteen articles of the Constitutions of Clarendon (1164). Becket refused them as a matter of Church principle. Alexander III canonised him by bull on 21 February 1173, and Henry did public penance and was scourged at the tomb on 12 July 1174. The Church teaches that martyrdom is the shedding of blood out of love for the faith, not a prize to be sought for reputation. The Catholic Encyclopedia counts it as a baptism of blood.
production: Film Traders Ltd produced the film. It premiered at the Venice festival in 1951, opened in Britain in March 1952 and in America on 25 March 1952. It won the Venice award for production design, credited to Peter Pendrey.

title: Word and Utopia
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a Jesuit's vocation, missions and preaching, much of it in Vieira's own sermons) and seriously reviewed by independent critics (Rosenbaum, BAMPFA, the São Paulo Mostra). The reservation is framing: the Inquisition trial is the spine, and the film presents Vieira as a 'freethinking' champion of Indians, slaves and New Christians persecuted by the Holy Office, whereas the trial actually turned on his prophetic writings (the Fifth Empire) and Rome later exempted him from the Portuguese tribunal. Vieira is not a canonised subject, so rule (a) does not apply. Subtitles of the trial scenes would show whether the film's case against the Inquisition goes beyond the history.
summary: Manoel de Oliveira's film of the Jesuit preacher António Vieira, three actors playing him across seventy years, built from his own sermons and his trial by the Inquisition.
synopsis: In 1663 the Jesuit António Vieira, once the intimate of King João IV, is summoned before the Portuguese Inquisition at Coimbra. Court intrigue and a misunderstanding have cost him his protection. Before his judges he goes over his life: a boyhood in Brazil and his novitiate at Bahia (Ricardo Trêpa), his first triumphs in the pulpit and his campaign for the Indians of Maranhão (Luís Miguel Cintra). Forbidden by the Inquisition to preach, he goes to Rome, where his sermons make him famous and Queen Christina of Sweden (Leonor Silveira) wants him as her confessor. Homesick, he returns to Portugal, but the new king, Pedro, receives him coldly, and the old man (Lima Duarte) goes back to Brazil, where he dies.
inclusion: Oliveira here gives the greatest preacher in Portuguese a feature built largely from his own words. Jonathan Rosenbaum notes that the sermons and letters are treated almost as libretti, with settings and period art arranged around them, and that Oliveira, in his nineties, directs his actors with unusual vigour; Renato Berta's photography is rich. The three Vieiras, Trêpa, Cintra and the Brazilian star Lima Duarte, chart youthful zeal, rhetorical mastery and the anger of age. It is demanding, with more than two hours of speech, static compositions and little conventional drama.
themes: Vieira's vocation, his sermons and his missions to the Indians are the core. The preaching draws on Scripture, the Fathers and the duties of kings and masters before God. The film's sympathies lie with his defence of the Indians and of Portugal's converted Jews, and the Inquisition appears as the obstacle. The BAMPFA note calls his views on God and prophecy unorthodox.
history: António Vieira (1608–1697), born in Lisbon and raised in Bahia, entered the Jesuit novitiate in 1625. Preacher and diplomat to João IV, he led the missions in Maranhão and opposed the enslavement of Indians. In Rome he preached before the cardinals. He died in Bahia.
liberties: Oliveira compresses seventy years into a trial frame and lets the sermons carry the story. The film emphasises Vieira's social causes over the prophetic writings that were the actual matter of his trial.
advisories:
No violence or sexual content reported.

Long, static and dialogue-heavy.

grey.question: Oliveira's film lets a great Jesuit preacher speak in his own words, and his vocation, missions and sermons are wholly Catholic. The frame is the difficulty, since the story is told from the dock of the Inquisition, and critics describe a 'freethinking' priest persecuted for defending Indians, slaves and converted Jews. Historically, his trial turned on his prophecies of a Portuguese Fifth Empire, and Rome later freed him from the Portuguese tribunal. Viewers should weigh how fairly the film treats the Holy Office and how far it endorses his prophetic speculations.

names: Sermons and letters of António Vieira, S.J. (17th century)

suitability.note: It runs about two hours, is slow and static, and is made up largely of sermon and debate in 17th-century Portuguese, so it suits adults and older students interested in the subject.

doctrine: The historical case against him was not a general quarrel with the Church. He was denounced to the Inquisition for heretical points, propositions 'smacking of heresy', in his sermons, conversations and writings, and jailed at Coimbra from October 1665 to December 1667, with a sentence barring him from teaching, writing or preaching. The matter was his belief in the prophecies of the shoemaker-poet Bandarra, which foretold a Fifth Empire (Quinto Império) under a Portuguese ruler. In the Clavis Prophetarum he tried to support this from Scripture. Vieira then went to Rome. He returned to Portugal in 1681 with a papal bull exempting him from the grand inquisitor's jurisdiction. The film's picture of the Holy Office as a persecutor of social reformers should be read against that narrower charge.
production: This is Oliveira's second tribute to Vieira. The same Sermon of St Anthony, in the series Vieira dedicated to the saint, was used in his earlier film No, or the Vain Glory of Command. The film was shown in competition at the 2000 Venice Film Festival and opened in Portugal on 17 November 2000, running about 130 minutes. It won the Best Director prize at the Portuguese Golden Globes. It reached the United States only in limited screenings.

title: Pastor Angelicus
decision: PUBLISH: Produced by the Centro Cattolico Cinematografico itself in 1942, and its American version, The Story of the Pope (1946), was classed A-I by the Legion of Decency. Independent treatment: Motion Picture Herald's 1946 review (good, though technically limited) and Cristina Formenti's 2017 study in Schermi. Focus, the British Catholic film review, praised it in 1951. The only question is political: Fascist circles withdrew it in January 1943 for its 'pacifist tendency'. That is history, not a reservation.
summary: The Italian bishops' film office's portrait of Pius XII for his episcopal jubilee, the first feature where a reigning pope appears himself; withdrawn by the Fascist authorities within weeks.
synopsis: The film traces Eugenio Pacelli's life from his Roman boyhood, ordination and legal training through his years as nuncio in Germany and Secretary of State to Pius XI, to the conclave of 1939 and his coronation. It then shows the Pope at work: receiving pilgrims and soldiers in audience, celebrating the great ceremonies of St Peter's, and directing the Church's relief in wartime, including the Vatican's information bureau for prisoners and missing persons. Scenes of the basilica, the Vatican palaces and Raphael's paintings are set to music and the singing of the Sistine Choir. The American version, The Story of the Pope, recut the material with a commentary by Mgr Fulton Sheen, an introduction by Cardinal Spellman and newsreel of the 1946 consistory.
inclusion: Pastor Angelicus matters as the first film made by the Church's own film office about a living pope, and as the first in which a pope appears on screen as himself. The Centro Cattolico Cinematografico deliberately released it without names in the credits, so that it would read as the Church's film and not a director's; the paperwork credits Romolo Marcellini, a documentarist from the Istituto Luce. Formenti shows that it was modelled on The March of Time's Vatican films and aimed at an international audience. Motion Picture Herald admired the Sistine Choir and the material but noted slow movement, poor editing and uneven sound. Focus, reviewing the British release, called it an excellent film essay and urged Catholic groups to ask cinemas to book it.
themes: The film presents the Pope as father of all the faithful and as a peacemaker above the warring nations. The office of Peter is shown in its liturgy, its audiences and its charity, with the Pope receiving soldiers of every nation. Focus singled out the scene of wounded soldiers of different countries waiting to be received by the Pope. The title comes from the prophecy of popes attributed to St Malachy, which the film uses as a devotional epithet. Its Catholic content is straightforward and devotional. Its political subtext, that the Pope and not Mussolini spoke for peace, is what got it withdrawn.
history: In December 1941 Luigi Gedda pressed the CCC, the Italian Catholic Action film office, to produce its own feature on Pius XII for his episcopal silver jubilee. The film received its Italian censorship certificate on 17 December 1942 and opened that month, but the Fascist authorities withdrew it on 8 January 1943, reportedly for a 'pacifist tendency'. It circulated in Europe after the war and was shown in France as Pastor Angelicus.
advisories:
Nothing objectionable; suitable for all ages.

Newsreel footage of wartime suffering and wounded soldiers.

The English-language version differs substantially from the Italian original; check which one you are watching.

doctrine: The First Vatican Council, in Pastor Aeternus (18 July 1870), defined that Christ gave Peter a true primacy of jurisdiction over the whole Church (chapter 1), that it passes to the Roman Pontiffs (chapter 2), and that the Pope has full, supreme, ordinary and immediate power over the Church (chapter 3). It also defined that when he speaks ex cathedra on faith or morals he is infallible (chapter 4). Pius XII's encyclical Mystici Corporis Christi (29 June 1943) teaches that Christ is the one chief Head of the Church, which He governs visibly through His Vicar, and that adhering to Christ while refusing the Vicar is dangerous error.
production: Pastor Angelicus was made in 1942 by the Centro Cattolico Cinematografico, the film office of Italian Catholic Action. The American version, The Story of the Pope, was released by Chapel Films on 19 December 1946. John Meehan adapted an original screenplay by Fr John O'Connor. The American Film Institute lists runtimes of 60 to 65 minutes.

title: Peter and Paul
decision: REJECT (content): the subtitles show James as head of the Church, with Peter declaring Jerusalem, not himself, the centre and deferring to James; Petrine primacy is denied in substance. Prior assessment: Identity from Wikipedia and the Internet Archive record (Universal Television; CBS, 12 and 14 April 1981). The dialogue of both parts (English, read 2026-10-12) settles the open questions against PUBLISH. Peter does not decide at the Council of Jerusalem: he gives his speech from Acts 15, but James rules, James is said to lead the Church, and Peter calls himself a failure whom Christ replaced with Paul. Paul, the hero, scorns the council's decree as James's capitulation and preaches salvation 'through faith alone' in those words. No Eucharist is shown. Both martyrdoms in Rome are there, and Peter's last sermon is from his first letter. Not REJECT: the Petrine texts are quoted, John contradicts Peter's self-reproach, and Paul's faith is set beside his hymn to charity.
summary: A CBS miniseries with Anthony Hopkins as Paul and Robert Foxworth as Peter, following the apostles from Stephen's martyrdom to their deaths in Nero's Rome.
synopsis: Saul of Tarsus (Anthony Hopkins) watches Stephen stoned and sets out to hunt Christ's followers, until he is struck blind on the road to Damascus. Peter (Robert Foxworth) tests the convert, shows him where Jesus ate the last supper and prayed, and sends him home to Tarsus. Herod Agrippa beheads James; Peter is freed from prison and flees. Barnabas brings Paul to Antioch, and they carry the Gospel to Cyprus and Galatia. At Jerusalem the apostles debate circumcision; at Antioch Paul rebukes Peter for yielding to James's men. Paul crosses to Macedonia with Luke, is jailed at Philippi, preaches at Athens and Corinth, is seized in the Temple, appeals to Caesar and is shipwrecked on Malta. In Rome he is beheaded. Peter arrives to lead the persecuted Christians and is crucified.
inclusion: This is a sober, well-cast television account of the apostolic Church, shot on Rhodes and written by Christopher Knopf and Stan Hough. Hopkins's driven, quarrelsome Paul is the main reason to see it; Movieguide, an evangelical review service, praises both leads and notes how much of the dialogue comes from Scripture. It is dialogue-heavy and its action is brief. Its weakness from a Catholic point of view is its reading of the early Church: it follows Galatians more than Acts, makes James the leader in Jerusalem, and turns Peter into a well-meaning waverer who comes to Rome only to die after Paul. The series won an Emmy for its makeup. It is a reasonable companion to Acts for viewers who know where it leans.
themes: The drama is Paul's struggle to open the Church to the Gentiles, and the series takes his side. Salvation by grace through faith is preached throughout, sometimes in the Protestant formula of faith alone, though Paul also prays that without charity his faith is nothing. Peter is the troubled conscience of the Jerusalem Church. He quotes Christ calling him the rock and giving him the keys, but says the commission passed to Paul; John tells him he stands alone in that opinion. Peter's final sermon in Rome, from his first letter, is the series' most Catholic moment, and he dies refusing to be crucified as his Lord was. The sacraments barely appear: baptism is assumed, and no Eucharist is shown.
liberties: The script follows Galatians' account of the dispute at Antioch and has Paul reject the Jerusalem decree as James's personal ruling, where Acts has Paul delivering it. Peter is sent to a literal Babylon rather than Rome. The slave girl with a spirit of divination at Philippi becomes a ventriloquist exposed as a fraud. Luke is a sceptical physician who calls a miracle an event that creates faith.
advisories:
Stoning, scourging, James's execution, riots, shipwreck and crucifixion, mostly implied.

No sexual content; a passage of Romans on homosexual acts is read aloud.

Suitable for families with older children.

Peter's primacy is muted and Paul's preaching uses Protestant formulas.

title: Quo Vadis
decision: GREY: Identity is established (Il Cinema Ritrovato 2024 record of the EYE Filmmuseum print; Wikipedia citing Ricci and Scodel–Bettenworth). Maria Wyke's programme notes, an independent scholarly treatment, describe a film that pushes Sienkiewicz's story to decadent extremes: half-dressed women thrown to Nero's eels with erotic underwater shots, orgies, attempted rapes and lurid martyrdoms, with the Christians emerging only late from the catacombs. The Catholic substance is real but subordinate to Nero's spectacle; the sensual material is a reservation a reader can weigh. The batch lead's 2012 Vatican Library print could not be verified and is omitted.
summary: UCI's lavish silent remake of Sienkiewicz's martyr novel is dominated by Emil Jannings's grotesque Nero and its decadent spectacle; the Christians come into their own only late.
synopsis: In Nero's Rome, the young officer Marcus Vinicius falls in love with Lygia, a Christian hostage in a Roman household, protected by her giant servant Ursus. Vinicius tries to take her by force; she escapes, and his pursuit of her draws him towards the Christians who shelter her. At court, Nero amuses himself with cruelties and banquets, egged on by Poppaea and Tigellinus, while the elegant Petronius watches with irony. Nero has Rome burned and blames the Christians, who are seized from the catacombs and sent to the arena or turned into living torches in his gardens. Lygia is exposed in the arena and saved by Ursus. Petronius and his slave Eunice take their own lives, and Nero's reign collapses.
inclusion: This was one of the most expensive Italian films of its day, an attempt by the Unione Cinematografica Italiana to recover the world market Guazzoni's Quo Vadis had conquered in 1913. Its biggest asset is Emil Jannings, whom Maria Wyke calls a satanic grotesque of a Nero; the New Yorker found him the one thing besides boredom in the film. The New York Times thought it excellent as spectacle but tedious. A restoration led by the Nederlands Filmmuseum, from two incomplete original negatives and a Dutch tinted print, allows it to be seen today.
themes: Sienkiewicz's novel is a story of conversion and martyrdom. A pagan learns from the Christians he despises, and the Church of Rome under St Peter wins by suffering. On Wyke's account, this film is more interested in the emperor's gaze than in the faith. The Christians appear only when they leave the catacombs, and their martyrdoms are staged as lurid spectacle and not as witness. The arena, the human torches and the Way of the Cross glimpsed in a vision of Christ are there, but the film's energy goes into Nero's palace.
history: Henryk Sienkiewicz wrote Quo Vadis in 1895-96, first in newspaper serial and then as a book. It draws on Tacitus's account of the fire of Rome in 64 and Nero's persecution of the Christians, and on the tradition that St Peter died in Rome. Sienkiewicz won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1905 for his work as an epic writer; the prize did not name Quo Vadis, though the novel made his name abroad.

Sensual material: half-dressed women thrown into a fountain of eels, with erotic underwater shots; an orgy; attempted rapes.

Lurid martyrdoms in the arena and Christians burned as torches.

The pagan Petronius and Eunice commit suicide.

Adults only.

grey.question: This Quo Vadis keeps the shape of Sienkiewicz's story of conversion and martyrdom, but its emphasis is on Nero's court. Maria Wyke describes erotic scenes with half-dressed women, an orgy, attempted rapes and lurid martyrdoms, with the Christians emerging only late in the film. Viewers should weigh whether the witness of the martyrs survives a production that dwells so long on decadence. Only adults should consider it.

suitability.note: The sensual material is prominent and the persecution is staged as spectacle, with Christians burned as torches and killed in the arena.

doctrine: The novel rests on the martyrdom of St Peter at Rome. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1911) treats his residence and death in Rome as 'established beyond contention' as historical facts, tied to Nero's persecution, with the date left open between July 64 and the beginning of 68, and gives Origen's report that he was crucified head downward at his own wish. Tradition places Peter's burial on the Vatican hill. The film sets Peter and the early Roman Church in the background, so the teaching on the Primacy and on martyrdom as witness is not developed.
production: Unione Cinematografica Italiana announced the film in 1921, and shooting began in 1924. Rudolph Valentino was approached but declined. The production ran far over budget, German backers stepped in, and they insisted that Georg Jacoby be added as co-director; one actor, Bruno Kastner, fell ill and his scenes were reshot. It premiered in Austria and Germany in October 1924, with First National handling the United States; running time is 90 minutes, 120 in the director's cut. It failed commercially and critically and effectively ended the career of its producer, Arturo Ambrosio.

title: The Holy Queen
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred: a life of St Elizabeth of Portugal, the Aragonese princess who became Queen of Portugal, canonised in 1625, made by Rafael Gil in a Spanish-Portuguese co-production. Identity is established by the Spanish and English encyclopaedia entries; the Spanish entry records good reviews and commercial success. But the sources give only an outline, centred on the queen's troubled marriage to King Dinis and a court intrigue, and no contemporary review describing its religious content, nor any Catholic rating, was found. Unverified until the content is checked.
summary: Rafael Gil's Spanish-Portuguese costume picture about St Elizabeth of Portugal, patient wife of an unfaithful king and peacemaker of her kingdom, with Maruchi Fresno.
synopsis: Elizabeth, daughter of the King of Aragon, is married as a girl to King Dinis of Portugal. At the Portuguese court she meets coldness and intrigue, led by the ambitious Nuño de Lara, and she bears with patience the infidelities of her husband, while devoting herself to prayer and to the poor. The film follows her through the troubles of her marriage and of the kingdom, in which she works to make peace within the royal family. Whether it includes the miracle of the roses, her intervention between her husband and their rebellious son Afonso, or her last years as a Poor Clare tertiary at Coimbra is not known.
inclusion: Reina santa was one of the prestige productions of Spanish cinema in 1947, made by Rafael Gil, who released La fe the same year, for Cesáreo González's Suevia Films, in co-production with Portugal and in separate Spanish and Portuguese versions. Maruchi Fresno played the queen, with the Portuguese star António Vilar as King Dinis, Luis Peña as Nuño de Lara and the young Fernando Rey. The Spanish encyclopaedia entry, citing Diego Galán, records good reviews and strong takings. Few films have taken up its subject, a married saint who was also a queen and a peacemaker.
themes: The life of St Elizabeth offers a model of sanctity in marriage and in public life, in fidelity and patience towards an unfaithful husband, charity to the poor, and peacemaking between king and heir and between kingdoms. The available outline stresses the marriage and the court intrigue. Whether the film gives equal weight to her prayer, her charity and her miracles, or treats her mainly as the heroine of a royal melodrama, is unknown.
history: Elizabeth of Aragon (born 1271), great-niece of St Elizabeth of Hungary, married King Dinis (Diniz) of Portugal. His morals were bad, and she bore it with patience. In 1323 war broke out between Dinis and their son Afonso, and she rode between the armies and reconciled them. After Dinis died in 1325 she took the Franciscan tertiary habit and retired to the Poor Clares' convent she had founded at Coimbra. She died in 1336, after again making peace between her son and the King of Castile. She was canonised by Urban VIII in 1625.
advisories:
The king's infidelities and court intrigue.

Probably suitable for families, but the content is unconfirmed.

grey.question: Rafael Gil's Spanish-Portuguese life of St Elizabeth of Portugal was well received in its day. No independent review of its religious content exists, and there is no contemporary Catholic rating; the available outline describes only her troubled marriage and the court intrigues against her. It is listed here until someone checks how it presents her faith, her charity and her miracles, and whether the saint or the royal melodrama is at its centre.

doctrine: St Elizabeth of Portugal is held up as a model of the Christian wife and peacemaker, and, in widowhood, as a Franciscan tertiary living by the Poor Clares at Coimbra. The Church canonises only after a long inquiry into heroic virtue and miracles.
production: Reina santa was a Spanish-Portuguese production by Suevia Films, one of Cesáreo González's most ambitious projects. Rafael Gil directed the Spanish version, with Henrique Campos and Aníbal Contreiras directing the Portuguese. title: Rita of Cascia
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred: a life of St Rita of Cascia, canonised in 1900, made with a priest as ecclesiastical adviser and shot on location at Cascia. Identity is established by the Italian and English encyclopaedia entries and FilmTV.it. But the only descriptions of the content are a one-line plot and two short modern judgments, both of which find the film weak; no contemporary review or Catholic rating was found, and nothing shows how the saint's forgiveness of her husband's killers, her prayer for her sons and her entry into the Augustinian convent are handled. Unverified until the content is checked.
summary: Antonio Leonviola's debut, a modest wartime life of St Rita, the wife and widow of Cascia who forgave her husband's murderers, with Elena Zareschi.
synopsis: In fourteenth-century Umbria, the young Rita longs to become a nun, but at her parents' wish she marries Paolo di Ferdinando, a violent and dishonest man, hoping by patience and prayer to reform him. Her husband is murdered in the feuds of the time, and her two sons grow up determined to avenge their father. How the film handles Paolo's change of heart, Rita's forgiveness of his killers, the deaths of her sons before they could take revenge, her repeated attempts to enter the Augustinian convent at Cascia, or the wound of the thorn and the other miracles of her last years is not known.
inclusion: Rita da Cascia was Antonio Leonviola's first film as director; he later remade the story as Il suo più grande amore. Fr Vittorino Callisto Vanzin was the ecclesiastical adviser. Modern judgments are lukewarm: FilmTV.it's editors find it poorly made but lifted by Zareschi's performance, and a viewer's review calls it harmless and anonymous. Its interest lies in its subject, one of the most popular saints in Italy, and in its being one of the few films about her.
themes: St Rita's story is of a marriage borne as a cross, with a wife's patience and prayer for a violent husband, his conversion, and his murder. The crux is forgiveness: Rita pardons her husband's killers and prays that her sons should die rather than commit murder in revenge. The widow's long-delayed entry into religious life ends the story. The outline covers the vocation, the marriage and the sons' wish for vengeance; whether the film keeps the saint's prayer for her sons, which modern versions often soften, is not known.
history: Margherita Lotti was born at Roccaporena near Cascia around 1381, married young, and was widowed when her husband was killed in a feud. After her two sons died, she entered the Augustinian convent of St Mary Magdalene at Cascia, where she lived for some forty years. She died in 1457, was beatified in 1627 and canonised in 1900.
advisories:
A murder and a family feud.

Probably suitable for families, but the content is unconfirmed.

sources.claims: Birth 1381, entry into the Augustinian monastery c. 1407, stigmata tradition, death 22 May, beatification by Urban VIII, canonisation by Leo XIII on 24 May 1900, patronage.

suitability.note: A mother loses her husband and then her two sons. Nothing is reported to be graphic, and the pace will suit older children better than small ones.

doctrine: Rita of Cascia (Margherita Lotti) was canonised by Leo XIII on 24 May 1900, and her feast is 22 May. Italian sources date her entry into the Augustinian convent of St Mary Magdalene at Cascia to around 1407, after she had been refused three times. Her forgiveness of her husband's killers, the film's centre, is the Gospel command to love one's enemies (Matthew 5:44) carried out. The wound on her forehead, from a thorn of the Crucifix, is a tradition: the usual account puts it on Good Friday, 18 April 1432, though another gives 1442. She is invoked as the patron of hopeless cases and of unhappily married women.
production: Made for Titanus, the film was shot in black and white and runs about 83 minutes. Celestino Spada wrote the story. The interiors were shot at the Farnesina studios in Rome and the exteriors at Cascia itself, where many townspeople appeared as extras. The editor, Gisa Radicchi Levi, went uncredited because she was Jewish. It opened in Italian cinemas on 31 May 1943.

title: Rosa de Lima
decision: GREY: Identity is established (UC3M Cine de movilidad catalogue; Decine21 credits), and the subject, canonised in 1671, raises no hard rule. The only treatment source is Decine21, a present-day Catholic-oriented Spanish site, which cannot make it PUBLISH. A 1962–63 Spanish review or Catholic classification (Hemeroteca Digital BNE, ABC hemeroteca) would settle it.
summary: José María Elorrieta's modest Spanish biography of St Rose of Lima, with María Mahor as the girl who refuses marriage to give her life to God and the poor.
synopsis: The film opens with the arrival in Peru of a Spanish arquebusier in the service of Philip III, and follows the life of his daughter Isabel, called Rosa, born in Lima in the late sixteenth century to him and María de Oliva. Her parents intend her for marriage, but Rosa has privately vowed her virginity to God. She refuses the match and gives herself instead to prayer and to the care of the poor and sick of the city, against the wishes of her family. The film follows her to her early death in Lima in 1617, at about thirty-one, after which the city took her as its patron.
inclusion: Few films have been made about St Rose, and this is the main screen biography of the saint. It was a Spanish production made for the Spanish-speaking world, with a script credited to Juan Antonio Verdugo, Elorrieta, Manuel Sebares and César González Ruano, and it made María Mahor's name. Decine21, a Spanish site that reviews films from a Catholic standpoint, gives it 4 out of 10 and calls the production humble but dignified. It suits viewers who want a straightforward, devotional life of a saint little known outside Latin America, and who can accept the conventions of a low-budget Spanish religious film of its time.
themes: The film is built around Rosa's vow of virginity. She refuses the marriage her family intends because she has already given herself to God, and spends herself on prayer and on the poor, which is also the core of her historical cult. How the film handles her penances and mystical life is unknown. The descriptions available call it a respectful biography, and none reports anything contrary to Catholic teaching.
history: Isabel Flores de Oliva was born in Lima in 1586. She took the habit of St Dominic in her twentieth year, lived in seclusion in a small grotto built with her brother's help in the family garden, leaving mainly to visit the Blessed Sacrament, and practised severe fasting and mortification. She died in 1617. Clement IX beatified her in 1667 and Clement X canonised her in 1671, the first saint of the Americas.
advisories:
No violence or sexual content is reported.

The saint's penances may be shown, but how is unknown.
