The only independent review is a short modern one on Decine21, which rates it 4 out of 10 and calls it humble but dignified. There is no contemporary review, Spanish Catholic classification or detailed account of how it treats Rose's vow, penances and mystical life. A period review in the Spanish press, the film's Catholic rating, or a check of its dialogue would settle it.

suitability.note: Decine21 classes it for all audiences. It is a slow, modest biography, so younger children may find it dull.

doctrine: Rose of Lima (1586-1617) took the vow of virginity as a girl and spent about ten years winning her parents' consent to keep it. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1912) says she kept severe penances for fourteen years, including fasting, an iron chain and a crown of spikes hidden under roses. She offered them for sinners, for her country and for the souls in Purgatory. She received the Blessed Sacrament daily and spent many hours before it. Her feast is on 30 August, and she is patroness of America.
production: The film is a Spanish production of 1961 (some catalogues give 1962; IMDb Pro lists a Mexican release in January 1963), directed by José María Elorrieta for Cooperativa Cinematográfica Unión. It runs 97 or 98 minutes. Decine21 calls it one of Mahor's most important roles.

title: Mystic Rose
decision: GREY: Identity from Rotten Tomatoes and the Biblioteca Nacional del Perú; content from Sebastián Zavala's Cinencuentro review (independent, substantive) and director interviews (El Comercio, Cinencuentro). Subject canonised 1671. Serious about penance but ambiguous on sanctity, with invented symbolic scenes: a reservation a reader can weigh.
summary: Augusto Tamayo's long, austere Peruvian portrait of St. Rose of Lima's penances and mystical life, which leaves open whether she was a saint or a troubled girl.
synopsis: Lima, early in the seventeenth century. Rosa, daughter of Gaspar and María, refuses the marriage her ambitious mother wants for her and deliberately spoils her looks to avoid it. She also declines to enter a convent, choosing instead to live at home in prayer and penance. She fasts, scourges herself and prays through the night, and her health gives way. She cares for the sick, confronts an old man she believes is the devil, and falls into ecstasy before a crucifix. Several priests counsel and question her, and a woman friend encourages her. Her mother calls her mad. The film is arranged in thematic chapters rather than as a continuous life.
inclusion: Tamayo, one of Peru's senior directors, worked on the project for some forty years, and the care shows in its colonial interiors. Sebastián Zavala of Cinencuentro praised its churches and cathedrals and, above all, Fiorella Pennano, who carries the film. It is slow, close to two and a half hours, shot with a restless hand-held camera, and its chapters do not always make Rosa's choices clear. It does at least take the penitential and mystical life seriously as a subject. Tamayo, who says he is not a believer, rejects the clinical diagnoses that have been made of her and insists she was not mad. He says most episodes come from documented testimony.
themes: The film puts St. Rose's penances (fasting, scourging and sleepless prayer) at the centre and does not soften them. Tamayo argues that bodily suffering has meant sacrifice, offering and forgiveness in every religious culture, and that modern incomprehension, voiced in the film by her mother, is the problem. He treats Rosa as a human figure and does not make her an object of devotion. Zavala found the film cool and leaning towards a psychological reading: Rosa appears capricious and manipulative with her parents, and her holiness is played down. Grace remains one possible explanation among others.
history: Rose of Lima was born in Lima in 1586 and took the name Rose at her confirmation in 1597. In her twentieth year she received the Dominican habit and lived in severe penance, with fasting, a spiked crown hidden under roses and an iron chain, while caring for the sick and poor. She died in 1617. Clement IX beatified her in 1667 and Clement X canonised her in 1671, the first saint of the Americas.
liberties: Tamayo calls the film an interpretation and says so on screen. Some episodes are invented symbols, notably a chapter in which Rosa drinks putrefied blood and a slave bears a wound in the place of Christ's. Her baptismal name, Isabel, is never used.
advisories:
Self-scourging and other bodily penances shown at length; the film opens with a warning.

Rosa drinks a sick woman's blood; scenes of illness among hospital patients.

No sexual content reported.

grey.question: Mystic Rose takes St. Rose's penances and mystical life seriously and refuses to call her mad, but its director, an unbeliever, presents her as a human figure whose sanctity is left open. The Peruvian critic Sebastián Zavala found it cool, sparing with her holiness, and likely to leave viewers leaning towards illness as the explanation. Some symbolic scenes are invented. Viewers should weigh whether its open question respects her sanctity or undercuts it.

sources.title: Asceticism
sources.claims: Penance is a means not the measure of holiness; prudence; extraordinary mortifications not proposed for imitation

suitability.note: Explicit bodily penance and illness make this a film for adults and mature teenagers.

doctrine: The Catholic Encyclopedia (1912) records that Rose of Lima was born on 20 April 1586 and died on 30 August 1617, which is also her feast. She vowed virginity and was devoted to the Blessed Sacrament. On penance the Catholic Encyclopedia article on Asceticism (1907) teaches that it is a means of holiness and not its measure: virtue is not to be judged by bodily austerities, prudence must govern them, and the saints' extraordinary mortifications are not proposed for imitation.
production: Rosa mística is a Peruvian film of 2018, directed by Augusto Tamayo. Alberto Ísola, Hernán Romero, Jorge Chiarella and Bruno Odar play the priests who advise Rosa. A review of 5 September 2018 describes it as presenting her as a devout woman who may also have had mental health problems.

title: Paul the Apostle
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (St Paul's conversion and the apostolic Church, with Peter, John and Our Lady present) and with no reported doctrinal error, but Peter Chattaway's independent review finds it the weakest of Lux Vide's Bible films: much invented material, above all an invented Sadducee, Reuben, whose wedding night includes nudity (the US distributor recalled the first video release for a censored version), while Paul's own missions are compressed into montages and his martyrdom is not shown. Under the clare-and-francis threshold the inventions do not change the saint's own choices, so not REJECT; the nudity and dilution make it a reservation.
summary: Lux Vide's two-part Acts of the Apostles for Rai, with Johannes Brandrup as Saul turned Paul, padded with invented intrigue and short on Paul's missions.
synopsis: In Jerusalem the young Pharisee Saul (Johannes Brandrup), a pupil of the tolerant Gamaliel (Franco Nero), joins the persecution of the followers of Jesus and approves the stoning of Stephen. His friend Reuben, a Sadducee, later turns against him, and Reuben's young wife Dinah is drawn to the new faith. On the road to Damascus Saul is struck blind; Ananias restores his sight, and he escapes the city by night. The second part follows the Church in Jerusalem under Peter (Ennio Fantastichini), Herod's persecution, and Paul's work with Barnabas (G. W. Bailey) at Antioch and Lystra, his dispute with Peter over eating with Gentiles, and his break with Barnabas. His later journeys pass in montage, and the film ends with his arrival as a prisoner in Rome.
inclusion: Few films deal with the Acts of the Apostles, and this one gives a full three hours to the early Church in Jerusalem, Saul's persecution and conversion, and the first Gentile mission. Its best scenes are the early ones, among them Gamaliel's counsel, Stephen's death and the Damascus road. It was popular in Italy, drawing over 8.7 million viewers, and Corriere della Sera's Aldo Grasso called the direction honest and expository. Peter Chattaway of Christianity Today, who has written more on Bible films than any other critic, is blunter. He finds it one of the weakest of the Bible Collection and spends far too long on invented characters, and narrates key events such as Cornelius's baptism instead of showing them. The 1981 Peter and Paul, with Anthony Hopkins, is the better film about the Apostle.
themes: Paul's conversion is presented as an encounter with the risen Christ, followed by baptism and a life given to preaching him to the Gentiles. Peter appears as head of the Jerusalem Church, and Our Lady is among the disciples. The dispute at Antioch over eating with Gentiles is only described, and the reconciliation of Jew and Gentile in one Church is the film's concern. Its weakness lies in proportion. Paul's letters and theology barely feature, and his martyrdom, the crown of his life in Catholic tradition, is left out.
history: Saul of Tarsus, a Pharisee trained under Gamaliel, persecuted the Church and consented to the death of St Stephen before his conversion near Damascus (Acts 9). With Barnabas he evangelised Cyprus and southern Galatia, then made further journeys through Asia Minor and Greece. Arrested in Jerusalem in about 57, he appealed to Caesar and reached Rome about AD 60. Tradition holds he was beheaded under Nero.
liberties: Reuben, a Sadducee friend turned enemy, and his wife Dinah, who becomes a Christian, are invented and given much screen time. Paul's journeys after Acts 15 are compressed into montages, and the film ends at Rome without his death.

grey.question: The film tells Saul's persecution of the Church and his conversion faithfully, with Peter at the head of the Jerusalem Church and Our Lady among the disciples. Its reservations concern proportion and content. Much of its three hours goes to invented characters, including a Sadducee whose wedding night contains nudity, cut from a later US video release. Paul's own missions are reduced to montages, his letters barely appear, and the film ends with his arrival in Rome, without his martyrdom. Younger viewers should have the censored version.

suitability.note: Violence and brief nudity, cut from the later US video, make it a film for teenagers; younger viewers should see the censored version.

doctrine: The Catholic Encyclopedia places Paul's conversion about AD 35, after the martyrdom of Stephen (Acts 7:58-60). It dates the first mission (Cyprus and southern Galatia) to about 45-49, the second (Macedonia, Athens, Corinth) to about 50-53 and the third (Ephesus and Macedonia) to about 53-57. At the assembly at Jerusalem, about AD 50, Gentile converts were declared exempt from the Mosaic law, though asked to abstain from food offered to idols, blood, strangled meat and fornication. Tradition places his martyrdom at Aquae Salviae (Tre Fontane) near Rome toward the end of Nero's reign, and he is buried at San Paolo fuori le mura. The Church keeps Peter and Paul together on 29 June.
production: Part of the Lux Vide 'Bible Collection', directed by Roger Young, who had also made Joseph, Moses, Solomon and Jesus for the series. It was made in English as a television film, with the studios at Ouarzazate, Morocco, used for filming. The story is by Gianmario Pagano.

title: Satan Never Sleeps
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred and supported by a contemporary pre-1965 Catholic judgment: Legion of Decency A-III in Motion Picture Exhibitor's 1962 alphabetical tables, with the Exhibitor's own review and the AFI Catalog. Reservation: the rape plot and the marriage of the victim to her repentant attacker, which critics (Poague, via Wikipedia) read as leaving her no choice; a weak film by all contemporary accounts.
summary: Leo McCarey's last film casts William Holden and Clifton Webb as missionary priests in 1949 China, harried by a Communist commander who was once a mission boy.
synopsis: In 1949, as the Communists overrun China, young Father O'Banion (William Holden) arrives at a remote mission to relieve the elderly Father Bovard (Clifton Webb). Siu Lan (France Nuyen), a girl whose life O'Banion once saved, follows him there and declares her love, which he rebuffs. Colonel Ho San (Weaver Levy), raised at the mission before he renounced Christianity, wrecks the dispensary, desecrates the chapel and jails the priests for refusing to confess to crimes against the state. With O'Banion tied to a chair, he rapes Siu Lan, who later bears his son. When his superiors order the killing of Christians, his own parents among them, Ho San turns and tries to smuggle the group out. Father Bovard puts on Ho San's coat and cap and draws the pursuers' fire, dying so the others can escape. In Hong Kong O'Banion marries the couple and baptises their child.
inclusion: McCarey made Going My Way and The Bells of St. Mary's, and his last film tries to carry the same pairing of a young and an old priest into the persecution of the Church in Communist China. Few Hollywood films dealt with the harassment and expulsion of missionaries there, and this one shows a desecrated chapel, priests jailed for refusing false confessions, and an old priest who gives his life for others. Webb's dry delivery is the best thing in it. Contemporary judgments were poor. Motion Picture Exhibitor found it over-long, with awkward and embarrassing scenes; A. H. Weiler of the New York Times called it a lacklustre imitation of Going My Way; and the studio's ending, which according to McCarey's biographer replaced his own, is pat. The Legion of Decency classed it A-III, unobjectionable for adults.
themes: The faith is shown under persecution. The priests lose their mission and staff, are imprisoned and threatened with torture for refusing to confess to crimes against the state, and Father Bovard lays down his life so that a mother, her child and his fellow priest may escape. O'Banion keeps his vow of celibacy against Siu Lan's open infatuation, which is played largely for comedy. The ending returns to the sacraments, as Ho San, a lapsed mission boy, comes back to the faith, marries the woman he wronged and has their son baptised. Whether a woman should marry her attacker is the film's moral problem. It presents the marriage as reparation, but the film scholar Leland Poague has argued that it leaves her no choice.
history: The film is set during the Communist victory in China in 1949. It was based on a story by Pearl S. Buck, The China Story, published as the novel Satan Never Sleeps in 1962, with a screenplay by Claude Binyon and McCarey. It opened in London, as The Devil Never Sleeps, and in New York in February 1962.
advisories:
A rape is part of the plot, committed while a priest is tied up nearby; the victim later bears a child.

A chapel is desecrated; priests are threatened with torture; a priest is shot dead.

grey.question: The film's Catholic substance is sound. Priests are persecuted for the faith, an old priest dies for others, a lapsed Christian returns and a baptism follows, and the Legion of Decency passed it for adults. The difficulty lies in the plot, which turns on a rape that the film resolves by marrying the young woman to her attacker, now repentant, with the priest officiating. Viewers should judge whether it shows that marriage as her free choice; critics have argued it does not. It is also, by every contemporary account, a weak film.

names: The China Story, original story by Pearl S. Buck

suitability.note: A rape is central to the plot and is resolved by the victim marrying her attacker, alongside torture threats, a desecrated chapel and a priest shot dead. Not for children or young teenagers.

doctrine: Pius XII's encyclical Ad Apostolorum principis (29 June 1958) describes the persecution the film dramatises: missionaries and bishops expelled from China, clergy imprisoned, forced confessions and people's courts, and a 'patriotic' association meant to make Catholics adopt atheistic materialism and to put the Church under civil authority. He tells the faithful to answer as the Apostles did: we must obey God rather than men. On the ending, the Church holds that marriage is made by free consent. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1909) teaches that grave, unjust, external fear inflicted to force consent invalidates a marriage (the impediment of vis et metus). A union forced on a woman by her violator would be no marriage; the film's marriage can be defended only if her consent is shown to be free.
production: Leo McCarey directed and produced for Twentieth Century-Fox. The story began as The China Story, an original screenplay by Pearl S. Buck sold to Fox; Hal B. Wallis acquired the property in 1950 and it reached McCarey in 1960. The film was shot in England and Wales. McCarey said he left in disgust over studio interference and script changes; an assistant shot the final week and he did not approve the final cut. It was released in the United States on 23 March 1962 and runs 125 minutes. It was also released as The Devil Never Sleeps and Flight from Terror. It lost money, with about 1.5 million dollars in rentals against a budget of about 2.9 million.

title: Say One for Me
decision: GREY: Priest-centred, with real ministry (a baptism, an alcoholic helped to sobriety, a marriage); Legion of Decency A-II (1958-59), no objection recorded. Content from AFI and Motion Picture Exhibitor (17 June 1959). Reservation: much of the film is set in a cheap nightclub with showgirl numbers, and the faith content is thinner than in Going My Way. Editor may prefer PUBLISH by analogy with Going My Way.
summary: Bing Crosby's third New York priest runs a show-business parish, rescues a drunken songwriter and steers a chorus girl away from a playboy, in a slack CinemaScope musical.
synopsis: Father Conroy (Bing Crosby) has a parish in New York's theatre district, where he says a 2 a.m. Mass for performers. When the old vaudevillian Harry LeMaise has a heart attack, Conroy promises to look after his daughter Holly (Debbie Reynolds). She secretly takes a job as a showgirl in a cheap nightclub, where the entertainer Tony Vincent (Robert Wagner) sets out to seduce her. Conroy keeps watch, has a chorus girl's baby baptised with Tony as godfather, and helps the alcoholic songwriter Phil Stanley (Ray Walston) back to sobriety and work. To separate Tony from Holly he offers him a place on a televised charity show. Tony, conscience-stricken, gives the spot to Phil's new song, and Conroy marries Tony and Holly.
inclusion: It is the last of Crosby's priest films after Going My Way and The Bells of St. Mary's, and it shows why the formula ran out. The parish is loosely modelled on St Malachy's, the actors' church off Broadway, and that is its most interesting feature, a priest whose flock is chorus girls, comics and drunks. Motion Picture Exhibitor found it a warm crowd-pleaser; Variety thought something went wrong and Crosby was oddly inhibited; Bosley Crowther called it a pleasant show-world entertainment. It runs nearly two hours, with Cahn and Van Heusen songs and nightclub routines, and Stella Stevens made her debut in it.
themes: Conroy's work as a parish priest is pastoral and seldom doctrinal. He moves his Mass times to suit his people, brings an unmarried mother's child to baptism, helps an alcoholic to sobriety and protects a young woman's chastity. The film ends with a church wedding that redeems the playboy's intentions. It has little sense of the supernatural beyond good counsel, a criticism also made of Going My Way, and more of the running time goes to nightclub numbers than to the parish.
advisories:
Nightclub showgirl numbers with costumes revealing for 1959; a playboy's pursuit of a young woman.

Alcoholism; an unmarried mother.

For teenagers and up. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.

The priest's bargain with the playboy may strike some as manipulative.

VII, can. v), which condemns anyone who denies this or says infants should not be baptised. The ordinary minister is the priest. title: The Song of Sister Maria
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a singer's vocation, convent hospital work and death on the missions). Identity is established (Wikipedia, Cervantes Virtual Rabal archive) and the plot by an independent Spanish review (DQVlapeli, which judges it one of the weakest of Gil's religious films) and decine21 (present-day, content only). No contemporary Catholic rating or substantive independent assessment of its religious treatment was found; the 'clandestine recordings' episode raises an unanswered question about obedience. A 1952 Spanish Catholic rating or review would settle it.
summary: Rafael Gil's comedy-drama of a famous singer who becomes a nursing sister, cheerfully bends convent ways to save its hospital, and gives her life on the missions in India.
synopsis: Soledad, a celebrated singer, astonishes her family, the press and the public by giving up her career to enter a convent, where she becomes Sor María de la Asunción. She works in the order's hospital, whose finances are failing, and her unconventional, high-spirited methods at first disconcert her superiors. She brings about a conversion and wins half a million pesetas from a television impresario in exchange for recordings of her voice, which save the hospital. Her goal is a leper settlement in India. There, a local couple are expecting a child; bandits threaten their lives, and Sor María gives her own life so that the newborn can be baptised.
inclusion: It belongs to the cycle of religious films Rafael Gil made with the writer Vicente Escrivá for their company Aspa, alongside La señora de Fátima, La guerra de Dios and Judas' Kiss. The French actress Dominique Blanchar plays the singer-nun. It received the state's National Interest classification and the first prize of the Sindicato Nacional del Espectáculo. The DQVlapeli reviewer admires Gil's handling of the early comic and pathetic scenes, a false Christmas and the cure of a crippled boy in a wheatfield among them, but finds the Indian third act rushed, under-financed and poorly motivated. Decine21 praises its restraint, Alfredo Fraile's photography and Blanchar.
themes: The film is about a vocation that costs everything, from fame and family approval to life itself. Sor María's religious life is active, nursing the sick and raising money for the order's hospital, and it ends in missionary self-sacrifice for the baptism of a child, a clear statement of the value the Church places on that sacrament. Its weakness is a cheerful view of convent discipline, since the recordings that save the hospital are made in secret. How the film reconciles this with religious obedience is unknown.
advisories:
A violent bandit attack and the heroine's death.

Nothing sexual of note is reported.

sources.title: Baptism
sources.claims: Necessity of baptism, Trent Session 7 canon 5, lay baptism in necessity per Florence, form of baptism

grey.question: Sor Intrépida is a popular Spanish vocation story that ends with a nun giving her life on the missions so that a child can be baptised. Its outline is clear, but no critic or contemporary Catholic body has assessed its picture of religious life. One episode needs checking: she saves the order's hospital with recordings made in secret, and her superiors are at first disconcerted by her ways. Whether the film treats this as disobedience rewarded or as permitted initiative is not yet known.

suitability.note: The only violence is a bandit attack near the end, in which the heroine dies. The tone is mostly light, and children can follow the vocation story and the comic convent scenes.

doctrine: The climax turns on baptism, which the Church teaches is necessary for salvation. Trent, Session 7, canon 5, anathematises anyone who denies it, and the Catholic Encyclopedia reads John 3 as admitting no exception for infants. In danger of death anyone may baptise, as the Council of Florence's Decree for the Armenians allows, 'not only a priest or deacon, but even a layman or woman', using water and the form 'I baptize thee in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost' with the intention of doing what the Church does. Sor María's death for the sake of a child's baptism also fits the Church's teaching on martyrdom, though the film does not present her as a martyr in the strict sense.
production: Sor intrépida was made in 1952 by Aspa Producciones Cinematográficas. Mercurio Films distributed it, and it opened in Spain on 10 November 1952 at about 85 minutes. It was known abroad as The Song of Sister Maria or Path to the Kingdom.

title: St. Patrick: The Irish Legend
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (St Patrick's slavery, vocation, ordination and mission as bishop to Ireland, drawn in part from his Confession and the early Lives by Muirchú and Tírechán), with no sex or language problems. The reservation is its picture of the Church: the main antagonist is a corrupt British bishop, Quentin, who tries to have Patrick excommunicated after he refuses to collect church taxes, and Patrick's churches are shown accommodating clan customs, a pattern that plays to the popular myth of a free Celtic Church set against a grasping institution. Critics (Variety, VideoHound) and Alan Bates's biographer judge it historically careless. A weighable reservation, not a heterodox thesis.
summary: A Fox Family television life of St Patrick, with Patrick Bergin as the slave turned bishop and Malcolm McDowell as a scheming British churchman.
synopsis: In fifth-century Roman Britain, Patrick, son of the decurion Calpurnius (Alan Bates) and Concessa (Susannah York), is seized at sixteen by Irish raiders and sold as a slave to a harsh Druid chieftain. Herding animals for six years, he turns to prayer, and a vision tells him a ship is waiting. He escapes home, but dreams of the Irish calling him back. He trains for the priesthood in Gaul and returns to Ireland as its first bishop (Patrick Bergin), facing the Druids, winning converts such as the boy Benignus and founding churches. At home in Britain, Bishop Quentin (Malcolm McDowell) regards the Irish as heathens, suspects Patrick of founding a church of his own, and moves to have him excommunicated when he will not collect the British church's dues.
inclusion: There are very few films about St Patrick, and this one covers the essentials of his own account, from the raid and the years of slavery and prayer to the escape after a vision and the call back to the people who had enslaved him. It was shot on Irish locations, with music by Inon Zur and contributions from The Chieftains and Clannad, and Patrick Bergin gives the saint a calm authority. The Dove Foundation's reviewer found its picture of faith growing under trial worthwhile. Other critics were cool. Variety praised the cast and scenery but called it a well-meaning, absurd costume drama, and VideoHound found it bland. Alan Bates's biographer Donald Spoto said it had no historical accuracy, was sentimentally pious and treated Patrick chiefly as a wonder-worker.
themes: The film is strongest on Patrick's conversion in slavery and his choice to return as a missionary to his captors, the heart of his own Confession. Prayer, visions and the courage to face the Druids carry the story, and the Dove reviewer notes its emphasis on salvation through Christ's sacrifice and God's mercy. Its picture of the Church is weaker. The British clergy are corrupt and unloving, Patrick is set against them over money, and his accommodation of clan customs is presented as a virtue against them.
history: Patrick, a Romano-Briton of the fifth century, was captured at sixteen and spent six years as a slave in Ireland before escaping. Ordained, he returned as a bishop and spent the rest of his life evangelising the Irish. His Confession, written late in life, answers charges brought by church elders in Britain. Muirchú and Tírechán wrote the first Lives in the seventh century.
liberties: Bishop Quentin and the tax dispute are invented; the film turns the elders' charges mentioned in Patrick's Confession into a corrupt prelate's vendetta. Patrick's miracles are staged freely from the later legends. The Roman connection of his mission is omitted.
advisories:
A raid with several killed and bloodied bodies; Patrick's capture and enslavement; Druid menace.

No sexual content or bad language.

Approved for 12+ by the Dove Foundation; suitable for older children.

grey.question: The film tells the core of St Patrick's own story: slavery, prayer, escape, ordination and his return as bishop to the people who had enslaved him. The question is its picture of the Church. Its villain is an invented British bishop who tries to have Patrick excommunicated for refusing to collect church taxes, the clergy at home are corrupt, and Patrick's adaptations to clan custom are set against them. Rome plays no part. Viewers should weigh that against the historical Patrick, whose quarrel with his elders concerned an old sin and not money.

suitability.note: A raid leaves several dead and bloodied, Patrick is enslaved, and the Druids are menacing, though nothing is graphic and there is no sexual content or bad language. The history is loose, so older children should be told that.

doctrine: Patrick's mission was commissioned by the Roman Pontiff. The Catholic Encyclopedia says Pope Celestine sent the bishop Palladius to the Irish in 430, that Palladius did little and returned to Britain, and that in 432 Celestine sent Patrick. Another article says that when Palladius's death became known at Rome in 431 Patrick was chosen and consecrated bishop for Ireland. This is at odds with the film, in which Rome plays no part and a British bishop threatens Patrick with excommunication. The encyclopedia dates Patrick's death to 17 March 493. It records that he was sold to Milchu, a druidical high priest, and escaped after a vision. It also says his Confession survives in the Book of Armagh.
production: St. Patrick: The Irish Legend was a Fox Family Channel television film, made with Sharpmist III Ltd. Robert Hughes directed and produced it, and wrote the script with Martin Duffy. It runs 92 minutes, and James Mathers was the cinematographer. It premiered on Fox Family Channel on 12 March 2000.

title: St. Wenceslas
decision: GREY: Identity is established (Wikipedia citing ČSFD and Czech Radio; the Czech Government Office and Czech Radio on the 2010 restoration). Content is known only in outline: St Wenceslas raised a Christian by his grandmother St Ludmila, opposed by his mother Drahomíra and a plotter, murdered by his brother Boleslav. Official sources say it stresses Czech statehood and peace (with the Germans, per the title of Petr Kopal's Cinepur article, not opened). No independent assessment of its religious treatment was found. A Czech critical study (Kopal 2009; Filmový přehled's 'Saint Wenceslas in film', which returned 403) would settle it.
summary: Czechoslovakia's costly millennium epic of the martyr-duke St Wenceslas, raised in the faith by St Ludmila and murdered by his brother Boleslav.
synopsis: Wenceslas is brought up as a Christian by his grandmother Ludmila, while his mother Drahomíra holds to the old gods. After his father's death, a schemer named Skeř stirs up Drahomíra, Wenceslas's younger brother Boleslav and the duke of Zlič against Ludmila and Wenceslas, and Ludmila is murdered. Wenceslas comes to the throne and rules as a Christian prince, seeking peace with his German neighbours, and the film stages great battles with thousands of extras. Boleslav finally kills his brother. Afterwards Boleslav is said to regret what he has done.
inclusion: St. Wenceslas was the most expensive Czech film yet made: a state-backed epic for the thousandth anniversary of the duke's death, with 5,000 extras, castle sets built at the Strahov stadium, location shooting in the Šumava forest and at Křivoklát, and a cast that included Vera Baranovskaya, Pudovkin's Mother, as Ludmila. It arrived in April 1930, a silent film just as sound took over, without the orchestral score by Oskar Nedbal and Jaroslav Křička that had been planned, and it flopped; most of its audience were schoolchildren.
themes: The film's subject is a martyr-king, a Christian prince formed by a saintly grandmother, opposed by pagan and political enemies within his own family and killed by his brother. Both Wenceslas and Ludmila were venerated as martyrs long before 1965. The official accounts of the 2010 restoration say the film puts strong emphasis on Czech statehood and peace, and the title of Petr Kopal's article suggests that peace with the Germans was its political theme. How far the drama's motive is faith and how far national history is not documented.
history: Wenceslas, born probably in 903, was raised a Christian by his grandmother St Ludmila, murdered in 921 at the instigation of his pagan mother Drahomíra. He ruled Bohemia as duke. He was murdered by his brother Boleslav at Stará Boleslav, probably on 28 September 935, and his relics were moved to St Vitus in Prague. He became patron of Bohemia.
advisories:
Battle scenes, the murder of Ludmila and the killing of Wenceslas.

Silent; the 2010 restoration carries the original orchestral score.

Suitable for older children and up.

grey.question: St. Wenceslas tells the life and martyrdom of the Bohemian duke, raised in the faith by St Ludmila and murdered by his brother, in a costly state-funded epic of 1930. Its outline is known, and official accounts say it stresses Czech statehood and peace with the Germans. No independent review describes how it treats Wenceslas's faith and death. A Czech critical study of the restored version would settle whether the saint or the national myth is its centre.

suitability.note: Battle scenes and the murders of Ludmila and Wenceslas are staged with restraint. Children who like history and knights will cope; younger ones will lose the thread.

doctrine: Wenceslas was killed as he went to Mass, and the Church counts him a martyr although his brother killed him for political as well as religious reasons. His feast is 28 September. His grandmother St Ludmila, who taught him the faith, was strangled and is also honoured as a martyr. Wenceslas favoured the Latin rite and German priests and placed Bohemia under the protection of the German king, which the Catholic Encyclopedia records. The film's 1929-30 date marks the thousandth anniversary of his death as then reckoned. Methodius, who appears in the cast, was the Apostle of the Slavs with his brother Cyril; Hadrian II approved their Slavonic liturgy in 867-869, and Wenceslas's period saw tension between the Slavonic and Latin rites.
production: The Czechoslovak government made the film part of the 1929 millennium celebrations and lent the producers 1 million crowns, and another million when filming nearly stalled. Prime Minister František Udržal also supplied army equipment and personnel. Jan S. Kolár directed and co-wrote it, and five cameramen shot it, among them Otto Heller. It had more than a hundred principals. Shooting began in September 1929, moved indoors in December and took 82 days. A 40-piece orchestra played at the premiere, since plans to record the music failed. František Balšán reconstructed it in 1971, supervised by Kolár himself. In 2009 the lost score was found in Czech Radio's archive, and the film was shown with live orchestra at the Rudolfinum on 28 September 2010.

title: The Awakening
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a missionary sister's vocation, obedience and charity). The contemporary Italian Catholic notice (Segnalazioni cinematografiche vol. 40, 1956, via Cinematografo) judged the very delicate subject not handled adequately or convincingly and called for more discretion. Legion of Decency A-II (Awakening (Ital.), 1957-58). Reservation, stated.
summary: Anna Magnani plays a missionary nun sent to close a failing island convent who reopens its school instead, and grows too attached to an abandoned boy.
synopsis: After twenty years in the African missions, Sister Letizia (Anna Magnani) is sent to an island in the Gulf of Naples to wind up a struggling convent, close it and take its last nuns back to the mother house. Offers for the land come quickly. Instead she takes pity on Salvatore, a fatherless boy whose mother Assunta (Eleonora Rossi Drago) means to leave him behind to go away with Peppino (Antonio Cifariello), who will not have the child. Against her superiors' wishes Letizia takes in Salvatore and other children and reopens the convent school. Her love for the boy grows possessive, and the other sisters notice. Recalled, she plans to take him with her, until the Mother Superior's words, and the boy himself, show her she must let him go. She goes to Naples and persuades Peppino to marry Assunta and take Salvatore in.
inclusion: The film is a vehicle for Magnani, and her energy carries it, as a forceful nun with years of mission work behind her who cannot leave a problem alone. Its subject is maternal feeling in a consecrated woman, and the danger that charity turns into possession. The contemporary notice in Segnalazioni cinematografiche, the Italian Catholic film office's review, was unconvinced: it found the delicate subject handled neither adequately nor convincingly, wanted more discretion, and thought the role did not suit Magnani's temperament, for all her spontaneity and passion.
themes: Religious life is treated as a vocation with demands. Letizia's virtues, zeal, pity and practical energy, lead her into disobedience, as she ignores her instructions and keeps the convent open on her own authority. Her love for Salvatore then becomes an attachment that draws her from her duties. The ending restores order: counselled by the Mother Superior, she gives the boy up for his own good and works to reunite him with his mother within a marriage. The film closes on obedience and self-denial. The Catholic reviewer's doubts concerned the handling of a nun discovering herself as a mother.
advisories:
No violence or sexual content reported.

A child is abandoned by his mother; emotional scenes.

For older children and up. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.

grey.question: Anna Magnani's nun disobeys her superiors to keep a convent open, then loves an abandoned boy so possessively that she neglects her duties and plans to take him away with her. The film ends with her giving him up on her superior's counsel and reuniting him with his mother. But the Italian Catholic film office's 1956 notice judged that its very delicate subject, a religious discovering maternal feeling, was handled neither adequately nor convincingly and needed more discretion. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.

suitability.note: The story turns on an abandoned child and a nun's possessive love for him, which younger children will not follow. The ending has her give the boy up on her superior's counsel.

doctrine: Sister Letizia disobeys her superiors, and the film treats this as a fault. The Catholic Encyclopedia says religious obedience is a submission made to God through the vow, and a promise to the superiors, and that it is not unlimited: a superior cannot command what lies outside his preceptive power or against higher authority. The convent's head draws her power to command from the vow, according to the approved constitutions. The film's resolution, in which Letizia yields to her Mother Superior and returns the boy to his mother, is consistent with that account of obedience.
production: Suor Letizia (The Awakening) was directed by Mario Camerini from a script by Cesare Zavattini. Anna Magnani won her fourth Silver Ribbon for best actress for the part, and the film was released in Italy by Columbia Pictures on 18 October 1956 at about 97 minutes, in black and white. It reached the US as The Awakening.

title: Tepeyac
decision: GREY: Identity is established (Il Cinema Ritrovato 2017 record of the Filmoteca UNAM 2K restoration; UNAM Gaceta; Wikipedia citing Wilt and Schroeder Rodríguez). Content is established by Shari Kizirian's San Francisco Silent Film Festival essay and the UNAM restorers: a 1917 frame story enclosing a reverent re-enactment of the 1531 apparitions, based on Becerra Tanco's account. No independent assessment of its religious treatment exists. Juan Diego (beatified 1990) is a character, not the subject: rule (a) does not apply, and he must not be called saint or blessed.
summary: Mexico's oldest surviving fiction feature: a woman praying to Our Lady of Guadalupe for her missing fiancé reads the story of the 1531 apparitions, which the film re-enacts.
synopsis: Lupita Flores is engaged to Carlos Fernández, a diplomat who has to sail for Europe during the war. News comes that his ship has been sunk by a German submarine. Lupita prays to Our Lady of Guadalupe for his safety and, unable to sleep, reads the story of the apparitions. The film then tells it: in December 1531 the Virgin appears to the Indian Juan Diego on the hill of Tepeyac and asks for a church to be built there. Bishop Juan de Zumárraga doubts him and asks for a sign. The Virgin sends Juan Diego to gather roses in winter; when he opens his tilma before the bishop, her image is on it. Back in the present, Carlos turns out to have survived, and the couple visit the Basilica of Guadalupe on 12 December.
inclusion: Made by Films Colonial in 1917, when the war had cut off European and American imports, it is the oldest surviving feature-length fiction film from Mexico and the first Mexican film about Guadalupe. The frame story is simple melodrama, and the apparitions are staged as a pious re-enactment based, according to the Filmoteca UNAM, on Luis Becerra Tanco's seventeenth-century account and Ignacio Manuel Altamirano's La fiesta de Guadalupe. It also preserves documentary images: a procession to Tepeyac carrying the banner Hidalgo raised in 1810. The Filmoteca UNAM restored it digitally, cleaning some 49,000 frames by hand, with a new score by José María Serralde.
themes: The film's Catholic content is direct. A woman in danger of losing the man she loves turns to Our Lady of Guadalupe, and her prayer is answered; the framing makes the 1531 story a lesson in trust. The apparition is told as the tradition tells it, with the Virgin asking for a church, the bishop asking for a sign, and the roses and the image on the tilma giving it. Shari Kizirian notes that the film presents what many believe to be historical fact.
history: According to the tradition, the Virgin appeared to Juan Diego at Tepeyac, near Mexico City, in December 1531 and left her image on his cloak as a sign for Bishop Zumárraga. Kizirian's essay outlines the later history: an inquiry in 1666, approval in the eighteenth century, and the title 'Empress of the Americas' in 1945. The hill had been a sanctuary of the Aztec goddess Tonantzin. Juan Diego was beatified in 1990 and canonised in 2002.
advisories:
No violence or sensual content reported.

Silent, with Spanish intertitles.

Suitable for all ages.

Running times vary between about 40 and 64 minutes in different sources and screenings.

grey.question: Tepeyac frames a re-enactment of the 1531 Guadalupe apparitions within a 1917 story of a woman praying for her fiancé, and every account describes the apparitions as told reverently and in the traditional form. No independent critical assessment of the religious treatment exists; the available writing concerns the film's place in Mexican film history and its restoration. A detailed review of the restored Filmoteca UNAM version, or a reading of its intertitles, would settle it.

sources.title: Our Lady of Guadalupe
sources.claims: 1666 inquiry; Benedict XIV 1754; Pius X 1910; Juan Diego beatification 1990

names: La fiesta de Guadalupe, by Ignacio Manuel Altamirano, and the account of the apparitions by Luis Becerra Tanco

suitability.note: The story of the apparitions is told with reverence. Children may find the pace slow.

doctrine: The cult at Tepeyac rests on the Church's own acts, not on the film. A cathedral inquiry took place in 1665-66, when painters examined the image on the tilma. On 25 May 1754 Benedict XIV, by the bull Non est Equidem, named Our Lady of Guadalupe patroness of New Spain and granted a Mass and Office for her feast, 12 December; the Sacred Congregation of Rites acted in the same year. On 16 June 1910 Pius X declared her patroness of the Republic of Mexico. The honour paid to her is the veneration due to the Mother of God, which is not adoration. The film's frame story, a prayer for a fiance answered, shows the ordinary Catholic practice of petitioning Our Lady.
production: Tepeyac was made in 1917 by the Mexican company Colonial. The directors were the writer José Manuel Ramos and the painter Carlos E. González, with Fernando Sáyago also credited; they had little film experience and modest equipment. The film was made in the year of the new Mexican Constitution, whose limits on religion in education made the apparitions a live political subject. A nitrate print was restored digitally by the Filmoteca UNAM (49,110 frames and 107 intertitles), with a new score by José María Serralde.

title: The Big Fisherman
decision: PUBLISH: Legion of Decency A-I (1958-59), and the dialogue (English, read 2026-10-12) removes the main reservation. Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi is given in full, with Christ's answer naming him the rock on which he will build his Church, promising that the gates of hell will not prevail and giving him the keys of the kingdom. The Sermon on the Mount, the Our Father, John the Baptist's rebuke of Antipas and his death, a healing by Christ and a healing by Peter in the holy name are all dramatised. The invented Arabian plot is long, but Peter's office is not left undeveloped, and nothing contrary to Catholic teaching was found.
summary: Frank Borzage's last film, a three-hour Lloyd C. Douglas epic in which Howard Keel's Simon Peter becomes Christ's chief disciple while an Arabian princess plots to kill Herod Antipas.
synopsis: Fara (Susan Kohner), a princess half Arab and half Jewish, learns that her father is Herod Antipas (Herbert Lom), who abandoned her mother. After her mother's death she vows revenge and rides to Galilee disguised as a boy. Robbed of her horse, she is taken in by Simon (Howard Keel), a big, self-reliant fisherman sceptical of the preacher from Nazareth. John the Baptist, soon imprisoned and beheaded for rebuking Antipas, points her to Jesus, whose teaching against vengeance she resists. Simon becomes Jesus' chief disciple and confesses him as the Christ. When Fara has her chance to kill Antipas, she remembers Christ's words and lowers the knife. Peter takes her back to Arabia, where he heals a jealous prince who later breaks his promise to reform and dies. Fara's suitor Voldi (John Saxon) becomes king; she will not marry him, and sails for Galilee to carry on Christ's work.
inclusion: Borzage was one of Hollywood's great romantic directors, and this was his last film, a 70mm Panavision production released by Disney's Buena Vista, with Oscar nominations for its photography, costumes and art direction. Motion Picture Exhibitor's reviewer was impressed by its scale and by religion presented in palatable form. Most critics were not: Variety called it pious but plodding, and Halliwell leaden. Keel makes a good physical Peter, the fisherman who trusts his own strength until he learns to trust Christ. Its weakness is proportion, since Lloyd C. Douglas's invented Arabian romance takes most of the running time. The Gospel scenes, when they come, are given whole and without hedging, Peter's confession and commission above all.
themes: Peter's conversion is the spiritual line, from self-reliance to dependence on Christ, from fisherman to the disciple called to be a fisher of men. The film gives his confession that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God, and Christ's reply in full. Peter is the rock, the Church will be built on him, hell will not prevail against it, and he receives the keys. Christ's teaching against revenge, from the Sermon on the Mount, is the turning point of Fara's story, and her renunciation of vengeance is the film's main moral act. Peter prays for a healing and later heals a prince in God's name; the prince breaks his vow to reform and dies. The film ends before the Passion, so neither the Cross nor the Resurrection is shown.
liberties: Fara, Voldi and the whole Arabian plot are Douglas's inventions. They grow from a historical fact: Herod Antipas married a daughter of the Nabataean king Aretas IV and divorced her for Herodias. The Gospel events are compressed and seen through Peter and Fara, and Peter's journey to Arabia and his healing of a prince there are invented.
advisories:
Fights and deaths; John the Baptist's execution, not shown graphically.

A chaste romance subplot.

For families, though very long. The Legion of Decency rated it A-I.

doctrine: The film's central scene is Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi. The First Vatican Council, in Pastor Aeternus (1870), taught that Christ gave Peter a true primacy of jurisdiction over the whole Church, directly and immediately, and not merely an honorary one (chapter 1), and that it passes to the Roman Pontiffs (chapter 2). The Catholic Encyclopedia reads Matthew 16:18 in the same way.
history: Simon, son of Jona, was a fisherman of Bethsaida who lived at Capernaum and owned his own boat. His brother Andrew brought him to Jesus, who named him Cephas, 'rock'. At Caesarea Philippi he confessed Jesus as the Christ, and Christ promised to build His Church upon him. The Catholic Encyclopedia holds that Peter laboured in Rome and died there, probably under Nero, between mid-64 and early 68, and was buried on the Vatican Hill.
production: Rowland V. Lee produced the film and co-wrote it with Howard Estabrook from Lloyd C. Douglas's 1948 novel. It was shot in Super Panavision 70 in the San Fernando Valley and at La Quinta, California, on a budget of about $4 million. Disney first rejected the project for its religious tone, but Roy Disney backed it, and Buena Vista released it on 4 August 1959. Reported running times range from 149 to 184 minutes.

title: The End of the Affair
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a vow to God, a priest's direction, a secret Catholic baptism, a conversion) and passed A-II by the Legion of Decency (1954-55). The English dialogue (read 2026-10-12) confirms the reservation and refines it: the affair is told with sympathy and never named as sin by the priest, Sarah is not shown receiving any sacrament and dies without a priest, her last letter speaks loosely of the lovers being part of God, and no miracle follows her death. In its favour, the vow is kept, the priest's counsel is sound, the childhood baptism is kept, and Bendrix ends conceding God's existence. Treatment established by AFI, Sterritt (TCM) and Schwartz.
summary: Deborah Kerr plays Graham Greene's adulteress who, believing her lover killed in an air raid, vows to give him up if God spares him, and is held by the promise.
synopsis: In London during the flying-bomb raids, the writer Maurice Bendrix (Van Johnson) is having an affair with Sarah Miles (Deborah Kerr), wife of the civil servant Henry (Peter Cushing). A bomb wrecks his flat; Sarah, finding him under a fallen door and thinking him dead, prays and promises God to give him up if he lives. He walks in, and she leaves him without explanation. A year later the jealous Bendrix hires a detective, Parkis (John Mills), who obtains her diary. It records her vow, her visits to a priest, and her talks with Smythe, an atheist orator whose hatred of God convinces her that God exists. She resolves to break the vow, then promises Henry she will not leave him. Bendrix pursues her through the rain to a church. She falls ill and dies; her mother reveals she was secretly baptised a Catholic, and her last letter declares her belief.
inclusion: Greene's novel is one of the central Catholic novels of the century, and this first film of it keeps its spine, a vow made in desperation that turns out to bind and a woman drawn to God against her own inclinations. Deborah Kerr was widely praised. Van Johnson was miscast, as Greene himself said, and Columbia's recut of Dmytryk's flashback structure leaves the film talky. Bosley Crowther of the New York Times found it muddy and Sarah irrational, while Picturegoer called it distinguished and provocative. David Sterritt, writing for TCM, thinks it tame beside Neil Jordan's 1999 remake but more thoughtful than most religious films of its day.
themes: The film takes seriously the idea that a promise made to God in terror binds. Sarah, who says she is not a Catholic, keeps her vow without knowing why. The priest first asks why she should keep a vow made to a God she does not believe in, then reminds her that God gave her free will to use for him or against him; later he tells her that one moment of acknowledging God was the first step of a long journey, and that to seek God is already to have found him. The film keeps Greene's revelation that her mother had her baptised a Catholic at two. Her last letter professes belief in loose words, and Bendrix ends conceding that God exists while asking for time.
liberties: Lenore Coffee's script reorders Greene's flashbacks. The sexual side of the affair is softened. The miracles after Sarah's death, including the healing of Smythe's disfigurement, are omitted; his affliction is mentioned but nothing follows. Bendrix's reluctant turn toward belief is reduced to a few closing lines.
advisories:
An adulterous affair is the starting point; it is treated sympathetically but not explicitly, and the priest never addresses it.

Wartime bombing; a woman's illness and death.

For adults. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.

grey.question: This is a Catholic story told through an adultery. Sarah Miles promises God to give up her lover if he survives a bomb, keeps the vow against her own wishes, seeks out a priest, and comes to belief; the film keeps Greene's revelation that she was secretly baptised a Catholic as a child. But the affair is told with sympathy and the priest never names it as sin, she receives no sacrament and dies without a priest, and the novel's miracles after her death are cut. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.

names: The End of the Affair, novel by Graham Greene (1951)

suitability.note: The subject, jealousy and a wasting death make it a film for adults.

doctrine: Sarah's promise to give Maurice up if he lives is a vow in the Church's sense only if it is a promise made to God with full knowledge and liberty. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1912) says a vow must have 'full consent of the will', that a vow binds according to the maker's reasonable intention, and that dispensation from a vow is ordinarily justified by great difficulty or a vow taken without due deliberation. Baptism with water, the Trinitarian form and the right intention is valid, and the Council of Trent (session 7, canons 13-14) rejected the claim that infants so baptised are not counted among the faithful or may be left to their own will later. By that teaching Sarah, who says she is not a Catholic, is a baptised Christian. The Encyclopedia notes that baptism of desire applies to adults who show perfect contrition or charity.
production: The producer David Lewis bought the novel rights, and the project was delayed about three years before Columbia took it. Lewis wanted Richard Burton as Bendrix, but Columbia insisted on Van Johnson. Greene had wanted James Agee as screenwriter; the backers refused. Lenore Coffee, a convert, wrote the script, and a British writer later rewrote it. It was shot mostly in London and at Shepperton, and entered at Cannes in 1955. Columbia recut it after shooting, and the miracles of the novel, including the one that shakes Smythe, were removed at the last minute over Lewis's objections. It opened in London in February 1955 and runs 106 minutes. Variety praised Kerr; Crowther found it 'cluttered and cold'.

title: The Fighting 69th
decision: GREY: The Legion of Decency classed it A-I, and Film Daily's January 1940 review calls it an outstanding war picture whose second strand is a finely etched study of Fr Duffy, played reverently by Pat O'Brien. The chaplain drives the redemption of the coward Plunkett. The open question is scope: the film is first a regimental saga and patriotic melodrama, and the sources do not show whether Duffy's ministry is presented in sacramental Catholic terms or as generic chaplaincy. Precedent (Men of Boys Town) rejects priest-led films whose subject is not religious; this one is closer to the line. A transcript would settle it.
summary: Warner Bros.' First World War saga of New York's Irish regiment, in which Fr Francis Duffy (Pat O'Brien) refuses to give up on a cowardly braggart (James Cagney).
synopsis: When America enters the war, Jerry Plunkett, a cocky New Yorker, joins the 69th Infantry, the old Irish regiment, sneering at its traditions and boasting that he will beat the Germans alone. In his first action he panics. Fr Francis Duffy, the regimental chaplain, believes the man can change and persuades Major 'Wild Bill' Donovan to give him another chance. On a night patrol Plunkett betrays the squad's position and several men are killed, including two brothers of Sergeant Big Mike Wynn. He is court-martialled and sentenced to death. Duffy visits him in his cell and refuses to help him escape. A German shell wrecks the prison; Plunkett frees himself, pulls Duffy from the rubble and watches him tend the wounded. He returns to the line, works a mortar for Wynn's crew, and dies throwing himself on a grenade to save Wynn.
inclusion: This is one of the classic Warner Bros. pictures of the period, with Cagney and O'Brien in their familiar pairing. Film Daily ranked it with the best war pictures made and praised O'Brien as born to play Duffy reverently and humanly. Later critics are cooler: Dennis Schwartz calls it a sentimental recruiting-poster account, sugary and patriotic, with exciting battle scenes and a fine Cagney breakdown. Its interest here is Fr Duffy, a priest from history, shown as a chaplain who will not give up on a soul.
themes: Duffy is the film's conscience. He sees good in a man everyone else has written off, argues for his second chance, visits him under sentence of death, refuses to connive at desertion, and keeps ministering to the wounded under shellfire. Plunkett's change of heart follows from seeing that example, and the film presents his self-sacrifice as redemption. The regiment's Irish Catholic identity is part of its colour, and Kilmer, a Catholic convert, is among the characters. It is unknown whether confession, absolution or the last rites are shown, or whether Duffy's role is that of a generic chaplain.
history: Fr Francis P. Duffy (1871-1932), a Canadian-born priest of the Archdiocese of New York ordained in 1896, was chaplain to the 69th New York (165th Infantry) in France and was much decorated. William Donovan commanded a battalion; the poet Joyce Kilmer, a sergeant, was killed in July 1918. Training at Camp Mills, the Rouge Bouquet dugout collapse and the Ourcq crossing are drawn from the regiment's history. Duffy's statue stands in Duffy Square, Times Square.
liberties: Plunkett is fictional, and his cowardice-and-redemption story, the court-martial and the shell that frees him are inventions. The film compresses the regiment's campaigns and shapes them around his personal story.
advisories:
Extensive battle violence and deaths; a soldier killed by a grenade.

A death sentence for cowardice.

grey.question: Fr Duffy is the moral centre of this war film: he refuses to give up on a coward, visits him under sentence of death and leads him, by example, to a redemptive death. But the film is first a patriotic regimental saga, and it is unclear how Catholic Duffy's ministry is on screen, whether confession or the last rites appear, or whether he is simply a good chaplain. Viewers should judge whether the faith is the film's substance or its colour.

suitability.note: The violence is of its period and not gory, so older children can watch it.

doctrine: Fr Duffy's part in the film is that of a priest in the field, a chaplain with the wounded and dying. The sacrament proper to the dying is Extreme Unction. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1909) says that, as the Council of Trent defined (Session XIV, chapter iii, canon iv), only bishops and priests can administer it, and that it is for Christians who are seriously ill. When death is near, a single anointing and a shortened rite suffice; the Holy Office approved a short form for such cases in 1906. This is why a chaplain was needed at the front at all. The laity can comfort the dying, but only a priest can give the sacraments.
production: Warner Bros. released the film on 26-27 January 1940, directed by William Keighley. It is loosely based on the 69th New York's service in the First World War. Duffy, Donovan, Kilmer and Lt Oliver Ames were historical figures. Most of it was shot on the studio's Calabasas Ranch, with John T. Prout, a former captain in the regiment, as technical adviser. It runs about 90 minutes and took roughly $2.3 million worldwide. Priscilla Lane was cut before production, so there are no women in it.

title: The Garden of Allah
decision: PUBLISH: The Legion of Decency classified it A-I (unobjectionable for general patronage, 1936–37 list), the contemporary pre-conciliar Catholic judgment. Identity and plot from Wikipedia (citing Thomson and Greene) and the Legion list; independent treatment from Graham Greene (Spectator, 1936, via Wikipedia), Sister Celluloid and Silver Screenings. A Trappist who fled his monastery marries without telling his wife; when his past is discovered she lets him return to make reparation. Vows upheld. The romance is foregrounded and the film is generally judged weak; stated in the prose.
summary: Selznick's Technicolor desert romance: Marlene Dietrich marries Charles Boyer, not knowing he is a Trappist who has broken his vows, and lets him go back.
synopsis: After her father's death, Domini Enfilden visits the convent where she was raised, and the Mother Superior suggests the solitude of the Sahara. At a Trappist monastery in Tunisia, Brother Antoine, the only monk who knows the secret of the house's famous liqueur, has fled. On a train Domini meets a troubled stranger who calls himself Boris Androvsky. In the desert he shows a strange hostility to religion, but they fall in love, and Father Roubier, uneasy, marries them. On their honeymoon caravan they rescue a lost patrol, and an officer recognises Boris as the runaway monk. Boris confesses his past and his vows. Domini, who loves him, lets him go back to the monastery to make reparation, and they part at its gate.
inclusion: The Garden of Allah is remembered for its colour. It was one of the first features in three-strip Technicolor, and the cinematographers received a special Academy Award; Max Steiner's score was nominated. As drama it is generally thought a failure. Graham Greene called its surrealism 'really magnificent' but mocked its 'superhumanly pious' Church. Modern reviewers are blunt: Silver Screenings calls it a mess with miscast leads and stilted dialogue, though Basil Rathbone and C. Aubrey Smith are good; Sister Celluloid enjoys it as gorgeous, ridiculous romance. A big Hollywood studio made a love story whose ending sends the hero back to the cloister because his vows bind him.
themes: The story turns on the permanence of solemn vows. Boris has fled the Trappists and lives in torment, hostile to the faith he has betrayed. His marriage to Domini, made by a priest who does not know his past, cannot stand, and the film does not pretend otherwise. Once the truth is out, Domini, raised by nuns and herself devout, gives him up so that he can return and do penance. The film's sympathy is with the lovers, and the cloister is shown as a sacrifice.
history: Robert Hichens published The Garden of Allah in 1904, and it became a bestseller. It had already been filmed in 1916 and 1927 before Selznick's version, the third feature made in the new three-strip Technicolor process.
advisories:
A love story between a woman and a runaway monk who has hidden his vows; an invalid marriage, treated with restraint.

A tense scene with a dancer and her jealous lover; desert hardship.

Rated A-I by the Legion of Decency; suitable for older children and up.

doctrine: The plot depends on the nature of solemn vows. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1912) says that canon law recognised as solemn only the vow of chastity, made by religious profession, and that solemn profession annuls even an earlier unconsummated marriage. The Pope may dispense even from it, but only for exceptionally grave reasons. A monk who leaves his monastery is therefore not freed, and Boris's marriage to Domini is no marriage in the eyes of the Church. The film follows this: Domini, convent-educated, does not argue the point but sends him back to make reparation. The priest who marries them does so without knowing who Boris is, which makes Father Roubier's unease no fault of his.
production: David O. Selznick produced the film through Selznick International, directed by Richard Boleslawski. Filming ran from 15 April to 3 July 1936, in California and at Yuma, Arizona. It was released in 1936 (Wikipedia gives 19 November) and runs 79 minutes. It earned about $2.7 million worldwide but lost money against its costs. It also received an Academy Award nomination for assistant director.

title: The Left Hand of God
decision: PUBLISH: Legion of Decency A-II, and AFI records the Production Code condition that Carmody is never shown hearing confessions or saying Mass. The dialogue (Portuguese subtitles, read 2026-10-12) settles the reservation in the film's favour: he refuses absolution to a dying man and leads only common prayers, declines to say Mass, performs none of the pending weddings or baptisms, calls his imposture a sacrilege, and submits to whatever the Church decides. The bishop's envoy rebukes him for letting a 'miracle' story grow, and the ruling to leave in priest's dress is framed as protecting the people's faith while he goes to judgement.
summary: Humphrey Bogart plays an American flier who escapes a Chinese warlord by posing as a dead priest at a remote mission, and finds the role changing him.
synopsis: China, 1947. James Carmody (Humphrey Bogart), an American pilot who has spent years in the service of the warlord Mieh Yang (Lee J. Cobb), escapes by taking the identity of a dead priest, Father O'Shea, and arrives at a Catholic mission as its new priest. Pleading that his chalice and vestments were lost, he avoids the sacraments; the mission doctor and his wife (E. G. Marshall, Agnes Moorehead) depend on him, and the nurse Anne Scott (Gene Tierney) falls in love with a man she believes is a priest. He confesses the truth to a Methodist minister and writes to the bishop. When Yang comes for him and threatens the villages, Carmody stakes his life on a game of dice and wins their safety. The bishop's envoy, Father Cornelius, rebukes him and orders him to leave still dressed as a priest and face judgement elsewhere.
inclusion: It is a star vehicle and an adventure about what a priest is. Bogart, near the end of his career, plays a hard man who takes up the cassock as a disguise and grows into what it stands for, without the film pretending that a disguise makes a priest. The script keeps with some care to the conditions the Production Code set for Carmody. Franz Planer's colour photography is handsome. Critics were cool: Bosley Crowther found it lacking credibility, the Monthly Film Bulletin disliked its mock religiosity, and the dice game strains belief. The New Yorker thought Bogart did a fine job.
themes: The film turns on the difference between the office and the man. Carmody is not a priest and knows it, and at a dying man's bed he gives no absolution and leads only the Our Father and Hail Mary, he finds excuses not to say Mass, and the weddings and baptisms waiting for him are never performed. The Methodist minister he confides in tells him he has offended the Church and must write to his bishop. After the dice game he insists there was no miracle, only luck, and that nothing he did had any authority. The bishop's envoy calls the imposture a sacrilege and doubts his sincerity for letting a miracle story grow. The ruling that he keep the cassock until he leaves is meant to spare the people's faith and does not excuse him.
advisories:
Warlord violence, killings and threats; a tense game of dice for lives.

A nurse falls in love with a man she believes to be a priest; nothing improper occurs.

For teenagers and adults. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.

A layman impersonates a priest throughout; he administers no sacrament, and the imposture is called a sacrilege.

cast.name: Humphrey Bogart
cast.role: James Carmody, posing as Father O'Shea

names: The Left Hand of God, novel by William E. Barrett (1951)

suitability.note: Nothing improper happens, and it suits teenagers better than young children.

doctrine: The film rests on the rule that only a priest can absolve. The Council of Trent (Session 14, chapter 6 and canon 10) condemned anyone who says that priests alone are not the ministers of absolution, and denied the power of the keys to anyone besides bishops and priests. Chapter 7 provides that at the point of death all priests may absolve every penitent from every sin and censure. It does not allow a layman to do so. Carmody therefore gives no absolution to the dying man and cannot say Mass or marry or baptise. The same council (Session 7, canon 12) teaches that a minister in mortal sin who observes all the essentials still confers the sacrament, so the validity of a sacrament depends on holy orders and not on the minister's merit. Carmody lacks the orders, which is why his assumed role is a sacrilege.
production: William E. Barrett's novel appeared as a Redbook serial in 1950 and as a book in 1951. Howard Hawks and Edward Lasker first acquired the rights, and Twentieth Century-Fox bought the property in early 1954, reportedly paying $110,000 for a William Faulkner screenplay and the novel rights. To win the Production Code Administration's approval (PCA No. 17462), the studio agreed that Carmody would not be shown hearing confession, saying Mass or doing other things that would be sacrilege from a non-priest. Filming ran from 7 March to 13 April 1955, with backgrounds shot in Hong Kong and location work at the Fox ranch in Malibu. It cost $1,785,000 and took about $4 million in the US. It premiered in Los Angeles on 2 September 1955 and in New York on 21 September. Reviews were mixed: the New York Times found it melodramatic, while Variety and Harrison's Reports praised its production values and Bogart.

title: The Miracle
decision: GREY: The Marian legend frames the film and is told straight; Legion of Decency A-II (Motion Picture Exhibitor Servisection; Legion list 'Miracle (War.) A-II'). The English dialogue (read 2026-10-12) confirms the frame (a habited 'Teresa' seen in the convent while she is away, the empty pedestal and drought, her prayer for forgiveness, her return and the rain) and corrects the plot: she is a postulant without vows, and her gypsy lover is shot before the wedding, so there is no marriage. Reservation unchanged: two hours of sympathetic romance, her open denunciation of Christianity, and religious life barely seen.
summary: Carroll Baker plays a Spanish postulant who runs off after a British officer while Our Lady takes her place, in Warner Bros.' Technicolor version of the legend.
synopsis: Salamanca, 1812. Teresa (Carroll Baker), a postulant at the convent of Miraflores, nurses a wounded British officer, Michael (Roger Moore), and falls in love. After praying for a sign she follows him; behind her the convent's statue of the Virgin vanishes from its pedestal, a figure in Teresa's habit is seen in her place, and drought follows. Teresa is taken in by gypsies and turns against her faith; Guido (Vittorio Gassman) means to marry her, but is shot before the wedding. In Madrid she becomes a celebrated singer, courted by a bullfighter who dies in the ring and by an old count. Believing she brings death to those she loves, she meets Michael in Brussels before Waterloo, sends him away, prays in a church for the first time since her flight and asks a priest for help. She returns to Miraflores, kneels at the empty pedestal, and the rain comes.
inclusion: Karl Vollmoeller's wordless spectacle The Miracle, staged by Max Reinhardt, was one of the theatrical sensations of the century, and Warner Bros. turned it into a Napoleonic romance in Technirama, produced by Henry Blanke after his success with The Nun's Story. The legend at its heart, the Virgin taking the place of a runaway nun, is a medieval Marian tale. The film keeps the frame of the legend, with the empty pedestal, the drought, the return and the restored statue. Between them come two hours of gypsies, bullfights and Waterloo. Critics were harsh, and the Monthly Film Bulletin called it a cloying confection. Motion Picture Exhibitor thought it had something for everyone. Elmer Bernstein's score and Ernest Haller's colour photography are handsome.
themes: The legend is about Mary's motherly care for a sinner. She covers the runaway's absence so the community is spared scandal, and waits for her return. The film keeps that shape. The Mother Superior tells Michael that Teresa is now the bride of Christ, and a habited figure is glimpsed in the cloister while Teresa is far away. Her flight is a fall, and her declaration among the gypsies that she is no Christian, and that Christianity betrays its believers, is its lowest point. In Brussels she prays to be forgiven and helped to atone, says a Hail Mary and seeks out a priest. The villagers read the drought as the Virgin's departure from a people who fell away from God, and the rain on her return ends the film with praise of God.
advisories:
A shooting before a wedding, a death in the bullring, the eve of battle; nothing graphic.

A postulant's several romances; nothing explicit.

The heroine renounces Christianity for a time and says so bitterly.

For teenagers and adults. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.

grey.question: The frame is a medieval Marian legend in which Our Lady takes a runaway postulant's place in the convent until she repents and returns. That frame is told straight, with the empty pedestal, the drought, her prayer for forgiveness and the rain on her return, and the Legion of Decency rated the film A-II. But most of its two hours follow Teresa's romances with an officer, a gypsy, a bullfighter and a count, treated with sympathy, and for a time she bitterly renounces Christianity. Religious life is barely seen.

names: The Miracle, play by Karl Vollmöller (1911)

suitability.note: The film is long and the religious frame is thin, so younger children will gain little.

doctrine: Teresa's flight from her postulancy and her return raise the Church's teaching on sin and repentance. The Marian frame belongs to pious legend, a sermon story and not a doctrine or an approved apparition. What it expresses is the traditional devotion to Mary as refuge of sinners. The film's Catholic content is devotional and legendary.
history: The story is a medieval Marian legend, not an approved apparition. The earliest written form known is by Caesarius of Heisterbach, in his Dialogus Miraculorum (Distinctio VII, chapter 34), which tells of Beatrix, the sacristan of a convent, who left the keys on the altar of the Virgin and followed a clerk. After years of sin she returned to the convent and learned from the doorkeeper that Beatrix had never left; the Virgin appeared and said she had done Beatrix's duties in her absence. Beatrix did penance for the rest of her life. Versions spread across Europe in the later Middle Ages.
production: Karl Vollmöller wrote the wordless play The Miracle in 1911, and an earlier film of 1912 was made from it. Warner Bros. moved the story from the Middle Ages to Spain in 1812 and added a climax at Waterloo. Irving Rapper directed Carroll Baker and Roger Moore. Filming ran from July to November 1958, partly in the Santa Susana Mountains. Baker was cast after Warner suspended her for refusing another film. It was released in the United States on 12 November 1959, the same week as MGM's Ben-Hur. It runs 121 minutes.
