title: The Power and the Glory
decision: GREY: Identity from the BFI record and Wikipedia; the dialogue of the CBS broadcast (English, read 2026-10-12) shows a close adaptation of Greene. In its favour: the priest's theology of the sacraments is stated plainly and more than once (only he can give the people Christ's body and blood; it would not matter if every priest were as bad as he), he returns knowingly to a trap to bring confession to a dying man, and he dies after a prayer of contrition. Against it: the faults the Holy Office objected to in the novel (1953) are all kept, including the child conceived in drunkenness, haggling over baptism fees, the married Padre José refusing him confession, and his admission that he is not sorry for his sin. The pre-conciliar verdict stands as the reservation.
summary: Laurence Olivier plays Graham Greene's hunted whisky priest in this lavish CBS adaptation, with George C. Scott as the police lieutenant who means to stamp out the faith.
synopsis: In a Mexican state where religion has been outlawed, the last priest at large (Laurence Olivier) is a drunkard who misses the boat to safety to visit a dying woman. Padre José (Frank Conroy) has married under the law. A police lieutenant (George C. Scott), an idealist who hates the Church, takes hostages from the villages and shoots them. The priest finds the village where Maria (Julie Harris) is raising their sullen daughter, says Mass and escapes; jailed overnight for carrying brandy, he goes unrecognised and is freed with a coin from the lieutenant. Across the border he baptises for fees and plans for an easier life. A mestizo (Roddy McDowall) lures him back to a dying American gunman, who refuses confession. The lieutenant arrests him. Padre José refuses to hear his confession, and he is shot at dawn.
inclusion: This was one of the most expensive American television dramas of its year, with a cast that runs from Olivier and Scott to Julie Harris, Patty Duke, Keenan Wynn, Mildred Dunnock and Cyril Cusack. Greene's novel is one of the great Catholic novels of the century, and Olivier's priest, frightened and weak but faithful at the last, is the reason to see it. Scott's lieutenant is given his argument fairly. The reception was cool: the New York Times called it a proverbial milestone and a major disappointment. Surviving copies are of poor picture quality, some with the original commercials.
themes: Greene's subject is the priesthood itself, and the sacraments do not depend on the holiness of the minister. The priest says it outright to the lieutenant. Drunkard and coward as he is, he can still put God in a man's mouth and give him God's pardon. He stays because only he can bring the people Christ's body and blood, even as hostages die for him. The lieutenant's charge that the Church served the rich is answered with the priest's insistence that damnation is no fairy story. His last night is a prayer of contrition: he has served badly and asks that his death be an atonement. In 1953 the Holy Office judged the novel 'altogether adverse', finding that human wretchedness prevails over the power of God and that the portrait injures the priesthood.
history: Greene wrote the novel in 1938 and 1939. The priest and the lieutenant are fictional. On 17 November 1953 Cardinal Pizzardo of the Holy Office wrote to Cardinal Griffin of Westminster about the novel, and Greene met Griffin in April 1954.
liberties: Dale Wasserman's script compresses the novel and gives the broken dentist, Tench, the opening scene. Coral Fellows becomes a girl who brings the priest food and loses her faith at ten, and a native child, not an adult, is the gunman's victim. The novel's closing scene, where a new priest arrives in secret, is replaced by the lieutenant's remark that the priest has more lives than he has bullets.
advisories:
The priest's drunkenness and the child he fathered are central; the conception is described, not shown.

Hostage shootings, the death of a child used as a shield, and the priest's execution by firing squad.

grey.question: This close adaptation of Greene's novel gives a strong statement of Catholic sacramental faith: a drunken, frightened priest who knows that only he can bring Christ's body and pardon to his people, goes back into a trap to hear a dying man, and dies after a prayer of contrition. But it keeps everything the Holy Office objected to in the novel in 1953, including the child he fathered and is not sorry for, the haggling over baptism fees, and a married priest who refuses him confession. Viewers should weigh that pre-conciliar verdict.

names: The Power and the Glory, novel by Graham Greene (1940)

suitability.note: The subject matter and the priest's execution make it a film for adults and older teenagers.

doctrine: The priest is a sinner, but the sacraments he gives are valid. The Catholic Encyclopedia teaches that their objective efficacy is wholly independent of the minister's personal sanctity, provided he intends to do what the Church does. St Optatus and St Augustine argued this against the Donatists. A priest alone can absolve: Trent, Session 14, chapter 6 reserves absolution to bishops and priests, and chapter 7, as the encyclopedia reports it, holds that absolution without jurisdiction has no effect. The priest's final prayer of contrition accords with the teaching on perfect contrition, which the encyclopedia cites from Trent, Session 14, chapter 4.
production: The Power and the Glory was a CBS television production, produced by David Susskind for Talent Associates-Paramount at a reported cost of $746,000, up from an initial $500,000, with a teleplay by Dale Wasserman written in seven days. It was Laurence Olivier's second American television role, after The Moon and Sixpence. Susskind first wanted Richard Burton as co-star. A Mexican township was built at the NBC studios, and taping began on 30 May 1961 and ran about four weeks. It ran 132 minutes. The Los Angeles Times thought it less than it could be.

title: The Red Danube
decision: PUBLISH: The National Legion of Decency classified the film A-I (its 1936–59 list on archive.org), a contemporary Catholic judgment. Independent secular sources (AFI Catalog, TCM, Jonathan Lewis at MysteryFile) establish a Catholic-centred story from Bruce Marshall's novel. The Spanish-dubbed dialogue (read 2026-10-12) confirms the open points: the Mother Superior tells the dying Maria she has sinned gravely but been given time to repent, and Maria dies repentant, commending her soul to God; no priest is called. The colonel's return to faith is understated, voiced in his refusal of an order as a Christian.
summary: MGM's talky Cold War drama, from Bruce Marshall's novel, sets a fierce Viennese Mother Superior against a faithless British colonel enforcing the forced repatriation of Soviet refugees.
synopsis: Vienna, 1946. Colonel Michael 'Hooky' Nicobar, a one-armed British officer who lost his faith when his son was killed in the war, is billeted with his staff in a convent run by a formidable Mother Superior. His job is to hand Soviet citizens back to the USSR. His aide falls for a ballerina, Maria Buhlen, who turns out to be a Russian the Soviets want. Hooky hands her over, then watches the consequences: a Soviet professor kills himself rather than go back, and on Christmas Eve a train of starving refugees is dumped in the British zone. Maria escapes; Hooky and the nun hide her. The Mother Superior flies to Rome with him and sees the Pope. Hooky refuses an order to return Maria and is relieved of command. Cornered again, Maria throws herself from a window and dies repentant. Forced repatriation ends.
inclusion: It is one of the few Hollywood films of its time to put a nun's argument for God at the centre of a political drama. Ethel Barrymore's Mother Superior is no sweet sister. She is blunt, anti-communist and certain, apologises when she has been uncharitable, and spends the film working on Walter Pidgeon's lapsed colonel. Bruce Marshall, a Scottish Catholic novelist, supplied the source. The subject, the Allies' forced return of refugees to Stalin, was a shameful fact, and the film says so. Critics in 1949 found it too long and too wordy, Variety complained of religious talk, and George Sidney, a musicals director, gives it little visual life. Angela Lansbury drew the best notices.
themes: The drama is a conversion story. Hooky's unbelief is grief, and the film adds a pointed detail. His son's last letter said he had come to believe in God and had been received into the Church, which the father dismisses as empty formality. The Mother Superior holds that only men who have abandoned God could treat refugees as the Soviets do, and carries Hooky's complaint about official Christianity to the Pope. The reply she brings back is that God does not abandon man; man abandons God. When Maria throws herself from a window, the nun tells her she has sinned gravely but been given time to repent; Maria asks forgiveness and dies commending her soul to God. No priest is called. Hooky's return to faith is understated, and he refuses an order as a Christian, or one trying to be.
history: In 1945-47 the British and American authorities returned Soviet citizens, including many who did not wish to go, under agreements made at Yalta; many were shot or sent to camps. Bruce Marshall (1899-1987), a Catholic convert, drew on this in Vespers in Vienna (1947).
liberties: The characters are fictional. The film compresses the end of forced repatriation into a single vote and a change of policy, and Hooky's promotion to carry out a humane line is a dramatic convenience. Its picture of Soviet officers is broad Cold War caricature, as reviewers have noted. The order's foundress, a saint said to have flown to Rome on an angel in 1585, is a comic invention.
advisories:
Two suicides: a professor shoots himself off screen, and the young heroine jumps from a window and dies; she repents before death, and her act is called a grave sin.

Refugees in distress; threats of deportation and imprisonment.

No sexual content of note.

Legion of Decency A-I.

names: Vespers in Vienna, novel by Bruce Marshall (1947)

suitability.note: The film is long and talky. Older children can watch it with a word about why the Mother Superior calls the girl's act a grave sin.

doctrine: The film turns on suicide. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1912) teaches that deliberate, direct suicide is a grave wrong, because life belongs to God and man has only the use of it. It adds that the Church denies Christian burial to those who take their own lives, to show her horror of the sin and to deter others. The same article admits that mental derangement can remove responsibility. The Mother Superior's words to the dying Maria, that she has sinned gravely but been given time to repent, follow this teaching, since the act is a grave sin but the Church does not close the door on repentance before death.
production: MGM bought Bruce Marshall's novel soon after its publication in 1947 and planned to shoot in June of that year. Background footage was filmed in Vienna and Rome in October 1947, but the project was shelved. When it revived, George Sidney replaced Victor Saville, and the first-announced stars (Irene Dunne, Spencer Tracy, Robert Taylor) dropped out. Angela Lansbury took the part first given to Audrey Totter, and Agnes Moorehead briefly replaced Ethel Barrymore in March 1949. The crew looked for 1,500 gaunt extras for the camp scenes and found that actual refugees looked too healthy. The film was released in the United States on 14 October 1949, runs 119 minutes and was nominated for an Academy Award for art direction. It cost about $1.96 million and lost money. Some critics called it anti-Soviet propaganda.

title: The Rite
decision: GREY: Identity from AFI and BBFC; treatment from Greydanus (Christianity Today), Moria (agnostic critic), KPBS and Den of Geek. Sound on the reality of the devil and the efficacy of the rite, but its horror content, the invented possession of the exorcist and an uncritical present-day setting are reservations a reader can weigh. Subtitles would settle whether Michael is shown giving sacramental absolution before ordination.
summary: Mikael Håfström's exorcism thriller, loosely drawn from Matt Baglio's book, sends a doubting American seminarian to a Vatican course and to an old Jesuit exorcist in Rome.
synopsis: Michael Kovak, a mortician's son, enters a seminary mainly to get away from the family business. Near the end of his studies he writes to resign, saying he lacks faith. After he ministers to a woman dying in a street accident, his superior, Father Matthew, persuades him to attend an exorcism course in Rome instead. There Father Xavier sends him to Father Lucas Trevant, a Jesuit with long experience, who is treating Rosaria, a pregnant teenager. Michael suspects mental illness and says so; a journalist, Angelina, is chasing the same story. Rosaria dies after a miscarriage, and then Lucas himself shows signs of possession. With Xavier away, Michael, still unsure what he believes, must perform the rite on his own mentor, and in doing so recovers his faith. He goes home, is ordained and is last seen hearing a confession.
inclusion: Steven Greydanus, writing in Christianity Today, called it probably the most sober and realistic treatment of exorcism in Hollywood history, and the most positive picture of the Church and Christian faith he could recall in a recent studio film. The first two thirds earn that. Exorcisms drag on for weeks, holy objects are not magic, and Michael's scepticism is given weight; Fr Lucas tells him to make friends with his doubts. The Roman settings, crucifixes and images of St. Thérèse and the Sacred Heart are used plainly. Anthony Hopkins is the reason to watch. The last half hour is weaker, and Den of Geek and Moria both note the lurch into stock horror once Lucas is possessed. Most secular critics were unkind.
themes: The film argues the old point that belief in the devil leads back to belief in God, and Michael cannot master the demon until he admits that he believes. The rite is shown as a prayer of the Church, said with crucifix, stole and holy water by priests acting under authority, and its power depends on faith, not technique. Doubt is treated with respect but not as a resting place. Its weakness is that the possession of a holy, experienced exorcist is a horror device, and that the film takes the present-day Church and its training course entirely at face value.
history: Matt Baglio's 2009 book The Rite: The Making of a Modern Exorcist follows Fr Gary Thomas, a California parish priest sent by his bishop to train as an exorcist in Rome, and his apprenticeship to an experienced Italian exorcist, Fr Carmine De Filippis. Baglio wrote the book partly to correct Hollywood clichés about exorcism.
liberties: The middle-aged parish priest of the book becomes a young seminarian without faith. Baglio, a male journalist, becomes Angelina, with a hint of romance. Fr Lucas is a composite based on De Filippis, and his possession, which fills the second half, has no equivalent in the book. The film opens by calling itself a true story; the end credits say only that it was suggested by the book.
advisories:
Sustained scenes of possession and exorcism, with contorted bodies, facial markings, a possessed girl beating her pregnant belly, and a bloody miscarriage. Rated 15 by the BBFC and PG-13 in the United States.

A possessed priest strikes a child. Mortuary scenes, including a boy helping prepare his mother's body.

Blasphemous and crude sexual taunts from the possessed; one strong expletive.

No sex scenes. For adults and older teenagers.

Michael is reported to absolve a dying woman before his ordination, which only a priest can do.

grey.question: The Rite is a horror film with Catholic convictions. It takes the devil, the rite of exorcism and the authority of the priest seriously, but its climax rests on an invented device, the possession of a holy and experienced exorcist, and it piles up stock shocks, a bloody miscarriage and crude demonic taunts. It also takes the present-day Church at face value. Viewers should weigh whether the horror serves the faith or simply sells tickets.

names: The Rite: The Making of a Modern Exorcist, book by Matt Baglio (2009)

suitability.note: The possession scenes and the bloody miscarriage make it unsuitable for children.

doctrine: Christ cast out demons by his own authority and gave the Apostles the same power; the Catholic Encyclopedia (1909) says the Roman Ritual's rite agrees with patristic teaching. The Ritual directs the exorcist to judge carefully whether a case is true possession or illness, to leave medical questions to physicians, to avoid superstition, and to prepare by prayer and fasting. It directs that the crucifix, holy water and relics be used, and that the Blessed Sacrament is not to be brought near the possessed, for fear of irreverence. The Encyclopedia adds that, under synod laws, only priests exercise the power and the bishop is consulted and his authorisation obtained.
production: Mikael Håfström began work in February 2010 and cast the leads in March. The script is loosely based on Matt Baglio's 2009 book, and the producers, Beau Flynn and Tripp Vinson, had made The Exorcism of Emily Rose. Håfström attended exorcisms in Rome to prepare. Fr Gary Thomas, the consultant and the subject of Baglio's book, called the exorcisms very accurate, with some expected licences. It was shot in Rome, Budapest and Blue Island, Illinois, and cost a reported 37 million dollars. Warner Bros. released it in the United States on 28 January 2011. It opened at number one and took about 97 million dollars worldwide. Critics were largely negative (22 per cent on Rotten Tomatoes), though Roger Ebert gave it three stars.

title: The Silent Witness
alternateTitles: The Silent Witness: An Investigation into the Holy Shroud
decision: REJECT (scope): a forensic, ecumenical documentary whose theological voice is the Anglican John A. T. Robinson; it never treats the Church’s own cult of the Shroud. Prior assessment: Identity from the Internet Archive record and Filmweb; content now from the film's own English narration (subtitle file, read 2026-10-12). Catholic-centred in subject, since the relic is kept in the royal chapel of Turin Cathedral and the film opens on pilgrims and a Roman priest-scholar, but not in treatment: its witnesses are forensic scientists, a Swiss criminologist, American Air Force researchers and the Anglican Dr John Robinson, and the narration speaks of 'the phenomenon that Christians call the Resurrection'. The Church's own judgment on the Shroud is not discussed. Reservation unchanged: an advocacy case for authenticity made before the 1988 radiocarbon test. Scope remains the editor's call.
summary: David Rolfe's BAFTA-winning documentary, narrated by Kenneth More, investigates the Shroud of Turin through history and science and ends by asking who the man on it is.
synopsis: The film treats the Shroud of Turin as a detective story. It opens at the locked shrine in Turin Cathedral and sets out the puzzle: a linen cloth bearing the faint image of a scourged and crucified man, documented at Lirey in the fourteenth century, which Secondo Pia's photographs of 1898 showed to be a negative. A Los Angeles forensic pathologist reads the wounds; Monsignor Giulio Ricci matches them to Roman scourges and a cap of thorns; the Swiss criminologist Max Frei finds pollen from Palestine and Turkey in the weave; the historian Ian Wilson traces the cloth back through the Templars and Constantinople to the Image of Edessa; and American researchers find three-dimensional information in the image and suggest it was made by a brief scorch. The narration closes by asking who the man is.
inclusion: It was a surprise success: by the archive record's account it broke box-office records in London and won a BAFTA, and it made the Shroud a popular subject in Britain. Rolfe, an independent filmmaker, began it as a sceptic and, as he told K. V. Turley, returned to Christian faith while making it. The film's strength is its method: it lays out the evidence piece by piece and lets specialists speak instead of preaching. Its weakness is age. It was made before the 1988 radiocarbon test, which dated the linen to the Middle Ages, so its scientific case is incomplete, and Rolfe has since made films disputing that test. It suits viewers drawn to the Passion and to the long Catholic veneration of the relic.
themes: The religious centre is the Passion. A pathologist reads on the image the scourging by two men, the bruised face, the fall, the cap of thorns, the nails through the wrists and feet and the pierced side, and the film draws the parallels to the Gospels without sermonising. The Shroud has been honoured in the Church for centuries: Julius II approved a Mass and Office for it in 1506. The film says nothing of that cult, nor of the Church's reserve about authenticity; it mentions only the fourteenth-century bishop who reported it to the Pope as a forgery. Its last suggestion, that the image may have been scorched in the moment of the Resurrection, is put as a question, and the closing words leave the viewer to answer it.
history: The cloth is first recorded at Lirey in the diocese of Troyes about 1360. By 1453 it belonged to the house of Savoy at Chambéry, where a fire in 1532 scorched its folds, and it has been at Turin since 1578. Photographs taken at its exposition in 1898 showed that the image behaves as a negative, which began the modern scientific debate.
advisories:
Detailed discussion and images of the wounds of crucifixion, including scourging.

No other content concerns.

The film's scientific case predates the 1988 radiocarbon dating and the later dispute over it.

title: The Silver Chalice
decision: GREY: An apostolic-age melodrama with a reverent conversion thread; Legion of Decency A-II; Motion Picture Daily (1954) records that Basil completes Christ's face only after learning the faith from Peter. The English dialogue (read 2026-10-12) confirms the Eucharistic words over the cup, Simon Magus drawn from Acts 8, and Peter called the Christians' acknowledged leader, but also the weight problem: Peter is on screen for a few minutes near the end, Basil is never baptised, and much of the film is his entanglement with Helena after his marriage. Still borderline with REJECT (scope); kept GREY because the Last Supper cup and the apostles drive the plot.
summary: Paul Newman's debut: a Greek silversmith commissioned to encase the cup of the Last Supper finds faith among the apostles while Simon Magus plots to destroy it.
synopsis: In Antioch the young sculptor Basil is cheated of his inheritance and sold into slavery. Luke buys his freedom and takes him to Jerusalem, where the aged Joseph of Arimathea shows him the cup of the Last Supper and commissions a silver casing carved with the faces of the Apostles and of Jesus. Basil can carve the Apostles but not his Lord. He marries Joseph's granddaughter Deborra (Pier Angeli) so that her inheritance can go to the Church, while still drawn to Helena (Virginia Mayo), his childhood companion and now partner of the magician Simon (Jack Palance). Simon sets out to outdo Christ's miracles and destroy the cup before Peter. In Rome Basil meets Peter, who has been watching him in disguise, and at last carves Christ's face. Simon, claiming to be a god, tries to fly before Nero and falls. The cup is lost, and Peter foretells its return.
inclusion: It is a curiosity of the 1950s biblical cycle, not a good film. Warner Bros. spent heavily on CinemaScope and stylised, nearly abstract sets that Variety thought wrong for the period and Fortnight admired. Jack Palance sneers through Simon Magus. Newman, in his first film, later called it the worst picture of the decade, and critics at the time largely agreed; Motion Picture Daily thought the long adaptation of Costain's best-seller drifted into religious soap opera. Its Catholic interest is the premise, the cup of the Eucharist kept as a relic by the first Christians, and a pagan artist who can carve Christ's face only once he has come to love him.
themes: The cup is introduced with the words of institution spoken over it, and Deborra sees a light around it that Basil cannot. His conversion is told through his art and is never formalised; no baptism is shown. He acquires a conscience through his Christian wife, meets Peter, who has watched him disguised as a porter, and hears him pray that Basil will one day see the face of Jesus. He finishes the carving only after asking Jesus to guide his hand. Simon Magus comes from Acts, where he is baptised in Samaria and rebuffed by Peter when he offers money; here he preaches a religion that calls lust and hatred natural and good, and dies boasting that he is a god. Peter heals a cripple. Little else of the Church's life appears.
history: Thomas B. Costain's novel was a best-seller of 1952. Basil, Helena and Deborra are fictional. Simon Magus appears in Acts 8, where he tries to buy the Apostles' power. The story of his attempt to fly before Nero comes from second-century apocryphal writing, not Scripture. According to the Catholic Encyclopedia Peter, a Galilean fisherman originally called Simon, laboured at Rome and died there, probably under Nero, and was buried on the Vatican Hill.
liberties: The plot is invented around legend. Simon dies through his own boast at Nero's court, refusing the hidden wire his trick depends on; in the apocryphal account he falls at Peter's prayer. Helena is forced to repeat the flight. Simon's fake Pentecost is presented as a miracle of Jesus. The Grail and its silver holder are not historical, and Luke, Joseph of Arimathea and Peter are drawn in as supporting characters.
advisories:
Swordplay, killings and Simon's fatal fall from a tower; Christians forced to build the tower; nothing graphic by modern standards.

Helena is a seductive figure in costumes revealing for the period. Basil marries Deborra for her inheritance's sake and, once married, keeps meeting and kissing Helena before he returns to his wife.

For older children and up. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.

The Grail story is legend; the film presents it as fact.

grey.question: This is a costume melodrama built on legend: an invented silversmith, a love triangle and the medieval Grail, with Peter, Luke and Joseph of Arimathea in support. Its religious thread is reverent, since the cup is introduced with Christ's words of institution, Simon Magus comes from Acts, and an artist carves Christ's face only after Peter prays that he will see it. But Peter appears only briefly, Basil is never baptised, and much of the film follows his pull toward Helena after his marriage. Take it as Hollywood legend, not as a picture of the apostolic Church.

names: The Silver Chalice, novel by Thomas B. Costain (1952)

suitability.note: There is swordplay, killings and Simon's fatal fall, and the romantic triangle includes a seductive woman and the hero's meetings with her after his marriage. Nothing is graphic, but it is long and melodramatic.

doctrine: Simon Magus is the Simon of Acts 8:5-24. The Catholic Encyclopedia treats the later story of a contest with Peter in Rome as largely legend. In the apocryphal Acts of Peter, Simon tries to fly in the Roman Forum and is brought down by the prayers of Peter and Paul; the encyclopedia calls these narratives legend and says later writers who placed Simon in Rome relied on Justin and those Acts. It doubts Justin's report of a statue to him on the Tiber island, which it thinks honoured the Sabine god Semo Sancus. The film also presents Peter as the leader of the Apostles. The Catholic Encyclopedia reads Matthew 16:18 as making Peter head of the community, with the primacy passing to the Roman bishops. The Grail itself is medieval legend, not Church teaching.
production: The film was made for Warner Bros. by Victor Saville's own company. The AFI Catalog records that Costain approved how closely the script followed his novel. It was shot in CinemaScope and WarnerColor in California, on a reported budget of $4.5 million, with semi-abstract sets by the stage designer Rolfe Gerard. Franz Waxman's score was nominated for an Academy Award. It premiered on 20 December 1954 at Saranac Lake, New York. The New York Times found it cumbersome, and Variety thought it overdrawn but sometimes exciting.

title: The Singing Nun
decision: GREY: The AFI Catalog and Motion Picture Exhibitor (Legion A-I and a 1966 review) establish a respectful convent drama with religious life in its pre-conciliar form and a nun who chooses obedience and the missions over fame. The 1966 classification comes months after the Council, so it is noted rather than decisive. The reservation is historical: the film presents itself as the story of a real nun whose life contradicted it (TCM).
summary: Debbie Reynolds plays a guitar-playing Belgian Dominican whose song 'Dominique' becomes a worldwide hit, in MGM's sweet, heavily fictionalised version of the Soeur Sourire story.
synopsis: Sister Ann (Debbie Reynolds), a young Dominican who loves to sing and play the guitar, leaves her convent near Antwerp for Samaritan House, a mission in a poor district of Brussels. There she befriends Dominic, a motherless boy whose unemployed, drinking father leaves him to his seventeen-year-old sister, Nicole, and she writes a song for him. Father Clementi (Ricardo Montalbán) brings her to Robert Gerarde (Chad Everett), a record executive who knew her at the Paris Conservatory. With the Church's permission she records an album, and 'Dominique' becomes an international hit; Ed Sullivan sends a crew to film her. Torn between success, Robert's interest in her and her vocation, she seeks Father Clementi's counsel. When Dominic is badly hurt in an accident, she prays for his recovery and promises to give up her music. He recovers, she gives her guitar to Nicole, and she leaves for a mission in Africa.
inclusion: This was MGM's family picture for Easter 1966, built on the surprise success of 'Dominique', the song a Belgian Dominican, Sister Luc-Gabrielle, recorded as Soeur Sourire. Reynolds sings it and the other songs well, Greer Garson is a calm Mother Prioress, and Harry Sukman's score earned an Oscar nomination. Motion Picture Exhibitor called it warm and appealing but found the story too pat to mean much, and TCM's Frank Miller records reviews that mocked its out-of-date wholesomeness. Its value now is as a picture of convent life in full habit at the very end of the pre-conciliar era, and as a story in which a nun chooses her vows and the missions over celebrity.
themes: Sister Ann's music is shown as an overflow of her love of God, but the success it brings, and the attentions of a man from her past, pull her away from the obedience and hiddenness of her life. She turns to her prioress and her confessor, and she settles the matter by prayer and a promise, offering up her music for the boy's recovery and going to the missions. Poverty, obedience and charity to the poor are presented as the heart of religious life, and the convent is treated warmly and without irony.
history: Jeanine Deckers was born in Laeken, Brussels, on 17 October 1933. In September 1959 she entered the Missionary Dominican Sisters of Our Lady of Fichermont at Waterloo and took the name Sister Luc-Gabrielle. Her superiors encouraged her to record her songs. Her single 'Dominique', released in 1963 as by Soeur Sourire, reached number one in the United States, the first Belgian record to do so. She appeared on The Ed Sullivan Show on 5 January 1964. She left the convent in 1967 to live as a tertiary, saying she had been forced out after a clash with her superiors, and she lost the right to the names Soeur Sourire and the Singing Nun. In late 1967 the Belgian finance ministry claimed back taxes of about $63,000, which she said her royalties had gone to the convent to pay. On 29 March 1985 she and her companion Annie Pécher died by suicide at Wavre. She reportedly dismissed the film as fiction.
liberties: Almost everything is invented: the slum mission, the boy Dominic and his family, the record executive who knew her before her vows, the Ed Sullivan crew as shown, and the departure for Africa. The real Sister Luc-Gabrielle did not give up her music for the missions.

A child's accident and a father striking his daughter; no other violence.

Nicole has posed for provocative photographs to pay the rent; they are discovered, not dwelt on.

The Legion of Decency rated it A-I (general patronage) in 1966.

The real nun later left the Church; the film is fiction.

grey.question: This is a pious, sentimental fiction in which a nun gives up fame for obedience and the missions, and the Legion of Decency passed it for all audiences. The reservation is historical. It is sold as the story of the real Singing Nun, Jeanine Deckers, but its plot is invented, and her life went the other way: she left the Church in 1967 and died by suicide in the 1980s. Take it as a parable of vocation, not as her biography.

suitability.note: A child's accident and a father striking his daughter are the roughest moments, and the convent is shown warmly.

doctrine: Religious life rests on the vows of poverty, chastity and obedience. The Catholic Encyclopedia explains that a vow is a promise made to God, so that breaking it is graver than breaking a promise to a person. Only the vow of chastity made by profession is solemn, and the vow of perpetual chastity is reserved to the Holy See. Dispensation from a vow is ordinarily justified by great difficulty in keeping it, and the Pope may dispense even from the solemn vow of chastity only for exceptionally grave reasons. This is the background to Sister Ann's decision in the film to offer up her music and obey her prioress.
production: John Furia Jr. wrote the story for MGM, with Sally Benson co-writing the screenplay. Henry King was first announced as director but left after disputes with the producer John Beck, and Henry Koster took over. Koster later called it probably the most difficult film he ever made, and it was his last. He blamed friction between Beck and Debbie Reynolds. It opened on 4 April 1966, runs 97 minutes, and earned an estimated $3.8 million in US and Canadian rentals. TCM reports that the Church agreed to the film only if the story was fictionalised.

title: The Story of the Vatican
decision: PUBLISH: The Legion of Decency classed it A-I (March of Time-RKO), the pre-conciliar Catholic judgment, and Film Bulletin's August 1941 review gives an independent account: splendid, sepia-toned photography and Sheen's fervent narration, but long and repetitive for general audiences. AFI's synopsis (via TCM) establishes the content: Vatican City's institutions, art and the career of Pius XII. Nothing post-conciliar is involved.
summary: The March of Time's feature-length tour of Vatican City under Pius XII, from St Peter's tomb to the post office, narrated by Mgr Fulton J. Sheen.
synopsis: The film opens with the career of Eugenio Pacelli: Secretary of State to Pius XI, visitor to the United States, and in 1939 the first pope crowned in public on the balcony of St Peter's. It then explains Vatican City as a sovereign state, independent since 1929, with its governor, its diplomatic corps of thirty-eight nations, its own radio station installed by Marconi, its currency, fire brigade, railway and post office. The Polyglot Press and the Osservatore Romano are shown at work, the latter noted as free of Mussolini's censorship. The camera moves through the Vatican Library and its manuscripts, Michelangelo's Sistine ceiling, Raphael's rooms, St Peter's Basilica and the papal crypts. It closes with the Noble Guard, the Swiss Guard, the Roman congregations and the pilgrims who come to Rome every year.
inclusion: This was a documentary whose crew were given unusual access inside the Vatican. Film Bulletin praised the photography as splendid and noted that the whole film was printed in sepia, which gives even the newsreel inserts a warmth. Fulton Sheen, then the best-known Catholic voice on American radio, wrote and spoke the commentary, and the reviewer found it fervent and dramatic. The same reviewer warned that the film would seem long and repetitive to anyone looking for entertainment, and it is essentially an illustrated lecture. Its value now is as a record of the papal court and the Vatican of Pius XII as it looked on the eve of war, decades before the Noble Guard and much of the papal court were abolished.
themes: The film presents the papacy as a visible institution, a sovereign state with its own guard, press and diplomats, serving a spiritual office. The Pope is shown as successor of St Peter, whose tomb lies under the basilica, and as teacher of the world through the Polyglot Press and the Osservatore Romano. The Noble Guard, the Swiss Guard and the Roman congregations, including the one that handles liturgy and canonisations, are shown as parts of a working Church government. It is reverent in tone, closer to a travelogue and art film than to a sermon, and it makes no doctrinal claims beyond the Pope's office.
advisories:
Nothing objectionable; suitable for all ages.

A documentary of about 54 minutes, slow and lecture-like by modern standards.

suitability.note: Nothing objectionable; the Legion of Decency rated it A-I. Children will need some interest in Rome, art or the papacy.

doctrine: The film shows the Pope as the successor of St Peter. The First Vatican Council defined this in Pastor Aeternus (18 July 1870): Christ gave Peter a primacy of jurisdiction over the whole Church (chapter 1); it passes to the Roman pontiffs, his successors (chapter 2); the pope has ordinary, immediate jurisdiction over every church and believer (chapter 3); and when he defines a doctrine of faith or morals ex cathedra he is infallible (chapter 4). The sovereign state the film shows has a recent origin. Italian troops entered Rome on 20 September 1870 and ended the pope's temporal rule. The Lateran Treaty, signed on 11 February 1929 by Cardinal Gasparri for Pius XI and by Mussolini, recognised the Holy See's sovereignty over Vatican City; Italy ratified it on 7 June 1929.
production: In summer 1939 Richard de Rochemont of The March of Time obtained permission for a crew, including the director Jean Pagès and the cameraman Marcel Rebière, to film inside the Vatican. Part of the footage became the two-reel The Vatican of Pius XII, released on 16 February 1940. The rest was expanded into this feature, written and narrated by Mgr Fulton J. Sheen, which RKO released on 18 July 1941. It is the second of only four full-length March of Time features and runs 53 to 54 minutes. Italy's Centro Cattolico Cinematografico modelled its 1942 film Pastor Angelicus partly on it.

title: The White Sister
decision: PUBLISH: Identity from the AFI Catalog; independent treatment from Bret Wood (TCM), James Patterson (Silent London) and the contemporary New York Times review (via Wikipedia). The heroine takes final vows believing her fiancé dead, refuses his plea to petition for release when he returns, and forgives the sister who wronged her. The Church advised on every religious scene. Vows upheld; no doctrinal problem. Pre-Legion, so no rating.
summary: Lillian Gish plays an Italian heiress who becomes a nun believing her soldier fiancé dead, and keeps her vows when he comes back, in Henry King's location-shot melodrama.
synopsis: Angela Chiaromonte loves Captain Giovanni Severini, but when her father dies her jealous half-sister, the Marchesa di Mola, burns his will and turns her out penniless. Giovanni leaves for Africa promising to marry her on his return. His camp is attacked and reported massacred. Grief-stricken, Angela is cared for by nursing sisters and decides to become one of them. Giovanni, in fact a prisoner, escapes and reaches Italy on the very day she takes her final vows. He finds her at the hospital and tries to persuade her to ask the Pope for release. She refuses. When Vesuvius erupts, the dying Marchesa confesses in a church and Angela forgives her; Giovanni drowns saving others, and Angela prays to be reunited with him in heaven.
inclusion: Bret Wood opens his TCM essay by saying that seldom has a Hollywood film embraced the Catholic Church with so much passion and reverence. Ronald Colman, in his first major part, is excellent as Giovanni, and Gish gives a restrained performance that contemporary critics thought among her best. The New York Times found the opening love story among the strongest ever filmed but thought the later disaster plot weakened it, and the film is long at over two hours. It was a large commercial success.
themes: Angela enters religion in grief, but once she has made her profession she treats it as binding, even when the man she loves returns and begs her to seek a dispensation. The film presents her fidelity as right and costly. Wood notes the near-fetishistic detail with which it stages her symbolic marriage to Christ. The church scene at the climax, where Angela forgives the dying sister who ruined her, is a plain picture of forgiveness at the hour of death. The ending looks to reunion in heaven.
history: F. Marion Crawford (1854-1909), an American novelist who lived in Italy, published The White Sister in 1909 and adapted it for the stage with Walter Hackett. It was filmed in 1915, 1923 and 1933, and in Mexico in 1960.
liberties: James Patterson notes that the novel ends happily while the 1923 film ends with Giovanni's death. The African expedition, the will and the Vesuvius eruption give the story a scale the play lacked.
advisories:
A massacre in Africa (reported), a carriage crash and the eruption of Vesuvius, with deaths.

No sensual content beyond a few embraces between the engaged couple.

Silent, about 2 hours 20 minutes in its full length; shorter release versions exist.

Suitable for older children and up.

sources.title: Vows
sources.claims: Solemn vow of chastity, dispensation by the Pope, effect of solemn profession

names: The White Sister, novel by F. Marion Crawford (1909), and the 1909 stage play by Crawford and Walter Hackett

suitability.note: Younger children will find it long and slow; older ones may enjoy the Italian locations and Lillian Gish.

doctrine: The plot turns on the difference between a promise and a solemn vow. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1912, Vermeersch) says the Church recognises as solemn only the vow of chastity made by religious profession, and that vows made earlier cease to bind a person once solemn profession is made. The Pope may dispense even from the solemn vow of chastity, but only for exceptionally grave reasons. Giovanni's plea that Angela seek a dispensation is therefore not absurd in Church law, and her refusal is a free choice to keep her word. Her forgiveness of the dying sister who wronged her at the end follows the plain command to forgive injuries.
production: Inspiration Pictures bought the rights for $16,000 and signed Lillian Gish in September 1922. Ronald Colman was cast after a screen test arranged following a stage performance. Shooting was planned for three months but lasted about six, partly because the Roman studios were ill-equipped. It was shot in Rome, at the Villa d'Este in Tivoli and in Naples, with the desert ambush filmed in Algeria. Monsignor Giovanni Bonzano, whom the company met on the way, arranged for Church officials to advise on every religious scene. Gish visited more than 30 cloistered communities and chose the Order of Lourdes as her model; the profession scene took 25 hours to film. The 15-hour assembly was cut to 13 reels (143 minutes). It opened in New York on 5 September 1923 and ran six months at the 44th Street Theatre, which led Metro to distribute it. The Times praised the performances but thought the story weakened after Giovanni's death.

title: The White Sister
decision: PUBLISH: Identity and full synopsis from the AFI Catalog; independent treatment from Danny Reid (Pre-Code.com) and the contemporary Variety and New York Times notices (via Wikipedia). Angela takes final vows believing Giovanni dead, refuses to leave the order when he returns and begs her, and he dies holding her cross: the vows are upheld. Pre-Legion (no rating found). Reid's complaint that her vocation is unconvincing is a matter of craft, stated in the prose.
summary: MGM's sound remake moves Crawford's story to the First World War, with Helen Hayes as the nun who keeps her vows and Clark Gable as the airman who returns.
synopsis: Angela Chiaromonte, a prince's daughter, is about to marry an older banker when a collision with the car of a dashing lieutenant, Giovanni Severi, starts a romance. Her father catches them kissing and forbids it. Running to Giovanni, Angela crashes into her father's car and he is killed. Stricken with guilt, she sends Giovanni away, but pledges her love when Italy enters the war. Giovanni is shot down and reported dead. Angela enters a convent, trains as a nursing sister and takes her final vows. Giovanni has survived as a prisoner, escapes in a stolen plane and finds her at a military hospital. He begs her to leave the order; she refuses. He leaves, is shot down by German fire, and dies in her arms holding the cross she gave him.
inclusion: This is a polished MGM production with Helen Hayes at the height of her screen reputation and Clark Gable in a part that, as TCM's account has it, was against type. Variety praised Hayes. Mordaunt Hall in the New York Times called it beautifully produced but less real than Henry King's silent version, and Harrison's Reports thought it lacked the earlier film's emotional pull. Danny Reid of Pre-Code.com is harder on it: a respectable, competent melodrama whose romance lacks chemistry and whose heroine's journey never quite convinces.
themes: As in the 1923 version, the subject is the binding force of religious vows. Angela enters the convent out of grief and guilt, and Reid finds that her spiritual journey is shown more as ritual than as inner change. But once professed she treats her vows as unbreakable, and the film supports her: when Giovanni sees her praying during an air raid, he understands that she no longer belongs to him. The Catholic rites, the veiling and the convent hospital are shown with care. The ending keeps the renunciation.
liberties: The novel's African expedition becomes air war on the Italian front. Angela's motive for entering the convent is changed: guilt over her father's death in a car crash replaces the destroyed will of the earlier version.
advisories:
Air combat, a fatal car crash and the hero's death from wounds.

The engaged couple kiss; later he pleads with her, now a nun, and they almost embrace.

sources.claims: Trent's full year of novitiate; novice free to leave

names: The White Sister, novel by F. Marion Crawford (1909), and the stage version by Crawford and Walter Hackett

suitability.note: Nothing is graphic, but it is a grief-laden wartime melodrama for older children and up.

doctrine: The plot turns on whether a professed religious can be released from her vows. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1912) says a vow is a promise to God that binds, and that the vow of perpetual chastity is among the vows reserved to the Holy See. The Pope may dispense even from the solemn vow, but only for exceptionally grave reasons. Angela's refusal to ask for a dispensation is therefore a free choice and not a legal impossibility. The same source records that the Council of Trent required a full year's novitiate, during which a novice may leave freely, and that vows taken before solemn profession cease to bind on that profession.
production: MGM's remake of the 1923 silent film (Henry King, with Lillian Gish and Ronald Colman) began principal photography in December 1932 with two units: Victor Fleming on the Culver City stages and backlot, and Cullen Tate on the aerial sequences in Reno, Nevada, with Paul Mantz supplying the aircraft, repainted as Italian and German fighters. Footage from Hell's Angels (1930) was used. The last scene was rewritten late. The film opened in New York on 17 March 1933 and was released on 14 April 1933, at 105 minutes. It cost $625,000 and made a profit of $456,000.

title: The World of Don Camillo
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a priest protagonist and Guareschi's speaking crucifix) and identity established (Wikipedia, Box Office Mojo). The English dialogue (read 2026-10-12) answers the rule (b) question in the film's favour: no Mass is shown or spoken of, Don Camillo wears the cassock, sets a boy to learn the Our Father in Latin, and answers to a bishop who calls himself old-fashioned. The crucifix speaks as Guareschi's Christ does, insisting on baptism, rebuking the priest's temper, bribery and card-sharping, and blessing him into exile; Don Camillo accepts the bishop's transfer as deserved. Reservation: a thin, Americanised remake whose comedy includes a gimmick skydiving wedding, girls roller-skating in church, and the priest's cheating and blackmail, played for laughs before Christ corrects them.
summary: Terence Hill directs himself as Guareschi's hot-tempered priest in a remake that moves his feud with the Communist mayor Peppone into the Italy of the 1980s.
synopsis: In a village on the Po, the parish priest Don Camillo and the re-elected Communist mayor Peppone (Colin Blakely) are old enemies who respect each other, and Don Camillo still talks with the crucified Christ in his church. He refuses to baptise Peppone's son with the name Lenin until Christ rebukes him. He goes poaching on a baron's land, hears Peppone's confession, and does penance by fasting. A football match between his 'angels' and Peppone's 'devils' is lost on a bribed penalty, and the bishop (Cyril Cusack) warns him. He befriends a lonely boy, Magrino, and his divorced mother. When Peppone secretly wins the football pools, Don Camillo extracts a gift for his youth centre. A violent rematch gets him sent to a mountain parish, and the village sees him off.
inclusion: Guareschi's stories were first filmed by Julien Duvivier in 1952 with Fernandel and Gino Cervi, and that film is the one to see. Hill, then best known for comic westerns, produced, directed and starred, working from a script by his wife, Lori Hill, and Guareschi's stories. The talking crucifix is kept and well used, and the contest between priest and Communist is still the engine of the comedy. Critics were cool, and the Filmtv.it reviewer found it a weak directing debut, glossy and Americanised, arguing that the stories lose their point without the post-war struggle between Christian Democrats and Communists.
themes: In Guareschi the crucifix is the priest's conscience, and the remake keeps that. Christ tells Don Camillo that he instituted baptism and that a child denied it through spite would be the priest's fault; he forgives those who crucified him and expects the same of his priest; he reminds him that the road to hell is paved with good intentions, that priests serve the king of heaven and not of money, and that winning at cards by trickery is confusing good with evil. Don Camillo does penance for poaching, admits he deserved the bishop's punishment, and goes into exile with Christ's promise to be with him wherever he goes. The parish is shown through baptism, confession, blessings and a procession; no Mass appears.
liberties: The setting moves from the late 1940s to the early 1980s, with football, roller skates, skydiving and cheerleaders in place of the post-war political battles. The football match, the pools win, the baptism and the priest's exile to the mountains come from Guareschi's stories, recombined, and a divorced American mother and her son are added.
advisories:
Comic brawling, a violent football match and a punch-up in the church doorway.

The Filmtv.it reviewer objects to scantily dressed girls on roller skates and cheerleaders at the children's match; the priest lets the girls skate in the church.

The priest bribes, cheats at cards and blackmails for comic effect; Christ rebukes him each time.

Probably suitable for families with older children, with those caveats.

title: Thérèse Martin
decision: PUBLISH: La Cinématographie française's review (June 1939), an independent trade notice, describes a simple, tactful and discreet life of St Thérèse from childhood to her death in the Carmel, with an invented parallel story of a childhood friend whose failing marriage is saved by the saint's death. The trade press reported that Cardinals Verdier and Gerlier saw it in Rome in 1939 and expressed their satisfaction. The Legion of Decency's A-I for 'Saint Therese of Lisieux (French)' (1940-41) very probably refers to this film but is not proved; it is not relied on. Thérèse was canonised in 1925.
summary: Maurice de Canonge's 1939 life of St Thérèse, with Irène Corday in her first role, follows her from a devout childhood to her death in the Lisieux Carmel.
synopsis: Thérèse Martin, the youngest daughter of a devout family in Normandy, loses her mother as a small child and grows up in an atmosphere of fervent faith with her father and sisters. Determined to give herself to God young, she enters the Carmel of Lisieux, where her sisters have gone before her, and lives a short, hidden life of prayer and sacrifice, ending in a long final illness. Alongside her story the film follows a fictional childhood friend, Elisabeth d'Estranges, who grows up, marries, and sees her marriage come close to ruin through misunderstandings. Thérèse's death holds Elisabeth back on the brink and saves her household. The film includes a scene with Pope Leo XIII, recalling the young Thérèse's petition in Rome to enter the Carmel early.
inclusion: This was the first sound feature about St Thérèse, made fourteen years after her canonisation and shot partly in Lisieux and the Normandy countryside. La Cinématographie française praised Maurice de Canonge's tact, discretion and feeling with a difficult subject, and the radiance and serenity that the young Irène Corday brought to the role in her screen debut. It was a popular success in France at the start of the war, and later in Canada. The parallel story of Thérèse's friend is a period device to show the 'little way' bearing fruit in an ordinary life, and the reviewer thought it cleverly done. The film is hard to see today, and its interest is partly historical, as an early, reverent attempt to film a modern saint whose family and sisters were still alive.
themes: The film follows Thérèse's hidden holiness through a pious home, an early call, the Carmel, suffering accepted and offered, and death. Contemporary publicity called her role a love brought into a world of hatred and quoted José Germain on her offering of herself as a holocaust in the Carmel, the language of Story of a Soul. The invented sub-plot puts the doctrine of the communion of saints into narrative form: Thérèse's death and intercession save a friend's marriage, as she promised to spend her heaven doing good on earth. The film is not reported to depart from the Church's understanding of her.
history: Thérèse Martin was born at Alençon in 1873, the youngest of nine children of Louis and Zélie Martin. After her mother's death the family moved to Lisieux. During the 1887 pilgrimage she asked Leo XIII for leave to enter the Carmel at fifteen, and in April 1888 the Bishop of Bayeux and the Carmel admitted her. She died of tuberculosis on 30 September 1897. Story of a Soul made her known worldwide.
liberties: Elisabeth d'Estranges, her family and the doctors in the cast list are inventions, and the friend's marriage plot is wholly fictional. Little is recorded of how the film treats the Carmel years, the papal audience or the illness.
advisories:
A long final illness and death.

A marriage in difficulty (the fictional sub-plot); nothing explicit is reported.

Suitable for all ages, but slow for young children.

doctrine: Thérèse was beatified by Pius XI on 29 April 1923 and canonised by him on 17 May 1925, twenty-eight years after her death. In 1927 he named her, with St Francis Xavier, patron of the missions, although she never left Carmel. Her teaching, the 'little way' of spiritual childhood, is a path of confidence, small offerings and charity for ordinary souls. It rests on the Church's doctrine of grace, merit and the communion of saints, and it does not replace the sacraments, the virtues or the counsels. Her Carmelite name was Sister Thérèse of the Child Jesus and of the Holy Face. Her feast was kept on 3 October in the pre-1960 calendar.
production: The film was made by Atlantic Film and Les Productions Françaises Cinématographiques and distributed by Filmsonor. Maurice de Canonge directed it, with music by Jacques Ibert. Irène Corday played Thérèse, and the Russian émigré actor Nicholas Malikov played Leo XIII. The picture ran 90 minutes and was released in France on 7 June 1939.

title: Thunder on the Hill
decision: PUBLISH: Legion of Decency A-II, a contemporary Catholic rating, and the English dialogue (read 2026-10-12) settles the two open questions. The order is plainly Catholic (the convent of Our Lady of Rheims; Mass, Latin prayers, the rosary, a bishop), and the nun's vocation and her reading of events as Providence run through the dialogue rather than decorating it. Her disobedience is named by her as a fault, the one order she refuses is to burn evidence that could save an innocent life, and the ending reconciles her with her superior on the note that being right is worthless without humility. It is a mystery first, and the record says so.
summary: Douglas Sirk's rain-soaked convent mystery: a nursing nun, haunted by guilt, sets out to prove that a condemned woman sheltering from a flood is innocent.
synopsis: Floods cut off the roads in Norfolk, and a convent hospital becomes a refuge. Among those stranded is Valerie Carns, convicted of poisoning her brother, a composer, and on her way to be hanged, with the officers escorting her. Sister Mary Bonaventure, who runs the hospital and entered religion troubled by her own sister's suicide, becomes convinced Valerie is innocent. She crosses the flood by night to fetch Valerie's fiancé and, against her Mother Superior's orders, presses on with the case, refusing to burn a love letter that points elsewhere. A lay sister's hoard of old newspapers yields the clue. The poisoner is the hospital's doctor, who lures Sister Mary into the bell tower and attacks her; the bell is rung, help comes, and he is taken. Sister Mary and her superior are reconciled.
inclusion: Sirk made it a few years before his great Universal melodramas, and it already shows his eye. William H. Daniels's dark, noir-style photography of the storm-bound convent is its chief pleasure. Claudette Colbert is better than her unlikely casting as a nun suggests, Gladys Cooper is a formidable Mother Superior, and Ann Blyth overplays the condemned girl. The source is Charlotte Hastings's 1949 West End thriller Bonaventure. Reviewers agree it is well made but contrived, with the murderer obvious too early. What lifts it is the serious treatment of the nun's inner story. Her guilt, her pride in being right, and her superior's patient correction are as much the subject as the poisoning. The Great Detectives reviewer credits it with treating religion more seriously than most Hollywood films of its day.
themes: Sister Mary's vocation is bound up with guilt over her sister's suicide, and the film asks whether that guilt has become charity or only a need to be right. The convent is plainly Catholic, with Our Lady of Rheims, Mass, Latin prayers and a rosary said over the potato peeling. She disobeys her Mother Superior, admits there is no excuse for it, and refuses only the order to burn a letter that could save a condemned woman. The superior answers her doubts with Christ's words that he chose his disciples, not they him. The ending reconciles them: the superior apologises, Sister Mary gives the credit to a lay sister, and the last word is that being right is a gift wasted without humility. Facing the murderer, she tells him to think of his soul.
liberties: The story and characters are fictional, taken from Hastings's stage thriller, whose device of a flood stranding a condemned prisoner in a convent the film keeps. Reviewers note that a nun conducting a murder investigation against the police and her superior strains belief.
advisories:
A murder by poisoning is the subject; a violent attack in a bell tower; a newborn in danger.

A sister's suicide is discussed as back-story.

No sexual content of note; an adulterous affair is part of the solution and is not shown.

A nun repeatedly disobeys her superior; the film treats this as a fault and ends in reconciliation.

Legion of Decency A-II (adults and adolescents).

suitability.note: Mild by modern standards, but the plot is adult and the pace slow for younger children.

doctrine: The nun's conflict is over the vow of obedience. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1908-1913) describes religious obedience as the general submission religious vow to God, binding them to be directed by their superiors toward perfection. It adds that the vow is not unlimited: it is bounded by the order's rule, does not reach the inward movement of the will, and is limited by higher laws, human or divine. A religious may also seek recourse to higher authority or the Holy See. The traditional teaching would judge her fault by that standard: zeal for justice does not dispense a religious from the vow, though a superior cannot lawfully command what is against the divine law.
production: Universal-International announced the film in August 1947 with Robert Siodmak to direct and Joan Fontaine and Burt Lancaster to star. It was postponed several times, partly because of the stars' other commitments and Fontaine's pregnancy. By the time filming began in January 1949 the director, producer and stars had all been replaced. It was shot in black and white, runs 84 minutes and was released in the United States on 17 October 1951.

title: True Confessions
decision: GREY: The AFI Catalog and Wikipedia establish identity and content; TCM (David Sterritt), Canby and Ebert (via Wikipedia) are independent. The Bishops' Conference of England and Wales note is post-conciliar and used for content only. Not REJECT: the portrait of clerical worldliness is a moral drama that ends in repentance, not an anticlerical thesis. Reservations: grave sordid material and the institutional portrait; adults only.
summary: Robert De Niro's ambitious monsignor and Robert Duvall's detective brother collide over a 1948 Los Angeles murder in a grim study of clerical worldliness and its cost.
synopsis: In 1948 Los Angeles, Monsignor Des Spellacy (Robert De Niro) is the cardinal's fixer, running the archdiocese's building programme with the help of Jack Amsterdam (Charles Durning), a former hoodlum turned contractor. His brother Tom (Robert Duvall), a homicide detective who once collected payoffs for Amsterdam, deals with the death of a priest in a brothel and then the murder of a young woman found cut in two. The trail leads to a stag film and to Amsterdam. The cardinal's office decides to honour Amsterdam as layman of the year and then drop him; Tom confronts him at the banquet and will not stop, whatever it costs Des. The scandal ends Des's career, and he asks for a remote desert parish. Years later Tom visits him there; Des, dying, tells him the ordeal was his salvation and shows him their graves.
inclusion: The film has a feel for the Irish Catholic Los Angeles of the 1940s, in Cyril Cusack's cardinal, the banquets and building drives, the brothers' shared past. De Niro plays Des with almost total restraint; William F. Buckley Jr. thought him miscast, and Duvall is the livelier of the two. Vincent Canby praised it highly, while Roger Ebert, who gave it three stars, thought it never finished its story. The Bishops' Conference of England and Wales calls it one of the best portrayals of a diocesan priest torn between administration and pastoral work.
themes: The Catholic subject is vocation corrupted by worldliness and recovered through humiliation. Des is not a bad priest in the obvious sense; he is an administrator who has made the Church's prestige and buildings his work, and he covers scandal in its name. His fall sends him to a poor desert parish, and the frame shows him at peace there, dying. The archdiocese is shown as powerful and compromised, with money and political ties, but the Church itself is not shown as false; its ritual is filmed with care, and the story belongs to a priest's repentance.
advisories:
A murdered young woman's mutilated body, cut in two, and an explicit investigation of the crime.

Prostitution, a pornographic film, a priest who dies in a brothel, and frank sexual talk.

Strong language and some violence.

Adults only (R in the US; 15 in the UK).

The archdiocese is shown as worldly; some Los Angeles priests refused the production access to their churches.

doctrine: The film's priest is a careerist who trades favours with a wealthy builder, and the story turns on an old scandal in the family of a priest and a policeman. In the Latin Church clerics in sacred orders are bound to celibacy; a candidate who comes forward for ordination after the solemn warning is understood to bind himself by a vow of chastity, and a later marriage is invalid. The Catholic Encyclopedia says the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) and the Council of Trent kept this law from becoming a dead letter, and that, under Trent, clerks in minor orders who wished to advance to sacred orders had to separate from their wives and take a vow of perpetual continence.
production: Robert Chartoff and Irwin Winkler bought the rights to John Gregory Dunne's 1977 novel in April 1978. Paul Schrader was first meant to direct, but Ulu Grosbard was hired. Dunne and his wife Joan Didion wrote the script, and Didion finally rewrote it. Bill Conti left the score after the shoot ran over, and Georges Delerue composed it. Filming took place around Los Angeles in 1979 and ended in mid-May 1980 near Lancaster, California. United Artists released it on 25 September 1981 at 108 minutes. It made about $12.9 million in the US on a $10 million budget. The character of Monsignor Spellacy is thought to be based on Msgr Benjamin Hawkes of Los Angeles.

title: A Day in the Life
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred and established by the Cinemateca Portuguesa's programme note (Manuel Cintra Ferreira, quoting Comencini, Palmieri and Aristarco) and the Italian and English encyclopaedia entries: enclosed nuns shelter wounded partisans, one nun is drawn to leave the cloister with them, the Germans shoot the nuns in reprisal, and the film ends refusing vengeance. Its treatment of the cloister and of the nun's temptation, and the political frame of Church and Left reconciled, are not independently assessed in any source I found, and no contemporary Catholic rating was found. Reservation, not PUBLISH, until the dialogue is checked.
summary: Blasetti's post-war drama about a community of enclosed nuns who shelter wounded partisans, are tempted and divided by their presence, and are shot by the Germans for it.
synopsis: Late in the war, a band of partisans hunted by the Germans takes refuge in a convent of enclosed nuns, who regard the presence of men in the enclosure as a sacrilegious violation. They try to keep apart but must nurse a badly wounded man, and the mother superior recognises in him the man who years earlier killed her husband. Allied bombing traps everyone together in the cellars, where the men and the nuns begin to understand one another, and one young nun wants to leave with the partisans. When they have gone, the Germans discover what the nuns have done and shoot them in reprisal. The partisans return with the Allies and want revenge on the prisoners, but the dead nuns seem to ask for none. The one surviving nun, out of her mind, keeps repeating that none of us knows what we do.
inclusion: Blasetti, best known for historical spectacles under Fascism, made this in 1946 with a writing team that included Cesare Zavattini and Diego Fabbri. Contemporary critics were divided. Guido Aristarco praised an intensely dramatic human story free of rhetoric; Luigi Comencini complained that it sacrificed the nuns as characters; Eugenio Palmieri called it a star vehicle rather than neorealism. Manuel Cintra Ferreira, introducing it at the Cinemateca Portuguesa, agrees that it is melodrama and singles out the ending, a single fixed shot in which the shooting of the nuns is heard while a German officer walks away, as one of the best things Blasetti did.
themes: The film sets the enclosure, prayer and the vow of separation from the world against the corporal works of mercy. The nuns break their seclusion to nurse the wounded, the mother superior must care for her husband's killer, and the community pays with their lives. The ending turns away from revenge, and the surviving nun's refrain echoes Christ's prayer on the Cross for those who 'know not what they do' (Luke 23:34). Against this, the cellar scenes show the nuns drawn towards the men and their cause, and one sister wanting to abandon her vows; how the film resolves her temptation is unclear. The film also offers the Church and the Resistance as reconciled in one national suffering.
history: Enclosed communities in German-occupied Italy in 1943-45 sheltered Jews, escaped prisoners and partisans, and several religious houses suffered reprisals. The film's convent and its story are fictional, a more dramatic variation on Vittorio De Sica's 1942 comedy Un garibaldino al convento.
advisories:
The shooting of a community of nuns (heard, then their bodies shown); war violence and bombing.

A nun is tempted to leave the cloister with the partisans.

The film presents the nuns' breach of enclosure for charity as heroic; its handling of the nun's temptation is unclear.

grey.question: Enclosed nuns give their lives for charity, and the film ends by refusing revenge. But the cellar scenes, where the nuns are drawn towards the partisans and one sister wants to abandon her vows, leave it unclear how the film judges her. sources.title: Nuns
sources.claims: Periculoso, Trent, Pius V, exceptions to enclosure

suitability.note: Teenagers will follow it; younger children may be frightened by the killing of the nuns and the bombing.

doctrine: Enclosure is the law behind the film. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1913) says that Boniface VIII's constitution Periculoso made enclosure an inviolable law for all professed nuns, that the Council of Trent confirmed it, and that Pius V in 1566 (Circa pastoralis) reaffirmed both and required tertiaries who took solemn vows to keep papal enclosure. Nuns could leave only in exceptional cases approved by the regular superior and the bishop, and some mitigations came by local usage or express concession from the Holy See. Receiving and nursing the partisans is therefore a grave step under that law, so the film makes the nuns hesitate.
production: Orbis Film produced it, from a story by Blasetti, Zavattini and Edoardo Anton. Sources give 117 and 95 minutes. It opened in Italy on 5 April 1946 and was in competition at the first Cannes festival. Blasetti won the Nastro d'argento for direction and Mario Craveri for cinematography. Italian receipts to the end of 1952 were 73,800,000 lire. It was shown again in 2009 at the Film Society of Lincoln Center.

title: A Missionary
decision: GREY: Identity is secure (French visa 16734; Wikipedia citing Crisp's critical filmography; cinefiches). Content is known only in outline: a young priest's disillusion at a West African mission, from a script credited to a priest, Father Bernier (an interested source). No contemporary review or Catholic rating has been opened. Unverified; a Radio-Cinéma or Centrale Catholique notice, or the Credic study in Mission et Cinéma, would settle it.
summary: Maurice Cloche's colour drama, written with a missionary priest and shot in West Africa, follows a young missionary whose dreams of heroism give way to hard daily work.
synopsis: Père Jean Maurel (Yves Massard), a young priest, arrives at a mission in French Guinea expecting a heroic destiny. He finds routine instead: thankless daily work, slow results and the difficulty of building a relationship with the people he has come to serve. He works under an older missionary, Père Gauthier, played by Charles Vanel, alongside a lay brother, Brother Timothée (Albert Préjean), and another priest, Père Duval (Jacques Berthier). The film follows his disillusion and his effort to understand the place; how it ends is not recorded.
inclusion: Cloche made Monsieur Vincent (1947) and, in Aristide Leucate's phrase, was saddled with an absurd reputation as the official Catholic director. Politique Magazine cites this among the films that earned it. A priest is credited with part of the screenplay, so the film comes from inside the missionary world. Unusually for a mission film, it is about a young priest's disappointment at how small and slow the work is, not martyrdom or adventure. Claude Renoir's colour location photography is a draw, and Vanel and Préjean head a strong supporting cast. A commenter on the French reference site cinefiches calls it a beautiful film for a religious audience, now hard to find.
themes: The film concerns the missionary vocation as it is lived: the priest's romantic idea of heroism has to give way to patience, obedience to his superior and daily service. The relation between the mission and the African population is the other subject, and summaries speak of his struggle to build a harmonious relationship with the people. What the film makes of the sacraments, catechesis and conversions, and how it treats colonial rule and local religion, is unknown.
advisories:
Nothing objectionable is reported, though the content is not fully documented.

A colonial-era mission film; its picture of African customs and religion has not been checked.

sources.claims: Missionary as lover of the adopted country; aim of a native hierarchy; respect for good native customs; no need to transplant European civilisation

grey.question: Maurice Cloche's film follows a young priest whose hopes of heroism at a West African mission give way to hard, unglamorous work. The outline comes from French film references and a script credited to a missionary priest. No independent review exists, so how it treats the mission, the sacraments and the African people is unknown. A period notice from the French Catholic film office or Radio-Cinéma would settle it.

suitability.note: A slow drama about a missionary's disillusion, probably best for older children and up.

doctrine: The Church's missions rest on Christ's command to teach all nations. Pius XII's encyclical Evangelii Praecones (2 June 1951) was written a few years before the film. It tells missionaries to regard the country they evangelise as a second fatherland and to seek the salvation of souls, not earthly advantage. It asks them to prepare by learning the language and useful subjects, and it names the aim as a Church established on firm foundations under its own native hierarchy. It adds that the Gospel should not destroy what a people possesses that is naturally good, and that missionaries are not required to transplant European civilisation. A 1955 film about a young priest's first years in Africa can fairly be measured against these standards.
production: Maurice Cloche's company Les Films Maurice Cloche made it with UGC, Cloche producing with André Halley des Fontaines. Cinefiches credits the screenplay partly to a missionary priest, 'Révérend Père Bernier'. It was shot on location in Guinea and Cameroon in Eastmancolor. It was released in France on 2 December 1955 and runs 98 minutes (some listings give 102).

title: Miracle of the White Suit
decision: GREY: Identity (Wikipedia citing Bentley and Carlos Aguilar's Guía del cine español; CEC medal) and plot (Santiago Aguilar's account; Decine21) are established. No contemporary Catholic rating or detailed assessment of the treatment of the First Communion has been found. Unverified.
summary: Rafael Gil's melodrama of a poor Castilian boy who will not make his First Communion without the white suit his dying mother promised him.
synopsis: In a village in Castile, Polonio tries on the white suit he will wear for his First Communion, and his poor friend Marcos looks on with envy. Marcos's mother promised him such a suit as she was dying, and he will not make his Communion without one. His campaign to get it takes him down a crooked road: he lies to his father, betrays his schoolmaster's trust, runs away to Madrid and even wishes for the death of the richest woman in the village. Betrayed by his brother, he takes clandestine work on the slag heap of a foundry and loses an arm in an accident. Only then does the press take up his story, and public sympathy gets him his suit.
inclusion: Rafael Gil and the producer-writer Vicente Escrivá were the leading makers of Catholic films in 1950s Spain, and this co-production with Italy's Lux Film is typical of their work: a child, a sacrament and a good deal of pathos. Cecilio Paniagua's black-and-white photography won the Círculo de Escritores Cinematográficos medal, and the Basque composer Jesús Guridi wrote the score. Decine21, a present-day Spanish review site, gives it 4/10 and calls it a social drama with a child's sensibility. Santiago Aguilar's retelling suggests the climax is staged as a spectacle of public compassion. It is little seen today.
themes: The film turns on a boy who makes his First Communion conditional on a fine suit, and on what that desire leads him to: lies, betrayal, an evil wish against a neighbour. Whether it presents this as vanity to be corrected or as a poor child's right finally honoured is unclear. The promise to his dying mother gives the wish a filial piety, and the loss of his arm a sacrificial colour. How the Communion itself is staged, and what part the parish priest plays, is not documented.
advisories:
A child is badly injured in an industrial accident and loses an arm.

A dying mother; poverty; a child's lies and dishonesty.

The story ties a child's First Communion to getting a costly suit.
