grey.question: A poor village boy refuses to make his First Communion without the white suit his dying mother promised him, and lies, betrays trust and finally loses an arm in a foundry before public sympathy gets him the suit. The film comes from Spain's leading Catholic film team and is plainly Catholic in intention. No independent review exists, so it is unknown whether it treats the boy's fixation as vanity corrected by grace or makes the suit the reward instead of the sacrament.

suitability.note: A poor boy lies, runs away and loses an arm in a foundry accident; a mother dies. It is sad but not frightening, and suitable for older children watching with an adult who can talk about what First Communion is for.

doctrine: The decree Quam singulari (8 August 1910) of Pius X's Sacred Congregation of the Sacraments set no fixed age for First Communion: the child is to be admitted when he reaches the use of reason and can tell right from wrong, with seven mentioned as the usual age. The child needs only a basic grasp of God as rewarder and punisher, the Trinity and the Incarnation, and must know that the Eucharistic bread differs from common bread and is the Body and Blood of Christ. He must fast from midnight. Admission rests with the father (or his substitute) and the confessor together. The decree's requirements concern age, instruction and the fast; the white suit is a custom, and the sacrament does not depend on it.
production: Rafael Gil directed it for Aspa Producciones Cinematográficas, with Lux Film of Italy as co-producer. It runs 93 minutes and was released in Spain on 26 November 1956, distributed by As Films. In Italy it was released as Il grande giorno and in English as Miracle of the White Suit.

title: A Time for Miracles
decision: REJECT (rule b): the story is framed by the 1975 canonisation inquiry and closes on footage of Paul VI, so the post-conciliar Church is the interpretive frame, not a passing coda. Prior assessment: GREY (reservations): Seton was beatified by John XXIII on 17 March 1963, so she is Blessed before the Council and rule (a) does not apply (the batch hint was wrong). The film is framed by her 1975 canonisation inquiry and closes with newsreel of Paul VI canonising her, which is a post-conciliar frame but a coda to a pre-conciliar life, so reservation rather than rule (b). Treatment of the conversion itself is unverified: subtitles or a transcript would settle whether the conversion and Eucharist are stated plainly.
summary: ABC's Christmas 1980 biography of Bl. Elizabeth Seton, with Kate Mulgrew as the Episcopalian widow who becomes a Catholic and founds the first American community of sisters.
synopsis: Elizabeth Bayley Seton, a New York Episcopalian and mother of five, is ruined when her husband's shipping business fails. She takes him to Italy for his health, and he dies there of consumption in 1803. Back in America she is received into the Catholic Church, which costs her friends, family and income. She opens a school to support her children and, at the request of Bishop John Carroll of Baltimore, takes vows and founds a school and convent at Emmitsburg, Maryland. Anti-Catholic mobs and more deaths from consumption mark the years of foundation. She dies at 46. A framing story set in 1975 follows a postulator who examines the evidence for her canonisation and searches for the miracle still needed.
inclusion: Seton's life is one of the plainest conversion stories in American Catholic history: a widow loses her husband, her money and her social place, and joins a church her neighbours despise. The cast is better than most television biographies: Kate Mulgrew in the lead, Lorne Greene as Bishop Carroll, Jean-Pierre Aumont, Rossano Brazzi and John Forsythe. America magazine's reviewer found the film "unusually poignant and uplifting" and singled out the scene of a mob outside a church, which shows how hostile early America was to Catholics. VideoHound's guide was less kind, giving one and a half stars out of four, so expect a television-movie look. America notes that it was nominated for an Emmy.
themes: The sources describe a conversion from the Episcopal Church that costs the convert dearly, the hostility of a Protestant majority, the founding of a teaching community under the authority of a bishop, and a death from consumption. The framing story brings in the Church's process for recognising saints and ends with newsreel of Paul VI's 1975 ceremony in St Peter's Square. No source describes how the conversion scenes treat the Real Presence or the claims of the Church, which are what a conversion to Catholicism turns on, and the film's own dialogue has not been checked.
history: Elizabeth Ann Seton was received into the Catholic Church on 14 March 1805, after her husband's death in Italy. She founded a community of sisters at Emmitsburg, Maryland, on 31 July 1809 and died there of consumption on 4 January 1821, aged 46. John XXIII beatified her on 17 March 1963, before the Council. Paul VI canonised her on 14 September 1975.
production: Henry Denker wrote the script with Sister Mary Hilaire. Michael O'Herlihy directed for ABC Circle Films and Jimmy Hawkins's company, with a score by Fred Karlin and photography by Donald Birnkrant, shot in Georgia. ABC aired it on 21 December 1980 as a Christmas special, 97 minutes long. America magazine says it was made after her 1975 canonisation and the 1976 bicentennial and notes an Emmy nomination. Dove.org rates it for ages 12 and up. No contemporary Catholic film-office rating has been found.
liberties: Sources say the film adds a modern frame: a postulator searching for one more miracle. Dove.org says the Church required proof of four miracles; America says she was short one. These accounts conflict, and the film's own presentation of the process has not been checked.
advisories:
A mob attacks a Catholic church and a priest, who is left with a bloody face. Several characters die of consumption, one coughing blood. Men drink in a tavern. Cleavage is shown. Dove.org rates the film 12+.

The film is framed by a 1975 canonisation inquiry and ends with footage of Paul VI: read the question above.

suitability.note: A mob attacks a church and a priest, and several characters die slowly of consumption. Dove.org recommends it for ages 12 and up; it suits families who want a gentle saint's life.

doctrine: Seton's conversion turned on the Catholic claim that Christ is truly present in the Eucharist. The Council of Trent, in Session XIII (11 October 1551), defined in canon 1 the real, substantial presence of Christ under the appearances of bread and wine, Body, Soul and Divinity, and the Catholic Encyclopedia notes that either kind therefore gives the whole Christ. She was beatified by John XXIII in 1963 and canonised by Paul VI in 1975, so for this site she is Blessed, not Saint. The film's canonisation frame follows the 1975 process, but she had already been declared Blessed before the Council.

title: Anthony of Padua, Saint of Miracles
originalTitle: Antonio di Padova, il santo dei miracoli
decision: GREY: Identity is established (Silent Era's detailed credits: SACRAS, scenario by Aldo Quinti and Antamoro from a novel by Vittorino Facchinetti, released April 1931, print exists; TMDB outline). Content is known in outline only, from Fernando's youth in Lisbon to his Franciscan vocation; no review found. Settled by a review, a CCC-type contemporary judgment or a viewing of a surviving print. Not the 1949 Francisci film (Legion A-I as Anthony of Padua), which is a separate record.

grey.question: Giulio Antamoro's life of St Anthony was made in 1931 by a Catholic production company, adapted from a novel by the Franciscan writer Vittorino Facchinetti, with music by Francesco Catalani, and a print survives. No independent review exists. The available outline follows Fernando from a Lisbon boyhood concerned for the poor to the Augustinians and then the Franciscans. A contemporary review or a description of the surviving print would show how it treats his preaching and miracles.

summary: Giulio Antamoro, director of Christus and Frate Francesco, returned for this late-silent life of St Anthony, released in 1931, seven hundred years after the saint's death.
synopsis: The film begins with the saint as Fernando, a boy in Lisbon, played by Ello Cosci, who also plays him as a youth; published outlines describe him as moved early by the sufferings of the poor. As a young man he renounces the world and enters the Augustinian canons, then joins the Franciscans and takes the name Anthony, played as an adult by Carlo Pinzauti. The title promises the miracles for which Anthony was famous, and the story follows him into his preaching life in Italy. No scene-by-scene account says which miracles are shown or how the film ends, though Anthony's death at Padua in 1231 is the obvious close.
inclusion: Antamoro had made two of the most successful Italian religious films of the silent era, Christus (1916) and Frate Francesco (1927), and this was his return to the genre for the seventh centenary of St Anthony's death. It was produced by SACRAS, a company set up for religious films, from a novel by Vittorino Facchinetti, a Franciscan writer, and it travelled widely: Portugal, Hungary and, years later, Mexico. Sources disagree on whether it is purely silent or has a synchronised music track by Francesco Catalani d'Abruzzo. A print survives, but its quality and approach are still open.
themes: Anthony's life as outlined runs through two religious vocations, from the Augustinian canons to the Franciscans, and the change of name marks his adoption of Francis's poverty. The emphasis on his concern for the poor, and the subtitle's promise of miracles, fit the traditional devotion to the saint of Padua. The source novel was written by a Franciscan, which suggests a conventional pious life. How the film shows his preaching, his miracles and the Eucharistic miracle of the mule, if it is included, is not recorded.
history: Fernando Martins de Bulhões was born in Lisbon about 1195, joined the Augustinian canons and in 1220 entered the Franciscans, taking the name Anthony. He became a renowned preacher in Italy and southern France and died near Padua on 13 June 1231. He was canonised in 1232 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1946.

doctrine: Baptised Fernando, Anthony died at Arcella, near Padua. Gregory IX canonised him at Spoleto on 30 May 1232, and his feast is 13 June. Pius XII gave him the title Doctor Evangelicus when he declared him a Doctor of the Church on 16 January 1946. The Church teaches that the saints reign with Christ and pray for men, and that it is good and useful to invoke them (Council of Trent, Session XXV, 3-4 December 1563). Devotion to Anthony as a worker of miracles rests on that teaching.
production: SACRAS (Società Anonima Cinematografie Religiose Artistiche Sonore) produced the film, with production management by Giovanni Pettine; Aldo Quinti and Antamoro also edited it. title: Aparecida: The Miracle
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (Marian shrine and devotion central, priests of the Sanctuary assisted), identity established, nothing alarming in the viewer reports, but no professional critic and no review by a Catholic authority of any date; treatment of the apparition story and of the shrine's liturgy is only known from user reviews. Dialogue or a published review would settle it.
summary: Tizuka Yamasaki's family drama follows a businessman who lost his faith when his father died at the Aparecida basilica and returns to Our Lady after his son's accident.
synopsis: As a boy, Marcos is devoted to Our Lady of Aparecida. His father dies in an accident at the Basilica, and the boy loses both his father and his faith. Thirty-five years later Marcos is a successful businessman, absorbed in money, a distant father who rejects his son's choices. A serious accident involving the son makes him remember his own father's devotion. His mother tells him of the mysterious grace that has guided the family. One viewer's account says the film includes a retelling of how the image of Our Lady was found in the Paraíba do Sul river.
inclusion: A modest Brazilian drama, no devotional pageant. The only reviews found are viewers' comments on AdoroCinema, which average 3.3 out of 5: some praise Murilo Rosa and Leona Cavalli and say the film treats faith without fanaticism, while one calls it overly melodramatic and says the story-within-a-story does not work. Its Catholic interest is the place and the devotion. AdoroCinema reports that the Sanctuary of Aparecida and its foundation were filming locations and that its priests helped the production, so the shrine's own account of the image probably shapes the story. The producers announced a sequel for the 300th anniversary of the image's finding in 2017.
themes: The film is about lost and recovered faith, tied to the devotion of Aparecida, the Marian shrine of Brazil. The wound is the father's death at the Basilica; the answer is the mother's account of an unexplained grace. Whether the film shows Mass, the rosary or confession, or presents the miracle of the title as a grace of Our Lady or as coincidence, is unknown.
history: Tradition holds that a statue of Our Lady was found in the Paraíba do Sul river and became the centre of the devotion of Aparecida. Pius X granted the image a canonical coronation in 1904, and Pius XI declared Our Lady of Aparecida patroness of Brazil by a bull of 16 July 1930. The film's Marcos and his family are invented.
production: RioFilme and Globo Filmes are named as producers. Besides the Sanctuary, the film was shot in Rio de Janeiro. It opened in Brazilian cinemas on 17 December 2010 and runs 90 minutes.
advisories:
A father dies in an accident at the Basilica, and the adult hero's son is seriously injured in another. Melodramatic family conflict; no violence or sexual content is reported by the viewers.

Its treatment of the faith has not been assessed; see the question above.

suitability.note: The death and the child in danger are sad rather than frightening, and children may find it slow.

doctrine: The film centres on the veneration of an image of Our Lady. The Council of Trent, Session XXV (3-4 December 1563), taught that images of Christ and of the Virgin Mother of God are to be kept, especially in churches, and given due honour, because the honour shown them is referred to the person they represent; nothing is to be asked of the image itself. The same session taught that the saints reign with Christ and pray for men, and that invoking them is good and useful. According to the tradition, the statue of Aparecida was found in the Paraíba River in 1717. Her feast is 12 October.

grey.question: No professional critic or Catholic film office has reviewed this film. The only evidence of its treatment is nine viewer reviews on AdoroCinema, which call it a father-and-son story that handles faith without fanaticism, with devotional passages and a retelling of the apparition; one finds it melodramatic. The shrine's priests helped the production, so the Sanctuary may have shaped its account. How it presents the apparition, the Mass and the miracle of the title is unchecked. The film itself or a published review would settle it.

title: The Priest from Kirchfeld
decision: REJECT (content): like the 1937 version of Anzengruber’s anticlerical play, it sides with the priest’s disobedience to his bishop — he secretly marries a couple the diocese refused and his transfer is framed as an injustice. Prior assessment: Catholic-centred (a priest's celibacy, a slander campaign, obedience). Identity and full plot from German and English Wikipedia; the Lexikon des internationalen Films verdict ('so oberflächenhaft wie möglich') and Der Spiegel's notice quoted there. Reservation: the priest secretly marries a couple against his diocese's refusal and the film frames his disobedience sympathetically; he keeps his vow. No other version of the play is catalogued.
summary: Hans Deppe's Heimatfilm moves Anzengruber's priest drama to post-war Bavaria: a well-loved pastor, drawn to a refugee girl, is undone by village gossip and his own disobedience.
synopsis: Vinzenz Heller (Claus Holm) is the well-loved pastor of Kirchfeld. He condemns the cohabitation of a war widow and a railwayman, who will not marry because she would lose her pension, yet lets her son Karli serve at the altar. He asks the diocese for leave to marry them secretly, and is refused. Anna Birkmaier (Ulla Jacobsson), a refugee girl who helps in the parsonage, grows attached to him, and he to her, though he holds back. The innkeeper Riedl, whom the pastor once denounced from the pulpit, spreads a rumour of an affair, and the village turns away from him. Heller marries the couple secretly against the ban. To end the scandal Anna agrees to marry the smith, whom she does not love; when she asks Heller to leave the priesthood for her, he cannot. His last act in Kirchfeld is her wedding, and he is transferred as a punishment.
inclusion: Ludwig Anzengruber's play was filmed several times; this version, by Hans Deppe, one of the busiest directors of 1950s Heimatfilm, moves it to the refugee-filled Bavaria of the post-war years and shoots the village in Sachrang. Ulla Jacobsson won the critics' prize for best actress at San Sebastián. Critics were less taken with the rest. The Catholic Lexikon des internationalen Films found it staged as superficially as possible, the landscapes apart; Der Spiegel called it a colourful Heimatfilm with Anzengruber's original dialogue and credited Deppe with a few natural village scenes. Its interest lies in its subject: a priest tempted, slandered and keeping his vow, in a film that leans towards him and against his superiors. It sits between the sentimental Heimatfilm and the problem picture, and belongs fully to neither.
themes: The film is about celibacy and obedience. Heller keeps his vow: when Anna asks him to give up the priesthood he refuses, and he officiates at her marriage to another man. That is the film's best moment, and it treats the vow as binding. But its sympathies lie with his disobedience. He secretly marries a couple after the diocese has refused permission, and his punitive transfer reads as the institution's injustice to a good priest. The villagers' gossip is the real villain and the diocese a cold one. Sin, scandal and the duty of a priest to guard his reputation are all present, but obedience is not weighed.
advisories:
No violence or sexual content is reported; the temptation is emotional and is resisted.

Unmarried cohabitation and a village slander campaign are central.

For teenagers and adults.

The priest's secret marriage of a couple against his diocese's refusal is presented sympathetically.

title: Father Cigarette
decision: GREY: Priest-centred comedy-drama (a parish priest's protection of a seduced, pregnant girl against the village's rich family). Identity: Wikipedia (citing Bentley) and Decine21; treatment only in Decine21's short note (4/10). A Biblioteca Virtual Cervantes article on the film and the Civil War, and a FilmAffinity review, returned 403. Unverified.
summary: Juan de Orduña films Arniches's comedy of a gruff Castilian village priest who takes the side of a pregnant, abandoned girl against the village's richest family.
synopsis: Don Froilán (Valeriano León), parish priest of a small Castilian village, is known as Padre Pitillo. He is irritable and gruff, but kind underneath, and he lives with his sister Camila (Aurora Redondo). Rosita (Margarita Andrey) is pregnant by Bernabé, son of the village's leading family, who has abandoned her, and her stepfather has shut her out of the house. Bernabé's family, meanwhile, is sending him away to the city. The priest takes Rosita's part and sets himself against the powerful family on her behalf. How the story ends is not recorded.
inclusion: Carlos Arniches was the great comic dramatist of Madrid, and his Padre Pitillo had already been filmed in Chile in 1946. Juan de Orduña, two years before his hit El último cuplé, directed this version with the comic actor Valeriano León as the priest. Decine21 calls it a more than competent adaptation, tender in its picture of village life and built on a priest whose bad temper hides a generous nature, though its own rating is 4 out of 10. The interest lies in that figure, a country priest who stands up to the rich for a poor girl.
themes: The priest's charity is practical. He shelters a girl who has been seduced, abandoned and turned out of her home, and he confronts the family whose son is responsible. It is a recognisably pastoral role, the parish priest as defender of the weak, guarding a mother and her unborn child against the powerful. How the film resolves the matter, whether by marriage, reconciliation or something else, and how it treats the pious villagers and the parish's other clergy, is not described.
advisories:
A young woman's seduction and pregnancy outside marriage are central; nothing explicit is reported.

The film's ending and its treatment of the parishioners are unverified.

title: The Portico of Glory
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a Franciscan friar leads a boys' choir on pilgrimage to Compostela for the Holy Year). Identity: Wikipedia (citing Castro de Paz and Cerdán) and Decine21 credits; content and an independent, sceptical reading from the Dqvlapeli review. A scholarly article, 'El pórtico de la Gloria: catequesis, melodrama y propaganda' (Biblioteca Virtual Miguel de Cervantes), returned 403 and was not read; it is the next source. Unverified.
summary: José Mojica, the Mexican singing star turned Franciscan, plays a friar who brings a boys' choir to Compostela for the Holy Year and reunites a mother with her lost son.
synopsis: Padre José (José Mojica), a Mexican Franciscan, travels to Spain with the Orfeón Infantil Mexicano, a boys' choir, for the Holy Year at Santiago de Compostela. The choir's success brings engagements across the country, and the middle of the film follows the tour from city to city. On the way the friar and the boys meet a wealthy, elegant woman with a troubled past (Lina Rosales), who takes them under her protection. She is an unbeliever from the side defeated in the Civil War, and she lost a son who was carried into exile in Mexico. The friar's care for the people around him draws the threads together, and at the end, at the altar of the Apostle in the cathedral, as the bells ring, mother and son recognise each other.
inclusion: José Mojica was a Mexican tenor and Hollywood musical star of the 1930s who became a Franciscan after his mother's death, and here he plays a friar much like himself; he also wrote the story. Suevia Films, Cesáreo González's company, made the film to catch the Compostela Holy Year, and the Dqvlapeli review credits González with business shrewdness in seizing the moment. The same review is sceptical. It finds the coincidences arranged so that nothing is left to chance, the central section a travelogue of Spanish cities, the Civil War approached on tiptoe while a montage celebrates the 1939 victory, and the whole in service of the National-Catholic message of the year of the Concordat. Its interest lies in Mojica himself, the boys' choir and its singing, and the pilgrimage to St James, which few fiction films have taken as a subject.
themes: Pilgrimage gives the film its shape. A friar leads children to the tomb of the Apostle for the Holy Year, and the journey ends at St James's altar. Along the way Padre José catechises the people he meets, and the climax reunites an unbelieving mother from the defeated side with her son, a reunion placed at the altar as if granted by the saint. Whether the recognition is also a return to the faith, and how the friar's preaching is handled, is unclear. The political framing sits alongside the religious one throughout.
advisories:
Nothing objectionable is reported. Suitable for all ages.

The Civil War and a montage celebrating the Nationalist victory form part of the background.

How the film treats the mother's unbelief and the friar's catechesis is unverified.

title: The Trial of Christ
decision: GREY: Identity and outline from a Crónica article by Daniela Muñoz (opened) and the Wikipedia list of Mexican films of 1966. Catholic-centred (the Passion, told in flashback by Peter, Pilate, Claudia and Barabbas) and nothing contrary to the faith is reported, but the only assessment says it gives "human perceptions" more than historical facts and does not discuss Christ's divinity or the Resurrection. Unverified: dialogue or a review would settle it. Year is disputed (1965 in Crónica, 10 March 1966 elsewhere).
summary: Julio Bracho's Mexican Passion film is told in flashback, twenty-seven years after the Crucifixion, by Peter, Pilate's household and Barabbas.
synopsis: Twenty-seven years after the Crucifixion, the apostle Peter comes to Rome and visits the house of Pontius Pilate. Their talk opens a series of flashbacks built from the memories of several people: Peter, Pilate, Pilate's wife Claudia, and Barabbas, the former rebel leader who has become a respectable citizen. The film is divided into four episodes, "The Trial of Christ", "Remorse", "Christ and Woman" and "The Sentence". Christ appears chiefly through these recollections, played by Enrique Rocha. Claudia tells how she was given proof of his miracles and reproaches Pilate for his indecision. The witnesses disagree about what happened, so the film offers several viewpoints on the trial.
inclusion: Julio Bracho, a figure of the Mexican theatre and cinema, made the film with the producer Blas López Fandos, who, according to Crónica, sent him to the Holy Land to study the setting. It tells the Passion through testimonies, with Peter, Pilate and Barabbas each carrying a different memory of Christ. Enrique Rocha, as Jesus, broke the habit of casting Spanish-looking actors in the role, which Crónica noted. The same article calls it a melodrama and says it offers human perceptions more than historical facts. Its quality and its handling of Christ's divinity remain unknown.
themes: The Catholic content is the trial and condemnation of Christ and the question of guilt and remorse among those who stood near it. Peter, Claudia and Barabbas are figures from the Gospel story. How the film presents Christ's divinity, the Resurrection or Peter's authority is not known. Because it is built on competing human accounts, a reader should check whether it affirms the Gospel account or leaves its truth open.
liberties: The Rome meeting between Peter and Pilate, twenty-seven years after the Crucifixion, is invented, as is the reformed Barabbas telling his story. The film also adds a chapter on Christ and women. Its structure of differing testimonies means the Gospel account is presented as one version among several.
advisories:
The Passion is shown in flashbacks; its intensity is not documented.

No content ratings are recorded; it was released in Mexico as a melodrama for a general audience.

The film is built on differing human accounts of the trial, which the one article describes as perceptions more than facts.

title: Faith of Millions
decision: GREY: Identity and content are established by the AFI Catalog (Chester Productions, six reels, Technicolor, copyright 26 April 1927, with a scene summary of the 1926 Chicago Eucharistic Congress). No review has been found and no archive holding is recorded, so survival is unknown; a separate eight-reel Fox film of the same Congress (Exhibitors Herald, December 1926) shows the subject was filmed more than once. Settled by a contemporary review or an archive record of a print.

grey.question: This six-reel record of the 1926 International Eucharistic Congress in Chicago is securely identified in the AFI Catalog, which summarises its scenes: the papal legate's high Mass, a children's choir of 62,000 at Soldier Field and the great procession of the Blessed Sacrament at Mundelein. No review of it is known, and no archive is known to hold a print, so it may be lost. A contemporary review, or the discovery of a surviving copy, would settle it.

summary: A six-reel Technicolor record of the 1926 International Eucharistic Congress in Chicago, from the papal legate's Mass to the great procession at Mundelein.
synopsis: The film follows the 28th International Eucharistic Congress, held in Chicago from 20 to 24 June 1926. According to the AFI Catalog's summary, Cardinal Bonzano, the papal legate, celebrates a high Mass at an altar raised before the Church of the Immaculate Conception, with eleven other cardinals in attendance. A Children's Day is held at Soldier Field, where a choir of 62,000 children sings. The film culminates in the pilgrimage of some 750,000 people to the seminary of St Mary of the Lake at Mundelein, Illinois, for the Eucharistic procession. Among those seen are Cardinals O'Donnell and Hayes, Bishop Hoban, Governor Al Smith of New York, the mayors of New York and Chicago and the US Secretary of Labor.
inclusion: The Chicago Congress of 1926 was the first held in the United States and one of the largest public acts of Catholic worship the country had seen, and this is a film record of it, released in April 1927 and listed by the AFI as a Technicolor film, unusual for a documentary of the time. Its value lies in the record: the scale of the crowds, a pontifical Mass before a dozen cardinals, a children's choir filling a stadium, and a procession of the Blessed Sacrament through the grounds of a new seminary. It was not the only film of the Congress; Fox showed an eight-reel picture that Cardinal Mundelein asked his clergy to promote. Nothing is known of this film's style or quality, so for now it is a title to look for rather than a film to watch.
themes: The subject is the Holy Eucharist. The Congress existed to honour the Real Presence, and its climax was the procession of the Blessed Sacrament. The Mass shown is the pontifical High Mass as celebrated before the Council, with the papal legate presiding and the hierarchy present in force. The children's day at Soldier Field, with a choir of 62,000, shows the Congress as a festival of Catholic schools and parishes as well as of the clergy. The AFI summary records what is shown and says nothing of how the film frames it.
history: The congress was hosted by Cardinal George Mundelein, with Cardinal Giovanni Bonzano as papal legate. Its closing day was held at the new seminary of St Mary of the Lake in the town of Mundelein, north of Chicago, with a procession of the Blessed Sacrament before a vast crowd.
advisories:
No objectionable content is recorded; a documentary of public worship.

Silent, with title cards; listed as Technicolor.

No surviving print has been traced; it may be lost.

suitability.note: A silent documentary record of public worship, with no objectionable content. Younger children may find the long processions slow.

doctrine: The Council of Trent, Session XIII (11 October 1551), taught that the body, blood, soul and divinity of Christ are truly, really and substantially present in the Eucharist (Canon 1) and that the whole substance of the bread and wine is changed, a change the Church calls transubstantiation (chapter 4, Canon 2). Chapter 5 taught that the sacrament is to be given the worship of latria, and Canon 6 condemned those who deny that it should be adored, kept in festal celebration and carried in public processions. The closing procession at Mundelein was such a public act of adoration.
production: Chester Productions, Inc. made the six-reel Technicolor documentary and claimed copyright on 26 April 1927; it was distributed on a State Rights basis. AFI lists no director or cameraman. Jean Conover is credited as film editor and for the art titles. Fox Film made a separate 96-minute documentary of the same Congress, released in New York on 8 November 1926.

title: Full of Grace
decision: REJECT (content): Peter is told he is “following, not leading”, setting aside the primacy (as with Peter and Paul, 1981), and Our Lady’s death and burial are shown with no sign of the Assumption. Prior assessment: GREY (reservations): Mary and Peter are the only principals, so it is Catholic-centred; no violence or sex, and the promotion is the only claim to Catholic approval. Two points can only be settled by dialogue: Mary is shown dying and being buried with no empty tomb (the producers cite Munificentissimus Deus as silent on how she died, which is accurate), and the premise that Peter "is following, not leading" may soften the primacy. Independent evidence is Video Librarian (trade, 3 of 5) and Movieguide (Protestant-leaning family site); Catholic outlets are post-conciliar and used for content only.
summary: Andrew Hyatt's quiet 83-minute drama imagines Mary's last days, when an exhausted Peter comes to her for counsel and she recalls her years with Christ.
synopsis: About ten years after the Resurrection the young Church is under pressure: persecution from outside, rival sects that mix Christian and pagan practice, and the question of how Jewish believers should live. Peter, worn out by years of travel and danger, comes to Mary, who is ill and cared for by her handmaid Zara. Over several conversations Mary remembers when she was called to bear God's Son, and recalls his life, his sacrifice and his victory over death. She counsels Peter to seek God's will rather than work everything out alone. Peter comes to see that he is following Christ, not leading alone. The film ends with Mary's last days.
inclusion: Reviewers agree that it is slow and short. Video Librarian's Tom Keogh gave it three stars out of five, found the tone solemn to the point of monotony, and praised Bahia Haifi's Mary and Noam Jenkins's Peter. Movieguide gave it three stars of four, "beautifully made but slow in places". The Catholic News Agency reviewer thought Haifi the true highlight. Notre Dame's Church Life Journal reports students admiring the atmosphere, the music and the restrained handling of Christ, who is never seen. It has no violence or sexual content, and Movieguide considers it suitable for all ages. Hyatt went on to direct Paul, Apostle of Christ (2018). It is a film for people who already love its subject.
themes: The film joins two themes: Mary as mother of the faithful and counsellor, and Peter as the man Christ chose to lead. A Church Life Journal article links her motherhood of believers to the scene at the Cross. Peter's lesson, in the Apple TV description, is that he is "following, not leading", which can be read as plain humility or as softening the primacy; no source quotes the dialogue. Mary is shown dying and being buried with no empty tomb. Pius XII's definition of the Assumption says only that she, "having completed the course of her earthly life", was assumed body and soul. The Notre Dame piece says the Eucharist is not addressed. Zara and the sects Peter must correct are invented.
history: Scripture says little about Mary after Pentecost, and the film's account of her final years is imagined. The Assumption of Our Lady was defined as a dogma of faith by Pius XII in Munificentissimus Deus on 1 November 1950. The definition says Mary, having completed the course of her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory; it does not say how or where she died.
production: Andrew Hyatt wrote and directed. T.J. Berden produced and Eric Groth was executive producer for Outside da Box of St. Charles, Illinois. The cast is Bahia Haifi, Noam Jenkins and Kelsey Asbille (credited elsewhere as Kelsey Chow). Cinedigm released it on DVD in January 2016; it runs 82 or 83 minutes. Groth said not everyone who worked on it was Catholic or Christian. The filmmakers say they met Pope Benedict at the Vatican and that he endorsed it as an example of the New Evangelization; this is their own account. Outside da Box also sells it for parish nights of reflection.
liberties: Zara, Mary's handmaid, is invented, as are the conversations with Peter and the sects he is asked to correct. Mary is shown dying and being buried with no empty tomb, according to the Church Life Journal. The producers say they consulted theologians and bishops and that Pope Benedict XVI endorsed the project when they met him; only promotional articles report this.
advisories:
None of the sources reports violence, sexual content, nudity or strong language; Movieguide scores it +4 for family content.

It is slow and talky, with long conversations and flashbacks.

Mary's death and burial and the question of Peter's authority: read the question above.

suitability.note: No violence, sex or strong language, per Movieguide. The pace is slow and conversation-heavy, so younger children may lose interest.

doctrine: The Assumption of Our Lady was defined by Pius XII on 1 November 1950 in Munificentissimus Deus: Mary, having completed the course of her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory. The document speaks of her having "passed from this life" but does not define the manner of her death or the fate of her tomb, so a film that shows her death and burial does not contradict the definition. The Council of Trent, Session XXV (3-4 December 1563), taught that the saints in heaven pray for men and that invoking them is good and useful, which is the basis of the film's picture of Mary as intercessor and counsellor.

title: Holy Year 1950
decision: PUBLISH: Legion of Decency A-I (1949-50), the pre-conciliar Catholic judgment, and an independent contemporary review in Motion Picture Herald's Product Digest (5 August 1950, reviewer's rating 'Good'); the AFI Catalog establishes identity and content. A record of the 1950 Jubilee under Pius XII, with nothing post-conciliar in it. Its 42-minute length is stated in the advisories.
summary: Fox Movietone's 42-minute record of the 1950 Jubilee in Rome: the opening of the Holy Door, pilgrims at the basilicas and catacombs, and Pius XII among the crowds.
synopsis: The film opens on Rome itself, with the Appian Way, the Colosseum and the Forum, and a short account of what a Holy Year is and when the first was held. It then follows the preparations for the Jubilee that Pius XII proclaimed in May 1949, and the opening of the Holy Door on Christmas Eve, when the Pope strikes the wall with a silver hammer. Pilgrims visit St Peter's, the catacombs and the College of Propaganda Fide, and tour the Sistine Chapel, the Vatican Library and the Raphael rooms. Highlights of the year follow: the Swiss Guards' oath, the beatifications of Vincent Pallotti and Dominic Savio, Cardinal Spellman leading 530 American pilgrims to a papal audience, and the Pope's own Jubilee visit to St Peter's among thousands of priests and seminarians. It closes with the Easter blessing given from St Peter's Square.
inclusion: A newsreel feature, not an essay, and best taken as one. Its value is the record. Fox Movietone's Rome crew filmed inside the Vatican with the approval of Pius XII and the Holy Year committee, and caught the Church of 1950 at full stretch: the Holy Door ceremony, the Pope celebrating Mass in St Peter's, the Swiss Guard, the beatification of Dominic Savio, John Bosco's pupil, and the Sistine Choir on the soundtrack. The commentary is spoken by Fr Robert Gannon, the Jesuit former president of Fordham and a well-known Catholic speaker. Motion Picture Herald's reviewer rated it good, called it the best newsreel technique, found the photography satisfactory and expected it to interest Catholics and non-Catholics alike. It is short and plainly a souvenir of a pilgrimage year, but few films show the papal liturgy and court of Pius XII so directly.
themes: The subject is the Jubilee: pilgrimage to the tombs of the Apostles, the Holy Door opened as the sign of a year of pardon, and the Pope as the visible head of the Church who receives the pilgrims and blesses the city and the world. The film shows Pius XII celebrating Mass in St Peter's and passing among the crowds, and it ties the living Church to the martyrs through the catacombs. The two beatifications show the Church raising up new models of holiness, one of them a schoolboy. The commentary explains the year, and the Herald thought it written for viewers who wondered what a Holy Year was about.
history: Boniface VIII proclaimed the first Jubilee in 1300. Pius XII invited the world to the Holy Year of 1950 and opened the Holy Door of St Peter's on Christmas Eve 1949. During the year he beatified, among others, Vincent Pallotti and Dominic Savio, both of whom appear in the film. The year's most important act, the definition of the dogma of the Assumption in Munificentissimus Deus on 1 November 1950, came after the film's release in August.
advisories: Nothing objectionable; suitable for all ages.

doctrine: A Jubilee is a year of special indulgence. title: Jesus, the Child of God
decision: GREY: Identity from 4enoch.org and a TMDB-mirror page (both opened); the second film of Zacarías's Gospel trilogy and a plain Nativity story. Nothing contrary to the faith is reported but no review or treatment source of any kind was found, so it stays unverified, like its sibling Jesús, nuestro Señor. Year disputed (1970 on FilmAffinity and in Wikipedia's Zacarías list; 16 December 1971 on the TMDB mirror).
summary: The Nativity instalment of Miguel Zacarías's Mexican Gospel trilogy follows Mary and Joseph, the Magi and Herod, with Gayle Bedall and Guillermo Murray as the Holy Family.
synopsis: The film tells the Nativity from the birth of Jesus at Bethlehem to the visit of the three Kings. Herod, played by Jorge Rado, orders the killing of the children under three years old, and the Holy Family is threatened. Guillermo Murray plays Joseph, Gayle Bedall plays Mary, and the Archangel Gabriel (Norma Kauffe) appears. The Magi are Melchior (Juan José Laboriel), Balthasar (René Cardona Sr.) and Gaspar (Dagoberto Rodríguez), and Alfredo Melher plays the child Jesus. The cast also lists characters who are not in the Gospels, Claudio (Jorge Rivero) and Voltigo (Luis Alarcón), with Archelaus (José Rafull). How these invented figures fit the story is not described.
inclusion: Miguel Zacarías, a Mexican-Lebanese director, made a three-part life of Christ in colour in the early 1970s: Jesús, nuestro Señor (the ministry and Passion), this Nativity film and Jesús, María y José (the hidden life). It is a popular devotional production with a large cast, including Jorge Rivero in an invented role. The running time is about 85 to 90 minutes. Nothing is documented about its quality, its tone or its faithfulness to Matthew and Luke.
themes: The film covers the Nativity, the Magi and Herod's slaughter of the children. Its cast includes the Archangel Gabriel and the Holy Family, so the Annunciation and the virginal birth may be shown. The Catholic reading of the Nativity includes the virginal conception and birth and the adoration by the Magi; whether the film keeps to these is unverified. Invented characters such as Claudio and Voltigo may carry subplots, and a reader should check whether they alter the Gospel account.
advisories:
The slaughter of the children under Herod is part of the story; the intensity is not documented.

No content concerns are reported.

title: Jesus, Mary and Joseph
decision: GREY: Identity from a TMDB-mirror page and 4enoch.org (opened, cast and runtime) and Wikipedia's Zacarías article (1970). The hidden life of Christ is a plainly Catholic subject, but sources say the film speculates on his whereabouts as a boy and shows Joseph as an old man, and no review of the speculation exists. Unverified rather than HOLD because identity and outline are established. Year: 1972 on most databases, 1970 on Wikipedia.
summary: The third film of Zacarías's Mexican Gospel trilogy dwells on the childhood of Jesus, speculating on his boyhood years with Mary and an elderly Joseph.
synopsis: The film is described as the first to concentrate wholly on the childhood of Jesus, filling in his boyhood with speculation about where he was. Guillermo Murray plays Joseph, shown as an old man acting as a guardian, and Gayle Bedall plays Mary. Jesus appears at five (José Alberto Castro), eight (Jorge España) and twelve (David Bravo). The cast list also includes grown figures from the Gospels, among them Peter (Juan Miranda), Andrew (Xavier Loyá), Caiaphas (Carlos Ancira), Barabbas (René Dupeyrón) and Judas (Luis Yañez), so it probably looks ahead to the ministry. The invented characters Zacchaeus (Enrique Rambal) and Amroth (Eric del Castillo) also appear.
inclusion: Few films take on the hidden life, the thirty years the Gospels cover in almost nothing apart from the finding in the Temple at twelve. Miguel Zacarías closed his trilogy with this attempt, in colour, giving three actors to the young Jesus and a veteran cast to the adults. The subject is daring and risky, since with so little to go on the film must invent. Nothing is documented about its quality or reception.
themes: The film centres on the Holy Family. Joseph is shown as an elderly guardian, an image from apocryphal tradition that the Catholic Encyclopedia calls unreliable and unsupported by early art. The point to check is the film's speculation about Jesus's whereabouts as a boy; what it adds, and whether it keeps to the Gospel account of Nazareth and the Temple, is unknown.
liberties: Joseph is shown as an old man, an apocryphal tradition rather than a Gospel fact. The film speculates on where Jesus was in his boyhood and adds characters not in the Gospels, such as Amroth and Zacchaeus. Jesus is played by three actors at ages five, eight and twelve.
advisories:
A family-oriented religious drama; no violence or sexual content is reported, though the later Gospel figures in the cast suggest a Passion element.

The film speculates about the boyhood of Jesus, which the Gospels do not describe.

grey.question: Jesus, Mary and Joseph is the third film of Miguel Zacarías's Mexican Gospel trilogy, centred on the boyhood of Jesus. Database entries say it speculates on where Jesus was as a boy and shows Joseph as an old man, which comes from apocryphal tradition, not the Gospels. No independent review exists, so it is unknown what the speculation involves or whether it stays within the Gospels' account of Nazareth and the finding in the Temple. The dialogue, or a 1972 Mexican review, would settle whether the invented years are devout or something else.

suitability.note: Its content is undocumented, but a childhood-of-Jesus drama with no reported violence suits families; older children will judge the invented material best.

doctrine: The Gospels record only the Nativity, the flight into Egypt, the hidden life at Nazareth and the finding in the Temple at twelve (Luke 2:42-51). The Catholic Encyclopedia calls the apocryphal stories about Joseph's marriage 'void of authority' and says it is most unlikely that he reached the great age they give. It reports that Aquinas, followed by most commentators, held the marriage to have been intended as virginal, and says we may well suppose Joseph died before Christ's public life. His feast is 19 March; Pius IX declared him patron of the Catholic Church in December 1870.
production: Panorama Films produced it, as the last of Zacarías's three films on the life of Jesus. A TMDB mirror gives a release date of 23 March 1972 and a running time of 1 hour 25 minutes; the Wikipedia article on Zacarías dates it 1970.

title: La manigua sin Dios
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (an 18th-century Spanish mission in the Chaco, ended by Charles III's expulsion of the religious). Identity: the ICAA catalogue (production 1948), the UC3M record and Decine21; release 7 April 1949 per TheTVDB. Content is known only in outline, and the two critical notices found (cinema.nl/VPRO, 2 of 5; Decine21, 4/10) give no account of the treatment. Unverified; a period review (ABC, Ya) or a Spanish Catholic rating would settle it.
summary: Arturo Ruiz Castillo's studio-jungle drama of a Spanish mission in the Chaco, harried by slavers and a hostile chief and finally ended by Charles III's expulsion of the missionaries.
synopsis: In the eighteenth century a Spanish caravan reaches the jungles of the Chaco in South America, and the priests who travel with it found a mission to evangelise the native peoples. The mission has enemies: slave traders, who oppose the missionaries' work, and a native chief whose people attack it. Jorge Mistral plays the warrior Yapacacú and Nani Fernández plays Panambí, and alongside the conflict runs a romance between a Spanish settler and a native woman. The missionaries hold on through the attacks, but the end comes from Spain, when King Charles III orders the religious expelled from his dominions. How the romance ends, whether the chief is won over and how the expulsion is staged is not recorded.
inclusion: La manigua sin Dios belongs to the missionary and colonial films of the early Franco years. Taurus Films made it with a historical adviser, José Tudela, and a cast led by Jorge Mistral, Nani Fernández and Luis Prendes. Its subject, the Spanish missions of the Chaco and their end under Charles III, is a historical one and seldom filmed. The director, Arturo Ruiz Castillo, had worked with Lorca in the Republican touring theatre La Barraca before making films for the new regime. Its reputation is poor. The Dutch film guide of the broadcaster VPRO gave it two stars out of five and called it a shameful religious film, and the Spanish site Decine21 rates it 4 out of 10. It is hard to see.
themes: On paper the film is about evangelisation: priests go into the jungle to convert its peoples and to protect them from slavers, and a royal decree, not its enemies in the forest, destroys the mission. That shape could be told as a lament for the missions, as martyrdom or as a defence of the Crown; which the film chooses is unknown. The synopses speak of 'religiosos' and do not name the order, though the expulsion by Charles III points to the Jesuits.
advisories:
Attacks on the mission; nothing graphic is reported.

How the film treats the missionaries, the conversions and the expulsion is unverified.

title: The Sword and the Cross
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (Christ, the Magdalene's conversion, the raising of Lazarus, the Passion). Identity: Wikipedia and the Cinematografo record (Ente dello Spettacolo), which gives the full synopsis and Ugo Tani's contemporary notice (Intermezzo, 15 June 1959). Reservation: an invented romance with the centurion who arrests Christ and a liaison with a Sanhedrin schemer carry much of the story. No Catholic rating found.
summary: Yvonne De Carlo plays Mary Magdalene in Bragaglia's Italian costume picture, torn between a Roman centurion and a Sanhedrin schemer until Christ's preaching and the raising of Lazarus convert her.
synopsis: The emperor sends the centurion Gaius Marcellus (Jorge Mistral) to Judaea to keep watch on Pontius Pilate. On arrival he meets Mary Magdalene (Yvonne De Carlo), and they fall in love. But Mary is the mistress of Anan (Massimo Serato), a nephew of the high priest Caiaphas who shields the bandit Barabbas, and the two men become rivals. Mary hears Jesus preach and is moved; her faith grows when he raises her brother Lazarus from the dead. Marcellus, who does not understand the change in her, is glad to arrest Jesus in Gethsemane, and Mary tries everything to save him. Anan betrays Barabbas, who is imprisoned. Offered the choice, the crowd demands Barabbas's release, and Jesus is crucified. Mary, repentant, stands among the holy women at the foot of the cross.
inclusion: A modest Italian costume picture of the late 1950s, shot at Cinecittà in English, in colour and CinemaScope, around a Hollywood star: Yvonne De Carlo, who had played Moses's wife in The Ten Commandments. Its religious story follows the Western tradition that makes the Magdalene the sister of Martha and Lazarus, and it ends with her at the cross, repentant. Around that the writers built a political intrigue and a love triangle with a Roman officer and a member of the Sanhedrin. Contemporary notices were lukewarm: Ugo Tani, in Intermezzo, said it took liberties with history and put spectacle first, and the Los Angeles Times found it sluggish. Gary Allen Smith's Epic Films rates it above average. It is one of the few films to give the Magdalene the title role.
themes: Mary is drawn by Christ's preaching, confirmed in faith by the raising of Lazarus, and found at the foot of the cross as a penitent, as the Gospels and tradition have it. The difficulty lies in the inventions. Mary is the mistress of a Sanhedrin intriguer and the beloved of the Roman who arrests Christ, and the romance, not her penance, carries much of the running time. How Christ himself is shown is not described.
advisories:
Costume-film violence and a crucifixion.

Mary is shown as a rich man's mistress and the object of a love triangle; nothing explicit is reported.

An invented romance between the Magdalene and the centurion who arrests Christ dominates the story.

grey.question: This Italian film tells the conversion of Mary Magdalene, moved by Christ's preaching and the raising of her brother Lazarus, and ends with her repentant at the cross. Around that it invents a love affair between Mary and the Roman centurion who arrests Jesus, and makes her the mistress of a member of the Sanhedrin. A contemporary Italian critic noted the liberties and the emphasis on spectacle. Readers must weigh how far the invented romance overshadows the Gospel story.

doctrine: The film follows the Western tradition, the common teaching and liturgical use of the Latin Church before the Council, that Mary Magdalen, the sinner of Luke 7 and Mary of Bethany, the sister of Martha and Lazarus, are one and the same. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) argues for this identification, which Protestant critics usually dispute. It names her as the first recorded witness of the Resurrection, who stood at the foot of the Cross. The raising of Lazarus (John 11) is the miracle the film uses for her conversion.
production: Incir De Paolis Studios produced it from a story by Ottavio Poggi. Yvonne De Carlo was signed in May 1958, and filming ran from August to November 1958. It was dubbed into Italian, with the working title The Great Sinner. The film opened in Italy in 1958 and in the United States in 1960 as Mary Magdalene.

title: The Life and Passion of Jesus Christ (Lumière)
originalTitle: La Vie et la passion de Jésus-Christ
alternateTitles: The Life and Passion of Jesus Christ
decision: HOLD: only Wikipedia sources so far; needs an independent archive or catalogue record (e.g. Library of Congress, Lumière catalogue) before it can be listed. Prior assessment: Identity is secure (Wikipedia, citing the Lumière catalogue numbers and the Library of Congress print). Content is known only as a list of scene titles; no critic or archive note describes how the tableaux are staged, and one catalogue number (935) is missing. Nothing suggests a doctrinal problem. A short series of one-shot views rather than a feature, so "Silent feature" is the nearest format. Settled by an archive or festival description of the surviving print.
summary: The Lumière company's Passion of 1898: a dozen one-shot tableaux, from the Magi to the Resurrection, sold separately so that showmen could assemble their own Life of Christ.
synopsis: There is no story in the modern sense. Each scene is a single view filmed with a fixed camera, issued under its own catalogue number so that exhibitors could buy and order them as they wished. The surviving sequence opens with the Adoration of the Magi and the Flight into Egypt. It then passes to the public life with Judas's betrayal and the Raising of Lazarus, and to the Last Supper. The Passion follows in the order of devotion: the arrest, the scourging, the crowning with thorns, the nailing to the cross and Calvary. The series ends with the entombment and the Resurrection. The catalogue reserved thirteen numbers for the series, but number 935 is not listed and surviving compilations usually contain twelve scenes.
inclusion: This is one of the very first attempts to film the Gospel, made in Paris in 1898 by Georges Hatot for the Lumière company, with Alexandre Promio, one of the Lumières' best-known cameramen, behind the camera. It belongs to the same short burst of Passion films as the American Passion Play pictures of 1897 and 1898, and it predates Pathé's better-known Life and Passion of Jesus Christ, with which it is often confused. The film historians Paul Spehr and Terry Lindvall treat these French tableaux as the start of conventions that later Passion films took over. A 35mm print is held by the Library of Congress. It is a historical document rather than a film to watch for its own sake: short, static and theatrical, with value mainly for anyone interested in how the life of Christ first reached the screen.
themes: The choice of scenes follows Catholic devotion rather than a single Gospel. The infancy appears through the Magi and the Holy Family's flight; the Passion is laid out in the sequence of the Sorrowful Mysteries of the Rosary, from the scourging and the crowning with thorns to the crucifixion. The Raising of Lazarus stands for the miracles. Crucially, the series does not stop at the tomb but ends with the Resurrection. How reverently each scene is staged has not been described by any source consulted.
history: The Lumière company sold its films as single views, each a short fixed shot. Georges Hatot staged several of its dramatic subjects in the late 1890s. This series was issued as catalogue numbers 933 to 945. Pathé began its own, longer Passion film in 1902 and remade it entirely in 1907.
advisories:
Brief, stylised scenes of the scourging, the crowning with thorns and the crucifixion.

No detailed description of the surviving print has been published.

grey.question: Pathé's second Life of Christ was a new production of 1906–07, directed by Lucien Nonguet under Ferdinand Zecca, in four parts and thirty-eight stencil-coloured scenes, with prints at Lobster Films and in Dutch and Swiss archives. Its content scene by scene is undocumented. Only the four part titles are given, from the Birth of Jesus to the Passion and Death, and none says whether it ends with the Resurrection. No independent review exists. A description or review of the restored print would settle it.

summary: Pathé's second, wholly new Life of Christ: thirty-eight stencil-coloured tableaux in four parts, directed by Lucien Nonguet under Ferdinand Zecca, with effects by Segundo de Chomón.
synopsis: Like Pathé's earlier Passion film, this is a chain of tableaux, each scene introduced by a title. It is divided into four parts. The first, the Birth of Jesus, covers the Annunciation and the Nativity; a still of the Annunciation from this version is widely reproduced. The second follows the Childhood of Jesus. The third, Miracles and Public Life, gathers the ministry. The fourth, Passion and Death, takes the story to Calvary. Thirty-eight scenes in all ran to some 990 metres, about half an hour at silent speed. No scene list is available, so it is unclear which miracles are shown or whether the film closes with the Resurrection and Ascension, as the earlier Pathé version did.
inclusion: In late 1906 Pathé started again from nothing. The result is shorter than the 1903–05 version but more polished: Henri Bousquet's note for Il Cinema Ritrovato singles out the Pathécolor stencil colouring, applied mechanically to each print, for its extraordinary precision, and the trick photography was handled by Segundo de Chomón, Pathé's effects specialist. Stencil-coloured nitrate prints survive at the EYE Filmmuseum in Amsterdam and in Bern, and Lobster Films restored a version that was shown at Bologna in 2006. Because Pathé kept reissuing its Passion films, the versions are easily confused; the archivist Camille Blot-Wellens published a study in 2017 sorting them out.
themes: The four part titles cover the whole Gospel life: the infancy, the hidden life, the miracles and teaching, and the Passion. That follows the shape of Catholic devotion, as Pathé's earlier version did with its Annunciation, Veronica's veil and Ascension. Whether this version keeps those traditional episodes, and whether it ends on the Resurrection or at the tomb, is not recorded.
history: Pathé first filmed the Passion in 1902 and kept extending that film until about 1905. The 1907 film was a new production, made between the end of 1906 and early 1907, and was itself reissued for years afterwards; edge marks on surviving prints date from 1909 and 1911.

Stylised scenes of the Passion and crucifixion.

summary: Georges Pallu's silent life of St Bernadette Soubirous, released in 1929, which stages the Lourdes apparitions with an actress as the Virgin.
synopsis: The film reconstructs the life of Bernadette Soubirous (1844–1879), the miller's daughter of Lourdes who, at fourteen, saw the Virgin Mary eighteen times in the grotto of Massabielle. Its cast list sketches the story it tells: Bernadette (played by an actress billed only as Alexandra), her mother and father, her godfather, the Virgin herself, played by Janine Lequesne, and a paralysed little girl, which suggests that one of the Lourdes cures is staged. No scene-by-scene account is available. Contemporary listings disagree on its form: Wikipedia's list of French films of 1929 calls it a documentary, while other databases class it as a historical drama, which may mean a dramatised life framed by footage of Lourdes itself.
inclusion: One of the earliest feature-length lives of Bernadette, it was made fourteen years before The Song of Bernadette and released four years after her beatification, while her canonisation was in preparation. Georges Pallu, a former lawyer and army officer who directed more than forty films between 1912 and 1939, made it for ISIS Films the same year as his Sister of Mercy. Its running time, ninety-six minutes, is long for a late silent devotional film. Nothing is known about its quality. It is of interest chiefly to those tracing how Lourdes was filmed before Henry King's version fixed the popular image.
themes: The film rests on the Lourdes apparitions: the Virgin appearing to a poor, unschooled girl, and the cures that followed at the spring. Casting an actress as Our Lady shows the apparitions as real events, not as Bernadette's private experience. The paralysed child in the cast points to the healings that made Lourdes a place of pilgrimage. How the film handles the parish priest's scepticism, the civil authorities and Bernadette's later religious life at Nevers is not recorded.
history: Bernadette Soubirous was born at Lourdes in 1844. Between February and July 1858 she reported eighteen apparitions of a Lady at the grotto of Massabielle, who on 25 March named herself the Immaculate Conception. She joined the Sisters of Charity at Nevers in 1866 and died there in 1879.

title: The Virgin of Guadalupe
decision: GREY: Identity and cast from the Wikipedia list of Mexican films of 1976 (opened) and search-result entries for FilmAffinity and IMDb (pages blocked). The apparitions are Church-approved and Juan Diego is a character, not the subject, as in La virgen morena (1942), so rule (a) does not apply. But reference entries conflict on the plot, with IMDb's synopsis describing an Aztec leader kidnapping the viceroy's daughter, and no review exists. Unverified.
summary: Alfredo Salazar's Mexican remake of the 1942 Guadalupe film, from a narration by the Jesuit Carlos M. de Heredia, with Fernando Allende as Juan Diego.
synopsis: In December 1531 Our Lady appears on the hill of Tepeyac to the Indian Juan Diego, played by Fernando Allende, and asks that a church be built there. Viola Trigo is cast as the Virgin. The cast also lists Doña Blanca (Angélica Chain), Uncle Bernardino (Enrique Lucero), Xochitl (Diana Torres), Captain Delgadillo (Carlos Agostí) and the Viceroy (Carlos Petrel). Reference entries disagree on the plot: one tells the apparitions, while IMDb's synopsis describes an Aztec leader who kidnaps the viceroy's blonde daughter, which may belong to another film or to a subplot.
inclusion: The Guadalupe story is the best-known Marian devotion in Mexico, and this 1976 version of it follows the 1942 La virgen morena, which had Heredia's text as its source. Fernando Allende plays Juan Diego, and the film runs 105 minutes in colour. Nothing is documented about its quality or its fidelity to the traditional account. A published scholarly article mentions that a 1976 film called Nuevo Mundo treated the legend from a revisionist angle; that is a different film, but a reminder that the 1970s also produced doubting treatments of the story.
themes: The film concerns a Marian apparition approved by the Church. Its treatment is unknown. The point to check is whether it tells the apparitions straightforwardly or mixes them with a different, invented story about an Aztec leader and the viceroy's daughter.
history: According to the Nican Mopohua, Our Lady appeared to the Indian Juan Diego four times on 9 to 12 December 1531 (Julian calendar) on Tepeyac hill, and once to his uncle Juan Bernardino. A manuscript of the Nahuatl account is dated to about 1556. Benedict XIV declared her patroness of New Spain by the bull Non est equidem of 25 May 1754. Leo XIII granted a decree of canonical coronation on 8 February 1887, and the coronation took place on 12 October 1895. Pius X named her patroness of the Republic of Mexico by the decree Gratia quae of 16 June 1910. Her feast is 12 December.
advisories: A religious drama about the apparitions; content is not documented. If the film includes the reported Aztec-warrior subplot, expect some battle scenes.

title: The Priest of Cucugnan
decision: GREY: Identity from the Marcel Pagnol site (opened) and Aleteia (content only); the film is Pagnol's black-and-white television adaptation of Daudet's tale, made 1967 and broadcast, per two sources, on Christmas 1968. Catholic-centred (the sermon turns on confession, hell and purgatory) and sound on its face, but there is no independent assessment of the adaptation: Aleteia is a present-day Catholic outlet and cannot be approving evidence, and a Film Review page and Time Out could not be read. Unverified.
summary: Fernand Sardou preaches the story of a dream of heaven, purgatory and hell to a village that never confesses, in Pagnol's television version of Daudet's tale.
synopsis: Father Martin, the parish priest of Cucugnan in Provence, finds that his people never come to church. He tells them in a sermon that he has dreamed of dying and going to heaven to look for them. Saint Peter consults his book and finds no one from Cucugnan; in the Provençal tale the villagers are sent first to purgatory and then to hell. Fernand Sardou plays the priest, speaking to a camera that stays largely on him, as the village and the writer Alphonse Daudet listen. According to the Pagnol site the angel says there are no Cucugnans in paradise because all are in hell. The next day the whole village comes to confession.
inclusion: Marcel Pagnol turned this short piece of folk preaching into a black-and-white television film in 1967, thirteen years after his Lettres de mon moulin. Fernand Sardou, who also appeared in the 1954 film, carries it. The story is Daudet's, taken from the Provençal tale by Roumanille, and its comedy comes from a priest who frightens his flock into confession. Aleteia, writing from a Catholic standpoint in 2023, quotes the priest's plea that people confess because they speak to God, not to him.
themes: The film is about the sacrament of Penance, which the sermon dramatises with a comic dream of the next life: heaven with no villagers, purgatory and hell. The dream is a device invented to scare the village; it is folk rhetoric, but it presents the doctrine seriously. How closely Pagnol follows Daudet, and how the film frames the priest, has not been independently reviewed.
advisories:
A short television piece for a general audience; no violence or sexual content is reported.

The sermon uses frightening images of hell and purgatory in a comic register.

The runtime is unconfirmed; one source says 2 hours 40 minutes, which looks wrong for a sermon-based piece.

grey.question: The Priest of Cucugnan is Marcel Pagnol's 1967 television adaptation of Daudet's tale of a priest whose dream sermon about heaven, purgatory and hell sends his whole village to confession. The doctrine is sound on its face and the story is a classic. No independent review exists, so how the film treats the priest and the sermon is unknown; the only accounts come from the Pagnol site and a present-day Catholic website. A review, the script or the dialogue would show whether the film plays the sermon straight.

names: Le Curé de Cucugnan, tale in Lettres de mon moulin by Alphonse Daudet (1866)

suitability.note: A short, humorous sermon-story for television; younger children may find the descriptions of hell frightening.

doctrine: On Penance the Council of Trent, Session XIV (25 November 1551), taught that penance is necessary for salvation for those who fall after baptism, as baptism is for the unregenerated (chapter II); that full confession of sins is necessary by divine right and all mortal sins must be enumerated (chapter V); and condemned those who deny this (Canons VI and VII). The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) says the eternity of hell's pains is a truth of faith. Its article on purgatory (1911) records that Trent, in Session XXV, affirmed purgatory and that the souls there are helped by the faithful, chiefly by the sacrifice of the altar. The priest's dream is a literary device, not a revelation.
production: Pagnol made this television film with Marcel Château and Jacques Pagnol, adapting Daudet's tale from Lettres de mon moulin, and Gaumont distributed it. It completes Pagnol's adaptation of that collection, 13 years after his film Letters from My Windmill. Interiors were shot in Marseille studios, with exteriors at the Daudet mill in Fontvieille, the abbey of Saint-Michel de Frigolet and the priory of Ganagobie. Aleteia dates it 1968; the Pagnol site gives 1967.

title: The Village Priest
decision: GREY: Priest-centred Quebec film. Identity: Wikipedia (citing Pratley, Pallister and Melnyk) and Robert Daudelin's Vingt ans de cinéma au Canada français (1967, on Wikisource), which records divided contemporary reviews but says nothing of the treatment. No Catholic rating and no account of how the story is resolved were found. Unverified; a contemporary Quebec review (Le Devoir, Front ouvrier) or the film would settle it.
summary: Robert Choquette's Quebec radio serial brought to the screen: a village curé shields a young bride-to-be from scandal when her fugitive father comes home.
synopsis: Robert Choquette wrote the film from his own radio serial, broadcast on Montreal's CKAC in the 1930s. In a small Quebec village the curé (Ovila Légaré) is the centre of parish life. Juliette (Lise Roy) is about to marry Lionel Théberge (Denis Drouin). On the eve of the wedding her father, Leblanc (Paul Guèvremont), a criminal on the run who came from the village and has long been estranged from her, comes back to see her. His return threatens a scandal that would fall on the girl just before her marriage, and the curé steps in to prevent it, a test of his standing among his parishioners. How the affair is resolved is not recorded.
inclusion: This was one of the films with which Quebec Productions tried to build a French-Canadian feature industry after the war. Paul Gury had just made Un homme et son péché, and the village scenes were shot at Saint-Damase. The historian Pierre Véronneau grouped it with Gury's Séraphin films as 'cowboys in cassocks', Westerns of a kind with a priest as hero. Contemporary critics were divided. Jacques Giraldeau, in Front ouvrier, saw in it proof that Canadian cinema would exist; Pierre Gascon thought the script more radio than cinema; Radiomonde called it a short film stretched to feature length.
themes: The curé is the village's moral authority and its protector. The story turns on scandal in the old sense, a father's sin that, once known, would fall on an innocent daughter on the eve of her marriage. The priest's task is to guard her good name and see the marriage take place. Véronneau's reading suggests a heroic, almost Western figure and not a study of the priesthood. How the film handles sermons, sacraments or devotions, and how the priest deals with the father, whether by conversion, persuasion or force, is not recorded.
advisories:
A fugitive criminal and the threat of exposure; nothing graphic is reported.

The film's handling of the priest's ministry and of the father's crime is unverified.

title: Marcelino Bread and Wine (2010)
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred remake of a story already catalogued as The Miracle of Marcelino (1955). Identity established; no independent critic found; the only evidence of treatment is Catholic-press promotion (ACI Prensa) and a 2011 festival prize organised by a post-conciliar Vatican office, neither of which is approving evidence. Dialogue would settle whether the miracle and the friars are presented soundly.
summary: A Mexican remake of Marcelino, pan y vino sets the foundling raised by Franciscan friars, and the bread and wine he brings to the crucifix, in the Mexican Revolution.
synopsis: In the middle of the Mexican Revolution a baby is left at the door of a Franciscan friary. The friars adopt him and raise him as Marcelino. After a revolutionary attack on the friary the frightened boy hides in the attic, where he finds a figure of the crucified Christ. Believing it to be hungry, he brings it bread and wine, talks to it and says he wants to meet his mother. The film's promoters say that a miracle occurs through the child's faith. The cast includes Mark Hernández as the boy, Alejandro Tommasi as the Father Guardian and Jorge Lavat as Fray Ernesto.
inclusion: Marcelino is one of the best-loved Catholic children's stories, and the 1955 Spanish film by Ladislao Vajda remains the standard version: it won at Berlin and Cannes, where Pablito Calvo received a special mention. This remake, directed by José Luis Gutiérrez Arias, moves the story to the Mexican Revolution. It is the only version in that setting, and the Revolution's dangers, part of the plot, give a Mexican friary a new edge. The praise comes from ACI Prensa, a Catholic news agency that calls it a Catholic film, and from a festival run by a Vatican council, which named Gutiérrez best director in 2011.
themes: The story centres on the Eucharist. A child offers bread and wine to the crucified Christ, and the plot depends on what follows. The friars' poverty and the boy's simple faith are the subject, set against a revolution that attacks their house. How the film treats the Mass, Holy Communion or the friars' own prayer, or whether the miracle is presented in the way the friars would understand it, is unknown. The 1955 film is in the catalogue and can be compared.
history: The story comes from José María Sánchez-Silva's novel Marcelino pan y vino, first filmed in Spain by Ladislao Vajda in 1955. The 2010 version moves it to the Mexican Revolution, which began in 1910. Which events or measures against the Church it shows is unknown.
production: It is a Mexican drama of 2010. The producers told ACI Prensa that it follows the 1955 version and an orphan adopted by a community of poor friars, and ACI Prensa's article of 23 January 2013 says the new version had been released.
advisories:
A child is left alone and frightened during a revolutionary attack on the friary. None of the sources describes violence beyond the attack.

No critic has assessed the film; see the question above.

names: Marcelino pan y vino, novel by José María Sánchez-Silva; earlier film by Ladislao Vajda (1955)

suitability.note: A foundling child, a revolutionary attack and a child alone in an attic. The 1955 original suits children; for this version no content guide exists, so judge from the setting.

doctrine: The bread and wine the boy offers are ordinary food, not the consecrated Eucharist. The Council of Trent, Session XIII (11 October 1551), Canon 1, condemned anyone who denies that the body, blood, soul and divinity of Christ are truly, really and substantially contained in the Eucharist, or who holds that he is there only as in a sign or figure. That presence follows consecration, not an offering of bread and wine. A miracle at an image would therefore not be the sacrament. Trent also taught, in Session XXV (3-4 December 1563), that images of Christ are to be kept and honoured because the honour is referred to the person they represent.

grey.question: No independent critic has assessed this remake. The sources are a Catholic news agency's promotion, a 2011 festival prize from a Vatican office and a wiki entry. They say the story is moved to the Mexican Revolution and that a child brings bread and wine to a crucifix and a miracle follows, but not how the friars, the Mass or the Revolution's attacks on the Church are treated. A viewing or the dialogue would show whether the miracle and the friars' faith are presented soundly, and whether the new setting adds anything doubtful.
